See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
Catastrophic flash floods along the Nepal-China border have killed at least 353 people and left more than 1,300 missing, sweeping away villages, roads and hydropower facilities.
Authorities say people from more than 30 countries are unaccounted for, including hundreds of foreign tourists and Hindu pilgrims traveling to the sacred Mount Kailash region in Tibet.
New satellite images from Vantor Satellite Imagery show the shocking devastation along a roughly 10-mile swath of the Trishuli river stretching south from the northern border with China.
The steep slopes and lush valleys below the Himalayan mountain range — home to many of the world’s highest peaks and remaining glaciers — are especially vulnerable to flooding and landslides. Melting glaciers have become more common because of human-caused climate change.
The image below shows the Rasuwagadhi border post on the Nepal-China border, at left, on April 19, 2024 and, at right, on Thursday, after the devastating flood.
The entire structure appeared to have been wiped out by the flood, with hardly any evidence of what once existed at the border.
The deadly flash flood in Nepal on Wednesday likely was caused by a huge chunk of a glacier that broke off and temporarily dammed a river, according to preliminary investigations by scientists. That may have led to the backed-up water surging downstream with enormous force a few hours later, they suggested.
The image below shows a power plant and bridge less than a mile downriver from the border post before and after the flood.
The power plant was part of a network along the Trishuli river that provided about 10% of Nepal’s power production, the Associated Press reported.
India’s Ministry of External Affairs said Thursday that 288 of their nationals, including 73 workers on a power project, were missing. Additionally, South Korean government officials said nine citizens working on building a hydropower plant were missing.
Water levels in rivers across the flood-affected region rose by as much as 29½ feet in 30 minutes as a result of the surge from the glacial detachment upstream, researchers at the Kathmandu-based climate research group said.
The image below shows the Syapru Besi village 8½ miles downriver from the border post before and after the flood.
Much of the village was swept away in the surging floodwaters, with dozens of structures wiped off the map.
Rescuers found bodies in Chitwan district hundreds of miles downstream from the hardest-hit areas.
Bishal Kumar Bhandari, chairman of the Nepal Red Cross Society, said they have shifted their focus from rescue to large-scale relief operations in the flood-hit districts. He said that around 1,200 people were displaced from at least three villages.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

Tropical Storm Dolly forms in the Atlantic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
19:45:26 UTC
04:45:26 KST

On Tuesday the legendary and beloved music icon Dolly Parton passed away. On Thursday a tropical disturbance managed to overcome headwinds to become a tropical storm. And the next name on the list of Atlantic storms was, you guessed it, Dolly.
Here’s how this unlikely meteorological coincidence happened.
The Atlantic hurricane season officially runs from June 1 to November 30, but late August through September is a peak time for storm formation. That’s when ocean waters are warmest, providing ample fuel for storm convection. It’s also when the winds that can rip apart a storm are typically at their weakest.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
A remarkably strong El Nino has kept a lid on Atlantic activity so far this season, meaning we’re still toward the beginning of an alphabetical list of storm names for 2026 that was created by the World Meteorological Organization. There are actually six lists that we rotate through each year, and we replace names on the lists when particularly damaging or strong storms cause them to be retired.
In its forecast discussion, the National Hurricane Center (NHC) said, “The timing of the use of the name Dolly for this storm is purely coincidental,” an unusual statement about a storm name.
The name “Dolly” has actually been on one of the lists of hurricane names since 1953, the first year that storms were given names based on lists from the NHC—when Dolly Parton was only seven years old. Back then only female names were used. The lists began alternating between male and female names for Atlantic storms in 1979. Dolly had dropped off the lists before that but was added back in 1990 and first used for a storm in 1996. (Fun fact: In the western Pacific, typhoons—which are the same phenomena as hurricanes but go by a different term—are named for national symbols, local animals and other features of affected countries.)
Though Dolly Parton had an enormous effect on people around the world, with efforts that included promoting childhood literacy and funding one of the COVID vaccines, Dolly the storm is expected to have little impact. Wind shear will make it hard for the storm to strengthen and will eventually deconstruct it before it reaches the Leeward Islands.

Turkish Ambassador to the US Sedat Onal on Thursday marked the 104th anniversary of Victory Day, commemorating Türkiye’s decisive victory over the occupying Greek army at the Battle of Dumlupinar in 1922, and highlighted Ankara’s growing role in regional and global security.
Speaking at a reception in Washington, Onal said the Aug. 30 victory holds significance not only for Türkiye but for world history.
"The kind of bravery that was demonstrated during this victory was not only significant in terms of opening up the path to the foundation of the Turkish Republic, but it also went into the identity of Turkish nation," Onal said.
He paid tribute to the Turkish soldiers and civilians who made sacrifices in the war, as well as to Mustafa Kemal Ataturk, who served as commander-in-chief and later founded the Republic of Türkiye.
Onal said the spirit of Victory Day remains an “enduring source of inspiration and a point of reference” for Türkiye as the country enters its second century.
Turning to relations with the US, Onal said ties between Ankara and Washington are “in a positive trajectory in many ways,” both bilaterally and multilaterally.
He cited the NATO summit hosted by Türkiye in the capital Ankara as one of the year’s highlights, noting that President Donald Trump’s participation was an important element of the meeting’s success.
"As we go through difficult, turbulent times regionally and internationally, I think the unity of NATO allies remains essential," Onal added.
 
'Victory demonstrated to the world the Turkish nation’s determination'
Brig. Gen. Alpaslan Guldal, defense attache at the Turkish Embassy in Washington, described the Battle of Dumlupinar as a "major turning point" in Türkiye’s struggle for independence.
"This victory demonstrated to the world the Turkish nation’s determination to protect its independence and sovereignty.
"It also opened the way for the establishment of the Republic of Türkiye on October 29, 1923," Guldal said.
Aug. 30 is also celebrated as Turkish Armed Forces Day, providing an opportunity to highlight the military’s role beyond Türkiye’s borders, Guldal said.
“Today, the Turkish Armed Forces continue to contribute to regional and global peace and security,” he said, noting that Turkish personnel serve in operations and missions under NATO, the UN and EU, as well as through bilateral partnerships.
Turning to Türkiye-US relations, Gudal emphasized the longstanding security partnership between the two NATO allies.
“As two NATO Allies, our countries have worked together for many years to support peace and security,” he said.
The Great Offensive – one of the greatest military victories in history – was launched by the Turkish Armed Forces on Aug. 26, 1922, under the leadership of Ataturk, and ended on Sept. 18 that same year.
From Aug. 26 to Aug. 30 of 1922, Turkish forces fought the Battle of Dumlupinar in Türkiye's western Kutahya province, where Greek forces were decisively defeated.
By the end of 1922, all foreign forces had left the territories which would collectively become the new Republic of Türkiye a year later.

====================================================================================================

Helping Every Student Find Their Story
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
19:43:37 UTC
04:43:37 KST

I often tell people I have the best job in the building. As a school librarian, I’m in a unique position: I don’t just see one grade level or one department. I’m one of the few staff members who works with every child, every teacher, and every member of the school staff. This vantage point gives me a clear view of how our school functions, and more importantly, where our students are finding success or facing barriers.
Moving from a small neighborhood school in southern Oregon to a regional Chinese immersion public charter school in western Massachusetts was a significant professional shift. In Oregon, the student population was largely homogenous. Here, the student body is diverse, and I encounter five-year-olds who are already navigating three or four different languages. They come from rural, suburban, and urban communities and from countries all over the world. Entrance to the public charter school is purely by lottery. My job is no longer just about finding a good book; it is about finding the specific tools and resources that will appeal to a diverse group of learners while building bridges between their home languages, their cultures, and their academic requirements.
In a dual language immersion setting, the library is the “common room.” It is the space where everyone feels they belong, and that is a functional necessity for multilingual learners.
The Library as a Flexible Hub
The school library collection should reflect the people who walk through its doors. In my experience, the library often becomes the place where students bring questions that don’t always find a home in the traditional classroom. Whether they are looking for information about their home country or trying to understand a complex cultural nuance they encountered in a textbook, they come to the library because they know it’s a space built for exploration.
As multilingualism becomes more prominent in US schools, we have to be conscious about how we provide library services. We are currently navigating a complex social climate in which powerful platforms are stoking fear about immigrants in order to implement more restrictive policies. It is essential that library resources provide a counterweight to that. We need to offer books and digital resources that celebrate the scientific, mathematical, and artistic achievements of world cultures and provide stories of people from all over the world who are thriving in this country.
This requires flexibility on the part of the librarian. We need to be able to pivot to the important stuff happening in a student’s life right now, even if it wasn’t on the curriculum for the day. Representation in a collection isn’t something that can wait for a six-month book-buying cycle. When a student needs to see their own story reflected in a book, they need it today. This is where modernizing our approach to collection development becomes a matter of equity.
Leveraging Digital Tools for Language Gaps
While I am a proponent of physical books—and many students still prefer a hardcover for pleasure reading—digital platforms have changed how we support students with language gaps.
In an immersion school, we sometimes face a proficiency gap. We see students who arrive with high academic ability but limited English proficiency. Their Chinese-language classes might feel too easy, while their English-language classes feel incredibly difficult. I have seen ninth-grade students with beginning English skills tasked with reading Romeo and Juliet. This is a heavy lift for native speakers, but for a multilingual learner, it can feel like a wall.
Digital resources, like the Sora student reading app, provide a ladder over that wall. They allow us to offer side-by-side comparisons of texts. A student can look at a complex English text alongside a simplified version or a version in their primary language. They can listen to an audiobook while reading the words on the page.
This on-the-fly accessibility can be a life-changer. It allows the student to stay involved in the classroom conversation and understand the content while they are still building their language skills. Without this kind of scaffolding, these students risk being sidelined during academic discussions.
There is also a social–emotional component to this. For middle and high school students, there is often a stigma attached to reading “easier” books or graphic novel adaptations. No one wants to be the only person in the room holding a book that looks like it’s the easy version. Digital tools remove that embarrassment. When every student is accessing resources on a screen, no one but the teacher knows if a student is accessing a simplified version, a translation, or a graphic novel adaptation. Similarly, a student can access database content at an elementary reading level while the screen still looks exactly like the middle school version. These tools provide a level of privacy that allows students to focus on comprehension rather than their status among their peers.
Collaborative Curation
Building a collection that is both linguistically diverse and culturally authentic is a massive undertaking, particularly when physical space and budgets are limited. Our school serves grades K–12, so I have to manage a significant age and complexity range in a relatively small footprint.
I’ve found that the most effective way to build a quality collection is through collaboration. I am fortunate to work with staff members from China, Taiwan, Venezuela, Trinidad, Puerto Rico, India, and Korea. They are my best resources. When I’m looking for authentic texts, I go to the people who have a deep, lived understanding of those cultures.
I also rely on a professional learning community (PLC) of local librarians. We meet monthly, visiting each other’s libraries to see what resources are being promoted and to discuss struggles and successes in our buildings. This collaborative approach ensures that our collections stay relevant, our practices remain rooted in our profession, and we aren’t duplicating efforts in a time of limited resources.
When a teacher comes to me and says, “I have a student who is struggling with this content. Is there something you can find to help them engage?,” it’s an opportunity to dive deep into our resources. It allows me to work with the teacher to identify what’s missing and see what new materials can be integrated into our system through our digital platform.
The Role of Pleasure Reading
I spend time talking to students about the benefits of pleasure reading. Beyond the academic advantages and improved test scores, there are recorded mental health benefits.
I recently worked with a ninth-grade student who was vocal about her dislike for reading. She had been placed in a reading elective and felt stuck. After we talked for a while about the “vibe” of stories she might enjoy, we found a book that hooked her. A few weeks later, she told me she was sleeping better because she had replaced her phone with a book before bed. She realized that the screen time was keeping her up, while the reading was helping her wind down.
Similar breakthroughs have come with our Battle of the Books program. I’ve seen students who only felt confident reading graphic novels get involved in the program and suddenly find themselves mastering chapter books and novels in verse. One earnest student told me she didn’t think she liked to read at all until she had to read an autobiography for Battle of the Books. She discovered she loved the genre; she just hadn’t known it existed. Providing these options is how we move students from being reluctant readers to confident ones.
Advocacy and Media Literacy
Looking ahead, school libraries have to be more than just quiet rooms; they have to be centers for advocacy. We need to be role models for the rest of the school in how we reach out to families in multiple languages and ensure that everyone’s freedom of information is protected.
We also have a responsibility to teach kids how to navigate the modern information landscape. I often describe the internet to my students as a big city. There are incredible things to experience —theaters, museums, and great food—but there are also areas you don’t want to go to and people on every corner trying to sell you things you don’t need.
We talk extensively about clickbait, misinformation, and how to evaluate a source. This is the cornerstone of what we do as educators now. In a world where students are bombarded with information, they need to know how to vet what they see. This is especially true for our multilingual students, who may be navigating information in multiple languages and cultures simultaneously.
The Value of the Librarian
As schools face economic challenges, it is more important than ever to protect the role of the school librarian. We are the advocates for inclusion. We are the people who see the students in between classes and activities and understand what they need to succeed.
The school library supports multilingual learners by providing a space where their language and culture are an integral part of their academic life. By utilizing digital tools to bridge the proficiency gap and focusing on authentic representation, we ensure that every student has the chance to be involved in the conversation.
It’s a role that requires constant pivoting, content curation, budget finesse, and a deep commitment to accessibility. And that’s why this is the best job in the school.
Becky Sniffen ([email protected]) is the librarian at Pioneer Valley Chinese Immersion Charter School in Massachusetts.

Pakistan, Kuwait sign defense agreement amid expanding regional security ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
19:38:57 UTC
04:38:57 KST

ALBAWABA- Pakistan and Kuwait have signed a defense cooperation agreement aimed at strengthening their existing military relationship, as Gulf states and regional powers increasingly expand and diversify their security partnerships amid heightened tensions across the Middle East.
The agreement, announced by Pakistan’s Ministry of Defense, builds on the two countries’ existing military cooperation framework and is intended to expand coordination between their armed forces. The two sides have maintained defense ties for decades, including cooperation in military training, education and professional exchanges.
The new defense arrangements have emerged in the aftermath of the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, which exposed vulnerabilities in the Gulf's traditional reliance on the United States for security.
Iranian retaliatory attacks during the conflict demonstrated that even countries hosting substantial U.S. military facilities could remain exposed to regional escalation, while Washington's ability to provide comprehensive protection faced practical and strategic limitations. The prolonged conflict and damage to critical infrastructure have consequently encouraged Gulf states and their regional partners to reassess their security calculations.
This has accelerated a search for more diversified security mechanisms, combining existing ties with Washington with stronger military partnerships among regional and neighboring powers. The clearest example is the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement signed by Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan on August 7, which commits the three countries to treating an armed attack against one member as an attack against all. The agreement is evidence of a broader move toward a more multipolar regional security order, although it does not eliminate the Gulf's dependence on U.S. military capabilities.
Pakistan's expanding defense ties with Kuwait fit into this broader trend. Rather than replacing U.S. security partnerships, such arrangements give regional states additional options by strengthening military cooperation with countries capable of providing training, manpower, technology, and strategic support.
The emerging architecture, however, is far from unified. Qatar has maintained a particularly close defense relationship with Türkiye, while the United Arab Emirates has pursued its own security and defense partnerships, including deeper cooperation with India and Israel. These choices reflect different threat perceptions and strategic calculations among Gulf states rather than a common regional alignment.
The result is an increasingly fragmented but more diversified Middle Eastern security landscape. The U.S. remains deeply embedded in the region's defense architecture, but the experience of the Iran war has encouraged several regional powers to hedge against the possibility that American protection may be insufficient, delayed, or constrained in a future crisis.
The emerging strategy is therefore not necessarily to replace Washington, but to reduce exclusive dependence on it by building stronger regional and extra-regional security partnerships.

Spain: Thieves steal Bronze Age gold in lightning raid on Villena Museum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
19:38:00 UTC
04:38:00 KST

Spain: Thieves steal Bronze Age gold at Villena Museum
August 27, 2026
Thieves on Thursday raided one of the world's greatest Bronze Age gold collections in the latest of a series of high-profile heists on European museums in recent months.
The early morning raid on Villena Museum in eastern Spain lasted just a few minutes.
A group of thieves described by one official as "super-fast and super-professional" made off with almost the entire Treasure of Villena collection, leaving behind only a few items.
What happened in the heist?
"The alarm at the Villena Museum went off around 5:20 a.m.," said a spokesman for the town council, adding that within four minutes, they had all left the building again in an extremely rapid and professional operation.
The collection of Bronze Age gold, some of which we now know hailed from a meteorite, was a centerpiece at the small museum in the Alicante province.
"They've taken most of the treasure," the mayor of Villena, Fulgencio Cerdan told journalists. "We are absolutely devastated, I'm even trembling. The truth is that for those of us from Villena, this destroys us. It's part of our heritage, our wealth."
The thieves arrived in several vehicles and apparently entered the museum "through a window," according to the Spanish government's deputy representative in Alicante, Manuel Pineda.
Mayor Cerdan said that only three silver vessels, a bracelet, an earring and one of four crowns in the collection — which the thieves appeared to have "dropped" while making their exit — remained behind.
 "All security systems were activated," according to the Villena spokesman, who insisted there had been "no failure" by the museum.
 
What is the Treasure of Villena?
The Treasure of Villena is a collection of more than 50 mainly gold objects, discovered in 1963 by archaeologist Jose Maria Soler in a sunken vessel in a dried out riverbed.
They are dated to between 1300 and 1000 BCE.
The gold pieces include 11 bowls, three bottles and 28 bracelets.
The collection has been exhibited beyond Villena in cities including Madrid, Alicante, Tokyo and Kyoto, and two sets of replicas were later made to showcase the collection without taking it away from the armored display at the Villena Archaeological Museum.
The relics' historical value is incalculable, although thieves might struggle to sell them even on the black market after having famously lifted them from a well-known display. The mayor said the gold alone would be worth around €1.7 million or $2 million.
According to the museum's website, specialist researchers consider it the most important collection of gold tableware from the Bronze Age. It also represents the earliest known example of iron use in Western Europe, two pieces crafted from a metal that recent studies showed hailed from a meteor.
Several slick heists on European museums recently, most famously the Louvre
Thursday's lightning dawn raid is the latest in a series on European museums in the last year.
Most famously, the Louvre Museum was hit in broad daylight last October, escaping in less than 10 minutes with jewelry worth millions. This led to the director's eventual resignation and a protracted political scandal, as well as forcing part of the museum to close for an extended period.
Italy's Culture Ministry announced on Sunday that four works of "extraordinary value" by Renaissance artist Antonello da Messina were stolen from a museum in Sicily.
Shortly before that, Italian police said they had recovered three paintings by Renoir, Cezanne and Matisse stolen from a museum near Parma. Again this involved a highly-organized group of thieves who were in and out in a matter of minutes.

====================================================================================================

Australia on track to eliminate cervical cancer 20 years on from vaccine launch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
19:35:07 UTC
04:35:07 KST

Twenty years on from Gardasil vaccine launch, Australia on track to eliminate cervical cancer
In short:
Twenty years ago, Australia launched the Gardasil vaccine, the world's first vaccine against cervical cancer.
Griffith University professor of infectious diseases Nigel McMillan said Australia was on track to eliminate cervical cancer in the next 10 years.
Despite that, Australian Immunisation Register data shows HPV vaccine coverage for girls and boys is dropping.
Twenty years on from the launch of the world-first vaccine against cervical cancer in Australia, more than 800 million doses have been administered worldwide in a breakthrough expected to save tens of millions of lives by early next century.
The vaccine, co-developed at the University of Queensland by Ian Frazer and his late colleague Jian Zhou, protects against strains of the sexually transmitted human papilloma virus (HPV), which cause most cases of cervical cancer and genital warts.
It also safeguards against many cases of throat, genital, and anal cancer.
Professor Frazer, the 2006 Australian of the Year, was dubbed by a magazine as "God's Gift to Women" because of the revolutionary vaccine's impact on cervical cancer, but HPV also causes cancers that affect men.
Dr Zhou died aged 42 in 1999, seven years before the vaccine was approved for use.
The Gavi Vaccine Alliance — a public-private partnership that assists in vaccinating children in high-risk countries — estimates the vaccine would have prevented 1.4 million future deaths across low and middle-income countries during a three-year immunisation program beginning in 2023.
In 2020, the World Health Organization released its global strategy to accelerate the elimination of cervical cancer as a public health problem, which seeks to save 62 million lives by 2120, underpinned by the HPV vaccine.
'A disease of the past'
Griffith University professor of infectious diseases Nigel McMillan, whose daughters Rachel and Emma were among the first Australian teenagers to be vaccinated on August 28, 2006, said Australia was on track to eliminate cervical cancer in the next 10 years.
"We'll have a few sporadic cases, but generally, it will be a disease of the past," Professor McMillan said on the eve of today's 20th anniversary.
"This will really be the first cancer vaccine in the world that will have achieved that sort of result.
"European countries are now reporting that they also see that this is incredibly effective."
While a hepatitis B vaccine, approved in the 1980s, was the world's first anti-cancer jab because it helps prevent liver cancer, Australia still sees about 3,000 new diagnoses of the cancer annually, with causes extending beyond hepatitis B.
Professor McMillan, who worked in the adjourning laboratory to Professor Frazer as the cervical cancer vaccine was being developed, said its "spectacular" results were helped by the fact that almost all cases were caused by HPV.
Public health expert Julia Brotherton, a professor of cancer prevention policy at the University of Melbourne, has spent most of her career studying the HPV vaccine.
She was part of the working party that recommended to the Australian Government that the vaccine should be included in the national immunisation program.
Australia was the first country to fully fund a HPV immunisation program, but only after the nation's Pharmaceutical Benefits Advisory Committee (PBAC) in early November 2006 controversially knocked back funding for Gardasil, a cervical cancer vaccine made by Merck and marketed in Australia by CSL.
But after a public backlash, political pressure by then Prime Minister John Howard, whose wife Janette had survived cervical cancer, and CSL made a price compromise, the PBAC reversed its decision and recommended funding at an extraordinary meeting later the same month.
The vaccine has been provided free to Australian girls and young women up to age 26 as part of the national immunisation program since 2007 and boys and young men were added in 2013.
Professor Brotherton said the cervical cancer vaccine was now included in the immunisation programs of 165 countries.
"It's really difficult to overstate the significance of this vaccine," she said.
"It's an incredibly effective vaccine. It's the backbone of what is now a global cervical cancer elimination strategy where we're going to make this a rare disease around the world.
"Cervical cancer is an absolutely devastating disease if it's not caught early. The suffering is absolutely immense. It strikes down women who are in their peak age of having kids and their career. It's an absolutely avoidable tragedy."
Vaccination numbers down
Professor Brotherton joined Professor McMillan in describing the vaccine as extremely safe.
Professor McMillan said he had "no hesitation" to allow his own daughters to be vaccinated after he had followed the HPV vaccine trial results as it went through testing worldwide.
"I'd looked at the safety profile. This was actually one of the safest vaccines we'd ever made," he said.
Despite that, Australian Immunisation Register data shows HPV vaccine coverage for girls by their 15th birthday fell from 86.6 per cent in 2020 to 78.7 per cent in 2025.
And coverage for boys by age 15 plunged from 84.9 per cent in 2020 to 75.6 per cent last year.
Professor Brotherton said the drop below 80 per cent was "really concerning".
"I go around the world and see countries struggling to try and afford this vaccine. We're so lucky we can prevent cancer in our kids with a single dose of a very safe vaccine," she said.
"There seems to be a lot more concerns and hesitancy. But the evidence for this vaccine is incredibly robust.
"It's been very carefully studied for 20 years. I absolutely am confident in recommending this vaccine as an incredible thing you can do for your kids. It's a single dose, it's free, it's easy, it prevents cancer, go get it."

This Australian crisis is entering a 'confronting' new phase
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
19:33:52 UTC
04:33:52 KST

IN BRIEF
- More than 2,500 Australians died from drug-induced overdose in 2024, the highest on record.
- Older Australians accounted for almost half of reported deaths.
This article contains references to substance abuse and suicide.
Drug-induced deaths have hit a record high, with older Australians accounting for more than half of the fatalities.
Australia's Annual Overdose Report, released by the Penington Institute, documented 2,596 drug-induced deaths in 2024, with 80.5 per cent being from unintentional overdose.
Since 2008, more Australians have died from drug-induced deaths than road fatalities — with an average of 31 years lost per death.
"The data is quite confronting," Jake Dizard, director of research at the Penington Institute, told SBS News.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
The report found that the median age of people dying from drug overdose is increasing.
For the first time, those aged between 50 and 59 accounted for almost half of all unintentional overdose deaths.
Dizard said it could be attributed to "an ageing large cohort of people who started using drugs in the 1990s and early 2000s".
"As that cohort has got older, they have become more vulnerable to drug-induced death because of the length of time that they have been using drugs and the accumulating sort of comorbidities," he said.
The report also noted that of the 428 drug-induced suicides, 39 per cent were people aged 60 and over.
Australian Alcohol and Other Drugs Council CEO Melanie Walker said the report confirms that overdose is not a "young people problem".
"Overdose is something that affects the whole community," she told SBS News.
"It affects young people. It also affects older people. Overdose can be from illicit drug use, or it can be from prescription drug use."
The report also found that men accounted for 72.7 per cent of unintentional drug-induced deaths, people living in regional and rural areas had higher rates of death than those living in capital cities, and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people experienced higher rates of overdose.
In 2024, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people experienced an overdose rate of 29.3 per 100,000 compared to 6.6 per 100,000 for non-Indigenous people.
Opioids were responsible for 42 per cent of all drug-induced deaths in 2024, with heroin-related deaths rising from 101 deaths in 2001 to 488 deaths in 2024.
Amphetamines were involved in 772 deaths, a record high for the drug, and cocaine was involved in 141 deaths. Benzodiazepines, alcohol and antidepressants also contributed to drug-induced deaths.
Dizard said that the use of prescription opioids, such as oxycodone, has declined since 2021 — a trend seen across "a number of categories of prescription drugs".
Cocaine was the only recorded drug that saw a decrease in the median age of people dying from overdose.
Two-thirds of Australians turned away from services
The majority of drug-induced deaths in Australia are preventable, Dizard said.
The report listed a range of recommendations to reduce the number of deaths, including increased access to the medicine naloxone.
"It's an opioid overdose reversal drug, which is very safe and can be administered by anybody," Dizard said.
"It's important not just for people who habitually or routinely use opioids, but also people who might be using other drugs, including cocaine, that might be contaminated with some sort of opioid."
Dizard noted the importance of community education on how to identify signs of overdose and respond — and greater investment in services, specifically opioid pharmacotherapy.
While stigma hinders people's ability to seek support for drug and alcohol addiction, Dizard said a major issue is a lack of funding for services.
He said law enforcement is heavily funded, and a "more balanced approach to drug policy" is needed.
"Funding has been incredibly unbalanced throughout the last several decades of Australian drug policy."
Australia's National Drug Strategy has three pillars: supply reduction, which includes law enforcement; demand reduction, which refers to treatment; and harm reduction, including preventative measures such as drug checks.
"The supply reduction pillar has traditionally had double the funding of treatment," Walker said.
She said that more than two-thirds of people seeking help for drug and alcohol use have been turned away from services because of funding insufficiency.
Walker said there's currently no forum for governments, both federal and state and territory, to come together and "talk about the implementation of the national drug strategy and do coordinated planning".
"For at least the last 10 years, half a million Australians have been missing out on getting to alcohol and other drug treatment because there's simply no place for them," she said.
"It's really obvious what the problem is in terms of why overdose deaths are rising, and until we come to terms with that and get proper resources — I can't see that changing."
SBS News has contacted the Department of Health for comment.
Readers struggling with their use of alcohol and other substances can contact the National Alcohol and Other Drug Hotline on 1800 250 015 for free and confidential support 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. More information is available via Lifeline.
Readers seeking crisis support can ring Lifeline on 13 11 14 or text 0477 13 11 14, the Suicide Call Back Service on 1300 659 467 and Kids Helpline on 1800 55 1800 (for young people aged up to 25). More information and support with mental health is available at beyondblue.org.au and on 1300 22 4636.

Exclusive: Memo reveals why NT Police were not charged over this death in custody
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
19:33:43 UTC
04:33:43 KST

This article contains references to a deceased Indigenous person.
SBS News can reveal Northern Territory Police waited four months to send the NT's Director of Public Prosecutions (NTDPP) an 'opinion file' seeking advice after the death in custody of a 24-year-old Warlpiri man.
Known as Kumanjayi White for cultural reasons, the young man who also lived with disabilities died in May last year after he was restrained by two plain-clothes police officers in the confectionary aisle of an Alice Springs supermarket.
His death sparked nationwide protests over government inaction on Aboriginal deaths in custody, with protestors echoing calls by his family for an independent investigation.
White's family launched legal action against NT Police after it was announced the two officers involved would not be prosecuted in May — but discontinued the action earlier this month.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Now, an internal memo obtained by SBS News via a Freedom of Information (FOI) request offers an insight into the reasoning behind the NTDPP's decision not to prosecute.
Internal memo anticipates 'anguish'
The email obtained through FOI is dated 26 May 2026 and was sent by the then acting director of the NTDPP Patrick Williams to all NTDPP staff announcing the news that no charges would be laid over White's death.
"Shortly following your receipt of this email, it will become public knowledge that I have determined there are no reasonable prospects of securing a conviction on any charge arising out of his death on the basis of the evidence provided by police," Williams writes in the memo.
He explains the decision would likely cause some "anguish" for White's family.
"For that reason, I have met with them on country this morning to inform them of the view that I have reached."
Williams goes on to explain the decision, noting that the department "may be the subject of some media criticism" as a result.
"That criticism may include questioning the integrity and independence of our office, noting the relationship between the NTDPP and NT Police Force," he writes.
You can be confident that the decision that has been reached in this case is one that has been made without fear or favour. It is a determination based solely on the available evidence.
To reassure staff further, Williams provided a timeline:
It notes that a police opinion file was delivered in September 2025, four months after White's death.
At that time, acting NT police commissioner Martin Dole told media that investigators had "compiled a full and comprehensive brief of evidence".
But the internal memo obtained by SBS News reveals prosecutors had asked police to obtain an additional independent report into the use of force in White's arrest "within days" of receiving the opinion file in September.
It was later revealed by Dole that this 'use of force' report was conducted by Queensland Police.
The email also shows Williams sought advice from external interstate senior and junior counsel on whether the evidence provided by police was sufficient to warrant prosecution.
Following news of White's death in custody, federal member for Lingiari Marion Scrymgour had called for the Australian Federal Police to run a separate investigation. White's family and community, based in Yuendumu, an Aboriginal community about 300km north-west of Alice Springs, also publicly called for an independent investigation.
The document suggests no other agency was approached to conduct an investigation, besides NT Police. The Northern Territory's coroner Elisabeth Armitage is now examining the case, with an inquest expected to occur next year.
A suppression order by Armitage prohibits the publication of anything in the brief of evidence, including CCTV of the incident inside Coles supermarket in Alice Springs.
Several interested parties will appear at the inquest including representatives for Coles Supermarkets, NT Police, Talice Security and sergeant Steve Haig.
'Stonewalled' for nearly a year
More than a year after the incident with police, White's cause of death remains undetermined.
Speaking on behalf of his family, CEO of the National Justice Project and lawyer George Newhouse tells SBS News that while the released memo provides some clarity about the decision not to prosecute the officers involved, little remains known about the charges that were considered.
"There is a charter of victims' rights in the Northern Territory, and it explains that people are entitled to be consulted. They're entitled to know the basis and the reasons behind a decision not to charge, and they're actually entitled to a review," he says.
Newhouse launched the now-discontinued legal action in the NT Supreme Court on behalf of White's senior next-of-kin, Ned Jampajimpa Hargraves, seeking further information about the decision not to charge anyone.
"The family had been asking for transparency for independent oversight of this investigation and the inquiry into Kumanjayi White's death. They got virtually stonewalled for nearly a year." The court action was withdrawn this month after police revealed the name and rank of one of the officers who made the call following the NTDPP's advice.
The decision over whether to pursue criminal charges in a death in custody case ultimately lies with the Director of Public Prosecutions. For White, this will also involve a referral from the coroner once the inquest into his death is complete.
White's family is now considering their options to take further action to find out what charges were considered by NT Police and the NTDPP.
Newhouse says the family were "horrified" to learn that the request by the NTDPP for an "independent interstate expert" to conduct the use of force report was ultimately fulfilled by Queensland Police.
"There are many academics who specialise in the use of force, including former police officers that could have been used to provide some independence," Newhouse says.
"The family are horrified that instead of seeking a truly independent report, the NT police and the DPP went to another police force with not the best track record of deaths in custody themselves.
"It gives the family absolutely no comfort that this report's been received."
Calls for reform
Following the decision not to prosecute in May 2026, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander social justice commissioner Katie Kiss renewed calls for justice reform.
"This case yet again highlights the urgent need to ensure that deaths in custody should be independently investigated. Police should not be investigating other police," she said in a statement.
Investigations must be conducted by organisations and individuals who have no potential or perceived conflicts of interest.
The call was initially backed by the Central Land Council in June 2025, which argued federal funding should be withheld from the NT until an independent investigation was set up.
Newhouse argues it's "not a transparent system".
"You can understand why First Nations people do not trust the police to investigate themselves when there's a death in custody," he says.
SBS News contacted the Northern Territory Police Force with a series of questions, including why it did not seek an independent use of force report prior to the NTDPP requesting it, why Queensland Police were ultimately commissioned for this, and why it isn't standard procedure for deaths in custody.
A spokesperson for police declined to answer specific questions, saying "the coronial investigation into the death of Kumanjayi White remains ongoing".
"It would be inappropriate for the Northern Territory Police Force to comment further."
Coronial inquest to be held
A four-week coronial inquest starting in April next year will examine the 24-year-old's death.
At a directions hearing in June, counsel assisting the coroner, Peggy Dwyer SC, said the inquest had not been able to be listed until the criminal investigation was finalised and would examine "the circumstances of why and how he [White] came to be restrained".
"The aim of an inquest is to get a truthful and proper account of what happened in the lead-up to Kumanjayi's death.
"We get that evidence to determine if there was any opportunity to do something differently that might have preserved Kumanjayi's life and to understand the circumstances."
The inquest was delayed until next year at the request of White's family so that all the evidence could be heard in one sitting block.
But Newhouse says the process is unlikely to satisfy the family's calls for accountability as it will focus on the circumstances.
"The family are also asking whether the police are investigating this death internally and trying to determine whether the officers involved complied with police policy and whether there will be any accountability through the normal internal police processes."
NT Police did not respond to questions put by SBS News as to whether an internal investigation had been conducted in line with its Code of Conduct, or if any internal mechanisms, processes or policies have changed since White's death.
Newhouse says the family remains committed to getting answers.
All the family have been asking for is justice, transparency, and independent oversight to ensure that the death of their loved one did not go without accountability.

Six months into Iran war, nuclear threat remains, Hormuz is disrupted and US forces are wearing down
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
19:32:54 UTC
04:32:54 KST

Six months after the war with Iran began, Washington is shifting from sustained military pressure toward an effort to choke Tehran economically, even as Iran refuses to surrender, traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remains disrupted and no diplomatic breakthrough appears close.
President Donald Trump said Thursday that the United States was not negotiating with Tehran despite continuing regional efforts to restart diplomacy.
“We don’t want to talk to them,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. “We’re not looking to meet with them either.”
At the same time, Qatari Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani arrived in Tehran for meetings with senior Iranian officials in an attempt to create what his office described as a more favorable environment for dialogue.
Al Thani met Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf and President Masoud Pezeshkian.
According to the Qatari government, Al Thani and Araghchi discussed a proposal concerning the Strait of Hormuz that includes establishing a temporary joint shipping corridor and cooperating on a mine-clearing project.
Against the backdrop of Iranian attacks in the Gulf, Al Thani stressed “the need to respect the sovereignty of neighboring states and freedom of navigation.”
In his meeting with Ghalibaf, he called for a renewal of diplomacy.
Ghalibaf, meanwhile, blamed Washington for the continuing confrontation.
“The Trump administration makes wrong decisions based on false information,” he said. “America’s miscalculations attack the interests of the Iranian people and contribute to expanding insecurity in the region. The economic siege plan against Iran will also fail, and the Iranian people will regain their rights.”
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said Thursday evening that “Iranian sovereignty over the Strait of Hormuz remains firm.”
‘An operation to destroy their economy’
White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt told Fox News that Trump continues to keep “all options on the table” regarding Iran.
She said Iran’s military had been devastated during the fighting and that Washington had now moved toward an economic campaign.
“There is now an ‘economic boycott’ operation underway to destroy their economy,” she said.
Leavitt said no negotiations were taking place.
“This will continue until the president feels that perhaps they will come to the negotiating table in a meaningful way,” she said. “We have not seen that yet.”
A senior Iranian official described the U.S. measures as “all-out economic warfare” after the Treasury Department this week announced plans aimed at cutting Iran off from its trading partners, part of what Trump has called an “economic D-Day.”
Qatar’s intervention also strengthens its position as a regional mediator, despite having itself come under Iranian attack during the war.
The conflict began on February 28. Six months later, shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains disrupted and Iran continues to attack tankers periodically.
Washington wants traffic through the strait restored to its prewar state, when the waterway served as one of the world economy’s most important oil arteries.
Iran, however, has refused to relinquish control and says the strait will remain closed unless the United States accepts its conditions, including an end to the blockade of Iranian ports, compensation and sanctions relief.
Six months later, no clear victory
Trump initially described the conflict as a “little excursion” and repeatedly suggested it would end within weeks.
Instead, it has become a costly stalemate with political, military and economic consequences spreading well beyond Iran.
Iran has not surrendered. Maritime traffic through Hormuz remains disrupted. There is no clear path toward ending the war.
After Washington concluded that airstrikes alone were unlikely to force Tehran to capitulate, the administration returned to economic pressure in hopes of weakening the regime further.
Reuters has mapped several of the consequences for the United States, Iran and the global economy after six months of war.
Trump’s political cost
The conflict was unpopular in the United States from the beginning, and public opposition has grown as fuel prices increased amid disruptions to oil exports through Hormuz.
Trump’s approval rating has fallen from 40% to 33% since the fighting began, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll, putting him at a low point.
The political cost is particularly sensitive because Trump campaigned in 2024 on promises to reduce costs for Americans and to end wars rather than start new ones.
Only 31% of Americans support the war, according to the poll.
That level of support is lower than for several previous U.S. military campaigns at a comparable stage, including the war in Afghanistan, which retained support above 50% for years in Gallup polling.
Rising prices could also hurt Republicans in November’s midterm elections, when the party must defend narrow majorities in both the House and Senate.
The war has also deepened divisions inside the Republican Party.
More isolationist Republicans, including parts of the MAGA movement, want the conflict ended quickly. Others argue that Trump should maintain or even intensify military pressure on Tehran until Iran is decisively defeated.
Global economy absorbs the shock
The U.S. and Israeli attacks immediately raised fears of severe damage to the global economy because of disruptions through the Strait of Hormuz, a roughly 34-kilometer-wide passage between Iran and Oman through which about one-fifth of the world’s energy supply moved before the war.
Oil prices surged, fueling concerns over a possible global recession.
The damage remains significant because higher fuel costs affect shipping, logistics and supply chains worldwide, although the impact has been less severe than many economists initially feared.
The International Monetary Fund has lowered its global growth forecast twice since the war began. It now expects the world economy to grow by 3.0% this year, compared with a 3.3% forecast in January.
Still, the global economy has proved more resilient than during the oil shocks of the 1970s.
Reuters noted that major economies have used substantial spending and investment to soften the impact, while the continuing boom in artificial intelligence has also helped support economic activity.
Iran wounded, but not defeated
Iran’s military and economy have suffered severe damage, but Tehran retains the ability to launch attacks across the Middle East and continue disrupting traffic through Hormuz.
In May, U.S. Central Command chief Adm. Brad Cooper told Congress that American forces had destroyed 161 Iranian naval vessels and neutralized 82% of Iran’s air-defense systems.
Iran’s air force, which once flew as many as 100 sorties a day, was no longer conducting missions, he said.
Yet Iran still retains stocks of drones and missiles of varying ranges and has continued carrying out successful attacks on ships and U.S. military facilities around the region.
Reuters reported in March that the United States could say with certainty that it had destroyed only about one-third of Iran’s vast missile arsenal.
The fate of another third was less clear. Intelligence assessments suggested those missiles had either been damaged, destroyed or buried in tunnels and underground bunkers, according to sources cited at the time.
Thousands of members of the Revolutionary Guards and Basij have been killed during the war, while Iran’s economic crisis has deepened. Inflation has worsened and trade has been disrupted.
At the same time, the war has prompted the regime to intensify repression at home, while political divisions have been pushed aside under what authorities portray as an existential external threat.
Middle East left more unstable
The war was initially framed as an effort to remove Iran as a threat to the Middle East.
But regional officials and experts cited by Reuters believe Tehran’s position has, in some respects, strengthened and that the region is currently less secure, particularly because the conflict remains unresolved and Iran continues to issue threats and demands.
Gulf states also remain divided over how to deal with Tehran.
Iranian missile and drone attacks on Arab Gulf states, including U.S. allies, have damaged military facilities, caused casualties and disrupted regional air travel.
Iranian attacks on tankers, combined with a blockade by Yemen’s Houthi rebels targeting Saudi-linked shipping in the Red Sea, have also driven up insurance and transportation costs.
The effect stretches far beyond individual attacks, disrupting supply chains and increasing uncertainty across Gulf economies.
Nuclear threat remains unresolved
U.S. and Israeli strikes in June 2025 and during the opening phase of the current war severely damaged Iran’s three known enrichment sites at Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan, as well as sites suspected of being linked to weaponization.
Israel also killed leading Iranian nuclear scientists who played significant roles in the program.
U.S. intelligence assessments in May put Iran’s estimated nuclear breakout time, the period needed to produce enough fissile material for a bomb, at up to one year, compared with up to six months before the war.
But preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon remains Trump’s central stated objective, and that goal appears far from assured.
The true condition of Iran’s nuclear program remains unclear because inspectors from the International Atomic Energy Agency have not returned to Iranian nuclear sites.
As a result, the agency has been unable to verify the location of roughly 440 kilograms of uranium enriched to 60% since the June 2025 strikes.
That stockpile could potentially be enriched further to weapons grade at an undisclosed facility.
Iran continues to publicly deny that it is seeking a nuclear weapon.
US military under growing strain
The war has also taken a significant toll on the U.S. military.
American forces have lost drones and aircraft to both Iranian fire and accidents. A Congressional Research Service report in May said 42 U.S. military aircraft had been lost.
Munitions stocks have also become a major concern, particularly interceptor missiles.
Reuters reported that the U.S. military had used “almost all” of its global inventory of certain precision weapons.
An assessment by the Center for Strategic and International Studies said that by July, the United States had used about 65% of its Patriot interceptors and reduced its stock of THAAD interceptors by at least 38%.
Washington has moved fighter jets, warships and other military assets to the Middle East from Europe and Asia and extended deployments in the region, raising questions about readiness elsewhere.
The aircraft carrier USS Gerald R. Ford spent more than a year on deployment, its longest mission since the Vietnam War.
Lawmakers have also raised concerns about conditions aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln after 200 consecutive days at sea. The Lincoln was replaced last week by the USS George Washington, which had been operating in the Pacific.
Six months into the war, Iran is badly damaged but still fighting, the Strait of Hormuz remains a global pressure point, the nuclear issue is unresolved and the U.S. military is being stretched across multiple theaters.
And despite new diplomatic efforts by Qatar, neither Washington nor Tehran appears ready to make the concessions needed to end the conflict.

US President Donald Trump told reporters that he does not believe Moscow will attack a NATO nation amid rising concerns that Russian President Vladimir Putin will strike a Baltic country or other member state to test the Western alliance’s resolve.
Trump on August 27 told reporters in the Oval Office that he had engaged in "good talks" with Putin and that "he's not going to be attacking a NATO territory." He did not specify when those talks were held.
"I am not concerned...at all. There is no problem," Trump was quoted earlier as saying by news publication Axios when asked about a possible Russian provocation against a NATO state.
The remarks come as the Kremlin at the same time dismissed as "scare stories" reports in the US media suggesting Moscow could attack NATO and following a surprise visit by the CIA director to Moscow.
NATO Article 5 Assurances
Western European security has long been tied to NATO's mutual defense clause, Article 5, which states that an attack on one member nation constitutes an attack on all.
Many Western leaders and officials have expressed concerns over Trump's commitment to the military alliance. Trump has at times put into question a possible US response to an attack on a member state, while at other times reaffirming support for NATO.
A letter seen by RFE/RL reveals growing concern about Russian aggression in the Baltic states, speaking of a "deteriorating security environment" amid an "increased frequency of airspace violations and drone incursions."
The letter was sent to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and signed by the three Baltic European commissioners, Kaja Kallas, Andrius Kubilius, and Valdis Dombrovskis, as well as the Polish and Finnish commissioners.
Dated July 30, the letter was one of a series of alarm bells sounded about Russian aggression over the course of the summer that culminated in CIA Director John Ratcliffe's surprise visit to Moscow on August 25.
Ratcliffe flew to Moscow to urge the Kremlin against escalating with US allies -- particularly Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania -- sources briefed about the visit confirmed to RFE/RL on August 26.
'Every Six Months'
Axios quoted Trump as denying Ratcliffe had issued such a warning to the Russians.
"Ratcliffe sees his Russian counterpart once every six months or once every year. They have a very good relationship. There was no message and there was nothing unusual," Trump said.
But when asked about the matter later by reporters in the Oval Office, Trump appeared to back off, saying: "I don't want to comment on that, but they're not going to attack [NATO]."
The New York Times, citing current and former officials, said Ratcliffe gave his counterpart a bleak assessment of the state of the Russia's war against Ukraine and to urge the Kremlin to reach a deal before its military and economic situation becomes worse.
The Wall Street Journal earlier cited US intelligence as stating Russia may test NATO resolve with a limited incursion as early as this fall.
Baltic diplomats who spoke to RFE/RL on condition of anonymity confirmed there was additional intelligence during the summer of Russian false-flag operations but no indication about an imminent conventional attack.
They were also keen to point out that such operations might not be limited to the Baltics, a concern reinforced by recent cases of alleged or suspected Russian involvement in assassination attempts, fires, and drone incursions in several NATO countries, including Germany, Poland, and Slovakia.
NATO Members Pressed
Separately, a senior Pentagon official on August 27 pressed NATO allies to outline how they were answering US demands that they take more responsibility for Europe's defense as Washington reviews its force levels on the continent.
The US administration under Trump has ignited fears among allies that the US could cut back its forces in Europe following a six-month review that began in July.
"The spirit that we come in is obviously one...of consultation, of engagement. We want to hear from our allies," US Defense Under Secretary Elbridge Colby said during a visit for talks at NATO's headquarters in Brussels.
Washington has sent out a questionnaire asking European countries to explain their efforts in taking the forefront in protecting the continent.
"We're actually having a kind of down-to-business conversation about how we go forward together in a world in which Europe, which is obviously a very wealthy continent, can and is taking primary responsibility for its own conventional defense," Colby said.

The man behind Srebrenica: Ratko Mladic dies at 84
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
19:28:00 UTC
04:28:00 KST

The man behind Srebrenica: Ratko Mladic dies at 84
August 27, 2026
More than 30 years after the end of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina (1992-1995), Srebrenica remains emblematic of its brutality. And no one is more closely linked to the genocide that took place in the small town in eastern Bosnia than Ratko Mladic, the former commander-in-chief of the Bosnian Serb army.
Although the United Nations had declared Srebrenica a "safe area," Bosnian Serb forces attacked the town. Within just a few days in July 1995, they expelled women and children, then killed more than 8,300 unarmed Muslim boys and men in the nearby village of Potocari — on Mladic's direct orders, according to the verdict handed down by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) in The Hague 22 years later.
At the time, Srebrenica was the largest massacre in Europe since World War II. The ICTY classified it as genocide. Mladic was also held responsible for other war crimes beyond the Srebrenica genocide. Under his command, the years-long siege of Sarajevo began at the start of the war. The city was shelled for more than 40 months, killing around 11,000 people, including more than 1,600 children.
Mladic always claimed that he targeted only military objectives. But numerous reports and intercepted radio communications indicate that civilian facilities and residential areas were also deliberately attacked. Around 100,000 people were killed during the four-year war in Bosnia, while some 2.2 million were driven from their homes in cities and villages across the country, half of its total population at the time.
'The butcher of the Balkans'
In 2017, Mladic was sentenced to life in prison by the tribunal in The Hague.
International media dubbed him "the Butcher of the Balkans."
He was found responsible for some of the most serious war crimes and the genocide committed during the Bosnian War.
Mladic consistently denied any responsibility. He saw himself as an avenger of the Serbs for centuries of Ottoman rule in the Balkans, and viewed Bosnia's Muslims, who today call themselves Bosniaks, as direct descendants of the Turks. In front of his soldiers, he referred to them simply as "the Turks" and showed no empathy.
"Borders are always drawn with blood, and states are marked with graves," he is quoted as saying.
Career in the Yugoslav army
At the beginning of the Croatian War in June 1991, when Serbs living in Croatia rose up against the independence of the former Yugoslav republic with active support from Serbia, Mladic's role fundamentall changed. As a colonel in the Yugoslav army, he became commander of the 9th Corps in the Croatian city of Knin. His task was to organize Serb militias and support them in their fight against Croatian independence.
Under Mladic's command, the Croatian cities of Sibenik and Zadar were bombarded, and Croatian civilians were driven from surrounding towns and villages. In May 1992, he took on the same role in Bosnia. By then promoted to general, Mladic became commander-in-chief of the Bosnian Serb forces, seeking to establish a territorial link between Serb-held areas in the east and west of the former Yugoslav republic.
Flight, arrest and final verdict
At the height of his career, Colonel General Ratko Mladic was a fervent Serbian nationalist. But he began his career as a committed communist. Born in eastern Bosnia in 1943, Mladic was just two years old when his father, one of Tito's Partisans, was killed by fascist Croatian Ustasha militia. The loss is often described as a formative influence, shaping his later worldview.
As a young man, Mladic embarked on a military career, attending the Military Academy in Belgrade. He later graduated at the top of his class. He quickly rose through the ranks of the Yugoslav army, which for many years was regarded as one of the most stable institutions in the multiethnic state.
Serbian nationalist
Before the end of the Bosnian War in late 1995, Mladic was indicted by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. But he evaded arrest for years. Supported by networks within the Serbian military and political establishment, he lived largely undisturbed underground and was even seen in public. He was finally arrested in 2011, after 16 years on the run and mounting international pressure.
The subsequent trial in The Hague lasted a total of 523 days. Nearly 600 witnesses testified, while numerous documents and other pieces of evidence were examined. Mladic was ultimately sentenced to life in prison at trial, among other charges for genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes. In 2021, an appeals chamber upheld the verdict, making it final. Legally, this established his responsibility as one of the principal figures behind the crimes committed during the Bosnian War.
A war criminal who saw himself as a hero
Internationally, the verdict was hailed as historic. United Nations officials saw it as a signal that accountability can still be pursued decades after crimes are committed. For many survivors and relatives of the victims, the verdict was a long-overdue but important acknowledgment of their suffering.
Mladic himself, however, remained defiant to the end. Throughout the trial, he maintained that he was innocent, calling the charges against him "disgusting" and the tribunal "satanic."
Many of his supporters in Serbia and among Bosnian Serbs still see him as a hero. While he is regarded internationally as a war criminal, his admirers continue to portray him as a defender of Serbian interests and a hero — even painting his likeness on walls.
While he was still on the run, Mladic threatened his pursuers, claiming he always carried a poison pill and that he would never be captured alive. But he never swallowed the pill during his decades in hiding. He survived several strokes while in prison.
Ratko Mladic died on August 27, 2026, at the prison hospital in The Hague at the age of 84.

Toys, Groceries and Electronics Become New Targets—Russian Strike Hits Warehouses Serving Ukraine’s Biggest Retailers
A massive Russian overnight attack tore through logistics infrastructure in Ukraine’s Kyiv region, damaging or destroying distribution centers serving some of the country’s largest grocery, electronics, toy, home-improvement and consumer brands.
Among the companies affected were Fora, Budynok Ihrashok, Comfy, Epicentr, Aurora, Silpo and Roshen, according to Forbes Ukraine and statements from company executives on August 27.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
One of the facilities hit belonged to Fora, a large Ukrainian neighborhood supermarket chain operating hundreds of smaller-format grocery stores. The warehouse had opened only days earlier, on August 23.
No employees were inside when the strike occurred, and no casualties were reported.
It was already the third Russian attack on Fora logistics infrastructure during August. The company is now rerouting deliveries while assessing the damage, although its stores continue operating normally.
Another strike destroyed the distribution center of Budynok Ihrashok, one of Ukraine’s largest specialist toy retailers and a business broadly comparable in format to Toys “R” Us.
CEO Maria Nazarenko said the warehouse held a substantial share of the products used for daily shipments to customers across Ukraine.
Employees had moved into shelters during the air raid alert and escaped injury. The company’s physical stores and online shop remain operational, although customers were warned that some previously placed online orders could face delays.
Russian drones also hit a distribution center belonging to Comfy, one of Ukraine’s largest electronics and appliance retailers—a chain similar in concept to Best Buy.
Comfy CEO Hennadii Verbylenko said a Russian drone deliberately struck the company’s facility in the Kyiv region. Employees survived because shelters had been prepared in advance.
“Comfy continues to operate. Teams are in contact, all necessary processes have been launched, and we are working in an enhanced mode to ensure the operation of stores, online channels, and order fulfillment,” Verbylenko said.
Other affected facilities included the Epicentr Kalynivka logistics center. Epicentr is Ukraine’s dominant home-improvement and household-goods retailer, broadly comparable to a combination of Home Depot or Lowe’s with a large-format general merchandise store.
A warehouse complex operated by Alfa Development Group was also affected. The site housed inventory belonging to several prominent companies and retail chains.
Among them was Aurora, Ukraine’s rapidly expanding discount variety chain, which follows a format similar to Dollar General in the US or Action in Europe, selling inexpensive household goods, personal-care products, toys and everyday essentials.
Warehouses serving Silpo were also located at the site. Silpo is one of Ukraine’s largest supermarket chains and is known for its large grocery stores and more premium-oriented retail format.
Comfy and Budpostach inventory was also stored at the complex. Budpostach is a major Ukrainian supplier and distributor of tools, machinery and equipment.
Berger Cargo Ukraine, a freight and logistics operator, was also among the businesses whose facilities were affected.
One of the most significant losses was a Roshen warehouse in Chubynske, which was destroyed during the Russian attack.
Roshen is one of Ukraine’s biggest confectionery manufacturers—a company operating in the same broad consumer category as major international producers such as Hershey or Mars—and supplies chocolates, candies, cookies and other products across Ukraine and export markets.
The destroyed Chubynske warehouse had been used to store finished confectionery products before their distribution.
No Roshen employees were injured. Workers followed air raid procedures and were inside shelters when the strike occurred, according to the company.
Previously, a Russian drone attack on Kherson sparked a fire at a Ukrainian Red Cross warehouse, destroying and damaging humanitarian supplies worth around $626,000.

Red tape or essential regulation? Why the new ASIC boss is pushing back
Almost a hundred days in and, right on cue, another domino has fallen.
Sarah Court, who ascended from the deputy to the leader of Australia's corporate regulator just on three months ago, has spent the past few days closely monitoring a corporate collapse, among a host of other issues.
Construction group Bathla — with more than 520 subsidiaries, about 2,000 homes under construction, and roughly 13,000 more in the development pipeline — was this week placed into administration.
But that's not the worst of it.
Bathla owes creditors more than $3.5 billion.
And the bulk of that debt comes, not from banks or financial institutions, but from ordinary Australians who have invested in a fast-growing new financial fad; private credit.
It is a high-risk lending operation that operates outside the banking system and largely under the radar, pulling in money from self-funded retirees and other investors and lending it out to mostly property developers.
A year ago, the new Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) chief and her predecessor Joe Longo, identified what they believed could become a potential systemic problem and ordered a deep dive into this murky new industry.
With the promise of high returns, it had attracted close to $250 billion.
What Court and Longo found was concerning.
Late last year, ASIC ordered an overhaul of some of the industry's practices, particularly around asset valuations, fee transparency, and conflict management. It also proposed new law reforms.
But, while the regulator can identify risk and attempt to minimise it, it can't eliminate it, as many aggrieved investors often demand after the event.
"It's not possible to eliminate risk," Court tells the ABC.
"We have a very permissive investment regime in Australia and people do very well from that permissive regime. But the consequence is that investors can suffer losses."
The investigations into private credit uncovered an opaque industry operating well below the radar. But it proved valuable in other ways.
It's a strategy that has become part of ASIC's new modus operandi; to gather intelligence on shifting markets and get ahead of potential issues rather than being hit by a freight train at full speed.
A brief history of ASIC ineffectiveness
Sarah Court now heads a regulator with a deeply chequered past.
After decades of failure at almost every level, from policy through to enforcement, the Australian Securities and Investment Commission notched up one embarrassing failure after another.
Even the global financial crisis, which exposed rampant misconduct within a group of collapsed corporations, resulted in not one conviction and precious little investigation.
A decade later, the lethargy was brought to a halt in a withering take-down by Kenneth Hayne, the man who led the royal commission into banking misconduct, with a call for a complete regulatory overhaul.
For years, there was constant dismay at ASIC's inability to emulate its cousin, the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) which had a ferocious reputation when it came to upholding the law.
Cue Sarah Court.
Given her 13 years as a deputy commissioner of the ACCC where she headed, among other things, enforcement and compliance, her appointment as deputy chair of the corporate regulator in 2021 was seen as a coup.
Since Court's arrival at ASIC, the organisation has dramatically lifted its game, taking on financial giants such as Macquarie and tearing into the failures at the Australian Securities Exchange (ASX).
Spare the rod
The new approach hasn't exactly been met with universal approval.
The business sector is ramping up calls for less regulation, reduced "red tape", to help lift the shackles costing Australian businesses an estimated $160 billion a year and arguably putting a handbrake on national productivity.
Loading...
Many senior business leaders have become alarmed that, instead of a quiet word or a discreet phone call from the regulator, they've found themselves facing the full glare of the courts.
But in an address to the Committee for the Economic Development of Australia (CEDA) this week, Court argued that strong law enforcement was essential for the country to have a stable environment for business and investors.
"Strong enforcement sets expectations, deters misconduct and protects both market confidence and market participants," she said.
Loading...
Failure to do so exacerbates and entrenches problems that are only ever addressed once a scandal erupts, often with even more onerous laws and regulation.
"Every failure leads to calls for new rules," she said.
"Every new rule adds a layer of complexity. That is how regulatory burden creeps into the system, with flow-on effects to productivity.
"When misconduct is addressed promptly, visibly and at the right level, it can prevent harm from spreading or repeating."
Too big to operate?
The uncomfortable truth, however, is that ASIC's remit is huge and its resources limited.
Brutal assessments are often made not to pursue what could be legitimate complaints.
"We have to make hard choices on a daily basis," she tells the ABC.
"In some ways, that's a more heightened challenge than during my time at the ACCC because we are often talking about people's money, their retirement savings."
But while every case may not be followed up, often they can form the basis of a campaign, to be put on an investment alert list or a scam list.
ASIC is tasked with covering financial services, big banks, corporate behaviour, market oversight and soon, since the KPMG and PWC debacles, auditors and liquidators. Then there's data collection, the business registry, and a raft of other avenues over which it must keep watch.
Is it too broad?
"I don't think it's too big," she says. "A lot of the factors are complimentary."
Court explains, for example, that ASIC's investment protocols neatly fit alongside financial services, which then relate directly to consumers.
Separating them out could hamper the overall picture the organisation has of the investment landscape.
Even the data it collects from its registry, which until now has been a cash cow for the federal government and largely separate, is planned to be used to support its regulatory role.
"The danger in separating some of our roles is that things could fall between the cracks," she explains before adding: "We've just got to get better at joining the dots."
