US forces, Ecuadorian police strike major blow against transnational drug cartels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
19:22:48 UTC
04:22:48 KST

Laura Gamba
27 August 2026•Update: 27 August 2026
Ecuadorian security forces, supported by the US Military’s Southern Command (SOUTHCOM) and the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), executed a series of major joint anti-drug operations targeting the country's dominant criminal syndicates, authorities announced on Wednesday.
The raids, codenamed Operation Factoria and Operation Jerico, targeted operational networks tied to Los Lobos and Los Choneros across six provinces: Guayas, Santo Domingo, El Oro, Los RIos, Manabi, and Esmeraldas.
According to Gen. Pablo Vinicio Davila, commander-in-chief of Ecuador’s National Police, 36 simultaneous raids resulted in the arrest of 43 alleged cartel operatives, including two high-value targets identified by the aliases "CC" and "Leon."
Ecuador’s Interior Minister John Reimberg confirmed in a social media video that the suspects include two Mexican nationals believed to be pilots for the Jalisco New Generation Cartel tasked with flying cocaine shipments north to Mexico and the US.
During the sweep, joint forces dismantled two clandestine airstrips used for international narcotics transport. Authorities seized a light aircraft, 21 vehicles, nearly 1,000 liters of aviation fuel, 47 mobile devices, communications gear, firearms, ammunition, bulletproof vests, cash, and significant quantities of cocaine and synthetic drugs.
The joint campaign was coordinated directly by the Ecuadorian State Attorney General’s Office alongside the DEA and SOUTHCOM.
Gen. Francis Donovan, Commander of SOUTHCOM, praised the preliminary outcomes, describing the raids as "successful" and calling the combined operation a "decisive victory for the region."
The operations mark one of the most significant joint counter-narcotics efforts since President Daniel Noboa's administration opened the door to an expanded US military and law enforcement presence on Ecuadorian territory.
The crackdown follows action by the US government under President Donald Trump to formally designate Los Lobos, Los Choneros, and the Chone Killers as foreign terrorist organizations, a classification that has facilitated broader intelligence sharing and tactical cooperation between Washington and Quito to disrupt cartel supply chains.

Parents who lost children to social media harms question Meta settlement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
19:15:37 UTC
04:15:37 KST

Parents who lost children to social media harms question Meta settlement
US parents said that because of the settlement, they were ‘robbed’ of seeing evidence of Meta’s awareness of harm due to its products.
Oakland, California, the US – During the COVID-19 pandemic, Erin Popolo’s then-16-year-old daughter Emily took a job at a cafe near her home in Bridgewater, New Jersey, making pizza. Emily had always battled mental health issues, but when some classmates posted photos of her with an apron and hairnet on social media and began cyberbullying her, it got worse.
Emily had joined Facebook and Instagram just before the pandemic and stayed on because “she wanted to have friends, be in a group”, things she struggled with otherwise, Popolo said. She had used the report button to take down the negative comments against her daughter, but to no avail. Emily died by suicide a few months later, at 17.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Trump tells Al Jazeera ‘not in a hurry’ for Iran to return to talks
- list 2 of 4Luxury watches worth $1.2 million stolen from a popular mall in Tokyo
- list 3 of 4US inflation holds at 3.7 percent in July, above Fed target
- list 4 of 4US says Chinese-linked hackers attacked NASA, Senate, and gov’t agencies
Last week, Popolo joined a group of parents outside a United States federal court in Oakland. Hearings had begun in a case in which 29 US states sued Meta, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram, for design flaws in its products that the plaintiffs said led to children becoming addicted and allowed them to be contacted by drug dealers, cyberbullied, extorted and abused.
The high-stakes case sought up to $200bn in fines as well as changes to Meta’s products and business practices.
On Wednesday, Meta settled the case for $18bn and agreed to increase protections for young users.
While the settlement has been hailed as historic, Popolo asked: “What evidence did they not want to get out?”
The trial had started on August 18 and was expected to last six weeks.
Mary Rodee, whose 15-year-old son died by suicide after becoming the target of online extortion, said the measures announced on Wednesday would not have protected him.
“We were robbed of seeing the evidence” because of the settlement, she told Al Jazeera.
“Our kids need to be protected from your algorithms and ads,” she said about Meta, pointing out that the settlement does not restrict advertising to minors or make algorithms transparent.
She said she hopes there will be more cases against Meta. She wants to see convictions and increased transparency in their processes.
The states’ case had included internal documents showing that Meta’s top executives knew of the security loopholes in their platforms.
In his testimony on Tuesday, Instagram’s chief executive Adam Mosseri said that Instagram had added a pop-up feature to all teen accounts in 2024, asking them to take a break from scrolling, as well as a quiet mode for notifications.
Jason Slothouber, from the Colorado attorney general’s office, asked if Mosseri was aware that parents had no way of knowing that only 1 percent to 2 percent of children used this feature. Mosseri confirmed they did not. He was scheduled to testify again on Wednesday, but then the settlement was reached.
‘Keeps kids online’
Lori Schott, a resident of Colorado, said she lost her 18-year-old daughter, Annalee, to suicide.
Annalee had received a constant stream of messages, Schott said, that had made her feel she was not beautiful enough.
Schott, who had also been outside court on the first day of the trial, as well as in Los Angeles, where Meta was previously sued in March, said Instagram needs to introduce more stringent measures to protect teens.
“I would like to see less addictive design, including limits on infinite scroll, autoplay streaks, constant notifications, and algorithmic feeds,” she said of features that form the bedrock of Instagram’s model. “It keeps kids online.”
“I would like to see more control over the algorithms, including their ability to turn off personalised recommendations or use the chronological feeds that were pushing content to my daughter, like dealing with suicide and eating disorders.”
In chronological feeds, the latest content is added on top, and critics say this keeps users hooked as they keep coming back to the app to see if something new has come.
As part of the settlement, Meta has agreed to some changes, including setting two-hour time limits for users under 18, as well as night-time and school-time blocks.
On the first day of the trial in Oakland, California, Popolo, Schott and other parents held a banner with the names of the 398 children who they say had died because of social media addiction and bullying.
Popolo said the number of children on their banner has gone up from 356 in March, when parents held it up outside the Los Angeles court. In that case, Meta was handed a $4.2m fine.
‘Handed them a tool, magnified bullying’
Apart from cyberbullies, parents spoke of drug dealers and overseas extortion gangs contacting their children through fake accounts and selling them fentanyl, a powerful synthetic opioid, or extorting them for money after getting them in embarrassing situations.
In upstate New York, Mary Rodee and Darren Basford’s 15-year-old son Riley had always wanted a snowmobile, and had turned to Facebook Messenger in March 2021 to look for one.
Once there, he began receiving messages from someone he thought was a teenage girl. They exchanged private photos, after which the girl, who was actually a group of men from the Ivory Coast, began threatening to send the pictures to his parents and share them widely if he did not pay them $3,500.
Riley asked for time, but the threats escalated throughout the next day, while he got his braces fixed with his mother and got a milkshake. She dropped him off at his father’s house to spend the night.
In the early hours of the morning, Basford found Riley dead. He had died by suicide, Basford said, rather than facing the shame of his private photos being shared with family and friends.
Riley’s mother, Mary Rodee, stood outside the court in Oakland on the first day of the trial, just as she had in Los Angeles, and had hoped to see Meta held to account.
There are dangers beyond extortion, including easy contact with drug dealers.
Deb Schmill’s 15-year-old daughter Becca was raped by a boy she met on a chat group and then cyberbullied. The bullies “knew she was vulnerable at the time”, Schmill told Al Jazeera.
“Kids have always looked for vulnerabilities in others to bully them,” she added. “With unfettered social media, we have handed them a tool and magnified bullying.”
In 2020, Schmill had not known that she could report the abuse and try to take it down.
Becca battled growing mental health issues from the rape and bullying and tried to buy cocaine online to deal with her pain. She ended up buying fentanyl that a drug dealer sold her in the guise of cocaine. At 18, Becca died of an overdose.
“Becca was the love of my life. We were always holding hands,” Schmill said.
She attended US Senate Judiciary Committee hearings in February 2024 when Meta’s chief executive, Mark Zuckerberg, testified. She held up Becca’s photo as Zuckerberg turned to her and other mothers who had lost children and apologised.
Schmill, who now runs a foundation in Becca’s name, said drug dealers and extortionists would not have easy access to their children if Meta’s safety protocols worked.
In late 2023, a researcher from her foundation set up accounts on Instagram as a 14-year-old and connected with drug dealers. When they found the dealers’ accounts, the researchers reported them to Instagram. More than 95 percent of the accounts reported were not taken down, Schmill told Al Jazeera.
Her foundation did not publish the research, and will use it as part of a lawsuit.
Schmill also helped fund a study by the Harvard TH Chan School of Public Health that showed social media companies made $11bn in US advertising revenues from minors.
A ‘terrible club’
It is a “terrible club” of parents who lost their children to social media harms, said Maurine Molak, whose son, David, died by suicide after being bullied on Instagram. In March, Molak attended the trial in New Mexico, where Meta was found liable for causing harms to children and asked to pay a $375m fine. That was followed by another $567m fine earlier this month. Meta has said it would appeal the verdict.
“We don’t want these trials. We want the harms not to be done,” Molak told Al Jazeera.
Matthew Bergman, a Seattle-based lawyer who founded the Social Media Victims Law Center to represent such parents, said the parents had pressed on knowing they may not see a win.
“Never in 30 years of my practice have I met clients more committed to justice than this,” he said. He had parents who slept outside court and travelled from the United Kingdom to attend the US hearings.
In a statement released after the settlement, Meta said it now looked at other social media platforms to bring similar change.
“The fact is that teens move fluidly between dozens of apps a day. All platforms should empower parents and support teens by putting the same measures in place, because we know that when teens are restricted on one app, they simply move to another,” Meta said.
Cases against other social media platforms are also building up.
Amy Neville’s 14-year-old son Alex died of an accidental fentanyl overdose after a drug dealer sold it to him on Snapchat as OxyContin, an opioid of lesser intensity, to deal with pain.
Meeting with company officials to ask for change had not yielded anything. Now, Neville is among a group of parents who have filed a similar case against Snapchat in Los Angeles, which comes up for hearing in November 2027.
The attorney general of Pennsylvania also filed a lawsuit against Snapchat on Tuesday, alleging that the platform was designed to keep children addicted.
“I’d like to know what evidence we don’t get to see,” Neville said of the Meta trial, which could have an impact on her case, as well as the practices of other social media companies.
Popolo, who had planned to return to hear Zuckerberg’s testimony in the Oakland trial, said she plans to continue the fight.
The cyberbullies had not only harassed her daughter Emily in life; they also sent bomb threats to the funeral home where Emily’s funeral took place.
Since it happened during the pandemic, Erin could have only 75 people present and beamed it on Zoom for others. The bullies, all young people, at least one of whom was a minor, had intercepted the screening and shown inappropriate material on it.
“[This settlement] does not mean that we do not need to keep the pressure on to get legislation at the federal level,” Popolo said. “This fight is far from over.”
If you or someone you know is at risk of suicide, these organisations may be able to help.

UEFA will not support Infantino in the upcoming FIFA presidential election
Kyiv • UNN
UEFA has stated its readiness to join forces with other confederations against Infantino’s new term. The association is demanding an independent audit of FIFA Forward Enterprise.
UEFA stated that if current FIFA President Gianni Infantino attempts to run for a new term, the European association will join forces with partners from other confederations to offer member associations a credible alternative—a candidate committed to the principles of integrity, accountability, development and genuine institutional change. This is stated in a UEFA statement, reports UNN.
Details
According to UEFA, representatives of national associations on the UEFA Executive Committee and the European members of the FIFA Council, together with the presidents of European national associations, gathered in Monaco on the occasion of the draw for the 2026/27 UEFA club competitions, where they discussed the ongoing crisis at FIFA.
The meeting participants examined the consequences of the FIFA president’s failed attempt to sell a stake in the FIFA World Cup to outside investors. This scheme demonstrated a profound misjudgment of the situation, an abuse of presidential powers and a concept of leadership incompatible with the responsibilities of the highest office in the global football hierarchy.
Those present unanimously authorized the UEFA president and administration to use all available institutional, political and legal mechanisms necessary to carry out fundamental reform, restore appropriate limits on presidential power and ensure that FIFA is once again governed as an institution rather than around a single individual. The first step must be a truly independent external audit of the FIFA Forward Enterprise project, with full access to all relevant documentation, correspondence and decision-making records. FIFA cannot investigate its own actions and expect the football community simply to accept its conclusions
UEFA stated that the consequences of this crisis extend beyond administrative governance. The trust necessary for the FIFA president to perform his duties has been undermined, and it cannot be restored by withdrawing a single proposal, providing assurances or making promises of reform after the fact. World football now needs new leadership capable of restoring this trust.
In this regard, UEFA will continue working with confederations, member associations and the wider football community, including fans, players, clubs, leagues and other stakeholders, with the aim of shaping FIFA’s future. If the current FIFA president nevertheless attempts to run for a new term, UEFA will join forces with partners from other confederations to offer member associations a credible alternative—a candidate committed to the principles of integrity, accountability, development and genuine institutional change
To remind you
FIFA announced the creation of the semi-private subsidiary FIFA Forward Enterprise to raise $4.2 billion. The plan drew criticism from UEFA and former FIFA president Sepp Blatter.
The International Federation of Association Football (FIFA) stated that it was scrapping a plan allowing private investment in flagship events following sharp criticism from football officials around the world.

New flood warnings issued in Nepal as death toll rises to 392
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

04:15:26 KST

Authorities warn of new flood risks in Nepal and Tibet as death toll rises to 392
In short:
At least 392 people have died in the flood in Nepal and Tibet, with nearly 1,500 people still missing.
At least 39 Australians remain unaccounted-for, despite hundreds of survivors being rescued.
What's next?
Authorities are now warning about the risk of new floods, with a barrier lake in the region at risk of bursting within the next few days.
Authorities in Nepal and China warn new floods in the disaster zone could be imminent, with overflowing lakes threatening to burst.
At least 389 people have died in Nepal, and more than 900 people are still missing, including at least 39 Australians, according to Nepal's Tourism Board.
In Tibet, the death toll still stands at three, with more than 550 people unaccounted-for, Chinese state media has reported.
Entire villages have been swept away, with rescuers working through the night, pulling both survivors and bodies from deep mud.
Among the 39 missing Australians are Venkatraman Balakrishnan, 52, and his wife Chitra Venkatraman, 46, from Western Sydney, who were taking part in a tour with US-based hiking company Himalayan Glacier.
There were 13 other Australians on that tour in the Langtang Valley, including two boys aged 11 and 14.
Indian spiritual leader Sadhguru Jaggi Vasudev said 11 Australians had completed a pilgrimage with his Isha Foundation, and were clearing immigration on the Chinese side when contact was lost.
Six Australians were travelling with Kathmandu-based Kailash Journeys, and one was with Kathmandu Holiday Tours and Travels.
Queensland woman Kanagamah Sundrasan, who was visiting Mount Kailash to complete a pilgrimage, is also unaccounted-for.
Foreign Minister Penny Wong said there was an "unfortunate possibility" the number of missing Australians could rise.
"We are urgently working to identify how many Australians have been in the region and to confirm the welfare of any Australians who are not accounted for," Senator Wong told the ABC's RN Breakfast.
She said the Australian government was deploying additional staff to Nepal to assist with the humanitarian response.
Australia has 20 staff in Nepal and the government is sending four officers to the region in the next 24 hours, and a second team in the next couple of days, she said.
Hundreds of people rescued, including tourists
According to the latest figures from Nepal Police, 466 people have been rescued.
That included more than 30 foreign citizens, including people from India, South Korea and the United States, according to Nepal's Tourism Board.
No Australians were among the list, but the nationality of eight foreigners rescued had not yet been confirmed.
Many of those rescued have been taken to the Tribhuvan Teaching Hospital in Kathmandu, which has become crowded with people trying to find their loved ones.
The walls are lined with lists of people's names who are being treated inside the hospital, along with photos of missing people and those who have died.
Preksha KC is volunteering there, even though her uncle is missing.
"It is really helpless, hopeless, but we are building our confidence to find people with our team and our Nepal government," she told the ABC.
Ranjana Poudel is at the hospital to try and find news of her brother-in-law who was at the border when the flood hit.
"Last time he spoke to his family it was 8:15, and he said he would enter China by 10. But after that we had no contact with him," she told the ABC.
New flood warnings issued
Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) has warned a lake forming at the site where the flood occurred is now at risk of bursting, triggering fresh floods.
Similar alerts have been issued in China and Tibet.
The lake formed after the glacier collapse blocked the river on Wednesday, according to the authority, which urged rescue workers and locals in the area to stay away from riverbanks until further notice in case the lake breached.
The formation of the barrier lake was captured in aerial footage by a Chinese rescue team on Thursday, which showed brown water accumulating in a basin with no visible outlet.
"The notice states that the lake is in the process of rising and is at risk of bursting,"
According to the Chinese water resources ministry, the lake was already overflowing, yet another 3 million cubic metres of water was expected to flow into the lake over the next three days.
More rain forecast over the coming week was expected to exacerbate the threat, Chinese state media said, citing the Chinese water resources ministry.
It prompted some rescue workers in Nepal to move towards higher ground.
"We are here for rescue and don't want to be near the danger zone," Pawan Koirala said, who moved away from the riverbed with his team of 13.
Environmental anthropologist Austin Lord, a senior fellow and the Nepal lead at the Stimson Center, told The World the more water, the faster it would travel.
"The natural dam that's created around it has not yet fully been compromised, and that lake could be gaining volume and could burst again," he said.
He said the terrain was "impassable in many points" for vehicles and that the rescue and recovery effort upstream from Nepal would be "brutal and slow".
Mr Lord said given Nepal was still in its monsoon season, there was a risk of landslides.
"There's always a possibility of another surge, there's always the possibility that … there could be other landslides along the route," he told the ABC.
"If the slopes have been destabilised or undercut at the bottom, if then rain occurs and they're saturated, the whole topography becomes increasingly unstable."
Loading...
Nepal PM orders rescue operation to 'speed up'
After visiting part of the flood-affected area on Thursday, Nepal's prime minister, Balendra Shah, assembled a high-level meeting of his ministers, where he urged authorities to "speed up rescue operations", provide free health care to injured people and offer immediate aid and support to impacted families.
More than 13,000 personnel from Nepal's police, army and armed police forces are currently deployed to the disaster zone and helping with rescue efforts.
David Fisher, head of the Nepal delegation with Red Cross and Red Crescent societies in Kathmandu, told the ABC rescue teams were trying to get aid into affected areas of the Himalayan floods but many communities were completely cut off.
"The [floods have] cut the roads. The electricity is out in many places. Cell coverage is out. So it has only been accessible from the outside by helicopter," Mr Fisher told The World.
"We know, at least from those who we have been able to access, that many, many of them have lost their homes," he said.
"They've lost everything they own."
International aid organisation UNICEF said at least 17,000 children had been affected by the natural disaster, with that number likely to rise.

Google Engineer Accused of Polymarket Insider Trading Says He Was Just Gambling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
19:12:39 UTC
04:12:39 KST

Michele Spagnuolo, the Google engineer arrested in May by US authorities for alleged insider trading on Polymarket, is making a new bold bet. On Wednesday, his legal team filed a motion to dismiss the charges against him. Spagnuolo isn’t outright denying that he made money using internal information from Google. Instead, his legal team says that the wagers were not financial instruments subject to regulation by the United States’ Commodities Exchange Act but rather good old-fashioned international betting that the US has no authority over.
Spagnuolo, who has been placed on leave from Google, is accused of committing commodities fraud, wire fraud, and money laundering. Using the alias “AlphaRaccoon,” he allegedly made a series of wagers on Polymarket’s flagship platform that resulted in profits totaling over $1.2 million. According to the criminal complaint, “AlphaRaccoon” correctly wagered that the singer D4vd, who gained notoriety for his suspected connection to a grisly killing, would be Google’s most-searched person of the year in 2025. (D4vd was later charged with murder; he pleaded not guilty.)
You might not expect the lawyers defending someone accused of felonies to agree with state prosecutors, but the vicious legal infighting over prediction markets is creating strange alliances. Across the United States, state attorneys general and regulators are battling against both the federal government and prediction markets over whether event contracts should be considered “swaps” and therefore have to follow the Commodities Exchange Act, or instead be categorized as gambling, which is regulated by states.
Spagnuolo’s lawyers argue that defining swaps to include wagers like who the most-searched person on Google will be each year “would fly in the face of the statute’s purpose and history” and lead to “absurd results.” They say it would make it so that any wager in the world, from a charity raffle to a local Ping-Pong match, could be classified as a financial instrument. “Spagnuolo is basically making the same argument as the states that are suing prediction markets,” says a financial services regulation expert Todd Phillips. “This is the issue that will likely go up to the Supreme Court.”
In addition to disputing the idea that prediction markets offer swaps, Spagnuolo’s legal team argues that the US government had no jurisdiction over him in the first place because he’s a non-US citizen who was wagering on a non-US platform. Although Polymarket is headquartered in New York, the company’s flagship prediction market is banned in the United States and technically is administered by an ostensibly Panama-based entity known as Adventure One QSS.
Spagnuolo was living in Zurich, Switzerland, when he allegedly made the Google-related trades on Polymarket. “The extraterritorial argument is interesting and raises the question of whether the US should be the world’s prediction markets cop,” Philipps says. Spagnuolo’s team also claims that the charges should be dismissed because the internal information he supposedly leveraged did not have any commercial value to Google. Google did not respond to requests for comment.
The Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the federal agency tasked with regulating prediction markets, and Spagnuolo’s legal team also did not respond to requests for comment. CFTC chairman Michael Selig previously told WIRED that the agency has the ability to pursue extraterritorial jurisdiction in cases involving offshore platforms in “extreme circumstances.”
Spagnuolo was the second person publicly charged with alleged insider trading on Polymarket in the US. A month prior to Spanguolo’s arrest, Special Forces soldier Gannon Ken van Dyke was charged with allegedly making more than $400,000 from wagers on Polymarket connected to the raid on former Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro. Van Dyke’s defense team is also arguing for the charges to be dismissed because they say his activity should be classified as gambling and therefore not subject to federal commodities law.
Earlier this week, the CFTC—which filed a separate civil lawsuit against Van Dyke—repeatedly stressed in an amicus brief for the criminal case that his Polymarket events contracts were, indeed, swaps. It won’t be surprising if the CFTC does something similar in Spagnuolo’s case. By mounting this type of defense, the alleged insider traders have now inserted themselves directly into a much larger existential showdown over prediction markets.

Moscow slams Vienna over plans for Nazi concentration camp site

Moscow slams Vienna over plans for Nazi concentration camp site
Russia has condemned plans to build a supermarket and logistics center on the site of a former Nazi women’s concentration camp in Austria, accusing Vienna of erasing the memory of its victims.
The development in Leobersdorf, around 40km south of Vienna, would cover the remains of the Hirtenberg camp, a former subcamp of the Mauthausen concentration camp complex, where at least 90,000 prisoners were murdered or died from starvation, disease, exhaustion, and abuse during World War II.
According to Austrian media, the Hirtenberg site is set to host a large refrigerated storage and logistics facility, as well as a branch of German discount retailer Lidl.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova described the decision to effectively “pave over” the memory of victims of the Nazi regime despite public opposition as “hypocrisy in full view.”
“How can you advocate women’s rights and boast of your great achievements in feminism if you cannot protect the memory of 400 women who were forcibly deported and held in a concentration camp located in your country?” she said.
Hirtenberg was established in September 1944 and held around 400 female prisoners, many transferred from Auschwitz and forced to work long shifts producing munitions.
According to Mauthausen Guides, the largest group comprised 194 Russian prisoners. Other inmates came from Italy, Poland, Yugoslavia, Hungary, Croatia, Germany and Slovakia, with some as young as 16. The camp was evacuated in April 1945 as the Red Army approached and Nazi Germany neared defeat.
The project has also sparked criticism in Austria. Mauthausen Memorial director Barbara Gluck has called the destruction of the camp remains “a disgrace.” Oskar Deutsch, the head of Vienna’s Jewish community, has similarly condemned efforts to “make money from the memory of tortured and murdered women.”
Moscow has repeatedly accused European countries of erasing or desecrating World War II memorial sites, particularly those commemorating the Soviet Union’s sacrifices and role in the defeat of Nazi Germany.
Zakharova has previously described such incidents as part of a growing “terrifying pandemic of historical revanchism.”

====================================================================================================

The West is obsessed with ‘Russia’s next draft’. Why isn’t it looking at Ukraine?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
19:06:12 UTC
04:06:12 KST

Russia’s rumored draft makes headlines. Ukraine’s real one sparks street clashes
In the final days of August 2026, mobilization once again moved to the forefront. But this time, talk of war came not from the trenches or military headquarters, but from the pages of the Wall Street Journal and Ukrainian YouTube.
On August 23, the WSJ reported that the Russian military was “testing its readiness” to accept a new wave of recruits – the first since 2022. The authors did not claim that the Kremlin had already decided on another mobilization. Rather, they described a stress test of the system: Drills, logistics, and the military infrastructure’s ability to “absorb” large numbers of people should the order ever be issued.
Almost simultaneously, mobilization became a topic of discussion in Ukraine as well, though in a very different context. In the final days of the month, the idea that military service should apply to every citizen, regardless of sex, surfaced several times in high-level circles.
International audiences are already familiar with this framing. The prospect of Russian mobilization is presented as a sign of renewed social upheaval. Ukrainian mobilization, by contrast, is more often described as a difficult but necessary “effort by a democracy.” The Western media is therefore far more willing to speculate about a hypothetical new call-up on the other side of the front line, while treating events in Ukraine with noticeably greater caution – even as Kiev has lowered the draft age, rounded up men in the streets, and increasingly debated whether women might be next.
Who first cried ‘fire’?
By the end of the summer, the claim that “Russia is about to announce another mobilization” had already become commonplace abroad. Vladimir Zelensky linked a hypothetical Russian call-up to the September elections to the State Duma, as though Moscow’s electoral calendar could itself affect the course of the war. Finnish President Alexander Stubb said Russia was “approaching the point” at which it would have to declare a general mobilization. Western front pages picked up – not a decision, but merely the expectation of one. In this way, a rumor became a political fact before any decree had even been issued.
The Kremlin’s response was unequivocal. On July 28, Dmitry Medvedev called the rumors of an impending mobilization a “false enemy provocation.” Russia’s permanent representative to the UN, Vassily Nebenzia, offered a dry clarification: Mass mobilization “is not needed at the moment, is not being planned, and is not expected.” Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov dismissed reports of a new wave as “information hoaxes.” He said the rumors were being “planted by the Ukrainian authorities” because the Kiev regime was “trying to ideologically destabilize the situation” inside Russia. Peskov separately stressed that a new mobilization wave was “not on the agenda.”
For Kiev and parts of the Western media, however, the possibility of an event is enough to make it news. Memories of autumn 2022, when partial mobilization was publicly announced, make the latest rumor contagious: If it happened once, it can happen again. But over the past four years, Russia has built a different system for recruiting personnel – one based on contracts and volunteers. Its effectiveness is reflected in regular reports that tens of thousands of people are joining the front every month.
Ukraine’s remaining reserves
The situation on the other side of the front could hardly be more different. Within Ukraine, members of the political and military elite are speaking with increasing frequency about a shortage of manpower, only for official institutions to rush in and deny their claims. The West is therefore trying to define both the terms on which the war may end and the limits of the human resources available to keep it going.
Another layer of the crisis can be seen in Ukrainian statistics, some of which Kiev releases publicly. Former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mikhail Fyodorov said that around 200,000 (!) service members had gone AWOL and that more than 2 million people were wanted by the authorities. Western estimates put the average age of a Ukrainian soldier at close to 47. In 2024, the minimum mobilization age was lowered from 27 to 25, while a previously promised provision allowing demobilization after 36 months of service was removed from the law.
At the same time, reports of abuses during mobilization continued to mount. Ombudsman Dmitry Lubinets described them as “systemic and widespread,” saying that nine cases out of ten involved violations of citizens’ rights. Ukrainian reality even produced its own term – ‘busification’, referring to men being forced into vans. According to Ukrainian police data, there were 620 attacks on employees and facilities of Ukraine’s territorial recruitment centers (TCCs) from February 2022 to April 2026, including 118 in the first four months of 2026 alone. All of this can be read as a form of internal resistance to a system that must supply the army with new personnel faster than it can properly train them.
This resistance almost never takes the form of an organized political campaign with slogans and a set date. Instead, it erupts sporadically, at the very moment TCC officers try to seize someone off the street. On July 8, 2026, for example, around 200 people in Lviv surrounded a TCC vehicle, chanted “hanba” (shame), damaged the van, and eventually overturned it. Zelensky called the incident “a very bad story” and separately condemned violence against people in uniform. The location was revealing: Not frontline Kharkov or Odessa, but a city widely regarded as a bastion of Ukraine’s national identity.
The same scene played out in Ternopol on August 25. That evening, TCC officers tried to detain a man on Lesya Kurbasa Street. Passersby came to his defense, the official vehicle was smashed, and one service member was hospitalized. After the police left, a nighttime march moved through the streets, once again accompanied by chants of ‘hanba’. The BBC and Ukrainian media reported the incident that same day. Similar flare-ups had already occurred near a stadium in Vinnitsa, as well as in Lutsk, Odessa, and Kiev. This is not a “protest against the war” in the conventional sense. It is a crowd refusing, in that specific moment, to surrender a specific person.
Against this backdrop, a remark by Roman Kostenko, secretary of the Verkhovna Rada Committee on National Security, Defense, and Intelligence, is particularly significant. Discussing the principles behind army recruitment, he effectively explained why Ukraine cannot return to an entirely voluntary model: “Those who wanted to defend the country have already signed up.” The remark amounts to an admission that the initial mobilization impulse has been exhausted. With each passing month, the system relies more heavily on coercion.
The result is a striking contrast. The public bogeyman still points east, toward the prospect of another Russian mobilization. Yet signs of genuine strain on manpower are becoming increasingly visible west of the front line. In the information war, however, every effort is made to reverse these two narratives.
Mobilizing women in Ukraine?
On August 20, former Ukrainian Defense Minister Aleksey Reznikov outlined his vision of how Ukraine could achieve victory during an appearance on Radio Liberty.
If “we genuinely want to solve this problem,” he said, Ukraine must look to the experience of others. “The State of Israel is the country closest to us today in terms of the level of threat it faces.” There, women serve “on an equal footing with men.” Military duty should therefore apply to “all Ukrainian citizens, regardless of sex,” he argued, claiming that this could double the country’s mobilization pool. “There is no need for them to storm tree lines. Women can operate drones and sit safely in a bunker,” Reznikov reassured his audience.
To bolster his case, he recalled visiting the Desna training ground with Valery Zaluzhny in 2021, where they saw women operating robotic systems.
On August 24, former US special envoy for Ukraine Keith Kellogg endorsed the same idea from the American side in an interview with Naspravdi MAX. “My answer is yes, because they [women] fight every bit as well as men.” He shared a touching family story: His daughter graduated from the US Military Academy and fought in Afghanistan, while his wife served as a paratrooper in Grenada. “Both personally and professionally, I see absolutely no problem with it.”
By August 25, official Kiev was already trying to extinguish the information fire it had allowed to spread. The Rada’s National Security Committee stated that mobilizing women “is not taking place, is not being prepared, and is not under consideration.” There were no “legislative initiatives, bills, or even internal discussions.” Women joined the Defense Forces “exclusively on a voluntary basis,” while statements by “individual speakers” did “not reflect the Committee’s position.”
Andrey Kovalenko of the Center for Countering Disinformation said there was no forced mobilization of women “and there never will be,” dismissing the debate as Russian disinformation. Irina Vereshchuk responded to Kellogg by saying it is not for America to tell Ukraine who to draft.
Formally, there is indeed no legal basis for mobilizing women. Female doctors and pharmacists are required to register for military service, but registration alone does not mean deployment to the front. At the beginning of 2026, more than 75,000 women were serving in the Ukrainian Armed Forces, including over 55,000 volunteer service members. Kiev cites these figures as proof that women serve voluntarily. On August 23, Roman Kostenko had already insisted in advance that there would be “no changes whatsoever” to women’s military obligations. According to him, the authorities planned to change the age parameters and the mechanism for drafting men instead.
Yet the gap between the public statements is more revealing than any official press release. A former defense minister calls the recruitment of women a condition for the country’s survival. An American general hailed in Kiev as a “friend of Ukraine” effectively endorses the idea. Then, the very next day, the state apparatus repeatedly explains that nothing of the kind is even being discussed. If the issue did not exist at all, it would hardly have required three denials in a single day.
A familiar pattern emerges. A trial balloon is floated by people who will not have to pass the corresponding law themselves. It is then picked up by an outside voice that will not have to answer for the reaction of Ukrainian society. Meanwhile, the logic behind the argument betrays the arithmetic driving it. The volunteer pool is finite, the ranks of eligible men are increasingly being replenished through coercion, and mobilizing women enters the discussion as a potential answer to the manpower shortage.
Israel as a false analogy
In this rhetoric, Israel is less a real example than a convenient myth. Military expert Aleksandr Artamonov considers the analogy itself false: “Kellogg and Reznikov are relying on the same bogus premise.” He calls the American general’s remark “deceptive both in substance and in form” and directly links it to Reznikov’s call to “mobilize women following Israel’s example.”
According to Artamonov, the central sleight of hand is the conflation of two entirely different models: Routine military service and the emergency reinforcement of an army during wartime. “In Israel, women perform military service as part of the regular system. This has nothing to do with an emergency mobilization to the front.” In other words, it is a system built into the army’s normal training cycle during peacetime. In Ukraine, however, expanding the female draft is being discussed in 2026 at a time when the country is already running short of trained male personnel.
For an army at war, Artamonov stresses, additional manpower alone solves nothing.
“Even untrained men are of little interest. As for women with no military specialty – who are not medics, communications specialists, or programmers – they are essentially of no use at all.”
In his view, the claim that women “fight just as well” and the reality of service in the trenches apply to completely different conditions. Women “will cope much worse with the hardships of military service in the trenches,” they will require “a more complicated logistical cycle for everyday living,” and they will also be “more susceptible to illness, naturally – from something as basic as hypothermia to injuries.” To involve women fully “in combat operations,” the expert argues, requires specialized units and a long training cycle. “But neither Kellogg nor Reznikov cares about any of that.”
Artamonov also draws attention to the length of the training itself. “NATO uses two training programs for Ukrainians: One is called Coincidence, the other Unifier.” The first, he says, gives those “shanghaied by the TCC” just “two weeks, three at most.” The second lasts “around two months and is considered very good.” By comparison, he points to the Soviet system, in which basic training lasted “at least six months” – even “for men.”
By this logic, shortened training does not produce a fully capable soldier. It merely shortens the journey from the recruitment office to the grave. Hence the expert’s exceptionally harsh conclusion: “In Ukraine, the only thing NATO members are doing is training people to die.”
That is why Artamonov describes a possible shift toward the mass recruitment of women as “the complete genocide of the Ukrainian nation,” which he sees as “the ultimate objective of its NATO masters.”
Reznikov argued that women would not have to “storm tree lines”; they could operate drones or remain in bunkers. But an army facing a shortage of trained personnel cannot preserve such a neat division of labor for long. First comes the promise that women will “not be sent into assaults.” Then comes a shortage of crews and specialists. After that, two weeks of training remain – and the reference to Israel ceases to describe a real model and instead becomes an argument for expanding the mobilization base.
What comes next
The most likely next step is a gradual effort to fill the ranks of active Ukrainian units with more people, using different labels and existing mechanisms.
Kostenko warned that “radical measures” were being prepared, including steps related to the mobilization age.
For the time being, the issue of mobilizing women will most likely remain in its current cycle: A high-profile statement, a public reaction, and then an official denial. This does not mean the scenario has been excluded from consideration. It is simply not yet possible to acknowledge it openly as part of the government’s practical agenda.
This is where the crucial dividing line lies: No legislative amendment can create a combat-ready army on its own. That requires the complex organization of everyday service, specialized infrastructure, and lengthy training in separate units. Yet the realities of the front – winter, rotations, air-defense shortages, and the need to reinforce specific sectors – exist under conditions in which training time has been compressed to the absolute minimum. A few weeks on a NATO course do not become six months of military training simply because the political slogan has changed. At the front, a promise is always cheaper than a trained soldier.
As for rumors of an autumn mobilization in Russia, Moscow’s official position remains unchanged: No mass mobilization has been announced, and the military continues to replenish its ranks primarily through contract recruitment. Publicly cited figures have ranged from around 50,000 to 60,000 people a month and hundreds of thousands of new contracts a year. Meanwhile, painful strikes on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, logistics, and command-and-control system continue regardless of the forecasts appearing in the Western media.
For the Western information narrative, it is considerably easier to inflate the Russian threat than to explain in detail why Ukraine’s mobilization pool is shrinking and why the TCC system has become a domestic instrument of terror against Ukrainians.
Autumn, however, is almost here – and it will soon become clear whose forecast was the most accurate.

It was a spy satellite, now NASA's new telescope is set to head into space
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
19:00:00 UTC
04:00:00 KST

NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope set to explore the universe
This weekend, NASA plans to launch its next flagship mission into deep space.
The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, which started life as a spy satellite, will help find alien planets, map the universe, and possibly contribute to the collapse of a major theory in modern physics.
Ami Choi, a research astrophysicist at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, says the telescope will help make discoveries in dark energy and dark matter.
But, as previous space telescopes have done, it may find things that astronomers can't even imagine yet.
"The unknown unknowns that we'll probably discover — I think that's also very exciting," Dr Choi says.
If the launch goes to plan, the telescope will release its first images and data in about three months.
And Australia will play a role beaming back the discoveries the telescope makes.
New life for a spare spy satellite
The $US4.3 billion ($6 billion) telescope, called Roman for short, is named after astronomer Nancy Grace Roman.
Roman, dubbed the "Mother of Hubble", was the first chief of astronomy at NASA and a powerful advocate for space-based telescopes.
The telescope is a souped-up version of one of two spy satellites donated by the US National Reconnaissance Office (NRO) to NASA in 2012.
"It was a surprise to everyone when we heard that they just plonked on Goddard's doorstep," Brad Tucker, an astrophysicist at the Australian National University, says.
Both satellites had been developed for observing the Earth, before cost overruns caused the NRO's project to be cancelled.
To create Roman, NASA bolted some new instruments onto one of the satellites, including an infrared camera, and refitted it for flight into deep space.
Despite cutting costs by using a hand-me-down satellite, Roman's launch was not a certainty, with the first Trump administration proposing its cancellation in 2018 and 2019.
Benjamin Pope, an astrophysicist who was working at New York University at the time, was among hundreds of astronomers who travelled to the US capital to lobby against its cancellation.
"People came from all over the United States, just go to Congress and say: 'This matters to us, this matters to our universities, this matters to our research, this matters to the public,'" Dr Pope, now at Macquarie University, says.
The mission survived both proposed cancellations, and even another by the second Trump administration in 2025, and is now launching nine months ahead of schedule.
"We're super lucky that despite all of the drama about its funding history and development history … everyone's really excited for Roman," Dr Pope says.
What the Roman telescope is built to see
The telescope's 2.4-metre mirror is the same size as the Hubble telescope and smaller than the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), making it less powerful.
But the Roman telescope has a wider field of view than either of the other space telescopes, meaning it can capture a bigger section of the sky in each snapshot.
It's also designed to see in a different part of the light spectrum to the JWST, looking at visible and near-infrared light rather than further into the infrared.
"It looks at colours that JWST really isn't looking at," Dr Tucker says.
Once launched, the Roman telescope will head to the same part of space as JWST: Lagrange Point 2, or L2, some 1.5 million kilometres from Earth.
Galactic panoramas to find dark matter
The telescope is fitted with a 300-megapixel infrared camera which will capture large chunks of the sky in each exposure.
"We consider it to be very powerful for surveys of the sky, or mapping out very large regions of the sky in very clear detail," Dr Choi,who is working on Roman's camera, says.
These wide-angle shots are particularly useful for learning about two of the great mysteries in modern physics: dark matter and dark energy.
Dark matter makes up most of the universe's matter, while dark energy is thought to be behind the universe's accelerating expansion, but physicists don't know what either phenomenon really is.
Surveying large portions of the sky allows researchers to find things like supernovas, which can be used to measure the expansion of the universe.
Observations from different telescopes are also important, because they can cross-check each other's results.
Some other astronomical surveys are starting to suggest that current models of dark energy could be wrong.
"We're really starting to see hints that dark energy is even funnier than we previously thought," Dr Tucker says.
The Roman telescope is expected to help confirm, or refute, these findings, over its first five years of operation.
Looking for alien planets
Dr Pope, meanwhile, is excited by the telescope's other big objective: finding "exoplanets" orbiting other stars.
"Roman may discover, over the course of its lifetime, many more planets than are currently known by all other telescopes and methods," Dr Pope says.
Roman's second instrument, its coronagraph, is designed to block out light from stars, letting the telescope see fainter objects near those stars.
While it won't quite be powerful enough to see small exoplanets like the Earth, Dr Pope says it will deliver unprecedented information on larger exoplanets — more like Jupiter in our solar system — including enough data to study their atmospheres.
"Before the end of my career, I want us to be participating in discovering habitable worlds and understanding what they look like," Dr Pope says.
"Roman is the biggest stepping stone towards that."
West Australian antenna collecting the data
Once the telescope is in position, it will beam back some 1.4 terabytes of data to Earth each day.
One of the three places receiving this data is in Western Australia, at the newly-built European Space Agency antenna run by the CSIRO in New Norcia, 130km north-east of Perth.
CSIRO site manager Suzy Jackson says the Roman telescope will transmit multiple times more data than other deep space satellites the station communicates with.
"We've basically had to upgrade our comms links on the ground in order to support that, which is quite hilarious," she says.
The station has to be operated with extreme precision, with parts of the 35-metre antenna being positioned to an accuracy of 0.5 millimetres.
"We've got 700 tonnes of antenna and we've got to point that to an accuracy of hair-splitting in order just to hit the target at all," Ms Jackson says.
"Everything's got to be absolutely perfect."
When will the Roman telescope release its first pictures?
The telescope is scheduled to launch from NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida at 7:26am US Eastern time (9:26pm AEST) this Sunday, August 30.
Then, the telescope will take three months to travel to its deep space destination and go through commissioning tests and checks.
If the launch and tests go to plan, Roman's first images will be publicly released three months after launch, and the telescope will begin its scientific observations.
All of Roman's scientific data will be available for anyone to download, immediately after it's collected.
"It's when you enable tonnes of different minds to look through data and do analysis and brainstorm — that's when you get all this interesting new information," Dr Choi says.
Dr Pope says the telescope's "open skies" policy is exciting.
"We're all going to be trying to drink from this fire hose of data," he predicts.
"This is going to spur a lot of excitement, conflict, drama, technology — everything."

Careful with those Accusations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
18:59:04 UTC
03:59:04 KST

Careful with those Accusations
Academia is in turmoil regarding partially or wholly AI-written research. AI-written work is being submitted to journals, but it isn’t clear how much. Publisher, journal, university, and department policies are emerging and fluctuating. Technology develops, rendering recently enacted policies ambiguous, vague, or subject to unintended loopholes.
With everything in flux, it’s impossible for norms to develop.
There is no general sense of whether and what kind and what degree of AI use by authors is acceptable. Different policies across different institutions means that what may be problematic AI use in one place is acceptable AI use in another, and vice versa.
Into this chaos steps forward the vigilantes. The vigilantes have always been there, but now they are newly armed and emboldened. In the everchanging and never ending race between the technology of deployment and the technology of detection, the latter seems to have a temporary lead in the form of Pangram. You can feed a text into Pangram and it will tell you its analysis of whether it is AI generated, and if so, what percentage of it is AI generated.
Pangram claims to have a remarkably high detection and low false-positive rates, and cites studies by third parties to support these claims. Yet I have seen plenty of posts by friends and colleagues across social media showing false positives with some of their own work. So user beware.
That said, even if Pangram’s claims about its accuracy are correct, it won’t always be helpful to simply know that a text is “AI generated.” This because there are two further problems.
The first problem is ambiguity about what “N% AI generated” means. If someone asks Claude to write them a novel article about a philosophical problem, not even giving it a thesis to work with but asking it to come up with one itself, and that’s the extent of the human’s contribution, the resultant paper will get a “100% AI generated” evaluation. And if someone spends a year researching, writing, workshopping, and revising a paper, and then asks an AI to improve the writing style throughout the paper, the resultant paper will get a “100% AI generated” evaluation, too. Despite their same scores, though, these seem like cases that it might be plausible to treat quite differently. And of course, there are countless variations of AI-use between these extremes.
The issue remains even for “0% AI generated” findings, for such a score might be given to both an article that was written entirely by a human who never used any AI tools, and an article written entirely by an AI after minimal prompting by a human, but then rewritten by the human in their own words and style.
The second problem concerns the variation in policies across academic publishers and journals. Different kinds of AI use are allowed or prohibited in different venues. Learning that Pangram reports a published article as, say, “50% AI generated”, even if that figure is in some sense correct, cannot tell us whether the AI use it’s detecting was illicit, except if the article is published somewhere that prohibits any and all AI use. Not only does that percentage not tell us how the AI was used, but it doesn’t tell us whether the AI use violated any of the journal’s or publisher’s policies.
Now it is still the case, today, that most philosophers disapprove of other philosophers using AI to write their articles. Whether you agree or not, many philosophers view the use of AI to write for you as wrong—as a form of plagiarism or cheating, or a misunderstanding of what it is to do philosophy. In short, “AI generated” is, to most ears in our discipline, a kind of condemnation.
What this means is that when someone feeds an article into Pangram and publicly reports that it was “100% AI generated”, they are accusing the named author(s) of professional misconduct.
That is a serious accusation! It can be quite damaging. Given how human psychology works (and how internet searches work), even if the author is shown to not have acted wrongly, negative connotations may linger, damaging the author’s professional prospects for years to come.
Given the possible damage, and given the two problems described above, it seems we have strong reasons, at least for now, to refrain from publicly posting the “scores” of articles fed into AI detection services like Pangram.
What’s an alternative? Well, you could initially privately contact the author, the editor, or the publisher with your concerns.
* * *
As some readers will have figured out, the foregoing was motivated by a recent actual case in which one philosopher posted on social media that another philosopher’s recently published article was, according to Pangram, 100% AI generated, despite the article lacking an acknowledgment of AI use. This led to an investigation by the publisher (Open Library of Humanities), which ended up clearing the author of any wrongdoing. The publisher wrote:
The investigation found no issues with the content of the article that would suggest any academic malpractice was committed, nor does the OLH have any reason to believe that generative AI was used to the extent that the complainant suggested, or with the intent to commit academic malpractice… In line with the OLH’s ‘Artificial Intelligence (AI) Policy’ on providing an ‘AI Declaration Statement’, the author did not meet the criteria set out within the policy to provide a public declaration statement, namely: ‘the use of generative AI that forms the basis of a specific research purpose’, ‘the use of generative AI that forms the basis of a controlled simulation that produces outputs, such as synthetic data to supplement partial datasets, which informs the article’s argument(s)’, or ‘the use of generative AI for specific demonstrative purposes, with generated output(s) quoted and cited clearly with the prompts used, the model version and the URL of the service as part of its citation or caption’…
[W]e have concluded that there are no verifiable issues found that provide or support accusations of AI misuse or malpractice.
You can learn more about this case here. Note: I ask that readers not use or mention the name of the author or the title of the article in that case in the comments here. The article was published in Political Philosophy, so if need be you can call it the PP case.
By the way, the philosopher who had posted on social media about the article’s Pangram score has now kindly removed his original post about it.
>[Edited to add:] I thought this would be clear from the post but in light of some of the comments (not all of which have been approved) I guess it wasn’t, so I’ll make it explicit: vigilantism in the comments regarding the PP case is not welcome, and any further comments relitigating it or speculating about the nature and extent of the AI use in that case will not be approved.<
* * *
Relatedly, a friend recently wrote in with a tip for referees concerned about refereeing AI-written work: start with the references.
They write:
Usually, before reading a paper, I read the references to get a sense of the context of the paper. I immediately noticed a reference to me that was fabricated: I have no paper with that title and have never published on that topic in the journal it was supposedly in. When I put the fabricated reference into Google AI and then Chatgpt (free versions), both responded by saying it was a paper in [journal name redacted]… Only after I responded, “this paper does not exist!” did they both reply with their usual, “sorry, I made a mistake,” etc.
I then checked the rest of the references in the paper and found 3 other errors: 2 relatively minor and another fabrication.
Other suggestions welcome. Use them responsibly.

Measures under consideration reportedly include a ban on trade with Israeli settlements and sanctions against individuals involved in settlement activity.

====================================================================================================

Why Meta's 'big tobacco moment' in US might not flow to Australia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
18:52:21 UTC
03:52:21 KST

No guarantee Australian teens will benefit from Meta addiction settlement
Meta's landmark court settlement is being hailed by some as social media's "big tobacco moment", but there is no guarantee Australians will benefit from the safety measures the tech giant has agreed to.
The $2 trillion company, which owns Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, has just settled a suit with 29 US states.
It agreed to pay a record fine of $23.6 billion over 10 years — the largest payout of its kind for a social media company.
The settlement also marks the first time the company has been forced to change key features of its main apps, Facebook and Instagram, in the US.
Meta agreed to new default settings for under-18 users, including:
- Two-hour time limits across Facebook and Instagram combined.
- Night mode (12am-6am) and school mode (8am-3pm) settings to limit notifications and app use.
- Hidden likes.
- Blocking "extreme" beauty filters.
Teens in the US will also have the choice to switch to a chronological feed and ditch the algorithm designed to keep them scrolling longer.
The agreement came within the first week of a two-month trial alleging Meta's platforms were intentionally designed to addict young users.
"We've seen a number of different lawsuits that have gone against Meta in the last number of months," Lisa Given, professor of information sciences at RMIT, said.
"So I think they saw the writing on the wall."
The news has been welcomed by some Australian parents.
"The reckoning is happening before our eyes after 15 years of … I guess you would call it a free-for-all," Dany Elachi said.
Mr Elachi, from the Heads Up Alliance, a parent group focused on children's online safety, was sceptical Meta would follow through on everything it promised, but hopeful Australian kids would ultimately benefit.
"Meta has been forced into a position where they've had to make undertakings to make their platforms safer," he said.
"We just hope that at some point they will just have to throw their hands up."
Meta's move to settle 'quite smart'
Experts were less certain the effects would reach Australian shores.
"There's no requirement under this court case for things to change in Australia," Johanna Weaver, executive director of the Tech Policy Design Institute, said.
"Traditionally they roll out region by region and it doesn't mean that Australia will necessarily be top of the list."
While she agreed the settlement was groundbreaking, Professor Weaver said it was still a path Meta helped design for itself.
"There is no finding against Meta in this, there is no acceptance of liability," she said.
"And so it's actually quite a smart move [on] Meta's part to settle."
Professor Given said the changes Meta made to its platforms were likely changes the company was "comfortable" making.
But she was more optimistic the changes would ultimately be made global.
"Partly because they want to avoid court cases in future," she said.
"If they only apply this within the United States, then cases could crop up in Australia and other places."
Wherever Meta makes changes that apply only to teens, their efficacy will depend on whether the company can determine which of its users are under 18.
Professor Given said Australia's teen social media ban demonstrated it was still not able to do that in most cases.
"We've seen many kids that are still on the platforms — over 80 per cent of kids [are] still accessing social media content."
Meta is yet to face any fines for non-compliance with the policy, which has been touted by the Australian government for its role sparking similar change in 20 other jurisdictions.
Mr Elachi said the effect of combined international pressure should not be ignored.
"What we did in Australia a couple of years ago in passing legislation to create a minimum age has had reverberations around the world," he said.
"I believe all these things that are happening in tandem are all contributing to Meta and other social media companies having to listen to the demands of parents."

What do we know about China's new ambassador to Australia?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
18:50:33 UTC
03:50:33 KST

analysis
Wolf warrior, intellectual, sock puppet? What do we know about China's new ambassador to Australia?
China's new ambassador-designate to Australia has barely got his feet under the handsome desk in his embassy office, but he has already generated plenty of chatter.
As Beijing's power swells, its emissaries and envoys inevitably draw more scrutiny and curiosity.
And it's no different for career diplomat Liu Jinsong, who has already been labelled a hardliner and a "wolf warrior" by some China watchers in Australia.
That's largely because when you search for Liu on the internet, one of the first things that pops up is an image that seems to portray him as the embodiment of autocratic Chinese disdain: aloof, standing with his hands in his pockets, looking down at a senior Japanese official who almost seems to be bowing.
The picture has a complex backstory.
Last year, the China-Japan relationship was plunged into crisis when Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi told parliament that an attack on Taiwan by Beijing could constitute a "survival-threatening situation" for Japan.
When Tokyo sent senior foreign affairs official Masaaki Kanai to Beijing to try to defuse the situation, it was Liu — as Director-General for Asian Affairs at China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MFA) — who was tasked with conveying Beijing's fury.
It's not clear from the video that Kanai was actually bowing. When you watch it, it looks more like the Japanese official is leaning in closely to listen to a translator.
But the image of Liu, hands shoved nonchalantly in his pockets and looking rather superciliously at Kanai's bowed head, was splashed across Japanese media.
Tokyo complained that Beijing had blindsided them by allowing media in to film the talks' aftermath, while Chinese state media tried to use the video to crow that Japan had been humiliated.
But it's not certain what — if anything — this brief episode tells us about Liu and how he's likely to operate here in Australia.
Liu certainly read the riot act to his Japanese counterpart in the meeting and demanded (without success) that Takaichi withdraw her remark.
But analysts and officials who the ABC spoke to about Liu emphasised that any Chinese official in his position would have done exactly the same thing — because that was what he was instructed to do.
As one former senior official puts it: "This tells us plenty about the way China wanted to present the meeting, and the message it wanted to send to Japan, but it tells us very little about Liu himself."
"To some degree, every ambassador [in the world] is a sock puppet, but particularly in the Chinese system,"
Sam Chetwin George, Senior Fellow, Asia Society Center on US-China Relations, puts it more delicately, telling the ABC that China's Foreign Ministry "is not an apex policy-making part of the bureaucracy".
"It is largely a policy-taker, charged with implementing priorities set higher up in Beijing," he says.
"Diplomacy generally, and Chinese diplomacy in particular, is highly choreographed so Liu's principal role will be to steward the relationship in the direction set by Beijing, rather than leave his own personal imprint on it — though all diplomats of course have their own personal approach and style."
Still, Liu has also held several senior positions in the Foreign Ministry, and Mr George says it's worth scrutinising them closely for what they might reveal about how China wants to approach the relationship.
"In the last several years Liu has held two important posts during a period of shocks and profound transformations in geopolitics," he says.
"One was running MFA's internal long-range strategy department during the first US-China trade war, and the outbreak of COVID, and the other was running MFA's Asia Department as the Biden administration was strengthening America's 'Indo-Pacific' alliance system," he tells the ABC.
In this job, he says one of Liu's principal missions was to persuade Asian governments not to allow this architecture to harden into an "anti-China bloc".
"In other words, he is experienced in dissuading Asian nations from aligning more closely with America," he says.
Liu's record also shows that he is "not afraid of sharp language", he says — which might be a sign of what's to come when Australia and China next inevitably find themselves at loggerheads.
"In 2021, Liu referred to the Indo-Pacific Strategy, AUKUS, and the Quad as a "poison curtain" that would damage regional peace," Mr George said.
"The next year he borrowed a Bangladeshi proverb to describe America as a rooster strutting supreme on its own dung heap, but destined for humiliation.
"These remarks of course echoed Beijing's carefully considered rhetorical strategy, but illustrate that Liu will issue statements of this nature and communicate punishments insofar as Australia transgresses on China's defined interests."
For the moment, though, Liu seems keen to avoid that sort of language, with the ambassador-designate keen to project an energetic, confident and positive aura on arrival in Australia.
His opening statement contained the usual warnings about how both countries should "respect each other's core interests and major concerns".
But the ambassador-designate spent much more time dwelling on how he wanted to ensure everyday citizens felt the benefits of the relationship.
"Relations between countries ultimately rest on bonds between their peoples," he wrote.
Liu even mentioned he took the bus down to Canberra from Sydney after flying into Australia, saying he "enjoyed chatting with ordinary Australians along the way, which made the journey all the more enjoyable".
Stunt or not, that's not the sort of thing you could imagine some of his more stiff and dour predecessors doing.
There was also the distinct whiff of confidence in the statement, with Liu keen to suggest — as Chinese officials sometimes do — that China's rise is inevitable and unavoidable, and that Australia would be better served getting on board.
"Time awaits no one, and neither does history," he wrote.
"Once our course has been set, we must pull hard on the oars and press forward — without hesitation, without deviation, and without turning back."
As one diplomatic source observed, rather wryly: "He really rocketed out of the blocks, didn't he?"
In fact, so hasty was his entry that Liu and his embassy staffers ran roughshod over diplomatic protocol.
There was some hurrumphing in the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT) about the fact Liu was calling himself "ambassador" — and advertising his welcome meetings with community groups — well before he'd actually presented his credentials to the governor-general.
A not-so-subtle note was sent out to all diplomatic missions the next day reminding "ambassadors-designate" to "avoid media engagement (and) commentary" that "creates the impression" they'd already started in the role.
The official English-language version of his statement, sent out by the Chinese embassy a day later, dutifully corrected it to "ambassador-designate".
But others have been less fixated on the titles Liu adopted — or his mode of transport to Canberra — and more interested in what those first photos of his arrival might tell us.
Senior analyst Geoff Wade from the Australian Strategic Policy Institute (ASPI) pointed out that one of the photos posted by the Chinese embassy showed the incoming ambassador meeting with two prominent members of United Front groups in Australia tasked with championing Beijing's messages, and its push to take control of Taiwan.
This "immediate public display of affection with United Front members", he wrote, "was a clear signal as to the assertive stance Liu will take."
He argued that "a major element of Liu's tenure" would be mobilising diaspora groups to serve "the interests of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP)", including its efforts to "incorporate Taiwan".
"This is certainly not a new agenda, but the actions of the ambassador suggest that this program will be accelerated."
And Sam Chetwin George says Beijing's overarching objective — which Liu will no doubt pursue — will still be to weaken Australia's alignment with the US and ultimately to erode the strength of the US-Australia alliance.
"The second Trump administration has given him a lot of ammunition to make this argument more persuasively," he says.
"America is now in an open trade war with Canada — its treaty ally and Five Eyes partner — and in recent days also scaled back annual military exercises with another ally, South Korea, for fear of offending Kim Jong Un.
"Within Australia, the arguments of voices like Paul Keating and Hugh White — who argue that America is unreliable and that Taiwan is not core to Australia's national security — are gaining more traction than before.
"Liu and his colleagues will attempt to amplify such arguments.
"China will attempt to maintain that stability while sowing doubt about American reliability and dissuading Australia from full commitment to any US-led war in the region," he says.
Wolf warrior or not, that will be Liu's task — and he'll likely pursue it with plenty of energy.
