Albanese is seeking the icing on the international cake
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
18:48:55 UTC
03:48:55 KST

analysis
Albanese about to hit campaign trail for United Nations Security Council seat
Like many of his predecessors, Anthony Albanese has grown to enjoy the international diplomatic round that goes with the prime minister's job.
These days it's quite a thing, with an extensive "summit season" that dominates the latter months of the year.
Summit season includes the international climate conference (COP), ASEAN, APEC and the G20 — a string of meetings where Mr Albanese can rub shoulders with dozens of world leaders.
Ahead of the summits, he will be at the United Nations during leaders' week in September.
That is an excellent opportunity for a prime minister with lobbying on his mind.
Mr Albanese, who will address the General Assembly for the second year running, will launch Australia's bid for one of the non-permanent places on the UN Security Council in 2029–30.
If Australia can secure a seat, it would be icing on the international cake for the Albanese government.
The council period would fall in a Labor third term which, given its huge majority and the chaos on the conservative side, appears a fair bet as things stand.
Foreign Minister Penny Wong says:
"At a time when the world is more contested and more uncertain, a seat on the Security Council would give Australia a stronger voice in the decisions that affect us and our region.
"As an active middle power, we have a practical contribution to make to international peace and security, standing up for the rules and working with others to deliver outcomes."
Labor places much more faith in the UN than the conservatives do, so obtaining that seat would be a high priority for Senator Wong and Mr Albanese.
Australia has had five stints on the Security Council: 1946–47, 1956–57, 1973–74, 1985–86 and 2013–14. Norman Makin, Australia's ambassador to the United States and a former Labor minister, was president at the council's first session in 1946.
The last time Australia had a seat turned out to be particularly significant, after the downing of the Malaysia Airlines MH17 flight over Ukraine by pro-Russian forces killed 38 Australian citizens and residents. Then-foreign minister Julie Bishop carried Australia's reaction in the council.
Bids for the non-permanent seats can have long lead times, and it was actually Ms Bishop who, in September 2015 under the Turnbull government, announced the current one.
The Liberals had not always been so keen on pursuing a spot. In 2012, while in opposition, Tony Abbott lambasted the Labor government for the cost.
But Opposition Leader Angus Taylor is giving in-principle support to the current bid.
There is no doubt such campaigns can be expensive, especially if contested. They can also distort foreign aid, with some money spent effectively to buy votes.
So far, however, there is no contest.
Two spots are available for the Western European and Others group — of which Australia is part — and the only other nomination is Finland, which Australia and Luxembourg beat for the 2013–14 places. The government believes a late new runner is unlikely, but it is not complacent.
The UN election is in June 2028, just after the federal poll's due date. Even if the spot is uncontested, a country must be elected by a two-thirds majority of those voting at the General Assembly (about 129 votes if all 193 member states are present and voting).
Leaders' week should be an easy run for Mr Albanese. By contrast, the diplomacy around the UN climate summit is more complicated, requiring a good deal of dexterity.
The government wanted to host the COP, in partnership with Pacific countries, but found itself in an arm-wrestle with a very determined Türkiye. That led to a less-than-satisfactory co-hosting compromise. But Energy Minister Chris Bowen is the "president of the negotiations".
This year's COP has become more challenging for Australia than might have been expected when Labor proposed, ahead of the 2022 election, to bid for a COP.
Domestically, as the cost-of-living crisis has gripped the nation, climate change has slipped down the list of people's concerns.
Internationally, this will be one of the less notable COPs — more focused on nitty-gritty issues than on making major strides. Also, it comes when it is clear the world is not going to meet earlier ambitious goals.
Loading
Ritchie Merzian, chief executive of the industry body Clean Energy Investor Group, foresees the November COP as "workmanlike" but "symbolically" important.
It comes at a time when the multilateral system is being undermined. There is also pushback on environmental standards, with companies stepping back from earlier commitments. So it will be a "rallying cry of support around processes and the ultimate objective," Mr Merzian says.
Among the specific issues will be the perennial one of money — in this case, finance for small islands' battle with climate change.
Australia's progress in meeting its own targets is mixed. There are two main ones: a reduction of 43 per cent below 2005 emissions levels by 2030, and having 82 per cent of its electricity coming from renewables in 2030.
Grattan Institute senior fellow Tony Wood says Australia will come close to meeting the first. But "despite Chris Bowen's heavy lifting", it is unlikely to meet the second.
With the economics of large wind farms becoming difficult, and other investment problems, the government is stepping on the accelerator wherever possible to promote the renewable rollout.
Mr Albanese has sought to insist, in the government's specifications for data centres, that all proposals must bring an accompanying new renewable energy source to provide the power.
But pushback from Queensland and the Northern Territory at Wednesday's National Cabinet led Mr Albanese to provide some flexibility.
"In Queensland, you have public ownership of power generation, transmission, and distribution. So, if there is surplus, then that, of course, could be available," he told a news conference.
The COP is preceded by a "pre-COP" in Fiji in early October that includes a special leaders' event in Tuvalu, a tiny nation seriously threatened by rising sea levels that has been dubbed "a country without a future".
But hopes of attracting a good turnout of leaders were overoptimistic.
Even under this government, Australia remains on the defensive in the Pacific on climate issues — with countries always wanting their big neighbour to do more.
Mr Albanese flagged he will be at pre-COP when he told parliament recently the Thai prime minister would be there.
Given both Australia's hosting responsibilities and the government's concerted effort, for strategic reasons, to promote special relationships with Pacific countries, staying away would be a diplomatic misstep.
Michelle Grattan is a professorial fellow at the University of Canberra and chief political correspondent at The Conversation, where this article first appeared.

At least 37 Sudanese migrants died during a sea journey from Libya to Greece after fleeing the war in their country, a Sudanese relief committee said Thursday.
The El-Fasher Resistance Coordination, a grassroots committee, said in a statement that the victims included women, children and families who had left Sudan in search of safety.

It said the victims came from several areas across Sudan, including El Fasher, El Geneina, Nyala, Gedaref, East Nile, Babanusa and other towns and cities.

According to local and international institutions, the RSF seized control of El Fasher on Oct. 26, 2025, amid accusations of massacres against civilians and warnings that the development could deepen Sudan’s geographic fragmentation.
Sudan has been engulfed in conflict since April 2023, when fighting erupted between the military and the RSF over plans to integrate the paramilitary force into the armed forces. The war has triggered one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, killing tens of thousands and displacing nearly 13 million people.
Millions of Sudanese have been forced to flee their homes, with many seeking refuge in neighboring countries or attempting dangerous migration routes across the Mediterranean.

03:40:39 KST

Jackson Hole preview: US Fed’s Warsh to deliver keynote amid bond markets fears
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh is due to deliver the keynote address at this year’s Jackson Hole Economic Policy Symposium on Friday. It will give markets their first chance to hear from the new Fed chief at the central bank’s annual gathering in Wyoming.
It comes at a fraught time. A recent Treasury market intervention announced by Secretary Scott Bessent with the aim of pushing long-term Treasury yields lower raised eyebrows on Wall Street, to put it mildly. It was a move that seems to be at cross-purposes with the Fed’s messaging.
The Jackson Hole gathering is normally a chance for the Fed to lay out its views on the economy and its interest-rate strategy. How much Warsh will divulge is unclear. He has tended to play things close to the vest so far. One thing is clear, though: The market is hardly convinced by what it has seen coming out of Washington.
RT breaks down the latest developments in the world’s most important market and what the Fed chair might have to say on Friday.
Bessent’s ill-fated move to tame yields
A little over a week ago, Bessent announced that the Treasury would at least double its buyback operations of long-dated Treasuries. It was, as many such things are, framed as a mere liquidity operation. It was hard not to notice that the operation involves buying long-dated bonds at a moment when the Treasury very much wants long-dated yields to come down.
With the US operating with a $40 trillion debt anvil around its neck, any rise in yields entails a sharp increase in borrowing expenses. The US is already paying over $1 trillion a year in interest, more than it doles out on its military. However, the added expense of higher rates may not even be the main point of concern. The highly financialized US economy is extraordinarily sensitive to interest rates. On several occasions in recent years, rising rates have threatened to tip the financial system into turmoil.
Bessent’s move was widely seen to have failed, given that about a day later, long-dated yields had risen above their pre-intervention levels. With the Iran war dragging on, fears are mounting that another surge of inflation could be around the corner. Investors would therefore demand higher yields on bonds, making Treasury’s task considerably harder.
What the market is saying
Billionaire investor Stanley Druckenmiller recently penned an op-ed for the Wall Street Journal in which he wrote that “governments defending prices against fundamentals always lose. The only variable is how much they spend before conceding,” The fundamentals, in this case, are rising inflation expectations and runaway US debt that has many wondering if Treasuries are losing their hallowed safe-haven status.
Economist and strategist Philip Pilkington claimed that a “desperate” Bessent is “fighting against gravity” and that the intervention indicated that the Treasury chief fears that high yields could trigger a financial crisis, noting that last time yields were this high, the 2008 crisis was just around the corner.
Politico, meanwhile, wrote an article titled ‘Wall Street turns on Scott Bessent’ in which it surmised that the Treasury secretary’s credibility as a steward of US financial markets is “under threat.”
On the heels of another intervention
Earlier this month, the US and Japan carried out a coordinated foreign exchange intervention to prop up the ailing yen. Over the last 12 months, the Japanese currency has sunk to its weakest level against the dollar in around 40 years.
One may wonder what it is about the yen’s weakness that is keeping Bessent and his colleagues up at night. Officially, the intervention was taken to counter “excessive volatility and disorderly movements” in the yen. Lurking underneath is the fear that Japan could have to resort to unloading a portion of its massive US Treasury holdings in order to support its beleaguered currency. This move would, among other things, push US rates higher.
The intervention achieved little, however, with the yen edging higher before giving up around half of the gains within a week. It was a quixotic effort to begin with. The road is littered with the bones of interventions not supported by economic policy adjustments. When the monetary authorities intervene in markets, they have a tendency to get tested and end up having to defend the move over and over.
Two people trying to drive the same car in opposite directions
At the press conference following the previous Fed meeting in late July, Warsh said the increase in long-term bond yields “has provided us some comfort.” He meant that the uptick in yields was helping fight inflation, thus reducing the immediate pressure on the Fed to hike interest rates.
Evidently not feeling much comfort, however, was Bessent, who a few weeks later would go on to announce the intervention with the aim of pushing long-term yields lower.
Despite incessant calls for lower rates by President Donald Trump, Federal Reserve officials are debating possibly hiking rates at their next meeting in mid-September. Inflation remains above the Fed’s 2% target while the inflationary repercussions of the Iran war may yet be forthcoming.
Warsh has also discussed reducing the Fed’s $6.7 trillion portfolio of government bonds and mortgage-backed securities, a move that would represent a tightening of monetary policy – not least because reducing the Fed’s holdings would remove a source of demand for longer-dated securities.
This would put the Fed at cross-purposes with the Treasury, which is seeking to increase its own balance sheet of Treasuries in order to suppress yields at the long end.
The Fed and Treasury are under no obligation to coordinate their moves – indeed, they are not supposed to. They have different jobs. But visibly conflicting policy, particularly when the moves effectively cancel each other out, is not typical and tends not to go over well on Wall Street.
The $40 trillion elephant in the room
The US fiscal situation continues to deteriorate with no end in sight and little prospect for improvement. In fact, it is beginning to snowball under the weight of its own interest expense. The national debt crossed the $40 trillion threshold earlier this month. It has been climbing at a pace of roughly $1 trillion every five months, adding the equivalent of a whopping $7-8 billion a day.
What gives the US so little room for maneuver is the composition of its spending. A large and growing share of federal spending is effectively locked in by existing programs and political commitments. Entitlements, interest expense, and veterans’ benefits are already equivalent to 105% of federal receipts, according to calculations by analyst Luke Gromen. Those outlays are growing 7.5% year-to-date, he estimates, while receipts are growing by just 4%. The gap, in other words, is widening.
Entitlements – such as Medicaid and Social Security – are sacred cows in the US. No administration has succeeded in materially reforming these systemic pillars in generations, and few have seriously tried. The Trump administration has shown little appetite for the kind of spending restraint that would alter the country’s fiscal trajectory. That has left investors wondering whether the only source of restraint left is the bond market.
What to expect from Warsh
Investors are hoping that Warsh will weigh in substantially on the economy and the Fed’s inflation strategy at Jackson Hole. It may be too much to hope that he will address Bessent’s recent efforts. The Fed has often used the Wyoming gathering to shed light on its thinking about rate policy. So far since heading up the central bank, however, Warsh has given markets slim pickings, an approach that represents a break with his predecessors.
In fact, Warsh has floated the idea that the Fed should hold rate-policy meetings less frequently and is apparently considering scaling back the post-meeting press conferences. There is logic to this approach: When the market is kept guessing, it might indulge in less risk. Highly telegraphed interest rate policy can become a fat target for investors.
Trump picked Warsh to head the Fed in hopes that he would deliver the aggressive interest rate cuts that the president has been unabashedly advocating. Warsh, however, has demurred, but has also managed to avoid Trump’s wrath, which has more times than not been directed toward the remaining FOMC members, many of whom are holdovers.
That may make Friday’s speech all the more interesting. With the Treasury trying to push long-term yields down, the Fed arguing that higher yields can help restrain inflation, and the fiscal outlook putting pressure on both, Warsh will have plenty to talk about. Whether he chooses to do so is another matter.

Unknown

Adel Abdelrheem and Lina Altawell
27 August 2026•Update: 27 August 2026
Heavy rains and floods displaced 168 families and destroyed or damaged 271 homes in Abu Kershola locality in Sudan’s South Kordofan state, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said on Thursday.
In a statement, the IOM said the rains and floods forced families to flee around 10 villages in the locality.
Its field teams reported that 138 homes were completely destroyed, while 133 others were partially damaged.
The displaced families took shelter in temporary sites in open areas within the same locality, the UN migration agency said.
Sudan usually experiences heavy rains during the autumn season from June to October, causing floods in several parts of the country.
The impact of the rains and floods comes as Sudan continues to suffer from a war between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces since April 2023, limiting the country’s ability to respond to such disasters.
The war has killed tens of thousands of people, displaced around 13 million and triggered one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises.

David vs Bunnings: Mitre 10 franchisee wins crucial legal costs case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
18:37:25 UTC
03:37:25 KST

Mitre 10 franchisee wins crucial legal costs case against hardware giant Bunnings
A Mitre 10 franchisee has won a crucial legal costs fight against Bunnings, allowing him to take on a high-stakes case to try to stop the hardware giant from opening up next door to his Queensland store.
David Woodman's story was detailed by the ABC's Four Corners program last year, with the family-owned retailer airing concerns about competition in the hardware sector.
Mr Woodman is trying to use the Competition and Consumer Act to stop Bunnings from opening a site in the town of Jimboomba, which he argues would put him out of business.
He had applied to the Federal Court to be protected from paying Bunnings' legal costs if he lost, under laws designed to help smaller businesses take on corporate titans.
Justice Robert Bronwich has now ruled in Mr Woodman's favour.
"I am delighted for the client," his lawyer Michael Daniel told the ABC.
Mr Daniel estimates Bunnings could easily spend $6 million fighting the case, a sum Mr Woodman could not risk paying.
"If we didn't get this order, the chances are that David wouldn't be able to pursue the case," Mr Daniel said.
"This decision improves that risk and increases access to justice."
What is a no adverse costs order?
Typically, when a civil action is brought, the entity lodging the case faces the prospect of paying the legal fees of the party they lodged against, known as an adverse costs order, if they end up losing.
The laws Mr Woodman used — known as a no adverse costs order (NACO) — were introduced for business owners in 2019.
Mr Daniel thinks today's ruling is the first time NACO has been granted for an anti-competitive conduct case.
"I was hoping we'd get the result, but I was apprehensive we'd get it," he said.
"The client had spent a lot of money just getting to this stage."
Bunnings, which is owned by the giant retail, mining and industrial conglomerate Wesfarmers, had already brought in a high-profile barrister, Garry Rich SC, to argue against the NACO application.
The barrister recently won a bombshell case against another high-profile retailer, Coles, on behalf of the competition regulator, the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC).
Only today, Wesfarmers posted its annual results, showing a statutory net profit after tax of $2.87 billion, up 8.3 per cent from the previous year.
"Bunnings has the resources to fight at every point and do so with very expensive experts and lawyers," Mr Daniel argued.
"I expect them to keep going, quite frankly."
What does Bunnings say?
Mr Woodman's family has been in the hardware business for 90 years.
He bought the store in Jimboomba with his brother and father in 2018 under a franchise agreement with Metcash, the second-largest hardware retailer in Australia after Bunnings.
Bunnings purchased the vacant lot next door a year later, in 2019, and was later approved for a warehouse eight times larger than Mitre 10 Jimboomba.
Mr Woodman's case argues this will put him out of business, saying:
As a result of Bunnings's conduct, Woodman abandoned plans to expand the size and product range of Mitre 10 Jimboomba, because once Bunnings Warehouse opens at the Jimboomba site, it is commercially likely that Mitre 10 Jimboomba will become non-viable within the short to medium term and therefore would have to close.
Mr Woodman is seeking damages for losses and is ultimately seeking an injunction to stop Bunnings from opening its store.
There are already several Bunnings stores in the surrounding region. However, Bunnings argues the Jimboomba site is needed and will enhance choice and jobs for locals.
"We note the Court's decision on costs and will continue to respond to the proceedings through the appropriate legal process," the company said in a statement.
"We believe opening a Bunnings store in Jimboomba will bring more choice and competition to the local community, while providing local employment opportunities."
In an interview with ABC's The Business, Wesfarmers boss Rob Scott reiterated that "competition is great".
"It offers better choice and value for consumers," he said.
"So we will compete very competitively against all competitors, and ultimately customers are the ones that decide.
"Bunnings is still very interested in growing its network."
In his ruling, Justice Bronwich noted the still significant challenge ahead for Mr Woodman to win his case against Bunnings.
"The case brought by Woodman is novel, as it freely acknowledges," he noted.
"The discretion to make the NACO is appropriate in all the circumstances.
"That does not entail underestimating the challenges that Woodman faces in bringing this proceeding.
"But in my view, a case such as this is precisely what the NACO regime was intended to facilitate."
Mr Woodman's lawyer said he thinks the case could drag on for years.

Nationals' deputy Chester says Joyce departure 'sad for him, sad for party'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

Nationals' deputy Darren Chester on Barnaby Joyce and the rise of One Nation
Darren Chester has spent 18 years in parliament as the National Party's member for Gippsland in Victoria.
In that time, he has served as a minister under both the Turnbull and Morrison Coalition governments, twice watched bushfires sweep through his electorate, collapsed in parliament due to fatigue and at one point even took a break from his own party.
Today he's the National's deputy leader, facing a looming threat from Pauline Hanson's One Nation, although it doesn't appear to be something the MP is too concerned about.
"In terms of my own future and in terms of One Nation, I don't even worry about what they're doing in Gippsland," he told Annabel Crabb on ABC iview's Kitchen Cabinet.
'Sad for our party'
But it's difficult to avoid the elephant in the room. Barnaby Joyce, a former leader of the Nationals, has left the party to join One Nation.
Mr Chester doesn't believe the New England MP's actions have made it harder for voters to distinguish the Nationals from One Nation and said there's no suggestion other National Party members would follow Mr Joyce.
"That's a decision he made for reasons that he has never fully explained, really,"
Mr Chester called the move "self-indulgent" and said it was sad that Mr Joyce had undermined his own legacy.
"The idea that a leader — someone who had been the deputy prime minister — would leave the party and join another party just because they didn't get the job they wanted in opposition is quite extraordinary."
The job in question was a position in the shadow ministry, according to Mr Chester.
At the time of his decision to leave the Nationals, Mr Joyce said his relationship with the leadership of the party "had broken down" and he had been relegated to the "ejection" seat on the backbench.
In a recent episode of Australian Story, speaking on Mr Joyce's move from the Nationals, his wife Vikki Campion asked: "How long do you have to be loyal to a party that mistreats you?"
Mr Chester said Mr Joyce's defection is not only "sad for our party" but also "sad for him".
"Our party had made him the Member of Parliament that he was; given him those opportunities," he said.
'Loose coalition of independents'
According to Mr Chester, the National Party is like a "a loose coalition of independents" who are "very independently minded" and "hard to lead".
"People in the [party] room expect to be treated as equals and get to have their say on behalf of their community," he said.
"There are issues which reflect the differences in the people we represent, and we are specialists in rural and regional Australia.
"They're the only seats we contest so there will be issues that impact rural and regional Australia disproportionately, and quite rightly, the Nats will have a stronger view than any other party with [those] issues."
Mr Chester said communicating the concerns of regional Australia — particularly those in industry — was becoming increasingly difficult.
"A lot of people in metropolitan areas now don't have a point of reference to a regional community,"
"They don't have a cousin who lives on a farm, they don't visit a farm, so they don't understand how farms work.
"The lack of understanding is a real problem for us."
Getting climate policy wrong
There has been a shift in climate policy within the Coalition since the early days of Net Zero, when the Morrison Coalition government pledged net zero greenhouse emissions by 2050.
Mr Chester initially supported Net Zero but has since changed his position, aligning himself with National Party leader Matt Canavan, who has long been one of its loudest critics.
He said his initial support for Net Zero was due to his belief at the time that Australia's trading position would otherwise be jeopardised.
"A lot has changed since that time and I have no hesitation in saying that Matt was right and I got it wrong," he said.
Mr Chester says he and Senator Canavan are working "really well" together.
Mr Chester is now arguing for nuclear power in Australia, advocating for a power station to be located in the place of the coal-fired power stations currently in Gippsland's Latrobe Valley.
He said it would come with enormous benefits, including the ability to link into existing transmission corridors while avoiding farmland.
Latrobe Valley residents are divided at the prospect of a nuclear power station in the region. Some cite safety and waste disposal as an issue, but others argue it would provide a boost to the local economy.
Despite his backflip on Net Zero, Mr Chester said he is not anti-renewables and believes it's about finding the "right energy solution for our country".
"We're going to have nuclear-powered submarines. We've had a reactor at Lucas Heights for 60-odd years. And we've got a moratorium in place based on some … Simpsons' episode about three-eyed fish?
"If your point of reference is a Simpsons' episode, you've kind of lost your credibility in [the] broader energy debate," he said, referring to the time Labor MPs shared a meme mocking the Coalition's nuclear plan.
'Waking up in the middle of the night'
Mr Chester's electorate has seen challenging times over his term in parliament, perhaps one of the toughest being the bushfires of Black Summer.
By February 2020, the bushfires had been burning for several months, incinerating millions of hectares along the east coast, including in Gippsland.
Mr Chester said this was partly behind his widely reported collapse in parliament at the time.
"It was during the Black Summer bushfires. You had 30-odd days in a row doing the recovery work. I was fatigued — I know that now," he said.
At the same time, there were rumblings taking place in the party's backrooms.
"Barnaby [Joyce] was hunting [then National Party leader and deputy prime minister Michael] McCormack relentlessly. I was waking up in the middle of the night, your mind was just staying active."
Mr Chester said he was "frustrated" by Mr Joyce's actions.
"There was a natural disaster of quite epic proportions, [and] we were again being distracted by a leadership conversation, which we should not have been having."
"I wasn't aware I wasn't getting enough rest until my body just basically shut down for a few seconds and gave me a wake-up call."

Most movies take months to film. This Australian director did it in six days
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

One email to Sharknado royalty landed director his first feature film
A single email was all it took for Anthony Frith to secure his first feature film with The Asylum, the infamous B-movie studio responsible for unleashing Sharknado and hundreds of other 'mockbusters' upon the world.
The aspiring Melbourne filmmaker had just welcomed his first child, and his CV mostly consisted of comedic skits he posted to YouTube which went nowhere and cutting commercial videos for his parents' business.
So Frith reached out to the high-ups at The Asylum.
One email exchange and a Zoom call later and Frith found himself appointed director of the new Asylum movie and the first to be filmed in Australia: The Land That Time Forgot.
He was also bestowed with the fodder for his own film — Mockbuster — which documents the process.
It was a dream come true.
But after travelling to The Asylum's LA headquarters, the stars in Frith's eyes were quickly knocked out when he was informed that there was almost no budget, a mere outline of a story and that it would all have to be shot in Australia in six days.
Frith always had a soft spot for B-movies; not the kind you would rush to the cinema to catch but the ones on streaming services with bad acting, terrible stories and even worse effects.
"What I kind of like about bad movies is that sort of earnest naivety that goes into making them," Frith tells ABC News.
"I think people discredit bad movies and specifically Asylum films as shameless cash grabs, which to a point they are, but they are made by people who are passionate who put their time and effort into making them.
"There's something kind of special about that."
What is The Asylum?
The Asylum is far from the first studio to pump out mockbusters — low-budget, low-quality spins on already popular movies or stories in the public domain. The genre has roots in everything from 70s Blaxploitation classics to CGI animations that can almost pass for Pixar (if you really squint).
But The Asylum turned the subgenre into an art form of its own. Originally founded in the late 90s by David Michael Latt, David Rimawi and Sherri Strain as a basic distribution company, the trio quickly realised they couldn't compete with the big studios.
So they pivoted to a different business model: pump out as many movies as they could, for as little money as possible, in order to always make profit or at least break even.
But Frith wasn't prepared for just how committed they were to their short filming windows, which they lovingly dub 'the six-day special'.
"I thought it was 10 or 12 days because that's what I read on Wikipedia," Frith laughs.
"What actually happened was during COVID in LA, you had to test on the first day of shooting and the seventh day of shooting. So they thought if they shot in six days, they wouldn't have to pay for the second test. So they just ran with it, and never stopped."
Despite everyone at The Asylum having full faith in Frith, he landed in Melbourne with a massive task: find a local cast and crew who would work for less, scout dozens of locations and then hope a script comes together in time for a six-day shoot.
"It was a stressful, crazy time. There were moments where I was like, 'This is the stupidest thing I've ever done in my life. Why do I do this to myself?'" Frith says.
"But then I was also contractually obligated to deliver the movie AND the documentary. I'm glad I did it in retrospect, like, you know, hindsight's 20-20."
Dinos everywhere
It's nailbiting to watch Frith stumble through costuming mishaps, arguments between the cast and crew and a missing producer (The Asylum sends a can-do LA implant over at the last second), but it's just as exciting to see Frith move mountains to pull the whole thing off.
Frith is in awe of the work and dedication his cast and crew pulled out.
"We never had overtime. We had to move scenes to the following days and stuff but we never went over time, which was insane to me," he says.
"One of my favourite scenes in The Land That Time Forgot, one where we have someone tied up on the tree. It's got tension and it kind of works. We shot that in like 15 minutes because the light was fading," he says.
"It's like those moments where everything kind of coalesces in a nice way and just works. Everyone might think I'm an idiot once they see it but that's okay. I'm proud of it."
And while they might have been a few million dollars shy of a regular feature, there was still enough in the budget for a small wrap party.
"We had like a carton of beer in the Surf Lifesavers club after. I think one of the actors, Dave Margetts, bought some doughnuts to share with everyone. It was nice," Frith says.
Once the Australian crew had wrapped, all that was left to do was send the film back to The Asylum for their trademark special effects, in this case ravaging dinosaurs.
The Land That Time Forgot has the bittersweet honour of being one of the last films under supervision of legendary special effects artist Glenn Campbell, who died in late 2024.
"He worked on the original Tron, the original Star Trek motion picture, all these incredible films that he kind of pioneered a lot of those sort of things that they still use today," Frith says.
"There's still super talented people there, but he left a big hole to fill. So, then they started just using generative AI because it was like it could keep up with Glenn's speed and talents."
While Frith understands the rationale, especially after seeing how The Asylum business operates, he still feels something will be lost for future mockbuster lovers.
"I think what's fun about bad movies is the human touch. The imperfections come from a person and they're unique to that person and that film," he says.
"Whereas if you're using generative AI, it all inevitably feels the same or looks the same aesthetically."
Send the email
A year after The Land That Time Forgot's premiere and as Mockbuster hits Australian cinemas, Frith still can't believe what he experienced.
"I've got copies of my movie on DVD in my lounge room, which is crazy to me that I've made something that's being sold on DVD. It's such a dream. It's something you dream about when you're a teen, and you're wanting to be a filmmaker," Frith says.
And while The Asylum has been knocking on his door to direct another mockbuster, Frith has some other dreams that need tending to.
"I kind of fell into documentary a bit, and fell in love with it. You can just like meet real people who are funny, doing interesting things, I really love that," he says.
But the director would 100 per cent push any prospective filmmaker to send their own email to The Asylum.
"Say what you want about The Asylum, I think the fact that they give someone a shot to make a film is really important. It's something that's dying and inaccessible," he says.
"The fact that you even get to make a film is kind of important in itself, because you learn so much. Sure, not a lot of people might watch it, but you can say you've directed this feature film.
"That's all that matters."

North American aliyah hits record month as over 1,100 olim arrive, with 4,000 expected in 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
18:29:54 UTC
03:29:54 KST

More than 1,100 North Americans have immigrated to Israel this month through Nefesh B’Nefesh, marking a new monthly aliyah (immigration to Israel) record for the organization, Nefesh B’Nefesh said on Thursday.
“It’s record-breaking for us,” Nefesh B’Nefesh’s Vice President of Diaspora Partnerships Marc Rosenberg told The Jerusalem Post at Ben-Gurion Airport that day, as some 150 more North American olim (immigrants) arrived in the country.
“It’s quite a summer,” he said. “Over 2,300 people are arriving. It’s really been a very busy summer.”
Founded in 2002, Nefesh B’Nefesh facilitates aliyah from North America in partnership with Israel’s Aliyah and Integration Ministry, the Jewish Agency for Israel, Keren Kayemeth LeIsrael and Jewish National Fund-USA. The organization recently marked the arrival of its 100,000th oleh.
According to Nefesh B’Nefesh, more than 2,200 North Americans are expected to make aliyah over the summer, including olim arriving on nearly 100 group flights or completing the process from within Israel.
Approximately 2,700 North Americans have made aliyah since the beginning of 2026, and the organization estimates that more than 4,000 will do so by the end of the year, making 2026 one of its strongest years.
Among the new olim were seven families from the Persian Jewish community of Great Neck, New York, who arrived at Ben-Gurion Airport earlier this month.
Rosenberg said one factor driving the wave of aliyah was parents’ desire to raise their children in Israel.
“They want to be a part of the project that built Israel,” he said. “They see a big quality of life here, and they admire what young people in Israel are doing. And they’re saying they want to be a part of it.”
Aliyah on the rise
Nefesh B’Nefesh has seen “a significant increase in interest in aliyah,” Rosenberg said, with numbers rising between three and five percent annually in recent years.
Among them are a growing number of singles under 30, many of whom are required to serve in the military. Others are set to study at Israeli universities. Families making aliyah are also getting younger.
“The average age of families last year, two years ago, used to be around 32. It’s 29 this summer,” Rosenberg said. “So we see some younger families that are coming.”
Nefesh B’Nefesh said this summer’s olim include approximately 1,100 singles, 480 families and 250 retirees, ranging in age from five months to 98 years old.
Some 700 school-aged children also made aliyah this summer, including 80 who will begin first grade next month.
“As we recently celebrated our 100,000th Oleh, it is particularly inspiring to see so many young people choosing to make Israel their home, to build their careers and families here, put down roots and invest their futures in this country,” Nefesh B’Nefesh co-founder and executive director Rabbi Yehoshua Fass said.
One of those arriving Thursday was Marlene, who landed with her husband, Michael, and their baby.
Marlene told the Post that, for her, the timing was right.
“We got married last year, so it’s something that I’ve been trying to make happen,” she said, adding that Michael, who had made aliyah a few years earlier, “just made it easy for me.”
“This is always where I wanted to be, wanted to raise my children, have my future,” she said.
Marlene, from Brooklyn’s Syrian Jewish community, said she was the last of eight families from the community who had made aliyah over the past week, and that the trend appeared to be spreading.
“The trend started years and years ago. It was one family, then another family, and then over the years, more and more families were getting it into their heads,” she said. “This summer was a really big deal that eight of us made it happen at the same time. And I think there’s already a group in talks to do it next summer.”
Aliyah and Integration Minister Ofir Sofer: 'Inspiring' to see young people choose Israel
Aliyah and Integration Minister Ofir Sofer said it was “inspiring to see so many young people and families choosing to build their futures in Israel,” adding that government programs were intended to help new olim integrate into Israeli communities and the workforce.
Jewish Agency chairman Maj.-Gen. (res.) Doron Almog similarly described the month’s 1,100 olim as families and young people who had chosen “to build their lives here and be part of the future of the State of Israel.”
Chava, from Richmond, Virginia, also said it was “the time” to make aliyah and that the move was what was “best for our family.”
“Our kids are the right age, and also I’m approaching middle age, and it just seems like the right time,” she said. “Just everything lined up.”
“We were kind of done with the US and all of the craziness that’s happening there. But at the same time, we were just drawn to the Holy Land. We need to live as our authentic Jewish selves.”
Another new oleh, Gedalia, who has worked in the rabbinate in the US for several years, said he had wanted to move for a long time and was now joining several of his children who already live in Israel.
“Another rav came and listened to a shiur (lesson) of mine, and he told me it was the best shiur he had heard,” Gedalia, who was making aliyah from Silver Spring, Maryland, recalled.
“He was going all up and down the East Coast, and he said it was fantastic. And I said, ‘I need to go somewhere people will really appreciate this skill.’”
Rivka and Rella, a mother and daughter from New York whose family also made aliyah on Thursday, voiced their elation at becoming Israelis.
“We love it here, and this is where we feel like we’re home,” Rivka told the Post.
“Why wait?” Rella asked. “You know, we could have done it two years from now, but take the risk! Do it!”
Jerusalem, Tel Aviv-Yafo, Modi’in, Ra’anana and Beit Shemesh are among the most popular destinations for this summer’s North American olim, according to Nefesh B’Nefesh. Some 650, however, are moving to communities in Israel’s North and South, bolstering peripheral communities.

France relaxes strict cheese-making rules after prolonged drought
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
19:29:38 BST
03:29:38 KST

France relaxes strict cheese-making rules after prolonged drought
- Published
France has temporarily relaxed rules for making some of its best-known cheeses after the summer drought drastically reduced the amount of grass available to feed milk herds.
Government decrees to grant dispensations to manufacturers of Abondance, Beaufort and Comté cheeses - which come from mountains in eastern France - appeared on Wednesday.
Several other cheeses are expected to receive similar waivers, allowing farmers to feed livestock with grass and hay brought in from outside their strict geographical zone.
These include Cantal, Bleu d'Auvergne, Fourme d'Ambert, Bleu du Vercors-Sassenage, Reblochon and the goats cheese Rocamadour.
The National Institute for Origin and Quality (INAO), which regulates France's labels of origin, has also approved temporary changes to the rules for other protected produce because of the effects of the summer heat.
Products that will benefit include some types of Calvados and cider from Normandy, Crémant d'Alsace fizzy wine, lamb from Poitou-Charentes, and Reine-Claude plums.
Certificates of origin allow farmers to sell at a premium, but they come with strict regulations governing the location and method of production.
The aim is to preserve the unique identity of cheeses, wines and other foodstuffs, supposedly linked to their particular terroir - a French concept that links locality and tradition.
Because of a 2026 drought - which the INAO now describes as "historic" - farmers are being allowed to bend the rules for a short period.
Makers of Abondance cheese in the Alps, for example, will be authorised to reduce the amount of pastured grass in their animals' diet from 50% to 15%. They will be entitled to import forage from outside their zone, and use some supplements.
Makers of Comté cheese in the Jura mountains will be able to replace the local green maize they usually give to their cattle with maize from elsewhere.
The derogations are allowed in French and European law for periods of exceptional weather. Similar measures came in after the dry summer of 2022.
It will be interesting to see if the changes lead to any detectable change in the taste or quality of the cheeses - or to the quantity produced and how it is priced.
Longer term, the measures raise questions over the viability of the existing labels of origin in France and elsewhere.
If changing climate means that certain foodstuffs can no longer be produced in their traditional localities, then the idea of terroir will be stretched to its limits.

Will Eating a ‘Retinol Salad’ Really Improve Your Skin?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
18:29:03 UTC
03:29:03 KST

Applying serums or creams with retinol—a vitamin A-derivative known for its anti-aging and acne-fighting properties—may be a mainstay in your skin-care routine. Some social-media influencers claim you can benefit by “eating your retinol” in the form of carrot-dense salads. Is that true?
“The answer is yes and no,” says Dr. Lawrence Green, a clinical professor of dermatology at the George Washington University School of Medicine and Health Sciences and vice president of the American Academy of Dermatology.
The “eating your retinol” trend centers on the “retinol salad,” which typically includes ribboned carrots, garlic, vinegar, peppers, sesame oil, and lime juice, though recipes vary. The idea is that carrots are packed with beta-carotene (a precursor to vitamin A), which some influencers claim your body converts to retinol, similar to what’s found in skin-care products.
“This is a great skin-saving salad, but I think the name is misleading,” says Dr. Rajani Katta, a dermatologist and author of Glow: The Dermatologist’s Guide to a Whole Foods, Younger Skin Diet. The retinol salad provides vitamin A, which is good for the skin, but it’s not the same as applying an over-the-counter retinol or prescription retinoid topically, she explains.
Here’s what to know about the role of vitamin A and skin health, and whether the “retinol salad” offers any skin benefits.
What’s the difference between the vitamin A in carrots vs. retinol?
Vitamin A helps maintain the health of several vital organs, including the heart, reproductive system, eyes, and skin, says Amy Bragagnini, a spokesperson for the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics.
Beta-carotene, a natural pigment that gives red and orange fruits and vegetables their color, is a precursor to vitamin A, meaning your body needs to convert it to the vitamin, Bragagnini says.
It’s true that the body converts beta-carotene into retinol (which is preformed vitamin A, or its active form). But it’s “not an efficient conversion,” Green says. “It happens, but it takes a lot of beta-carotene to get a lesser amount of retinol.”
You can actually get retinol directly from foods, including eggs, milk, and beef liver, Katta adds.
Is eating vitamin A the same as applying retinoids or retinol?
A 2025 systematic review found that topical and dietary carotenoids (a group of plant compounds that include beta-carotene) offer anti-aging skin benefits, including lowered inflammation and improved hydration and elasticity.
However, eating a retinol salad or other forms of beta-carotene “nowhere compares to putting retinol directly on your skin as a cream,” Green says.
When applied topically, retinol penetrates your skin, where it can speed up cell turnover and boost collagen production, Katta says. Research shows that topical retinol can improve fine lines, hyperpigmentation, roughness, and signs of sun damage. Retinol can also exfoliate and plump the skin and help treat and manage acne.
Consuming carrots or other foods rich in beta-carotene is an inefficient way to get these benefits, since your body has to go through the process to convert it into vitamin A, Katta explains.
The retinol salad is still good for your skin. But its benefits mainly come from the antioxidants in the ingredients, rather than the potential to add retinol to your diet, Green says.
Antioxidants help maintain skin health by reducing the effects of oxidative stress from the environment, such as ultraviolet light radiation and pollution, research shows. Antioxidants also protect against free radicals, or unstable molecules that lead to premature aging and collagen breakdown, Katta says.
Are there any downsides to the ‘retinol salad’?
Beta-carotene from dietary sources is typically safe for most people, even in high levels, according to the Harvard School of Public Health. However, too much preformed vitamin A, which you could get from overusing vitamin A supplements—or, less commonly, by eating too many vitamin A-rich foods—could be toxic, potentially causing blurry vision, dry skin, nausea, or vomiting.
One potential downside to the salad, Bragagnini says, is that eating too many carrots could cause beta-carotene to build up in your blood and possibly turn your skin a “yellow-orange color.”
If you don’t normally consume vegetables, which are fiber-rich, eating too many at once could upset your digestive system, she says.
What’s the best diet for healthy skin?
“I encourage my patients to make sure they are eating a variety of colorful fruits and vegetables,” at least five servings a day, Bragagnini says.
Fruits and vegetables contain different antioxidants that protect your skin from damage from UV rays and pollution, she says. Omega-3 fatty acids, found in oily fish, walnuts, and flaxseeds, reduce inflammation in the body, which may guard against skin conditions.
Also, limit sugar, alcohol, and ultra-processed foods, like cookies, bacon, and sugar-sweetened beverages, Bragagnini adds. These foods may increase oil production in the skin and affect collagen production.
Overall, Green recommends the Mediterranean diet, which incorporates many of these principles and has been shown to benefit overall health. Research shows that the diet can also help manage inflammatory skin conditions, like acne or psoriasis.
Yet diet alone is “not going to necessarily change your skin in a month,” Katta says. It’s a long-term approach.
When to see a dermatologist about your skin
If you’re struggling with acne or are bothered by age-related changes like wrinkles, sagginess, or sun spots, see a dermatologist.
For acne, doctors can prescribe topical retinoids like tazarotene or tretinoin, oral retinoids such as isotretinoin, or other types of medications, Green says. The goal is to clear breakouts, prevent new ones, and minimize scarring, Katta adds. Dermatologists may also recommend dietary or other lifestyle changes.
Addressing wrinkles, pigmentation changes, and other age-related changes depends on the individual person and their skin issue, Green says. For example, dermatologists may prescribe retinoids or recommend Botox, fillers, laser treatments, or microneedling.
“We can look at your skin and help direct you,” Green says, and that includes helping you develop a tailored skin-care routine.
Over-the-counter retinol serums, creams, and other products are available, too. Katta says they’re beneficial but not as potent as prescription retinoids. Retinol also hasn't been studied as extensively as retinoids, so there’s not as much evidence on its effectiveness, Green says.
Taking care of your skin should be a holistic approach that includes diet, and the retinol salad can be a part of that. Green says the dish is a “nice idea for the antioxidant benefits,” but won’t treat acne or address any unwanted signs of aging.

Most people know that Labor Day is one of the best times of the year to buy tools (get it? Labor?), but if you’re a newly minted homeowner or DIY-er, the landscape can be intimidating. Just the basics will do: a drill, a saw, a set of manual screwdrivers, and a stud finder, for example.

In fact, after examining all the major sales, I was able to find a rather encyclopedic house-repair kit for any new homeowner or DIY-er for under $375 (minus tax and shipping) with deals from Home Depot, Lowe’s, and Walmart. Any of these would also be great to stash away for a holiday gift.
Here’s what I chose:
Power-Tool Workhorses: Ryobi 4-Tool Kit for $199
Look, you’re not going to take Ryobi tools to a jobsite or use them to build a house from scratch (a former WIRED editor once deemed them “the Kia of tools”), but if you’re just using them for basic, casual home use, they’ll do the job. Ryobi’s 18V ONE+ batteries (this set comes with one) are fully backward compatible with all Ryobi tools ever made, and this set has a three-year warranty. I live in a DeWalt household, so I don’t have a lot of firsthand experience with Ryobi, but my brother, a contractor, says the brand is great for the average DIY homeowner and offers a much broader range of tools than competitor Bauer from Harbor Freight.
This set packs a ½-inch drill/driver, an impact driver (which WIRED reviewer Scott Gilbertson said had a profound 'I can't believe I didn't own one sooner' impact on him, though his is Milwaukee), a circular saw, and an LED light. The impact driver packs 1,800 pounds of torque, which is pretty decent for a consumer-level tool. If you need a sander, there's also another kit with a sander plus drill/driver and circular saw, which may be worth a look if this set sells out.
The Hand-Tool Essentials: Workpro 408-Piece Set for $144
I don't have this exact set, but I do have remnants of a similar one. Again, you're not going to bring these to a construction site, but this kit is a knockout deal for everything you get—pliers, screwdrivers, Allen keys, wrenches, sockets, bits, tape measure, knife, hammer, wire stripper … there's even a metal box in which to store everything. A lot of the “pieces” are doodads like screwdriver heads and drywall anchors, but it still contains pretty much any non-power tool you might need for light home repairs and even basic car maintenance. (There's no level, but you can always use an app on your phone for that.) However, note that this is a flash deal, so it's likely only live for a limited time.
Wall-Hanging Must-Have: Franklin Sensors Stud Finder for $22
No household repair kit is complete without a stud finder. (And if you're a dad, it will give you years of built-in dad jokes.) In fact, you can't—or, at least, shouldn't—hang anything even slightly heavy on your wall without one. I have a Franklin Sensors stud finder, though not this exact model, and it's done well to help my family hang pictures, shelves, mirrors, and pretty much everything else for the past decade or so. This is the best deal I could find, though it's not technically on sale. However, Lowe’s is having a sale on plenty of other tools, including outdoor furniture, appliances, and grills.

Burnham recently suggested £500k political donation cap that would be ‘reduced over time’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
18:24:06 UTC
03:24:06 KST

Andy Burnham recently supported an even lower donations cap than previously reported, according to correspondence seen by the Guardian, as the row over next week’s elections bill escalates.
The prime minister wrote to a campaigner in May outlining his support for a £500,000 individual donations cap, which he said would “guard against the perception of any one party being unduly influenced or swayed by one person or organisation”.
In a follow-up email seen by the Guardian, Burnham went on to say he believed the cap should gradually be reduced – a proposal now being put forward by the Labour MP Stella Creasy.
Campaigners are accusing Burnham of a U-turn after the Guardian reported the prime minister had decided not to back the attempts by Creasy and others to introduce a donations cap in next week’s elections bill.
In his first message to Shaun Bowler, who runs the website wakeupgb.co.uk, Burnham wrote: “I do think there should be a cap on political donations. This would guard against the perception of any one party being unduly influenced or swayed by one person or organisation.
“As to the level, I think that would have to be subject to wider review of political funding but my gut feeling would suggest somewhere in the region of £500k.”
In a second message, the then would-be MP for Makerfield said: “[I] would definitely want to see that reduced over time. I am in complete agreement that there needs to be wholesale culture change in Westminster.”
Bowler has now written to the prime minister accusing him of abandoning his previous commitments. He wrote: “It appears you are going to break your promise to me – and the nation …. Weeks after being elected, you have made your first major U-turn.”
He added: “This is your chance to actually deliver the start of that cleanup. Show us that politics can be clean and trustworthy. Don’t surrender to the mess.”
Other campaigners, including the broadcaster Carol Vorderman, are also urging the prime minister not to back down in the face of opposition from trade unions, who have warned that a donations cap could undermine their ability to contribute to the Labour party.
Senior figures at groups including Transparency International, Spotlight on Corruption and Greenpeace have also written to Burnham. In an open letter, they call for a “low and hard cap on all political donations”, adding: “We know you agree that politics should not be for sale. Please take action now to ensure it will not be under your leadership.”
The issue will come to a head next week when MPs debate the next stage of the elections bill. The bill will lower the voting age to 16 and cap donations by Britons based abroad, but not on domestic donations.
Creasy had put forward an amendment to cap domestic donations at £100,000, while her colleague put forward an amendment to cap them at £1m.
Creasy has now changed her amendment to set the cap at £500,000, reducing in the second year to £100,000 unless ministers intervene to set it at a different level. The proposal, which has cross-party backing, mirrors what Burnham told Bowler he would support in May.
The prime minister’s aides say that while he is not backing a donations cap next week, he is not ruling one out in the future. A Labour source said: “This bill was designed to deliver our manifesto commitments on votes at 16 and to strengthen political donation rules to guard against foreign interference and that’s what the government is prioritising. But we’re not ruling out taking further steps to protect our democracy in the future.”
Officials also said the government would not support an attempt by the Labour MP Anneliese Dodds to reduce the amount political parties can spend during an election campaign after the limit was raised by the previous Conservative government.

The NBU disclosed details of its supervision of Sense Bank: more than 100 decisions and 21 notifications to law enforcement agencies
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
21:22:22 EEST
03:22:22 KST

The NBU disclosed details of its supervision of Sense Bank: more than 100 decisions and 21 notifications to law enforcement agencies
Kyiv • UNN
The NBU reported more than 100 decisions and 12 inspections concerning Sense Bank since the end of 2022. The regulator expects personnel decisions from the government.
The National Bank of Ukraine (NBU) stated that from the end of 2022 through 2026, the regulator’s relevant committee adopted more than 100 decisions concerning Sense Bank, while, based on the results of supervisory measures, 21 notifications were sent to law enforcement and other government authorities. UNN reports this, citing an official statement by the Board of the national financial regulator.
The NBU also expects the government, as the bank’s shareholder, to promptly complete the formation of the supervisory board and remove from their duties the employees mentioned in the information released by NABU.
Details
The Board of the National Bank reviewed a report by the Committee on Banking Supervision and Regulation and Oversight of Payment Infrastructure concerning supervisory actions regarding the state-owned Sense Bank during the period from 2022 to 2026. It emphasized that it supports the work of independent anti-corruption bodies and is interested in establishing all the circumstances of the case fully and impartially.
"The NBU Board supports the actions of independent anti-corruption bodies and is interested in establishing all the circumstances of the case fully and impartially. A necessary condition is the maximum openness of the parties within the law and without harm to the pretrial investigation," the NBU said in its published statement.
The National Bank separately explained the decision-making mechanism in the area of banking supervision. The powers related to licensing, supervision, and financial monitoring are exercised not by the regulator’s head alone, but by the relevant collegial body—the Committee on Banking Supervision and Regulation and Oversight of Payment Infrastructure. These powers were delegated to it by the NBU Board in accordance with the law.
After hearing the Committee’s detailed report, the NBU Board stated that the available materials, in its view, confirm the consistency of supervisory and regulatory actions concerning Sense Bank. The National Bank also noted that the regulator responded to new circumstances, including those subsequently made public by law enforcement authorities.
More than 100 decisions and 12 inspections
According to the NBU, from the end of 2022 through 2026, the relevant Committee adopted more than 100 decisions concerning Sense Bank. In addition, based on the results of supervisory measures, the regulator sent 21 notifications to law enforcement authorities, the State Tax Service, and the State Financial Monitoring Service.
During this period, the National Bank conducted three inspections concerning compliance with banking legislation, six inspections in the area of financial monitoring, as well as three inspections concerning compliance with sanctions and currency legislation. In total, this amounted to at least 12 inspections of various types.
The NBU announced previously unknown confidential minutes
The regulator’s statement devoted particular attention to an inspection that concluded in April 2025.
According to the National Bank, during the inspection, a substantial body of previously unknown confidential minutes of Sense Bank’s collegial bodies was discovered. The NBU informed law enforcement authorities about the documents. The regulator said that analysis of the materials is ongoing. In addition, the Ministry of Justice of Ukraine is using these documents while formulating the state’s position in international arbitration in a case initiated by the bank’s former sanctioned owners.
The situation will be brought before the Financial Stability Council
Against the backdrop of recent events, the National Bank plans to initiate a separate review of the situation surrounding Sense Bank at the next meeting of the Financial Stability Council. The regulator also publicly addressed the government, which represents the state as the bank’s owner.
The NBU expects the Cabinet of Ministers to promptly complete the formation of Sense Bank’s supervisory board, as well as to suspend or otherwise remove from the performance of their duties the bank employees mentioned in the information published by the National Anti-Corruption Bureau.
For its part, the government announced on August 19 that it had decided to suspend the chair of the supervisory board of the state-owned Sense Bank from performing his duties and initiate the suspension of the bank's chair of the management board. The Cabinet of Ministers then stated that similar decisions should also be made regarding other bank officials mentioned in the pretrial investigation materials.
In addition, the NBU previously found Sense Bank Supervisory Board Chair Mykola Hladyshenko not to meet the independence requirements established by law and demanded that the state, as the shareholder, terminate his powers.
What is known about the NABU case
The National Bank's latest statement came amid an investigation by NABU and SAPO as part of the "Forrest Gump" special operation.
On August 19, anti-corruption agencies announced that they had exposed a group of individuals who, according to the investigation, organized the legalization of UAH 150 million in cash. According to detectives, the funds were put into legal circulation through the accounts of a number of companies so that bail could subsequently be posted for one of the defendants in the "Midas" case. In the media and case materials, these operations were linked to bail for former Energy Minister Herman Halushchenko.
According to NABU, among those appearing in the investigation are representatives of the Office of the President, former and incumbent members of parliament, as well as executives of a state-owned bank. The investigation alleges that accounts at Sense Bank and accounts of controlled companies were used to conduct the operations. These circumstances reflect the investigation's version of events, and the guilt of specific individuals must be established by a court.
According to the published data, UAH 50 million was transferred directly from accounts at Sense Bank to the account of the High Anti-Corruption Court: UAH 46 million from Hiran Construct LLC and UAH 4 million from Pellet Service LLC.
After this information emerged, the NBU stated that, as part of unscheduled inspections, it intended, in particular, to clarify the circumstances of possible interference with Sense Bank's automated system during the relevant operations, verify possible instructions from the bank's management to employees, and examine compliance with legislation in the area of financial monitoring.
What is known about the chair of Sense Bank's management board
On August 25, the High Anti-Corruption Court began considering the issue of a preventive measure for Sense Bank Management Board Chair Oleksii Stupak, who appears in the NABU and SAPO case.
The SAPO prosecutor asked the court to remand him in custody with an alternative bail amount of UAH 150 million. According to the prosecution, Stupak may have facilitated the use of part of the funds and actions aimed at concealing their origin. These are allegations made by the investigation, not guilt established by a court.
The bank had previously conducted its own audit
The situation surrounding Sense Bank had been developing even before the August events.
In May 2026, the bank's supervisory board initiated an internal audit after information emerged during a meeting of a parliamentary temporary investigative commission, in NABU investigation materials, and in journalistic publications related to the so-called "Mindich tapes."
On June 4, Sense Bank announced the completion of this review. According to the supervisory board, the audit had not established any instances of preferential treatment, the application of nonstandard service conditions, or violations of the bank's internal procedures concerning the individuals and companies mentioned in the relevant materials.
At the same time, the subsequent NABU and SAPO investigation in August led to the emergence of new circumstances and additional allegations against certain representatives of the bank's management.
Sense Bank is being prepared for sale
The events are taking place against the backdrop of preparations for the privatization of the state-owned Sense Bank.
At the beginning of August, the bank announced the creation of a separate working group tasked with preparing the financial institution for sale. Its responsibilities include analyzing the corporate governance system, financial statements, liabilities, capital structure, loan portfolio quality, and potential risks.
After the anti-corruption investigation materials were made public, the government instructed the Ministry of Finance to accelerate the process of selling Sense Bank. The Cabinet of Ministers stated that the procedure should be as transparent and competitive as possible, and that the proceeds from the sale were planned to be directed toward the needs of Ukraine's Defense Forces.
Sense Bank itself reported on August 21 that it continues to operate as usual, fulfill its obligations to customers, and prepare for an open competitive sale.
The NBU rejected accusations of unilateral influence
In its statement, the Board of the National Bank also separately responded to public criticism of the regulator's actions.
The NBU emphasized that it is ready for parliamentary oversight, substantive criticism, and scrutiny of its actions. The regulator has already sent a detailed report on its supervision of Sense Bank to the government and members of the Verkhovna Rada's Temporary Investigative Commission.
At the same time, the National Bank stated that regulatory decisions cannot be made under the influence of political pressure or based on unsubstantiated personal accusations.
"Regulatory decisions cannot be a response to political pressure or unsubstantiated personal accusations; they must be based exclusively on verified facts and the logic established by law," representatives of the national financial regulator insist.

A Georgia Cop Used Flock to Track 2 Other Cops: His Ex and Her Friend
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
18:12:17 UTC
03:12:17 KST

In recent months, there has been a surge in reports of police officers misusing automatic license plate readers (ALPRs) sold by Flock Safety to stalk former romantic partners—but details about these incidents are often scarce.
Now, with documents obtained via a public records request, WIRED can reveal specific details about one extensive Flock-fueled surveillance campaign and the subsequent investigation and fallout.
Dustin Bozzo, who until this month worked as a patrolman in the Atlanta-area suburb of Alpharetta, Georgia, allegedly used Flock 56 times between March and May to search for the license plate of a former romantic partner—a fellow member of the Alpharetta Police Department. (Their relationship itself violated the city’s ban on workplace dating, documents show.) When Bozzo noticed that his ex’s car was often near that of another police officer, he began searching for that officer’s vehicle as well. He did so 29 times between March and May.
Lieutenant Jason Hiott of the Alpharetta Police Department tells WIRED that Bozzo was placed on paid leave on July 20 and resigned on August 5 following an internal investigation. He adds that an “ongoing criminal investigation” is underway in the department's Criminal Investigations Division.
Alpharetta police chief Trent Lindgren tells WIRED that the investigation will likely be finished soon, adding that the department holds itself to a “high standard,” and took “immediate action” when misuse was identified. Flock did not respond to a request for comment.
Bozzo did not respond to multiple requests for comment. He changed his Facebook profile picture and name after WIRED messaged him on the platform.
In the civilian world, a breakup may tempt people to check up on their former lovers by pulling up their social media profiles. But in the police world, many officers have instant access to Flock—a powerful, informative, and invasive tool for tracking people’s locations. Across the country, there have been at least 45 documented incidents of police officers misusing Flock in order to look up or track current or former romantic partners.
According to the documents—which include the full internal report written by Alpharetta police Sergeant Jabbar Braithwaite—Bozzo says that he didn’t use Flock with the intent to intimidate or cause harm. The sequence of events they describe nonetheless show that even in such a case, the misuse of this technology can quickly and easily escalate into a serious offense.
Per the internal report, Bozzo admitted to Braithwaite that he had a fling with a then-fellow officer that started in late 2025. (That officer is now a civilian employee of the department.) The other officer, for her part, claimed that most, if not all of their romantic communications happened on Snapchat.
It’s unclear how much of the relationship may have played out during work hours. Bozzo, upon first being asked if he “had ever been romantically involved” with the former officer, responded by asking, "At work?" according to the documents.
“To clarify the question, I asked whether, at any time, either while employed together or otherwise, he and [redacted] had engaged in a sexual relationship,” Braithwaite wrote. “Patrolman Bozzo responded that they had.”
The former officer also admitted that they had been sexually intimate, but both maintained that it never occurred while they were on duty. Nevertheless, their behavior had caught the attention of multiple people within the department.
According to the documents, multiple people reported that Bozzo and the other officer “frequently spent personal time together while on duty” and were “not engaged in their assigned responsibilities” while doing so. The reports prompted the police department to separate the officers, who had been assigned to the same squad and patrol beat, and issue them a “written directive” about “acceptable workplace interactions.”
However, the officers seemingly continued the affair. One sergeant reported that he saw the pair meeting in a “dark, secluded park,” per Braithwaite’s summary, at about 2:30 am while Officer Bozzo was on duty but the other officer was not.
Bozzo claimed that the fling lasted approximately one month, and that their eventual breakup was mutual—though the other officer claimed that the relationship lasted several months, and that she initiated the breakup. Both said that it had ended on good terms.
It’s unclear exactly when the relationship ended, but Bozzo’s Flock searches for her vehicle began in early March. Citing Flock audit logs, Braithwaite claims that when Flock’s system would prompt Bozzo to specify the reason for each query, he almost always selected either “Wanted Person” or “Traffic Infraction."
“When asked why he routinely selected those categories, Patrolman Bozzo explained that doing so was ‘just a quick keystroke,’” Braithwaite wrote.
Bozzo claimed that he was trying to make sure that the officer had arrived home safely, claiming she often drove around late at night. He began searching her uncle’s license plate after learning that she got into a car accident and was borrowing his car, the documents show. Between April 5 and April 14, he searched for the uncle’s vehicle 18 times.
At some point, while reviewing the search results, Bozzo claimed that he began noticing a particular vehicle that was often in close proximity to her. The car belonged to an Alpharetta Police Department officer who recently transferred from a nearby police department.
Bozzo claims he found the search results “weird,” prompting him to start searching the officer’s vehicle. Though Bozzo denied being motivated by jealousy, he knew the officer personally: They had both helped the Alpharetta officer when she was moving. (Both men corroborated this claim.)
Bozzo’s former romantic partner, upon being interviewed by Braithwaite, claimed that she didn’t know what motivated Bozzo to search for the vehicles she and the other officer were driving. Both she and the other officer insisted that they had always been platonic friends. The other officer, for his part, told investigators that his interactions with Bozzo had been friendly and respectful.
Bozzo told Alpharetta investigators that he understood that his actions were wrong, and Braithwaite did not find any evidence to undermine his claim that he hadn’t acted with “malice or an intent to harm.” However, Braithwaite ultimately told Bozzo that “regardless of his stated motivation,” his use of Flock was “inconsistent with Department policy and the authorized use of the system.”

Has Canadian travel to the U.S. declined since Trump returned to office?
Prior to Eby’s tourism plea, Canadian travel to the U.S. had shown a jump in visitors after a widely-reported decline.
In May, the number of Canadians visiting the U.S. was up by 9.9% compared to the same month a year prior, according to Statistics Canada. In June, the number of Canadian-resident return trips from the United States increased 5.0% year over year. The number of Americans visiting Canada was also higher, with a 6.1% rise year over year.
However, in the first quarter of 2026, Canadian residents took 5.5 million trips that included an outbound visit to the United States, a year over year decline of 10.6%. Spending while visiting the U.S. by Canadians during this period was also down by 13.6%.
Figures for the start of 2026 fall in line with a trend that has seen Canadian travel to the U.S. decline since Trump returned to Office last year.
Cell phone data analysis published by the University of Toronto in May found a 42% year-over-year median decline in Canadian travel to U.S. metropolitan areas.
The research also found that “when Canadians travel to the U.S., they are visiting fewer locations and staying for less time than they used to.”
Some metro areas such as Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, and Panama City, Florida, saw drops in Canadian tourism of at least 60%. In Florida, the decline in visits has persisted with an average decrease of just under 14% across the state during the first six months of 2026.
How U.S.-Canada talks collapsed into an all-out trade war
Relations between the U.S. and Canada have deteriorated further since the collapse of high-stakes trade talks last week resulted in U.S. tariffs of 50% on various Canadian products going into effect on Aug. 22, with no CUSMA exception.

Vice President J.D. Vance during a speech in Brewer, Maine, on Monday said: “We have to remember, Canada is a state—sorry, Freudian slip.”
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, meanwhile, has drawn focus to Canada’s burgeoning trade relations with other countries.

Carney in January met with China’s President Xi Jinping to forge what he called a “new strategic partnership” to end Canada's economic reliance on the American market.
