Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico is out with a new plan, first shared with CNBC, to break up what he says are healthcare monopolies and bring down the cost of prescription drugs. And he's teaming up with entrepreneur Mark Cuban to launch it.
Talarico, a member of the Texas House of Representatives who is running against state Attorney General Ken Paxton in one of the most closely-watched Senate races of the 2026 election cycle, will appear with Cuban for a live event and podcast recording in Fort Worth on Saturday to discuss the plan.
"Mark and I agree it's time to break up the Big Medicine monopolies that control our broken healthcare system," Talarico said in a statement to CNBC. "Healthcare corporations are ripping us off — jacking up premiums and profiting off our pain. This plan will break up monopolies, lower medical debt, bring down the cost of prescription drugs, and ensure doctors decide what medication their patients need — not insurance companies."
Talarico is trying to become the first Democrat elected statewide in Texas since 1994, in a seat that would be key for the party if they want to win control of the Senate from Republicans. The Cook Political Report with Amy Walter rates the race a "toss-up," and recent polling shows Talarico and Paxton neck-and-neck.
Democrats across the country have hammered home a cost-of-living message heading into the November election, criticizing President Donald Trump and the GOP-controlled House and Senate for enacting policies they say have hurt the economy and raised prices.
Talarico is taking the same approach on healthcare, arguing that consolidation is causing the cost of health insurance and care to rise; small, physician-owned practices to be bought out by larger hospital groups; and revenue for large insurance companies to skyrocket.
He cited recent reports that found 90% of all hospital beds are controlled by large hospital systems and just three pharmacy benefit managers — CVS Caremark, Cigna's Express Scripts and UnitedHealth Group's Optum RX — process roughly 80% of prescriptions nationwide.
Representatives for CVS Caremark, Express Scripts and Optum RX did not immediately reply to requests for comment.
In an announcement of the plan, Talarico voiced his support for antitrust legislation that he said would take aim at vertically integrated health-care conglomerates, like pharmacy benefit managers, insurance companies and hospital networks.
It would bar PBMs from hiding pricing data, create incentives to develop and approve generic drugs and institute caps on out-of-pocket costs, according to the announcement.
A representative from the American Hospital Association did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Thursday.
Greg Lopes, a spokesperson for the Pharmaceutical Care Management Association, the trade group representing PBMs, said in a statement that "PBMs are the only part of the drug supply chain lowering prescription drug costs." He argued there is no evidence that vertically-integrated plans lead to higher costs.
"One of the things American patients and families most dislike about our health care system is how fragmented and complex it is, and this legislation would only make that problem far worse — sending patients into a deeper maze of discontinuous care," Lopes said.
"Health plans operate in highly competitive markets and are the only part of the healthcare system with a clear incentive to keep coverage and care as affordable as possible," Chris Bond, a spokesperson for AHIP, the trade group representing health insurance providers, said in a statement. "Commonsense policy solutions are needed to rein in hospital systems and brand drugmakers' anti-competitive practices and ever-higher prices which are the root causes of the affordability crisis."
Cuban, the billionaire entrepreneur who in 2022 founded the Mark Cuban Cost Plus Drug Company, which is focused on lowering the consumer cost of generic prescription drugs by cutting out PBMs and negotiating directly with pharmaceutical manufacturers, has spoken favorably of Talarico.
In an Aug. 21 appearance on the "Pivot" podcast with Kara Swisher and Scott Galloway, Cuban called Talarico "honest" and said he would "do the right thing instead of the politically expedient thing."
In a statement, Cuban said Talarico's healthcare plan would "break up healthcare monopolies and lower the price of medicine."
"I've spent a long time working to reduce the cost of healthcare for everybody – politicians in Washington have not. Whether you're a Republican, Democrat, or an independent – you want more affordable, better quality healthcare. The plan James has put together will accomplish exactly that, which is why I am supporting it," Cuban continued.

Keto diets may offer health benefits the Mediterranean and other diets don’t

01:32:42 KST

It’s possible to lose weight following any one of three diets, a new clinical trial has found—but one diet stands out for its substantive health benefits that the other eating regimens just don’t seem to offer.
In the trial, researchers put three popular weight-loss regimes—a low-fat, plant-focused diet, the Mediterranean diet and the ketogenic, or keto, diet—to the test. The Mediterranean diet has long been lauded by nutritionists for its health benefits and is high in healthy fats, plants and whole grains. The plant-focused diet used in the trial is similar and highlights plant-based foods. The keto diet is rather different: it is typically high in fat and very low in carbohydrates, with a little protein thrown in for good measure.
Keto diets are specifically intended to limit your body’s access to sugars, forcing it to consume fat for energy by entering a metabolic state called ketosis. They can be used to treat certain diseases, such as epilepsy, and may have some benefits in other psychiatric conditions such as depression and schizophrenia.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Now, in a new head-to-head clinical study of the three diets, researchers found that people with obesity who lost weight on the keto diet saw better metabolic outcomes than their peers who lost a similar amount of weight on another diet. These benefits included a reduction of liver fat and lower rates of prediabetes.
The trial was small—it involved 55 participants with obesity who were prediabetic and had fatty liver disease. The participants met with a dietician every week, and they got precooked, frozen meals for one of the three diets.
The keto diet that the participants followed was rich in food such as fruits and vegetables, cheese, eggs, meat and fish, says Samuel Klein, the study’s senior author and a professor of medicine and nutritional science at the Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis. The Mediterranean diet, meanwhile, included items such as fish, chicken, legumes, seeds, nuts and olive oil, and the plant-focused diet included beans, rice, and fruits and vegetables.
Klein and his colleagues weren’t interested in whether the diets helped people lose weight. “That’s already been studied in multiple studies, and the differences are quite small between these three different diets,” Klein says. Instead the team assessed the participants’ health before and after they lost a similar amount of weight—about 10 percent of their starting weight.
All three diets had clear health benefits, such as greater sensitivity of muscle tissue to insulin, says Max Petersen, the paper’s lead author and an assistant professor at the Washington University School of Medicine. Blood cholesterol profiles were also similar across all diets.
But the keto diet had “much more profound beneficial effects on the liver,” Klein says. Participants on the keto diet saw a decrease in the liver’s production of triglyceride, a type of fat that is unhealthy in high amounts, and increased liver insulin sensitivity, which helps regulate blood sugar, as well as a reduction in liver fat.
The latter was a critical metric, Klein says: liver fat can have serious complications, including inflammation and cancer. Half of the participants on the keto diet also saw remission of their prediabetes.
The results suggest that reducing the intake of carbohydrates, particularly sugars, can help people lose weight and support their metabolic health, Klein says. “Reducing sugar intake would be a number one thing to do for anybody ... trying to change their diet to improve their health if they have obesity, independent of weight loss itself,” he says.
The study is well designed, says Jeff Volek, a kinesiologist at the Ohio State University, who was not involved with the study. Research by Volek and others has shown that ketosis can help with liver insulin sensitivity, triglyceride production, and more. The study adds to that body of evidence, he says. “It is nice to see these researchers finally coming around on ketogenic diets, as the evidence has been strong for a long time,” Volek says.
Sai Das, a nutrition science professor at Tufts University, who was also not involved in the study, says that the results suggest keto is a “highly promising” choice for people who need to reduce their liver fat and triglyceride levels ahead of surgery, whether for weight loss or any other chronic condition. “This diet offers a better option to do this in a timely manner,” Das says.
The study’s short timeline and small sample size, however, mean more research is needed to better understand the long-term effects of the keto diet compared with those of other diets, she says. On the Mediterranean diet, she notes, participants saw greater reductions in body fat mass and smaller reductions in fat-free mass, which includes muscles and bones.
Klein, for his part, hopes the results inspire future research combining keto with popular glucagonlike peptide 1 (GLP-1) weight-loss drugs such as semaglutide, tirzepatide, and more.
“All medications have costs and side effects,” he says. “How can we use diet in conjunction with medication to enhance the therapeutic effect with the least amount of cost and least amount of side effects?”
The findings were published on Thursday in the journal Cell Metabolism.

West Bank has become 'a lawless land,' says top Catholic in Jerusalem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
16:32:19 UTC
01:32:19 KST

Ilayda Cakirtekin
27 August 2026•Update: 27 August 2026
The Latin patriarch of Jerusalem, the top Catholic in the holy city, said Thursday that the West Bank has turned into "a lawless land" as the Israeli settlers’ aggression in the region continues, Vatican News quoted the cleric as saying.
The West Bank has now become “a lawless land," Cardinal Pierbattista Pizzaballa told reporters at a Catholic festival in Rimini, northern Italy, adding that the situation continues "without any effective security or legal restraints.”
Speaking at the Meeting for Friendship Among Peoples in Rimini, he urged further diplomatic engagement by the West to stop escalating violence in the Middle East.
“The fact that there is a situation of continuous aggression by settlers is well established," Pizzaballa stressed.
"The West must help raise its gaze somewhat, create perspectives, and also help calm this continuing downward spiral through ever greater diplomatic efforts."
He stressed the need for diplomacy as the "only way" to resolve the conflict "while avoiding the use of weapons, violence and military force.”
On the deteriorating situation in Gaza, Pizzaballa called it "very devastated from a human point of view.”
The two-state solution is "the only way to recognize the right of Israelis and Palestinians to have a home in their own land,” he said.
“Sooner or later the pope will come to the Holy Land — it is only a matter of time. I think it is necessary to prepare the conditions for this visit so that it can truly bear fruit," Pizzaballa added.
He also stressed the need to prevent the dehumanizing logic of war from becoming our “way of thinking, of surviving."
"War steals from young people the most beautiful years of their lives, when it does not take their lives altogether,” he said.
“This is true for Ukraine, but also for the Middle East. War has its own dynamics, and they brutalize you. The other person is exorcized, because if the other is human and close to you, it becomes difficult to strike them.”
He further said they should avoid "reducing peace to a slogan, as well as naive approaches to a complex reality."
Pizzaballa also said the sense of the common good had been lost in the Middle East as institutions seemed to be guided by what is good for themselves or for their own political side.
In a Middle East “so torn apart, burdened by hatred, resentment and hardship,” cultivating hope is not easy, he added.
“We must be realistic because the situation has deteriorated,” he added.

Israeli socialist group plans left-wing settlement in West Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
16:31:30 UTC
01:31:30 KST

Breadcrumb
Socialist-Zionist Israeli group plans Jordan Valley settlement to 'ensure left-wing presence'
A left-wing Israeli youth movement is seeking to establish a kibbutz-style community in the occupied Jordan Valley, prompting criticism from anti-settlement campaigners who say the politics of its prospective residents do not alter the project’s implications for Palestinians.
HaMachanot HaOlim, a youth movement that identifies as socialist-Zionist, has been exploring the creation of a new settlement in the Jordan Valley in recent months, according to reporting by Israeli newspaper Haaretz. The initiative is presented as a bid to establish a left-wing Israeli presence in an area increasingly associated with far-right settler groups and violence against Palestinians.
The organisation’s director Ilan Gazit – himself a resident of the Na’aran kibbutz north of Jericho – explained to the Israeli outlet the rationale behind the move: since new illegal settlements will likely be built in the West Bank, it’s preferable to populate them with leftists rather than right-wing settlers.
But Hagit Ofran, co-director of Settlement Watch at Israeli peace movement Peace Now, said the initiative should be judged by its location and political function, rather than by the political outlook of those behind it.
"In terms of the conflict and the political meaning of a settlement – it’s just the same," Ofran told The New Arab. "A settlement is a settlement: it’s not part of Israel, it’s occupied territories. And if we bring Israelis to live there, it’s not only a violation of international law – it’s also destroying the possibility to have peace and to have Palestinian independence."
The proposal has revived a longstanding tension in Israeli political history: while the settler movement is commonly associated internationally with the religious right and its most militant factions, settlement-building has never belonged solely to Israel’s right wing.
Labour’s settlement legacy
The kibbutz itself is inseparable from the history of Labour Zionism: a collective agricultural community model central to the Zionist movement’s project of establishing and consolidating Jewish communities in historic Palestine.
After Israel occupied the West Bank in 1967, Labour-led governments drove the early phase of settlement construction, with the Jordan Valley at its centre.
The approach was shaped by the Allon Plan, developed by Labour minister Yigal Allon soon after the war. Though never formally adopted, it envisaged Israeli control over a broad eastern strip of the West Bank, including the Jordan Valley, as a strategic buffer.
"The settlements that started there actually started under the Labour Party, not the right wing," she said. "There were many kibbutzim there, and they didn’t see themselves as messianic settlers."
She argued, however, that the security argument used to justify the valley’s continued control is obsolete.
"We grew up on the myth that the West Bank is a security asset for Israel," Ofran said, referring to historic fears that armies from Jordan, Syria or Iraq could advance through the valley towards Jerusalem.
"That myth that it’s needed for security is already very old. The threat on Israel is not from tanks. We have today ballistic rockets that can hit any point in Israel, and the fact that you have more land or less land does not change this vulnerability."
"The way to get peace is through agreements," she added. "We need to allow the Palestinians some independence, so that we can solve this conflict and not control them forever."
Palestinian displacement and Israeli settler violence
For Palestinians, the Jordan Valley is a major part of the occupied West Bank whose future is central to the possibility of a geographically contiguous Palestinian state. Israel has imposed sweeping restrictions on Palestinian construction and development across much of the area while settlements, outposts and Israeli-controlled infrastructure have expanded.
"Except for the enclave of Jericho and the adjacent town of 'Auja, the Jordan Valley went through something that you cannot really define differently but ethnic cleansing," Ofran told The New Arab.
"Palestinians were kicked out of their lands and not allowed to cultivate the land, starting already in ’67, when the Israeli authorities declared most of the Jordan Valley a military zone."
She said restrictions on Palestinian development had been compounded by recent settler violence. "We have dozens of communities and families that lost their homes because of settler violence," she said.
Numerous human rights organisations, including Peace Now, have documented an intensified Israeli drive to displace Palestinian shepherding communities in the northern Jordan Valley since October 2023, alongside the expansion of settler farms and outposts.
Ofran said the newer sites are often small, with only a few residents, but can wield control over extensive areas.
"It’s not a dramatic increase in the number of settlers in the Jordan Valley," she said. "It’s small settlements, those that are referred to as farms, where you only have, I don’t know, 10 people sometimes living in one place. But it’s a dramatic increase in the number of settlements."
The initiative also raises a wider question on whether rejecting settler violence is enough to distinguish a purportedly progressive settlement from the settlement enterprise itself.
"People tend to think that the problem is only their violence," Ofran said. "Had it been that they were nice, there wouldn’t be occupation, and I think that’s wrong."
"The violence of the settlers is a huge problem, and it’s the responsibility of the government that supports them and [is] not doing anything to them. But the problem of occupation is not if you are nice or not. If you are taking Palestinian land politely or violently, that’s not the problem. The problem is that we are taking other people’s land and we keep them without rights."
The proposal comes amid an acceleration in settlement activity. Peace Now said in April that a secret Israeli security cabinet decision had approved 34 new settlements, illegal under international law, adding to 68 new settlements it said the government had already decided to establish since taking office.

Israeli defense chief renews threat to punish Gaza for flying kites

2026-08-27

01:28:31 KST

Abdel Ra'ouf Arnaout and Lina Altawell
27 August 2026•Update: 27 August 2026
Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz on Thursday renewed his threat to expel Palestinians from any area in the Gaza Strip from which kites or balloons were being flown.
Katz made the threat during a high-level security meeting with army chief Eyal Zamir, the head of Israeli air defense, and other top military officials, according to a statement released by his office.
Katz said the warning was issued after balloons and kites were flown from areas inside the Gaza Strip.
Katz warned that the flying of kites or balloons would be met with a “firm response” against those responsible and against areas from which they were being flown.
“Based on the instructions of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and my instructions, the Israeli army will use all necessary tools, including evacuating Gaza residents from any area or neighborhood from which [kite and balloon] launches are carried out,” he said.
Katz and Netanyahu issued similar threats on Sunday, warning of stepped-up assassinations and expulsions of Palestinians in the Gaza Strip if the flying of kites and balloons toward Israel did not stop.
Israel has not reported any deaths or injuries from the kites and balloons that it says originated from the Gaza Strip.
Typically flown by children, lightweight kites are controlled by strings pulled from the ground.
If a string breaks, wind can carry the kites beyond the Gaza Strip towards nearby Israeli communities, some of which are located only a few kilometers away.
On Tuesday, the UN’s human rights office criticized Israeli threats to evacuate areas in the Gaza Strip over the flying of children’s kites, saying such threats contravened international legal obligations to protect civilians.
Nevertheless, the threats have prompted some local groups in the Gaza Strip to urge families to stop their children from flying kites, fearing Israel could use the practice as a pretext to escalate attacks.
Separately, Netanyahu denied that Israel plans to reopen the Erez (Beit Hanoun) crossing to goods entering Gaza following Israeli reports that the crossing might soon resume operations.
“There are absolutely no instructions to open the Erez crossing for goods,” Netanyahu said in a joint statement with Katz.
“Israel’s policy in Gaza is clear and has not changed: there will be no reconstruction before Hamas is disarmed and the Gaza Strip is fully demilitarized,” he added.
Israel’s Channel 24 reported on Thursday that Israel was expected to reopen the Erez crossing on Sept. 1 amid mounting Western pressure to increase humanitarian aid deliveries into the northern Gaza Strip.

US faces critical missile interceptor shortage in Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
16:27:00 UTC
01:27:00 KST

The U.S. military is grappling with a severe shortage of advanced missile interceptors in Europe after the war with Iran depleted key stockpiles, raising concerns about NATO’s ability to counter a potential Russian attack, U.S. and alliance officials said.
The U.S. defense official said the most concerning shortfall involves Patriot missile interceptors, which can shoot down Russia’s high-speed ballistic missiles. The NATO official confirmed the low inventories of Patriots among American and NATO forces in Europe. Both spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive military matters.
In the event of a Russian ballistic missile assault on, for example, a military headquarters or power plant, NATO could be in a similar position to Patriot-starved Ukraine and be forced "to take punch after punch in the mouth,” the U.S. defense official said.
In Europe, the American military "definitely” does not have enough Patriots to stop any possible sustained ballistic missile attack and would have "very limited” capability to defend against a single ballistic missile strike or a stray Russian missile that goes off course, the U.S. official said.
It illustrates the cascading fallout from Trump’s decision to launch a war against Iran, a conflict that reaches the six-month mark on Friday. U.S. missile stocks in Europe have been moved to the Middle East, where U.S. and Gulf allies have fired off significant numbers of interceptors, including Patriots, to thwart Iran’s drones and missiles. Some of those attacks have killed and wounded American troops.
Though a Russian ballistic missile attack against NATO countries is not imminently expected , CIA Director John Ratcliffe went to Moscow this week to warn Russia not to attack, The Wall Street Journal reported. Trump played down the significance of the rare and secretive trip, saying it was "sort of semi-routine.”
European and NATO officials say Russia could be in a position to attack countries in the alliance by 2030. Patriot stockpiles are projected to rebound by then. In the meantime, Russia’s war in Ukraine could hinder its ability to carry out any missile attack on Europe as it would be a challenge for Moscow to fight an air war on two fronts.
The Patriot missile shortage is most acutely felt in Ukraine, where officials are begging for more air defense support and where previous U.S. transfers also have drawn down some supply. Kyiv says only U.S.-made Patriots can stop Russia’s advanced ballistic missiles, which increasingly are getting through Ukrainian defenses, including as part of a barrage overnight into Thursday.
The U.S. supplied hundreds of Patriot missiles to Ukraine over the course of the 4 1/2-year-long conflict, but the Iran war was the tipping point for shrinking inventories, said Ed Arnold, senior associate fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, a military think tank in London.
The supply to Ukraine was planned for and reasonably measured, he said, whereas stocks in the Middle East have been unexpectedly and quickly drained, exposing supply chain constraints.
The U.S. military in Europe also is grappling with critical shortages of the Army Tactical Missile System, or ATACMS, a medium-range ballistic missile designed to strike behind enemy lines, the two officials said. But the overall munitions picture in Europe is less dire than on air defenses alone because some European militaries have their own offensive missiles, such as the Taurus and Storm Shadow, which are both long-range air-launched bunker-busting missiles.
The Pentagon said it would not discuss weapons stockpile levels for security reasons. U.S. Army Col. Martin O’Donnell, a senior NATO military spokesperson, said it is "simply not the case” that the number of Patriot missiles in Europe is beyond critical.
NATO, he said, is able to "block punches” and has enough air defense munitions available to defend itself as well as to donate to Ukraine.
The dearth of Patriot interceptors in Europe would leave few alternatives for shooting down Russia’s more advanced ballistic missiles, which can be combined with swarms of inexpensive drones to overwhelm defenses, experts say.
Ukraine and some allies already use systems that can destroy slower-moving drones without expensive missiles. But ballistic missiles are a challenge because they dive steeply toward targets at more than five times the speed of sound, leaving little time to stop them.
The Patriot system tracks the missile, predicts its path and launches within minutes, all while carrying out complex calculations to ensure the interceptor finds its target. One Patriot battery can only cover a limited area: for example, a small military base but not a whole city.
One alternative could be France and Italy’s SAMP/T NG air defense system. France has promised to speed up the delivery of the system - the upgraded version of the current SAMP/T - to Ukraine, which the manufacturer says is better able to counter ballistics.
The new iteration, however, has not yet been battle tested and the current version of the SAMP/T has a smaller range than the Patriot.
While U.S. and European militaries have warships that can serve as mobile air defense, they may be too far from a target to protect it and could risk getting sunk.
Ukraine has received Patriots from American and European stockpiles since Russia's 2022 invasion, with the U.S. providing about 600 of the interceptors during the Biden administration, said Mark Cancian, a retired Marine colonel who is now senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a Washington think tank.
But the greatest expenditure has been during the Iran conflict, which has used up 65% of U.S. Patriots, amounting to roughly 1,500 of the nation's 2,330 interceptors, CSIS says. About 600 missiles, including those destined for Europe, should be made this year, with a production goal of 2,000 Patriot missiles a year set for 2030, Cancian said.
NATO says Europe’s first Patriot missile production facility is expected to open in Germany in September, with deliveries possibly beginning early next year. The first deliveries should go to countries that have already placed orders, including Germany, the Netherlands, Romania and Spain, the U.S. defense official said.
But for now, that means some countries, such as Germany, have bought expensive Patriot systems but are in the "ridiculous” position of not having any ammunition to fire from them, said Arnold of the London think tank.
Germany's defense ministry said it does not comment on stockpiles.
Moscow likely cannot carry out a sustained air assault on a NATO target while it launches almost nightly attacks on Ukraine, Arnold said.
Ukraine's recent strikes into Russia also have exposed weaknesses in Russia's air defenses, which could prompt Putin to think twice about provoking a retaliatory attack.
"The uncomfortable truth is possibly the best air defense that we have is Russian constraints,” Arnold said.

Guidance: Scotland firing times
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
17:24:25 BST
01:24:25 KST

Scotland firing times
Firing times for ranges in Scotland including Barry Buddon, Kirkcudbright, Garelochhead, Tain, Cape Wrath, Fort George, Blackdog, Castlelaw Ranges and Dreghorn
Documents
Details
As seen in the Security Defence Review, the Army are at heightened readiness due to a new era of threat. This has placed greater demands on the Defence Training Estate across the UK, which is being used for training more regularly and at shorter notice.
As such, the firing time notifications published on Gov.UK have been standardised to show the daily timings for when live-firing is permitted on the UK DTE. This is a change from the previous method of showing when training bookings had been made in advance.
This to ensure safety of all users, as it is not possible to change Gov.UK notifications at short notice. Broadly, the only guaranteed safe times for access are before or after the firing times provided on this page, however there may be exceptional circumstances where extensions have been requested.
If you wish to use the DTE for recreation, please always refer to onsite safety warning signals to understand if the site is safe to access before doing so.
Your safety
Danger - When warning signals are displayed, regardless of the timings, do not cross the range boundary.
Warning signals are red flags by day and red lamps by night; range boundaries are marked by red and white poles.
Red flags and red lamps indicate that live firing is taking place within the range boundaries.
Do not enter the danger area when in use, this could result in loss of life.
Do not touch any military debris, it may be dangerous. Please note the location and inform a Training Safety Officer (TSO) via 07717542336 or the police.
Learn more about accessing MOD training areas

Russian psychiatric evaluation finds pro-Kremlin blogger Ilya Remeslo sane after anti-Putin posts
A psychiatric evaluation conducted at the Serbsky Institute of Psychiatry found blogger Ilya Remeslo sane, his defense attorney, Sergei Badamshin, said.
The evaluation also found that Remeslo “did not suffer, and does not suffer, from any illness,” Badamshin said.
On July 26, Remeslo was transferred to the Serbsky Institute of Psychiatry from the pretrial detention center where he is being held on charges of spreading false information. The pretrial investigation has concluded, and investigators have filed final charges against him, the Russian state news agency TASS said.
The Moscow City Court heard an appeal of Remeslo’s detention order on August 26 and upheld his pretrial detention. “Thank you for your attention to my case,” Remeslo said after the court’s ruling. “Everything will be fine. Russia will be free.”
Remeslo built his reputation on a years-long feud with Alexey Navalny. In March 2026, however, he posted a series of messages on his Telegram channel sharply criticizing Russian President Vladimir Putin, demanding that he resign and be convicted as a “war criminal and thief.” Remeslo was sent to a psychiatric hospital a few days later and was released after 30 days.
Remeslo was detained in mid-July on charges of spreading false information about the military. Sources told the Russian business news outlet RBC that the case stemmed from his posts. His defense attorney said the charges referred to “the very manifesto published exactly four months earlier.” Moscow’s Basmanny District Court ordered him held in pretrial detention on July 17.

Forensics unable to determine Eldar Dayan's cause of death, suspects released from house arrest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
16:23:29 UTC
01:23:29 KST

Police did not ask the court to extend the house arrest of seven suspects in the investigation into Eldar Dayan’s death on Thursday, allowing the house-arrest restrictions to expire after forensic experts were unable to determine his cause of death.
The decision does not close the investigation or clear the suspects. It does, however, leave all seven outside custody and reflects the central difficulty facing investigators: Without knowing how Dayan died, police have been unable to establish the evidence needed to sustain a murder allegation.
Two of Dayan’s friends, Omri Peretz and Maxim Barberman, were initially arrested on suspicion of murder. Police are now investigating them on suspicion of attempted murder.
Five other suspects from Petah Tikva are suspected of involvement in a fight that preceded Dayan’s disappearance and death.
Earlier this week, police asked the Petah Tikva Magistrate’s Court to place the seven under house arrest for two weeks. Judge Ronen Peleg instead ordered that they remain under house arrest only until Thursday.
Police did not file a request to extend that order, meaning the house arrest expired without a further court hearing.
Condition of remains makes it impossible to determine cause of death
The change followed a report from the L. Greenberg Institute of Forensic Medicine at Abu Kabir, which found that the condition of Dayan’s remains made it impossible to determine his cause of death.
The finding does not establish that Dayan was not killed. It leaves investigators unable to determine how he died or connect any of the suspects’ alleged actions to his death.
At the previous hearing, a police representative acknowledged that the evidence gathered did not support a murder allegation. Police nevertheless said additional laboratory findings were still pending and that the investigation could potentially support a suspicion of attempted murder against Peretz and Barberman.
Their attorneys rejected that suspicion and argued that police had not presented substantial evidence linking their clients either to Dayan’s death or to an attempt to kill him.
Dayan’s relatives have sharply criticized the handling of the investigation, alleging that delays in locating his remains allowed evidence to be compromised.
The investigation can continue despite the end of the house arrest, and police may seek to arrest the suspects again if new evidence emerges. Whether any of the seven will ultimately be charged remains undecided.

Halis Sunnetci
27 August 2026•Update: 27 August 2026
AC Milan have accepted an offer from Galatasaray for Portuguese winger Rafael Leao, but the player has yet to decide his future amid interest from Aston Villa, The Athletic reported Thursday.
Milan have accepted a Galatasaray proposal worth €45 million ($52.4 million) plus €5 million in potential bonuses, according to the report.
Galatasaray have offered Leao an annual salary of around €10 million plus €2 million in bonuses and could improve the proposal.
However, the 27-year-old’s representatives are reportedly seeking €12 million per season plus €3 million in bonuses.
Aston Villa are also in discussions with Milan and are proposing an initial loan with an obligation to make the move permanent.
The Premier League club is discussing a package comprising an €8 million loan fee and a mandatory €42 million purchase.
Villa have yet to submit a firm offer, however, with Milan preferring a permanent sale during the current transfer window, the report added.
The English club are reportedly offering Leao an annual net salary of around €7 million.
Leao, whose Milan contract runs until 2028, now has the final say over whether to join Galatasaray, pursue a move to Villa or remain with the Italian club.
He joined Milan from French side Lille in 2019 and has helped the club win the Serie A title and the Italian Super Cup.
The left winger scored nine goals and provided three assists in 29 Serie A appearances last season.

====================================================================================================

Race to get aid into Nepal and Tibet amid warnings flood lake could burst
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
16:22:31 UTC
01:22:31 KST

The international community was scrambling to get aid into flood-stricken parts of Nepal and Tibet on Thursday as authorities warned that a lake formed at the site where the deadly torrents occurred was rising and at risk of bursting.
The catastrophic flash floods that hit Nepal and Tibet on Wednesday, thundering down valleys and obliterating entire villages, killed at least 389 people and left more than 1,300 missing.
Efforts to locate those unaccounted for – including hundreds of tourists from India, the US, Britain, Australia and Canada – have been complicated by the destruction of dozens of bridges and 25 miles (40km) of roads in the mountainous region, which is popular with trekkers and pilgrims.
Rescue teams reported finding bodies hundreds of miles downstream from the disaster zone in the Chitwan district of Nepal, near the Tibetan border. Dozens of injured people were transported to Kathmandu for advanced medical care and more than 100 people were rescued by Nepali army personnel in helicopters.
Videos from Wednesday’s disaster showed a massive wall of water crashing down on the border as people tried to flee. The power, volume and speed of the floods gave little time for escape.
Trucks were overturned and houses, roads and power plants were swept away in Nepal, while officials in Tibet said they feared “major casualties” after a mudslide hit a border crossing.
Tom Fletcher, the UN’s humanitarian chief, described the flood as “horrifying”. He said emergency teams had been mobilised and an initial $2m (£1.5m) of disaster funds allocated to cover emergency medical care, shelter and water.
Nepal’s disaster authority warned of continuing danger on Thursday, appealing to residents and rescuers to stay away from a swelling lake that had formed at the flood site. Chinese authorities said a barrier lake at the confluence of the Tsogyal and Purupqiangzangbu rivers was overflowing and could burst.
Girilal Budhathoki, 36, who lives in the Rasuwa district of Nepal’s Bagmati province, said the flood waters swept away his wife and four children while he was away from the family home.
“A huge surge of water came,” he said. “Everything turned completely black, and I couldn’t understand what was happening. Suddenly, something heavy crushed me and I fell down.”
Budhathoki realised what had happened only when he returned to the place where his house had stood. “I searched desperately for my wife and children but I couldn’t find them,” he said. “They didn’t make it out. My wife was swept away too. I am all alone now.”
Kamal Kharel, who works at a hydropower plant in Chilime, also in Rasuwa district, was in the office when the floods hit. “The whole place shook as if there had been a huge earthquake,” he said. “But when I went outside, I saw everything a storm and raging water.”
Kharel and some of his colleagues managed to climb a hill, where they stayed until they were rescued by the army on Thursday morning. He said: “I had never seen waves crashing that high. You only see waves like that in the sea.”
People from the hard-hit districts of Nuwakot and Dhading, in Bagmati province, were seen gathering outside an army training centre – the base for helicopter rescue operations – seeking information about missing family members.
Police were recording the names of the missing outside the barracks gate. Mobile phone torches were their only source of light as the area remained without electricity because of damaged hydroelectric infrastructure.
The village of Soley, in Nuwakot, which had about 25 homes, was almost wiped out, according to Nirajan Paudyal, a Kathmandu-based journalist whose parents and other relatives lived there. Desperate for information, he had travelled to the area on Thursday for news of his family. “There is no update till now,” he said. “I fear there won’t be any update.”
More than 500 foreigners were among 826 people missing in Nepal, police and tourism officials said. Among those unaccounted for were 177 from India, 90 from the US, 34 from Australia, 33 from Britain and 25 from Canada.
Chinese state media said at least 558 were missing on the Tibet side of the border, of whom at least 260 were foreign nationals.
Police in Nepal said 389 bodies had been recovered by Thursday afternoon local time, while Chinese state media reported three dead on the Tibet side of the border.
Many of the victims were on a pilgrimage to Kailash Mansarovar, a high-altitude site in Tibet revered by Hindus and Buddhists among others.
Early reports from Nepali officials suggested an earthquake could have caused the lower part of a glacier to collapse and trigger the floods. But the US Geological Survey later said what was initially reported as a 4.4-magnitude earthquake was a seismic shock generated by glacial rock and ice collapsing, and the flow of debris. “No earthquake had occurred,” it said.
Srijana Gurung, the acting Nepal director for the international NGO Plan International, said communities across the Himalayan country were facing “climate shock after shock” with hardly any time to recover.
“Floods and landslides have always happened in Nepal but the climate crisis is making them far more frequent and intense,” she said. “The priority now must be reaching those affected, supporting families searching for loved ones and ensuring vulnerable communities have the assistance they need.”
Gurung said children and families who had lost their homes and livelihoods would be in urgent need of medical help, food, shelter and hygiene kits. “There is also a risk of waterborne disease as access to clean water and sanitation is likely to have been damaged,” she said.
Scant information has emerged from the Chinese authorities about the scale of the destruction. Tibet is the most tightly controlled part of China even under normal circumstances. Foreign journalists cannot visit the region unless they are part of a government-controlled tour and the authorities have cracked down harshly on calls for greater autonomy from the Tibetan people. Tibetans have almost no contact with the international media because of fears of retribution.
Only brief, state-controlled media reports about the floods have been allowed to circulate in China and the authorities have confirmed only three deaths. Chinese reports have focused on rescue efforts.
Maya Wang, the deputy Asia director at Human Rights Watch, wrote on X: “The floods raise questions about whether Chinese authorities could’ve done more to reduce disaster risks, given longstanding concerns from Tibetan diaspora groups & experts about rapid, state-led development in areas where Tibetans have little say.”
She called on Beijing to “allow Tibetans access to information and international researchers and journalists unfettered access to the region, and conduct a rigorous investigation into the disaster”.

Five missiles hit Zaporizhstal blast furnace shop, power and transport infrastructure, open areas – Metinvest
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
19:20:02 EEST
01:20:02 KST

At dawn today, Russian troops once again attacked the joint-venture Zaporizhstal steel mill, which had completely halted production following a previous strike on August 11.
According to Chief Operating Officer (COO) of the Metinvest Group Oleksandr Myronenko, five ballistic missiles struck equipment in the blast furnace shop, power and transportation infrastructure, and open-air areas of the plant, damaging civilian production facilities.
He said, however, that Zaporizhstal is a civilian industrial enterprise known worldwide for its pig iron, as well as for producing rolled steel for the manufacture of pipes, household appliances, and automotive components, and that it does not produce any military products, as it is not a military facility.
"Ordinary people work at the plant: metallurgists, blast furnace operators, maintenance workers, and power engineers who produce steel for civilian life. Until August 11, the plant continued to operate despite numerous attacks – we managed to restore and restart production on multiple occasions. But the attack two weeks ago was unprecedented in its consequences. First and foremost, in terms of human casualties. Second, in terms of the scale of the destruction, as it devastated production in a way not seen since the Second World War. The civilian enterprise had barely recovered from the August 11 strike when it happened again on August 27: the same type of munitions, the same launch sites," the chief operating officer of the Metinvest Group said.
Myronenko said people are alive – and that is the most important thing: after the air raid alert was sounded, the employees who were on shift managed to take cover. However, he said, "timelines for resuming production exist only in theory, because no sooner had we cleared the debris from the previous strike than we were hit by another one."
"Currently, experts are assessing the extent of the damage and losses and inspecting the production, energy, and transportation infrastructure to determine the next steps," Myronenko said.
The press release notes that the previous attack on August 11 claimed the lives of eight Zaporizhstal employees – civilians who were heading to shelters while performing their work duties. Another 26 employees were injured. Russian missiles struck the plant just two minutes after the air raid siren sounded. At that time, key blast furnace production equipment, power facilities, and the plant's infrastructure were damaged. Zaporizhstal had only experienced destruction on this scale during the Second World War.
After urgent emergency repairs, the plant began dismantling the damaged structures to gain access to the equipment, assess the extent of the damage, and determine the feasibility of restoration. Since production had come to a complete halt, the number of employees at the plant was reduced, while the core team remained in place.
Despite the complete halt in production and the limited presence of staff, Russia attacked Zaporizhstal again. This is yet another indication that Russian troops are systematically targeting civilian industrial infrastructure and the people who work there, according to a statement from Metinvest.

Pentagon says it found ‘hidden’ files on Afghan withdrawal
Pentagon investigators reviewing the chaotic US withdrawal from Afghanistan have uncovered classified documents that they say were deliberately hidden from previous probes. The discovery comes amid long-running accusations that the administration of former US President Joe Biden concealed failures surrounding the operation.
Sean Parnell, chairman of the Afghanistan Withdrawal Special Review Panel, said on Wednesday that his team had recovered “highly relevant classified documents” that “should have been disclosed.”
The material had been “stashed and hidden away in safes where they would not be found,” Parnell said in a video statement on X, five years after the deadly bombing of the Abbey Gate entrance to Kabul airport.
“After the team reviewed these documents, it became clear why someone tried to hide them,” he said.
Parnell did not disclose what the documents actually contain, who allegedly concealed them, or whether they relate to any specific decisions made by Biden or his officials.
However, he said his panel would follow the evidence “wherever it leads and to whoever it touches,” and promised veterans and the families of those killed “the full picture” of how and why decisions were made during the disastrous withdrawal.
Thirteen US service members and around 170 Afghans were killed when an ISIS-K suicide bomber attacked Abbey Gate during the August 2021 evacuation. During the chaotic withdrawal, the Taliban rapidly swept across Afghanistan, the Western-backed government collapsed, and thousands of people crowded Kabul airport in an attempt to flee the country.
Images of desperate Afghans clinging to a departing US military aircraft became emblematic of the withdrawal, which ended a 20-year American military presence with the Taliban back in power.
Republicans have since repeatedly accused Biden officials of ignoring or downplaying warnings that a complete US withdrawal could trigger the rapid collapse of the Afghan government and security forces, and of waiting too long to launch a full-scale evacuation.
House investigators have also consistently raised concerns that potentially relevant photographs, video, and other material from the evacuation were missing, deleted, or otherwise unavailable during subsequent probes. They have accused Biden-era officials of withholding information and frustrating congressional attempts to establish exactly how key decisions were made.
Biden administration officials have denied any cover-up and argued that the unexpectedly rapid collapse of the Afghan government severely complicated the evacuation.

Visa, Mastercard begin first Syria global card payments in years
- Visa and Mastercard processed Syria’s first international card payments in over 15 years, marking a key step in modernising the country’s payment system.
- This follows the US removing Syria from its state sponsors of terrorism list, easing economic restrictions and signalling warmer ties.
- Syrian officials expressed hope this will end economic isolation, attract investment, and support the country's post-war rebuilding efforts.
AI generated
DAMASCUS - Visa and Mastercard said they had carried out their first international card payments in Syria in more than a decade, days after Washington delisted the country as a state sponsor of terrorism.
Mastercard said in a statement that it and Qatar National Bank (QNB) Group “have processed Syria’s first international card payment in more than 15 years, marking an important milestone in the modernisation of Syria’s payments ecosystem”.
Visa in a statement on Aug 26 said it had “tested the first live international transaction in Syria”, also hailing “an important milestone in supporting the country’s financial services sector”.
It said the move came in cooperation with Lebanon’s Fransabank, which it called “the acquiring financial institution”, and with local electronic payments company Paymera.
Paymera said on Aug 27 that it had carried out the first electronic payment using Visa.
Since the December 2024 ousting of longtime Syrian ruler Bashar al-Assad, several Western countries have lifted sanctions imposed on the country after its nearly 14-year civil war erupted in 2011.
On Aug 24, the United States removed Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism, rescinding a decades-old designation that came with severe economic restrictions and marking another step in warming ties between the countries.
The Visa statement said the test was “the start of a historic step towards expanding digital payment capabilities in the market and providing international visitors with a familiar, secure, and convenient way to make payment”.
Central bank governor Safwat Raslan late on Aug 26 posted a video on social media of himself with Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa, who paid for coffee at a Damascus cafe by card.
The central bank chief described it as “the first payment made using a Visa card in the heart of Damascus” after Syria’s removal from the state sponsors of terrorism list.
“It is a feeling which is hard to put into words,” he said, calling it “a new beginning in which we carry great hope, and responsibility too.”
“We will keep working ceaselessly to build a modern, trusted, open financial system that keeps up with Syrians’ aspirations and opens up new opportunities for them,” he added.
After the civil war erupted, sanctions cut Syria off from the international banking system, with a ban imposed on dealing with the country’s central bank whose assets were frozen.
Damascus hopes this week’s de-listing will help end Syria’s economic isolation and strengthen its integration into the global economic and financial system, as well as attract investment and support development as the country seeks to rebuild. AFP

====================================================================================================

Iran’s Hormuz trump card is rapidly losing strategic value, expert tells 'Post' - interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
16:05:44 UTC
01:05:44 KST

Though the Islamic Republic of Iran has established a “sophisticated panoply” to protect itself against the possibility of regime change, its trump card, the Strait of Hormuz, is losing its strategic value and will continue to do so, Thomas O’Donnell, an American energy and geopolitics strategist and a Global Fellow of the Wilson Center, told The Jerusalem Post on Thursday.
With many of the regime’s regional proxies degraded over years of war with Israel and its nuclear ambitions delayed after the 12 Day War in June last year, Tehran only has its rockets, drones, and ability to threaten the Strait of Hormuz left as an insurance policy against attempts to topple the regime, he noted.
These remaining elements will be used to dissuade action while it restores the others, but they are losing the weight they once carried, O’Donnell added.
Though 14 to 15 million barrels of oil traveled through Hormuz per day before the war, he argued that it was very possible to manage without much of that supply.
Saudi Arabia’s East-West Crude Oil Pipeline moves around five million barrels per day for non-domestic use, while the United Arab Emirates moves an average of 1.5 to 1.8m. bpd through its own pipeline, he calculated.
Some 400m. barrels of oil and refined petroleum products were unanimously approved for release by the 32 member nations of the International Energy Agency (IEA), while the US government committed 172 million barrels from its Strategic Petroleum Reserve.
None of this even touches on the oil supplied by the Western Hemisphere, where roughly 32% to 40% of the world’s total oil originates.
“There’s more production in other places, but [the disruption of] oil has not been anything like it would have been 20 years ago if they closed the strait,” he said, explaining how the US’s own oil and fracking industries have helped mitigate much of the damage.
Could Iran’s weakening control of Hormuz force a deal with the US?
“The oil price, it’ll go up and down. The fact that it went over $100 [a barrel], and the next day it was $80, that means that’s geostrategic variability. That’s not fundamental.”
A number of planned pipelines, namely the UAE’s plans to double its oil output through a parallel pipeline and Iraq’s plans for an Iraq-to-Syria pipeline, will also weaken the strategic value of Hormuz as states develop alternative routes.
Reflecting on these developments, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent shared earlier this month the prediction that the strait “is going to become just another body of water” over the next two years, estimating that 50-70% of the exports passing through the waterway would instead travel through underground pipelines.
Noting that the Iran-backed militias operating in Iraq could still cause some issues with the planned pipeline, he reasoned that this would provide further motivation for Iraq to keep to its September 30 deadline to disarm the groups.
O’Donnell further argued that beyond Hormuz becoming less valuable as a transit point for fuel, Iran’s own ability to defend its claim over the waterway has also diminished, as has its ability to attack neighboring states’ alternative oil routes.
“The Americans systematically bombed the region and knocked out every radar that was ever turned on. Little by little… they systematically degraded it. And now you see [oil tankers] are sneaking or being escorted at night, where Iran can’t visually see the tankers very well,” O’Donnell explained.
“Iran had a more or less static defense or offense, missiles and drones that they can’t reproduce, and electronic eyes that undoubtedly the Americans can only degrade at some rate. And so their ability to control Hormuz will degrade over time.”
In other words, Iran is losing leverage over Hormuz from both directions: The waterway is becoming less indispensable to global energy markets, and Tehran is becoming less capable of controlling it.
The natural outcome of this will be vessels traveling largely unimpeded through the strait as Iran is left with degraded weapons and defenses, he continued, predicting that even the regime’s hardliners would eventually need to make a deal with the US despite their current “bravado” as the financial crisis hitting Iran worsens.
Aware of this, Iran may make a “desperate attempt” to step up its pressure campaign on the US through attacks on Gulf states, potentially even launching a ground incursion, O’Donnell said.
What will happen to Hormuz if Iran loses control?
Having rubbed shoulders with a number of diplomats and analysts in the region, O’Donnell said he had been told by a number of sources that Gulf states were aware, prior to the war’s outbreak on February 28, that Iran had strategized a plan to target them as a means to pressure the US into dropping or moderating any campaign against it should the need ever arise.
When the US continued to attack despite Gulf pressure, quickly eliminating Tehran’s leadership, the Islamic Republic went for the Strait of Hormuz, “because it’s so important globally.”
Despite not approving of the US’s attacks on Iran due to the consequences for them, O’Donnell said that Gulf states were unwilling to see Hormuz remain under Iran’s control for reasons outside of the issue of fees.
“As soon as there’s something on Asharq or on Sky News that they don’t like, they’ll hold up the UAE ships,” he said. “As soon as there’s something on Al Jazeera they don’t like, they’ll hold up the ships for a week.”
This, he reasoned, is why Gulf states would not allow the United States to leave the conflict, despite alternative oil routes becoming available in the not-so-distant future.
“If they’re going to make a deal, now’s the time to make a deal and get it over with. They can cause a lot of pain, but in the end, Iran is really going to become diminished. And if they go diehard, it’s going to be hard for everybody, obviously,” O’Donnell said.
“If you have a diminishing lever, best to make what deal you can… The US knows it’s going to take a long time, it’ll be fairly painful for allies, [but] in the end, it’s going to get better for us.”

Antisemitic ideology deeply embedded within the far-right German AfD party, new AJC report shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
16:05:40 UTC
01:05:40 KST

A new analysis published by the American Jewish Committee (AJC) claims that antisemitic ideas, conspiracy narratives, and historical revisionism are deeply embedded beneath the surface of Germany’s Alternative for Germany (AfD) party.
Authored by Prof. Dr. Lars Rensmann, a Professor of Political Science at the University of Passau who specializes in modern political ideologies, democratic theory, and the comparative study of antisemitism, the report, published on Tuesday, is titled “‘Friendly Faces’ of antisemitism? Political Antisemitism in the Alternative for Germany Party.”
Rensmann said that political antisemitism functions as a connective element within the party’s broader opposition to modern, pluralist democracy, noting that while the party does not present itself as openly antisemitic and regularly denies harboring antisemitism, “antisemitic ideas, codes, and narratives permeate its rhetoric, mobilization strategies, and memory politics.”
The report said that the AfD has evolved from a Eurosceptic protest party founded in 2013 into the central political force of Germany’s far Right, serving as a durable parliamentary actor and the largest opposition party in the Bundestag.
According to Rensmann, this transformation has been accompanied by a radicalization in which the party positions itself against liberal democracy while cultivating authoritarian, ethno-nationalist, and conspiratorial worldviews.
AfD frames politics into virtuous people versus corrupt domestic elites. external forces
The analysis outlines how the AfD frames politics through a stark friend-enemy logic, dividing society into a supposedly virtuous people versus corrupt domestic elites and external forces. According to Rensmann, this framework “closely mirrors patterns of modern antisemitism, which historically constructed Jews as hidden enemies linking internal ‘traitors’ with external threats.”
Rather than naming Jews explicitly, Rensmann argued that the AfD usually relies on coded language. He noted references to “globalists,” “cosmopolitan elites,” or “shadowy financial powers draw on long-standing antisemitic stereotypes.”
The study further stated that the conspiracy myth of a planned “Great Replacement” of the native population “echoes classic fantasies of a Jewish world conspiracy without explicitly mentioning Jews.” Investor George Soros serves as a recurring personification of these ideas, with Rensmann noting that “AfD representatives repeatedly portray him as a sinister puppet master orchestrating migration, climate policy, and social change.” The author argued that “such narratives revive the core motifs of antisemitic conspiracy theories while maintaining plausible deniability.”
The analysis explained how the party’s ideology has been shaped by ethno-nationalism and the demand for remigration, accompanied by the rehabilitation of Nazi rhetoric. Rensmann argued that this worldview is historically inseparable from antisemitism because it frames cultural homogeneity as a prerequisite for survival and attributes national decline to subversive outside influences.
Appropriation of Nazi slogans, ideas, and symbols by party leaders
The report highlighted political and legal responses to the frequent appropriation of Nazi slogans, ideas, and symbols by party leaders, such as the SA slogan “Everything for Germany,” noting that the AfD said these references are entirely innocuous and are criticized or prosecuted in bad faith by representatives of the state.
Rensmann noted that rehabilitating this language is structurally linked to antisemitism because it reactivates the national-revolutionary imagination of the Nazi era, which historically blamed Jews for modernity, liberalism, and pluralism.
Furthermore, the paper examines historical revisionism and secondary antisemitism arising from defense against memory as political motives of the AfD.
Rensmann argued that the party rejected the “cult of guilt,” claiming that this stance relativizes Nazi crimes, prevents national pride, and in effect marginalizes Jewish perspectives on history. According to the report, this promotes what scholars describe as secondary antisemitism, defined as “hostility toward Jews arising from resentment about Holocaust remembrance and perceived moral demands.”
Within this framework, Rensmann said that “Jews appear implicitly as those who prevent a positive national self-image by insisting on confronting German crimes.”
Party's attempts to shield itself from antisemitic accusations
The report also noted how the party attempts to shield itself from accusations of antisemitism by pointing to its supposed pro-Israel positions as proof that it harbors no hostility toward Jewish people.
Rensmann argued that this maneuver is entirely instrumental and defensive, noting that “instrumental ‘pro-Israel’ rhetoric” is deployed by the party “only insofar as it appears to confirm the AfD’s own ethno-nationalist and anti-migration agenda,” such as expressing hostility toward Muslim migrants.
Rensmann said that this supposed solidarity is selective and disingenuous by highlighting instances where the party exhibits underlying anti-Israel or hostile positions when Israel’s actions or existence do not serve nationalist talking points.
He noted that the party’s foreign policy positions frequently align with anti-Western and authoritarian regimes hostile to Israel, and that its leadership has routinely voted against or opposed cooperative diplomatic frameworks involving Israel while weaponizing the Jewish state merely as a rhetorical tool against political opponents and Muslim immigration.
The paper concluded by stating that far from being an isolated problem, political antisemitism functions as a key mobilizing resource within the AfD’s broader challenge to liberal democracy.
Rensmann argued that understanding this dynamic is essential for assessing the risks the party poses to democratic culture, minority rights, and social cohesion in Germany.

Pakistan: Protests continue in Azad Kashmir despite repression and internet blackout

Pakistan: Protests continue in Azad Kashmir despite repression and internet blackout
Harshly repressed protests that have shaken Pakistan-administered Kashmir since early June have continued through local legislative elections held in July and August. With internet access cut off and access by foreign media restricted, local residents are attempting to report on the situation on the ground.
To contact us, Usman*, a resident of Rawalakot, a city in the Pakistan-administered part of the disputed Kashmir region, has to climb into the nearby mountains, where he can pick up a few bars of mobile signal from outside the province.
This article was reported by the FRANCE 24 Observers, the network’s digital investigation team in Paris, via social media. No other FRANCE 24 staff contributed to the report.
*We have concealed the identity of people we spoke to inside Pakistan to protect them from reporting restrictions imposed by the Pakistani government.
Azad and Jammu Kashmir (AJK), an autonomous territory under Pakistani administration since the partition of Kashmir between India and Pakistan in 1947, has been gripped by widespread protests since June. The Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) – a local opposition movement founded in 2023 – is leading the mobilisation and is calling, among other things, for electoral reform, greater political representation and more resources for the territory.
After several rounds of protests that led to government concessions, dialogue broke down in the run-up to local legislative elections, held between July 27 and August 10. On June 5, the Azad Kashmir authorities designated the JAAC as a terrorist movement, and clashes subsequently intensified, particularly on June 7 and 8 in Rawalakot, following the death of activist Shahzeb Habib, who human rights groups say was killed by security forces.
The Pakistani government imposed an internet shutdown, on June 5, and restrictions on the supply of essential goods. Since then, protests have continued, some of which have been violently suppressed, notably in Rawalakot on July 27.
The Pakistani government denies that security forces have used force to repress peaceful political activity in the territory and says internet access is being "progressively normalised". [see statement below].
'They tried to kill the protesters by opening fire directly at them'
Usman* was present at the July 27 protest in Rawalakot.
 We began a march on July 27 towards Muzaffarabad, the capital of Azad Kashmir. Security forces were stationed at various locations. They had set up roadblocks and were using snipers, light machine guns, and tear gas grenades. It wasn’t just the police, but also Pakistani paramilitary forces. When they realised that the crowd was much larger than expected, they tried to kill the protesters by opening fire directly at them.
This is the first time I’ve witnessed such repression in Pakistan-administered Kashmir. Before this, we had never witnessed such bloodshed or such brutal attacks by the security forces.
To display this content from Instagram, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
'After two days, more than 30 people had been killed in a very confined area'
The Jammu Kashmir Human Rights Observatory (JKHRO) is a UK-based organisation that seeks to verify information coming from Azad Kashmir. One of its members, who wished to remain anonymous to protect his family in the territory, describes the situation in Rawalakot following the events of July 27:
 “After two days, more than 30 people had been killed in a very confined area. As the entire city had been sealed off by the security forces, it was impossible even for ambulances to reach the hospital. The injured had to travel more than 60 kilometres to receive treatment at a hospital in another city.”
To display this content from X (Twitter), you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
Protests also broke out in other cities across Azad Kashmir to denounce the violence carried out by the security forces in Rawalakot. They were also violently suppressed, leaving at least three people dead in Mirpur on July 28 and four dead in Muzaffarabad between July 31 and August 2, according to JKHRO.
To display this content from X (Twitter), you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
To display this content from X (Twitter), you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
In its latest report, published on August 5, the JKHRO stated that 89 people had been killed during the protests since June 5. However, the organisation believes that the death toll could rise further. The authorities in Azad Kashmir, for their part, have yet to release any figures.
Pakistani government denies use of force by security forces
In a statement to FRANCE 24, the ministry of information in Islamabad said: "The government categorically rejects the suggestion that security forces used force to repress peaceful political activity in Azad Jammu and Kashmir." The ministry accused the JAAC of promoting "anarchy and violence" and said the AJK authorities had evidence of the JAAC using weapons and taking civilians and security personnel hostage. [see full statement]
The AJK police on August 13 said the JAAC had "abducted" eight highway police officers. They did not immediately respond to a request asking for more information.
The JAAC denies using violence, and supporters deny targeting police officers .
Protests continue despite violence and internet outage
Despite the danger, the protests continue. Numerous sit-ins are still being organised in Rawalakot, as shown by videos shared on social media.
To display this content from Instagram, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
Usman* participates regularly in these gatherings. He explains :
 “Thousands of people gather at the sit-ins every day. A specific time slot, from 2pm to 6pm, is set aside to allow the general public, particularly women, to attend the protests.”
'There is a blockade on medicines'
Beyond the shootings, the internet shutdown and restrictions on the supply of essential goods coming from the rest of Pakistan are also having dramatic humanitarian consequences, as the JKHRO member we spoke to explains.
 “One of the major impacts has been the absence of banking services since June 5, due to the internet shutdown. There is also a blockade on medicines and other goods being transported to Kashmir from Pakistan. If you are sick and go to the hospital for a blood test, you may not be able to get your results because of the lack of internet or means of communication. Pregnant women, children, and people suffering from heart problems, diabetes, or chronic illnesses may therefore not be properly diagnosed. In addition, all schools are closed. This is therefore a catastrophe with multiple and far-reaching consequences.”
In its statement to FRANCE 24, the information ministry said on August 27 the internet outages were being "progressively normalised" and were "limited to areas affected by violence and imposed only for the period considered necessary for public safety".
'A further tightening of restrictions on press freedom in the country'
In addition to residents’ difficulties communicating with the outside world due to the internet shutdown, Pakistan’s Ministry of Information and Broadcasting imposed the “Foreign Media Facilitation Guidelines 2026” on August 4 (full text here).
A Pakistani digital rights activist explains the consequences of these directives :
 “Anyone working for foreign media outlets, even if they are a Pakistani citizen, must obtain a no-objection certificate issued by the government in order to report from outside the country’s three major cities [in Pakistan], which are Karachi, Lahore and Islamabad. This is evidence of a further tightening of restrictions on press freedom in the country, where the government essentially decides who has access to information and under what condition.”
On August 2, Al Jazeera’s website was blocked, with the information ministry accusing the network of “sensational journalism” following its coverage of events in Azad Kashmir.
Meanwhile, two independent local journalists have been detained since August 1, after covering a protest held in the capital in support of the Kashmir protesters.
Local journalists and even citizens who cover the protests on social media are facing significant pressure. Some of them have been included on a watch list of suspected terrorists by the government of Azad Kashmir. This means that their bank accounts, SIM cards and identity documents have been blocked.
The Azad Kashmir election was supposed to have a final round of voting on August 10, but elections in seven constituencies, including Rawalakot, were postponed for security reasons. As of August 10, 38 of the 45 directly elected seats had been filled, with the ruling Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) winning 25 seats, and the Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP) winning 12 seats.

A lawyer for the social media influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate urged a US judge on Thursday to release the brothers on bail from a Miami jail as they contest extradition to Britain, where they are wanted on rape charges.
Howard Srebnick, a lawyer for the Tate brothers, told the Miami-based US magistrate judge Lauren Louis that they had regularly appeared in court in Romania, where they are on pretrial release, which he said was evidence they were not a flight risk.
“The brothers have been fully compliant with their conditions of release,” Srebnick said.
Andrew Tate, 39, and Tristan Tate, 38, wore beige prison garb and sported beards to their hearing. They were arrested in Miami on 18 July after Britain requested their extradition to face charges of rape, assault and facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation. The Tate brothers, who have dual US and British citizenship, have denied any wrongdoing.
The arrests marked a new phase in the legal troubles for the former kickboxers, who have built a large online following promoting their views on masculinity and wealth. Andrew Tate has previously described himself as a misogynist.
The Tates recruited dozens of women to work for a webcam pornography business starting in 2014, and later ran online courses called “Hustler’s University”, prosecutors with the Miami US attorney’s office said in a 10 August court filing.
The prosecutors said in court filings there was a strong presumption in favor of detention in international extradition cases. They said the Tates could pose a danger to the community if released, citing British authorities’ allegations that they strangled victims during forcible rapes, and that they could try to flee.
The prosecutors also pointed to allegations by authorities in Romania, where the brothers face human-trafficking charges, that they sought to influence witnesses’ statements while released on judicial supervision there. Romanian authorities say the Tates threatened to release private information about alleged victims and bribed an alleged victim, the US prosecutors said.
The brothers’ defense lawyers have said in court filings there was no need to keep them behind bars while the extradition process played out because their “extraordinary public visibility” would make it impractical for them to flee.
They said the witnesses the Tates were alleged to have bribed were women who wanted to speak on their behalf, and said the Tates helped coordinate their travel to Bucharest and hired lawyers for them.
The defense lawyers proposed that Louis release them on the conditions they post bond, surrender their passports and submit to location monitoring.
The legal process for determining whether the Tate brothers may be extradited could take months. Prosecutors in Britain have until 16 September to submit a full extradition request to the state department, US court records show.
The impetus for the brothers’ arrests in Miami was a new set of charges brought by the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) in Britain relating to alleged offenses involving four alleged victims between July 2010 and August 2017.
They had previously faced rape and human-trafficking charges related to three alleged victims, the CPS said. A judge in Britain issued a warrant for their arrests in 2024. They have not appeared in court in Britain to enter a plea to those charges.
The brothers’ extradition is sought to face both sets of charges.
