SDF dissolution earns global praise, but questions remain over Syria's future - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
15:26:42 UTC
00:26:42 KST

Countries throughout the region have praised the decision by the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) to dissolve itself and integrate into the new Syrian security forces.
The process has been in the works since a meeting in March 2025 between SDF commander Mazloum Abdi and Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa. A new meeting this week in Damascus became the endpoint for the process. The SDF is now dissolved.
Regional leaders have praised the process. The concept is that this will lead to peace and unity in Syria and also guarantee Kurdish rights in eastern Syria. The SDF was founded with US support in 2015. It played a major role in defeating ISIS. Its leadership and many of its fighters were Kurdish.
Kurdistan Region President Nechirvan Barzani praised the SDF decision on Wednesday. “He also hailed the chief of the now-dissolved SDF and the Syrian president for the move,” Rudaw media noted.
“I welcome the significant progress made in the process of integrating the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) with the Syrian government forces, as well as the steps taken to implement the agreements reached between them,” Barzani said. “I see this as an important development toward strengthening Syria’s security and stability,” he added.
He added that “we hope that this step will contribute to building a secure future that preserves the rights of all components of Syria, opens broader horizons for developing its relations with Iraq and the Kurdistan Region, and expands cooperation in all fields in a way that serves common interests.”
Countries in the region, such as Qatar, also praised the move. “Saudi Arabia also welcomed the integration, saying it contributes to Syria’s security and stability, while Turkey described the SDF’s dissolution as an important development in strengthening Syrian state authority,” Rudaw noted.
Abroad, many countries are also enthusiastic. French President Emmanuel Macron praised the decision, especially Abdi’s “sense of responsibility.” France has been a key supporter of Kurds and Kurdish rights over the years.
The UK said that it welcomes “the recent announcement on the dissolution of the SDF as an independent military force and its integration alongside DAANES administrative bodies into Syrian state institutions – an important step towards a peaceful, stable and unified Syria.”
US supports new developments, calling them 'absolutely historic'
The US is also happy with how this has turned out. US Ambassador to Turkey Tom Barrack, who is also the US Envoy to Iraq and Syria, said the move is “absolutely historic.” He said that US President Donald Trump’s “far-sighted leadership opened the path for the SDF’s orderly integration into Syrian state institutions – transforming past division into lasting partnership and restoring to the Syrian people the opportunity to shape their common future.”
He added that “recognizing the Kurdish language in education and securing substantive roles for our valued partners Mazloum Abdi and Ilham Ahmed within the Syrian government pays due respect to their leadership, the sacrifices of our Kurdish partners, and the constructive contribution they have made to regional stability – turning yesterday’s separations into tomorrow’s shared purpose.”
Syria's next steps following SDF dissolution
What comes next? The deal to dissolve the SDF is supposed to pave the way for a number of key decisions in the next phase. Mazloum Abdi may take on a new role after having served as a military commander for a decade. Ilham Ehmed and other officials who served key roles in eastern Syria, either with the SDF or civilian components of it such as the SDC or AANES, may take on new roles.
Wladimir van Wilgenburg, a co-author of two books on Syrian Kurds who is an expert and journalist, noted that the terms of the agreement in Damascus will lead to Abdi becoming a presidential adviser. He based his post on the terms of the agreement on Ibrahim Hamidi, the editor-in-chief of al-Majalla.
According to the post, he noted that Ilham Ehmed would become a member of the People’s Assembly of Syria. In addition, Kurdish will become an official language for education, and the Kurdish women’s military unit called the YPJ will “join the Interior Ministry to fight terrorism (as CT units).”
The deal in Damascus could also lead to developments in Turkey with the Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK). This group is also supposed to be disbanding, ending decades of conflict in Turkey. Turkey has long viewed the PKK as linked to the SDF and viewed SDF leaders as “terrorists.” Now this may change. It remains to be seen how this actually develops. Many are concerned that now that the SDF is disbanded, Damascus will have no reason to proceed in good faith.

Kurdish language officially introduced in Syrian schools for first time marking historic shift
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
15:26:42 UTC
00:26:42 KST

DAMASCUS - For the first time, the Kurdish language will formally enter Syria’s education system beginning with the 2026-2027 academic year, after being approved as an elective subject taught for two periods per week, marking a significant shift after decades of restrictions on Kurdish language and cultural identity in Syria.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
The decision comes in implementation of Decree No. 13 of 2026 and executive instructions issued by Syria’s Ministry of Education, in a move aimed at safeguarding cultural and linguistic rights and promoting diversity within an inclusive Syrian national identity.
The introduction of Kurdish instruction is based on the decree issued by Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa on Jan. 16, 2026, which states that Syrian Kurdish citizens are “an essential and integral part of the Syrian people” and that their culture and language are part of Syria’s national identity.
The decree also recognized Kurdish as a national language and permitted its teaching in public and private schools in areas where Kurds constitute a significant proportion of the population, either as an elective subject or as a cultural and educational activity.
The decision marks a shift in the state’s approach to the Kurdish issue. For more than half a century, Syria’s Kurds faced policies of discrimination and exclusion, most notably after the 1962 special census in Hasakah province, which stripped Syrian citizenship from tens of thousands of Kurds.
Restrictions deepened after the Baath Party came to power in 1963, affecting political, cultural, and linguistic life.
Executive decree implementing Kurdish as an elective subject
On Jan. 26, Syria’s Ministry of Education issued executive instructions implementing the decree, approving Kurdish as an elective subject to be taught for two periods per week across all grades covered by the decree. The subject’s grade will be included in students’ overall scores, but the result will not determine whether a student passes or fails.
The National Center for Curriculum Development was tasked with preparing Kurdish-language curricula for all educational levels and began work on Jan. 29 after forming a committee of linguistic and educational experts.
On Aug. 17, the ministry announced that it was recruiting Kurdish-language teachers from both within and outside its existing workforce. Applicants will undergo written and oral examinations to verify their proficiency in Kurdish, as well as training and qualification programs.
Decree represents a 'qualitative shift' in approach to Kurdish issue
Education Minister Mohammad Abdulrahman Tarkou said in press remarks that the decree represents a “qualitative shift” in the historical approach to the Kurdish issue and reinforces a concept of citizenship based on rights and responsibilities.
Tarkou, who is himself a Syrian Kurd, added that the ministry is working to prepare curricula and secure teaching staff, including in eastern Syria, stressing that the goal is to make schools “a space for national belonging, not discrimination and exclusion.”
The decision comes amid broader changes in relations between Damascus and the Kurds, as well as the restructuring of state institutions in northeastern Syria. The 2026-2027 academic year will provide the first practical test of turning the new legal recognition of Kurdish into classroom instruction, after decades in which language remained one of the central issues surrounding the identity and cultural rights of Syria’s Kurdish community.

Nepal and China warn of new flood risks

UEFA to bring criminal complaint against Infantino
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
15:26:00 UTC
00:26:00 KST

UEFA to bring criminal complaint against Infantino
August 27, 2026
Just a day after UEFA reportedly agreed to remove their threat of boycotting FIFA tournaments, European football's governing body has launched a new wave of pressure on FIFA President Gianni Infantino to resign.
UEFA has asked a US federal court for permission to obtain testimony and documents about the creation of the failed FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) subsidiary. FFE was Infantino's plan to sell a stake in FIFA's commercial rights linked to men's and women's World Cups and the Club World Cup.
"UEFA and its counsel are contemplating a Swiss criminal proceeding against Infantino and possibly other FIFA officials for criminal mismanagement under Article 158 of the Swiss Criminal Code," UEFA's lawyers said in a 56-page document cited by several news agencies.
The association, which has been pushing against Infantino staying in power since early August, states that Infantino's development of FFE was not compliant with FIFA's usual governing processes and without consultation with the FIFA Council.
FIFA has not yet responded to UEFA's legal advance.
What do we know about the UEFA complaint against Infantino?
UEFA alleges that Infantino developed his infamous FIFA Forward Enterprise plan in secret with a small group of advisers and investors, bypassing FIFA's normal governance processes.
The European association also alleges that the valuation included in the plan significantly undervalued FIFA's commercial rights, arguing it was not subjected to an open auction or tested by an independent valuation.
UEFA is seeking access to a list of documents pertaining to the background of the FIFA Forward Enterprise plan. These include a meeting held in a New York City hotel on the eve of the World Cup final last month, where several senior FIFA directors were reportedly apprised of the plan.
The New York Times reported that two of the five directors attending refused to endorse the plan, including chief operating officer Kevin Lamour who has since left FIFA.
"Specifically, UEFA seeks documents and communications from FIFA Americas and from FWC2026 concerning.....the governance and internal approval process for the FFE proposal, including all materials presented to the FIFA Council, FIFA Congress, FIFA Bureau, or FIFA Management Board," the document read.
If it successfully obtains the documents, UEFA's plan is then to submit them as part of a complaint it wishes to lodge in Switzerland, where both the European football association and FIFA are based.
"Swiss counsel has confirmed, on the factual record described in this application, that the proceeding is within reasonable contemplation for purposes of Swiss law," it said. "On information and belief, Infantino's actions described herein rise to the level of criminal mismanagement."
Amid considerable pressure led by UEFA — but also from other continental federations like the AFC in Asia and CONCACAF in North and Central America — Infantino and FIFA abandoned the FFE plans altogether. But pressure on Infantino has nonetheless endured.

Canton Zug to invest CHF55 million in ETH research centre
The canton of Zug is to provide CHF55 million ($68.5 million) for the establishment of a joint learning and research centre run by the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology ETH Zurich and representatives of Zug’s business community.
The facility is intended to combine academic education with professional practice on the Tech Cluster Zug AG site in the Göbli area of Zug. According to a report to Parliament, students from ETH Zurich, researchers, lecturers and apprentices from Zug-based companies will eventually work together on industry-relevant, practice-oriented tasks.
The requested funding of CHF55 million relates to the implementation of Phase 1. This comprises the refurbishment of two existing buildings and ten years of operation, expected to commence in 2029/30. According to the documentation, the project is to be financed from the additional revenue generated by the OECD minimum tax.
+ Swiss tax revenues get bump from OECD minimum tax rate
The total cost for the first phase amounts to CHF110 million. In addition to the cantonal funding of CHF55 million, the City of Zug is to contribute CHF27.5 million, the industry partners CHF16.6 million and ETH Zurich CHF10 million.
The final vote will take place after the second reading. The parliamentary procedures are due to be completed by the end of the year. In addition to the Cantonal Council, the proposal also requires the approval of the Zug City Council and the voters in the city of Zug.
The proposal was uncontested during the session. All parliamentary groups, as well as the Education and Economic Affairs Committees, supported the initiative. It was noted that the learning and research centre would combine academic and vocational education. It would create a place “where students, apprentices and professionals work and conduct research together”, said cantonal parliamentarian Michèle Schmid.

Officials urge calm after malaria outbreak kills two staff at Frankfurt airport
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
15:23:22 UTC
00:23:22 KST

German health officials are seeking to reassure the public after two workers at the country’s biggest airport died of malaria.
Mosquito traps have been set up at Frankfurt airport and a mosquito monitoring process is under way. A detailed investigation is being conducted to clarify how the workers contracted the disease.
Since last month, six people are known to have caught malaria tropica – the most dangerous form of the disease – in connection with their work at the airport.
Of the two that have died, one began getting sick at the start of July and the other in mid-August. The four other people who were infected have been treated in hospital and are now out of danger, according to Frankfurt’s public health department.
Letters have been sent to all airport workers to raise awareness about symptoms and urge vigilance. Doctors are being asked to watch out for patients with unexplained fever who work in and around the airport.
In a statement on its website, the health department acknowledged the existence of “airport malaria”, where mosquitoes from malaria-endemic areas are transported in flight cabins or in baggage holds.
It said that because this was “a very rare occurrence”, malaria could easily be overlooked and diagnosis delayed, increasing the chance of death. It said human-to-human transmission was not possible.
The Robert Koch Institute, which is responsible for disease control and prevention in Germany, believes the Frankfurt infection was transmitted by an Anopheles stephensi mosquito imported by plane.
A spokesperson for Fraport, which operates the airport, confirmed that mosquito traps had been set up in and around the site and that mosquitoes had been caught. These are being examined in a tropical medicine laboratory in Antwerp, Belgium.
Peter Tinnemann, the head of Frankfurt’s health department, told the broadcaster Hessische Rundfunk: “The mosquito is probably already dead.”
He said higher temperatures in Germany increased the likelihood of mosquitoes surviving for extended periods but the risk to the population of Frankfurt was low.
“Not everyone should assume that just because they have a headache, fever and nonspecific symptoms they are now infected with malaria because of the case at the airport,” he added.
But he said the rise in malaria cases made it necessary to check whether existing measures, including the disinfection of aircraft and removing breeding grounds for mosquitoes, were being correctly followed.
A study that set out to record all cases of airport and baggage malaria in Europe from 1969 to 2024 found 145 instances, nine of them in Germany.
The Robert Koch Institute said Germany’s last outbreak of airport malaria was also at Frankfurt, in 2023, when a single documented infection was successfully treated.
About 90% of all malaria cases occur in sub-Saharan Africa. Countries from this region with direct flight connections to Frankfurt include Ethiopia, Kenya, Nigeria and Tanzania, all of which have a high to widespread malaria risk. Namibia and South Africa also have direct flights but are considered to be moderate to low risk.

As the world pays homage to the life and legacy of Dolly Parton, François Picard is pleased to welcome Nashville's Irene Kelley, Country musician and celebrated songwriter, alongside her daughter, Justyna Kelley, Country musician, songwriter, actress and producer. For the Kelley family, Dolly Parton’s significance lies in the extraordinary reach of her music, and even more in the way she turned intimate stories into something remarkably universal. Her songs were grounded in home and family, sharing life's immense struggles, while staying true to her values. The Kelleys see Parton as a national treasure who transcended generations, social class and the great political divide.
Her influence, her music, her voice was enough to change the trajectory of a young Irene Kelley. And her music subsequently was generational as Kelley passed on her passion for country, and most notably Dolly's music, to both of her daughters, Justyna and Sara Jean, each of them distinct in their own right. What made Dolly exceptional was her ability to hold qualities that are too often regarded as polar opposites: “glamorous and grounded,” “funny and profound,” commercially successful yet exceptionally generous to America's youth, the underprivileged and underrepresented.
During an era of deep polarization, her commitment to connect with all walks of life became part of her cultural legacy. She “loved everybody” and “accepted everyone.” That consistency between the stories she told, the values she held dear and the life she lived helps explain why her passing offers us all pause to reflect on a life fully lived, and celebrate Dolly's life, legacy and her art of celebrating all that it is to be human.

China and Nepal both warned on Thursday of fresh risks of flooding in the Himalayas as two lakes that have developed on either side of their border threaten to burst, in an area still grappling with this week's catastrophic flood.

Nepal's disaster authority issued a notice on Thursday warning that a lake formed by debris blocking a river at the flood site is rising and at risk of bursting.
Heeding the warning, some rescue workers in Nepal began moving towards higher ground on Thursday.
Among them was Pawan Koirala, who began moving away from the river bed along with his team of 13 after the warning was issued.

====================================================================================================

After two decades, Palestinians prepare to vote for a new political leadership. But will it change anything?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
15:20:30 UTC
00:20:30 KST

Palestinian factions that have spent two decades in bitter — and at times violent — division are joining forces ahead of elections announced for November, forming the broadest political coalition seen in the occupied territories in years.
Following a series of talks in Cairo, the “Alliance of National Forces” was formed with the specific objective of running together in the next Palestinian legislative elections. This coalition includes Hamas, the Palestinian Islamic Jihad (PIJ), the Democratic Reform Current (a dissident Fatah current led by the UAE-based former Fatah Gaza leader, Mohammad Dahlan), the National Democratic Forum (another dissident Fatah current led by Yasser Arafat’s nephew, Nasser Al-Qudwah), and the Popular Resistance Committees (a Gaza-based organization founded by former Fatah member Jamal Abu Samhadana in 2001).
Palestinian left-wing factions, namely the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine and the Democratic Front for the Liberation of Palestine, are expected to announce in the coming days whether they will join.
The alliance, set in motion by a decree from Palestinian Authority (PA) President Mahmoud Abbas calling for new elections in late November, disrupts two decades of political stagnation that have weakened Palestinian political leverage at a moment of accelerating Israeli annexation.
According to the Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics (PCBS), about 64% of Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza are under the age of 30 – for most, this would be their first voting experience.
For many Palestinians, the mere prospect of elections is in itself a chance to reunite Palestinian politics and more efficiently confront Israel’s destruction of Gaza and annexation of the West Bank under a united national leadership. The fact that the coalition itself is so diverse proves the point: Palestinians across the board have a desire for change after two decades of Palestinian politics being reduced to the division between the mainstream Fatah leadership and Hamas.
However, neither elections nor political alliances guarantee a united Palestinian leadership or a repaired Palestinian political system. Whatever outcome emerges will face serious internal and external challenges, including private interests that have accumulated over years of stagnant politics, international pressures to limit Palestinian political expression, and the fundamental constraints of democratic reforms under military occupation.
All of this is taking shape in a political climate that has never been more hostile to Palestinian political life. Since October 7, 2023, Israel has de facto banned organized Palestinian politics — through mass arrests, administrative detention, the targeting of community leaders, and the criminalization of political expression — even as elections are being announced and coalitions formed. A new legislative council, if it ever convenes, would need to produce a united Palestinian vision and project to unite the West Bank and Gaza, at precisely the moment when the conditions for doing so have been most severely undermined.
Repressed politics
Political activity has always been a risk for Palestinians under Israeli occupation. Most Palestinian political groups were born in the context of resistance to occupation, and have been targeted with arrest, even in the social branches, student movements, and unions affiliated with those parties — including parties that have never engaged in armed resistance, such as the Palestinian People’s Party (formerly the Communist Party).
The First Intifada, between 1987 and 1993, produced an irreversible outburst of political activism, creating a space for political expression within Palestinian politics, even under the Palestinian Authority, which was founded in the wake of the Oslo Accords. Even Hamas, which opposed the Accords, joined this framework in 2006, running for seats in the PA’s legislative council.
Following October 7, 2023, Israel’s crackdown on Palestinian politics spiked dramatically. The number of Palestinian detainees in Israeli prisons doubled – from 5,000 on the eve of October 7 to more than 10,000 by the end of 2025, half of them held without charges under “administrative detention orders.”
“Arrests extended to former detainees, social activists, community leaders, and basically anybody with a leading role in their community,” Ayah Shreiteh, from the Palestinian Prisoners’ Club, told Mondoweiss. “Before October 7, the detention conditions of Palestinian prisoners had already been deteriorating, but then everything deteriorated.”
Shreiteh details that in Israeli jails, “food quantity and quality deteriorated, Israeli prison guards raided cells on a weekly, sometimes daily basis, medical neglect became widespread, and cells with an average surface of five or six square meters that usually held up to six prisoners were now being crammed with nine to 12 prisoners.” This, added to reports of sexual assault on Palestinian prisoners in Israeli jails, raised the stakes on doing any kind of politics in Palestinian society, especially under the label of parties or groups.
This impact was palpable in the weak participation in the April municipal elections earlier this year. During the previous local elections in 2022, Nablus had six electoral lists, Hebron had six, and Ramallah had five. This year, only two lists competed in Hebron, while in Nablus and Ramallah, there was no contest at all, since only one list registered for each city.
The competing forces
Hamas, which led the attack on October 7, has come under the most direct pressure from Israel’s crackdown and the devastation of Gaza. The wiping out of Gaza, and the pounding of Hamas’s fighting force, subsequently leading to its acceptance of the once-unacceptable principle of disarming under the urgency of reconstruction, the group has lost much of its capacity to advocate for its traditional program centered around armed resistance. Through its alliance with other forces — including dissident Fatah currents with strong support bases within Fatah itself — Hamas is attempting to stage a comeback as an opposition force to the dominant Abbas leadership.
The PRC has remained outside electoral politics since its formation as an armed resistance group in 2001, while the PIJ has historically been disinterested in elections across its 40-year existence. Both groups have their main social base in Gaza and a legacy of resistance independent from Hamas. Their alliance with Hamas signals building a political case for resistance that extends beyond Hamas alone.
The most surprising aspect of this alliance is the inclusion of Muhammad Dahlan’s “Democratic Reform Current.” The former Gaza Fatah leader built his reputation as a former Palestinian intelligence officer whose crackdown on Hamas in Gaza in the late 1990s and early 2000s made him the main internal nemesis of the Islamic group at the time. He retains strong support within Gaza’s Fatah base.
Naser al-Qudwah’s National Democratic Forum rounds out the alliance. A former diplomat, physician, and nephew of the late Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat, he presents himself as a statesman holding an institutionalist and legalist line, with support among the Palestinian upper-middle classes.
Together, these forces pose a serious challenge to the dominant leadership of Fatah’s Mahmoud Abbas and his deputy-president, Hussein al-Sheikh, who have monopolized Palestinian representation for the past two decades. If the left-wing PFLP and the DFLP join the coalition, the challenge would be overwhelming. This could produce one of two familiar scenarios: Abbas could call off elections as he did in 2021, or if elections proceed, a coalition government forms, and Western countries boycott it because Hamas and the PIJ are a part of it. That’s what happened in 2006.
But if a new legislative council gets to form a new government and exercise its legislative and oversight authority, it would confront a whole other set of challenges.
International pressure and private interests
These elections do not unfold in a vacuum. The U.S. and European countries have been pushing the PA to reform. Two years later, Trump’s peace plan included the same demand.
In November 2025, a European Commission spokesperson said that the PA needs to “implement reforms” to continue receiving EU aid.
In responding to these demands, the PA has already revoked its financial support program to families of those killed or imprisoned by Israeli forces. The PA also agreed in 2024 to remove content referring to historical Palestine or to the history of the Palestinian struggle from school books.
This pressure appears to be one driver behind the most significant amendment to the Palestinian elections law, passed by presidential decree last month: any candidate or group running for elections must adhere to the political platform of the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO), which means they accept all agreements signed with Israel and adhere to a two-state solution framework through U.S.-mediated negotiations as the sole path to Palestinian statehood. The condition is already generating controversy.
Limits of free politics under occupation
A new legislative council would also face challenges that go beyond internal politics. The status of the Gaza Strip and its relationship to U.S. President Donald Trump’s so-called “Board of Peace,” Israel’s violations of signed agreements through expanding settlement activities into areas of the West Bank supposedly under PA control, and changes to land and building permits laws facilitating annexation — all of these are political questions any new elected body would have to address. All would be subject to pressure by the U.S., the EU, and Arab countries with the leverage and interest to contain any new Palestinian political stance.
“The new legislative council might have to clash with internal private Palestinian interests, but also with the Israeli occupation, and possibly with Western countries who are pushing for reforms, and who would set the limits and the direction of these reforms,” Isam Abdeen, a lawyer and human rights advocate, told Mondoweiss.
For Mustafa Barghouthi, the new elections are more than a political competition. “These elections are about the Palestinian people’s right to democratic participation, which they have been denied for many years, and therefore they need to be free, without political conditions,” the General Secretary of the Palestinian National Initiative told Mondoweiss. “The coming elections need to be a tool, not only to reunite Palestinians, but also to serve as a tool to resist Israeli plans, the first of which is the separation of Gaza and the West Bank.”
Barghouthi added that “there needs to be a national dialogue to agree on these basics, to guarantee that the elections will fulfill their goal.”
Although Palestinian elections are a genuine and longstanding demand of Palestinians, their effectiveness and the scope of change remain bound to Palestine’s capacity to sustain a free, independent, and inclusive political life – a basic condition made very difficult under the continuity of Israeli occupation, and the threat of full annexation and displacement.

Kremlin Asks North Korea for Heavier KN-30 Ballistic Missiles Ahead of Winter Strikes on Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
15:19:19 UTC
00:19:19 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Kremlin Asks North Korea for Heavier KN-30 Ballistic Missiles Ahead of Winter Strikes on Ukraine
Russia is negotiating with North Korea for a new military aid package that could include more powerful KN-30 ballistic missiles for use against Ukraine during the coming fall and winter, Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence (HUR) representative Andrii Cherniak told Ukrainian media outlet LIGA.net on August 27.
According to HUR, Moscow has requested the KN-30, a heavier member of North Korea’s short-range ballistic missile family that Ukrainian intelligence assesses as roughly three times more powerful than the KN-23 and KN-24 missiles Russia already uses against Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Cherniak stressed, however, that Ukrainian intelligence has not yet detected any transfer of KN-30 missiles from North Korea to Russia.
The talks are part of a much broader package of military support Moscow reportedly hopes to secure from Pyongyang.
Ukrainian intelligence previously said Russia expects to receive as many as 120 ballistic missiles and six launchers, along with a separate missile unit of up to 90 North Korean personnel and between 30,000 and 50,000 additional North Korean troops.
Russia has already received 40 KN-23 and KN-24 ballistic missiles from the requested package, according to Cherniak. He said Russian forces used two of those missiles during a recent attack on Ukraine.
“Missile terror is part of the Kremlin’s strategy aimed at increasing fear, fueling destructive processes and conflicts within Ukraine. In this way, the aggressor is putting pressure on Ukrainian society and trying to undermine our resilience,” Cherniak said.
The KN-30 is a Western designation associated with North Korea’s Hwasong-11C ballistic missile, also referred to as Hwasong-11Da. It is an enlarged member of the Hwasong-11 short-range ballistic missile family and is launched from a mobile ground-based platform using a solid-fuel propulsion system.
The missile was first publicly displayed during a military parade in Pyongyang on January 14, 2021, and its first known test launch followed on March 25 of that year.
During testing, the missile demonstrated a range of at least 600 kilometers, or roughly 370 miles.
North Korea has claimed the weapon can carry a warhead weighing as much as 2.5 metric tons, although that figure has not been independently confirmed.
Such a payload would make the missile particularly destructive against fixed targets, while its road-mobile launcher could complicate efforts to locate and destroy the system before launch.
The reported request comes as Russia continues relying heavily on ballistic missiles in large-scale attacks against Ukrainian cities and critical infrastructure, particularly during combined strikes involving drones and other missile types.
Final details of the next North Korean military aid package could be determined during expected September talks between Russian leader Vladimir Putin and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, according to Cherniak.
Previously, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha stated that Ukraine would treat any North Korean missile launchers deployed on Russian territory as legitimate military targets and move to destroy them.

Defense Forces test new robotic turrets with assault rifles on front line
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
15:19:00 UTC
00:19:00 KST

Defense Forces test new robotic turrets with assault rifles on front line
According to Ukrinform, the Ministry of Defense reported this on its website.
The strike systems were developed based on technical specifications provided by Brave1, a defense innovation cluster.
The project received grant funding, and the developers needed less than six months to go from the initial idea to a working prototype.
Using standard Kalashnikov assault rifles makes it possible to reduce production costs and rapidly scale the deployment of ground robotic systems on the front line.
The system is built on a four-wheel chassis with airless tires and features a protected body. This design makes it resistant to shrapnel, bullets, and punctures while allowing it to maneuver across difficult terrain.
The weapon module features a twin turret capable of mounting two assault rifles simultaneously. This significantly increases the density of fire during offensive and defensive operations against enemy infantry. The turret can also be mounted on other wheeled and tracked ground robotic systems.
Several Ukrainian Defense Forces units are already testing these systems in combat conditions. In particular, there are confirmed cases of the Security Service of Ukraine's Special Operations Center "A" successfully using them against enemy ambushes involving "waiting" drones.
The Ministry of Defense is systematically working to introduce robotic systems. These systems are intended to take over the most dangerous tasks on the front line, minimizing the presence of infantry in areas of direct fire contact.
"We are robotizing the front to reduce risks to infantry and save the lives of our soldiers," the ministry said.
As Ukrinform reported, since the beginning of 2026, ground robotic systems have carried out more than 100,000 missions in place of Ukrainian troops on the front line.

Nepal flooding: 'We are disconnected from Kathmandu'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
15:15:00 UTC
00:15:00 KST

Nepal flooding: 'We are disconnected from Kathmandu'
August 27, 2026
With the death toll in Nepal well into the hundreds and rising following a massive flash flood on Wednesday, the full scope of destruction remains unclear.
People from the affected areas told DW that many villages remain both physically and electronically cut off from the capital, Kathmandu.
Bidhya Rajput, a journalist based in the capital, said her home in the Sole village in Nepal's Nuwakot District was swept away by the Trisuli River.
"As far as we know, only four or five people from Sole village could save their lives by fleeing towards the hills. Others couldn't make their way as the floods came up suddenly," she told DW.
The government has declared Nuwakot, along with Rasuwa and Dhading districts, to be the most affected by the deadly floods.
Rajput told DW her husband's parents remain missing. Her father-in-law, a teacher, may have been caught in the flood while returning home after work, according to the school principal.
Rajput's husband has left for the village in search for news on his family members, despite the roads being damaged and swept away in many places. Rajput said that there are no further updates from the village as there has been no electricity or mobile communication since early morning on Thursday.
"The state's rescue and relief efforts have been centered mostly on bigger cities," she said, adding that "state assistance is yet to reach Sole."
Villagers said the same area was affected by flooding last year, but many villagers managed to get to higher ground and the water did not reach as high as on Tuesday.
"Had the villagers received early warning information, [and] could have presumed that this time floods would be so massive, they could have fled to safe locations like last year," Rajput said. "This time, they couldn't get even that chance."
'Two of my close relatives are missing'
But Usha Kiran Timsena, an opposition politician from Nuwakot, said police and local officials did issue a warning that a massive flood was coming. However, many people in the area simply didn't account for the scale and speed of the mass of water.
"Many those who were a bit far from riversides took it lightly and couldn't flee once the flood reaches to their places," she told DW.
"Two of my close relatives have been missing since yesterday morning. There has been no further update or contact since then."
Authorities said that more than three dozen bridges, including vehicular and suspension bridges, as well as a dozen hydropower dams, have been destroyed by the floods.
Sujan Lohani from Dhading told DW that he never imagined that the flooding and destruction caused by the Trishuli River could be so massive and widespread.
The main bridge over the Trishuli River, connecting his district headquarters with the capital Kathmandu, has been swept away.
"I am worried that my cousin is now in the village," he told DW. "We are disconnected from Kathmandu."
Hundreds of survivors airlifted from affected areas
Nepal's authorities are racing to reach survivors in the affected areas. With over a 1,300 people still missing, including hundreds of foreign nationals, as of Thursday, Nepal's neighbors India and China are coordinating with Kathmandu on the disaster response.
Rescue teams are airlifting stranded and injured people to the capital, while police, military and ordinary citizens are building temporary shelters for the displaced.
"We are putting our all-out efforts to rescue people alive," Nepal's Minister for Information and Communication Bikram Timilsina told DW.
Timilsina represents the flood-hit Nuwakot-1 constituency in the House of Representatives and is currently in the affected region. He described the destruction as enormous
"Entire villages have been swept away. Many have tragically lost their lives. Many are out of contact," he said.
"I don't think our state mechanism had ever imagined a flood and disaster of such magnitude," Timilsina said.
At the same time, Timilsina noted said the state has mobilized all its resources, including more than a dozen helicopters, to transport survivors to safety and deliver aid. At least 414 stranded people, including 164 foreigners were airlifted by mid-day Thursday, according to the minister.
What do experts say about the cause of the flood?
Scientists are still debating the exact cause of the natural disaster, despite Beijing claiming it was triggered by a high-altitude glacier collapse.
Sudip Thakuri, a climate scientist and associate professor at Central Department of Environmental Science at Nepal's Tribhuvan University, told DW that preliminary assessments indicate the flood was likely triggered by an avalanche on the Nepali side of the Nepal-China border.
"So far, what we have concluded is that a massive avalanche initially blocked a river flowing southwards from the Tibetan Autonomous Region of China. Once the avalanche-created landslide dam burst, it might also have swept away a subglacial lake downstream, triggering massive flooding," he said.
Another climate scientist, Rijan Raj Kayastha, who teaches at Kathmandu University, warned of the possibility of further flooding due to other glacial lakes in the area.
Separately, Chinese authorities also warned that another lake in Tibet's Gyirong, upstream from the flooded area in Nepal, was already overflowing and that another 3 millions of tons of water were expected to enter the lake over the next three days.

UN envoy welcomes US removal of Syria from state sponsors of terrorism list, urges election preparations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
15:14:48 UTC
00:14:48 KST

Berk Kutay Gokmen
27 August 2026•Update: 27 August 2026
UN Deputy Special Envoy for Syria Claudio Cordone on Thursday welcomed the US decision to remove Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism, saying the move could support economic recovery, while stressing the urgency of preparing for elections at the end of the country’s political transition.
Briefing the UN Security Council, Cordone said the decision could help create “more favorable conditions for economic recovery, investment, and broader international engagement with Syria.”
Citing an International Monetary Fund mission to Damascus last month, he said economic recovery was accelerating, with double-digit growth projected for 2026. However, he warned that “widespread poverty and renewed inflation mean conditions remain very difficult for most Syrians.”
Cordone said Syria could not address the challenges of its transition alone and called for greater international support for humanitarian, recovery and development needs, as well as for creating conditions that enable safe, dignified and voluntary returns.
“The success of the political transition will ultimately be measured by whether all Syrians feel represented in state institutions and able to participate meaningfully in shaping their country’s future,” he said, relaying a message delivered by UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres during his recent visit to Syria.
On security, Cordone expressed concern over continued Israeli military activity in southern Syria, including ground incursions, house searches and the destruction of private and agricultural property.
He said Israel’s continued presence east of the ceasefire line violates Syria’s sovereignty and territorial integrity and is inconsistent with the 1974 Disengagement of Forces Agreement. He also reiterated that the Golan Heights remain occupied Syrian territory under international law.
At the same time, he welcomed recent direct Israeli-Syrian contacts and talks in Jordan, as well as US efforts to mediate a security arrangement.
“Diplomacy must prevail, and negotiation should progress within the framework of international law,” Cordone said.
He said the UN would continue working closely with Syrian authorities and the UN country team, with the goal of expanding cooperation through the restructured UN presence in Damascus and supporting a “serious, successful transition.”

00:13:56 KST

HANGZHOU, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- East China's Zhejiang Province raised its typhoon emergency response to Level I, the highest level, at 8 p.m. Thursday as Typhoon Saudel, the 18th typhoon of this year, is forecast to make landfall in the province.
At 5 p.m., the typhoon's center was located about 320 km east of Wenzhou, packing maximum wind speeds of 45 meters per second near its center. It is moving at 10 to 15 km per hour and is expected to make landfall along the coast of Zhejiang from early morning to afternoon on Friday.
Hu Yaowen, chief engineer of the Zhejiang Provincial Emergency Management Department, warned that the typhoon's impact coincides with the astronomical high tide, likely creating a combination of strong winds, towering waves, high tides and heavy rainfall.
He added that previous continuous heavy rains have kept rivers, lakes and reservoirs at high levels, and the new round of downpours could easily trigger mountain torrents, mudslides and landslides.
To prepare for the typhoon, Zhejiang has carried out comprehensive risk inspections. More than 4,000 monitoring personnel have conducted over 19,000 patrols at more than 7,200 geological hazard potential sites and risk zones, while 564 geological experts have been dispatched to 73 counties to assist in risk identification.
In terms of flood control, plain river networks across the province have drained 437 million cubic meters of water, and large and medium-sized reservoirs have pre-released 456 million cubic meters.
All 14,682 marine fishing vessels in Zhejiang have taken shelter in harbors, and 47,983 crew members and 1,906 aquaculture workers have been evacuated ashore, ensuring that no people, vessels or activities remain at sea. ■

by sportswriters Zhang Zewei and Yuan Yukuan
TIANJIN, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- Japan and Thailand both clean swept their opponents 3-0 in the quarterfinals here on Thursday to reach the semifinals of the 2026 Asian Women's Volleyball Championship.
Japan raced to an 11-4 lead in the opening set and then scored six straight points behind powerful serving from outside hitter Yukiko Wada to widen the gap before comfortably taking the set 25-14.
Chinese Taipei improved in the second set, taking a 6-2 lead. However, the team faced pressure midway as Japan's two outside hitters consistently scored with attacks, sparking an 8-1 run and reversing the momentum. Japan ultimately overcame Chinese Taipei to win the set 25-21.
The Japanese women took full control in the third set where they prevailed 25-13.
Japan outblocked Chinese Taipei 11-1 and produced four aces, compared to nil for Chinese Taipei. Three Japanese players scored in double figures, with Wada Yukiko recording a match-high 19 points.
Despite missing out on the semifinals, Chinese Taipei middle blocker Yeh Yu-Wen said the team was fortunate to compete on a world-class stage against top Asian teams.
"We have played two strong teams, China and Japan, over the past two days and learned a lot from them. Japan in particular are similar to us in stature. What they are able to do in terms of physical conditioning, mentality and tactical execution is something we also need to learn from and strive for," Yeh said.
Thailand defeated South Korea 25-20, 25-18 and 25-21 in Thursday's other quarterfinal match to set up a semifinal clash with Japan.
Opposite Pimpichaya Kokram scored a match-high 19 points for Thailand with outside hitters Sasipapron Janthawisut and Chatchu-On Moksri adding 16 and 12 respectively. Thailand was also better from the service line, firing six aces, compared to South Korea's one.
"Thailand play at a very fast tempo. We will carefully study their match videos and prepare accordingly. We hope to perform at our best," said Japan outside hitter Mayu Ishikawa.
The other two quarterfinals will be played on Friday with China facing Vietnam and Indonesia taking on Iran. ■

====================================================================================================

Feature: Beyond palace -- Chinese, Turkish folk wares tell shared story of everyday life
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
23:13:28 CST
00:13:28 KST

ISTANBUL, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- Entering the historic Tiled Pavilion in the tranquil courtyard of the Istanbul Archaeology Museums, visitors are immediately greeted by the refined geometry of Ottoman imperial tiles.
Tucked among the pavilion's grand displays is a distinctly different style of pottery: rustic plates and pitchers decorated with loosely painted sailboats and playful depictions of lions, camels, and horses.
These are Canakkale ceramics, a vibrant folk tradition that emerged in the late 17th century. Unlike the highly regulated Iznik tiles produced for Ottoman palaces, these wares were crafted for everyday use by ordinary people, offering a glimpse into daily life in the past.
Thousands of kilometers away, a parallel tradition with roots stretching back over a millennium flourished in China, particularly in the historic porcelain center of Jingdezhen: Minyao, or folk kilns. This tradition continues today, with household wares made by and for ordinary people, often featuring freely painted scenes of everyday life.
Both folk traditions are gaining renewed attention today. In July, Jingdezhen's traditional ceramic handicraft sites were added to the UNESCO World Heritage List, while traditional Canakkale ceramic production, which ceased in the mid-20th century, is now also undergoing a revival.
"Historically, cultural links between China and the Ottoman Empire have been studied largely through the lens of imperial porcelains," Turan Takaoglu, a researcher at the Archaeology Department of Canakkale Onsekiz Mart University, told Xinhua.
However, Canakkale ceramics and China's Minyao provide richer soil for cultural study.
"When we study Canakkale ceramics, China's Minyao tradition has always been an important reference," Takaoglu said. "Comparative studies could bring the two ceramic communities together at the academic level, allowing both sides to learn from each other."
For Ke Guoxing, general manager of the Jingdezhen porcelain official flagship store in Istanbul, the importance of Minyao lies in what it reveals about ordinary society.
"Imperial ware tells us about the court; Minyao tells us about society," he said.
Unlike imperial porcelain, Minyao was produced in far greater volumes for everyday use -- from family tableware and storage jars to tea-house cups and pieces for weddings and festivals. Freed from strict palace regulations, its decoration drew instead on daily life and popular beliefs, featuring fish, birds, auspicious symbols, and folk tales, Ke said.
Now, with this renewed attention, cooperation between museums and cultural institutions of the two countries can be further elevated.
Rahmi Asal, director of the Istanbul Archaeology Museums, said temporary exhibitions, expert exchanges and joint publications could provide practical avenues for deeper cooperation between Türkiye and China.
He proposed a joint exhibition of Jingdezhen Minyao and Canakkale ceramics, allowing visitors to explore both traditions through the lens of everyday life and reframing Chinese-Turkish ceramic exchange as a story not of emperors and sultans, but of the craftsmen and communities behind these objects. ■

Foreigners jostle to secure UK residency rights before rules tighten
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
15:12:22 UTC
00:12:22 KST

Foreigners jostle to secure UK residency rights before rules tighten
The proposed reforms to a scheme offering permanent residency would double the qualification period from five to 10 years
The United Kingdom has seen a spike in the number of migrants applying for citizenship and permanent settlement ahead of a planned government clampdown.
Government data shows what appears to be a rush to secure residency rights in response to changes announced by Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood that would force migrants to wait longer before they can gain them.
The Home Office said 199,628 people were granted settlement, giving them the right to live, work and study in the UK permanently, in the year through June 2026. Most granted indefinite leave to remain can then apply for citizenship after 12 months.
These figures represent a 24 per cent increase from a year earlier and the highest number since 2010. Over the same 12 month period, 245,520 people were granted British citizenship.
Although that was slightly lower than a year earlier, the number of citizenship applications surged 17 per cent to a record 315,224. There was a 44 per cent increase in the number of citizenship applications refused.
The proposed reforms to indefinite leave to remain, which offers permanent settlement rights and a route to citizenship, would double the qualification period from five to 10 years and are controversial among members of the governing Labour Party.

Ukraine to get 90% of drones under planned Finnish production deal, Finland’s president says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
15:09:22 UTC
00:09:22 KST

Finnish President Alexander Stubb said Ukraine would receive about 90% of the drones that Finnish companies build under a planned Finland–Ukraine framework agreement, Mi-Ukraina reported on 26 August. Three days earlier in Kyiv, he said the other 10% would stay in Finland.
The planned arrangement follows a broader European shift toward co-production with Ukraine rather than supplying weapons from existing stockpiles. Drones have shaped much of the fighting on both sides since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, and Russia has repeatedly struck defense plants inside Ukraine—a Bayraktar plant under construction in Kyiv was hit four times in six months by August 2025—pushing Ukrainian makers to expand production into allied countries, Finland among them.
Asked what still had to be agreed before production could begin, Stubb said nothing did.
"Everything is done. There is a so-called framework agreement on drones that we're working on. It's more about cooperation between states—that is, Zelenskyy and me. And the companies between themselves do what they have to do. I think the doors are already open," Stubb said.
He said the 90/10 ratio is common practice in corporate contracts and that companies would determine the pace of production after finalizing their decisions. Some details could remain classified because of military secrecy, he said.
At a press conference on 23 August after the Nordic-Baltic Eight summit with Ukraine, Stubb had described the deal as still taking shape. He said seven Finnish defense companies interested in cooperation with Ukraine, including on maritime drone production, had traveled to Kyiv with him and that one had already provided production estimates.
"The companies are making actual deals. I'm looking forward to the results, but it seems one of the companies has already provided data on the number of drones that can be produced in Finland. And I think the deal will follow approximately the so-called 90/10 proportion. So 90% of the output is supplied to Ukraine, and 10% stays in Finland," Stubb said, according to Unian.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on 23 August that three of the seven Finnish companies present had already signed agreements for joint production, including drones. Yle identified the three as Patria, Insta, and Boomeranger, saying they had signed letters of intent with Ukrainian counterparts. Patria and the Ukrainian company General Chereshnia signed a memorandum of intent to produce defense drones in Finland, Patria announced.
Separately, Ukrainian drone maker Airlogix and Finnish technology company Innokas signed a letter of intent to establish joint drone manufacturing in Finland under Ukraine's "Build with Ukraine" initiative. Ukrainian firm TAF Industries and Finnish company Summa Defence had signed a similar agreement earlier under the same initiative.
Zelenskyy said the cooperation would combine Ukrainian combat experience with Finnish technology. Stubb said Finland already faces hybrid attacks, from undersea cable sabotage to drones, and treats sabotage as a standing risk to the plants, adding that Finland ranks among the largest per-capita suppliers of military equipment to Ukraine.
From support to co-production—and a two-way expertise swap
Stubb said the planned arrangement is not far from Denmark's model of directly financing Ukrainian defense production, according to Yle.
Zelenskyy said the agreements cover drones built in Finland for Ukraine and Europe, expanded maritime unmanned systems, and a plant for ground robotic systems, and Stubb said the documents signed during the visit concerned air, land, and sea.
The Finnish president said in the Mi-Ukraina interview that Europe's relationship with Ukraine has changed since the full-scale invasion. Ukraine once needed European support, while Europe now needs Ukraine's battlefield experience, he said. What Finland learned, by his account: trench warfare is over, a 40-kilometer kill zone means tanks firing at shorter range have no role, and Ukraine holds more data on modern war than the rest of Europe combined.

Poland does not want nuclear warheads on its territory, deputy defence minister says
BRUSSELS, Aug 27 - Poland does not want to have nuclear warheads on its territory, Deputy Defence Minister Pawel Zalewski said on Thursday.
"No — that is what I would like to say very clearly and openly. Poland does not want to have nuclear warheads on its territory," Zalewski told reporters when asked whether future U.S. military presence in Poland could include nuclear capability.
"We want to participate in NATO nuclear deterrence, which does not mean having nuclear warheads on our territory," Zalewski said at NATO headquarters in Brussels.
He added that Poland was interested in increasing the permanent U.S. military presence under Washington's Force Posture Review and referenced U.S. President Donald Trump's remarks earlier this year on the possibility of sending additional troops to Poland.
Washington announced a six-month review of U.S. troop deployments in Europe in June. According to a document seen by Reuters it will create at least four sets of options for Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth by November 6, well ahead of a December deadline.
"We treat President Trump's decision as a tool to improve European security, aligned with the Pentagon's concept of NATO 3.0. It means that it's due to Europeans to defend conventionally, but the U.S. maintains an extremely important role to support European armed forces," he said.
"Of course the starting point is a message sent to the public opinion by President Trump about sending 5,000 American soldiers to Poland on a permanent basis," he added.
In May, Trump surprised NATO allies by pledging to send an additional 5,000 troops to Poland. REUTERS

USS Abraham Lincoln to visit port in Thailand after more than 250 days at sea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
15:05:55 UTC
00:05:55 KST

The USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier is set to make a temporary stop in Thailand next week as it heads back to the United States, Thai navy officials said, after spending more than 250 consecutive days at sea supporting US operations against Iran amid recent reports of poor living conditions and low morale onboard the vessel.
The Lincoln left the Middle East several days ago after being relieved by the USS George Washington, and is now heading home to San Diego. A Thai navy official told Reuters this week that the carrier was expected to make a brief port visit in Thailand next week for the crew to rest and recuperate before continuing their journey home.
“The stop is a routine port visit intended to allow personnel to rest and recuperate … as well as to receive logistical support,” the spokesperson for the Thai navy said.
Earlier this week, the Thai navy said that three ships from a US navy carrier strike group would be making a brief port call in eastern Thailand to allow personnel to rest. No military exercises would take place during the visit, the statement added. The Thai navy did not identify the vessels or provide a date.
The planned stop comes as the Lincoln’s deployment has faced scrutiny in recent weeks amid reports of poor living conditions onboard among its crew. Family members of sailors have described shortages of supplies and water, plumbing problems, low morale, and worsening mental health among the roughly 5,000 personnel on the carrier. The Navy Times also reported that there had been several attempts by sailors to jump overboard.
On Wednesday, the wife of a sailor who jumped overboard told MS Now that her husband, who she said had since returned to the US, was now facing disciplinary action from the navy.
Charging documents viewed by MS Now reportedly accuse the sailor of violating Article 83 for “malingering”, which is defined as someone who, “with the intent to avoid work, duty, or service”, fakes “illness, physical disablement, mental lapse, or mental derangement” or “intentionally inflicts self-injury”.
The document also reportedly accuses the sailor of violating Article 86 for “absence without leave” which is when the service member, without authority, “fails to go to his appointed place of duty at the time prescribed”, “goes from that place” or “absents himself or remains absent from his unit, organization, or place of duty at which he is required to be at the time prescribed”.
The couple, both 19, have a three-year-old son and welcomed a daughter in February while he was deployed. His wife told the outlet that he had requested paternity leave but was denied.
The sailor is now reportedly facing non-judicial punishment, which MS Now notes is typically used by commanding officers to address minor rule-breaking without a court martial.
The navy did not immediately respond to a request for comment from the Guardian. In a statement to MS Now about the decision to pursue a non-judicial punishment for the sailor, a navy official said that “the Navy is fully committed to the health and wellbeing of every Sailor”.
“We strive to foster environments that support mental health by removing barriers to seeking help, increasing awareness of resources, and taking appropriate action when someone is in need,” they added. “Mental health resources are available to our Sailors 24/7, and asking for help is a sign of strength.”
The Lincoln left San Diego on 21 November bound for the Pacific, but was redirected to the Middle East. It has since spent more than 250 consecutive days without a significant port visit.
Reports about the conditions onboard have prompted several Democratic lawmakers to demand answers from the Pentagon.

Meta’s $18bn settlement: How social platforms will change for child users
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
15:01:57 UTC
00:01:57 KST

Meta’s $18bn settlement: How social platforms will change for child users
From a night curfew to a two-hour limit, Instagram and Facebook will introduce new features for children in the US.
Meta has agreed to a landmark $18bn settlement in a major US federal case accusing it of endangering children, the terms of which will force the social media giant to introduce new safety features to platforms including Instagram and Facebook.
The social media giant has faced an avalanche of legal cases against it this year, mostly arguing that it deliberately designed its platforms to be addictive and that they have harmed children. It has already lost two of these and been forced to pay damages.
Under the agreement, child users under the age of 18 will see a slew of changes to their Facebook and Instagram accounts, ranging from night curfews to two-hour usage limits, which Meta must implement as part of the settlement reached on Wednesday with 48 US states.
The agreement could have a global ripple effect as several countries around the world are already taking regulatory action against Meta and other social media companies over their platforms.
So, what is in the settlement Meta has reached in the United States, and how will Instagram and Facebook change for users?
What was the lawsuit about?
Twenty-nine US states sued Meta, accusing it of designing its platforms in ways that “encourage addictive behaviour, fail to verify users’ ages, encourage adolescents to bypass parental controls, and inadequately safeguard against harmful content and/or intentionally amplify harmful and exploitative content”, according to filings at the Court of Appeal in California.
The first four of the states that originally filed their federal lawsuit against Meta in 2023 – California, Kentucky, Colorado and New Jersey – began their cases in a California federal trial last week.
The attorneys general bringing the case also asked the court to order that changes be made to Meta’s platforms to protect young social media users. In particular, they demanded that Meta introduce a process of parental verification for teenage users; change its “dopamine-manipulating” algorithms; remove image filters for users’ personal images; forbid the creation of multiple accounts; and end “disappearing” messages and posts.
The lawsuit also alleged Meta had violated the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act by collecting, retaining and using personal data from children under 13 without proper parental consent.
In February this year, Meta lost a multimillion-dollar case brought on similar grounds by a young woman referred to as KGM in Los Angeles, over platform features linked to addiction in younger users.
In March, a US jury ordered Meta to pay $375m for endangering children in a case brought by the state of New Mexico.
Last month, a judge in New Mexico also ordered Facebook and Instagram owner Meta to pay a further $567m in a second phase of the trial.
What has Meta agreed to do?
Meta denied wrongdoing but agreed to settle after evidence was heard that Meta knew its products harmed children’s mental health. The total payout – to be paid over 10 years – is a fraction of Meta’s 2025 revenue of $201bn.
The company, which was originally founded as Facebook in 2004 by Mark Zuckerberg, agreed to make maximum payments totalling $16.7bn to 47 US states as well as Washington, DC; Puerto Rico; American Samoa; and the Northern Mariana Islands.
Among those, California could receive a $2.2bn payout, while New York could receive $1.1bn. Texas reached a separate settlement worth more than $1bn. Some states will deposit funds they receive in general accounts, while others will earmark portions to address children’s mental health services.
The settlement does not require Meta to discontinue personalised recommendations or targeted advertising.
It also does not address some content researchers found particularly problematic, including posts that made Instagram users uncomfortable with their body image.
“Ensuring teens have a safe and productive experience on our platforms is an absolute imperative for Meta,” Meta said in a blog post. “We want to get this right for parents and teens.”
What changes will be seen on Instagram and Facebook?
Under the agreement, children under 18 using Meta platforms will be restricted to two hours’ use per day, with a night curfew in place from midnight to 6am. Meta will limit “social comparison” features by hiding likes and reactions to children’s accounts, and will ban “cosmetic procedure filters” that alter the appearance of a user’s image, as a default setting. These settings will only be able to be overruled by parental consent.
The company also agreed to disable the majority of push notifications from the platforms during school hours – 8am to 3pm – for teenage users.
It will also facilitate much closer parental supervision of social media accounts by giving designated adults the ability to more extensively monitor and change settings on a social media account.
Parents and guardians will be able to receive information about time spent on platform apps, and usernames of social connections and accounts sending messages to children.
Supervising parents will also receive daily notifications from Meta any time the teen account messages an adult account for the first time, as well as a link to the adult’s account. Parental accounts will also be notified any time the teen account searches for keywords related to suicide, self-harm or eating disorders.
Meta also agreed to improve the technology used to check children’s ages, using its own as well as third-party tools, with regular outside audits on how well this monitoring is working. This measure is particularly notable because Australia banned under-16s from using social media platforms in December last year. However, the Australian internet watchdog, eSafety, found in August this year that more than eight in 10 young Australian teens and preteens continue to use them – largely because age-check procedures are ineffective.
So far, Meta has only agreed to pay 70 percent of the settlement, or roughly $12.7bn, over the next 10 years. It will only pay the remaining amount, about $5bn, if its rivals – including Snapchat, TikTok and Alphabet-owned YouTube – adopt similar measures and agree to pay the same. It also said it would reduce time restrictions to one hour per day if other platforms do the same.
These changes would be phased over time. Once the court approves the settlement, non-personalised feeds would be introduced within four months; broader compliance measures within six months; and major age-assurance requirements within one year.
While these changes will apply to users in the US, it is unclear if Meta plans to introduce them worldwide. However, Meta is already under rising regulatory pressure in European Union countries and those elsewhere to implement similar changes.
How much difference will these changes make?
Critics and child safety advocates have acknowledged that this settlement has forced landmark changes by Meta, the world’s biggest social media company, which owns Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp and Messenger, each of which has more than two to three billion monthly active users.
However, critics say the central plank of Meta’s latest settlement deal is the move to restrict teens to two hours per day on platforms, rather than fundamentally changing their addictive algorithms.
Sacha Haworth, executive director of The Tech Oversight Project, which campaigns for youth safety online, said the deal is a “historic settlement that will have a lasting impact, but we cannot truly protect all children and teens until these protections are required on every platform and are permanent – that’s something only Congress can do”.
Ella Bradshaw, policy officer for child safety online at the NSPCC, a UK children’s charity, welcomed moves to rein in “addictive” design features like personalised algorithms and likes. “These are the things that we know keep children hooked and feeling out of control of their screen time, so action here is necessary and welcome. However, important gaps remain,” she told Al Jazeera.
Bradshaw described the settlement as taking “piecemeal action” on tackling risky features and addictive design choices which drive harm of children.
“This means features like disappearing messages, infinite scroll, the ability to gift and livestreaming remain unaddressed. Similarly, little has been announced on how Meta’s AI chatbots will be made safer – better guardrails are needed, particularly when children raise safeguarding concerns.”
Bradshaw also called for stronger protections for younger children as well as protections that “don’t suddenly drop away the moment a teenager turns 18.”
Furthermore, she said: “Not all children have families they can rely on to oversee their online worlds and help them to stay safe. We know that the issue of patchy online protections extends across the online world.
“This settlement must spur governments and regulators to go further faster; taking stronger action across the online ecosystem including private messaging, AI tools and online gaming. Without that wider shift, children will continue to face avoidable harm.”
What action are other countries taking against Meta?
While action against social media giants in the US is mostly taking the form of lawsuits, elsewhere it is regulators who are leading the charge.
In the European Union, regulators are pursuing several legal and regulatory cases against Meta, covering antitrust rules for artificial intelligence (AI) on WhatsApp, as well as child safety protections and addictive platform features under the Digital Services Act (DSA).
The EU specifically accused the group of designing Facebook and Instagram to be “addictive”, adding that Meta has failed to adequately assess the danger its products pose to users’ physical and mental health.
On Thursday, a European Commission spokesperson said it is waiting on Meta to present changes to limit the addictive designs of its social networks.
“We have been very clear … Meta knows what we are expecting from them. … the ball is in Meta’s court,” Thomas Regnier said. “Now it is for the company to offer these commitments in the European Union to protect our kids here, too.”
In June, the UK government also announced a sweeping ban on social media for those below 16 to come into force next year, following a global trend after Australia pioneered it. The UK is also considering overnight curfews and ways to prevent infinite scrolling for those under 18.
In Brazil, a prominent consumer rights organisation, the Collective Defence Institute, filed twin lawsuits for three billion reais ($525m) in damages against the Brazilian subsidiaries of Meta, TikTok and Kwai in October 2024.
Those lawsuits also accuse the groups of failing to implement safeguards against addiction and use by children and adolescents. Since March this year, platforms have been required to link the accounts of children below 16 to legal guardians under Brazil’s Digital Statute for Children and Adolescents.
South Korea’s media regulator also reacted on Thursday to Meta’s settlement, calling for better protections for young users to be ideally applied worldwide, rather than just in specific markets.

Russia may use disposable agents for sabotage in the Czech Republic: facilities providing aid to Ukraine under threat
Kyiv • UNN
Czech counterintelligence warned about Russian disposable agents who may attack facilities providing aid to Ukraine. Suspicions regarding last year's incidents have not been confirmed.
The risk remains in the Czech Republic that Russia will use so-called one-time agents to carry out acts of sabotage—individuals recruited to conduct a single operation. If they are exposed, Russian entities deny any connection with such agents and do not intervene in their fate. Radio Prague reports this, citing data from the counterintelligence service—the Czech Security Information Service (BIS)—as reported by UNN.
Details
The threat of sabotage primarily concerns facilities connected with the production or distribution of aid to Ukraine. The Czech counterintelligence service BIS reported this in its report for 2025, which was published today.
None of last year's incidents in the Czech Republic that were investigated as possible acts of sabotage by Russia have so far been reliably confirmed as supporting those suspicions.
Czech counterintelligence reports that Russian entities regulate the intensity of sabotage attacks intended to exert pressure on European countries depending on how the situation on the battlefield in Ukraine and on the international political arena develops.
The number of acts of sabotage organized by Russia decreased in the first half of last year, but an increase was recorded again in the second half, BIS notes.
The counterintelligence service reports on one-time agents because, if such individuals are arrested, Russia disclaims responsibility for their actions and does not intervene in their subsequent fate in any way. "They are often inexperienced amateurs and, at the same time, people of low social status or with a criminal past. Their predominant motivation is the prospect of receiving financial compensation," BIS writes.
According to BIS, agents usually receive specific instructions from their coordinators only after they report which targets within their reach they are capable of targeting. "Thus, the risk of a sabotage attack against a specific facility depends more on the capabilities of individual agents than on an integrated plan of the Russian state authorities," the report emphasizes. However, BIS notes, this circumstance makes it more difficult to detect preparations for such attacks.
In 2025, a Czech court sentenced Colombian citizen Andrés Alfonso de la Hoz de la Cruz to eight years in prison for setting fire to three buses in the garages of Prague Public Transit Company. According to information obtained by the media, he had planned larger-scale actions, including setting fire to a cinema in a Prague shopping center.
In Poland, the Colombian was linked to two arson attacks on warehouses containing construction materials. Both the Polish special services and the Czech counterintelligence service BIS agree that de la Cruz was recruited by Russian intelligence.

An Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer facing state charges over a shooting in Minneapolis was released from a Texas jail Thursday after a three-month extradition dispute between Republican officials in Texas and Democratic officials in Minnesota, The New York Times reported.
Christian Castro was released shortly before 7 am local time (1200GMT) from the Cameron County jail, Sheriff Manuel Trevino said. Minnesota prosecutors charged Castro in May with four counts of assault and one count of falsely reporting a crime. They allege he fired through the door of a home after a vehicle chase and foot pursuit, striking Sosa-Celis in the leg.
Federal officials initially supported Castro and accused Sosa-Celis and his roommate of attacking officers with a broom and shovel.
