====================================================================================================

124 reports in nine days: Inside Israel’s fake think tank bid to shape ChatGPT
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
14:26:50 UTC
23:26:50 KST

A purported U.S. research institute with no apparent legal existence, no physical address and no named researchers published more than 560,000 words in just nine days as part of an Israel-backed effort designed to influence what artificial intelligence systems tell users about Israel, according to an investigation by The Guardian.
The Hanover Institute for Public Policy published 124 reports between August 6 and 14, averaging about 4,500 words each. On August 12 and 13 alone, it released 73 reports totaling almost 354,000 words.
The reports address some of the most contentious allegations involving Israel, including accusations of torture of Palestinian prisoners, war crimes, genocide and the deliberate starvation of Palestinians in Gaza. They are presented as neutral, quasi-academic research and heavily sourced to institutions including the World Bank, UN agencies, Amnesty International and the Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics.
But the institute itself apparently does not exist as a legal entity in any jurisdiction, according to The Guardian. It lists no physical address, names no employees or researchers and publishes its reports without bylines.
Its terms of use say they are governed by the laws of “the state in which the Institute is established,” without identifying that state.
The site was registered with the U.S. Justice Department this month by New York media production company Piro Inc. under the Foreign Agents Registration Act, or FARA, as material distributed on behalf of the Israeli government.
The operation appears to represent a new frontier in Israel’s public diplomacy campaign: producing online material not simply for human readers, but specifically to be discovered, cited and potentially absorbed by AI systems including ChatGPT, Perplexity, Claude and Gemini.
124 reports built around chatbot questions
Almost every headline on the Hanover Institute website takes the form of a question a user might type into an AI chatbot.
Among them are “Is Anti-Zionism Antisemitism?”, “Did Israel Expel Palestinians From Their Land?” and “Is Israel Carrying Out a Genocide in Gaza?”
According to The Guardian, the reports consistently frame evidence in ways that blunt criticism of Israel.
When human rights organizations accuse Israel of genocide or apartheid, for example, the reports repeatedly note that no court has issued a final verdict on the allegation. The Guardian counted that formulation in 20 of the 124 reports.
Casualty and humanitarian-aid figures are repeatedly attributed to “a party to the events,” language used in 55 reports and applied to Israeli figures as well as Palestinian ones.
One 2022 academic study examining antisemitic comments on Facebook pages belonging to British, French and German media outlets was cited 454 times across 88 Hanover reports, including pieces dealing with subjects ranging from the Gaza death toll and the 1948 Palestinian displacement to land registration and AIPAC.
Nick Cleveland-Stout, a research associate at the Quincy Institute who has investigated the site, said its presentation initially appears convincing.
“It succeeds in masquerading as very academic – the website design, the logos, everything just looks good. But the more you read it, you’re able to realise that a lot of it makes no sense.”
He said the reports frequently return to the possibility that discussion of criticism directed at Israel could fuel antisemitism.
“Almost every article concludes with saying, well, just talking about this though could contribute to antisemitism,” he said. “And it’ll throw in the study about Facebook comments in Britain.”
Built for machines, not just readers
One of the clearest indications of the site’s intended audience was hidden in its technical infrastructure.
The Guardian found that Hanover initially carried an llms.txt file, a type of file intended to tell AI systems what a website contains and how to read it.
The file did not originally describe the Hanover Institute. Instead, it was the standard file belonging to Res, a company that markets itself as an “AI-native content platform” helping businesses get cited by ChatGPT, Perplexity, Claude and Gemini.
Res specializes in what the industry calls generative engine optimization, or GEO, the AI-era equivalent of attempting to optimize material for search engines.
The file was later replaced with a Hanover-specific version and references to Res disappeared from the site.
Res founder Hai Tran registered with the U.S. Justice Department on July 22 as a subcontractor to Piro on the Israeli account, listing his role as “digital strategist.”
Piro itself advertises a service called “AI Story Optimization,” promising to “author content engineered for how LLMs evaluate credibility” and publish that material either on clients’ own sites or on third-party properties it builds.
The strategy can work in two ways.
The first is relatively straightforward: publish material online and hope AI chatbots find and cite it when answering users.
The second could have a much longer-lasting effect: getting that material into large web archives such as Common Crawl, whose datasets are used in training commercial AI models.
“There’s kind of two ways to do it,” Cleveland-Stout said.
The latter, he said, is “the more concerning and potentially more effective thing.”
“When it regurgitates narratives the chatbot is trained on, it won’t even cite the sources,” he said. “You won’t be able to fact-check it.”
Hanover’s reports were published too late to appear in Common Crawl’s July index. But another network involved in the broader campaign already has.
Seven websites operated by Clock Tower X, a company run by former Trump campaign manager and digital director Brad Parscale, appeared 294 times in Common Crawl’s July index.
Chatbots are already finding the material
The Hanover effort may already be having some effect on chatbot responses.
The Guardian tested ChatGPT by asking it for recent research published by the Hanover Institute. The chatbot returned links to four Hanover reports.
At the same time, however, it warned that the institute was subject to “significant controversy over who funds it and why it exists,” and also directed users to critical reporting about the organization.
That distinction is important.
Israeli officials have increasingly questioned whether large public diplomacy campaigns are improving Israel’s image overseas. But influencing public opinion and influencing the information surfaced by an AI system are not necessarily the same thing.
Cleveland-Stout argued that the campaign could succeed technically even if it fails politically.
“Parscale is having success in influencing chatbots, and the Hanover Institute is and will continue to have success at influencing the responses that chatbots give,” he said. “But they’re not changing the polls, which is what Israel actually cares about.”
The multimillion-dollar chain behind the campaign
The Hanover Institute forms part of a much larger influence operation involving companies in the United States and Europe.
Piro is contracted for $1 million through two work orders, according to U.S. foreign-agent filings.
It and Clock Tower X are subcontractors to Havas Media Germany, part of the international Havas advertising group.
U.S. Justice Department records list Havas as the intermediary in the foreign-agent registrations of five American companies: Clock Tower X, Piro, Targeted Communications Global, Bridges Partners and Davis Media NY.
The filings show Havas paid Clock Tower X $15 million in six installments between October 24, 2025, and March 3, 2026, while Targeted Communications Global received nearly $9.9 million between October and December 2025.
A contract between Havas and another American company involved in the campaign calls for the “deployment of websites and content to deliver GPT framing results on GPT conversations.”
The financial structure also makes the overall cost of the operation difficult to see in one place.
Seven days after the first payment to Clock Tower X, Havas’s U.S. subsidiary terminated its registration as an agent of the Israeli government. While registered, it had been required to disclose payments received on the Israeli account.
After the German Havas entity began paying U.S. contractors directly, only the individual American contractors’ filings remained publicly visible.
Israeli procurement records show the government advertising agency LaPam awarded Havas entities contracts without competitive tender worth $39 million, $29 million and $17.5 million during 2019, followed by another $58.3 million contract in March 2023 for planning and purchasing media abroad.
That contract expired in March 2024.
The Guardian said it found no later public procurement award to Havas covering the period in which the company was paying almost $25 million to American contractors.
Not just AI
The broader campaign extends beyond attempts to influence chatbots.
Targeted Communications Global disclosed a social media campaign called Freedom Not Terror. A 30-second video uploaded to YouTube in October 2025 has received 28.1 million views.
Its TikTok account, by contrast, has 425 followers, and the campaign has published nothing since December 2025.
The campaign website states that it was “Paid for by LAPAM.”
Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar allocated 545 million shekels, about $181.6 million, for international public diplomacy after taking office, followed by another 2 billion shekels, about $666.3 million, for 2026 and 2027.
Yet Israeli officials have privately voiced frustration over what that spending has achieved.
In July, one official told ynet: “The government paid a lot of money, but the situation only got worse.”
A former senior figure in Israel’s public diplomacy system described the effort as “a terrible hoax on the scale of Pollard,” referring to Jonathan Pollard, the former U.S. intelligence analyst imprisoned for spying for Israel.
Another official, speaking to Israel’s Kan public broadcaster about Parscale, said: “He was supposed to improve the situation. We paid him a lot of money. But what did he do with it?”
The polls keep moving against Israel
Those concerns come as Israel’s standing among Americans has deteriorated sharply.
Gallup found in February that Americans sympathized more with Palestinians than Israelis for the first time, with 36% siding with Israel.
Pew Research Center reported in April that 60% of Americans held an unfavorable view of Israel, nearly 20 percentage points higher than in 2022, with the steepest decline among younger Americans.
An AP-NORC poll published July 7 found that 31% of Americans believed Israel’s military actions in Gaza constituted genocide. Among Democrats, the figure was 52%.
The same survey found that 58% of Democrats believed the United States was too supportive of Israel, compared with 45% in January 2024.
Cleveland-Stout said such figures point to a more fundamental limitation of the campaign.
“There is a lack of reflection on the fact that the policies themselves are the ones that are leading to a lot of Americans questioning their support for Israel,” he said. “They view what is a political problem as a marketing one.”
He also cited the late Israeli politician Yossi Sarid, who once joked that “Hasbara is always the refuge of all failures. Everything is going great – only the hasbara is garbage. If only the hasbara was ok, then everyone would realize the ideal situation.”
A new battlefield for influence
Israel’s Foreign Ministry has said the state does not conduct “influence operations” in the United States and is “scrupulously careful to implement the provisions of American law.”
Piro co-founder Daniel Rosenberg has said the company was hired “to put accurate, sourced facts into the public record and to counter misinformation about Israel with verifiable information.”
Neither Piro nor the Israeli government responded to The Guardian’s requests for comment on its investigation.
For Cleveland-Stout, however, the significance of the Hanover experiment extends well beyond Israel.
“Whether it’s foreign governments, whether it’s companies, whether it’s even just a guy who owns an ice cream shop – LLM grooming, poisoning, whatever you want to call it, is part of the new reality that we live in.”
The question is no longer simply whether online campaigns can persuade people. It is whether governments, companies and other interested actors can deliberately flood the information ecosystem with material engineered to shape what AI systems learn, retrieve and ultimately tell their users.

Feature: Chinese-donated rice brings relief to vulnerable households in Cameroon
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
22:26:43 CST
23:26:43 KST

YAOUNDE, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- At dawn in Mbende, a neighborhood in the resort town of Limbe in Cameroon's Southwest Region, 89-year-old Vivian Njie lit her firewood stove. This time, the pot on it was not empty.
Inside, long-grain white rice donated by China bubbled gently. Njie, a grandmother of 15, stirred the rice prepared for the 19 people in her compound.
"Before, we would cook a small quantity of rice and divide it into five plates," she said. "Today my grandchildren will eat until they say, 'I'm full.' That alone is peace."
For nearly a decade, Cameroon's English-speaking Northwest and Southwest regions have borne the brunt of an armed separatist conflict.
Farms have been deserted, roads to markets have become dangerous, and cultivated land has declined by 20 to 40 percent in the worst-hit areas, pushing up food prices.
In early 2026, humanitarian agencies warned that 2.9 million people across Cameroon, including 1.5 million children, needed assistance.
It was against this backdrop that aid from China arrived. In June, Cameroon received food commodities from China, including 1,630 tonnes of rice and 880 tonnes of wheat bound for conflict-affected regions.
To date, 9,000 bags of rice have been sent to Buea, the capital of the Southwest Region, where distribution has already begun. Another 10,700 bags have been sent to Bamenda for distribution across the Northwest Region.
In Limbe, City Council Mayor Paul Efome Ngalle supervised the handover of the supplies to community leaders, saying the aid came as the city was "stretched to its limits."
"This rice donation from China is not just food; it is solidarity," Ngalle said. "A lot of vulnerable groups in our municipality were really touched."
At a distribution point in Buea, families lined up with ration cards. Each household received rice.
James Nkemasong, 48, fled his village in the Lebialem division two years ago with his wife and five children. He now rents a single room in Buea.
"This rice will feed us for weeks," he said, lifting a 25-kg bag onto his shoulder. "Things have been really tough for me and my family. We barely eat three square meals a day. But this rice has brought us relief."
A similar story is unfolding in Muyuka, another town in the Southwest Region, where Judith Mbah, 38, cooks for 12 internally displaced persons.
"The rice from China is soft, and it doesn't waste firewood," she said. "We mix it with beans and a little oil. The children call it 'sweet rice' and ask for it every day."
When the rice arrived in Limbe, it was not only for those displaced by war; it was also for people who had nothing left.
Early August brought hard, fast rain to the coastal town at the foot of Mount Cameroon. Runoff poured down the slopes with no outlet, flooding neighborhoods and triggering landslides that crushed homes. Three people lost their lives.
For a community already carrying the weight of displacement caused by the separatist conflict, the floods meant a new crisis: not just lost homes, but also lost food.
John Molua lost much of his property in the flooding. "The rain keeps coming. But this rice gave us stability and hope for weeks. Most of the victims got some, and we were very relieved. It came right when we needed it," he said.
Xiao Guofeng, economic and trade counselor at the Chinese Embassy in Cameroon, said the donation was one of 10 concrete actions announced at the 2024 Beijing Summit of the Forum on China-Africa Cooperation.
"This food donation is a concrete example of China-Cameroon friendship. It embodies China's policy toward Africa, which is guided by the principles of sincerity, solidarity, friendship and candor, as well as a sound understanding of friendship and shared interests," Xiao said.
Mayor Ngalle noted that the gesture reflects more than 55 years of Cameroon-China cooperation. "That gesture alone deepens not only the relationship between nations, but also the relationship between citizens, the people-to-people relationship," he said.
In places like Buea and Limbe, where conflict and flooding have stretched families thin, the sacks are doing what aid is meant to do: keep people going.
Back in Mbende, Njie served the rice. Her grandchildren ate quickly, then ran outside to play. She watched them and smiled.
In a region that has seen too much hardship, a hot plate of rice is feeding hope, one bowl at a time. ■

An aerial drone photo taken on Aug. 26, 2026 shows tourists enjoying the scenery on a glass observation deck on Jinyun Mountain, Beibei District, southwest China's Chongqing.
Located along the Jialing River, Jinyun Mountain Reserve is an important ecological barrier in Chongqing and one of the best-preserved subtropical evergreen broad-leaved forest ecosystems in China.
Years ago, ecological conservation in the reserve was under severe strain, as unauthorized construction, irregular business activities, and unregulated expansion of farm-stay tourism ran rampant.
In June 2018, Chongqing launched the comprehensive ecological environment improvement project of Jinyun Mountain.
To date, the reserve has restored 774,000 square meters of ecology and planted about 1 million ornamental plants. The forest coverage rate has increased from 94 percent to 98 percent.
In 2025, the collective economic income of villages in the Jinyun Mountain area reached 27.784 million yuan (about 4.13 million U.S. dollars), and villagers' per capita annual income increased by 9.5 percent year-on-year, achieving a win-win situation for ecological protection, industrial development, and villagers' income growth. China, Zimbabwe pledge to deepen economic, trade ties
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
22:26:30 CST
23:26:30 KST

Zimbabwean Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Trade Amon Murwira (R) and Chinese Assistant Minister of Commerce Zhang Li pose for a group photo in Harare, Zimbabwe, on Aug. 26, 2026. China and Zimbabwe have reaffirmed their commitment to deepening bilateral economic and trade ties at the 11th Session of the Joint Commission on Economic, Technical and Trade Cooperation in the Zimbabwean capital of Harare. (Photo by Tafara Mugwara/Xinhua)
HARARE, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- China and Zimbabwe have reaffirmed their commitment to deepening bilateral economic and trade ties at the 11th Session of the Joint Commission on Economic, Technical and Trade Cooperation in the Zimbabwean capital of Harare.
The session, held on Wednesday and co-chaired by Zimbabwean Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Trade Amon Murwira and Chinese Assistant Minister of Commerce Zhang Li, provided a platform to translate existing bilateral agreements between the two countries into tangible economic opportunities, including increased trade and investment, value addition and job creation.
Both sides agreed to fully implement the 10 partnership actions initiated at the 2024 Beijing Summit of the Forum on China-Africa Cooperation, further expand and optimize bilateral trade, and accelerate negotiations on the Economic Partnership for Shared Development agreement.
They also agreed to encourage more Chinese enterprises to invest and operate in Zimbabwe, support Zimbabwe in extending and upgrading its mining industrial chain, and advance industrial upgrading.
Murwira said China and Zimbabwe enjoy a long-standing friendship based on mutual respect and strategic partnership, noting that the partnership has delivered monumental development across critical sectors of Zimbabwe's economy, including energy generation, agricultural productivity, and infrastructure.
"Zimbabwe is committed to expanding trade, promoting investment, and strengthening economic linkages between our two countries," Murwira said.
He also welcomed China's zero-tariff treatment for 53 African countries, which presents vast opportunities to expand local exports, as demonstrated by Zimbabwe's first blueberry consignment to China in July.
For his part, Zhang commended the expanding bilateral trade and Zimbabwe's growing exports to China, noting that Zimbabwe has become a major African destination for Chinese investment.
China stands ready to work closely with Zimbabwe to translate all consensus into concrete actions and steadily advance the high-quality development of bilateral economic and trade cooperation, said Zhang. ■

UK failed to follow UN recommendations to protect vulnerable asylum seekers: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
14:24:38 UTC
23:24:38 KST

Burak Bir
27 August 2026•Update: 27 August 2026
The British government acted against UN recommendations aimed at protecting vulnerable asylum seekers, a rights watchdog said on Thursday.
In its report, the Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) said the government has taken "inconsistent action" – the lowest EHRC ranking – and failed to uphold the rights of migrants and asylum seekers in line with UN recommendations.
Citing the National Human Rights Institution, it found gaps in social security provisions and failures to provide protection from poverty and destitution.
The EHRC said it found major gaps in the government’s approach to promoting integration and fostering good relations between all groups.
"The UK government ended its Refugee Employability Programme after less than two years," it said, mentioning that the program was designed to help refugees with CV writing and interview skills so they could find work.
"At the same time, it also revoked its legal duty to support asylum seekers at risk of destitution this year."
It noted that the government had also not acted in line with a UN recommendation to prevent poverty among migrants and asylum seekers.
The watchdog stressed that instead of revising rules which do not allow many migrants to access social security, the government has consulted on proposals to extend no recourse to public funds conditions to people granted Indefinite Leave to Remain in the UK.
"When the government fail to protect the rights of one group, it puts everyone’s rights at risk," said Mary-Ann Stephenson, chair of the Equality and Human Rights Commission.
The chair called on the government to implement the outstanding recommendations for promoting economic, cultural and social rights in full, ahead of the UN’s follow-up review next year.

Work ability appeals fall as success rate climbs, data shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
14:24:00 UTC
23:24:00 KST

Work ability appeals fall as success rate climbs, data shows
The number of appeals against work ability assessment decisions has steadily declined over the years, Minister of Economic Affairs Erkki Keldo (Reform) wrote in a letter to an MP.
Keldo was responding to Center Party MP Aleksandr Tšaplõgin and noted while the number of successful appeals has remained more or less unchanged, the share of successful appeals has gone up at the same time the total number of appeals has declined.
In 2023, 17.5 percent of appeals were upheld, compared with 23.1 percent in 2025. Last year, 2,564 work ability assessment decisions — or 5.8 percent of all work ability decisions — were challenged, while 577 of those appeals were upheld.
In the bulk (89 percent) of successful appeals, the reason was new information about the individual's health that had been submitted or emerged during the appeal process. In the remaining 11 percent of cases, the existing data was assessed on a different basis.
The number of court disputes has remained stable, with 51 work ability assessment decisions reaching the courts in 2023, and 48 in 2025.
According to the ministry, the decline in challenged decisions has been aided by continuous quality control of work ability assessments, improvements to guidelines and better-quality health data. A change in the outcome of a work ability assessment does not necessarily mean there is an error in the system, as a person's health may improve or deteriorate over time.
Last year, the work ability assessment remained unchanged in about 72 percent of reassessments. In 17 percent of cases, work ability was assessed as lower than previously, meaning the person's health had deteriorated. In 12 percent of cases, work ability was assessed as having improved.
There were 1,234 cases in which a person previously assessed as having no work ability was assessed as in fact having partial work ability upon reassessment. In 140 cases, people previously assessed as having no work ability were found upon reassessment not to have a reduced work ability.
The number of people with reduced work ability may be partly affected by hazards arising from the working environment, which in turn can reduce life expectancy and can reduced the number of years being employed while in good health. A safe and health-preserving working environment must support the maintenance of work ability and help prevent its decline, it was found.

====================================================================================================

Rohingya suffering deepens as UN flags child labour by Myanmar rebels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
14:23:38 UTC
23:23:38 KST

A child no older than six was forced to clear bones and skulls from the ground in Buthidaung town in Myanmar’s Rakhine State, where Rohingya were killed in a 2024 massacre in Hoyyar Siri village.
The child was among Rohingya labourers forced to build a displacement camp, a settlement for non-Rohingya residents and a military base on land where three Rohingya villages once stood, according to a new report from the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights.
The Rohingya are a Muslim minority in Myanmar who have endured decades of systematic oppression and discrimination.
Denied citizenship and stripped of basic rights, they have faced severe violence and forced displacement, making them one of the world's most persecuted communities.
The new figures offer a glimpse into the scale of abuses Rohingya communities continue to face. In northern Rakhine, local sources recorded at least 2,353 forced labour instances in January 2026 alone, 75 of them involving children as young as six.
Villages were required to provide workers to the Arakan Army, an ethnic-armed group based in Myanmar’s Rakhine State, for a set number of days each week or month, turning forced labour into a system imposed at the community level.
What is being documented, however, may only scratch the surface of what Rohingya children are enduring, according to Ravina Shamdasani, the Chief Spokesperson for the UN Human Rights Office.
“Due to the lack of access to Rakhine and the ongoing restriction on communication, the full extent of abuses against Rohingya children is indeed challenging to quantify and detail,” Shamdasani tells TRT World.
“We have received many reports of extreme cases of children being forcibly recruited as well as subjected to forced labour, early marriage, and sexual violence,” she adds.
About 600 displaced Rohingya are currently held at the camp for survivors of the 2024 massacre.
They are under continuous guard and cannot leave. Sources in the report say that their detention is meant to prevent information about the massacre from spreading.
One escapee described the camp's conditions as appalling, with eight deaths in a few months, including a pregnant woman and five infants and young children.
Women and girls have also faced sexual violence, including rape, according to the report.
The abuse does not end there. Rohingya detainees have described being beaten with bamboo and rubber pipes, burned with matches and cigarettes, and suspended upside down until they lost consciousness.
One man said he woke up in scrubland after his captors, believing him dead during torture in Buthidaung prison, disposed of his body.
His son, arrested alongside him, later died in custody. Families said they were forced to sign statements attributing the deaths to natural causes.
Endless suffering
For the Rohingya, today's abuses are the latest chapter in a persecution that dates back decades.
In August 2017, Myanmar's military launched a campaign of killing, arson and mass displacement across northern Rakhine State, driving more than 700,000 Rohingya into Bangladesh within weeks.
UN investigators later concluded that the campaign was carried out with "genocidal intent", citing mass killings, widespread sexual violence and the systematic destruction of Rohingya villages.
For decades, the Rohingya had been denied citizenship under Myanmar's 1982 law, leaving most of the population stateless and subjecting them to restrictions on movement, marriage, healthcare and education.
The 2017 campaign turned that institutionalised exclusion into mass atrocity.
The abuses reflect a deliberate strategy toward this population, according to Shamdasani.
“What is clear is that since the coup, the military has pursued a strategy of terrorising, surveilling, and limiting the exercise of rights and freedoms against civilians more broadly as a means to crush opposition to their unchecked power,” she says.
“The impunity for these violations, and for the abuses committed by other armed actors, only encourages further violence.”
Nine years later, most of those displaced remain in camps in Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh, now the world's largest refugee settlement, with little prospect of a safe or dignified return.
The situation inside Myanmar has since become even more complicated.
The February 2021 military coup plunged the country into a broader civil war, leaving the Rohingya caught between competing armed actors and vulnerable to abuses from more than one side.
In northern Rakhine, the Arakan Army has taken control of territory once held by the military, but that shift has not brought safety for the Rohingya living there.
“The abuses and violations are widespread and systematic - that much is clear,” Shamdasani says.
“Forced recruitment in particular, including for portering or other logistical reasons, has been a hallmark of operations by the military and armed ethnic organisations.”
“What is included in the report does not mean to be exhaustive, but it should help paint a picture of the suffering, and the threats to which civilians in Myanmar are continuously exposed,” she adds.
Documentation without a verdict
In 2019, The Gambia filed a lawsuit against Myanmar at the International Court of Justice, accusing the state of violating the Genocide Convention through its 2017 campaign against the Rohingya.
The case has moved through the Court since then, and the Court has not yet set a date for judgment.
Since the case focuses on Myanmar's state responsibility under the Genocide Convention rather than individual criminal guilt, new evidence like this report's findings contributes to the overall factual record before the Court rather than being directly incorporated into the case file at this point.
A separate track runs through the International Criminal Court, where the Prosecutor has requested an arrest warrant for former Senior General Min Aung Hlaing over the 2017 Rohingya campaign.
The OHCHR notes no public developments on that request during the latest reporting period.
Beyond these two UN-linked bodies, accountability efforts have spread further. Universal jurisdiction cases have been brought in Argentina, Timor-Leste and Indonesia, with domestic courts asserting jurisdiction over alleged international crimes linked either to the Arakan Army or to Min Aung Hlaing himself.
This multiplication of legal tracks strengthens the overall push for accountability, but they are not enough, according to Shamdasani.
“States’ use of universal jurisdiction legislation signals an unwillingness to tolerate grave violations and the indiscriminate use of force against civilians. This is very welcome,” Shamdasani says.
“However, the need for justice of the Myanmar people is larger than the scope of the ongoing processes. There needs to be a stronger push for accountability by all,” she adds.

====================================================================================================

Ratko Mladić, the ‘Butcher of Bosnia’, dies in The Hague
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
14:21:24 UTC
23:21:24 KST

Ratko Mladić, the infamous Serbian general who was serving a life sentence for genocide committed during the Bosnian war, has died in prison in The Hague.
Mladić had been one of the main architects of the policy of ethnic cleansing during the Bosnian war. He was convicted of genocide for orchestrating the 1995 killing of at least 8,000 Muslims in the UN-designated “safe area” Srebrenica, the worst massacre in Europe since the second world war.
Mladić, who was nicknamed the “Butcher of Bosnia”, had been in ill health after having a series of strokes.
A UN international tribunal confirmed Mladić’s death, saying he had died in hospital in The Hague earlier in the day.
“Mladić passed away today while hospitalised in The Hague,” the International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals said in a statement, adding that judge Graciela Gatti Santana had ordered “a full inquiry into the circumstances” of his death.
Described by the former UN rights chief Zeid Ra’ad al-Hussein as “the epitome of evil” after his conviction, Mladić was one of the most notorious figures of the war that killed more than 100,000 people and left more than 1 million homeless.
He commanded his troops to “scorch the brains” of Bosnian Muslim people and had boasted of being a “Serbian god”.
The news of Mladić’s death was first broken on Serbian state television after his son, Darko, had spoken earlier about his father’s declining health.
Mladić was sentenced by a UN tribunal to life imprisonment in 2017 over genocide and war crimes committed during Bosnia’s 1990s war. He was arrested in Serbia in 2011 after 16 years on the run.
The slaughter in Srebrenica was the culmination of a brutal war that had lasted more than three years, during which Mladić oversaw the siege of Bosnia’s capital, Sarajevo, which was pounded daily by artillery, tank and sniper fire, killing 10,000 people.
The goal of the Serbian leadership, which Mladić was tasked with implementing – as determined by the UN’s international criminal tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) – was the forcible expulsion of Bosnian Muslims, Croats and other non-Serbs to clear Bosnian land for the creation of a greater Serbia.
The tribunal found that Mladić, together with the late Serbian president Slobodan Milošević and the Bosnian Serb political leader Radovan Karadžić, were part of a criminal conspiracy to implement the plan.
“I do not recognise this court,” Mladić said at an ICTY hearing on his case in 2014. When he was sentenced, he shouted: “This is all lies, you are all liars!”
The Serbian campaign culminated in the horror of Srebrenica when, after the withdrawal of Dutch UN peacekeeping forces, thousands of Bosnian men and boys were rounded up, killed and their bodies bulldozed into mass graves.
Mladić had the siege filmed to show him praising his “lads” and haranguing the UN peacekeepers who misguidedly accepted his solemn word that the inhabitants would be safe in his hands.
“We give this town to the Serb people as a gift,” Mladić said to the camera, claiming the victory as revenge against Muslim Turks, who had once held the area as part of the Ottoman empire.
The next day, Mladić’s forces were filmed handing out sweets to children, promising their safe passage. Meanwhile, thousands of men and boys were being readied for slaughter.
When Nato tried in 1995 to rein in his forces with the threat of limited airstrikes, his troops seized UN peacekeepers as human shields, chaining them to likely targets.
The son of a second world war partisan fighter killed in 1945, Mladić was, according to his family, born in March 1943 in the tiny Bosnian village of Bozinovici, putting his age at death at 83 (though official documents recorded his date of birth a year earlier, in 1942).
Mladić was an officer in the communist Yugoslav People’s Army (JNA) when Yugoslavia’s disintegration began in 1991.
When Bosnian Serbs rose in 1992 against Bosnia’s Muslim-led secession, Mladić was chosen to command the new Bosnian Serb army that swiftly overran 70% of the country.
Dozens of towns were besieged with heavy weapons that once belonged to the JNA and villages were burned down, as 22,000 troops with the UN Protection Force stood by, more or less helplessly, under orders not to take sides.
A combination of western pressure, Nato strikes and covert US arms and training for Croats and Muslims gradually turned the tide against Mladić’s army. After the war, Mladić went into hiding, with the reformists ruling post-conflict Serbia not daring to move against a man who was a hero to a core of nationalist Serbs.
Mladić continued to insist he was “a simple man” chosen to protect his people. When he was finally arrested in 2011, he put up no resistance. He had a heart attack in 2013 and seemed older than his years. By his own account, he felt like a frail old man.
This month, a UN doctor said Mladić’s death “may occur at any time”, possibly within weeks, but his application for release was again rejected.
Munira Subašić, from the Mothers of Srebrenica group, said she deplored that Mladić’s crimes were still being denied by many Bosnian Serbs. “Today, a major war criminal died, the criminal of the Balkans,” Subašić said. But while 31 years later mothers of victims were “still carrying the pain in our souls … we are still listening to denials, we are still listening to how Ratko Mladić was a hero for the Serbs”.
Elizabeth Evenson, the international justice director at Human Rights Watch, said: “The death of Ratko Mladić, the former Bosnian Serb army commander found guilty of genocide, including the massacre of up to 8,000 Bosnian men and boys after the fall of Srebrenica, Bosnia, in July 1995, is a reminder of the ongoing need for justice, truth, and reparations in the western Balkans.
“Full accountability for such terrible crimes, in Bosnia and elsewhere, demands commitment by governments to justice, even decades after the events themselves.”

A new live train map lets users track rail journeys across France, Spain and Belgium, including delays, cancellations and what type of facilities are available at stations.
For the age-old question of “where’s my train?”, there's now a new live map for that which tracks rail traffic across France, Spain and Belgium.
Launched in August with an initial focus on the three countries, TrainTracker24 lets users browse Europe’s railway network in real time, from how many trains are active, average delay time in minutes, percentage of on-time trains as well as the percentage of cancellations. The map itself can be rotated, zoomed and explored to your heart's content.
Users can filter the map by a country’s train operator, with TrainTracker24 also including data on Eurostar and Italy’s Frecciarossa service. Other filters focus on infrastructure, such as stations that are without any rail service, those with high-speed lines, and stations that are operational, but closed to members of the public. There are also widgets with live rankings of the most delayed trains and most disrupted stations.
And if you have a train number handy, even better. Train enthusiasts can look up scheduled runs, past journeys as well as live tracking. Other search functions include departures, arrivals, punctuality and facilities available at stations in France, Germany, Spain and Belgium.
There is also a section to search rail operators, their routes and performance. For instance, when Euronews Travel looked at France’s high-speed SNCF performance, at the time of writing, the operator had 601 trains running, 80 of which were delayed by 15 minutes or more and 22 were cancelled. This network snapshot is refreshed every 20 seconds, so you can quite literally watch any rail dramas unfold there and then.
While the above basics are free, paid features include a personalised journey map, live data on interrupted services shown on the map, the ability to sort trains by delay, as well as more map details highlighting infrastructure, track types and an expert reading, among other features.
The platform gets all of its information from open data from operators, regions and infrastructure managers about timetables, real-time updates and disruption information.
According to a post via X, the platform is on track to expand further into Europe.
Sounds familiar? It should
Does this concept sound familiar? TrainTracker24 joins other platforms, including TrainTracker.live.
The latter is also free to use and offers users a live map and details on train positions, timetables and punctuality statistics for rail networks. Boasting data on almost 11,000 live trains as of when I browsed the website, TrainTracker.live’s reach span across four continents, including Europe, the Americas, Asia and Oceania.
In fact, train enthusiasts are spoiled for choice on where to get these insights from, with other available platforms, such as TrainsTracking, which offers live information as well as fare comparisons with links to official booking operator pages across 76 countries. However, its insights are most detailed in Europe, Japan, India, Pakistan and the US.
Meanwhile, the SignalBox live train map focuses solely on trains and rail networks within the UK.
Perhaps all this sounds slightly reminiscent of Flightradar24, too? Well…
Elric Battello, TrainTracker24’s founder, told Luxembourg-based media outlet Virgule: “When you’re flying, or waiting for someone at the airport, it’s easy to open Flightradar24 to track the flight live on a map; the same goes for shipping. With trains, it’s different. You’ll often see a display at the station or receive a notification in the event of a delay. But you don’t really know what’s going on”.

Srebrenica war criminal Ratko Mladić dies in The Hague
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
14:20:09 UTC
23:20:09 KST

Srebrenica war criminal Ratko Mladić dies in The Hague
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Ratko Mladić, the Bosnian Serb general convicted of genocide over the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, has died aged 84 in the United Nations detention unit in The Hague, a UN official has confirmed.
It was Mladić’s forces who overran Srebrenica – a UN “safe area” guarded by lightly armed Dutch peacekeepers known as Dutchbat – and killed more than 8,000 Bosniak men and boys in July 1995. It was the worst mass killing in Europe since the Second World War.
Mladić had been held in the UN detention unit in Scheveningen since his arrest in Serbia in 2011, after 16 years on the run. Known as the “Butcher of Bosnia”, he had been in poor health for years and reportedly suffered another stroke over the summer.
An international tribunal convicted him in 2017 of genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes, and jailed him for life; the verdict was upheld on appeal in 2021. He showed no remorse during his trial.
His death comes days after the tribunal rejected a request from his defence team, backed by the Serbian government, to release him on humanitarian grounds so he could spend his final days in Serbia.
Dutch guilt and apologies
 For the Netherlands, the memory of Srebrenica is an open wound. Dutchbat’s failure to protect the victims led to a 2002 inquiry whose findings pushed the government at the time to resign, and to years of court action by survivors against the state.
Prime minister Mark Rutte apologised to Dutchbat veterans in 2022, saying they had been sent on an impossible mission and unfairly blamed for the killings. The government also repeated its “deepest apologies” to survivors in 2025.
Thousands gathered in Srebrenica to mark 30 years since the genocide last year. In the Netherlands, campaigners are still pressing for a national monument to the victims in The Hague.

Asylum seekers housed in UK hotels halve in year, data shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
14:15:27 UTC
23:15:27 KST

Burak Bir
27 August 2026•Update: 27 August 2026
The number of asylum seekers housed in hotels across the UK has fallen by half in a year, with more than 16,000 people in hotel accommodation as of June, according to Home Office data released Thursday.
In its quarterly immigration report, the Home Office said around 16,000 supported asylum seekers, or 17% of the total, were living in hotel accommodation, down 50% from more than 32,000 people, or 34%, in June 2025.
The data also showed declines in legal migration arrivals, asylum claims and small boat arrivals compared with a year earlier.
The Home Office said the figures indicated that policies aimed at curbing migration were having an effect but warned that more remained to be done to address small boat crossings.
It said there were 136.8 million arrivals to the UK in the year ending June 2026, with British nationals accounting for 57% of the total.
Of the non-British arrivals, most were short-term visitors, while smaller numbers arrived for other reasons, including work, study or joining family members.
Meanwhile, 2.2 million visitor visas and 19,684 transit visas were granted during the same period.
The figures also showed a decline in the number of family members arriving in Britain to join someone already in the country, while asylum claims fell by a fifth.
Around 38,000 irregular arrivals were detected in the year to June, including 33,000 people who crossed the English Channel in small boats from France.

MOSCOW, August 27. /TASS/. Russia’s international reserves amounted to $761.2 bln as of August 21, 2026, having increased by $5.6 bln in one week, the Central Bank reported.
"International reserves amounted to $761.2 bln as of the end of the day on August 21, 2026, having increased by $5.6 bln, or by 0.7%, in one week mainly due to positive revaluation," the regulator said.
As of August 14, the country’s reserves totaled $755.6 bln.
Russia's international reserves reached a record high of $826.8 bln on January 30.
Russia’s international reserves are highly liquid foreign assets available with the Bank of Russia and the Russian government. They comprise foreign currency, Special Drawing Rights (SDRs), a reserve position in the International Monetary Fund and monetary gold. Following the onset of Moscow’s special military operation in Ukraine Western countries slapped sanctions against the Bank of Russia. Apart from freezing Russia’s gold and foreign currency reserves, all transactions related to management of the regulator’s reserves and assets, as well as transactions with any legal entity, organization or body acting on behalf or at the direction of the Central Bank, were prohibited.

Four EU countries renew push to use Russia's €210bn assets to support Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
14:12:18 UTC
23:12:18 KST

Ukraine is facing a budget crunch, and EU member states are under pressure to find a solution ahead of next year's election season.
A group of four countries have relaunched the push to unlock immobilised Russian assets to fund Ukraine's budgetary and military needs before European Union member states become distracted by their own domestic elections.
The EU holds €210 billion of these assets, most of it in Belgium.
"Ukraine needs more financial support in both the short and long term. The EU, in dialogue with its partners, should continue to provide comprehensive, predictable and structured financial support to Ukraine in line with its need," the letter reads.
The letter was led by Sweden and co-signed by the Netherlands, Spain and Poland, a selection meant to represent Northern, Western, Southern and Eastern Europe.
It is addressed to High Representative Kaja Kallas and Irish Foreign Minister Helen McEntee, as Ireland currently chairs the Council's rotating presidency.
Earlier this year, the bloc gave the final green light to a €90 billion support loan for Ukraine. But Kyiv is still strapped for cash, and EU capitals want a solution that does not further strain national budgets.
There is also urgency to lock in funding before next year's election season, when key member states, including France, Poland, Italy and Spain, head to the polls.
"We believe now is the time to revert to the issue of how we can make further use of Russia's immobilised assets for the benefit of Ukraine," reads the letter, drafted on the initiative of the Swedish government.
"While we should be proud of our achievements, we cannot afford to rest on our laurels."
At a press conference on Thursday, a European Commission spokesperson said it was "ready to provide any assistance that might be needed in this context" and would study the letter "carefully"
Old struggle, new push
Using Russia's immobilised assets was intensively debated last year as the EU grappled with the withdrawal of US assistance for Ukraine.
Under an inventive proposal, the Commission planned to convert the €210 billion into a zero-interest loan to cover Kyiv's budgetary and military needs. Brussels insisted the scheme would stop short of confiscation, which is illegal under international law, since Russia could recoup the money if it paid war reparations.
Belgium opposed the plan from the outset. As the host of Euroclear, the assets' main custodian, it feared being left exposed to Russian litigation.
Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever demanded "full mutualisation" of the risks to shield his country from Moscow's retaliation and damage claims. Euroclear called the proposal fragile and overtly experimental, warning it risked an investor exodus.
"There is no free money in the world. It just does not exist," De Wever said then.
Despite a strong push from a group of proponents led by Germany, the plan eventually fell apart at a make-or-break summit in December. Now, supporters believe the timing is right to bring it up again.
Budgetary hole
As a fallback, the 27 leaders agreed to issue an extraordinary €90 billion loan for Ukraine, backed by common borrowing and repayable only once reparations are paid. Hungary, Slovakia and Czechia negotiated a full opt-out.
The loan was meant to cover Kyiv's needs for both 2026 and 2027, split evenly at €45 billion a year. The first payment went out in June.
But Russia's relentless bombardment has upended Kyiv's calculations. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has urged allies to plug a €23 billion deficit in the Ministry of Defence budget, telling them he needs "more money, much more" to stay "competitive" in deep strikes. He also raised the matter of the assets.
Zelenskyy's request caught Brussels off guard, raising fresh concern over how long the bloc's €90 billion credit line will last.
Brussels has so far disbursed €3.2 billion in budgetary aid and €8.35 billion in military aid. In total, €22 billion has been allocated for weapons purchases this year.
As Moscow escalates its campaign of ballistic missile strikes, prompting a scramble for air defence systems for Kyiv, capitals are realising the €90 billion loan may not stretch to cover 2026 and 2027 in full, as originally planned.
The new EU budget, with a dedicated Ukraine envelope, will not kick in until 2028.
Looking for 'new options'
Earlier this month, Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha raised the question of reallocating Russia's assets during a visit to Kyiv by his Belgian counterpart, Maxime Prévot.
Prévot said the risks Belgium had previously flagged had not gone away, but signalled an openness to considering new proposals, noting no objection in principle to using the money to support Ukraine.
In other words, Belgium's position has not shifted: if the debate reopens, it will again demand uncapped guarantees, Belgian officials say.
Euroclear, which also remains opposed, is meanwhile fighting a legal challenge from the Russian Central Bank.
As allies gathered in Kyiv for its 35th Independence Day, Swedish Foreign Minister Maria Malmer Stenergard raised the issue again, signalling her intention to put it on the table at the next informal meeting of foreign ministers, set for Ireland on 1-2 September.
"We therefore propose that the Commission's technical experts are invited to explore, in close consultation with member states, new options on how to use the immobilised assets for the benefit of Ukraine, which ensure that the risk rests with all EU member states and where no member state holds a disproportionate burden," the letter says.
"Managing financial and economic risks, as well as compliance with international law, will constitute important components of this technical analysis and discussion," it adds, acknowledging "the question is complex".

Kansas City Federal Reserve President Jeffrey Schmid said Thursday that inflation is still too high, though he stopped short of calling for an interest rate hike.

Schmid does not vote this year on the FOMC, though he still gets to express his views at meetings. When he was a voter last year, he twice dissented against rate cuts.
However, Schmid said he is not sure whether he would support a rate increase now.
"I think we need a little bit more information. What I'm trying to figure out is the demand side of what's driving both growth and inflation," Schmid said.
Separately, Schmid said he sees "some room" to consider an idea that Chairman Kevin Warsh raised in July to reduce the number of FOMC meetings per year to six from the current eight.

Bosnian Serb war criminal Mladic dies in prison at 84
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
14:10:00 UTC
23:10:00 KST

Convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic, known as the "Butcher of Bosnia," whose forces besieged the Bosnian capital for several years in the 1990s and carried out the worst massacre in Europe since World War II, died Thursday while serving a life sentence for his crimes, U.N. officials said. He was 84.
Mladic died at a hospital in The Hague, Netherlands, U.N. court officials said.
The U.N. tribunal for war crimes committed during the wars in the former Yugoslavia in the 1990s sentenced Mladic to life in prison in 2017 in what was considered a key step toward bringing justice to the victims. He had been in custody since 2011 after many years on the run.
The ruthless, former communist officer-turned nationalist warlord was one of the most notorious figures of the Bosnian War that left more than 100,000 people dead and over 1 million homeless. He commanded his troops to "scorch the brains" of the Bosnian Muslims and boasted of being a "Serbian God."
When the ethnic war in Bosnia-Herzegovina started in 1992, Mladic became the commander of the Bosnian Serb troops and took control of large swaths of the country to form a Serb mini-state.
Serbs under Mladic's control laid siege to the Bosnian capital, Sarajevo, and other cities and villages, established concentration camps for detained non-Serb civilians and enemy soldiers, and systematically killed prisoners.
In Sarajevo, Serb troops kept the city isolated while killing civilians with snipers and heavy artillery. In 1995, Mladic's troops slaughtered more than 8,000 Muslim men and boys in Srebrenica – the first case of genocide in Europe since WWII.
But Mladic and his admirers have never repented. He was seen by many as a patriot fighting for the first pan-Serbian state. Defiant, Mladic acted bullishly during his trial and yelled at the judges when sentenced to life in prison.
Munira Subasic, from the Mothers of Srebrenica group, said she had mixed feelings about Mladic's death and deplored that his crimes are still being denied by many Bosnian Serbs.
"Today, a major war criminal died, the criminal of the Balkans," Subasic said. But while mothers of victims "are still carrying the pain in our souls" 31 years later, "we are still listening to denials, we are still listening to how Ratko Mladic was a hero for the Serbs," she said.
"I am sorry that he died and that he did not suffer for a little while longer, that he didn't wait for more and dream about the eyes of our children," she said.
Emir Suljagic, head of the Srebrenica Memorial, said "there is not much to say" about Mladic's death. "Nor does that fact change much."
"It doesn't bring back the dead. It doesn't clear mass graves. It does not change judgment. It does not turn the criminal into a historical figure," Suljagic said.
"Now the hardest part of the job remains: not to let the truth, responsibility and memory die with him. Mladic's death is another moment in which we must decide what we will remember and more importantly, what we will not allow to be erased."
To this day, many Serbs still see him as a hero. Local authorities in Bosnia's Serb entity, Republika Srpska, called on residents to pay their respects to Mladic in churches across the entity.
Residents of Pale, a Bosnian Serb stronghold just outside of Sarajevo, mourned Mladic.
"He was murdered there, in those dungeons," said Janko Seslija, a former Bosnian Serb soldier. "I feel sorry for Gen. Mladic. He was an honorable man, honorable soldier and commander."
Former Bosnian Serb leader Milorad Dodik lit a candle at a church in Banja Luka, calling Mladic "a great figure for the Serbian people" who "took command of the army at a difficult time."
The pro-Russian Dodik has pushed for the separation of Republika Srpska to join neighboring Serbia. His policies have stoked fears of renewed instability in the country.
Mladic was born March 12, 1942, in the tiny Bosnian village of Bozinovici, in the hills 40 kilometers (25 miles) south of Sarajevo. Like other protagonists in the Yugoslav conflict, he imbibed nationalism from his family's fate in WWII – his own father was killed by Croats.
A communist-era officer, Mladic sided with the Serbs as Yugoslavia disintegrated into war. Mladic first led a Serb insurgency in Croatia before taking over the Bosnian Serb army that was backed by Serbia and then-President Slobodan Milosevic, who also died in the custody of the Hague court in 2006 while on trial for genocide.
Mladic was known for his obsession with his nation's history. He saw Bosnia's war as a chance for revenge against the onetime 500-year-long Ottoman control of Serbia. He often referred to Bosnia's Muslims as Turks and boasted of revenge when his troops overran the protected U.N. enclave of Srebrenica in 1995.
Carried away by Serb dominance in firepower and international ignorance, Mladic was convinced of his final victory.
"The time has come... for revenge against Turks in these regions," Mladic said after taking over Srebrenica.
What happened in Srebrenica remains a mark of shame for the international community, as the town had been declared a U.N. "safe haven" for civilians in 1993.
Instead, the Dutch U.N. peacekeepers watched as Serb troops took men and boys, forced them to strip, killed them and bulldozed their bodies into mass graves in a brutal rampage that lasted for over a week.
Many of the bodies were dug back up and reburied in order to try to hide the evidence. The few who escaped told harrowing stories of murder, torture and rape by the Bosnian Serb forces.
The Srebrenica survivors said one image forever will be imprinted in their minds: Mladic handing out candy to Muslim children who had been rounded up on the town's square and reassuring them that everything would be all right – even patting one child on the head.
Convinced of the power of his army, he used to tell his soldiers: "When I give you guarantees, it's as if they are given by God." To clear the way for his helicopter to land, he would tell air traffic controllers: "Here speaks Ratko Mladic - the Serbian God."
Sarajevans still remember his commands to the Serb gunmen pounding the Bosnian capital in early 1992. He issued his orders through a military radio system, not bothering to scramble the signal, which was picked up and taped by the Sarajevo police.
"Turn toward Velesici, there are no Serbs there," Mladic said as he ordered his artillery to pound the Sarajevo suburb.
"Scorch their brains," he told his gunmen.
Faced with the U.N. tribunal's genocide indictment, Mladic in 1996 began his fugitive years in Han Pijesak, a military compound in eastern Bosnia built for Yugoslavia's longtime communist leader, Josip Broz Tito, and designed to withstand a nuclear attack.
With his wife, Bosa, Mladic settled down to imposed domesticity, passing the time caring for bees and goats. His 23 goats reputedly bore the names of foreign dignitaries he despised, such as Madeleine Albright, the former U.S. secretary of state.
Surrounded by security guards, he occasionally ventured out of the dense pine forest to mark events such as the anniversary of the Bosnian Serb army and St. Vitus Day, a religious festival marking the 1389 Serb defeat by the Turks at Kosovo.
When his trail grew too hot in Bosnia in the late 1990s, Mladic moved with family to a villa near the Serbian capital, Belgrade. There, he was seen at his son's wedding, football games and fancy restaurants, refusing to give interviews and smiling quizzically when photographed.
When Milosevic was ousted from power in 2000, and Serbia's new authorities signaled they might hand Mladic to the tribunal, tabloids reported he had left Belgrade for Bosnia.
But true to his style, Mladic countered those rumors and others that said he was terminally ill, and before going underground in 2002, he was repeatedly seen driving around the Serbian capital in a Yugo.
He completely disappeared from public view in 2008 and was finally arrested in May 2011 in a village near Belgrade where he was hiding at a relative's house.
The frail-looking old man who appeared in court at the Hague was a far cry from the robust image Mladic exuded in wartime. But his defiance was intact.
"Everything you said is pure lies. Shame on you!" he yelled at the U.N. judges when they handed down the conviction.
The tribunal said at the time the crimes committed were "amongst the most heinous known to humankind." Former U.N. rights chief Zeid Ra'ad al Hussein described him as "the epitome of evil."
Russia on Thursday criticized the Hague, saying the tribunal that had convicted Mladic had shown "deliberate disregard for basic rules of impartiality and fair treatment of convicted persons for political reasons."
Already in poor health upon arrest in 2011, Mladic is believed to have suffered multiple strokes during his years on the run and was hospitalized on several occasions while in custody.
Serbian state officials and Mladic's family had appealed for his release due to his failing health, but the Hague tribunal rejected those calls.
Kada Hotic, 82, whose 29-year-old son and 56-year-old husband were killed by Serb forces in 1995, said she was grateful to the tribunal because it sentenced Mladic to life and has not released him.
"Justice was served on the day he was sentenced to life," Hotic said.
"He died in disgrace, because he killed so many people."
U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said he stood "in solidarity with the victims, survivors and their families who suffered the crimes" for which Mladic was found guilty, his spokesperson told reporters.
Gutteres reiterated his call on all those in positions of power to refrain from denying the seriousness of the crimes that have been adjudicated.
"He (Guterres) strongly condemns any denial of the Srebrenica genocide as a historical event, and any actions that glorify those convicted of war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide by international courts," his spokesperson, Stephane Dujarric, said.

====================================================================================================

Torn apart by war, Palestinian basketball players reunite in ‘second family’ to keep the dream alive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
14:09:41 UTC
23:09:41 KST

The ball hits the hardwood with a steady thud in an Istanbul sports hall. Shoes squeak, coaches call out instructions, and players move through drills as a single unit.
It looks like an ordinary national team training session. For Palestine's basketball players, however, simply getting everyone onto the same court is an achievement.
The Palestinian national team is based in Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, but its players are scattered across Palestine and several countries abroad. Checkpoints and movement restrictions make assembling the squad inside the occupied territory difficult, while some diaspora players cannot enter at all.
So, ahead of the FIBA Asia Cup 2029 Pre-Qualifiers, the team came together in Istanbul.
Türkiye's Ministry of Youth and Sports, through its Istanbul Provincial Directorate, hosted the camp and provided the team with training facilities. For a squad that spends much of the year separated, Istanbul became both a practical meeting point and a temporary home.
"Some of our players come from Europe, America and Vietnam, while others come from the West Bank," German-Palestinian forward Elias Marei, who wears No. 2 for Palestine, tells TRT World.
"Four years ago, we had players from Gaza, but that is no longer the case."
For those travelling from the occupied West Bank, reaching the team's camp in Türkiye means navigating a journey shaped by checkpoints, border controls and lengthy delays.
Palestine's No. 45 Ramzi Qumsieh made the journey from Bethlehem.
"Our journey was hard. We first go through the Palestinian border, then the Israeli border and then Jordan. From Jordan, we fly to Türkiye. We cannot travel directly from Palestine because of the borders," he tells TRT World.
Some players spent more than 12 hours reaching Jordan before they could continue to Türkiye, according to head coach Harry Savaya.
"My players came from everywhere, including the occupied territories," Savaya tells TRT World. "Travelling here was very difficult, and they faced many problems on the road to Jordan."
The difficulties are not confined to international travel. Even bringing players together for training inside the occupied West Bank can be a logistical exercise.
Before arriving in Istanbul, only seven players had been able to practise together. For some, reaching a training session can take four or five hours.
Journeys between the occupied West Bank cities that would ordinarily take about an hour can stretch to as long as eight because of checkpoints and road closures.
Players sometimes have to leave their jobs and families behind and stay in Ramallah for an entire week simply to train.
That makes the time they have together in Istanbul particularly valuable.
"Türkiye is like our second family," Savaya says.
"The people, the courts and the facilities make this one of the best places for us to be. This camp is very important because it brings the team together, helps us develop chemistry and prepares us for the qualifiers in the short time that we have."
The players trained for up to six hours a day under Savaya and his coaching staff, trying to compress months of preparation into the limited time they had together.
"Some of us have been together for five or six years, while we also have new players and new coaches," Qumsieh says.
"The coach is giving us a really hard time – we are practising for around six hours a day. But the coach is good, the staff is good and everyone is doing everything possible for us."
Their preparations also included an August 17 friendly against Qatar, which Palestine lost 89-72, giving the squad a competitive test before travelling to Kazakhstan.
For Mohammed Mousa, Palestine's No. 88, however, the importance of being together in Istanbul extends beyond preparing for the next game.
"This camp is very important because it brings together the Palestinian players who are in the homeland and the players who have come from the diaspora," he tells TRT World.
"We are preparing and training well. God willing, our hard work will not be wasted."
More than a jersey
For players who spend much of the year separated by borders and occupation, coming together also reinforces what it means to wear the Palestinian jersey.
When Abu Shamsiya pulls on his No. 34 shirt, he sees more than a basketball uniform.
"It carries a much greater meaning. We have lived under occupation since 1948, and we are trying to represent Palestine in the best possible way – not only to the Middle East, but to the whole world," Abu Shamsiya, who has represented the senior national team since 2023, says.
For him, continuing to compete internationally despite the circumstances facing Palestinians carries a message of its own.
"After everything that has happened, we are still standing and we will continue," he says. "Nobody can stop us. I am certain of that, and the whole team is certain of it."
That sense of responsibility extends beyond the players on the court. For a team representing a people scattered by occupation, war and displacement, playing for Palestine also means representing those who cannot be there.
Qumsieh describes the players as "sports ambassadors" for Palestinians at home and those forced into exile.
"We represent Palestine. We represent our people in Gaza, everyone inside the country and everyone outside it who was forced to leave," he says.
"We are the voice of every boy who wants to play basketball and every girl who wants to play basketball."
For Marei, a 24-year-old German-Palestinian professional who plays in Germany's ProB league, basketball offers another way to make Palestine visible internationally – one that is not defined solely by conflict.
"We can show our sport, and we can show our identity to the world," he says. "Sport is a good way to put Palestine on the map."
But Marei is reluctant to portray the players themselves as heroes.
"The real fighters and the real heroes are not us," he says. "They are the Palestinians living in the West Bank, Gaza; the occupied land. We are privileged simply to play basketball and to be able to represent Palestine."
For Mousa, the connection to Gaza is deeply personal.
He left the enclave in 2017, but his family remains there. His brother and brother-in-law have been killed during Israel's war on Gaza, along with many of his friends.
His brother, Firas Khaled Mahmoud Mousa, known as "al-Sharkh", was also a basketball player.
The 26-year-old playmaker had risen through school, university and youth teams before joining Khadamat al-Maghazi's senior side.
He also played for Shabab al-Maghazi and dreamed of reaching the occupied West Bank to compete for its clubs and represent Palestine.
He never got the chance.
Firas was killed on November 4, 2024, after an artillery strike hit the club's premises in the Maghazi refugee camp.
For Mousa, taking the court for Palestine is now also a way of honouring those he has lost.
"My brother was a basketball player with Khadamat al-Maghazi," Mousa says. "This is the least we can offer them – to bring them some happiness. May God have mercy on our dead, heal our wounded and free our prisoners."
Mousa's loss illustrates how deeply the war has reached into Palestinian sport. But even outside Gaza, occupation shapes whether and how Palestinian athletes can train.
Abu Shamsiya says players in the occupied West Bank contend with restrictions on movement, economic hardship and constant concern for their families, while sporting facilities themselves have not been spared.
"It is not only what is happening in Gaza," he says. "Many things are happening in the West Bank as well. Everyone is affected – the players, their families, businesses, the economy and life in general."
He recalls tear gas being fired near a national-team training camp and sports halls being bombed.
"Imagine being in a normal national-team training session and someone fires tear gas at you," Abu Shamsiya says. "You cannot do anything. This actually happened. No one can understand what it is like without living through it."
Qumsieh says conditions in the occupied West Bank cannot be compared with the devastation in Gaza, but even there, training can be disrupted by violence.
"We have courts where we practise, especially in Bethlehem and Beit Sahour," he says.
"But sometimes they fire tear gas, and sometimes there is shooting when things happen. Most of the time we are safer than the people in Gaza."
From Istanbul to Almaty
After completing their preparations in Istanbul, the players left the training court that had briefly brought the scattered squad together and travelled to Almaty, Kazakhstan, for Group B of the FIBA Asia Cup 2029 Pre-Qualifiers.
They began their campaign at Baluan Sholak Sports Palace on August 26 with a commanding 110-69 victory over Kyrgyzstan.
Palestine next faces Sri Lanka on August 27, host nation Kazakhstan on August 28, and the Maldives on August 30.
Twelve teams from the opening stage will progress to the second round, with the top four sides in each second-round group advancing to the main FIBA Asia Cup 2029 Qualifiers.
"We have not qualified for a long time, so our motivation is to win and reach the next round," Qumsieh says.
"We have been training together in Türkiye, and everybody – from the players and coaches to the federation president – is trying to do everything possible. We have no excuses."
For Palestine, however, the campaign's significance goes beyond qualification.
The Istanbul camp offered something the players struggle to find at home: a place where those from the occupied West Bank and the diaspora could simply gather, train and function as one national team.
They arrived there by different routes, after checkpoints, border crossings and flights. Some carried memories of family members killed in Gaza. Others had spent hours travelling between West Bank cities just to attend training.
For a few weeks in Istanbul, those separate journeys converged on the same basketball court.
Then they travelled to Kazakhstan wearing the same jersey.
"We are still standing," Abu Shamsiya tells TRT World. "And we will continue."

Tunisia recovers bodies of last missing migrants from sunken boat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
14:09:06 UTC
23:09:06 KST

Tunisia recovers bodies of last missing migrants from sunken boat
TUNIS, Aug 27 - Tunisian authorities said on Thursday they had recovered the remains of the last migrants missing from a boat that sank off the coast last week, bringing the death toll to 14.
The boat was carrying mostly young people, including seven members of the same family, as well as a man and his pregnant wife, the Tunisian Observatory for Human Rights said over the weekend.
The central Mediterranean route from the North African coast is one of the world's deadliest migration routes, used by migrants from Africa and the Middle East seeking to reach Europe, often in overcrowded or unseaworthy boats.
Earlier this week, the Coast Guard said it had found the bodies of 11 Tunisian migrants. One person was rescued alive.
The National Guard said on Thursday it had now ended search and rescue operations and handed the bodies over to their families.
Migrant departures from Tunisia have declined over the past two years amid a crackdown on migrants, backed by European support that has included funding and modern surveillance equipment. REUTERS
