Mladić and the monstrous crimes of the 'Butcher of Bosnia'
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
14:48:09 BST
22:48:09 KST

The monstrous crimes of Ratko Mladic, the 'Butcher of Bosnia'
- Published
Ratko Mladić, who has died at the age of 84, was the bull-necked "Butcher of Bosnia".
As Commander of the Bosnian Serb army, he oversaw a brutal campaign of "ethnic cleansing" as Yugoslavia splintered in the 1990s.
The phrase was a chilling euphemism for the massacre of tens of thousands of men, women and children - in pursuit of what he saw as a chance to fulfil the historic destiny of Greater Serbia.
It was a goal he pursued with single-minded determination and studied brutality - and it made him responsible for the bloodiest atrocities Europe has witnessed since Hitler's Third Reich.
His fanaticism made him a hero to his people. He told them their Muslim neighbours planned to "impale Serbs, burn them alive, crucify them and put out their eyes".
He led the long and bloody siege of Sarajevo; killing and maiming its citizens in a daily hail of shells and sniper-fire.
When his troops overran the UN-declared safe area of Srebrenica, he promised they were safe. Later, 8,000 men and boys were led to unmarked graves.
He and his political counterpart, Radovan Karadžić, ripped Bosnia apart - committing acts of genocide and vicious crimes against humanity.
The barrel-chested warlord displayed no remorse, giving relatives of his victims a cheery thumbs-up at his eventual trial in the Hague.
"Borders are drawn in blood," he is reported to have said. "And states marked out with graves."
Ratko Mladić was born on 12 March 1942 in a small mountain village near Sarajevo, then part of the German-controlled Independent State of Croatia - although he always claimed to be a year younger.
Two years later, his father was killed fighting for Tito's partisans against Nazi-backed Croat nationalists.
Mladić was brought up in the new, post-war construct of Yugoslavia. After a short apprenticeship as a tinsmith, he chose a military career.
He graduated from officer school in 1965. Proving himself an ambitious and capable soldier, he rose rapidly through the ranks, commanding army units in Macedonia and Kosovo.
Tito's death in 1980 was the beginning of the end for Yugoslavia - always an uneasy confederation of opposing factions, competing nationalisms and simmering hatred.
In June 1991, Croatia declared independence. Mladić was sent in with the Yugoslav army in an effort to re-impose control.
He gained a reputation for courage bordering on recklessness, ever-present in frontline trenches and personally leading expeditions to clear mines.
His men loved him for it, their devotion bordering on religious.
As the war spilled over into Bosnia, his force switched uniforms - pledging support for the breakaway Republika Srpska.
He saw the Muslim population as invaders - the result of an ancient occupation by Ottoman Turks.
Mladić vowed to right what he considered a historical injustice, drive out the intruders and then build the ethnically pure nation of his dreams.
So began the siege of Sarajevo - the Bosnian capital defended by a rag-tag multi-ethnic force of Serbs, Croats and Bosniaks (Bosnian Muslims).
With his troops dug in on surrounding hillsides, the blockade lasted 1,425 days. It was the longest city siege in the savage history of modern warfare.
On 22 July 1993, nearly 4,000 shells rained down on its terrified people.
By the end of the siege, 13,000 were dead from shell-fire or a sniper's bullet; almost every building in the city either damaged or destroyed.
In the villages around the capital, legions of men were killed or carted off to prison camps; thousands of women were mercilessly raped.
A communiqué from Gen Mladić's headquarters captured his attitude. "Shoot at slow intervals until I order you to stop," it said.
"Target Muslim neighbourhoods - not many Serbs live there. Shell them until they are on the edge of madness."
Revelling in the power of his army, he gave orders by radio, the messages deliberately left unscrambled so they would be picked up and broadcast worldwide.
"Burn their brains," he screamed as his soldiers took aim at one enclave, telling them to follow his orders "as if given by God."
At weekends, he would visit his family, his wife and two children kept safe in Belgrade.
They would play board games, the conversation deliberately avoiding politics. But his 23-year-old daughter, Ana, had fallen in love with a young doctor and human rights activist.
The doctor gave her an ultimatum: renounce your father or never see me again.
Torn between dreams of love and bonds of family, Ana took her father's favourite gun from its display case. Moments later, she pulled the trigger.
Mladić struggled to come to terms with her suicide, preferring wild conspiracy theories which blamed the tragedy on everyone but himself.
Finally, in 1995, Nato lost patience.
It launched fighter attacks and cruise missile strikes on Mladić's positions around Sarajevo, most of them with devastating effect.
The siege was broken but his murderous campaign to cleanse the country was far from over.
That summer, tens of thousands of Bosniak civilians were gathered in Srebrenica: a small mountain town in eastern Bosnia.
They were under the protection of the United Nations, which had declared it a "safe area".
Bosnian Serb troops bombarded them with heavy shells and rockets. Five days later, Mladić strutted into town surrounded by TV camera crews.
In the main square, he handed out sweets, patted children on the head and assured them all would be fine. They were not fooled.
The handful of Dutch peacekeepers did nothing as men were shot and women were raped.
There followed the single most heinous act on European soil since World War Two.
Mladić's troops rounded up every Bosniak male they could find, marched them to remote sites and murdered them on an industrial scale.
In just a few days, 8,000 men and boys were tied up, blindfolded and shot. Some of them were as young as twelve, others in their late seventies.
All of them were cruelly pushed into mass, unmarked graves.
It was genocide: a black moment in European history and the UN's darkest hour.
It was a crime that took a high degree of organisation; the people had been promised UN protection and all this had happened right under its nose.
Later, the UN Secretary General, Kofi Annan, wrote that responsibility lay "first and foremost with those who planned and carried out the massacre". However, the international community had "made serious errors of judgement, rooted in a philosophy of impartiality", he added.
Mladić was accused of war crimes.
America offered $5m for information leading to his capture. A year later, Bosnian President Biljana Plavsic buckled to international pressure and dismissed him.
But it would be 14 years before he stood trial at the Hague.
He returned to Belgrade, enjoying the support and protection of President Slobodan Milošević.
Mladić lived openly; deer-hunting with friends, eating in swanky restaurants and even attending football matches.
He remained a hero to swathes of his countrymen, who saw in him the Serbian martial spirit and an echo of the past glories of their nation.
They were determined not to give him to an International Court. The president even established a military force dedicated to Mladić's personal protection.
The net began to tighten when, in October 2000, Slobodan Milošević was himself arrested and later delivered to the Hague.
International politics was beginning to bite, Serbia's entry to the European Union held up by its protection of the fugitives.
That night, Mladić fled; no longer guaranteed the sanctuary of his state.
He spent the next decade moving from safe-house to safe-house, first protected by a loyal team of bodyguards and, when they dwindled away, by his family.
In July 2008, his former political ally, Radovan Karadžić - now a long-bearded faith-healer - was arrested on a bus in Belgrade.
The new Serbian regime delivered him to the International Court, with which it had formalised co-operation. General Mladić was next.
Three years later, he was found.
The police tailed his children to a remote, squalid farmhouse where they stood alone in the courtyard for no apparent reason.
Too nervous to meet them, Mladić was watching through a window. When the security forces went in, they found a dishevelled 69-year-old man who had suffered several strokes.
The trial itself took four years.
The court sat for more than 500 days, heard from nearly 600 witnesses, and examined nearly 10,000 bits of evidence.
Due process was followed, although few doubted what the verdict would be.
Ratko Mladić was shown giving orders to his troops immediately before the Srebrenica massacre and convicted of genocide, crimes against humanity and violations of the "customs of war".
He entered the courtroom with a smile and a thumbs-up to the cameras but exploded with anger at the verdicts.
Screaming that it was "all lies", he was forcibly removed. His sentence meant he would die in prison.
Among the many victims and their relatives present at his trial was Fikret Alic, a prisoner famously filmed in a skeletal state in a Bosnian Serb concentration camp in 1992.
"Justice has been done," he said. "The war criminal has been convicted". Others simply dissolved in tears.
But the widespread joy at the verdicts was far from universal.
Some Bosniaks were disappointed he had not been convicted of crimes outside Sarajevo and Srebrenica. And many fellow Serbs reacted with rage.
One leading politician in Republika Srpska condemned the trial as a plot to demonise his people, and called for them to "forever erase every mention" of the court proceedings from school history books.
In 2024, the court turned down his application to serve the rest of his sentence in Serbia. Having suffered heart attacks and strokes, Mladić claimed that his health would be better protected in his home country.
His lawyers continued to reapply unsuccessfully for his release, on the grounds that he had only months to live.
Both Serbia and Russia have supported his legal appeals. In Bosnia, by contrast, an opposition politician was sentenced to three years in prison for "glorifying" Karadžić and Mladić in January 2026.
For many of his people, the "Butcher of Bosnia" was just a simple soldier and the protector of their way of life. But he will be remembered by Bosniaks and most of the international community as a murderous thug who disgraced the European stage.
In Bosnia, Muslims and Serbs live side-by-side in uneasy cohabitation. The violent nationalist war waged by Mladić and Radovan Karadžić in the 1990s may be over, but tension still exists.

Polish Olympic chief Radosław Piesiewicz arrested in crypto-linked graft probe, officials say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
13:47:16 UTC
22:47:16 KST

Authorities launched an investigation in April, which prompted most of Poland's sports federations to call for Piesiewicz's resignation.
Police arrested the head of the Polish Olympic Committee on Thursday on suspicion that he took bribes from a crypto trader in return for sponsorship deals, officials said.
Radosław Piesiewicz, who is considered close to Poland's nationalist right, is suspected of receiving kickbacks from Zondacrypto, which the government accuses of having links to nationalist opposition groups, organised crime and Russian intelligence services.
"Radosław Piesiewicz has been arrested," Poland's Sports Minister Jakub Rudnicki confirmed in a post on X.
"Such a person should never have been president of the Polish Olympic Committee...Piesiewicz has discredited Polish Olympics," he added.
Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski described Piesiewicz as a "symbol of the extreme corruption plaguing the Olympic movement."
He said Piesiewicz's election as head of the Olympic committee had been backed by the former government, led by the nationalist Law and Justice (PiS) party.
Authorities launched an investigation in April, which prompted most of Poland's sports federations to call for Piesiewicz's resignation.
Crypto prizes for athletes
They said Piesiewicz was responsible for signing a sponsorship agreement for the Olympic committee with Zondacrypto, a crypto fund which has stopped trading.
Under the deal, Olympic medallists at the Winter Olympics in Milano-Cortina in February would be awarded prizes in cryptocurrency.
The payment of the bonuses was random at best.
The government estimates that Zondacrypto's disappearance caused 350 million zlotys (€80 million) in losses, with around 30,000 people falling victim to the company. The interior minister said that Zondacrypto was "in reality a Ponzi scheme."
Media reports said Piesiewicz received a watch worth some €40,000 from Zondacrypto chief Przemyslaw Kral. Piesiewicz has said he paid for the watch himself.
The reports said Kral was now cooperating with prosecutors in a bid to get a lighter sentence when he faces a trial.
Piesiewicz is one of many names cited by prosecutors in the Zondacrypto investigation.
Former justice minister and attorney general Zbigniew Ziobro has since fled to the United States, while his former deputy Marcin Romanowski is said to be in a pro-Russian separatist region of Moldova.
Prosecutors are also looking into Zondacrypto's links to the pro-nationalist Republika broadcaster.
President Karol Nawrocki, a nationalist elected in 2025, has blocked draft laws aiming to regulate the crypto market in Poland three times.
Prime Minister Donald Tusk, an opponent of Nawrocki, has told parliament that Zondacrypto's founder had "disappeared" and was "very probably" dead. He said the Zondacrypto scandal involved "Russian mafia" money.
The cryptocurrency was founded in 2014 by Sylwester Suszek who disappeared in 2022. His place as head of the company was taken by Kral.

A Malaysian court charged former Prime Minister Ismail Sabri Yaakob on Thursday with failing to disclose his assets to the country’s anti-graft agency. According to state news agency Bernama, the 66-year-old is accused of failing to declare local and foreign currencies totaling nearly $40 million, as well as five gold bars, to the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission (MACC) on February 7 last year at the agency's headquarters.
Ismail Sabri, who served as Malaysia's prime minister from August 2021 to October 2022, pleaded not guilty to the charges and was released on 300,000 ringgit (about $74,500) bail.
He submitted a wealth declaration to the MACC in March last year after the agency seized the $40 million in assets allegedly linked to him as part of a broader investigation into corruption and money laundering.
The next hearing in the trial is set for September 29.

MSI wins contract for naval gun systems with unnamed NATO buyer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
13:46:57 UTC
22:46:57 KST

MSI Defence Systems has won a £16.6 million ($22.6 million) contract to supply three 30mm naval gun systems to an unnamed NATO country, according to Navy Lookout.
The deal includes MSI-DS’s own radar and optical fire-control system, which the company says allows the gun mounts to engage aircraft, drones, surface vessels and semi-submersible threats. Deliveries are expected to begin toward the end of 2027.
MSI Defence Systems, based in Norwich, England, is the only UK-based manufacturer of medium-caliber naval gun mounts and has exported its Seahawk 30mm systems to more than 40 countries. The company specializes in stabilized mount architecture rather than the guns themselves, allowing cannons of different calibers to be integrated with minimal redesign.
MSI’s gun mounts are already in service with the Royal Navy, where the DS30M has been fitted across much of the fleet since it entered service in 2005. The lightweight variant of the Seahawk mount has also been selected by Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence for its patrol vessels.
The company has expanded significantly into the U.S. market in recent years. After supplying eight systems to the U.S. Navy for trials and evaluation in late 2023, MSI received a $23.4 million low-rate production order for 15 Mk38 Mod 4 gun mounts, with work split between its factories in Norwich and Rock Hill, South Carolina. USS Mustin became the first U.S. Navy warship to receive the Mk38 Mod 4 in late 2024, and the system underwent test firing at sea in July 2025. Arleigh Burke Flight IIA and Flight III destroyers are slated to receive the mount going forward. A second U.S. contract worth $29.2 million covers manufacture and support of the Mk48 Mod 2 Electro-Optical Sight used to guide the gun.
MSI’s 30mm Seahawk system was also selected for the German navy, beginning with installation on Brandenburg-class frigates.
Navy Lookout did not name the NATO country receiving the new order, and MSI has not disclosed further details on the contract’s scope or the specific vessels the gun mounts will be fitted to.

Convicted Bosnian Serb war criminal Mladić dies aged 84
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
14:46:40 BST
22:46:40 KST

Convicted Bosnian Serb war criminal Mladić dies aged 84
- Published
Convicted Bosnian Serb war criminal Ratko Mladić has died in a UN prison at The Hague aged 84.
He was jailed for life in 2017 for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity during the wars in the former Yugoslavia in 1992-95.
After the Bosnian war, he went on the run for 16 years until he was finally tracked down in rural Serbia in 2011 and put on trial in the Dutch city.
The sentence for the man known as the "Butcher of Bosnia" was upheld on appeal by the UN court in 2021. He was being given palliative care in the hospital of the UN detention facility, where he died.
In a statement confirming the death on Thursday, the UN Court said Dutch authorities have begun an investigation.
It added that the court's top judge"has ordered a full inquiry into the circumstances" of Mladić's death.
In May, the court rejected a bid for his release from jail as he was nearing the end of his life.
The judge agreed his situation was "dire" but ruled that he was receiving "comprehensive and compassionate treatment" in prison.
Mladić's lawyers said at the time that he had already been bedbound or in a wheelchair for a long time and later had suffered a suspected stroke that left him almost unable to speak.
Mladić - who never recognised the UN court - had been held at The Hague detention facility since 2011.
He commanded Bosnian Serb forces in the 1990s against the Bosnian Croat and Bosniak (Bosnian Muslim) armies.
During the war his troops committed what became known as "ethnic cleansing" in Bosnia-Herzegovina in a bid to expel the non-Serbian population by force. They besieged the main city of Sarajevo with the deaths of more than 10,000 people, and carried out the massacre of 8,000 men and boys at Srebrenica.
Hasan Hasanović , a Srebrenica survivor who lost his twin brother and father in the massacre, told the BBC World Service's Newshour programme that Mladić's death "does not bring closure because the people who were killed in Srebrenica cannot come back".
"His death is just a biological necessity, and it doesn't bring to an end the political project and military project that created that legacy of genocide. And we now live with the consequences of a divided country, genocide denial," said Hasanović, who now works at the Srebrenica memorial centre.
However, Bosnian Serb separatist leader Milorad Dodik told Reuters news agency that Mladić "was respected by Serbian people. As a commander he stood to defend Serbs."
In Serbia's capital Belgrade, some local residents also praised him.
"I genuinely believe he protected the Serbian people, because after all, that was his duty," a man called Milan was quoted as saying by Reuters.
Another man, Vasilije, said: "It's a massive shame, it really is. Personally, I think it's a total injustice that he was even thrown in The Hague."

Israel claims assassination of 'Sinwar's bodyguard' in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27

Breadcrumb
Israel claims assassination of 'Sinwar's bodyguard' as Gaza ceasefire violations continue
The Israeli army and security agency Shin Bet on Thursday claimed they had assassinated two members of Hamas' military wing in Gaza, one of whom was allegedly the personal bodyguard of slain Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar.
The army identified one of the deceased as Hamas elite military wing member Hazem Moussa, saying he was killed in a raid on Sunday. It accused Moussa of participating in the attack on the Re'im military base on 7 October 2023.
A seperate raid on Monday resulted in the killing of Rizq Suhail Suleiman Abu Shahma, who the army claimed was also an elite military unit member and Sinwar's bodyguard. The military released a photo of Abu Shahma alongside Sinwar during an event, though it provided no further evidence that he was part of Sinwar's security detail.
The statement claimed that Moussa and Abu Shahma were planning attacks on Israel and attempting to rebuild Hamas' military capabilities, what it called a "violation of the ceasefire agreement".
The attacks, which took place in Khan Younis, are part of Israel's continued raids on Gaza despite the US-brokered ceasefire agreement which came into force in October.
Gaza's health ministry on Wednesday said Israel had killed 1,303 Palestinians since the ceasefire, bringing the total death toll since October 2023 to 73,438.
On Thursday, Israel continued its attacks, bombing the roof of a house in the Al-Shati camp, west of Gaza City. The attack wounded several Palestinians, including one who remains in intensive care.
On Wednesday, the high representative for US President Donald Trump's 'Board of Peace' slammed Israel's attacks on Gaza, questioning why Tel Aviv has continued its offensive.
Nikolay Mladenov highlighted that Hamas has agreed to disarm under Trump's peace plan, but said that Israel's attacks continue to kill Palestinians.
“After three years of war and 20 years of military operations, I ask, will another strike on a munitions depot stop Hamas from rearming or tightening its grip on Gaza?" Mladenov said. “It will not. It only delays the demilitarisation that would happen”.

CIA chief John Ratcliffe reportedly made secretive Moscow trip to warn Russia against attacking NATO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
13:45:57 UTC
22:45:57 KST

U.S. CIA Director John Ratcliffe made a surprise trip to Moscow this week to warn Russia against attacking NATO, according to multiple media reports, amid growing fears of further escalation in the Ukraine war.
Ratcliffe's first publicly known visit to the Russian capital as CIA chief came to light on Tuesday, when a U.S. Air Force jet was spotted arriving at a Moscow airport, and footage of a diplomatic motorcade moving through the city emerged on social media.
The purpose of Ratcliffe's trip to Moscow was first reported Wednesday by The Wall Street Journal, citing unnamed sources briefed on the trip.
Politico and CBS News separately reported the same motive, citing multiple people familiar with the matter. CBS News added that Ratcliffe also brought up Iran, warning of additional sanctions if the strategically vital Strait of Hormuz does not reopen to shipping traffic.
The Trump administration has threatened Iran's trading partners with so-called secondary sanctions as it seeks to ratchet up the pressure on Tehran's economy following six months of war between the U.S., Israel and Iran.
China, the United Arab Emirates and Turkey are known to be among Iran's top trading partners, while Russia has long shared close economic and military ties with Tehran.
Spokespeople for the CIA and the Russian Embassy in London were not immediately available to comment when contacted by CNBC.
U.S. President Donald Trump on Wednesday described Ratcliffe's meeting with figures from Russia's intelligence services as "semi-routine." He added that "something may come out of" the Moscow visit and Washington would like to see the Russia-Ukraine war come to an end. His comments came during an interview with conservative talk show host Glenn Beck.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov, meanwhile, said Ratcliffe did not meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin during his visit to Moscow and declined to specify whether the meeting concerned issues such as Ukraine or Iran.
"I can only tell you that contacts took place through the intelligence services," Peskov said Wednesday, according to Russian state news agency Tass.
Russia and Ukraine have exchanged an intensifying series of drone and missile strikes far beyond the front lines in recent weeks, amplifying fears of further escalation in the conflict.
Alongside analysts and external observers warning that Russia's full-scale invasion could soon enter a more dangerous phase, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that Putin is preparing to escalate the war.
In comments posted on X earlier this month, Zelenskyy called on the country's partners to ramp up sanctions pressure on Moscow and provide Kyiv with further air defense support.
Russian forces have increased the number of missile strikes on Ukrainian cities in recent weeks, likely as part of a push to exploit Kyiv's shortage of ballistic missile interceptors.
Zelenskyy has repeatedly called on international partners to expedite the supply of ballistic missile interceptors to Ukraine, saying the technology could have saved the lives of those killed in Kyiv on Aug. 5.
'Quite an unusual visit'
Katia Glod, deputy head of foreign policy at the New Eurasian Strategies Centre think tank, said Ratcliffe's trip to Moscow was "quite an unusual visit" but not the first of its kind.
The last known visit by the head of the CIA to Moscow was in November 2021, when William Burns warned Russia against sending troops into Ukraine. Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine just weeks later in late February 2022.
"I think it is indeed important that [Ratcliffe] went there. He is one of the strongest supporters of Ukraine and I think the current wave of escalation of hybrid attacks against Europe is indeed something that perhaps the U.S. also wants to have some discussion with Moscow about," Glod told CNBC's "Europe Early Edition" on Thursday.
"We have seen the cases recently in Germany. Again, there have been many cases in Britain and I think this just shows us that the level of communication is needed to be stepped up, because the situation … has been escalating," she added.

The president of the Polish Olympic Committee (PKOl), Radosław Piesiewicz, has been detained as part of a criminal investigation into Zondacrypto, a cryptocurrency firm that collapsed earlier this year and was a major sponsor of Poland’s Olympic team.
The development comes a day after Waldemar Żurek, Poland’s justice minister and prosecutor general, revealed that prosecutors are investigating possible crimes relating to Zondacrypto’s financing of various individuals and organisations, including PKOl, Piesiewicz, and figures from Poland’s right-wing opposition.

Under Piesiewicz’s leadership, PKOl signed an agreement in 2025 with Zondacrypto that made the crypto firm the main sponsor of the Polish team at this year’s Winter Olympics in Italy.
However, in April, Zondacrypto began to come under scrutiny after customers began reporting being unable to access their funds. The firm subsequently collapsed and Kral went into hiding abroad. Prosecutors estimate losses to its clients of at least 350 million zloty (€81.4 million).
At a press conference today, Żurek confirmed that Piesiewicz had been detained in connection with the investigation into Zondacrypto, which concerns suspected large-scale fraud and other criminal activity.
The development comes days after two leading media outlets, Wirtualna Polska and TVN, published a joint investigation in which they alleged that Piesiewicz received a watch worth €40,000 and other gifts from Kral.
The gifts were allegedly given in exchange for Piesiewicz intervening on behalf of Zondacrypto with Poland’s consumer protection authority, UOKiK. Piesiewicz denies the allegations and says he bought the watch with his own money, with Kral simply helping facilitate the purchase.

“Cash for watches worth €40,000 euros, [financing] for media, election parties, foundations of right-wing politicians,” he continued. “And the ‘Zonda’ show is just getting started.”

He noted that no evidence had been presented and no indictments made against PiS politicians. “Instead, we have ministers threatening to hold others accountable, and nothing has happened. This is simply meant to cover up the incompetence of the current government.”

Arsonists target planned asylum shelter for teen refugees

Someone tried to set fire to a building in Valkenswaard in Noord-Brabant, which is being prepared as a shelter for teenage refugees, police have said.
The fire was started at two points on the former business premises on Leenderweg late on Wednesday, several windows were also broken.
Police said on Thursday that they were treating the incident as arson. A flammable liquid may have been thrown against the building, according to reports.
News emerged less than two weeks ago that COA, the refugee settlement agency, had approved a plan to house 40 unaccompanied minors aged 14 to 18 at the site for up to five years, a term that could be extended to 10.
Valkenswaard council stressed that no final decision had yet been taken, and that it would work through the details with COA over the coming months.
Run of attacks
 The arson is the latest in a wave of vandalism, fires and bomb scares at sites earmarked for asylum seekers. In June, explosives were found at a planned centre in nearby Nuenen.
Earlier in the year, an explosion damaged a building in Den Bosch earmarked for teenage refugees, and a disused town hall in Loosdrecht was targeted during weeks of riots and arson.
The domestic security service AIVD is still investigating whether organised groups are behind the unrest.

EU’s frugals push for cuts but can’t agree on how much as budget talks enter key phase
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
13:41:36 UTC
22:41:36 KST

The EU's frugals gathered in Berlin to push for cuts. But they still cannot agree on how much as European budget talks enter key phase.
Germany, Austria, Denmark, Finland, the Netherlands and Sweden want to cut the EU’s proposed long-term budget for 2027–2034, but have yet to agree on how much.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz hosted the leaders of Finland, Austria and Denmark for a lunch meeting in Berlin on Thursday to discuss cuts to the EU’s next seven-year budget. The prime ministers of the Netherlands and Sweden joined by video conference.
The meeting of the so-called “frugals” — vocal net contributors to the EU budget — was intended to reaffirm their shared demand to reduce the budget’s overall size. But they again failed to agree on a figure.
“We will continue to handle this in the same way as a group. We agreed on this today because we share a common interest in advocating for realism and reforms in these negotiations,” Merz said at a subsequent press conference.
“We finance around 40% of the European budget. This means that we are, so to speak, the group of major contributors to the European budget,” he added.
Opposing camps
In July 2025, the European Commission proposed a €2 trillion EU budget, which is now being negotiated by the 27 member states. Two camps have emerged.
The “Friends of Cohesion” want to protect agriculture, fisheries and regional funding, which the Commission’s proposal would cut compared with the current budget. The group includes 17 member states, among them Spain, Italy, Poland, Hungary and Portugal.
The “frugal” camp wants to significantly reduce the overall budget and redirect spending towards priorities such as competitiveness and defence. They have increasingly styled themselves as the “modernisers”.
In June, Cyprus, which was then chairing the member states’ discussions, proposed a compromise involving a €32.8 billion cut, focused on programmes favoured by the modernisers.
“The European budget must prioritise competitiveness and security. We also need, as the Chancellor just said, to build a stronger economy,” Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said.
She called for an EU budget that is “responsible and understandable for our citizens”.
Fresh proposal needed
Cyprus traditionally belongs to the Friends of Cohesion camp but did not sign the group’s May letter, in line with the neutrality expected of the rotating presidency. For the frugals, however, the Cypriot compromise fell well short of a genuine middle ground.
They argue that the Commission’s proposal would increase the budget by up to 60% at a time when national finances are already under pressure from rising defence spending and aid for Ukraine.
Ireland, now chairing the talks, must produce a fresh compromise before the European Council summit in mid-October — the key target of Thursday’s show of unity.
European Council President António Costa is also touring European capitals to discuss the budget, with the aim of securing a deal by the end of the year.
With 2027 set to be a major election year in several member states, including France, Italy, Poland, Finland, Greece, Spain, Slovakia and Estonia, EU leaders face pressure to reach an agreement before campaigning gets underway.
Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo reiterated his commitment to reaching a deal by year-end, but “not at any cost”.
“We are not stingy, but allocations such as those proposed by the Commission are simply out of step with the times. We want a European budget that is commensurate with our aspirations for a sovereign and strong Europe,” Merz said.
No figure agreed
While the frugal countries broadly agree on the need for cuts, they have yet to converge on a target for the overall budget or how deeply to cut the Commission’s proposal.
German government spokesman Stefan Kornelius told Die Zeit that Berlin wants the total EU budget reduced to €1.6 trillion — around €400 billion below the Commission’s proposal.
Other governments have focused on national contributions rather than the overall budget. The Dutch government told parliament it wants to ensure that Dutch contributions from 2028 onwards increase by €1.6 billion less than currently proposed.
Sweden, expected to take a tougher line after its upcoming election, wants national contributions capped at 1% of gross national income, compared with the Commission’s proposed 1.26%.
The group’s joint statement remains vague, saying only that the Commission’s “nearly €2 trillion” proposal must be reduced by “several hundred billion euros” in a balanced manner.
Those differences could ultimately weaken the frugals’ leverage: the group of wealthy net contributors has traditionally wielded significant influence in budget negotiations precisely because it has acted as a united bloc.

New Turkish law allows children to be sentenced to life in prison outrages human rights groups
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
13:38:30 UTC
22:38:30 KST

A new Turkish law allowing children aged 15 and above to be sentenced to life in prison, and those aged 12 and above to receive a maximum sentence of 27 years, has been widely condemned by human rights groups since it came into effect earlier this month.
The amendments to the Child Protection Law, which took effect on August 8, violate children’s rights by allowing those younger than 14 to be tried as adults, Human Rights Watch claimed. The organization also criticized provisions requiring detained children to be held in closed prisons rather than educational institutions aimed at rehabilitating them.
Children serving sentences over 3 years, if found guilty of criminal intent, and over 5 years, if found guilty of criminal negligence, are to be imprisoned in “closed juvenile correctional institutions,” with transfers to educational centers only possible if sanctioned by an assessment panel.
“Any serious crime committed by a child deserves a serious response, but locking up children for decades is neither just nor effective, and can be harmful and potentially counterproductive,” said Bill Van Esveld, associate children’s rights director at Human Rights Watch. “Child justice standards are grounded in science that establishes that children have the ability to grow and reform, so they should not be punished like adults.”
Under Turkey’s penal code, those sentenced to life in prison may only apply for conditional release after 24 years, though children sentenced to “aggravated life imprisonment” will need to wait 30 years for such a right.
"While some of the proposals may be positive – such as those that aim to ensure better coordination between child protection and education services and to prevent children from accessing firearms – others raise serious human rights concerns. I am particularly alarmed by the possibility that child offenders could be sentenced to life imprisonment,” UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk said. “...A focus on rehabilitation and reintegration is essential to protect victims and to reduce re-offending. It contributes to safer communities for everyone”
Courts will decide if children over 12 understand the legal meaning of their actions
Courts will now decide whether children above the age of 12 are capable of “understanding the legal meaning and consequences of the act and of controlling their behavior in relation to the act.” If the child is not criminally responsible, the court may impose “security measures specifically designed for children.” However, if the child is deemed responsible, they may receive sentences of up to 27 years for serious crimes, including intentional murders.
“Punishing children as if they were adults ignores years of scientific findings as well as international law,” Van Esveld said. “With this law, the Turkish government has taken a step backward for public safety as well as children’s rights.”
Ankara made the changes to the criminal law seemingly in response to the fatal stabbing of a 15-year-old and a 16-year-old boy by 14-year-old Mattia Ahmet Minguizzi in January 2025. Minguizzi was sentenced to 24 years in prison for the crime, the maximum sentence he could receive at the time, angering a number of politicians who argued that the sentence was not a sufficient deterrent for young people.
Turkish child rights expert, Seda Akço, objects to new legislation
Though the legislation was pushed for by a number of lawmakers, it has also met with some domestic backlash. Seda Akço, a prominent Turkish lawyer, human rights defender, and child rights expert, told the Bianet news agency that the “real issue” of youth crime is not being addressed by the amendments.
"What kind of interventions exist in the execution system for children that will truly ensure behavioral change and eliminate the reasons driving them to crime? Can the execution system succeed here? Does it have appropriate psychosocial programs, or a suitable and adequate number of personnel? We need to talk about these,” she said. "The purpose of the penal execution system should not only be to deprive the child of liberty, but to create the conditions that will prevent them from being associated with crime again."

Do not refer to 9/11 as 'terror attacks,' leaked Canadian broadcaster memo instructs reporters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
13:38:30 UTC
22:38:30 KST

Ahead of the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC) has circulated a memo to reporters and editors instructing them not to refer to them as “terrorist attacks.”
This was first reported on by Canadian journalist Warren Kinsella, who received the memo. CBC then confirmed the existence of the memo to The Jerusalem Post.
According to the screenshot of the memo shared by Kinsella, the memo was authored by Basem Boshra, senior director of journalistic standards and public trust at CBC News, to reporters and editors.
In bold letters, Boshra states the attacks are not to be referred to as terrorist attacks.
He then said that “the hijackings led to passenger jet crashes in Washington, DC, Pennsylvania and Manhattan. The World Trade Center was destroyed.”
CBC spokeswoman Kerry Kelly told the Post that it is the practice of the CBC to “exercise extreme caution before using the words terrorist and terrorism.”
“The memo was a reminder of the longstanding practice that favors the use of these terms with attribution in our reporting,” she said.
She also pointed the Post to an October 2023 blog by Brodie Fenlon, CBC news editor-in-chief and general manager, where he said “CBC News does not itself designate specific groups as terrorists, or specific acts as terrorism, regardless of the region or the events, because these words are so loaded with meaning, politics and emotion that they can end up being impediments to our journalism.”
“While the language is not seriously disputed in some cases, it’s less clear if not highly contested at other times – which can lead to virtually endless questions about consistency and impartiality in our coverage of various attacks around the world,” he advised.
Fenlon said this rule applies to the attacks against the United States in 2001, which CBC News prefers to call “the Sept. 11 attacks,” as well as the deadly suicide bombing at an airport in Moscow in January 2011, the London bombings in July 2005, and the Madrid train bombings in March 2004.
Canadian MP Rachel Thomas said the memo is “absolutely shameful.”
Memo 'downplays the atrocity of 9/11'
“The CBC is choosing to redefine terrorism in a way that downplays the atrocity of 9/11. Refusing to call it an act of terrorism dishonors the victims, their families, the survivors, and the first responders who witnessed the horrors of that day. 9/11 was an act of terrorism. Full stop.”
The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is the public broadcaster for both radio and television. It received over $1.5 billion in taxpayer funding in 2025-26.

Latvia arms its new combat vehicle against drone threats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
13:38:13 UTC
22:38:13 KST

- Latvia will demonstrate GDELS-Santa Bárbara Sistemas counter-drone systems mounted on the Hunter infantry fighting vehicle on Thursday at Ādaži.
- Latvia has ordered 84 Hunter vehicles total, with initial deliveries to the National Armed Forces scheduled for October 2026.
Latvia tested a new way to protect its infantry vehicles from one of the biggest threats on today’s battlefield: cheap, swarming drones.
The country’s Ministry of Defence held a demonstration Thursday at the Ādaži military base, mounting counter-drone systems onto its new Hunter infantry fighting vehicle to see how well they work. The systems came from Spanish defense company GDELS-Santa Bárbara Sistemas.
The concept is similar to tests the U.S. Army has run on its own vehicles: bolting on hardware meant to shoot down or jam small drones before they can drop a grenade or crash into an armored vehicle from above. Both active systems, which actively engage incoming drones, and passive systems, which detect and warn crews, were tested. So were ground-based drones of Latvia’s own, meant to work alongside the vehicle rather than against it.
The Hunter, called “Mednieks” in Latvian, is built on the ASCOD platform, a tracked armored vehicle design used by several NATO countries and localized for Latvia’s own requirements. The vehicle has been modified for modern mechanized infantry operations, with an emphasis on firepower, modular armor, and the ability to work alongside equipment used by other NATO militaries. Soldiers from Latvia’s Mechanized Infantry Brigade, who will actually crew the vehicle, picked the “Hunter” name themselves.
This test matters because of timing. Latvia’s military signed its first contract for 42 Hunter vehicles with GDELS-Santa Bárbara Sistemas in January 2025, then doubled the order to 84 vehicles that June. The first Hunters are due to arrive with Latvia’s National Armed Forces this October, just weeks away. Thursday’s demonstration was Latvia’s chance to figure out which drone defenses to install before that happens, rather than bolting them on later.
The threat driving all this is well understood in the region. Russia’s war in Ukraine has shown how cheap first-person-view drones can knock out armored vehicles worth millions of dollars, and Latvia sits directly on NATO’s eastern border with Russia.

Missing Swiss woman found alive in Nepal floods
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
13:35:19 UTC
22:35:19 KST

Missing Swiss woman found alive in Nepal floods
A Swiss woman who had been reported missing by the Nepal tourism authority following a flash flood between Nepal and China has been found alive.
The online paper 20min.ch had first reported on the rescued Swiss woman. Among the foreigners rescued and found are 30 other nationals from India, Italy, Bulgaria, the US, South Korea, Russia and those with as yet unknown nationalities.
Following the floods in Rasuwa, Nepal, the tourism authority reported 644 people missing. Most of those missing are Indian or Nepalese nationals.
FDFA travel service
The Swiss Federal Department of Foreign Affairs (FDFA) had previously received no information regarding Swiss nationals who had been injured or killed. Investigations into this matter are currently underway.
Currently, around 20 travellers have registered with the government Travel Admin service. Around 120 people are registered in the Register of Swiss Citizens Abroad. The FDFA was unable to provide any information on how many people were in the affected region. Swiss nationals in the area are advised to follow the instructions of the local authorities.
Switzerland pledges $1 million for relief efforts
On the X platform, Swiss President Guy Parmelin said he was “deeply saddened by the devastating floods” and paid tribute to the victims and their families. Switzerland stands in solidarity with all those affected and with everyone working tirelessly to support the local community, he added.
In response to the devastating floods in Nepal, Switzerland is providing around $1 million (CHF800,000) via the United Nations for humanitarian aid in Nepal, the FDFA announced on Thursday.
More
Switzerland ‘deeply saddened’ by Nepal flash floods
The funds are to be channelled into clean drinking water, emergency shelter, food aid, medical care and psychosocial support for the affected communities. According to the FDFA, the humanitarian aid will be delivered using resources available on the ground.
Swiss aid organisations provide emergency aid
The Swiss aid organisations Helvetas and the Red Cross have now launched emergency relief operations. To fund the aid, both organisations have launched a fundraising appeal in Switzerland.
The aid organisation Helvetas has sent a team to the disaster area. Local staff will assess the extent of the damage and prepare the emergency aid, as Helvetas announced on Thursday. The organisation has allocated CHF100,000 for this purpose. The priority is to provide the population with emergency shelter, drinking water and hygiene items.
The Swiss Red Cross (SRC), with the support of the federal government, is providing a further CHF50,000 for emergency aid. The SRC stands ready to support the local Red Cross, which has been on the ground since the very beginning, “with specialist staff and further aid funds”.
More than 1,300 people missing
On Wednesday, massive masses of mud and rock had wreaked havoc in the mountainous region between Nepal and south-western Tibet, stretching along the Bhotekoshi River as far as central Nepal.
The cause of the flood is still under investigation. However, following initial analyses of satellite images, the Nepalese Disaster Management Authority suspected that a glacial avalanche may initially have blocked a tributary of the Bhotekoshi, which rises in the Tibetan highlands, as reported by the Kathmandu Post. This is said to have formed a temporary lake, which subsequently burst its banks. A flood wave of water, ice and debris then swept downstream into the Himalayan nation.
According to official figures, the number of people missing in Nepal alone has risen to 826. This brings the total number of people missing in Nepal and China to more than 1,300. Among those missing are also numerous tourists. The affected region is a popular hiking destination and a stop on the route for Buddhist and Hindu pilgrims travelling via Nepal to the sacred Mount Kailash in Tibet.

Iceland waits referendum; fish could decide outcome
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
13:35:04 UTC
22:35:04 KST

Iceland will hold a referendum on the 29th of August to decide whether the country will reopen talks on joining the European Union, and polls are currently showing the outcome is uncertain, the BBC reports.
At a factory near the coast, workers in blue overalls and hairnets sort freshly caught cod and haddock, and machines process the fish, which will mostly end up in Europe. Pétur Pálsson, head of fisheries at Visir, fears that the price of joining the EU will be job losses in Iceland and factories forced to relocate abroad. He says that if Iceland is in the EU, everything will be decided by Brussels.
On the 29th of August, the nation of 400,000 people will decide whether to reopen accession talks, and polls are showing the outcome is uncertain. EU supporters say closer ties with Europe could help curb Iceland’s currency volatility and rising cost of living. Opponents say the stakes are high for Iceland’s independence and control over its invaluable fishing waters.
The EU has been a divisive issue for Icelanders for decades, but after winning snap elections in 2024, Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir’s center-left government promised to hold a referendum on whether to reopen accession talks in 2027. Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, escalating rivalry in the Arctic, and U.S.S President Donald Trump’s threats of tariffs and plans for Greenland have prompted the referendum to be rushed.
Iceland is located in the North Atlantic Ocean, on the edge of a strategically important sea area known as the GIUK corridor,
where Western powers are closely monitoring Russian shipping activity. Iceland is a founding member of NATO, but it does not have its own army.
Eirikur Bergmann, a professor of politics at the University of Bifrist, said the outcome was impossible to predict because both sides were using all available means.
Supporters of resuming talks say EU membership would strengthen Iceland’s trade and security positions and protect it from larger powers. They also talk about the advantages of switching to the euro. A vote to resume talks would allow discussions with Brussels to resume, but joining the bloc would require another referendum. If voters reject the resumption of talks, they would be postponed.
Although Iceland is not a member of the EU, it is part of the European Economic Area,
along with Norway and Liechtenstein. Iceland is also part of the single market and the Schengen area.
Reykjavik began accession talks in 2008 after the devastating international financial crisis, but they stalled in 2013. The main obstacle then was fishing, and it remains so now. Fishing and other sea-related industries account for almost 40% of Iceland’s exports, and many who oppose reopening the talks are concerned that the EU’s common fisheries policy could take away control of the tempting fishing grounds. Opposition leader Guðrún Hafsteinsdóttir has vowed not to give up Icelandic waters.
Professor Bergman said fishing was an integral part of Iceland’s cultural and political identity, and no politician would ever give it up, or they would be expelled from the country.
The Icelandic government plans to secure special conditions to protect fishing and agriculture. Meanwhile, eurosceptics doubt that this is possible.
When the BBC visited Keflavík Air Base in August, fighter jets were taking off, and the US flag was flying alongside the Belgian and NATO flags.
Iceland has no army, so its security depends on its NATO allies and a 1951 treaty with the US.
Trump’s repeated threats to take over Greenland and the risk of NATO unity weakening are other concerns that have gripped Iceland. Officials see increased Russian activity near Iceland as a major security threat.
Supporters of the accession talks say joining the EU will offer financial stability, and the introduction of the euro could curb the country’s stubbornly high inflation. Since separating from Denmark in 1944, Iceland has gone from a poor island to one of Europe’s wealthiest nations. However, prices in Iceland are on average 84% higher than the EU average, and interest rates have climbed to 8%.
Skeptics believe that joining the EU will be too expensive.
The referendum on the 29th of August will be closely watched across Europe. If Icelanders decide in favor of resuming negotiations, they could take months, not years, as 11 of the 35 rounds of talks had already been completed when they were suspended.

Russian forces have advanced toward the outskirts of Slovyansk within eastern Ukraine’s so-called “fortress belt” of heavily fortified cities in the Donetsk region, Chief of the General Staff Valery Gerasimov said Thursday.
Speaking at an undisclosed location while inspecting troops from Russia’s “South” grouping of forces, Gerasimov said that Russian troops are positioned just 4 kilometers (2.5 miles) from the eastern outskirts of Slovyansk.
The general noted that Russian forces captured at least three villages to the northeast and southeast of the city over the summer, with active street fighting continuing in two other settlements.
Gerasimov added that Russian operations are currently advancing along a 160-kilometer (99-mile) front.
The Washington-based Institute for the Study of War (ISW) said earlier this week that Russian troops have intensified efforts to push toward Slovyansk from the east and southeast following unsuccessful assault attempts from the northeast.
Slovyansk and neighboring city of Kramatorsk represent Ukraine’s primary defensive strongholds in the region following the Russian capture of Kostiantynivka last month.
Kostiantynivka had served as the southern end of the “fortress belt,” while Slovyansk anchored the group of cities in the north.
In response to the offensive, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Wednesday that he had appointed two prominent military commanders to lead defensive operations in the region.
Zelensky claimed in June that the Kremlin had ordered Russian forces to fully capture the Donetsk region by Dec. 31.
Russian President Vladimir Putin continues to demand that Ukraine cede full control of the Donetsk region as a prerequisite for any ceasefire agreement — a condition Kyiv has repeatedly rejected.

Students lose shared rooms to studios as landlords sell
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
13:34:32 UTC
22:34:32 KST

Students lose shared rooms to studios as landlords sell
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Small private landlords are selling off cheap, shared housing that students depend on, new figures from the land registry Kadaster show.
Across the Dutch cities with a university, these private landlords cut the number of homes they rent out by 19% on average over three years, according to NRC, which reported the figures.
Bigger property companies bought and built enough to keep the total number of rental homes almost steady, and student cities are attractive to investors, but these tend to be smaller studios rather than shared houses.
For a student hunting a room, that means there are likely fewer affordable shared rooms and more competition.
Hardest on internationals
 International students are hardest hit by this, as they cannot join the years-long waiting lists for social housing, which the Kadaster figures don’t include, and often have to rent from abroad without seeing the room first.
That leaves them relying on the private market, which is shrinking, and more exposed to scams and overcharging.
It is not the same everywhere though – the number of rental homes actually rose in Amsterdam, Leiden and Eindhoven, while The Hague and Utrecht saw the steepest falls.
The national shortage stood at 21,500 rooms last year, and more students are giving up the search and staying with their parents, according to student housing centre Kences, which has linked the sell-off to lost rooms. Its next report is due on September 3.
Housing minister Elanor Boekholt-O’Sullivan this week asked councils to be more flexible about shared student houses, after 10 students in Groningen faced eviction because their council would not treat them as one household.

World Bank urges Ghana to anchor fiscal consolidation on revenue mobilization
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
21:30:22 CST
22:30:22 KST

ACCRA, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- The World Bank Group has urged the Ghanaian government to anchor its fiscal consolidation on aggressive domestic resource mobilization to ensure sustainability.
In its latest Ghana Economic Update report, launched Wednesday in Accra, the Ghanaian capital, the World Bank acknowledged that the country achieved a strong fiscal turnaround in 2025 and remained ahead of the targets set in the reform program backed by the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
"The 2025 fiscal results showed a big improvement from the problems in 2024, with the government's actions leading to a primary surplus of 2.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) by the end of 2025, which is much higher than the 1.5 percent of GDP target set in the IMF-backed reform program," the report said.
According to the report, Ghana recorded a primary surplus of 0.9 percent of GDP during the first half of 2026, against a planned deficit of 0.2 percent.
It explained that the better-than-expected results were mainly due to a significant reduction in capital spending, which was 38 percent less than what was planned, as the government denied some payment claims following an audit and slowed down project work after finalizing debt restructuring deals.
It added that the government also contained current expenditure through wage caps, restraint on goods and services spending, and a reduction in energy-sector transfers.
"Fiscal adjustment anchored primarily in spending cuts, particularly capital expenditure, is less sustainable than adjustment supported by structural revenue gains," it said.
Robert Taliercio, World Bank division director for Ghana, Sierra Leone and Liberia, said that the report offers a clear message for the country: "Sustained fiscal consolidation over the medium term will require strengthening revenue mobilization." ■

China and Iran sanctions: what US moves mean for Beijing, and its retaliation options
Washington’s new measures seen testing a recent bilateral detente with Beijing, and room for escalation remains, threatening trade, payments and supply chains
The United States has imposed sweeping sanctions on nearly 60 Iran-linked entities, spanning digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping, as Washington seeks to “sever every economic lifeline” that sustains Tehran.
With the fresh sanctions complicating an already delicate diplomatic detente, we examine the Chinese entities targeted, delineate Beijing’s red lines and assess the potential economic countermeasures that China’s leadership could utilise if tensions escalate.
How do Washington’s new sanctions on Iran affect China?
More than a dozen Hong Kong- and mainland-based entities and individuals were named in the latest round of sanctions, primarily for helping to procure sensitive goods or for shipping Iranian oil.
This included Hong Kong-based Sweet Ocean, which the US alleged had acted as an intermediary for the acquisition of sensitive equipment, such as laser optics, bound for the heavily sanctioned Malek Ashtar University in Iran.
Other Hong Kong-based firms, including Feili Co, Minvur and Feisu, allegedly transferred capital to Sweet Ocean and acted as front companies to facilitate payments for Iran’s “shadow banking” networks.
Also on the list were Hong Kong-registered Riqueza and China-based Lilimoon Navigation, which US authorities accused of owning foreign-flagged ships transporting Iranian crude to China – Tehran’s biggest oil buyer.
Washington also signalled a readiness to deploy secondary sanctions on countries that refuse to cut economic ties with Iran.

Slovakia's industrial producer prices up 2.7 pct in July

BRATISLAVA, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- Slovakia's industrial producer prices for the domestic market rose by 2.7 percent year-on-year in July 2026, Slovak Statistics Office reported on Thursday.
As many as 15 of the 16 monitored industrial sectors recorded price increases in July. Producer prices in the food manufacturing sector declined by 2.8 percent year-on-year, making it as the only sector to see a price drop since the beginning of the year.
The price growth was driven in particular by the production of coke and oil products (up 17.5 percent), electric appliances (8.4 percent) and metals (3.5 percent).
In the first seven months of 2026, meanwhile, industrial producer prices were 1.3 percent higher than the year before, while they went up by 1.8 percent in monthly terms. ■

Japanese army uses own soldiers in mosquito-borne disease experiments during WWII: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
21:29:51 CST
22:29:51 KST

HARBIN, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- Japanese troops conducted live human experiments involving mosquito-borne diseases on their own soldiers during World War II (WWII), according to new research released Thursday.
The study was released by the Exhibition Hall of Evidences of Crime Committed by Unit 731 of the Japanese Imperial Army in Harbin, capital of northeast China's Heilongjiang Province. It shows that during WWII, Japanese forces in China conducted insect-based bacteriological weapons research using mosquitoes, fleas and flies through two major biological warfare units -- Unit 731 in Harbin and Unit 1855 in Beijing -- along with military medical institutions in Japan proper.
According to the study, Japanese biological warfare units conducted detailed research on disease-carrying insects, using fleas to transmit plague, flies to spread cholera, and mosquitoes as the primary vector for malaria. Both Unit 731 and Unit 1855 established dedicated insect sections to breed these vectors as part of their bacteriological weapons development.
Jin Shicheng, a researcher at the Exhibition Hall, said a paper documenting live human experiments using malaria-infected mosquitoes, conducted from May to August 1940, was published in a journal by the Japanese Army Medical Corps on Jan. 10, 1943.
At a military hospital in Japan's Chiba Prefecture, Japanese military personnel first had mosquitoes feed on soldiers who had contracted malaria in China, then allowed the infected insects to bite 10 Japanese soldiers hospitalized with mental illnesses. Multiple test subjects subsequently developed symptoms including fevers exceeding 40 degrees Celsius, headaches and loss of appetite.
"This case exposes the criminal nature of the Japanese forces' practice of treating human beings as mere 'experimental material,'" Jin said. "It also confirms that their experiments extended to the Japanese mainland, with even their own soldiers not spared."
The records further reveal that Japanese forces conducted cross-institutional collaboration in bacteriological weapons research, according to the study. ■

BEIJING, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- China has made phased progress in emergency communication support and infrastructure restoration after a mudslide hit a border port in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology said Thursday.
As of now, one telecom base station has been successfully restored, two new base stations have been put into operation, and 5G inter-network roaming functionality has been simultaneously activated, the ministry said.
The mudslide struck Gyirong Port in Gyirong County, Xizang, on Wednesday morning. As of 8 a.m. on Thursday, three people had been killed, 558 others remained missing, while two local villagers had been rescued.
The mudslide has cut off roads leading to the port on the Chinese side, as well as communications and power supplies.
Local telecom operators have since mobilized emergency crews and equipment for line checks, fault repairs, and network optimization to ensure communications for rescue operations and the affected public.
Chinese authorities have launched full-scale rescue operations after the mudslide. The National Health Commission (NHC) announced on Thursday that it sent senior officials to Xizang to guide medical rescue and emergency response efforts.
The NHC, working with Xizang's regional government, is coordinating and deploying medical resources to ensure that all necessary measures are carried out, the NHC statement said.
Medical and disease control professionals have been dispatched from Lhasa to the disaster-hit area with emergency medical supplies, disinfection and disease-control medicines, and specialized vehicles, while ambulances, medical personnel and psychological support workers from neighboring counties have also been mobilized. ■

BEIJING, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- China's central bank has added 5 billion yuan (about 737 million U.S. dollars) to its relending quota for agriculture and small businesses in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region to support disaster relief and post-disaster reconstruction, the People's Bank of China said Thursday.
The move is aimed at guiding and encouraging financial institutions to step up credit support for market entities in disaster-hit areas after a mudslide caused significant casualties along the China-Nepal border, according to the central bank.
Relending is a monetary policy tool under which the central bank provides low-cost funds to financial institutions to encourage lending to targeted sectors.
A mudslide struck Gyirong Port in Gyirong County, Xizang, on Wednesday morning. As of 8 a.m. Thursday, three people had been confirmed dead and 558 others remained missing.
The central bank said it will urge its Xizang regional branch to make good use of the additional relending quota and guide financial institutions to actively respond to financing needs in affected areas.
China's insurance sector has also moved swiftly to provide claims services and financial support following the disaster. Major insurers, including PICC and Ping An P&C, activated emergency response mechanisms, dispatched teams to affected areas and opened fast-track claims channels.
The first team of 141 rescuers has arrived at the mudslide-stricken border port of Gyirong Thursday morning. ■

BEIJING, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- A massive mudslide that caused casualties and left a large number of people missing at the border port of Gyirong in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region was triggered by the collapse of glacier on the Nepalese side at a higher elevation, an expert said.
The collapse sent masses of debris rapidly downhill, which swept up moraine material along the way to form a mudslide that struck Gyirong Port before moving downstream toward Nepal, said Guo Zhaocheng, an expert with the Ministry of Natural Resources.
The mudslide struck Gyirong Port in Gyirong County, Xizang, on Wednesday morning. As of 8 a.m. on Thursday, three people had been killed, 558 others remained missing, while two local villagers had been rescued.
The mudslide is estimated to have traveled at about 50 meters per second, an extremely high speed leaving people with little time to react, while the affected area stretched more than 20 kilometers, resulting in severe losses.
Therefore, the disaster prevention and mitigation work on the Qinghai-Xizang Plateau must take a bottom-line and worst-case approach and fully account for such complex conditions, Guo said. ■

Trump administration weighs sweeping semiconductor tariffs: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
13:28:19 UTC
22:28:19 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
27 August 2026•Update: 27 August 2026
The Trump administration is considering sweeping new tariffs on semiconductors that could also cover a broad range of technology products containing computer chips, Politico reported Thursday.
One approach under discussion would apply duties not only to imported chips but also to goods made with them, including laptops, gaming consoles, and servers used in data centers, the report said, citing eight people familiar with the deliberations.
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick reportedly favors tying tariff relief for foreign companies to their investments in US semiconductor manufacturing, aiming to encourage more production on American soil.
Under the proposed system, companies would be permitted to import a certain volume of chips duty-free, with the allowance determined by how much production they pledge to establish in the US.
Officials are also considering a phase-in period as well as separate tariff rates and import quotas for individual countries, according to the report. The tariff rate and other key details have not yet been finalized, and the framework could be substantially revised in the coming weeks or months.
The proposal has raised concerns in the technology industry, which is already facing shortages of advanced semiconductors amid surging demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure.
Industry representatives have warned that broader tariffs could increase the cost of data center construction, slow US investment in AI infrastructure, and raise prices for servers, computers, televisions, and other electronic products.
The measures could also affect US chip designers such as Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices, which rely on overseas manufacturers to produce their semiconductors.
White House spokesperson Kush Desai defended the administration’s trade policy, saying reshoring semiconductor manufacturing is a “top priority” for President Donald Trump.
“The Trump administration remains focused on delivering more investments and economic relief for the American people while safeguarding our national security,” Desai said.
In polls, the American public largely disapproves of higher tariffs, but Trump has pledged that his tariff policy will make the US, in his words, “rich as hell.”

Afghan man to be deported from Switzerland for assaulting wife
The Valais Cantonal Court has dismissed the appeal of an Afghan man who stood trial for the attempted murder of his wife. It has upheld his sentence of 10 years’ imprisonment without parole and a 15-year ban on entering Swiss territory.
On November 21, 2022, the defendant pushed his wife to the ground. He then picked up an 80 cm branch and struck her on the back of the head, and then all over her body. The victim suffered a head injury, damage to a cervical vertebra and fractures to the eye socket and the left maxillary sinus.
+ Swiss court clears Afghan repatriations if conditions allow
“The day I hit my wife, I was being a fool, but the alcohol I’d consumed may have influenced me,” the defendant told the Criminal Court on June 17. “The victim survived only by sheer luck, or rather, thanks to the intervention of third parties,” stated the prosecutor, Alexandre Rosset.
The defendant’s lawyer, Luis Neves, had argued for a conviction for simple bodily harm, to spare him deportation and a return to a country where his life would be at risk. This view was not shared by the Criminal Court.

Rescue teams waded through mud searching for more than 1,400 people missing after flash floods and landslides struck the Nepal-China border, as the death toll rose sharply to at least 362, with entire villages swept away.
Experts warned of the risk of further floods on Thursday, a day after the devastating tsunami-like wall of freezing water and mud wiped out towns under a torrent of sludge, engulfing homes, smashing bridges and dams, and sweeping vehicles away like toys.
Many of the missing are foreign tourists, including scores of Hindu pilgrims to Tibet's sacred snow-capped Mount Kailash.
According to the US Geological Survey (USGS), the disaster was caused by a glacial collapse that triggered a vast flow of icy debris.
Emergency teams were racing to pluck survivors from affected zones, while Nepali soldiers used sniffer dogs to search for bodies buried under the suffocating dirt.
"Everything is finished," Omkar Joshi, a 35-year-old Nepali customs agent rescued from a hilltop in the border town of Timure, said.
"It is a giant graveyard. All that is left are sand and pebbles, soaked red by human blood."
Nepali police said they had recovered 359 bodies.
Another 910 people, including 517 foreign tourists, were out of contact in the country. Beijing said 100 Chinese citizens are missing in Nepal.
In China, state media said the "mudslide disaster" at the Gyirong Port in Tibet killed three people, while 558 people, including 260 foreigners, are missing.
Chinese Premier Li Qiang visited the area on Thursday, state media said, to oversee "emergency rescue and relief work, and to visit rescue workers and affected people".
Li Qipu, a member of China's paramilitary People's Armed Police, cited "the instability of a reservoir lake upstream" and "the narrow mountain road" as elements complicating rescue efforts.
'Inland tsunami'
Prime Minister Balendra Shah, who urged the Himalayan nation to "stand together" hours after the disaster, visited some of the hardest-hit areas on Thursday.
Shah told local authorities to "provide immediate relief to displaced families" and to open blocked roads, his office said in a statement.
The foreigners out of contact included Indians and others from Australia, Britain, Malaysia, the Netherlands, Portugal, South Africa, South Korea and the United States, Nepal's tourism board said.
The sudden rush of mud and debris was "like an inland tsunami", travelling nearly 170 kilometres (105 miles) south into Nepal, said environmental historian Ruth Gamble, of Australia's La Trobe University.
Rasuwa, in the north of Nepal, was the first district to be affected, but deaths were reported as far south as Chitwan, on the border with India.
Chinese government officials in Tibet mobilised nearly 800 emergency workers, as well as sniffer dogs and speed boats to help the rescue efforts, the official Xinhua news agency said.
Promises of aid and assistance came in soon after reports of the scale of the disaster.
The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies said it was sending emergency supplies including blankets, first aid kits, stretchers and body bags.
Glacial collapse
The USGS said the flood was sparked by a glacial collapse, which caused seismic activity and the "catastrophic" downstream impacts in Nepal and Tibet.
"This event was initially reported as a magnitude 4.4 earthquake," it said, but the seismic recordings were analysed, and it was found instead to be a "glacial collapse and debris flow".
The climate crisis is causing glaciers to melt worldwide, increasing the risks of glacial lake floods and glacial collapses.
Fears of more potential floods remain, with water trapped by the immense piles of debris blocking the valley.
"With a blockage still lodged upstream on the Nepal-China border river, authorities warn a second flood may occur," said Qianggong Zhang, head of climate and environmental risks at the Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development.
Kathmandu's Flood Forecasting Division issued a "special notice" on Thursday, warning of a growing lake behind debris left by the landslide.
"Residents of downstream areas of the Bhote Koshi River, travellers, rescue personnel, and all concerned are requested to exercise extreme caution," it said.

The Ministry of Climate and Energy (KEM) has withdrawn the draft order submitted for inter-agency approval on Wednesday, the 26th of August, which envisaged declaring a state of emergency in the healthcare, energy supply and water management sectors in Latvia’s eastern border region, according to information published on the Draft Legal Acts (TAP) portal.
KEM representatives told the LETA news agency that, in light of discussions in the public domain and what the ministry considers to be some inaccurate interpretations of the document’s substance and purpose, the document is currently no longer publicly available on the TAP portal.
To reduce the risk of further communication problems and misinterpretation, the ministry also plans to clarify the title of the document. At the same time, the information provided by KEM does not indicate that the initiative itself or the draft order has been abandoned.
The ministry is continuing work on a temporary legal solution, while
the next step will be to develop permanent regulations governing the provision of critical services
during an aerial threat over the long term.
KEM also stated that it initiated the drafting of the relevant Cabinet of Ministers order on the basis of a government instruction requiring all ministries, where necessary, to submit proposals to the Ministry of Justice by the 30th of September this year for the legal framework needed in their respective sectors to ensure continuity of operations in the event of threats to Latvia’s airspace.
The ministries were instructed to clearly define the objective or problem, propose a conceptual solution for achieving that objective or addressing the problem, and explain why the issue cannot be resolved under the existing legislation governing their respective sectors.
As previously reported, KEM had prepared and submitted for inter-agency approval a draft order proposing that a state of emergency be declared until the 1st of December this year in the healthcare, energy supply and water management sectors in Latvia’s eastern border region.
The proposal was justified by the threat of an escalation in Russia’s military activities
and the need to address potential threats to Latvia’s airspace.
The proposed state of emergency would have applied to the municipalities of Alūksne, Augšdaugava, Balvi, Daugavpils, Krāslava, Līvāni, Ludza, Preiļi and Rēzekne, as well as the cities of Daugavpils and Rēzekne.
KEM explained that unmanned aerial vehicles and other unidentified objects are being detected with increasing frequency in Latvian airspace or near the country’s border, potentially posing a threat to public safety, human health and the operation of critical infrastructure.
The draft order provided for temporary exemptions from working-time and overtime regulations, additional remuneration and employee protection measures to ensure the continuity of critical services during an aerial threat.
Minister of Climate and Energy Jānis Vitenbergs (National Alliance) explained on Thursday that the draft order concerning a state of emergency in Latvia’s border region was not a signal of an imminent invasion, but rather a preventive measure intended to ensure the continuity of critical services in the event of an aerial threat.
KEM stressed that the draft order, entitled “On Declaring a State of Emergency in Latvia’s Eastern Border Region,” did not itself provide for the immediate declaration of a state of emergency, but instead set out measures to be taken if such a state of emergency were declared.
