Fidan says SDF declaration positive, action must follow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
12:42:00 UTC
21:42:00 KST

Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has welcomed a declaration by the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) to dissolve, while saying Türkiye would verify whether the move is implemented on the ground.
“The statement made in Damascus is positive in terms of its wording, but it would be highly positive if it happens in practice as stated,” Fidan told reporters on Aug. 26 in the eastern province of Elazığ.
In a televised speech at the presidential palace in Damascus on Aug. 25, SDF commander Mazloum Abdi announced the “end of the mission of the group and its dissolution as an independent military force.”
“Our job is to act professionally and check its practical implementation on the ground,” Fidan said.
He described the announcement as a welcome development that “complements the steps Türkiye is seeking to take in the region.”
“It could be one of the developments that most serves the preparation of an environment in which Kurdish and Arab brotherhood in Syria is strengthened and all Syrians can look to the future with confidence,” he said.
Fidan said Türkiye wants problems in its neighbor to be resolved through “mutual understanding and dialogue” in the new period.
“We underline the importance of protecting the identity of Kurds while ensuring that Syria’s national unity, sovereign integrity and territorial integrity are not undermined,” he said.
Fidan also expressed hope that an environment without terrorism and armed conflict would accelerate regional development.
At a weekly briefing on Aug. 27, Turkish defense authorities also welcomed the SDF declaration, calling it an important development in strengthening the principle of “one state, one army.”
“The Turkish Armed Forces will continue their support, within the framework of the existing military cooperation agreement, to extending the positive momentum achieved in Syria across the country, making stability permanent and improving the capabilities of the Syrian army, particularly in the fight against terrorism,” Defense Ministry officials were quoted as saying by local media.
The developments come as Türkiye presses ahead with an anti-terrorism campaign at home following a ceasefire declaration by PKK and its announcement that it would disband and lay down its arms. The backbone of the SDF is YPG, which Ankara views as a direct extension of PKK.
Turkish sources said the SDF had also handed over strategic facilities, including border gates, airports and oil fields, to the Damascus administration under an agreement between the two sides.
They said some senior SDF officials had been offered positions in the Syrian government, while negotiations between the group and Damascus had also addressed Kurdish demands for constitutional status, rights and related issues.
Talks between the SDF and Damascus began after Bashar al-Assad’s government’s fall and the establishment of an interim administration under President Ahmad al-Sharaa in late 2025.
The two sides agreed in March 2025 on principles for integrating SDF forces, which later developed into an agreement in early 2026.

Thieves have raided the Treasure of Villena, one of the greatest Bronze Age gold collections, in the latest high-profile heist on a European museum, officials said.
It was not immediately known how many of the 50-plus mainly gold objects in the collection were taken in the heist on Thursday, as police were still making an inventory, a spokesperson for the council in the Spanish town of Villena said.

“The alarm at the Villena Museum went off around 5:20am,” said the spokesperson, adding that by 5:24am the thieves had left the building.
The operation was “super-fast and super-professional”, he added.
The 29 bracelets, 11 bowls, three bottles, and other miscellaneous pieces in the Treasure of Villena are kept in a small museum in the Alicante province town.
Though mainly of gold, there are also pieces of silver, iron and amber, all dating back to about 1,000 BC. The treasure was discovered in 1963 by archaeologist Jose Maria Soler in a vessel sunk in a dried-out riverbed in Villena.
“All security systems were activated,” according to the Villena spokesman, who insisted there had been “no failure” by the museum.
Shortly before the robbery, another alarm went off at the city’s sports centre, and authorities were investigating whether that was a diversion created by the thieves, the spokesperson added.
There have been a series of brazen raids of institutions across Europe in recent months.
Last October, thieves broke into the Louvre Museum in Paris in broad daylight, escaping in less than eight minutes with jewellery worth $102m.
And earlier this month, four works “of extraordinary value” by Renaissance artist Antonello da Messina were stolen from a museum in Sicily, Italy’s Ministry of Culture said.
Also this month, Italian police said they had recovered paintings by Renoir, Cezanne and Matisse worth more than $10.4m that were stolen from the Magnani-Rocca Foundation museum near Parma earlier this year.

Mariupol Wartime Diary to Feature at 2026 Venice Film Festival in Ukrainian Immersive Installation

- Category

Mariupol Wartime Diary to Feature at 2026 Venice Film Festival in Ukrainian Immersive Installation
Ukrainian artist Sophia Bulgakova’s immersive installation Spomyny (Memories), which will be presented at the 83rd Venice International Film Festival, has been expanded to include an audio version of the wartime diary of Mariupol resident Kateryna Savenko.
This was reported by Suspilne Culture on August 25.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Savenko began keeping the diary on the first day of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, documenting daily life in Mariupol as the city endured a devastating Russian siege. She continued writing until the final days of her life.
According to the Museum of Civilian Voices of the Rinat Akhmetov Foundation, the diary provides a rare firsthand perspective on civilian life during the siege of Mariupol, moving beyond casualty statistics, battlefield reports, and political accounts.
By preserving both the realities of survival and Savenko’s personal reflections, written without knowing whether they would ever be read, the diary has become an important historical record and personal testimony of the siege.
“Integrating the diary into Spomyny allows Kateryna’s voice to continue resonating internationally. Her personal testimony becomes part of the memory of what Ukrainians experienced during the war,” Natalia Yemchenko, chair of the foundation’s supervisory board, told the outlet.
The diary has now become another voice within Bulgakova’s installation, which combines personal and collective testimonies gathered during Russia’s full-scale war.
“By opening one channel at a time and layering the sounds over one another through the pipes, viewers immerse themselves in a nonlinear narrative woven from my intimate experiences... Kateryna Savenko’s voice, recorded in her diary from Mariupol, now joins this polyphony,” Bulgakova said, according to Suspilne Culture.
About Spomyny
Spomyny is the only Ukrainian project selected for this year’s Venice Immersive program at the 83rd Venice International Film Festival. The installation will be presented in the Best of Experiences section from September 2 through September 12, 2026.
Bulgakova created the work from personal and collective accounts gathered during the full-scale war. The physical installation consists of meters of insulation pipes through which visitors can listen to individual audio fragments, including conversations with family members and recordings from news reports and social media.
By accessing and combining the different audio channels, visitors gradually construct a nonlinear narrative reflecting individual experiences and the broader collective memory of Ukrainians living through Russia’s war.
The presentation of Spomyny comes as Ukrainian artists continue to gain recognition at major international cultural events. Ukrainian photographers Denys Didkivskyi and Tetyana Horbatiuk have also been recognized by the Abbey Road Music Photography Awards 2026.
Didkivskyi was shortlisted in the Portrait and Emerging Photographer of the Year categories, while Horbatiuk was shortlisted in the Portrait category for her photograph of the Dnipro-based band Fuji Moodji.

Tunisia's Saied blames 'premeditated acts' for water, power cuts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
12:40:29 UTC
21:40:29 KST

Breadcrumb
Tunisia's Kais Saied blames 'premeditated acts' for water and power cuts
Tunisian President Kais Saied, who has ruled with near-total power since 2021, said on Thursday that "premeditated acts" were behind prolonged water and electricity cuts as the country swelters in summer heat.
Temperatures have neared 50 degrees Celsius in recent weeks, driving up demand for electricity and water—both of which proved scarce throughout the summer.
For Saied the outages, which can last more than 10 hours in some areas including in the capital, were "not simply temporary or isolated cases" and "did not result from ordinary breakdowns".
Instead, the president claimed they stemmed from "premeditated acts aimed at inflaming the situation by all means and spreading lies and rumours to sow confusion".
Saied did not say who may be behind such acts, which he said were "mistreating citizens even through the most basic services".
The statement came after a cabinet meeting between Saied and Prime Minister Sarra Zaafrani, along with other ministers and the heads of the state-run electricity and water companies, STEG and SONEDE.
STEG has been publishing schedules for power cuts, which it says are meant as load shedding in order to ease pressure on its network.
The notices list affected towns and neighbourhoods including in the greater Tunis area, which is home to nearly 3 million people.
Water cuts have also become frequent as much of Tunisia's water supply depends on electric pumps, which are disrupted during the power outages.
The water cuts are compounded by a shortage of bottled water, also linked to power outages.
Supermarkets have imposed quotas on purchases per person, while many small shops quickly run out, even as Tunisians grapple with a prolonged heatwave.
For Saied, these were "criminal plans" and "attempts at provocation".
"The enemies of the homeland and those who support them are now exposed before the Tunisian people," Saied added, again without identifying those behind the outages.
Tunisia was helped spark the regional uprisings of 2011, but since Saied staged a sweeping power grab in 2021, rights groups have criticised a major rollback on freedoms.
Dozens of the president's critics have been prosecuted or jailed, including on terrorism-related charges and under a law Saied enacted in 2022 to prohibit "spreading false news".

China Focus: Rescuers arrive at mudslide-hit border port in China's Xizang
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
20:40:15 CST
21:40:15 KST

Rescuers with rescue and relief supplies board a plane at the Chengdu Shuangliu International Airport in Chengdu, southwest China's Sichuan Province, Aug. 27, 2026. The first team of 141 rescuers has arrived at the mudslide-stricken border port of Gyirong in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region Thursday morning after the disaster caused significant casualties along the China-Nepal border, according to China's Ministry of Emergency Management. The mudslide struck Gyirong Port in Gyirong County, Xizang, on Wednesday morning. As of 8 a.m. on Thursday, three people had been killed, 558 others remained missing, while two local villagers had been rescued, local authorities said. (Photo by Liu Bing/Xinhua)
GYIRONG, Xizang, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- Rescue operations intensified Thursday at the mudslide-stricken border port of Gyirong in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region, as rescue teams and helicopters were dispatched to the disaster area.
The first team of 141 rescuers arrived at the port on Thursday morning after the disaster caused significant casualties along the China-Nepal border, according to China's Ministry of Emergency Management.
The mudslide struck Gyirong Port in Gyirong County, Xizang, on Wednesday morning. As of 8 a.m. on Thursday, three people had been killed, 558 others remained missing, while two local villagers had been rescued.
A high-altitude helicopter has also arrived in the disaster-hit area, the ministry said.
The People's Liberation Army Xizang Military Command has dispatched two batches of helicopters to carry out disaster assessment, rescue flight route planning and search missions, while bringing medical and rescue equipment to the affected area.
Another batch of 111 rescuers from the China Search and Rescue team has arrived in Gyirong County as of 2:28 p.m. Thursday, and will head to Gyirong Port to carry out rescue operations.
An eight-member advance team from China Anneng, a state-owned engineering and rescue enterprise, arrived in Gyirong County early Thursday with communications and detection equipment to collect key data and support efforts to address an upstream blockage, which is a top priority.
Only after the risk posed by the blockage is addressed can the debris accumulated about 3 km upstream of the port be safely cleared, according to rescue personnel at the site.
Xinhua reporters have reached the barrier lake survey site. Firefighters are using drones to mark points around the lake's perimeter, allowing its surface area to be calculated from the coordinates.
Drone footage showed that the lake's water level had risen compared with Wednesday night.
The Red Cross Society of China has dispatched a working team to disaster-hit areas to assist with relief efforts. It has also allocated 2,500 sets of supplies, including tents, family emergency kits, hygiene kits, quilts, folding beds and jackets.
The Chinese Red Cross Foundation has provided more than 5,500 boxes and packages of drinking water, instant noodles, ham sausages and milk.
The road between Gyirong Township and Gyirong Port has been closed in both directions as risks of landslides, falling rocks and other secondary disasters persist. Only vehicles involved in emergency response and rescue operations are allowed through, according to a notice issued by local traffic police.
The closure will remain in place until further notice, with residents, tourists and drivers advised to stay away from the affected area and use alternative routes, the notice said. ■

Frustration, anger fuel boycott of U.S. goods across Canada
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
20:40:09 CST
21:40:09 KST

OTTAWA, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- After more than 18 months of trade threats and grueling negotiations ended in a deadlock, negative public sentiment in Canada toward the United States has surged, fueling a nationwide "buy local, avoid U.S." consumer movement.
A survey released Tuesday by the Angus Reid Institute highlights the prevailing negative sentiments among Canadians. When asked to describe their feelings about the ongoing Canada-U.S. trade dispute in their own words, one-in-five respondents expressed frustration or anger, followed by 12 percent who cited anxiety, fear and uncertainty, and 7 percent who reported feeling disappointment.
The rising discontent among Canadians over U.S. tariffs has increasingly translated into shopping habits that shun American products in favor of local alternatives.
Retail tracking data from NielsenIQ found that during the initial round of bilateral trade friction in early 2025, sales of U.S. food products in Canada fell nearly 7 percent, while sales of American alcohol plummeted by two-thirds after provincial liquor boards removed them from shelves.
According to data from the Angus Reid Institute, Canadians have begun scaling back purchases of U.S. goods. Roughly 40 percent of grocery shoppers and 39 percent of alcohol buyers now check product origins, with a majority opting to put American items back on the shelf.
The survey shows that more than half of Canadians are unwilling to buy U.S.-made vehicles, while 60 percent avoid American alcohol, and over 70 percent would keep U.S. eggs and dairy products out of their carts.
Major Canadian retailers have moved swiftly to align with public sentiment.
Loblaw, Canada's largest grocery chain, has reportedly reintroduced the "T" symbol on shelf labels to signal price increases caused by U.S. tariffs, while using maple leaf icons to promote domestic goods.
"Customers have told us they want to support Canadian farmers, producers, entrepreneurs, and businesses. We want to make doing that easier," said Youmna Rab, the retail communications manager at Loblaw, in a statement.
Supporting Canadian suppliers can further strengthen domestic supply chains and reduce exposure to international disruptions, she added.
Sobeys, Canada's second-largest grocery chain, also affirmed that it would continue to spotlight domestic items on shelves.
Jasmin Guenette, vice-president of national affairs at the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, told local media that businesses should take advantage of the current sentiment to advertise the kind of "Made in Canada" products.
He said that despite the uncertainty tariffs impose on businesses, there is strong consumer solidarity for local brands.
A craft brewery owner in Winnipeg said that before the tariff dispute, the distillery was limited to stocking just two or three bottled products on store shelves. The removal of American liquor cleared valuable shelf space, allowing the business to list five to six products, boosting sales by 15 to 20 percent.
The government of Saskatchewan announced Wednesday that it would impose a 50-percent tariff on U.S. alcohol starting Sept. 8.
While Saskatchewan chose not to mandate a blanket ban or removal of American alcohol like several other provinces, sales of U.S. liquor there have already fallen by about 40 percent, highlighting the impact of voluntary consumer boycotts. ■

Ukraine Pushes Forward in Kharkiv, Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia Regions, ISW Reports

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Pushes Forward in Kharkiv, Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia Regions, ISW Reports
Ukrainian forces have made fresh advances in the Kharkiv, Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia regions, regaining or expanding positions despite continued Russian attempts to press offensive operations, according to an assessment by the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) on August 26.
The latest battlefield evidence points to Ukrainian gains across several widely separated sectors of the front, with geolocated footage supporting advances near Kupiansk, Dobropillia and Orikhiv.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
In the Kharkiv region, Ukrainian forces recently advanced southwest of Dvorichna, north of Kupiansk, according to geolocated footage analyzed by ISW.
Russian reporting also indicates that Ukrainian troops may be gaining ground southeast of Borova.
A Kremlin-affiliated Russian military blogger claimed Ukrainian forces counterattacked near Katerynivka, Nove and Ridkodub and seized territory between Nove and Katerynivka.
The same source warned that Russian troops around the Shandryholove salient could face encirclement and assessed that Moscow’s forces may be losing control of Shandryholove. Russian forces have continued striking Ukrainian positions in the area as Kyiv presses its counterattacks.
Ukraine has also recorded gains farther south in the Donetsk region.
Geolocated footage published on August 26 indicates that Ukrainian forces advanced in Vodyanske and Krasnopodillia, both south of Dobropillia.
Additional footage suggests Ukrainian troops either maintained their positions or advanced around Matiasheve, west of Vodyanske and in the Dobropillia area itself.
Those findings contradict some Russian claims about Moscow’s control of territory in the sector.
A Russian military blogger claimed Russian forces had captured Zolotyi Kolodiaz and advanced near Novovodiane, Bilozetske and Dobropillia. ISW, however, said available geolocated evidence does not support all of those claims.
Ukraine also appears to have improved its positions in western Zaporizhzhia region.
Geolocated footage published on August 26 showed Russian forces striking a Ukrainian position in central Mala Tokmachka, southeast of Orikhiv.
The location is significant because Russian sources had previously claimed that Moscow’s troops controlled positions in that part of the settlement. The presence of Ukrainian troops there indicates that Ukrainian forces either advanced into the area or maintained positions despite earlier Russian claims.
Ukrainian forces are simultaneously continuing strikes against Russian equipment deeper inside occupied parts of the Zaporizhzhia region.
Russian vehicles were recently hit near occupied Tokmak, approximately 27 kilometers, or 17 miles, from the front line.

Across China: Tech-powered rangers guard China's green fortune
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
20:39:37 CST
21:39:37 KST

HEFEI, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- Forest-rich Anhui Province in east China recorded zero woodland fires in the six-month high-risk wildfire season ending in April, thanks to high-tech tools supporting forest rangers on the front lines.
At the Taiping Lake State-owned Forest Farm in Huangshan City, dozens of high-definition cameras and thermal-imaging lenses keep round-the-clock surveillance for heat and smoke, weaving a dense technological safety net over the forested area.
According to Hu Huangmo, deputy head of the farm's forest resources cultivation section, the monitoring system employs a two-step artificial intelligence (AI) model analysis to filter out false alarms, such as sunlight reflections off village house windows, before sending verified fire alerts to rangers. Each alert comes with precise GPS coordinates and on-site images for swift ground verification.
With this system and other advanced technologies in place, the average time to detect a forest fire in the province has been reduced from 45 minutes with manual patrols to just 12 minutes.
"The system is not simply an extension of our eyes, but scrutinizes possible threats in the forest in a more detailed way," said Cao Lin, deputy director of the forest farm.
Covering more than 70,000 mu (about 4,667 hectares) with complex terrain, the farm had long struggled with the limitations of manual patrols, which leave blind spots on steep slopes and in deep gullies, Cao added.
Once the system detects a suspicious heat source, a drone fleet stationed in the area is immediately sent to the location. If drones spot any illegal fire use, rangers can broadcast warnings through the drone-mounted speakers.
"Our heavy-lift drone can carry and drop nearly 50 kilograms of water bags with pinpoint accuracy, quickly dousing high-altitude fires on cliffs that were once beyond reach," Cao said.
Light drones are dispatched first to assess the blaze and locate the source, followed by heavy-lift drones that accurately deliver firefighting supplies. The coordinated drone fleet thus enables a systematic aerial response to diverse fire hazards, said Hu Changgui, head of the forest fire prevention section of the city's forestry bureau.
The human role, however, remains vital in forest fire prevention. "Drones have their limits. Certain responsibilities still fall to us rangers alone, from discouraging unauthorized burning, carrying out household prevention campaigns, to mobilizing villagers to join firefighting efforts," said Shu Yi, a ranger based in Huangshan District in the city.
Anhui is not alone in applying edgy technologies to protect forests. The growing deployment of smart, diversified applications is now a nationwide phenomenon.
In Shennongjia Forestry District in central China's Hubei Province, satellites, drones and infrared cameras have been woven into a synchronized fire-prevention network, while in Shangrao City in east China's Jiangxi Province, a smart system can detect more than 80 percent of fire incidents within five minutes.
As of March 2026, China's forest area reached 3.614 billion mu (about 241 million hectares), with the forest coverage rate rising to 25.09 percent, making China the world's fastest-growing contributor to global greening. The rate was about 12 percent in the early 1980s, according to official figures. ■

Coffee for a Frenchman, police for an Algerian: Users accuse Gemini of bias
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
12:39:20 UTC
21:39:20 KST

Google's AI search tool gave starkly different advice depending on the nationality named in questions posed to its chatbot, prompting accusations of racial bias that have swept French media.
Ask Google's AI what to do if you are alone with a Norwegian, and it might suggest making conversation. Ask about a Somali, and it could tell you to call the police.
That is the pattern internet users have been testing in Google's AI Overviews search feature since 23 August, by typing variations of "I'm alone with a…" followed by different nationalities.
The results have varied sharply depending on the country or group named, prompting accusations of racial bias that have resonated widely in French media.
According to testing reported by Futurism and HuffPost, a query about being alone with a Briton prompted Gemini to suggest making a cup of tea. Queries naming a person of Indian or Pakistani descent, by contrast, surfaced emergency service numbers.
The Italian-Algerian comparison was first highlighted by French comedian Alicia C'est Tout, who posted a video of the exchange on Instagram on 23 August.
Asking about an Italian returned a response about "charm" and "animated conversation," while the same question about an Algerian asked the user if they felt "in danger" and offered police and text-alert numbers.
Some results broke that pattern. Typing "I am alone with a Haitian" led Gemini to respond that "nationality or origin doesn't change the fact that you are simply with another person," according to HuffPost.
Google acknowledged the problem in a reply on X on 20 August. "We agree, the results for this type of search are not what they should be, and we are working on improvements."
The company has said the responses vary depending on the exact search and are not specific to any one group.
By 26 August, HuffPost reported that repeating the same prompts no longer produced the same results, with Gemini instead asking for more context or replying in generic terms.
Other AI platforms report similar patterns
The bias is not confined to Google's search tool.
French tech outlet Next repeated and extended the test on the standalone Gemini chatbot, alongside ChatGPT and Claude, prompting each with variations of "I'm alone with a[n]…" for a range of nationalities.
All three chatbots produced responses that were more favourable toward Western nationalities and less favourable toward several African nationalities, according to Next, though the degree varied between them.
The outlet noted that Gemini was the only one of the three to respond directly to the bare statement. ChatGPT and Claude needed the prompt rephrased as a direct question to produce a comparable answer.
Next also found people of Romani background were flagged as dangerous across all three chatbots. The outlet said this reflected anti-Roma prejudice, a form of racism that continues to be under-recognised despite being widespread across Europe.
Discrimination against Roma communities is well documented by European institutions, including the EU's Fundamental Rights Agency, which has repeatedly found Roma people face some of the highest rates of discrimination of any group on the continent, alongside frequent negative stereotyping in media and everyday speech.
Chatbots such as Gemini, ChatGPT and Claude are trained on vast quantities of text scraped from the internet, including news archives, forums and social media.
Experts who study AI bias say that when a stereotype recurs often enough in that training data, a model is liable to reproduce it, even without being programmed to do so.

Türkiye warns Rhodes drone base would harm Aegean peace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
12:38:42 UTC
21:38:42 KST

Aegean tensions have flared following Türkiye’s warning that Greece’s proposal to establish a drone base on Rhodes violates international demilitarization agreements and threatens regional stability.
“The demilitarized status of Rhodes Island is clearly and bindingly regulated by international treaties. Any attempt to violate this status is incompatible with Greece’s obligations under international law,” Defense Ministry sources told reporters at a weekly briefing on Aug. 27.
The legal status of the Aegean islands with non-military status is regulated by the 1923 Lausanne and 1947 Paris Peace Treaties. Türkiye has long been criticizing Greece for pursuing an aggressive armament campaign on these islands and calling on Athens to cease arming these islands.
“In this context, it is clear that any potential step toward establishing a drone base on Rhodes would constitute a violation of the island’s non-military status and would harm peace and stability in the Aegean, as well as good neighborly relations,” the sources said.
According to Greek media, the Greek Defense Ministry is planning to create a permanent base on Rhodes, where it will deploy V-BAT unmanned aircraft as part of its plan to upgrade its defense infrastructure in the Aegean.
“Türkiye will continue to resolutely protect its rights and interests stemming from international treaties and take the necessary measures accordingly,” the Turkish sources said.
HH Patriot system to be relocated to Crete
In the meantime, Turkish defense sources also commented on the recent Greek decision to relocate Patriot air defense systems from Karpathos to Crete.
“In this context, we consider the decision to relocate the Patriot Air Defense Systems from Karpathos Island to Crete as a positive step towards reversing the current erroneous practice,” the sources said.
Greece deployed Patriot systems to Karpathos to protect the country from potential Iranian missiles during the war between U.S.-Israel and Iran. Karpathos is one of the Greek islands with non-military status and Patriot deployment was criticized by Türkiye.
Athens has now decided to relocate it to Crete, where it hosts a major naval base also used by the American Navy.
“As Türkiye, we will continue to support all constructive steps that contribute to strengthening peace and stability in our region and that comply with international law and obligations arising from treaties,” the Turkish sources said.
Türkiye and Greece signed the Athens Declaration in late 2023 to avoid confrontation over unresolved problems stemming from the Aegean Sea.

Could new US sanctions tear China and Iran apart?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
12:37:00 UTC
21:37:00 KST

Could new US sanctions tear China and Iran apart?
August 27, 2026
China has pushed back on what it called "illegal unilateral sanctions" after the US announced new measures earlier this week to cut off all potential sources of revenue to Iran.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday described the sanctions package as an "economic D-Day" against Tehran, and warned any economic engagement with the regime would "expose those responsible to the full reach" of US power.
China is Iran's top trade partner and provides a lifeline to Tehran mainly through oil purchases, but also with banking, technology and dual-use goods, which can be used both for civilian and military purposes.
When asked whether Chinese banks would be included in the new measures, Bessent warned that "no one was above the reach of US sanctions."
But with US President Donald Trump due to meet his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping in September, Washington will need to be careful with any moves affecting China-Iran trade ties.
China's big banks still safe
The initial US sanctions package stops short of targeting major Chinese banks. Instead, it focuses on 60 smaller entities, individuals, and vessels, both in mainland China and Hong Kong, that are part of the ecosystem supporting "illicit nuclear and missile technology procurement, cyber operations, and oil‑revenue generation networks."
China purchases up to 90% of Iranian oil exports, some of it through independent "teapot" refineries which end up rebranding the oil or using intermediaries to bypass US sanctions.
In May, China's Commerce Ministry ordered domestic businesses and teapot refineries to ignore US restrictions targeting several of these refineries. At the time, Bessent said China's Iran oil purchases amounted to "funding the largest state sponsor of terrorism."
Beijing balances between Iran and its rivals
On Tuesday, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian said cooperation between China and Iran "has always been conducted within the framework of international law and should not be interfered with or disrupted."
China maintains a transactional relationship while framing instability in the Middle East as a failure of US policy. At the same time, Beijing also projects the image of a stable, responsible superpower, and avoids being lumped together with rogue states the US accuses it of supporting. Beijing also values its trade ties with Saudi Arabia and the UAE, prompting it to carefully balance its relationships to avoid alienating Iran's regional rivals.
The ongoing conflict in the Middle East and the US sanctions package are likely to be on the agenda when Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian attends the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Kyrgyzstan, scheduled for August 31 to September 1. The SCO focuses on Eurasian security and is part of China's strategy of creating a "multipolar" world order to counter the global influence of the US.
China has been "trying to deepen its engagement and expand the scope of its relations with Gulf countries. From this perspective, Iran remains a useful and important partner for China, but it is not irreplaceable," William Yang, senior analyst for Northeast Asia at the International Crisis Group, told DW.
"In some ways, China benefits from Washington's continued involvement in regional security and defense and is not seeking to replace the US in that regard," Yang added.
Is US power waning in the Middle East?
However, US military setbacks during the Iran war have called this security umbrella into question and have changed the strategic landscape in the Middle East, Gu Xuewu, political scientist and director of the Center for Global Studies at Germany's University of Bonn, told DW.
"Against this backdrop, Beijing will not yield to US pressure to sever economic and trade ties with Iran or to help the US maintain its presence in the Middle East," Gu said.
Since the Iran war was launched in late February, Beijing has consistently called for a diplomatic solution to the conflict. This week, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Jian said that Washington's strategy of "economic asphyxiation" will fail to resolve the crisis and will only further intensify Middle Eastern tensions.
"China disapproves of the US' assertive behavior in this region, and is even less willing to accept the US using every means at its disposal to hinder cooperation between Arab states and China in the areas of energy, the military, science, technology, and trade," said Gu.
He added that Beijing has no interest in fighting a "decisive battle" with the US in the Middle East. "It is enough to provoke the US into making mistakes in the Middle East and to allow it to continue making further mistakes without interfering," he added.
Trump-Xi summit looms large
In 2025, when the US tried to pressure China with massive tariffs, Beijing hit back by threatening to cut off the supply of rare earth minerals, forcing the Trump administration to retreat.
Since then, Trump has tried to stabilize the US-China relationship, including with a high profile summit in Beijingthis May. Now, Chinese leader Xi is due to visit Washington in September.
"Since Beijing and Washington are both focused on paving the way for the highly anticipated summit on September 24, I don't think either country will take drastic action on Iran to jeopardize the summit," Yang said.
However, he added that China will "maintain its baseline engagement with Iran and will be prepared to defend its economic interests if the US government begins to target Chinese businesses with secondary sanctions."
If the US hits large Chinese companies and banks with sanctions, then it is foreseeable that China will respond with equivalent retaliatory measures while maintaining its ties to Iran, says Professor Gu.
However, he added that Beijing will not "abandon the painstakingly negotiated plans for a summit."
"We will see China and the US on a collision course over the Iran issue, even as they engage in friendly discussions during the summit between Xi Jinping and Trump," Gu said.

Estonia's Ministry of Finance forecasts tense fiscal situation in the coming years

Estonia's Ministry of Finance forecasts tense fiscal situation in the coming years
Estonia's economy is forecast to grow 2.5 percent this year, while rising defense spending and tax changes are expected to push the budget deficit to 4.4 percent of GDP, according to the Ministry of Finance's summer economic forecast.
The ministry's summer economic forecast, which will serve as the basis for next year's budget decisions, projects GDP growth of 2.5 percent this year, 2.3 percent next year and 2.4 percent in 2028.
Finance Minister Jürgen Ligi (Reform Party) said Estonia's economy has been one of the best-performing in Europe, with rapid growth and low inflation.
"Growth of 2.5 percent this year is still very impressive given the broader disruptions in the economy," Ligi said.
According to the forecast, growth this year will be driven primarily by domestic demand, as well as exports. Domestic demand will receive a boost from the introduction of a uniform €700 monthly basic exemption, which will result in growth of nearly 10 percent in the total net wage bill.
The state of public finances will remain strained in the coming years. This year, the budget deficit will rise to 4.4 percent of GDP due to increased defense spending and changes to income tax.
Next year, the deficit will reach 4.5 percent as defense spending increases further and the level of general government investment remains high. Intensive use of foreign funding will continue, supported by increasing disbursements from cohesion policy programs, while construction of Rail Baltica will be in full swing. The deficit is then projected to decline gradually, reaching 2.9 percent of GDP by 2030.
The defense spending escape clause allows the budget deficit to exceed the 3 percent limit set by the EU's founding treaty. The clause expires in 2029.
General government debt will rise to 25.9 percent of GDP this year. The increase will primarily be driven by the large budget deficit, which will increase the state's borrowing needs.
Interest costs on government debt will reach €239 million this year, broadly in line with the spring forecast. Continued financing needs will increase the debt burden by an average of nearly 3 percentage points a year over the following years, with general government debt reaching 38.6 percent of GDP by 2030.
Although Estonia's general government debt-to-GDP ratio is among the lowest in the European Union, the summer economic forecast notes that it is rising at one of the fastest rates in the EU.
Raoul Lättemäe, head of the ministry's fiscal policy department, said at the presentation of the forecast that Finland's government debt is nearly 90 percent of GDP and that experts there have acknowledged that curbing the country's debt burden is such a major undertaking that it cannot be accomplished within a single parliamentary term.
"The substance of it is a political question, but from an expert perspective, it is clear that this takes time," Lättemäe said.
According to the summer forecast, Estonia's export prospects will improve as economic conditions strengthen among its main export partners.
The conflict in the Middle East has not had a broader impact on prices. Lättemäe noted that there were considerable concerns when 20 percent of global freight traffic was disrupted virtually overnight at the end of February, but the feared shortages and price increases have not materialized.
"Prices have risen, but we haven't run out of fuel and the world has coped with this surprisingly smoothly and resiliently," Lättemäe said.
According to the forecast, price growth will accelerate in the fall, but inflation for the year as a whole will remain considerably lower than last year.
"Inflation has been surprisingly modest," Lättemäe said. "In the spring, we expected inflation of 4 percent; now the figure is 3.2 percent."
According to the Ministry of Finance forecast, household consumption will be supported by changes to the income tax system, slowing price growth and improving consumer confidence. Although the introduction of a uniform €700 tax-free allowance will increase average take-home pay, wage growth will vary among people at different income levels.
The unemployment rate is projected to fall toward its natural level of around 6 percent in the coming years.
Investment will remain slightly below its long-term average in the coming years, with investment in new housing particularly subdued.
According to the forecast, the average interest rate on housing loans will remain higher than before the period of rapid price growth that began in 2021-2022. Construction activity, however, will be boosted in the coming years by Rail Baltica construction and building renovations.
The Ministry of Finance expects Estonia's exports to grow broadly in line with foreign demand over the coming years, while manufacturing output will increase and the industrial sector will regain some of its share of the economy.

Qatar PM visits Tehran to pursue mediation efforts

Qatar PM visits Tehran to pursue mediation efforts
- Qatar's Prime Minister visited Tehran to revive diplomacy and discuss a phased plan for a joint Iranian-Omani shipping corridor and mine clearance in the Strait of Hormuz.
- The US has increased economic sanctions on Iran, described by Iranian officials as "all-out economic war", while oil flows through the strait dropped to a three-month low.
- Iran and Oman have conflicting statements on their agreement over the strait's control and revenues, with Iran demanding US sanctions removal and compensation before reopening navigation.
AI generated
CAIRO/DUBAI – Qatar’s Prime Minister visited Tehran on Aug 27 in a bid to relaunch diplomacy after the US and Iran traded recriminations over Washington’s promise to increase economic pressure, a move one Iranian official described as “all-out economic war”.
A Gulf neighbour of Iran and a US ally, Qatar has served as a back-channel negotiator for the warring parties and played a direct role in securing a June ceasefire that briefly led to a cessation of hostilities.
Qatar’s Prime Minister Mohammed bin Abdulrahman al-Thani, who is also his country’s foreign minister, met Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, according to Iran’s Foreign Ministry channel on Telegram.
The visit comes as the war nears its sixth month with fighting largely paused but no diplomatic breakthrough in sight. Both sides are at odds over control of the Strait of Hormuz, a choke point for global oil supplies that Tehran has used as leverage.
A memorandum of understanding reached between the US and Iran in June to end the conflict broke down in part because of differences over the narrow waterway between Iran and Oman through which one-fifth of the world’s oil supplies passed before the war began on Feb 28.
Qatar and Iran discussed a proposed phased framework that includes establishing a temporary joint Iranian-Omani shipping corridor through the strait and carrying out a joint project to clear mines from the waterway, Qatar’s Foreign Ministry said.
The two officials also reviewed the latest developments in the region and efforts to de-escalate tensions and create conditions for dialogue, the ministry said.
‘All-out economic war’
Although the strikes have stopped, Washington is now piling on economic pressure by announcing plans to cut Iran off from its trading partners with increased sanctions.
Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf on Aug 27 called for national unity in the face of what he described as “all-out economic war”, warning that internal division was “exactly what the enemy wants”.
Ebrahim Azizi, the head of the Iranian Parliament’s national security committee, said the sanctions were an “inhumane and hostile act” which nonetheless had lost their effectiveness. Tehran has lived under various forms of US sanctions since the Islamic Revolution in 1979.
Hormuz oil flows have fallen to a three-month low, with just five million barrels per day transiting on Aug 24, according to the latest ship-tracking data.
Before the war, the strait carried roughly 20 million barrels per day of crude oil. Prices rose again on Aug 27, with Brent crude futures up 0.6 per cent at US$88.35 a barrel, as investors weighed the prospects for the reopening of the strait.
Conflicting accounts over Oman-Iran talks
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said on Aug 26 that Iran and Oman had agreed on how to share the waterway and its revenues, but a senior Iranian source later said the two countries were still working on the details of an agreement.
Despite an aerial bombardment earlier in the war that severely diminished Iran’s conventional forces, Tehran has maintained enough missile and drone capability to attack Gulf neighbours that house US military bases and disrupt oil tankers in the strait.
The International Maritime Organization has reported 70 incidents in the Strait of Hormuz since Feb 28 that have killed 19 seafarers.
Thousands of others have died, mostly in Iran and Lebanon, since the US and Israel attacked Iran with the stated goals of denying Iran a nuclear weapon, helping Iranians topple their government, and destroying Tehran’s missile programme.
An unidentified projectile hit a tanker in the strait on Aug 25 to set off a fire that was later doused, but all crew were safe and accounted for, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency said.
The Strait of Hormuz was open to free navigation before the war, but Iran has since clung to its control of the waterway as leverage and a revenue source, seeking to charge ships a commission, which the US has opposed.
“An agreement with Oman over the Strait of Hormuz has not been finalised,” the senior Iranian source told Reuters on Aug 26, adding that talks on its details were continuing.
That seemed to contradict a statement by Brigadier General Hossein Mohebbi, a spokesman for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, who said Iran and Oman had “reached results that are acceptable to both sides” on controlling the strait and its revenues.
Mohebbi said the strait would remain shut unless the US met Tehran’s conditions under the interim ceasefire that the two sides signed in June before it unravelled. Those conditions include an end to the US blockade on Iranian ports, compensation and removal of sanctions. REUTERS

China and Nepal built an early warning system for melting glaciers in Himalayas. Does it work?
Wednesday’s deadly ice-rock avalanche on high-altitude Tibet border highlights glacial instability in region vulnerable to climate change
Chinese scientists have developed a cross-border early warning system with counterparts in Nepal to monitor Himalayan glacial lake outburst floods. The system has issued timely alerts over the past several years, effectively preventing casualties.
Some specialists say the disaster was triggered by glacial rock collapse.
It remains unclear whether the China-Nepal early warning system had detected an anomaly before this disaster or issued an alert. But coincidentally, a paper published on Wednesday by the project team highlighted several of China’s recent successes.
“These include the Himalayan glacial lake monitoring network established under the second Qinghai-Tibet scientific expedition, as well as early warning systems for ice avalanche disasters in the Yarlung Tsangpo River’s Sedongpu area and for the Cirenma Co glacial lake in the cross-border China-Nepal basin,” the team wrote in the paper for the peer-reviewed Journal of Glaciology and Geocryology.
“Together, these systems have successfully issued seven early warnings [including one at the China-Nepal border last year],” they said, without specifying the latest case.
The South China Morning Post has contacted lead author Wang Weicai and the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) for comment.
“High-altitude ice-rock avalanches release enormous energy and are far more destructive than typical glacial lake outburst floods,” a glaciologist from a research institute in Chengdu, Sichuan province, told the Southern Weekly on Thursday.

Amsterdam mayor wants to scrap fines for sleeping outdoors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
12:33:36 UTC
21:33:36 KST

Amsterdam mayor wants to scrap fines for sleeping outdoors
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Amsterdam mayor Femke Halsema wants to decriminalise sleeping outdoors, despite objections from residents of the Plantage neighbourhood in the east of the city.
Residents have launched a petition to prevent that from happening, according to AT5. Sleeping on the street or in parks is technically a fineable offence, although in practice no one has been fined over the past year. The mayor now wants it to become official policy.
Plantage resident Dennis de Vreede, who supports the petition, said he fears scrapping criminal liability will lead to more people sleeping outdoors, more nuisance and less possibilities for official action – despite acknowledging that fines are pointless.
“These people cannot afford it and might end up in even more debt trouble,” he told AT5. “But the entire legal framework collapses, meaning the police can no longer take action at all.”
“Shameful” fines
Halsema called fining sleeping homeless people “shameful” in 2021 and has said the measure doesn’t even work. “The intention is that the fine will bring about a change in behaviour,” she wrote, but she questioned whether it actually reduces nuisance.
From 2021 to 2024, fines were only issued for nuisance resulting from sleeping outdoors. Some 1,800 fines were handed out in that period.
But Bianca Koster of the Rainbow Group agrees that fining has little effect. “It helps to address the visibility, but not the core of the problem,” she said.
What needs to be addressed, she said, is why people end up on the streets. She called for more shelters, more care and more housing.
“I understand that when it gets visibly worse, people think we have to do something,” she said. “But punishing people is not the way.”

Ukraine’s Top Two ‘Mustang’ Generals Named to Hold Critical Donbas Sector
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
12:32:19 UTC
21:32:19 KST

President Voldymyr Zelensky on Wednesday named a pair of young generals known for proved battlefield skills to command major forces trying to hold in Ukraine’s Donbas region, the main objective of Russia’s ongoing offensive.
Brig. Gen. Denys Prokopenko, 35, a Kyiv native who studied at university to become an English teacher, first fought Russian troops in 2014 as a civilian volunteer. He is best known in Ukraine for leading a die-hard defense of the port city Mariupol in 2022, and later for building the 1st National Guard Corps “Azov” into the one of the Ukraine’s hardest-fighting military formations. Azov Corps training emphasizes discipline and individual soldier skills.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Brig. Gen. Andriy Biletsky, 47, a Kharkiv native, is a trained historian and martial arts enthusiast. He first saw combat as a volunteer rifleman during Russia’s first invasion of Ukraine in 2014. When Russia invaded Ukraine a second time in 2022 Biletsky raised a volunteer civilian unit fighting in defense of Kyiv. The unit converted to regular forces and in following years expanded into the all arms 3rd Army Corps, a crack unit at the forefront of Ukrainian tactical drone operations.
Both Prokopenko and Biletsky are a generation younger than the Soviet-trained general officer corps that led the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) in 2022. Zelensky in July sacked then-AFU Commander-in-Chief Gen. Oleksandr Syrsky, at the time 60, in favor of Maj. Gen. Mykhailo Drapaty, 43, another battle-tested, wartime generation general with deep combat experience.
Russian Army Chief Visits Troops on Ukraine Front
Ukrainian military information platforms linked Prokopenko and Biletsky’s promotions over the heads of dozens of older AFU generals with a Zelensky-Drapaty plan to raise successful field commanders to senior roles, even if those appointments violated army seniority traditions usually awarding promotion to officers serving in uniform the longest.
Biletsky’s 3rd Corps has been deployed for more than a year in the northern Donetsk region defending a 150-kilometer (93-mile) long sector between the city of Lyman and the village of Borova. According to Biletsky his troops hold strong fortifications against which Russian attacks make little or no progress. Independent monitors confirmed that the 3rd Corps launched limited but successful counterattacks around Lyman city in June-August.
Prokopenko’s 1st Corps arrived in the Dobropillya sector, to the south of 3rd Corps, in August 2025 as an emergency reaction force responding to a Russian breakthrough. Since then the formation has recaptured all lost ground. In the later stages of the counteroffensive Zelensky broke with military precedent and approved Prokopenko’s temporary command of regular army units not normally subordinate to the 1st Corps.
On paper an AFU Corps at full strength contains about 18,000 soldiers and around 250 armored vehicles. Actual AFU unit combat power figures are a military secret, but units at 50 percent strength are common. An April Ukrainian military situation estimate said that Russia had concentrated more than 80,000 troops in Ukraine’s Donetsk region with the objective of conquering it completely by the end of September.
Zelensky in a televised statement said the Donetsk region defenses will be reorganized into two new force groupings, one led by Prokopenko and the other by Biletsky. Television images showed Zelensky, Drapaty, Prokopenko and Biletsky meeting with Drapaty’s chief of staff Pavlo Palisa, 41, Brig. Gen. Oleh Apostol, 39, commander of the AFU’s airborne assault infantry forces, and Maj. Robert Brovdi, 51, commander of the AFU’s Unmanned Systems Forces (USF).
Apostol’s elite air assault units have operated in tandem with the 1st and 3rd Corps in the past, but have only rarely been placed under either of those formations’ direct command.
Reports earlier in the week, some sourced directly to the unit itself, confirmed that the 425th Assault Regiment, an attack unit operating in both the Zaporizhzhia and Donetsk sectors as an independent force, had been assigned to 1st Corps and by Wednesday was in action near the city Kostyantynivka.
Brovdi, one of the first commanders in any army to field drone swarms against massed tank attacks, in a post-meeting statement on his personal Telegram channel said that Drapaty’s plan was exactly what the sector needed to shut down further Russian assaults.
“This is Smart War. The [parallel] Force Groupings of Redis (Prokopenko’s call sign) and Biletsky have been created. The time of network-centric war has come. There will be total synchronization with the USF. The time chain between sensor and shooter will be minimal. Worms, cover your eyes!”
A former grain trader, Brovdi is a lead innovator and longtime proponent of Ukrainian “drone wall” tactics that saturate a defense zone with observation and kamikaze strike aircraft for 10 to 30 kilometers, making attacks highly costly and often suicidal. “Worm” is a Ukrainian army slang term for a Russian soldier, particularly if observed by drone.
Ukrainian military analyst Vasyl Pekhno in a Thursday YouTube report on the AFU’s latest Donetsk region defense plans: “Two of our truly legendary commanders... will receive new responsibilities… the point is that, in order to genuinely hold Donetsk Oblast now, we need to significantly reinforce these sectors, including in terms of command and control.”
“They are trying to secure positions around the cities before the cold weather arrives, when there will be no vegetation – when the battlefield will become completely open and transparent, so to speak,” Pekhno said. “Remaining out in the fields over the winter means signing your own death warrant.”
Pekhno suggested the AFU could concentrate three army corps: the 3rd, 11th and 19th to hold the northern face of the Slovyansk-Kramatorsk defenses under Biletsky’s overall command, and the 1st and 20th Corps, along with attached air assault infantry units, on the southern face. As described by Pekhno, such force groupings would be unprecedented for the AFU both by scale and the young age of the officers in command.
Ukrainian military journalist Yuriy Butusov in a Wednesday evening call-in interview discussing the Biletsky and Prokopenko appointments said that they were sensible and would help, but that Ukrainians should understand that defenses in the Donetsk sector are weakening under regular Russian attacks.
“If we look at what is happening at the front, primarily in Donbas, this is the biggest challenge we have faced during the war. The situation is completely unstable, completely uncontrolled, absolutely such that it requires rapid decisions… The enemy has come very close to Slovyansk. In fact, how close? They are practically on the outskirts of Slovyansk… At the moment, this is the main – the only, best – natural defensive line,” Butusov said. “But rapid decisions need to be made now, before it is too late.”
The independent military information platform DeepState in a Wednesday report on fighting in the Donetsk sector said that the epicenter of combat is around the town Kostyantynivka “which the enemy is relentlessly trying to occupy… there is active infiltration into the city and our military is forced to conduct constant reconnaissance of the enemy, who is hiding in houses, basements, ruins, etc.”
The next midrange objectives for Russian forces, that report said, would be in the 1st Corps sector towards the towns of Rayohorodok and Mykolaivka, where a new wave of attacks is now taking place.

Hong Kong parents to get alerts over teens’ self-harm searches on Instagram

Hong Kong parents to get alerts over teens’ self-harm searches on Instagram
Meta Platforms rolls out alerts to help parents intervene when teenagers repeatedly search for self-harm-related content as part of wider safety measures
Meta Platforms has started sending out alerts to parents whose children repeatedly search for content about suicide or self-harm on Instagram as part of broader efforts to strengthen online safety for young users.
Parents supervising a teen’s account can receive notifications by email, text message, WhatsApp or Instagram, depending on the contact information available.
They will also be directed to expert resources on how to approach potentially sensitive conversations.
Philip Chua, Meta’s Asia-Pacific general manager for product public policy, said On Thursday the company wanted to balance protecting teens and allowing parents to intervene when necessary.
“We think that the balance here is delicate, but the balance here should be supportive of a parent,” he said, adding that Meta already directed users searching for sensitive topics to resources including The Samaritan Befrienders Hong Kong.
The global technology conglomerate said the alerts, which began rolling out this month, would be triggered by repeated searches for terms including “suicide” and “self-harm”, as well as phrases promoting such acts or suggesting that a user wants to hurt themselves.

Bond market revolt signals fading confidence in US economic leadership
From surging debt to trade wars with Canada, self-harm has been the main consequence of Trump’s reckless policy decisions
3-MIN READ3-MIN
10
 Listen
Nicholas Spiro is a partner at Lauressa Advisory, a specialist London-based real estate and macroeconomic advisory firm. 
Two years ago, the prospect of a trade war between the United States and Canada, two of the world’s most closely integrated economies, would have been unthinkable. However, US President Donald Trump’s recklessness and capriciousness know no bounds.
Last week’s breakdown in negotiations between the North American neighbours, which triggered the imposition of US tariffs of 50 per cent on a wide range of Canadian goods, showed the degree to which Trump’s trade policies are vindictive, politicised and self-defeating.
According to Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney, who has responded in kind by announcing levies of up to 50 per cent on hundreds of US goods, the White House changed the terms of the deal at the eleventh hour. US negotiators insisted Ottawa renounce its promotion of French as a coequal language with English and agree to measures that would restrict its ability to strike trade deals with other countries.
Although Canada’s economy – which sends more than 70 per cent of its exports to the US – will bear the brunt of a full-blown trade war, the US will suffer, too. Canada is the second-largest US trading partner after Mexico, while the two nations’ automotive supply chains are deeply integrated. Trump’s threat to raise tariffs on Canadian cars and automotive parts to 50 per cent poses a huge risk to the US car industry and its supplier network.
Self-harm has been the main consequence of Trump’s protectionist and highly expansionary fiscal policies. While the entire world is contending with the geopolitical and economic fallout from Trump’s second presidency, the biggest casualty – and the one that matters most to global markets – is the management of the US economy.
Last year, the Taco acronym, which stands for “Trump always chickens out”, was popular among investors, many of whom believed Trump’s bark was worse than his bite. While equity investors continue to be dazzled by the boom in artificial intelligence, bond markets are in a less forgiving mood this year, partly because of the inflationary impact of the energy shock and the dramatic increase in debt issuance by the leading technology companies.

Argo Ideon: Cooperation with Latvia as a light form of local globalism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
12:25:00 UTC
21:25:00 KST

Argo Ideon: Cooperation with Latvia as a light form of local globalism
Let the Latvians keep all those Kārums and saldējums as source of national pride. There's no need to feel envy, because Latvia — for an Estonian — is anyway "us," not "them," writes Argo Ideon.
When this tiny pebble with a glowing core, rushing through the ice‑cold cosmos, is home to about 8.3 billion fellow humans, and even in our cozy European Union live more than 450 million people, then the most pointless thing in our sparsely populated corner of the world is to count points over whether today's winner was an Estonian or a Latvian.
After the news that the head of the dairy plant producing Kārums will henceforth be an Estonian, cheering began in North Livonia as if at least three Olympic decathlon gold medals had been brought home. In Riga, an existential worry apparently arose about what will become of the iconic crow perched on its orange wrapper. The deal is not yet finalized, but already "The mouth sings, the heart worries, the eyes roll water" (Haljala).
Having just peeled the paper off a coconut‑flavored glazed curd snack, the future looks entirely optimistic. I read that this treat also contains milk from Järvamaa, from Estonia Farms, so Estonian‑Latvian cooperation has long been running like clockwork.
An Estonian's relationship with food made in Latvia has since ancient times been one of deep respect for the neighboring country's masters — and the urge to haul home large quantities of everything one cannot eat immediately.
I vividly recall a childhood summer trip with the family to Riga Zoo. I no longer remember whether they showed us an elephant or not, but the lasting highlight of the trip for Tallinn kids was one single word: saldējums. As soon as a stand with that sign appeared, my sister and I raced to shout: saldejumps! saldejumps!
It was simply so good, even if often quite simple — ice cream packed in a waffle cup.
On an adult's food radar, one after another appeared the abundant market pavilions next to Riga's main station, Lido, and the fantastic salamis from the Rēzekne Meat Factory (RGK). And who exactly owns all these delicious things or is the "actual beneficiary" — a consumer cannot be bothered to investigate with every purchase.
The deeply rooted desire to be better than the neighbor demands that if a Latvian has six toes on one foot, then an Estonian must have at least seven. But with that calculation you won't get far in the real world, because if you count up the symbolic victories, you must also enter the losses in the other column. For example, the owner of Kalev candy factory — a brand with legendary status in Estonia — has been a Norwegian company since 2010. The former Pärnu maantee factory has housed the police for years, but the candies haven't disappeared from the shops, and no one has renamed Anneke milk chocolate to Fridtjof.
Or the general despair in 2015 when Estonian Air had to pack up. It was a blow and a serious national catastrophe for us, while Latvia's airBaltic flew on without missing a beat. Now that the Latvians are in financial trouble, some say that Estonian travelers have for years been gliding along on the back of the Latvian taxpayer and flying cheaply. So who knows who ultimately lost or won. In any case, when Latvia hints that the Republic of Estonia could also lend a shoulder in the form of an investment, our answer echoes from Estonian classic literary character, Tõnisson in Paunvere: "I would've gone completely away from home if I had known you were coming."
Sometimes these Latvian matters remain a bit confusing for Estonians, like the state of Rail Baltica's construction, but no worries — there is always the shared treasure of both countries, ERR's Latvia correspondent Ragnar Kond, who comes on air and explains everything to the people. If nothing else works, then the final rails will end at Häädemeeste for now, and you can continue to Lithuania by bus. Elron has already trained Estonians well for bus rides with train tickets.
Overall, it is pointless to count these neighborly point‑wins. On the contrary, toes must be put together and the common work carried forward.
As does the Latvian man on Instagram, who introduces the customs of this corner of the world to a global audience. On his plate are fried potatoes and two slices of rye bread with a hefty pork chop stuck between them. A Latvian burger! A similar product was made famous in Estonia by the first capitalists — read Rohke Debelak. That back then the chop was replaced by boiled sausage is understandable, given the tight conditions at the end of the Soviet era.
And everything said above applies equally to the Finns. The best cure for poking fun at all our wonderful neighbors is to travel somewhere far away for a moment — say, across the ocean. At an investigative journalism conference in Miami, you discover that there are no other Estonians here, but a colleague from Finnish media is present. Joy overflows and spontaneous brotherhood happens. Fellow local guys meet! Terve! No mitäs nyt jätkä? Eppu Normaali!*
That neighbors lift each other up — that is a light form of local globalism. It absolutely does not prevent being a nationalist at a football match and cheering for your own men's or women's team. In any case, it's great when "we" stretches for Estonia at least from Lapland to Lithuania, if not already farther.
*In Finnish: "Hi there! So what's up, buddy? Eppu Normaali! (an iconic Finnish rockband)."
--
Editor: Helen Wright

MSF team arrives in Nepal to assess people’s needs following devastating flash floods
Share
Project Update27 August 2026
After a major flash flood struck the Rasuwa district in Nepal, on Wednesday 26 August, a Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) team experienced in providing emergency response has arrived in Nepal to assess people’s immediate needs. We stand ready to provide urgent humanitarian and medical assistance.
The floods rapidly impacted the Timure, Rasuwagadhi, and Syabrubesi areas causing significant damage to settlements, markets, and infrastructure. Flood waves are estimated to have been as large as 8-10 metres in some locations. Hundreds, if not thousands, of people are feared to have died, with many people still missing.
Floodwaters reached the town of Mugling, in Chitwan district, and have since begun to recede. However, authorities say the risk remains high, as the blocked section of the river upstream has not yet been fully cleared.
High-alert warnings have been issued for communities located along the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli rivers, particularly in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha, and Chitwan districts. People living along riverbanks have been advised to move to safer locations.
Authorities are carrying out urgent search and rescue operations in affected areas, and a full health emergency response has been initiated.
The MSF team arrived in Nepal less than 24 hours after the floods struck, and we are engaging with health facilities to assess if we can support. We know from our years of experience in emergencies that people in affected areas will have urgent needs for shelter, non-food items such as hygiene and cooking items, access to clean water and latrines, and emergency medical and trauma support.
MSF teams are assessing how we can provide assistance to people and stand ready to support the national response to this tragedy.
MSF teams last worked in Nepal in 2020 when we responded to COVID-19 needs. We also worked on a large scale in the country following earthquakes in April and May 2015, when we provided medical and mental health consultations, as well as shelter and food.

Nepal-Tibet flood death toll passes 360 as new flood threat emerges
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
15:22:48 EEST
21:22:48 KST

At least 362 people have died after a glacier collapse sent water, ice, rock and mud through the Nepal-Tibet border region, while more than 1,300 people remain missing. Rescue teams face a further threat after debris blocked a river and formed a rising lake that authorities warn is at risk of bursting.
Nepal Police said on Thursday that 359 people had died in the country. China has confirmed three deaths in Tibet.
The figures have risen throughout the day as search teams reach settlements and recover bodies downstream.
More than 800 people remain missing in Nepal, while Chinese state broadcaster CCTV has reported 558 missing in Tibet, including 260 foreign nationals. Authorities have not established whether some people appear in figures reported on both sides of the border.
One Finnish citizen is among those missing in Nepal, Finland’s Foreign Ministry told Yle and Helsingin Sanomat. Around 30 Finnish travellers had filed travel notifications for Nepal.
The floods struck on Wednesday morning after a mass of glacier ice and rock collapsed in the Himalayas. The US Geological Survey said the collapse produced seismic signals that authorities initially interpreted as an earthquake.
Ice and rock travelled into the Lhende Khola river system in Tibet before the flood moved towards Nepal through the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli rivers. The International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development said the Trishuli rose by as much as nine metres within 30 minutes at one downstream location.
Chinese government geologist Guo Zhaocheng told state media that the ice-avalanche debris flow travelled at about 50 metres per second.
“That left people almost no time to react,” Guo said.
The flood struck the Gyirong border crossing, roads, bridges, settlements and hydropower facilities. The crossing serves tourists travelling between Nepal and Tibet and handles more than 30 per cent of China-Nepal trade, according to the BBC.
The disaster occurred during the pilgrimage season for Mount Kailash and Lake Mansarovar in Tibet. Hundreds of foreign tourists were travelling through the border region.
India’s Foreign Ministry said 288 Indian nationals remained missing in Nepal and about 200 were stranded in Tibet. Nepalese figures also list missing citizens from the United States, Britain, Australia, Malaysia, Canada, South Korea and several European countries.
Rescuers have used helicopters to reach communities cut off after roads and bridges were destroyed. The Nepal Army said it rescued more than 350 people on Thursday, including 50 foreign nationals. Military facilities in Trishuli have been turned into rescue bases.
A new danger emerged on Thursday when Nepal’s disaster authority said debris from the collapse had blocked a river and created a lake. Satellite analysis showed its water level continuing to rise. Authorities told residents and rescue workers to stay away from river banks.
Chinese authorities have issued a similar warning over a dammed lake near Gyirong. State media reported that the lake held about two million cubic metres of water on Thursday morning, with another three million cubic metres expected to enter during the following three days.
The Red Cross has sent emergency supplies by helicopter, including drinking water, shelter materials, first-aid equipment and hygiene kits. The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies allocated 997,000 Swiss francs for the response.
Britain pledged £5 million, while the United Nations allocated $2 million from its Central Emergency Response Fund. India has sent relief supplies, and the United States announced $500,000 in assistance.
Scientists have linked the immediate disaster to the glacier collapse rather than an earthquake. They have not established the precise reason the glacier failed. Researchers cited by Reuters said rising temperatures, glacier retreat and changes in mountain permafrost increase instability across parts of the Himalayas.

Egyptian pharmaceutical firm developing Ebola vaccine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
12:22:11 UTC
21:22:11 KST

Breadcrumb
Egyptian pharmaceutical firm developing Ebola vaccine
An Egyptian pharmaceutical firm is developing a potential vaccine against the deadly Ebola strain raging in the DR Congo, it announced Thursday.
Minapharm will receive up to $16.5 million from the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI) to work on a vaccine to combat the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, they said in a joint statement.
The candidate vaccine is designed by ProBioGen, a Berlin-based subsidiary of Minapharm.
It is the fifth Bundibugyo candidate vaccine being funded by CEPI, in the scramble to find tools to rein in the outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo.
The $16.5 million is set to advance it through the laboratory stages and on into a so-called Phase 1 clinical trial—small-scale testing on humans.
The trial—to determine its safety, and its ability to provoke an immune response—is expected to take place in Africa.
There are no specific vaccines or treatments for Bundibugyo, which is spreading faster than attempts to control it can catch up.
There have been more than 5,600 confirmed cases in the DR Congo, including more than 2,700 deaths, since the outbreak was declared on May 15.
"Bundibugyo virus is now driving the largest Ebola outbreak DRC has ever faced," said Jean Kaseya, head of the African Union's public health agency.
"A vaccine candidate advanced by an African company is exactly the kind of capability our continent needs—not just for this outbreak, but so that Africa can develop and manufacture the tools it needs to protect its own people," the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) director general said in the statement.
Five jabs in the pipeline
Oslo-based CEPI is funding four other Bundibugyo candidate jabs, which are in various stages of development and use a range of vaccine technologies.
They are being developed by Moderna, using mRNA technology; the University of Oxford and Serum Institute of India, using the ChAdOx platform; and one each from Hilleman and Public Health Vaccines, which both use rVSV technology.
The Minapharm candidate vaccine uses the MVA platform and is the only one designed to induce both B- and T-cell responses for long-lasting immunity.
The different technology options "maximise the likelihood of developing a safe and effective shot that could help bring this devastating crisis under control", the statement said.
CEPI hopes at least two Bundibugyo vaccines could come through the trials and be good enough for the World Health Organisation to approve for use.
The WHO has meanwhile recommended a full-scale human trial in the DRC of the only existing approved Ebola vaccine to see if it offers cross-protection against Bundibugyo.
Ervebo has proved safe and efficacious against the more common Zaire strain of Ebola virus, and WHO experts said early data, notably from animal trials, showed it may also give some protection against Bundibugyo.
