How do we cope when we can no longer trust what we see and hear to tell us what is real? That’s a challenge that Alessandra Sala, senior director of AI and data science at Shutterstock, grapples with every day. One inciting incident: when her father received an AI-generated voicemail that sounded exactly like her sister, nearly fooling her family.
“Our senses were never designed to cope with this digital world where what’s synthetically generated seems so real that we cannot differentiate anymore,” says Sala. As the AI industry remains fixated on releasing more powerful and autonomous models, the Italian-born computer engineer is one of the leading voices pushing for safer and more inclusive AI systems.
One of those is in disinformation: Sala represents Shutterstock in the AI and Multimedia Authenticity Standards Collaboration, a group focused on developing authenticity standards for AI-generated multimedia and tackling the growing problem of deepfakes.
The other is in representation: Sala also serves as co-chair of UNESCO Women in Ethical AI and is the global president of Women in AI, which are both addressing the gender gap in the AI industry. In a world where algorithms can shape our reality and govern everything from hiring to healthcare, underrepresenting women or other minorities in training models could hold serious consequences for society. Many of the latest AI models don’t just automate the discrimination and institutional biases that already exist, she says—they amplify it.
“Those models converge to an average of the things that they see, and if they receive very [few] examples of women or any other minority, this information gets forgotten very early,” says Sala. “We see an amplification of the discrimination and the gap.”

Emil Michael led the Pentagon’s negotiations with Anthropic over military AI safety guardrails, attempting to strongarm one of the world’s fastest-growing companies into accepting terms it deemed unacceptable. When Anthropic refused in February, Michael helped trigger an unprecedented reaction: designating it a supply chain risk—the first time the label has been applied to an American outfit.
Michael, a former Uber executive, was no stranger to dealmaking. He pushed providers to permit “all lawful uses” of their models.
Anthropic has said the dispute came down to two exceptions: keeping Claude from conducting mass surveillance of Americans and from independently controlling lethal autonomous weapons. Michael rejects that account, saying Anthropic instead wanted the Pentagon to seek its approval for particular uses of Claude, effectively inserting the company into the military chain of command. Anthropic has called that characterization “patently false.”
After negotiations failed, the Pentagon imposed the supply chain risk designation. “They turned it into a PR thing,” Michael told TIME in March. “When you do that, you are a supply chain risk.” Though Michael did not persuade Anthropic, he won the broader fight. OpenAI, xAI, and Google subsequently reached agreements allowing the Pentagon to deploy their models under terms closer to those he had laid out.

During a trial excavation, archaeology firm BAAC uncovered a medieval cemetery beneath the Vlasmarkt or Flax Market in Ghent. The city authorities in the capital of East Flanders had planned to plant a tree on this location following roadworks. BAAC estimates that there may be up to 240 skeletons buried here. The tree will now not be planted for the time being. Ghent has also decided not to carry out any further excavations at the minute.
Archaeologists found four skeletons during a trial excavation on the Vlasmarkt. A small section of the market was examined at the spot where a tree was to be planted. The excavation took place whilst roadworks were underway. Ghent is removing the traditional cobblestones and resurfacing the market with tarmac.
It was known that the current Vlasmarkt was a cemetery from the 11th to the 18th century. The square is situated next to St James’s Church. Until now, it had been unclear how many people were buried here.
The archaeologists found the skeletons at a depth of just over 1 metre. A deeper borehole indicates that there are a further four burial levels underneath. This means that there are probably only 20 skeletons buried at that specific location. Based on this, the archaeologists have made an estimate for the entire site, which covers 23 square metres. Beneath the Vlasmarkt, there is thought to be a cemetery containing more than 240 skeletons.
Ghent has decided that the tree will now not be planted and that no further excavations will take place. The finds will therefore be preserved for the time being. The city authorities have, however, promised to take the remains into account during any future, larger-scale redevelopment.
Today the Vlasmarkt is one of the places where Ghent residents and visitors enjoy a night out. During the Ghent Festival, the square is the place to party until the early hours of the morning.

Iran's top diplomat met his Qatari counterpart on Thursday in Tehran for talks on the strategic Strait of Hormuz, as a US naval blockade squeezes oil supplies to Iran amid a domestic shortfall.
The visit by Qatar's Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani follows a week of intense diplomacy in Iran involving separate meetings with Oman's top diplomat and senior Pakistani officials seeking ways to end the Middle East war and reopen Hormuz.
It also comes as Washington threatens wider secondary sanctions against countries, banks and companies that continue doing business with Iran, part of a broader campaign it has called "economic asphyxiation".

Qatar's foreign ministry said they discussed de-escalation efforts as well as the proposed framework for Hormuz between Iran and Oman.
Al Thani "emphasised the necessity of respecting the sovereignty of neighbouring states and freedom of navigation", and pursuing dialogue, the ministry said.
Alongside mediator Pakistan, Qatar had played a key role in securing an April ceasefire and June deal between Iran and the United States, but those deals have since collapsed.
Fuel shortage
Since war with the United States broke out on February 28, Iran has maintained tight control over Hormuz, a vital global energy conduit, with Washington imposing a naval counter-blockade on Iranian ports.

On Wednesday, Iran's Vice President Mohammad Jafar Ghaempanah said the blockade had prevented his country from importing enough petrol to cover a shortfall in domestic production.

Iran, a major oil producer with some of the world's cheapest fuel, has for years heavily subsidised petrol, making changes to pricing politically sensitive.

Talks on Hormuz

Tehran has also sought to impose service fees on ships using the strait – a move strongly opposed by Washington and regional countries.

Persistent financial hardship is linked to later-life brain shrinkage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
12:00:52 UTC
21:00:52 KST

Money worries can keep us up at night, but could decades of financial stress leave a lasting mark on the brain itself? That’s the question my colleagues and I set out to answer in a new study – and the answer, it turns out, is yes.
Most research on money and brain health looks at people’s financial circumstances at just one point in time. This makes it hard to know whether a few difficult years have the same effect as decades of enduring struggle. For our study, published in the journal Innovation in Aging, we tracked the same people throughout their adult lives to find out.
We used data from the MRC National Survey of Health and Development, also known as the 1946 British birth cohort study. A cohort study follows a group of people born in the same period throughout their lives. This is the world’s longest continuously running study of its kind, tracking thousands of people born in one week in March 1946 – participants who celebrated their 80th birthdays earlier this year.
The study’s origins go back to the economic anxieties of the 1930s, when the Great Depression left many families worrying about money and the cost of raising children – making it a fitting dataset to revisit those same questions decades later. Using this rich resource, we examined the financial circumstances of 2,759 participants at multiple points across adulthood.
Participants reported their household income at ages 26, 43 and 53. We classed those in the bottom 20% of the group on at least two of these occasions as having persistent low income – about one in six people. Separately, we measured financial hardship by asking whether people struggled to manage on their income or had trouble paying bills, at least twice between ages 36 and 53. This applied to about one in eight.
At age 53, participants took tests of verbal memory and processing speed. A smaller group also had brain scans between ages 69 and 71, which let us measure brain atrophy (shrinkage) and ventricular expansion – the widening of fluid-filled cavities within the brain, a recognised marker of poor brain health.
We found that people who had experienced more financial hardship and low income scored lower on the cognitive tests at age 53. These links held even after we accounted for their childhood thinking skills, education and childhood disadvantage. Among those who had brain scans, persistent low income was linked to greater brain shrinkage in later life.
When we looked at how memory changed from age 53 to 69, those who had faced persistent hardship actually showed slower decline over that period. We believe this is because they had already lost more ground by age 53 – they started from a lower point, so there was less left to lose.
We also found that the link between financial adversity and brain shrinkage was stronger for men, for those who grew up in disadvantaged homes, and for carriers of a gene that raises the risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease.
For men of this generation – born in 1946, when the male breadwinner model was the norm – the pressure of being the main earner may have made financial stress more acute. Disadvantaged men also had higher rates of smoking and drinking than disadvantaged women.
The finding on genetic risk suggests that people who are already biologically vulnerable may be more susceptible to the effects of financial strain. These subgroup findings are based on smaller numbers within our sample, so we are treating them as suggestive rather than conclusive.
Why would money worries harm the brain?
How might financial hardship affect the brain over time? Chronic stress is known to increase inflammation, which accelerates brain ageing. There is also the simple fact that constantly worrying about money uses up mental energy, leaving less capacity for other thinking tasks – a cognitive load that competes with everything else the brain is trying to do.
We acknowledge that our study cannot prove cause and effect, and the results, drawn from a single generation of British adults, may not apply directly to other populations or countries. But following the same people over many years gives us a clearer picture than studies that only look at a single moment in time.
Financial hardship is increasingly recognised as one of several factors – alongside things such as hearing loss, smoking and physical inactivity – that may shape our risk of cognitive decline in later life. Our findings suggest that reducing chronic financial hardship among working-age adults, wherever they live, could help protect brain health and potentially reduce dementia cases in the future.

Russia sentences former ‘king of state contracts’ to 12 years in prison in absentia for bribing a colonel
Moscow’s Basmanny District Court sentenced Boris Usherovich, a former co-owner of the “1520” group of companies, to 12 years in prison in absentia for bribing former Interior Ministry colonel Dmitry Zakharchenko, the Russian business news outlet RBC reported.
Usherovich, who has been placed on an international wanted list, was arrested in absentia in 2019. The court, which began hearing the bribery case in October 2025, also fined him 500 million rubles.
Investigators said that from 2007 to 2016, Usherovich, his “1520” partner Valery Markelov, and former Inkredbank vice presidents Dmitry Motorin and Ivan Stankevich paid Zakharchenko bribes totaling more than 1.4 billion rubles.
Investigators believe the payments were meant to secure protection for a platform the men had set up to run shadow banking operations, including cash withdrawals and currency conversion. Zakharchenko initially received 150,000 euros a month; those payments stopped in 2009–2011, after which his cut rose to 20% of the platform’s monthly income in each currency.
Motorin, Stankevich, and Usherovich left Russia after the case was opened. Zakharchenko has denied protecting the bankers and businessmen. Valery Markelov was sentenced in 2019 to eight years in prison and fined 500 million rubles. He was diagnosed with cancer during the trial and died several months after the sentence was handed down.
The “1520” group of companies designs and builds railroads. In 2018, its owners — Alexei Krapivin, Valery Markelov, and Boris Usherovich — topped Forbes Russia’s ranking of “kings of government contracts,” after receiving government contracts worth 218 billion rubles that year, according to Forbes Russia’s calculations.

American Airlines adds batch of new international routes on its XLR planes

21:00:01 KST

American Airlines announced Thursday it will add seven international routes to its 2027 schedule, with many of those on its Airbus A321XLR planes.
Here are the additions:
- Charlotte, North Carolina, to Barcelona, Spain, starting May 27, on a Boeing 777-200ER.
- Chicago O'Hare International Airport to Tokyo's Narita International Airport, starting March 19, on a Boeing 787-9.
- New York John F. Kennedy International Airport to Amsterdam, starting March 28, on an Airbus A321XLR.
- New York JFK to Nice, France, starting May 6, on an Airbus A321XLR.
- Philadelphia to Porto, Portugal, starting March 28, on an Airbus A321XLR.
- Philadelphia to Reykjavik, Iceland, starting May 27, on an Airbus A321neo.
- Philadelphia to Vienna, starting May 6, on an Airbus A321XLR.
The carrier is also adding a fourth daily flight between JFK and London Heathrow Airport, on a Boeing 787-9, starting March 28.
The Airbus XLR, which stands for extra long range, has the ability to go up to 4,700 nautical miles. The single-aisle planes are smaller than others in the airline's fleet, like a Boeing 777 or Boeing 787 Dreamliner, which makes them cheaper to operate.
The airline rolled out a new interior and configuration with its inaugural XLR flight last year. It's allocated more space to premium seats — which take up a fifth of the plane — than it has on its other aircraft.
American's plan is to use the XLRs to focus on routes to smaller European cities from its Philadelphia hub or from New York City.
"It really opens up the menu for all these destinations that are just too small for a widebody," American's senior vice president of network and schedule planning, Brian Znotins, told CNBC last year.
The airline said its Vienna route will extend through early January 2028 to draw tourists who are aiming to visit European Christmas markets. That follows a growing trend, as airlines have been adding more capacity in the shoulder seasons and even in the off-peak winter period as travelers opt to fly in the fall and other cooler, cheaper times of the year.
American's announcement comes the same week that United Airlines unveiled its 2027 destinations. United is adding routes to less traditionally popular tourist destinations for U.S. travelers, spanning Ljubljana, Slovenia, to Okinawa, Japan.
United offers more international service than other U.S. airlines.
American has been trying to close a profit gap with rivals United and Delta Air Lines and said earlier this year that its flying is split about 80% domestic versus 20% international.
International flights often carry a high premium compared with domestic routes — and the planes serving them generally have more luxurious seats on board, which can be more profitable for airlines.

After Israeli seizure of Kalandia training centre, UNRWA warns of impact on youth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27

21:00:00 KST

After Israeli seizure of Kalandia training centre, UNRWA warns of impact on youth
The seizure of a vocational training centre in occupied East Jerusalem has left hundreds of Palestinian young people without access to skills and training that could help shape their futures.
Israeli authorities forcibly entered the Kalandia Vocational Training Centre on Tuesday, 24 August, and took control of the facility, according to the UN agency for Palestine refugees, UNRWA. The centre was the last UNRWA facility still operating in occupied East Jerusalem, after Israeli authorities closed the agency's other schools and clinics in the city.
The United Nations has strongly condemned those actions, saying that the entry of security forces into a UN facility without the Organisation's permission or approval was unacceptable.
Secretary-General António Guterres called for the Israeli Government to immediately cease its interference with UNRWA installations and to vacate, return and restore all affected premises to the United Nations without delay.
Earlier this month, there was misinformation circulating about the centre, which prompted UNRWA to issue a statement reaffirming its commitment to education and underlining that the agency remains “essential to ensuring that Palestine refugee children and young people can develop the knowledge, skills and opportunities they need to build their futures”.
Roland Friedrich, Director of UNRWA Affairs in the West Bank, told us that the incident was part of a wider effort by the current Israeli Government to end UNRWA's activities in occupied East Jerusalem, following the adoption of what he described as "anti-UNRWA" legislation almost a year and a half ago.
The Kalandia centre provides vocational training to young people from refugee camps across the West Bank. Mr. Friedrich warned that its closure would deprive 340 male youth of their right to education and opportunities for the future.
This interview has been edited for clarity and length.
Roland Friedrich: The situation at the Kalandia Training Centre remains critical. Israeli security forces are still deployed inside the centre, along with Israeli officials from the Municipality of Jerusalem, as they carry out work and alterations to the installation. This is an unacceptable violation – as the Secretary-General has underlined – of the privileges and immunities of the United Nations. The continuation of this situation will very likely deprive 340 male youth from the West Bank of their right to education.
UN News: Can you tell us exactly what happened? What happened to the UNRWA staff who were at the centre?
Roland Friedrich: On Tuesday morning, a large Israeli force arrived and forcibly entered the compound. We had 24 staff on site as we prepared for the new scholastic year, which is scheduled to start next week. Israeli security personnel searched the site, opened the buildings and temporarily held our staff at the site. They were later released. This is an unacceptable violation of the privileges and immunities of the United Nations.
UN News: Were you informed of any reason for the Israeli authorities' entry into the centre or what they were looking for? Do you have any information on the possibility of returning the centre to UNRWA, as requested by the United Nations?
Roland Friedrich: The Secretary-General has been very clear in his demand to urgently restore the situation to the way it was before. The background of what happened goes back to the Israeli anti-UNRWA legislation that was adopted roughly a year and a half ago. We saw the progressive closure of our six schools in Occupied East Jerusalem for 2025, depriving 800 children of education. In December, amendments were made to the anti-UNRWA laws, including a provision to cut water and electricity from UNRWA installations in East Jerusalem, and secondly, to authorize Israeli security forces to seize, our compound, the main headquarters, and the Kalandia Training Centre.
UN News: You talked about the immunities and privileges of the United Nations and its facilities. Can you explain what that means and why it is important to commit to it all over the world, especially in the occupied Palestinian territory?
Roland Friedrich: Any Member State of the United Nations, per its obligations under the Charter, but also through being a party to the general Convention, is obliged to respect the privileges and immunities of the UN. That means, for instance, the inviolability of UN premises, the respect for immunities relating to staff, to vehicles, as is the case anywhere in the world where we operate. What we saw yesterday and what continues to happen is exactly the opposite [of this]. And I think what is important to keep in mind is that this sets a precedent when it comes to making sure that our staff can work in a safe way, are protected anywhere else in the world in a very dangerous context.
UN News: Because we're talking about international law and international obligations, what is the UN planning to do now? What do you hope the international community will do about it?
Roland Friedrich: What we hope is that Member States take the responsibility to exercise pressure, so that we can resume our work at this training centre. The key thing is that we can go back to that centre, operate it, and serve the people that we are mandated to serve by the General Assembly.
UN News: In the context of the Israeli legislation you talked about regarding UNRWA, what can you still do in the West Bank to serve Palestine refugees?
Roland Friedrich: There are two laws. One law is a ban on UNRWA operations and presences in what Israel considers sovereign territory and that applies to our services in occupied East Jerusalem. The occupation of East Jerusalem is not recognized by the UN, nor is in fact the annexation of East Jerusalem. The second law provides for no-contact policy that bans Israeli authorities from being in touch with UNRWA and that has an impact on our operations in the Gaza Strip and the West Bank. However, we can continue to operate both in the Gaza Strip and the West Bank, providing critical humanitarian aid in Gaza through more than 11,000 staff members who work every day, providing education, health consultations, shelter and drinking water. Similarly, in the West Bank, we have 4,600 staff on the ground. We continue to provide education. Last year we provided 1.1 million health consultations through 50 health facilities, and we provided together with partners social protection, cash assistance, and food support to more than 270,000 beneficiaries. I pay the highest respect to my UNRWA colleagues on the ground, Palestinian teachers, nurses, social workers in the Gaza Strip and in the West Bank who work under extremely difficult conditions every day.
UN News: What is the main message you would like the international community to understand about UNRWA's presence, its work and the risks it faces in the West Bank?
Roland Friedrich: One thing that we clearly need to see is a restoration of respect for the United Nations at large, and for UNRWA as an agency mandated by the General Assembly by all State parties. Secondly, the humanitarian space in the West Bank overall is shrinking, and that is a trend that needs to be reversed. And thirdly, we need to reverse the trend of forcible displacement in the West Bank. These are dangerous trends because together with settlement expansion, they create a reality on the ground that makes the two-State solution ever more unlikely to be implemented. It is important to pull back from the brink that we're seeing in the West Bank now and return to a credible pathway towards the two-state solution, and eventually a situation where UNRWA as an agency does not have to do its work anymore because the conflict has moved towards a solution.

UN chief condemns “indifference” as Ebola cases mount in DR Congo

UN chief condemns “indifference” as Ebola cases mount in DR Congo
The Ebola Bundibugyo outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) requires “urgent” action and funding to rein in its alarming spread, the UN Secretary-General told reporters at UN Headquarters on Thursday.
Key points
- More than 5,600 cases and 2,700 deaths in six affected provinces in DRC since the outbreak began in mid-May
- The World Health Organization (WHO) believes it has slowed its spread, but has not yet managed to reverse the current trend
- Prevention work has already begun in neighbouring Burundi, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
“The challenge is immense,” he said, noting 500 new cases are being reported every week while the humanitarian response remains only 48 per cent funded.
Estimates show current resources will last only weeks, not months, as the epidemic spreads faster than the response to contain it.
“We know how to contain Ebola, how to interrupt transmission and how to save lives,” he underscored, “but we must also overcome another virus: the virus of indifference.”
Watch the UN chief’s press stakeout on UN Web TV:
More funds needed
“Without additional funding, vital operations will run out of money at the very moment they need to ramp up,” he warned, calling for an additional $1.1 billion.
Money, however, is only part of the problem. Ebola is spreading in a region where decades of conflict have displaced entire populations and weakened health infrastructure. In Ituri province alone, one million people have been displaced, and more than 12 million people in the region are in need of humanitarian aid and protection.
Insecurity is also directly hindering the response. More than 40 healthcare workers have lost their lives while treatment centres and ambulances have been attacked. Humanitarian teams must therefore simultaneously confront the virus and the violence while some communities remain difficult to access.
All corners of civil society mobilised
Local artists and social media influencers are joining the fight against Ebola by raising awareness through their respective medium, including renowned Congolese singer and songwriter Lokua Kanza.
A national UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) ambassador, Mr. Kanza called for people to implement preventive measures in a video posted on the agency’s social media account.
The Wedy duo and singer Drigo Eboma have also both published music calling for people to stop the spread, and 15 influencers – each with over 100,000 followers – have used their platforms to raise awareness among young people.
Religious leaders are also on the case, with over 50 of them in Ituri province – the epicentre of the outbreak – being briefed on how to prevent the spread and manage rumours.
Similarly, around 30 former combatants received special training from the UN and local partners on prevention measures and detection of suspect cases before being dispatched to heavily frequented areas north of Ituri province to share this crucial information with the local communities.
Prep work in Burundi
UN humanitarian agencies and partners are continuing to support government-led efforts in Burundi to prepare for the potential spread of Ebola in that neighbouring country.
While Burundi has not reported any confirmed cases, the country remains at higher risk due to its proximity to the affected areas in the DRC and continued cross-border population movements, UN agencies are reporting.
Some of the preparedness efforts are already under way, from strengthened surveillance at points of entry through temperature screening and deployment of thermal scanners to training healthcare providers, including nurses and community health workers, as well as journalists.
Uganda’s outbreak declared over
UN health officials and partners declared on Thursday that the Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak in neighbouring Uganda is over.
This follows 42 consecutive days without a new confirmed case since the country’s last patient was discharged from care on 16 July.
The 42-day benchmark – equivalent to twice the upper limit of the incubation period for Ebola – is the internationally established criterion for determining that an outbreak has ended.
During the outbreak, Uganda reported 20 confirmed cases of the disease, including two deaths. More than 800 contacts were identified and monitored to stop the spread.
What’s the UN doing?
- UN agencies and partners began expanding the response with 35 additional mobile safe and dignified burial teams and 286 community-based teams high-risk areas, with more than 2,500 volunteers and civil protection personnel, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
- WHO has deployed more than 260 experts, delivered over 330 tonnes of essential medical and logistical supplies
- The World Food Programme (WFP) continues to provide assistance and medical evacuations through its UN Humanitarian Air Service (UNHAS)
- The UN migration agency, IOM, launched a regional preparedness plan in June covering 11 countries and has helped to screen more than one million people
- In Burundi, WHO and partners are supporting the national authorities in updating their Ebola response guidelines and strengthening lab procedures for the safe collection and transportation of samples while nearly 30,000 Ebola prevention posters have been distributed in three languages: Kirundi, Swahili and French

Shock and devastation remain, a day after Himalayan flood disaster

Shock and devastation remain, a day after Himalayan flood disaster
Amid reports that hundreds of people are still missing in Nepal and China after a floodwater surge slammed into towns and villages on Wednesday, aid teams have been working to reach communities cut off by the disaster.
Key points
- Hundreds remain missing after devastating floods in Nepal and China
- $2 million funding released by UN emergency relief chief
- World Health Organization (WHO) sends medicines, supplies and tents
An initial $2 million has been released from the United Nations Global Emergency Fund (CERF) “to save lives with emergency medical care, shelter, water”, the UN’s relief chief Tom Fletcher said on X.
In Nepal, immediate humanitarian needs are huge in the districts of Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading and communities face immense challenges as families cope with loss, displacement and disruption to essential services.
The UN chief pledged swift support.
“The United Nations is mobilising supplies and humanitarian teams and we pledge to support national efforts to deliver emergency aid and support,” Secretary-General António Guterres said.
17,000 children affected
The flash floods have swept away or cut off entire communities, with roads, bridges, hydropower facilities, water systems and telecommunications networks badly damaged, leaving affected areas largely inaccessible and hampering the delivery of lifesaving aid, the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) said on Thursday.
At least 17,000 children have been impacted by the devastating flash floods that tore through Nepal’s Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading districts.
“Children across Rasuwa and Dhading saw their lives being literally washed away in front of their eyes in a very short span of time, with homes, classrooms, and medical facilities damaged,” said Alice Akunga, UNICEF Representative to Nepal.
“Too many lost their lives and loved ones. With the death toll still rising, we know this tragedy is far from over. Children who have survived the floods now face heightened risks of disease, malnutrition, violence and exploitation.”
For its part, UNICEF is on the ground and scaling up support, “but we urgently need more resources to reach every child in need”, Ms. Akunga said.
Still missing
“UN agencies are deployed to affected areas with food, medical supplies and relief materials in support of the government-led response and stand ready to do more,” the UN office in Nepal wrote on Facebook.
In China, around 560 people remain missing, according to the authorities, while the UN country office on Wednesday reported damage and significant numbers of casualties and destruction in the Tibet autonomous region of China.
Meanwhile, in support of the authorities and the wider response, WHO has dispatched an interagency emergency health kit, containing medicines and supplies sufficient to provide basic health services for up to 10,000 people. The UN health agency has also provided six multipurpose tents to help sustain health service delivery in affected communities.
“These supplies are intended to support frontline health workers as they continue providing critical care and responding to the immediate health needs of affected populations,” the UN agency explained on Facebook.
New deployments
“WHO remains committed to working closely with health authorities and partners to assess the evolving situation, support emergency health services and help ensure that people continue to access the care they need during this difficult time.”
In addition on Thursday, the UN World Food Programme (WFP) and the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) planned to start deploying staff and trucks carrying relief supplies.
Efforts also continued to rapidly assess the scale of the disaster, in particular from secure satellite imagery and analysis of the area impacted by flooding, provided by the UN platform for the UN Space-based Information for Disaster Management and Emergency Response (UN-SPIDER). Managed by the UN Office for Outer Space Affairs (UNOOSA), the initiative connects disaster management experts with space agencies to help disaster risk reduction, early warning and emergency response activities.
Collapsed glacier
A collapsed glacier high up in the steep-sided valleys of the Himalayas has been cited as a possible cause of the sudden flash-flooding and mudslides that have destroyed entire communities and washed away bridges and roads.
Rasuwa district some 80 kilometres north of Kathmandu in northern Nepal was hit particularly hard, including the towns of Timure, Rasuwagadhi and Syabrubesi, a popular trekking destination among tourists, climbers and pilgrims wanting to access the Langtang valley.
The area was also hit by a 7.8 magnitude earthquake in April 2015, which killed more than 8,800 people. Last October, torrential rains caused fast-moving floods and landslides across eastern and central Nepal, affecting more than 30,000 people.
Growing risk of disasters
UNDRR, the lead UN agency for the coordination of disaster risk reduction, projects that the world will experience 560 medium to large-scale disasters annually by the year 2030.
“Global disasters are projected to increase by 40 per cent between 2015 and 2030, driven by climate change and systemic underestimations of risk,” the agency said.
In addition to the human cost of such disasters, the annual cost is $2.29 trillion and rising, when indirect and ecosystem impacts are factored in, UNDRR said. This figure is nearly 10 times the annual direct losses reported in official figures.

Lebanon: UN warns of growing civilian risks as military activity continues
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27

Lebanon: Civilian risks grow as military activity continues, UN says
Damaged roads, disrupted services and ongoing military activity continue to put civilians at risk in south Lebanon as strikes between Israeli forces and Hezbollah continue, according to the UN’s peacekeeping mission in the country (UNIFIL).
Following reports of Hezbollah drone attacks and retaliatory Israeli strikes on Wednesday and Thursday, UNIFIL is urging restraint and renewed political engagement to avoid a further escalation of hostilities.
UNIFIL spokesperson Kandice Ardiel told UN News that while the latest strikes occurred outside UNIFIL’s area of operations, the impact of the conflict continues to be felt across southern Lebanon and along the “Blue Line”.
Find out more about the Blue Line in our explainer here.
UNIFIL is urging all parties to comply with Security Council resolution 1701 – the 2006 agreement intended to cease hostilities between Israel and Hezbollah – and use existing mechanisms to de-escalate tensions.
“It’s in no one’s interest to continue on a military path,” Ms. Ardiel said. “The only solution to this is political and diplomatic.”
Although violence has decreased compared to previous months, UNIFIL has observed a rise in military activity inside its area of operations, including logistical movements, demolitions and projectile launches.
The mission continues to monitor developments closely and report violations, warning that renewed military activity risks undermining the fragile stability achieved in recent months.
Scale of damage harms civilians
UNIFIL remains concerned about the scale of destruction across parts of south Lebanon. According to the mission, several villages and neighbourhoods have suffered severe damage, affecting homes, roads and civilian infrastructure.
The destruction has also restricted the movement of residents, many of whom face difficulties travelling between villages and accessing essential services. Humanitarian organizations and peacekeepers have faced similar logistical challenges while carrying out their work.
To help reduce risks on the ground, UNIFIL continues to coordinate with both the Lebanese Armed Forces and the Israeli Defense Forces, facilitating movement and helping prevent incidents through deconfliction mechanisms.
Peacekeepers regularly accompany certain movements to support safety and ensure humanitarian access where possible.
While peacekeepers continue to carry out their mandate, they have faced occasional delays at Israeli military checkpoints along the coastal road linking UNIFIL headquarters in Naqoura with Beirut.
“Peacekeepers have freedom of movement, and any interruption of that is a concern for us,” Ms. Ardiel said.
Political solution remains essential
With UNIFIL’s mandate set to expire at the end of this year, the UN remains concerned about the potential impact of a security vacuum left behind by its departure.
In a letter published in June, UN Secretary-General António Guterres outlined options for implementing resolution 1701 without UNIFIL’s presence, all of which involve a continued UN presence – albeit a smaller one – on the ground to monitor the Blue Line, plus a strengthened UN political office (UNSCOL) to promote peace and coordinate UN efforts.
UNIFIL continues to stress that a lasting solution cannot be achieved through military means alone. The mission is urging both parties to return to dialogue and implement measures that can restore security and stability for communities on both sides of the Blue Line.
Aid efforts hampered
On the humanitarian front, UNIFIL, in coordination with OCHA, facilitated humanitarian missions to reach those in need.
Since the Hezbollah-Israel conflict erupted in March, 900,000 people have received at least one round of emergency cash assistance, according to UN Spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric.
At the same time, humanitarian needs remain immense, yet available funding is insufficient to meet those needs, he said, noting that the six-month flash appeal requiring nearly $640 million to support people impacted by the escalation of the fighting is due to end in just four days and remains only half funded.
“We call for full respect for international humanitarian law, the protection of civilians, the protection of civilian infrastructure, the protection of humanitarian and aid workers as well as our peacekeepers while stressing that sustained humanitarian support is essential to meet the needs of communities affected by the ongoing hostilities,” he said.

How Widow’s Bay Supports a Mystic Epistemology
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Nathan Eckstrand is an editor at the Blog of the APA. The views expressed here are solely those of the author and do not necessarily represent the views of the American Philosophical Association or the Blog of the APA.
Mystical experiences, or non-sensory awarenesses of situations that can’t be accessed normally, are incredibly diverse. They consist of encounters with God, eerie coincidences, feelings of connection with others, awarenesses of spirits, and insights into the world’s nature. Research on near-death experiences shows that mystical experiences can have a profound impact on someone’s life. People come away with a greater sense of purpose or connection to their world. But what is the epistemological status of such experiences? While clearly not scientific facts, are they subjective opinions? Is it reasonable for someone to believe them or the accounts of others? As the main character of Apple TV’s show Widow’s Bay, Tom Loftis deals with this question when confronted with the island’s mystic past, transforming from a skeptic to a believer. His transformation illustrates why it is reasonable, though not necessary, to believe that mystical experiences are true.
Widow’s Bay, named after the island town in which the show takes place, has no lack of mystical experiences. There’s a bell that rings nine times despite being chained up, a book that puts people into trances, and a demon that communicates with the town’s founder. While some supernatural phenomena are presented as empirical, others take place in characters’ minds. The latter qualify as mystical experiences. At the show’s beginning, Mayor Tom Loftis is skeptical about the townspeople’s claim that the town is cursed. He’s more interested in providing a positive experience for a visiting New York Times reporter. Loftis wants Widow’s Bay recognized as “the next Martha’s Vineyard and definitely not cursed,” which will bring more tourists. Of course, it doesn’t help that the local museum—which Loftis obligingly brings the reporter to—is decked out with exhibits about the island’s mysterious history, including references to a possible deal the town’s founder, Richard Warren, might have made with a demon. Yet Loftis dismisses these as local superstitions that he, as a mainlander, knows are absurd. In episode two, Loftis even stays a night in the local hotel to show townsfolk that it is not haunted.
Loftis’s rejection of local mysticism is a clear appeal to scientific realism. The locals only refer to legends to prove their claims of curses and demons, and Loftis finds this unreliable. He wants something he can confirm empirically; anything else is a rumor at best. Yet, even as he rejects the islanders’ superstitions, Loftis appeals to a constructivist view of mysticism to explain them. For him, the superstitious beliefs are part of the island’s culture. Similarly, Steven T. Katz claims that the content of mystical experiences is partly the result of one’s culture. Unlike those who believe all mystical experiences have a common core, Katz says that language, society, and psychology necessarily influence every mystical experience. As Katz’s goal is to explain the origins of such content, he—unlike Loftis—doesn’t question whether it is true. Nevertheless, Loftis draws on Katz’s insight. Loftis believes is the islanders’ similar culture that produces similar mystical experiences, rather than the similar experiences signaling that the superstitions are true. Loftis believes he has a more rational view, given his upbringing on the mainland.
Loftis changes his perspective on mysticism midway through the series when he accidentally takes psychedelic mushrooms, leading him on a drug trip in which—among other things—he recalls his wife going blind when she tried to leave the island. While the hallucinations are mostly comedic, it is true that psychedelics can create or enhance mystical experiences, and neurological studies confirm this relationship. Notably, Loftis’s hallucinations include a revelation confirming Warren’s pact with a demon and indicating that the only way to end the island’s curse is to end Warren’s family line.
Despite no scientific evidence to confirm his revelation, Loftis accepts it as true, indicating a shift in how he views mystical experiences. He begins to accept them, in part because he has had a mystical experience and in part because his experience matches the experiences of others. Loftis embraces what philosophers who study mystical experiences call the Doxastic Practice Approach. Doxastic means “of or relating to beliefs,” and advocates of this theory argue that the truth of one’s beliefs can be established, at least in part, by referring to one’s society. Specifically, supporters claim everyone evaluates and forms beliefs using socially established methods, and no method can justify itself without referring to itself (i.e., it is “epistemically circular”). Epistemologies should not be judged on whether they produce “Truth”—an impossible task—but on whether they are consistent. As long as one does not ignore cognitive or perceptual experiences indicating one’s epistemology is unreliable, one can use socially accepted practices to decide if something is true. For example, Christians can accept the truth of their mystical experiences by referencing Christian scriptures and doctrines. Since every epistemology is circular, there is no reason to privilege epistemologies like scientific realism over those that accept the existence of mystical experiences (assuming those other epistemologies are consistent).
In addition to providing a reason to accept that one’s mystical experiences are true, the Doxastic Practice Approach argues that we can sometimes accept the truth of others’ mystical experiences. This is because: (1) the experience itself argues for its existence, (2) if there is agreement between people in different times and places (e.g., people provide similar accounts of experiences with God), that implies the experience is not simply subjective, and (3) if the experiences have a positive effect upon a person’s life, that testifies to its truth. This last criterion, while perhaps unusual, comes from the pragmatism developed by William James. James says that mystical beliefs have greater truth value the more useful they are. As we can’t assess them scientifically, we should prefer mystical beliefs that lead to the best outcomes. While not arguing that mystical experiences are objectively true, James argues that these criteria provide reasons to accept the truth of both one’s own mystical experiences and those of others.
After his hallucinations, Loftis accepts the mysticism of the islanders. Even though the weird phenomena he’s experienced could be explained by other ideologies, Loftis looks for explanations using the island’s lore, as the Doxastic Practice Approach suggests. Among other examples, he searches the town’s museum to find Warren’s last descendant. Additionally, he accepts the truth of his revelation, not just because he’s had it but because it is confirmed by people throughout the town’s history who’ve had similar experiences. This is illustrated by his new interest in island lore, which describes others who, like Loftis’s wife, went blind after leaving the island. Most importantly, embracing the truth of his revelation leads Loftis to better outcomes. He realizes that to be a good mayor he needs to stop the troubles plaguing the island, and this requires him to accept the mystical experiences of the islanders as true. His improved outlook and actions testify to the truth of the island’s mystical experiences.
Loftis wrestles with the island’s mystical beliefs throughout Widow’s Bay. While initially dismissive, he comes to embrace them as important. By doing so, he effectively adopts the doxastic practices of the Widow’s Bay community, symbolically giving up his mainlander identity. Loftis transforms from a scientific realist who rejects the island’s mysticism to someone who embraces it using the Doxastic Practice Approach. As Loftis’s journey demonstrates, mystical experiences don’t need to be accepted as true by everyone, but that doesn’t mean we should reject them. There are legitimate reasons to believe that mystical experiences, whether encountered by us or others, are still true.
The post How Widow’s Bay Supports a Mystic Epistemology first appeared on Blog of the APA.

Aid reaches hundreds of thousands in Gaza amid severe food insecurity
As hunger deepens across Gaza, humanitarian agencies continue to deliver food and other essential supplies to families in need.
In Gaza, about one in five families say that they are eating only one meal a day, and 50 per cent of them reported that they completely ran out of food at least once in the past month, according to latest UN figures.
This is because of cash shortages, but also because most food items have become exponentially more expensive since the escalation of hostilities in October 2023.
So far this month, three-quarters of households in Gaza have faced difficulties in accessing markets, according to the UN’s World Food Programme (WFP).
The UN on the ground
Yesterday, the UN and its partners collected hundreds of pallets of supplies from the Kerem Shalom crossing – a vital commercial and humanitarian entry point located at the junction of Israel, Egypt, and the Gaza Strip.
The pallets include fruits, vegetables and other food, as well as adult diapers, school supplies and fuel.
So far, partners have provided food parcels and wheat flour to more than 600,000 people as part of the August cycle.
A fragile peace
Despite a ceasefire signed by Israel and Hamas in October 2025, ongoing hostilities and security restrictions hamper local movement and recovery efforts.
Frequent Israeli military strikes continue to kill and displace people across Gaza. More than two million people, almost the Strip's entire population, have been driven from their homes, with most now living in makeshift or fragile shelters.
Around 90 per cent of civilian infrastructure – including homes, hospitals, water plants, and schools – is heavily damaged or destroyed.

After Israeli seizure of Kalandia training centre, UNRWA warns of impact on youth
The seizure of a vocational training centre in occupied East Jerusalem has left hundreds of Palestinian young people without access to skills and training that could help shape their futures.
Israeli authorities forcibly entered the Kalandia Vocational Training Centre on Tuesday, 24 August, and took control of the facility, according to the UN agency for Palestine refugees, UNRWA. The centre was the last UNRWA facility still operating in occupied East Jerusalem, after Israeli authorities closed the agency's other schools and clinics in the city.
The United Nations has strongly condemned those actions, saying that the entry of security forces into a UN facility without the Organisation's permission or approval was unacceptable.
Secretary-General António Guterres called for the Israeli Government to immediately cease its interference with UNRWA installations and to vacate, return and restore all affected premises to the United Nations without delay.
Earlier this month, there was misinformation circulating about the centre, which prompted UNRWA to issue a statement reaffirming its commitment to education and underlining that the agency remains “essential to ensuring that Palestine refugee children and young people can develop the knowledge, skills and opportunities they need to build their futures”.
Roland Friedrich, Director of UNRWA Affairs in the West Bank, told us that the incident was part of a wider effort by the current Israeli Government to end UNRWA's activities in occupied East Jerusalem, following the adoption of what he described as "anti-UNRWA" legislation almost a year and a half ago.
The Kalandia centre provides vocational training to young people from refugee camps across the West Bank. Mr. Friedrich warned that its closure would deprive 340 male youth of their right to education and opportunities for the future.
This interview has been edited for clarity and length.
Roland Friedrich: The situation at the Kalandia Training Centre remains critical. Israeli security forces are still deployed inside the centre, along with Israeli officials from the Municipality of Jerusalem, as they carry out work and alterations to the installation. This is an unacceptable violation – as the Secretary-General has underlined – of the privileges and immunities of the United Nations. The continuation of this situation will very likely deprive 340 male youth from the West Bank of their right to education.
UN News: Can you tell us exactly what happened? What happened to the UNRWA staff who were at the centre?
Roland Friedrich: On Tuesday morning, a large Israeli force arrived and forcibly entered the compound. We had 24 staff on site as we prepared for the new scholastic year, which is scheduled to start next week. Israeli security personnel searched the site, opened the buildings and temporarily held our staff at the site. They were later released. This is an unacceptable violation of the privileges and immunities of the United Nations.
UN News: Were you informed of any reason for the Israeli authorities' entry into the centre or what they were looking for? Do you have any information on the possibility of returning the centre to UNRWA, as requested by the United Nations?
Roland Friedrich: The Secretary-General has been very clear in his demand to urgently restore the situation to the way it was before. The background of what happened goes back to the Israeli anti-UNRWA legislation that was adopted roughly a year and a half ago. We saw the progressive closure of our six schools in Occupied East Jerusalem for 2025, depriving 800 children of education. In December, amendments were made to the anti-UNRWA laws, including a provision to cut water and electricity from UNRWA installations in East Jerusalem, and secondly, to authorize Israeli security forces to seize, our compound, the main headquarters, and the Kalandia Training Centre.
UN News: You talked about the immunities and privileges of the United Nations and its facilities. Can you explain what that means and why it is important to commit to it all over the world, especially in the occupied Palestinian territory?
Roland Friedrich: Any Member State of the United Nations, per its obligations under the Charter, but also through being a party to the general Convention, is obliged to respect the privileges and immunities of the UN. That means, for instance, the inviolability of UN premises, the respect for immunities relating to staff, to vehicles, as is the case anywhere in the world where we operate. What we saw yesterday and what continues to happen is exactly the opposite [of this]. And I think what is important to keep in mind is that this sets a precedent when it comes to making sure that our staff can work in a safe way, are protected anywhere else in the world in a very dangerous context.
UN News: Because we're talking about international law and international obligations, what is the UN planning to do now? What do you hope the international community will do about it?
Roland Friedrich: What we hope is that Member States take the responsibility to exercise pressure, so that we can resume our work at this training centre. The key thing is that we can go back to that centre, operate it, and serve the people that we are mandated to serve by the General Assembly.
UN News: In the context of the Israeli legislation you talked about regarding UNRWA, what can you still do in the West Bank to serve Palestine refugees?
Roland Friedrich: There are two laws. One law is a ban on UNRWA operations and presences in what Israel considers sovereign territory and that applies to our services in occupied East Jerusalem. The occupation of East Jerusalem is not recognized by the UN, nor is in fact the annexation of East Jerusalem. The second law provides for no-contact policy that bans Israeli authorities from being in touch with UNRWA and that has an impact on our operations in the Gaza Strip and the West Bank. However, we can continue to operate both in the Gaza Strip and the West Bank, providing critical humanitarian aid in Gaza through more than 11,000 staff members who work every day, providing education, health consultations, shelter and drinking water. Similarly, in the West Bank, we have 4,600 staff on the ground. We continue to provide education. Last year we provided 1.1 million health consultations through 50 health facilities, and we provided together with partners social protection, cash assistance, and food support to more than 270,000 beneficiaries. I pay the highest respect to my UNRWA colleagues on the ground, Palestinian teachers, nurses, social workers in the Gaza Strip and in the West Bank who work under extremely difficult conditions every day.
UN News: What is the main message you would like the international community to understand about UNRWA's presence, its work and the risks it faces in the West Bank?
Roland Friedrich: One thing that we clearly need to see is a restoration of respect for the United Nations at large, and for UNRWA as an agency mandated by the General Assembly by all State parties. Secondly, the humanitarian space in the West Bank overall is shrinking, and that is a trend that needs to be reversed. And thirdly, we need to reverse the trend of forcible displacement in the West Bank. These are dangerous trends because together with settlement expansion, they create a reality on the ground that makes the two-State solution ever more unlikely to be implemented. It is important to pull back from the brink that we're seeing in the West Bank now and return to a credible pathway towards the two-state solution, and eventually a situation where UNRWA as an agency does not have to do its work anymore because the conflict has moved towards a solution.

UN chief condemns “indifference” as Ebola cases mount in DR Congo

Unknown Publisher

UN chief condemns “indifference” as Ebola cases mount in DR Congo
The Ebola Bundibugyo outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) requires “urgent” action and funding to rein in its alarming spread, the UN Secretary-General told reporters at UN Headquarters on Thursday.
Key points
- More than 5,600 cases and 2,700 deaths in six affected provinces in DRC since the outbreak began in mid-May
- The World Health Organization (WHO) believes it has slowed its spread, but has not yet managed to reverse the current trend
- Prevention work has already begun in neighbouring Burundi, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
“The challenge is immense,” he said, noting 500 new cases are being reported every week while the humanitarian response remains only 48 per cent funded.
Estimates show current resources will last only weeks, not months, as the epidemic spreads faster than the response to contain it.
“We know how to contain Ebola, how to interrupt transmission and how to save lives,” he underscored, “but we must also overcome another virus: the virus of indifference.”
Watch the UN chief’s press stakeout on UN Web TV:
More funds needed
“Without additional funding, vital operations will run out of money at the very moment they need to ramp up,” he warned, calling for an additional $1.1 billion.
Money, however, is only part of the problem. Ebola is spreading in a region where decades of conflict have displaced entire populations and weakened health infrastructure. In Ituri province alone, one million people have been displaced, and more than 12 million people in the region are in need of humanitarian aid and protection.
Insecurity is also directly hindering the response. More than 40 healthcare workers have lost their lives while treatment centres and ambulances have been attacked. Humanitarian teams must therefore simultaneously confront the virus and the violence while some communities remain difficult to access.
All corners of civil society mobilised
Local artists and social media influencers are joining the fight against Ebola by raising awareness through their respective medium, including renowned Congolese singer and songwriter Lokua Kanza.
A national UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) ambassador, Mr. Kanza called for people to implement preventive measures in a video posted on the agency’s social media account.
The Wedy duo and singer Drigo Eboma have also both published music calling for people to stop the spread, and 15 influencers – each with over 100,000 followers – have used their platforms to raise awareness among young people.
Religious leaders are also on the case, with over 50 of them in Ituri province – the epicentre of the outbreak – being briefed on how to prevent the spread and manage rumours.
Similarly, around 30 former combatants received special training from the UN and local partners on prevention measures and detection of suspect cases before being dispatched to heavily frequented areas north of Ituri province to share this crucial information with the local communities.
Prep work in Burundi
UN humanitarian agencies and partners are continuing to support government-led efforts in Burundi to prepare for the potential spread of Ebola in that neighbouring country.
While Burundi has not reported any confirmed cases, the country remains at higher risk due to its proximity to the affected areas in the DRC and continued cross-border population movements, UN agencies are reporting.
Some of the preparedness efforts are already under way, from strengthened surveillance at points of entry through temperature screening and deployment of thermal scanners to training healthcare providers, including nurses and community health workers, as well as journalists.
Uganda’s outbreak declared over
UN health officials and partners declared on Thursday that the Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak in neighbouring Uganda is over.
This follows 42 consecutive days without a new confirmed case since the country’s last patient was discharged from care on 16 July.
The 42-day benchmark – equivalent to twice the upper limit of the incubation period for Ebola – is the internationally established criterion for determining that an outbreak has ended.
During the outbreak, Uganda reported 20 confirmed cases of the disease, including two deaths. More than 800 contacts were identified and monitored to stop the spread.
What’s the UN doing?
- UN agencies and partners began expanding the response with 35 additional mobile safe and dignified burial teams and 286 community-based teams high-risk areas, with more than 2,500 volunteers and civil protection personnel, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
- WHO has deployed more than 260 experts, delivered over 330 tonnes of essential medical and logistical supplies
- The World Food Programme (WFP) continues to provide assistance and medical evacuations through its UN Humanitarian Air Service (UNHAS)
- The UN migration agency, IOM, launched a regional preparedness plan in June covering 11 countries and has helped to screen more than one million people
- In Burundi, WHO and partners are supporting the national authorities in updating their Ebola response guidelines and strengthening lab procedures for the safe collection and transportation of samples while nearly 30,000 Ebola prevention posters have been distributed in three languages: Kirundi, Swahili and French

Nepal floods leave hundreds dead, thousands missing: As it happened
A catastrophic flash flood on Wednesday morning wreaked massive destruction upon Nepal’s northern mountainous region, bordering China. The torrent of water, rock, and mud wiped out entire villages, washed away roads and destroyed power infrastructure and dams.
Thousands of people are missing, Nepalese Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal has said, among them pilgrims to Mansarovar in Tibet, a sacred site for Hindus. “Town after town has been wiped out within hours,” he said. Nearly 400 of the 579 tourists missing are Indians.
Nepal’s army has pressed in helicopters to rescue people trapped in mud and in buildings that survived the deluge, and deliver emergency supplies. More than 100 people have been rescued so far, including foreigners.
In China, where the border customs post at Gyirong Port was wiped out by the rushing water and rocks, 558 people are missing – 260 of them foreigners. However, rescue efforts are hindered because of the lack of road connectivity and the thick mud covering the area.

Central Bank Makes Leap of Faith for Money Market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
11:59:17 UTC
20:59:17 KST

On July 30, Ukraine’s banking sector was surprised – the NBU announced banks could no longer place all their liquidity in 3-month deposit certificates and must now bargain on the rate.
Over the past three years of full-scale war, Ukraine’s central bank, the National Bank of Ukraine (NBU), has worked to preserve public confidence in the hryvnia and encourage Ukrainians to keep their savings in the national currency. Alongside capital controls and, for a time, a fixed exchange rate, the NBU linked banks’ excess liquidity to three-month deposit certificates after its initial wartime interest rate hike failed to raise deposit rates as effectively as intended.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Set up in spring 2023, the three-month deposit certificates let banks place an amount of liquidity tied to their existing portfolio of household deposits with a term of three months or more, multiplied by a coefficient of 3.0 for any growth in that portfolio since April 2023. The NBU said it worked, however, critics said the NBU overpaid banks and should have redirected that liquidity to loans instead.
Why rock the boat if the central bank stabilized the storm? The NBU warns that once the war ends and reconstruction capital flows in, deals will again jump to foreign currency. Ukraine needs a breathing money market with reliable benchmarks set by the banks themselves. In parallel, the NBU is developing a holding for future capital-market infrastructure.
Zelensky Joins Moldova’s Independence Day as Russia Violates Its Airspace With 5 Drones
Critics call the new updates a loosening of monetary policy exactly when liquidity should be locked down in a country at war. The banks are watching. They’re either neutral or don’t share the excitement.
The central bank is betting the credibility it earned through war on its ability to steer the economy through the invasion’s aftermath. The question is whether the strategy will deliver as intended.
                                                                                                                                                                         
How parked liquidity became the NBU’s weapon
Ukraine’s banking system evolved from corruption and ineffectiveness, into a healthy lender and keeper of deposits. During COVID-19, Ukrainians packed banks with cash, but banks couldn’t find enough businesses to lend to, so liquidity sat in correspondent accounts abroad and in government bonds.
After the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the pattern repeated with higher stakes. Banks sat on billions in liquidity even as inflation climbed, reaching 13.7% in March of that year, 16.4% in April, and finally peaking at 26.6% in December.
In June 2022, the NBU raised its key rate from 10% to 25% to curb panic currency-buying, but market rates didn’t follow.
According to Mykhailo Rebryk, former head of the NBU’s Monetary Policy and Economic Analysis Department and now Senior Macroeconomist at KSE Institute, transmission was weak as banks were awash with excess liquidity and yields on government bonds did not rise. “Transmission from the key rate to market rates is weak if no transactions actually take place at that rate,” Rebryk told Kyiv Post.
                                                                                                                                                                         
The three-month deposit certificates were a tool no other central bank had, but it was worth trying. “Ukraine does not have a financial market where the central bank can impact rates the way the Fed does,” Olesia Verchenko, associate professor at the KSE, told Kyiv Post.
It was framed as a win-win. Both sides protected their money from inflation and Ukrainians did not flee into dollars. But Concorde Capital’s Oleksandr Parashchiy calculated that the tool cost more than it saved, calling it an “anti-stimulus for lending” in a Facebook post, and more critics followed.
First deputy governor Serhiy Nikolaichuk closed the debate in a September 2025 interview with Interfax-Ukraine, calling the design “very effective in calibrating monetary conditions,” adding that changes could follow if the NBU wanted “to develop the money market” where banks could lend each other cash short-term. That moment has arrived.
Why the NBU is changing the rules
When the war ends, reconstruction capital won’t ease the central bank’s task. The NBU fears rebuilding finance will pour in foreign currency unless a functioning hryvnia market exists first. “When large-scale reconstruction projects already need financing, the market must already be working, not merely forming,” NBU governor Andriy Pyshnyi wrote in an op-ed.
Reliable market benchmarks will eventually underpin a “yield curve, interest rate and currency derivatives, long-term loans, and mortgages,” deputy governor Volodymyr Lepushynskyi told Kyiv Post
For now, the NBU wants to stimulate trading between banks on the interbank credit market, “but going forward, we may not limit ourselves to this,” he added.
Now banks will not have all their bids satisfied in full and need to wander around seeking market alternatives for liquidity. “It will not create a deep money market in a day, but it already changes the logic,” Lepushynskyi explained to Kyiv Post.
However, the only problem is that the central bank’s key rate may become a weaker signal while inflation is again sticky, or it may even lower hryvnia deposit rates.
                                                                                                                                                                         
From Aug. 7, the NBU began holding interest-rate tenders for the certificates every two weeks, with a pre-announced volume, instead of meeting every bid. The ceiling stays at the key rate plus 3.5 percentage points, but the market has started to lower it.
The first tender on Aug. 7 caught Rebryk off guard. The average rate fell 0.3 percentage points to 18.71%, even as the NBU had just raised its key rate by 0.5 points. “This could lead to a leveling-out of the July hike... in the worst case, reverse transmission,” he wrote on Facebook.
The second tender, on Aug. 21, pushed the rate down even further, to 18,59%. Bank profitability on these risk-free placements is gradually shrinking, a banking-sector source explained to Kyiv Post on the condition of anonymity.
“A release of liquidity ‒ freed up because it can no longer be parked in NBU certificates of deposit ‒ could be quite significant,” Rebryk told Kyiv Post. “To push it into lending quickly, banks may loosen credit standards ‒ but that risks a build-up of non-performing loans over time.”
But the demand for instruments is still higher than NBU’s pre-announced volumes. The central bank announced a Hr.30 billion ($675 million) limit for the first tender and banks placed bids of Hr.37.1 billion ($834.75 million). As the NBU announced a higher limit of Hr.40 billion ($900 million) on the second tender, banks placed bids for even more – Hr.52.1 billion ($1.17 billion).
Maksym Tsymbal, first deputy chairman of Bank Pivdennyi, also thinks the rate hike was “most likely an additional argument” to offset banks’ weaker incentive to attract deposits.
However, NBU governor Andriy Pyshnyi disagreed when Kyiv Post asked directly: “Of course, we understand that there will be a limited effect on the tightness of monetary policy from the introduction of interest rate tenders to place three-month certificates of deposit – that is truly so. Was this actually the main reason behind considering the need to raise the key policy rate? My answer is no.”
                                                                                                                                                                         
Will it work?
Markets aren’t convinced. Two banking-sector sources, speaking on condition of anonymity, told Kyiv Post they’re “intrigued and watching” while the effectiveness of the previous monetary policy framework needs to be reflected first. The third one said: “We will watch, but this first step in adjusting the monetary policy framework related to 3-month CDs seems, under conditions of excess liquidity in the banking system, to depend largely on the central bank’s decision regarding the volume of certificate issuance, which is why it feels somewhat artificial.”
But the fourth one thinks the new design will indeed make the monetary transmission more effective.
As of Aug. 24, the tender mechanism remains the only change made. “Nor are there any details,” Verchenko said. At the time of publication, the NBU has not announced any new rules.
“The biggest question for now is how narrow the corridor between the key rate and the three-month DCs can become before the NBU moves to the next stage … and what that next stage might be. The NBU might move away from tying this to the pace of term deposit attraction altogether,” Tsymbal says. He added that this part of the plan “was not communicated with full clarity by the regulator.”
The third source agreed that banks will compete at the NBU’s tenders, but the supply of 3-month CDs is currently “determined by a single institution.” “At the moment, the situation is not entirely clear. We can see that the rate on 3-month CDs is declining, but it is unclear at what level it may eventually stabilize,” the source told Kyiv Post.
The central bank says future steps depend on the results of the previous changes. Lepushynskyi told Kyiv Post the NBU will analyze “the impact on deposit rates, the money market, demand for hryvnia assets, and the overall tightness of monetary conditions.”
Verchenko argues the old design needs phasing out regardless, since both lending and borrowing have revived since it was built. “What are alternatives for excess liquidity? Either park it in the NBU, or lend out more – that’s it,” Verchenko added.
Lepushynskyi agreed the old design was only ever transitional: ”It strengthened a particular transmission link, but created almost no incentives for banks to trade hryvnia liquidity among themselves. Now the task is more complex: to develop a more market-oriented monetary transmission.”
                                                                                                                                                                         
NBU’s initiative alone is not enough – the market needs more private buyers of the excessive liquidity, Rebryk wrote in his Facebook post. Banks have borrowed aggressively, bought enough government bonds, wage growth lags B2C lending, and reliable B2B clients from retail and agro are suffering from devastating drone strikes. In this case, banks are not interested in more deposits – another surplus of liquidity. If the NBU does not absorb the surplus, he wrote, it risks the same flood of foreign currency, only worse, with lower deposit rates and an “inactivated interbank market.”
Nevertheless, the central bank has options: selling government bonds from its own portfolio, larger interventions, higher reserve requirements, or changing how much of those requirements banks can cover with benchmark government bonds instead of cash. But each carries a side effect – on the finance ministry’s borrowing costs, on reserves, or on corporate lending, Rebryk wrote.
However, that doesn’t seem to be stopping the central bank.
“We fully understand that under the previous operational design, the situation was comfortable for banks …. Now, with these changes, the NBU has begun to push banks out of their comfort zone, but there is no alternative to this decision if we want to achieve the activation of the money market,” Lepushynskyi explained to Kyiv Post.

France is also not ready for the threat posed by cheap drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
11:59:11 UTC
20:59:11 KST

The French Chief of the Defense Staff, General Fabien Mandon, warned on the 26th of August that the country is not yet ready to confront relatively cheap and mass-produced threats such as drones, writes Politico.
Since Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, financially sustainable defense against relatively cheap, mass-produced weapons, including the Iranian-made Shahed drones, has become one of the main challenges for Western militaries.
Mandon, at an event organized by France’s main business lobby, Medef, warned that there are enemies who have developed a large number of cheap solutions that can drain French defense resources. He said that this is not happening yet, there is no catastrophe, and the country is peaceful, but action must be taken.
NATO’s arsenal consists of sophisticated, high-tech missiles, each worth millions, that the army, navy and air force use to shoot down remotely piloted aircraft worth tens of thousands of dollars.
The main goal now is to reduce the so-called cost per kill — that is, to reduce the price of neutralizing a threat.
Recently, the French Air Force has used expensive missiles to shoot down cheap Iranian drones that it has been targeting in the Persian Gulf.
French arms manufacturers such as MBDA and start-ups including Alta Ares and Harmattan AI are working on cheaper, mass-produced weapons to counter the threat. Mandon said defensive weapons are not yet being produced in the quantities needed to stop intense waves of attacks. He added that he is working to accelerate the use of drones in the French armed forces. The general also noted that defense industry companies must be able to adapt to a rapidly changing world where competitors are adapting very quickly.
