Is it safe to buy airBaltic tickets? Tallinn Airport representative gives his assessment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
11:56:18 UTC
20:56:18 KST

Latvia’s national airline airBaltic needs to make changes in order to survive, but there is no reason to fear that flights will be suspended in the coming months, Eero Pärgmäe, a member of the management board of Tallinn Airport operator Tallinna Lennujaam, said in an interview with Estonian public television on Thursday.
He said there are two possible scenarios for airBaltic’s future.
“The first is that they will manage to complete the restructuring, continue operating with a smaller fleet and make the company profitable. The second scenario is that, at some point, it will be concluded that there is no place in the market for this kind of business model, that the major airlines have taken over the European market and that this smaller model no longer works. In that case, the company will be shut down,” Pärgmäe said.
In his assessment, the measures airBaltic is taking to reduce its fleet are a step in the right direction.
“Reducing the fleet is entirely reasonable. Here in the Baltic States, there is simply no use for a fleet of more than 35 aircraft — there is nowhere to deploy that many planes. So these measures are moving in the right direction. The question is whether they were taken in time,” Pärgmäe said.
airBaltic is the largest carrier at Tallinn Airport, with a market share of 29%.
Asked about the impact of the airline’s restructuring on Tallinn Airport, Pärgmäe said airBaltic aircraft are still operating according to schedule and tickets remain on sale.
However, the advance booking window for airBaltic has shortened — passengers are now booking tickets one or two months in advance, which is the period for which customers are currently willing to purchase tickets. Regarding January, the airline needs to provide additional explanations in order to strengthen market confidence, Pärgmäe said.
“If you ask me whether I would buy airBaltic tickets, then yes, I would — for the end of September. According to today’s flight schedule [from Tallinn], they are selling tickets on 12 routes. I think they will also continue flying during the winter. However, to make it through the winter, they will need both additional financial resources and positive signals to the market,” the Tallinn Airport management board member said.
He suggested that
airBaltic aircraft would likely operate somewhat less frequently from Tallinn during the winter season.
“airBaltic will most likely continue serving the so-called core routes that it has operated until now. If airBaltic reduces the number of flights, it will undoubtedly affect the market for some time. However, demand for air travel is currently strong. We can see that people want to fly, and I am completely confident that we will be able to introduce new routes to the market and attract new carriers,” Pärgmäe said.
He stressed that Tallinn Airport has deliberately sought to maintain as broad a portfolio of airlines as possible.
“For a small country like ours, having 15 scheduled carriers is a very good figure. If we look at our customer profile, 50% of our passengers travel through major hubs — Frankfurt, Helsinki, Copenhagen, Warsaw and Riga. This means that Estonia will by no means be left without air connections; such a problem will not arise,” Pärgmäe said.
The Tallinn Airport management board member predicted that low-cost airlines would see the strongest growth in the coming years.
He also noted that aviation fuel prices are having the greatest impact on airlines this year.
“If we look at last year, aviation fuel was 70–80% cheaper then. Because of the situation surrounding the Strait of Hormuz, aviation fuel remains very expensive. We can already see the consequences in the winter flight schedules — airlines are cutting longer and less heavily used routes that were operated last winter, simply because they are not profitable. Fuel is currently that expensive,” Pärgmäe concluded.
Pärgmäe is one of four members of the Tallinna Lennujaam management board and is responsible for commercial matters.
As previously reported, airBaltic’s Supervisory Board has approved a business plan that, among other measures aimed at improving liquidity, provides for raising 225 million euros in interim financing using the existing collateral pool securing the 2029 senior bonds.
In the longer term, the plan provides for the company’s recapitalisation through up to 225 million euros in new debt and 100 million euros in new equity. Part of the existing 2029 bonds will be converted into equity in the company, while
the remainder will be replaced with new, reduced debt of up to 125 million euros.
The business plan also provides for the airline to operate 36 Airbus A220-300 aircraft by the end of 2026, compared with 54 aircraft currently, with the fleet gradually increasing to approximately 40 aircraft by 2031.
The airBaltic Group’s revenue increased by 4.2% last year compared with 2024, reaching 779.344 million euros. Meanwhile, the Group recorded a loss of 44.337 million euros, 2.7 times lower than in 2024. In 2025, the airline carried a total of 5.2 million passengers, an increase of 1% compared with 2024.
Last summer, German flag carrier Lufthansa became a shareholder in airBaltic. The Latvian state currently owns 88.37% of airBaltic’s shares, Lufthansa holds 10%, Aircraft Leasing 1, a company owned by Danish businessman Lars Thuesen, holds 1.62%, while other shareholders own the remaining 0.01%. The company’s share capital amounts to EUR 41.819 million.
Taking into account the 2025 financial results and current market conditions, airBaltic has suspended its potential initial public offering (IPO) and does not currently consider it a potential source of capital in 2026, according to airBaltic’s annual report.

AI, Scams, the Law, and Governance: A Conversation With David Tan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
11:56:00 UTC
20:56:00 KST

Governments across Southeast Asia are struggling with the arrival of artificial intelligence, both its endless possibilities that can improve everyday life and the threats posed by organized crime and the scam industries that have taken hold in the region.
Singapore-based David Tan, co-director of the Centre for Technology, Robotics, Artificial Intelligence & the Law, says the predominant issues evolve around what he calls the three Ps: permanence, proliferation, and perniciousness.
“We only need to regulate what’s truly important – what’s really pernicious, that proliferates, and has that permanent digital memory,” he said, adding: “Intimate sexual images, child abuse images, whether digital or not, that should be a priority.”
Tan, who also heads Intellectual Property at the EW Barker Centre for Law & Business at the National University of Singapore, spoke with The Diplomat’s Luke Hunt about how to combat the negative impact and AI’s reach into financial markets, public health, and pop culture.
Common law and legislation are key, as are online safety commissions. These commissions have been deployed by a core group of eight countries, Singapore and South Korea among them, where national authorities coordinate across borders through the Global Online Safety Regulators Network.
But Tan said the industrialized scam industry is here to stay, with crime syndicates expected to grow and continue taking advantage of AI and in particular, deep fakes.
“I think that one just has to be more vigilant as to the kind of fakes we get,” he said.

Back to the office: learning Dutch at work is the new perk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
11:55:11 UTC
20:55:11 KST

Partner content
Back to the office: learning Dutch at work is the new perk
With working from home increasingly out of favour with employers, offering in-company Dutch courses can be a great way of getting your international staff back on location.
Earlier this month financial services group ABN Amro said it wanted its staff to come into the office for at least three days a week. The move was necessary, the bank said, to increase creativity, encourage contacts between staff and improve the differentiation between their work and private lives. It would also, the bank said, make it easier to integrate new colleagues into their jobs.
It’s a trend that is becoming increasingly apparent across Dutch industry. After all, work is about more than just sitting at a desk or being part of an online meeting. It is about interacting with colleagues, sharing experiences and learning something new. And this is one reason why in-company language courses are growing in popularity. They help people to develop skills together while strengthening intra-team communications. And they are also proving a popular perk!
“We’ve noticed that an increasing number of companies are offering Dutch courses at their offices,” says Margreet van ‘t Haaff, owner of language school Taalthuis, which recently expanded to Amstelveen, Rotterdam and Eindhoven and now offers lessons in 10 different cities.
From online to in-company
Taalthuis pioneered the development of online lessons during the coronavirus pandemic and found an enthusiastic market for learning Dutch when people were confined to their homes. Now, however, in-company lessons are becoming increasingly popular as employers seek ways of improving contacts between staff – and helping their foreign workforce settle into the Netherlands more quickly.
“Employers see language lessons as a way of encouraging people to reduce the amount of time they work at home as well as to boost team spirit,” says Margreet. “It’s not a question of forcing people to go back to the office, but of making it more attractive to do so. And of course, learning Dutch helps you to feel more at home as well as getting to know your colleagues.”
Dutch as teamwork
Taalthuis’s dedicated teachers come to the company itself to provide the lessons – either 14-week courses tailored to fit their students’ language level, or tailor-made conversation sessions to meet a particular need on a month-by-month basis. Every student is given a test to find out their Dutch level before they start.
The courses themselves cover beginners to C1 and emphasise conversation skills, which, says Margreet, are perfect for boosting chats between colleagues over lunch or during brainstorming sessions.
The lessons include discussion about typical Dutch themes such as Koningsdag, cycling culture and, of course, food. You will learn about the delights of bitterballen at the vrijmibo, and how to explain your disappointment to your colleagues when faced with a broodje kaas for lunch in the bedrijfsrestaurant.
Learn Dutch during office hours
Many classroom-based Dutch courses take place during office hours, and people who have been struggling to learn Dutch often say that they find it difficult to combine work with lessons and family duties. Offering lessons at the office is another way of getting round that hurdle.
One Taalthuis client, for example, offers its workers lunch combined with a Dutch language course. Others offer lessons towards the end of the day, but in company time, such as a session at 4.30pm, allowing staff to still go home at 6.15pm.
Engineering group Haskoning began offering Taalthuis language courses to its employees in Delft about two years ago and continues to do so. “We recognised a growing need among our international colleagues in the Netherlands to feel more integrated into Dutch society and workplace culture,” says Sofia Aguero from the company’s HR department.
Strengthening teamwork
“From a company perspective the Taalthuis courses strengthen team cohesion, support retention, and enhance our inclusive culture. And given all the positive feedback from students and a growing interest from other employees, we’re already planning future sessions and exploring ways to expand access.”
“Learning Dutch makes it more fun to go to the gym or to have a chat with your colleagues at the coffee machine,” says Taalthuis teacher Floortje, who specialises in in-company courses. “You can talk about the weather, your weekend, what you want to drink… it just makes it easier to have personal contact.”
If you are an employer who would like to offer your staff Dutch lessons, feel free to contact Taalthuis. And if you are a worker who would like your company to offer Dutch lessons at the office, ask your HR department to get in touch.

Farmers to recieve €26.4 million to offset rising prices and bad weather
Agricultural producers will recieve an additional €26.4 million next year to help alleviate the rise in prices following the Middle East crisis and losses resulting from adverse weather conditions.
The amendments to Estonia's strategic plan for the European Union's Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), approved by the government on Thursday, will increase next year's direct payments budget by the maximum possible amount, a statement said.
"The additional funds come from the European Union's long-term budget and their use does not require additional funding from the state budget," Minister of Regional Affairs and Agriculture Hendrik Johannes Terras (Eesti 200) was quoted as saying.
The money will reach producers mainly in December next year, helping to improve companies' financial position and cover sharply increased operating costs.
The distribution of the funding was agreed following proposals from the Chamber of Agriculture and Commerce, the Central Union of Farmers and organic farming organisations.
Cow and sheep and goat farmers, as well as cultivators of fruit and vegetables, berries, cereals, pulses, and seed potatoes will all recieve extra support.

Satellite images show destruction from Nepal-Tibet floods
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
11:54:59 UTC
20:54:59 KST

Satellite images show destruction from Nepal-Tibet floods
A glacier collapse high in the Himalayas on Wednesday triggered catastrophic flooding along the Nepal-Tibet border.
At least 359 people have been confirmed dead and more than 1,300 remain missing across Nepal and China’s Tibet region after a Himalayan glacier collapse sent a wall of water, mud and rock through border towns and valleys.
Rescue teams are searching for survivors in terrain that is hard to access at the best of times. At least 19 bridges and about 40km (25 miles) of road have been destroyed, further hampering the search.
Nepal Police spokesperson Abi Narayan Kafle said the death toll is expected to rise further.
Satellite imagery captured by Planet Labs before and after the flood shows how buildings and roads have been washed away.
The imagery also shows large parts of Syapru Besi village submerged in mud.
What happened?
At about 8:40am local time (02:55 GMT) on Wednesday, a large section of glacier broke away high above the Lhende river in Tibet. The falling ice and rock dammed the river and, shortly afterwards, when the blockage gave way, the surge tore through settlements in Nepal’s Rasuwa district, destroying homes, hydropower plants and border infrastructure.
The resulting ice and rock avalanche struck the river about 20km (12 miles) northeast of the Rasuwagadhi border crossing.
Early reports attributed the collapse to a magnitude 4.4 earthquake. But the United States Geological Survey later said the seismic signal was caused by the landslide itself, not an earthquake. The landslide packed enough force to register as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event.
Where did the floods hit?
Some of the worst damage was in Rasuwa district, on Nepal’s northern border with China. The surge travelled down the Lhende Khola (river) into the Bhotekoshi and then the Trishuli river, which rose by as much as 9 metres (30 feet) in 30 minutes, according to Nepali officials.
Timure and Syapru Besi were among the settlements hit in Rasuwa. Further downstream, the flooding reached parts of Nuwakot and Dhading. Bodies have since been recovered much further south, in Gorkha, Tanahun, Chitwan and the two Nawalparasi districts.
In Tibet, mud and debris struck Gyirong Port in Shigatse.
The Trishuli eventually joins the Narayani, which flows into India’s Bihar state, where it is known as the Gandak.

====================================================================================================

A stab in the back: Why an AfD victory in Saxony could pose a national security threat to Germany
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
11:54:20 UTC
20:54:20 KST

For the first time in its history, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party has a real chance of forming a regional government. On Sept. 6, voters in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt will go to the polls, and experts are already describing scenarios in which the AfD would have enough votes to govern alone. In that case, the German political system’s “firewall” — the voluntary commitment of other parties not to cooperate with the radical right — would prove powerless. The AfD’s rise to power even in a state as small and economically weak as Saxony-Anhalt could cause serious problems for Berlin — including in the key areas of defense and security.
The “plan for Germany” is under threat
In Germany, a regional government cannot directly influence the nation’s foreign or defense policy. This is the exclusive prerogative of the federal center, in the form of the Bundestag and the government. That said, the AfD makes no secret of its opposition to weapons deliveries to Ukraine and to broader European rearmament plans. The party describes Berlin’s actions as a “course toward war” and demands “the restoration of partnership with Russia.”
Even if a party representative were to take the premier’s seat in Magdeburg, they would be unable to change Germany’s current geopolitical course. Moreover, the authors of Germany’s Basic Law anticipated the possibility of conflict between the federal center and a state, embedding protective mechanisms in two separate articles.
Article 37 allows the federal government to apply coercive measures in the event that local authorities refuse to follow a national decision. Additionally under Article 85, the federal government may issue direct instructions to the states within the framework of so-called “federal supervision.” But the process isn’t simple.
If an event in Europe were to trigger NATO’s Article 5 mechanism, Germany’s civilian authorities and military would begin implementing the Operational Plan for Germany (OPLAN DEU) — a set of mobilization and logistics measures that include the redeployment of large military contingents and equipment from western and southern Europe to the east, and Berlin’s allies would be counting on the use of German territory as a key hub for defensive operations. Although the exact routes for convoy movements are classified, several factors suggest that Saxony-Anhalt has been assigned an important role in such plans.
First, the geographic location of the state is perfect, as it sits halfway between the western part of the country and Poland. As a result, virtually the only route for a rapid response runs through Saxony-Anhalt. After all, numerous key Bundeswehr bases and logistics centers are located in and around the state.
Second, this region has in recent years undergone large-scale rehabilitation of its rail network, autobahns, and secondary roads. Many of them are now considered to be among the best in Germany. Plans through 2029 call for further modernization of the central rail hubs in Magdeburg and Dessau, as well as capacity expansion on the Magdeburg–Berlin route.
A state government, if it chooses, could significantly slow down military convoy movements at precisely the moment when every hour counts. For example, a hypothetical premier of Saxony-Anhalt who opposes “escalation” and calls for “seeking compromises at the negotiating table” could refuse to issue the permits required for heavy — and especially tracked — military vehicles to pass through the region, as the issuance of such permits falls within the competence of the relevant state authority. In addition, military convoys are required to move exclusively with a police escort whose purpose is to close off civilian traffic, and law enforcement agencies are subordinate to local authority.
A state government could significantly slow down military convoy movements at the very moment when every hour counts
Finally, decisions about the use of regional infrastructure — such as allocating land for tent camps and ensuring supplies of electricity, water, and fuel — are made locally, not at the federal center. Even the exchange of information between central command structures and the operations hub in Magdeburg could be significantly hampered.
There is no doubt that in an emergency, Berlin would immediately invoke its powers under the relevant articles of the Basic Law, and it is also fair to assume that not every senior police officer would agree to openly sabotage defensive measures. But precious hours — or even days — could still be lost, creating grave ramifications for the defensive strategy of both Germany individually and NATO as a whole.
Red tape as a weapon
The reputation of German bureaucracy is renowned far beyond the country’s borders. On one hand, the meticulous observance of the letter of the law and strict adherence to procedure guarantee a functioning rule-of-law state, reducing the actual power of those in positions of authority.
On the other hand, what makes the system stable simultaneously renders it vulnerable to legalistically legitimate, functionally pointless legal challenges. Although the AfD’s core political demands are unachievable without the approval of the Bundestag and the federal government, authorities at the state level possess all of the necessary mechanisms to make life considerably more difficult for the chancellor and their ruling coalition in Berlin.
A state is a significant player on Germany’s political field. The Bundesrat, the chamber of the states, approves nearly 40% of the laws passed by the Bundestag — and that approval is far from automatic. Since the Federal Republic’s founding in 1949, the Bundesrat veto has been used more than 100 times.
Moreover, some initiatives approved by the government and the upper house of parliament — such as recent payments to the public that required co-financing from the states — were never unblocked. And even though Saxony-Anhalt has only four of the Bundesrat’s 69 seats, this by no means implies legal weakness.
Presently, AfD parliamentary groups in the Bundestag and the state parliaments frequently pressure the executive and legislative branches with a barrage of motions, bills, and inquiries. These often lack any legal basis, but the system is obliged to respond to them.
For the AfD, this is an opportunity to demonstrate activity to its voters and convince them of its own effectiveness as the “only genuine opposition.” Moreover, around 7,000 AfD inquiries concerning the state of critical infrastructure and the country’s defense between 2020 and 2025 raise serious concerns among politicians and journalists.
Armed with votes in the Bundesrat and a new lever of influence, the AfD could well push this process to the point of absurdity, creating tangible stress for government administration. A state is what is known as a “constitutional body,” meaning it has the right to file a complaint with the Federal Constitutional Court. Under the unwritten rules of the game, a state government hardly ever resorts to this instrument — only in cases where the state’s rights have been seriously violated and numerous mediation councils with the federal center have yielded no result.
Statistically, state lawsuits account for just 1% of all cases examined by the Constitutional Court, and referrals to the court to review the legality of a given federal law are almost as rare — in the range of two to three per year. However, there are no legal limitations on the number referrals that can be submitted, meaning that a state under AfD rule could well disregard the unwritten rules and flood the Constitutional Court with challenges to any law passed by the Bundestag. The focus would be, first and foremost, on the issues most sensitive to a radical electorate: the entry and residence of foreign nationals, refugee admissions, environmental policy, and funding for renewable energy development, gender equality programs, and measures to strengthen European unity.
A state under AfD rule could flood the Constitutional Court with challenges to any law passed by the Bundestag
Blocking tax legislation would also theoretically be possible, posing a potential threat to the smooth functioning of the country’s fiscal system. Admittedly, federal laws are not subject to suspensive effect — meaning their entry into force would not be suspended on account of a pending complaint. Still, a mass attack on the Constitutional Court would inevitably affect its productivity and, indirectly, the functioning of government bodies.
A state also has the right to file a so-called urgent application, which would indeed effectively block a law until a final decision is reached. As a rule, the Constitutional Court grants such an application only in exceptional cases of serious harm to the state and its residents, but here there is ample room for legal interpretation and hairsplitting.
Finally, while four seats in the Bundesrat represent a mere 3% of the total membership, even these could become a “golden share” under certain conditions. The AfD’s appearance in the Bundesrat as the ruling party in its state would further legitimize the far-right party, and in the event of a serious conflict between states or a deadlock in the body, one side might not be able to resist the temptation to form a temporary alliance with the AfD in order to secure victory in the dispute with the help of Saxony-Anhalt’s votes.
Reshaping the system
The intense focus of foreign — and indeed many German — observers exclusively on federal politics is understandable. The state level may seem dull and unimportant, but in Germany’s federalist model the region plays a significant role in the implementation of policy. The state commands numerous levers of government administration, and here, the AfD would obtain tangible opportunities to change a great deal if it were to come to power.
All school-level education, along with a significant share of higher education, is a state-level responsibility. In Germany, a teacher is not required to follow the textbook to the letter and enjoys considerable freedom in shaping lesson concepts, but a hypothetical AfD-led government in Saxony-Anhalt would be quite capable of reformatting the educational process.
The party’s attention is focused primarily on the subject of “history,” and it makes no secret of its rejection of the form of historical memory and perception of past events that has developed in the Federal Republic. Instead, it would prefer a departure from the sense of guilt — or more precisely, collective responsibility — of the German people for the crimes of Nazism, as well as from the negative assessment of the militarism of the Second Reich, the colonial period, and a number of historical figures from the last 150 years.
Ideally, the AfD wants to foster the development of German patriots who are proud of their country and do not dwell on the dark pages of its history. This approach could be reflected in new curricula, which teachers are not entitled to ignore.
The AfD wants to raise German patriots who are proud of their country and do not dwell on the dark pages of its history
The state Ministry of Education would also be able to exert sufficient administrative and financial pressure on schools and universities to shut down initiatives aimed at combating racism, xenophobia, homophobia, and sexism. The AfD has an extremely negative attitude toward gender equality and diversity, feminism, and the use of gender-neutral language, meaning all of these could become a thing of the past in the area under its authority.
Admittedly, under such a scenario, the human factor would play a considerable role. Would thousands of teachers, officials, and administrators be willing to comply with the new rules of the game? This is where the second important set of state-level powers comes into play: personnel policy. Saxony-Anhalt has approximately 115,000 public-sector employees — 12% of the entire working-age population — and in a region with high unemployment, low wages, and very poor prospects on the open labor market, some administrators may choose to adapt to the new realities rather than risk being dismissed. In the five years before the next elections, the AfD could well appoint “ideologically compatible” personnel to senior and mid-level positions. This also applies to the state Center for Political Education, an important government body promoting democracy, which the new government could restructure beyond recognition.
Finally, the state government controls the police and the Office for the Protection of the Constitution — the body that, back in November of 2023, classified the AfD’s state organization in Saxony-Anhalt as “definitively right-wing extremis.” Should the AfD come to power, it may be tempted to exact revenge on the agency. Meanwhile, the state police have already been mired in scandals on multiple occasions involving the discovery of racist and antisemitic messages in internal chats, while year after year, human rights activists record an increase in cases of police brutality.
Even worse, it is not inconceivable that some local police officers would welcome “a firm hand” in power. In addition, the state Interior Minister has the authority to block individual law enforcement operations, and a hypothetical AfD minister would undoubtedly make use of that privilege.
Not least, the emergence of an AfD-led government even at the state level would deal a crushing blow to the firewall. Germany’s Basic Law explicitly requires the states to cooperate with one another. Without this, German federalism would simply be unworkable. In practice, the regions are genuinely bound by political ties — from the Bundesrat, where the mode of cooperation is different from that in the neighboring chamber of parliament, to the format of joint conferences of relevant state ministers. Currently, such conferences are held in 21 areas — from meetings of state premiers to forums of interior, economics, justice and transport ministers.
The AfD’s rise to power in Saxony-Anhalt could provide the final contribution to the “normalization” of the far-right party on a wider scale.

DW users on life in Russia: 'People are mad as hell'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
11:54:00 UTC
20:54:00 KST

DW users on life in Russia: 'People are mad as hell'
August 27, 2026
Fuel shortages are disrupting daily routines. Discontent over pay is rising as job prospects weaken. Planning for the future has given way to short-term coping as anxiety spreads in Russia.
Even Russia's major pollsters, including state-run VCIOM and FOM, as well as the independent Levada Center, report a clear decline in public sentiment. The Kremlin, however, insists that conditions remain stable. DW invited its social media users to share their stories. All responses have been anonymised for safety reasons.
'If there is gas at all, there are massive queues of 50 to 100 cars'
A DW subscriber in Moscow's Pechatniki district described a recent attempt to refuel late at night, covering around 40 kilometers (24 miles) in search of stations with supply.
"If there is gas anywhere at all, there's a massive queue of 50 to 100 cars," he said. "We decided that waiting until 3 or 4 a.m. only to head straight to work was a terrible idea, so we went home to sleep. We're on half a tank for now, but by the end of the week we'll either have to hunt for fuel or stand still. Lately, we use the car almost exclusively for trips to the dacha to see our elderly parents."
"Now you have to hunt for gas at night. You don't always get lucky. Often there's no gas at all. If there is, it's a two-to-three-hour wait," said another subscriber.
Fuel shortages triggered by Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries have become a leading public grievance. Data from BenZinMap, a fuel tracking portal, show severe sales restrictions across 66 regions as of August 27, with another 16 reporting localized disruptions or sharp price increases.
Alexander Shokhin, head of the Russian Union of Industrialists and Entrepreneurs (RSPP), told news portal RBC that refining capacity has fallen by nearly a third, a view echoed by independent analysts. Government measures — including export bans, increased imports, and relaxed fuel-quality standards — have failed to close the gap.
The data provided by Russia's state statistics service Rosstat show average retail gasoline prices are up 7.4% this year, outpacing overall inflation of 4.19%. But the averages conceal sharp regional variation. Stations owned by major oil companies have kept price increases relatively modest, drawing long queues. Independent stations are charging significantly more, adding pressure on household budgets.
There are few signs of outright panic, though. Drivers appear to be adapting to intermittent supply. "Gas is tight, but St. Petersburg is still holding up for now," said one user. "There were disruptions with gas, but the situation is better now, though it's not available everywhere," said another.
'Getting a new job is becoming harder'
Official statistics point to exceptionally low unemployment in Russia, with Rosstat reporting a record-low rate of 2.2%. But the figure is misleading. Recruitment platforms hh.ru and SuperJob report a sharp rise in CVs alongside a decline in job postings, suggesting growing dissatisfaction among workers but limited alternatives.
Wage growth has also slowed. Companies in struggling sectors such as automaking and coal mining are increasingly shifting staff to reduced hours or mandatory leave. Some DW readers also describe a labor market under strain.
"Getting a new job is becoming harder and harder: There are no new openings, and the ones available are either low-paying or involve gruelling 12-hour shifts," wrote one subscriber.
"Wage delays make it hard to keep up with loan payments," said another. "I've been working for two-thirds of my salary all summer. It covers food and gym, and that's about it," noted a third. "Layoffs have hit many industries," added a fourth. "The race of inflated salaries is over. And life has gotten monstrously more expensive than before 2022."
This grim sentiment has spread even to prestigious white-collar roles. An IT professional from St. Petersburg described the shift: "There are no sudden economic shocks, just a gradual decline that has been dragging on for the last 10 years. Job prospects are tight, and finding a new role will be extremely difficult."
A 54-year-old Moscow entrepreneur recalled running a service firm for Western clothing brands before Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine. After major clients pulled out, he was forced to close the business. He later launched a new venture manufacturing apparel in Central Asia and Bangladesh for sale on Russian online marketplaces. Early on, rising consumer incomes drove rapid growth. But as economic pressure mounted, conditions worsened.
"At first, sales grew faster than we expected. But this business too got caught in the fallout of current policies, isolation, and economic instability," the businessman explained. "Revenues are collapsing catastrophically. And it's not just us. People are cutting back on almost everything."
'People plan nothing, withdraw cash, and buy dollars'
The dominant theme in responses received by DW is the absence of a positive vision of the future. Respondents, judging from their comments, are not preparing for a single shock, but for a prolonged period of stagnation or decline.
"In our region, the changes are not yet significant," wrote a woman from Sakhalin, an island in Russia's Far East. "Prices are rising, of course, but overall, it feels like people live just as they did before. Personally, the changes in daily life I feel most are with internet service. It has gotten slower, and the VPN is on almost constantly to bypass censorship. A huge number of people from my personal bubble left Russia, though that has been happening since 2022. We sent our son to another country, too."
When planning becomes difficult, day-to-day coping dominates. "Fuel shortages, drone attacks... Basic trips to Turkey have become unaffordable," said another subscriber. "People plan nothing, withdraw cash, and buy dollars. There are no hopes for a bright future or a change of power. Everyone lives for today. Drinking has increased significantly — even in Moscow."
Beyond anxiety and apathy, a notable number of responses point to growing social fragmentation, with people withdrawing into narrower circles and avoiding broader discussion.
"People are mad as hell and blame the West for all their troubles. Life has become far poorer, duller, and more dangerous than before the war," noted one subscriber. "People either shut down or cut off any conversation about life and the war immediately. Almost no one is left putting on a brave face or posturing."
"The issue isn't just fuel or the internet — it's the change in people, even quite decent ones," wrote another subscriber, a woman working in healthcare. "There's internal fear, deep irritation — even among those who understand nothing and want to know nothing. But everyone sees the prices. It frightens people. Internal social taboos are vanishing... The intelligentsia suddenly lost its dust, its cultural veneer — especially military-industrial engineers."
Edited by: Robert Mudge

Iran endures 6 months of US strikes as Trump’s war goals hit ‘dangerous impasse’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
11:53:30 UTC
20:53:30 KST

Iran endures 6 months of US strikes as Trump’s war goals hit ‘dangerous impasse’
‘I don’t think the administration is any closer to finding a way out of this,’ an ex-diplomat says, as Tehran bets time is on its side
The Iran war has reached its endgame: a costly stalemate.
Six months after US and Israeli forces attacked Iran, killing its supreme leader and maiming his son and successor, the Iranian government is under economic siege, but it still holds power and believes it has time on its side.
A threat by US President Donald Trump to impose crippling new sanctions on Iran faces a fundamental problem: Tehran is betting he will not take the final step to break the stalemate – aggressively enforcing secondary sanctions on the countries keeping its economy afloat, foremost among them China and India.
Washington’s latest measures, announced on Monday, mark a new phase in the conflict that began on February 28, shifting the battlefield from missiles and air strikes to Iran’s oil revenues, banks and trading partners.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has said the United States will cut off the financial lifelines sustaining Iran’s economy, while a US-led naval blockade restricts Tehran’s oil exports and access to hard currency.
“The [Trump] administration is groping in a sort of desperate fashion to try to find a pathway out of this,” said Aaron David Miller, a former US diplomat and senior fellow at Carnegie Endowment.

1968 seoul residence is reshaped with courtyard, annex and timber frame
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
11:50:40 UTC
20:50:40 KST

Tucked behind a long, narrow alley in Yeonhui-dong, Seoul, Saekdong House by Isak Chung and Jinpyo Hong transforms a residence originally built in 1968 through a combination of renovation and extension. Set deep within a landlocked plot and surrounded by neighboring buildings, the existing single-story house already sat unusually high, with elevated floor and ceiling levels intended to pull in more daylight and preserve views despite its enclosed position.
The architects chose not to correct these peculiarities so much as work with them. The entrance passage becomes a gradual transition from the city into a more secluded domestic world, while another inherited feature — an air-raid shelter beneath the house, typical of older Yeonhui-dong residences built amid tensions with North Korea — is folded into the new spatial sequence rather than treated as an inconvenient leftover.
Saekdong House transforms a 1968 residence in Seoul | images courtesy of Saekdong House
A COURTYARD REPLACES THE OLD LIVING ROOM
At the center of the intervention, the former living room was removed entirely to create an open courtyard, bringing daylight and ventilation into the previously enclosed plan. The building coverage released by this subtraction was then transferred to a new annex in the southern yard, an area that had previously received little light because of surrounding construction. In other words, one room disappears so another can appear elsewhere — a fairly productive bit of domestic accounting.
The existing structure was reinforced with timber framing, while a low-ceilinged internal corridor connects the reorganized spaces. Outside, a jade-green FRP eave protects circulation from rain, and the heavy original roof has been replaced with a lighter, restrained gable. Below ground, the floor of the former shelter was lowered to create usable headroom, with a sunken passage between the courtyard and annex bringing daylight and movement into the lower level.
a central courtyard brings light into the existing house
SAEKDONG TURNS CONTRAST INTO A DESIGN METHOD
The project takes its name from saekdong, a traditional Korean technique in which strips or patches of different colored fabrics are joined together to form a single textile. Chung and Hong translate that principle into architecture, allowing contrasting elements to remain visibly distinct while still belonging to the same composition. Old and new, timber and FRP, enclosed rooms and open courtyards all meet without being forced into visual uniformity.
That patchwork logic extends across scales: furniture and architecture, structure and finish, interior and exterior, main house and annex, as well as natural and constructed elements are treated as separate pieces within one domestic landscape. Rather than smoothing over the house’s oddities, the renovation makes them part of its character, turning a difficult urban plot, an aging structure and even a wartime shelter into ingredients for a home that feels intentionally assembled rather than simply updated.
timber framing reinforces the original structure
old and new elements remain visibly distinct throughout the house

Nepal flood fury: How it started
A sudden surge of water and debris unleashed devastation across Nepal.
From the Himalayas to the swollen Trishuli, the flood left a trail of destruction. Here is how the disaster unfolded, leaving a trail of death and destruction.
Then came the human toll

PM Modi offers India’s support
As the scale of devastation emerged, Prime Minister Narendra Modi reached out to Nepal PM Balendra Shah on August 26 and conveyed his condolences over the loss of lives.

Where Can Russian Athletes Compete After the IOC’s Provisional Ban Lift?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
11:45:00 UTC
20:45:00 KST

Russia’s return to international sports competition was already well underway long before the International Olympic Committee (IOC) provisionally lifted its ban on the Russian and Belarusian Olympic Committees this July.
The shift began in September 2025, when the International Paralympic Committee voted against maintaining its ban on Russian and Belarusian athletes, paving the way for them to compete at the 2026 Milano-Cortina Paralympic Games, where Russian competitors won eight gold medals.
By December, the IOC recommended that international federations lift their bans on Russian and Belarusian youth athletes.
However, some individual governing bodies acted even earlier. The International Judo Federation became the first to restore full participation rights to senior Russian athletes in November of last year. World Taekwondo followed this January by approving the full return of both junior and senior athletes from Russia and Belarus.
Since then, eight additional Olympic sports federations have restored full participation rights to Russian athletes and teams, allowing the use of the Russian flag, national anthem and team uniforms.
Below is a list compiled by The Moscow Times detailing where and how Russian athletes can currently compete on the international stage:
Federations that allow full senior and youth participation
Archery: On August 14, World Archery reinstated Russian athletes, allowing them to compete under their national flag and bringing their status in line with Belarusian athletes, who were reinstated in May.
Aquatics: The World Aquatics Bureau lifted its ban on senior Russian and Belarusian athletes on April 13, 2026, two months after it lifted its ban on Junior athletes.
In its statement, World Aquatics President Husain Al Musallam said, “Over the last three years, World Aquatics and the AQIU have successfully helped ensure that conflict can be kept outside the sporting competition venues. We are determined to ensure that pools and open water remain places where athletes from all nations can come together in peaceful competition.”
Boxing: On July 30, World Boxing announced that it was restoring full participation rights to all Russian athletes.
"The Executive Committee accepted that Russian athletes would now take part in World Boxing competitions like boxers from any other national federation. However, World Boxing will strictly monitor the behaviour of Russian delegations during events as well as compliance with anti-doping protocols," the statement read.
World Boxing previously lifted its restrictions on Belarusian athletes on May 12.
Fencing: The International Fencing Federation (FIE) reinstated Russian and Belarusian athletes on June 2, 2026.
“The decision reflects the FIE’s commitment to the fundamental principles of the Olympic Charter, including non-discrimination, equal treatment and the universality of sport, as well as the objectives and principles set out in the FIE Statutes,” FIE’s statement read.
On July 28, Russian fencer Pavel Graudyn won gold in the Men's individual sabre at the World Fencing Championships in Hong Kong, marking Russia's first gold at a major championship since the International Fencing Federation lifted its restrictions.
Gymnastics: The Executive Committee of World Gymnastics released a statement on May 18, 2026, that it had decided to lift all restrictions on Russian and Belarusian gymnasts.
On July 28, 2026, European Gymnastics voted to bring itself in line with World Gymnastics in allowing Russian and Belarusian athletes to compete with their national symbols.
Handball: On July 15, 2026, the International Handball Federation (IHF) lifted its ban on Russian and Belarusian teams and officials, citing the IOC’s recommendation.
“The IHF reiterates its longstanding commitment to the Ukraine Handball Federation and continues to stand in solidarity with Ukraine. It strongly condemns the ongoing war in Ukraine and its devastating consequences. It is the IHF’s sincere hope that the conflict will soon come to an end, paving the way for a return to peace, the restoration of normal sporting relations and the resumption of peaceful international cooperation,” the IHF statement said.
“At the same time, the IHF remains committed to safeguarding the values of sport, promoting dialogue within the international handball family, and ensuring that its decisions continue to reflect the recommendations of the IOC and the interests of the global handball community”
Judo: The International Judo Federation, calling sport the “last bridge for reconciliation and peace,” was the first to allow Russian and Belarusian senior athletes back, doing so on Nov. 27, 2025.
“Athletes have no responsibility for the decisions of governments or other national institutions, and it is our duty to protect the sport and our athletes,” the federation’s statement said.
“Sport must remain neutral, independent and free from political influence. Judo, rooted in the values of peace, unity and friendship, cannot allow itself to become a platform for geopolitical agendas. The decision to reinstate full national representation reflects the IJF’s confidence in its ethical safeguards, as well as in the strength and integrity of the sport,” it continued.
Modern Pentathlon: The International Union of Modern Pentathlon lifted its ban on Russian athletes on July 13, 2026, citing the IOC’s recommendation.
Taekwondo: The World Taekwondo Council allowed Russian and Belarusian athletes back into the fold on Jan. 31, 2026, at a meeting in the United Arab Emirates.
Triathlon: Mikhail Degtyarev, head of the Russian Olympic Committee and the Russian Minister of Sport, said on Aug. 21 that World Triathlon had granted Russian athletes full participation rights.
World Triathlon lifted its ban on Russian and Belarusian junior athletes in April 2026, while senior athletes continue to compete as neutral athletes.
"This was made possible by the restoration of the Russian Olympic Committee's status. Earlier in April, World Triathlon already admitted Russian junior and para-athletes," Degtyarev said.
Volleyball: The International Volleyball Federation (FIVB) announced on July 8, 2026, that Russian teams and athletes would be restored to the World Ranking with the same World Ranking points they had at the time of the initial ban.
“The FIVB remains deeply concerned about the ongoing war in Ukraine and strongly condemns all forms of violence. We continue to hope for a peaceful resolution as soon as possible and remain committed to supporting the Ukrainian volleyball community through the FIVB Volleyball Empowerment programme,” FIVB added.
Weightlifting: The International Weightlifting Federation decided on June 26, 2026, to reinstate Russian and Belarusian athletes.
“The IWF remains committed to promoting fair competition, safeguarding the integrity of the sport and ensuring that athletes have the opportunity to compete in an environment that respects the principles of neutrality, inclusion and excellence,” the decision read.
Wrestling: United World Wrestling announced on May 15, 2026, that Russian and Belarusian wrestlers would be able to compete without restrictions starting with immediate effect.
Federations that allow full youth participation
Baseball/Softball: On Jan. 19, 2026, the World Baseball Softball Confederation (WBSC) reinstated Russian and Belarusian youth athletes. However, senior athletes remain banned.
Chess: The International Chess Federation (FIDE) lifted its ban on Russian and Belarusian youth chess players on Dec. 14, 2025. Senior athletes may compete under a neutral designation.
Curling: World Curling announced on Jan. 30, 2026, that, following the IOC’s recommendation, Russian and Belarusian junior athletes would be able to compete in international competition. Senior athletes remain unable to compete.
Equestrian: On May 19, 2026, the International Equestrian Federation (FEI) approved a return to competition for junior athletes from Russia and Belarus, but did not change its stance that senior athletes should compete with neutral status.
Sailing: The Russian Sailing Federation published a statement on June 9, 2026, announcing that the World Sailing Federation had approved a return to competition for Russian junior athletes.
Ski Mountaineering: The International Ski Mountaineering Federation (ISMF) reinstated Russian and Belarusian youth athletes.

Across China: Green computing powers diverse industries in China's Inner Mongolia
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
19:43:21 CST
20:43:21 KST

HOHHOT, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- At a community health center in north China, an artificial intelligence (AI) system is used to undertake early screening instead of a doctor's traditional clinical consultations.
By leveraging big data and algorithms, the system analyzes basic blood test results to flag potential health risks, offering diagnostic support and enabling early medical intervention.
The Haidong Road Community Health Center in Hohhot, capital of Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, is one of the pioneering clinics showing how technology is reshaping everyday life, thanks to the region's burgeoning green computing infrastructure.
This AI-driven transformation is taking place across multiple sectors. In classrooms at a school affiliated with Inner Mongolia Normal University, smart blackboards respond to voice commands, while AI systems analyze student performance in real time and create personalized learning plans.
At a smart ecological ranch operated by Yili Group, China's leading dairy producer, in Hohhot, tens of thousands of dairy cows wear smart collars and ear tags that monitor vital signs around the clock, turning traditional herding into a precise, data-driven science.
These smart scenes are powered by a robust computing infrastructure. As a key hub in China's national "East Data, West Computing" project, Inner Mongolia is capitalizing on its abundant renewable energy and favorable climate to build a core base for green computing power.
With rich wind and solar resources, the region generated more than 270 billion kilowatt-hours of renewable power in 2025, ranking among the top nationwide. This clean energy provides a stable power supply for energy-intensive data centers.
As of July 2026, Inner Mongolia's total computing power reached 345,000 PFlops, with intelligent computing accounting for 326,000 PFlops -- a unit representing one quadrillion calculations per second. Notably, over 85 percent of the electricity used by regional data centers comes from green power.
The region has developed a dual-hub strategy centered on Hohhot and Ulanqab. The two centers operate in synergy and complement each other, efficiently handling high-intensity AI computing tasks for both industrial and public sectors.
Inner Mongolia's green computing initiative aligns with China's broader national strategy. The country's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) explicitly calls for the coordinated development of green power and computing infrastructure.
Nationally, the results of this green transition are already clear. By the end of 2025, China had built 42 supercomputing clusters, each with more than 10,000 AI acceleration cards. The country's eight national computing hubs now account for more than 80 percent of total intelligent computing capacity.
"Inner Mongolia's practice is a vivid microcosm of China's broader shift toward greener and more intensive computing," said Li Donghong, vice dean at the Institute for Global Industry, Tsinghua University.
By converting clean energy advantage into computing power, the region has not only bridged the gap between eastern China's computing demand and its energy constraints, but also offered a replicable model for the low-carbon development of global AI industry, Li said. ■

Economic Watch: New growth drivers power China's industrial profit surge
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
19:43:14 CST
20:43:14 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- China's burgeoning new growth drivers are fueling a sustained surge in industrial profits, reflecting the country's accelerating shift toward innovation-driven development.
Profits of China's industrial firms above designated size increased 17.6 percent year on year during the first seven months of 2026, data from the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) showed on Thursday.
These industrial firms with an annual main business revenue of at least 20 million yuan (about 2.95 million U.S. dollars) saw their combined profits reach 4.58 trillion yuan in the January-July period, according to the data.
In the three major sectors, mining industry profits jumped 34.9 percent to 666.05 billion yuan, and manufacturing profits climbed 18.8 percent to nearly 3.44 trillion yuan. However, profits in the power, heat, gas and water production and supply sector fell 5.8 percent to 478.42 billion yuan.
Among major industries, the computer, communications and other electronic equipment manufacturing sector saw profits surge 110 percent. Non-ferrous metal smelting and rolling processing jumped 91.8 percent, chemical raw materials and products manufacturing rose 56.6 percent, and coal mining and washing increased 50.4 percent. The petroleum, coal and other fuel processing sector turned from losses to profits.
Yu Weining, an NBS statistician, attributed the robust gains to the rapid expansion of the "AI Plus" initiative and booming demand for computing power, which boosted product demand, pushed up prices and underpinned rapid profit growth in AI-related electronic industries.
Pang Ming, a researcher with the China Chief Economist Forum, said that the remarkable growth fundamentally reflects the accelerated development of new quality productive forces and the synchronized cyclical resonance of the global AI and consumer electronics industrial chains.
Notably, high-end segments represented by integrated circuits, such as memory chips, have seen dividend-driven explosive growth. With the accelerated application of AI, big data, and cloud computing, the market space for the electronic information industry has expanded significantly, driving concurrent growth in upstream components and related manufacturing sectors, Pang said.
Meanwhile, the recovery of export orders and the improved domestic industrial chain support have also provided solid backing for the profitability of industrial firms.
Pang also noted that some traditional industries remain under pressure, highlighting the mismatch between energy costs and demand structure.
The NBS data also showed that in the first seven months, the combined revenue of these industrial firms reached 80.92 trillion yuan, up 6.5 percent year on year, while operating costs increased 5.9 percent to 68.79 trillion yuan.
Yu attributed the relatively fast profit growth to steady industrial production and the rapid expansion of new growth drivers.
Yu highlighted the electronic sector as the main pillar, with profits surging 110 percent and contributing 9.3 percentage points to the overall industrial profit growth.
High-tech manufacturing also showed strong momentum, with profits up 50.1 percent, contributing 9.6 percentage points to overall industrial profit growth. Raw material manufacturing profits rose 55.2 percent, adding 7.1 percentage points.
Yu noted that the profit margin on revenue stood at 5.66 percent in the first seven months, reaching the highest level for the same period since 2023.
However, Yu cautioned that the international environment remains complex and challenging, while the domestic imbalance of strong supply and weak demand is still prominent. He called for further efforts to expand domestic demand, optimize supply, and advance the upgrading of traditional industries, the growth of emerging sectors and the cultivation of future industries to consolidate the foundation for high-quality industrial development.
Pang said that the industrial economy remains in a transition period characterized by the strengthening of new driving forces and the pressure on old ones. Maintaining profit momentum continues to rely on policy support and market demand recovery.
In July alone, profits of major industrial firms grew 11.2 percent year on year, according to the NBS.
Looking ahead, with the ongoing release of policy dividends and the deep stimulation of endogenous momentum, the performance of industrial enterprises is expected to make solid progress toward high-quality development, Pang added. ■

Chinese art dialogue exhibition opens in New Zealand
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
19:43:06 CST
20:43:06 KST

WELLINGTON, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- An international art dialogue exhibition by China National Academy of Painting kicked off in the New Zealand capital on Thursday in celebration of the 20th anniversary of sister city relations between Wellington and Beijing.
The 39 art pieces on display were organized into four sections, namely Observing the Way with a Clear Mind, Figures in Myriad Forms, Scenery of the Four Seasons and Timeless Bronze and Stone Inscriptions. Together, they showcase contemporary creative practices in Chinese landscape, figure and bird-and-flower painting, alongside calligraphy and seal carving, tracing the evolution of these traditions from classical paradigms to present-day expressions.
A Chinese artist also painted a plum blossom on the spot.
Speaking at the opening ceremony, Wellington Mayor Andrew Little noted that 20 years ago, New Zealand and China were negotiating in the final stages of a free trade agreement. "It reminds us of the importance of diplomacy and relationships being conducted at all levels," he said, adding that relationships between citizens, people, cities, and communities are very important.
Different cultures have their own distinct histories and traditions, yet feelings for nature, life and beauty can resonate with one another through art, said Yan Dongsheng, chairman of the Artistic Committee of China National Academy of Painting.
"'Embracing Diversity' conveys an open and inclusive cultural spirit," he added. "We choose this as the title of this exhibition in the sincere hope that art can bring different cultures together, enable mutual learning, and enhance understanding through exchange and dialogue."
On behalf of Ambassador Wang Xiaolong, Minister Counsellor Zhang Xinyu at the Chinese Embassy in New Zealand stressed that both China and New Zealand are multicultural nations built on equality, mutual respect and cooperation. "Across mountains and seas, we hope this exhibition could serve as a bridge, channeling the spirit of the Global Civilization Initiative: equality, mutual learning, dialogue and inclusiveness," she said.
After the inaugural leg in Wellington, the exhibition will tour other major New Zealand cities until Oct. 7, including Christchurch, Hamilton and Auckland. ■

China urges Philippines to remove unlawfully "grounded" vessel from Ren'ai Jiao
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
19:43:01 CST
20:43:01 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese defense spokesperson on Thursday urged the Philippines to tow away a vessel unlawfully "grounded" at Ren'ai Jiao and cease all provocative acts in the South China Sea.
Zhang Xiaogang, a spokesperson for China's Ministry of National Defense, made the remarks at a press conference in response to a media query regarding the Philippine vessel BRP Sierra Madre (LT-57), which recently received a fresh shipment of supplies.
It was reported that the Philippine side has repeatedly attempted to use such resupply missions to smuggle in reinforcement materials in order to permanently anchor the vessel on the reef.
Ren'ai Jiao is part of China's Nansha Qundao, Zhang said, noting that China and the Philippines had reached a provisional arrangement on the humanitarian resupply of living necessities for handling the situation at Ren'ai Jiao.
China would not accept any attempt by the Philippines to deliver construction materials, build fixed facilities or establish a permanent outpost on the reef, Zhang said, adding that China would take measures to prevent such actions in accordance with the law.
He said China remained committed to safeguarding its territorial sovereignty and maritime rights and interests, while upholding peace and stability in the South China Sea. ■

Unknown Publisher

19:42:50 CST

ISLAMABAD, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- Pakistani security forces killed 11 terrorists in separate intelligence-based operations in the country's northwest and southwest, Radio Pakistan reported Thursday, citing security sources.
Two terrorists belonging to the banned Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) were killed during an operation in Bannu district of the northwest Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, the report said, adding that weapons and ammunition were recovered.
In a separate operation in the Ladha area of South Waziristan district in the same province, security forces killed five other terrorists, according to the report.
Meanwhile, four terrorists were killed in an operation in the Sasool area of Khuzdar district in the southwest Balochistan province, where security forces used a quadcopter to target the militants, Radio Pakistan said.

The prime minister said the entire nation stood alongside the security forces in the fight against terrorism and reaffirmed Pakistan's determination to completely eliminate all forms of terrorism from the country. ■

Feature: The ball and the crutches -- Gaza's amputee children reclaim a lost childhood
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
19:42:47 CST
20:42:47 KST

GAZA, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- Eleven-year-old Malak Khader balances on her crutches at the center of a five-a-side football pitch in Gaza City, her eyes fixed on the ball as it weaves between feet and metal poles.
One crutch forward, then the other, she moves cautiously into the game as her teammates pass the ball and coaches call out instructions.
For Khader and the other children here, football is not just a game. It is a way to process loss, regain confidence in bodies altered by war, and piece together a shattered childhood.
Khader lost her right leg during the war. She also lost her entire family after a bombing struck the school where they were sheltering.
"I was trapped under the rubble for hours," she tells Xinhua. "I'm the only survivor from my family."
Pulled from the rubble, the girl underwent multiple surgeries to treat injuries to her abdomen, leg and hand.
Before her injury, she had never played football. But afterward, she found the pitch, a place where, for a few hours, the weight of her new reality lifts.
Every Saturday, she joins other children who have lost limbs or suffered injuries during the conflict, "kicking" the ball across the dusty field.
"Football is the only thing that makes me feel happy and joyful these days," Khader says. "It makes me forget my injury, the tent I live in and the difficult life that has become our daily reality."
On the other side of the pitch, 13-year-old Hanin Ayoub Shaaban Ghanem moves with deliberate precision.
She extends one crutch, nudges the ball with her left foot, and pushes toward the goal in measured strides.
Ghanem lost her right leg during the war, and her sister was killed. Afterward, she withdrew into isolation.
"At first, I would sit alone and feel different from the other children," Ghanem recalls. "I kept thinking about my injury and my sister whom I had lost. I felt that everything had changed suddenly and that I could no longer live as I used to."
Then came football.
"When I started coming to the playground and playing with the other children, I began to feel that I wasn't alone," Ghanem says. "At first, I was afraid I wouldn't be able to keep up with them, but they encouraged and helped me."
"Now I try, I move, and I learn how to play using my crutch and my other leg. I feel that I can do things I never thought I could do," Ghanem says.
"When I play, I feel free, like any other child. I don't think about the injury, the tent or the war. I just want to play, laugh and feel that I can keep going."
Ahmed Badwan, a coach with the Palestine Amputee Football Association, says the group he coaches includes about 15 girls and a similar number of boys. The association currently supports more than 90 amputees across Gaza.
"The goal is not only to teach children how to play football," Badwan explains, "but also to help them overcome the psychological trauma they experienced during the war and after their amputations. We try to help them adapt to their new reality and regain their self-confidence."
According to the Gaza-based social development authorities, over 5,000 amputations have been recorded in the enclave, including 700 among children. About 10,000 children now live with permanent disabilities, while fewer than a quarter of those needing prosthetic limbs have received them.
Badwan dreams of one day taking the children to international matches and championships, so they might see themselves not only as survivors, but also as athletes.
For Khader and Ghanem, such stages may still feel distant. But for now, they keep coming back to the pitch, playing with friends, chasing the ball, and laughing in the dust. ■

Thailand's exports surge 21.6 pct in July
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
19:42:33 CST
20:42:33 KST

BANGKOK, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- Thailand's exports grew for the 25th straight month in July, driven by strong global demand for technology-related and digital infrastructure products and a rebound in agricultural shipments, official data showed on Thursday.
Exports, a key driver of the Southeast Asian country's economic growth, expanded 21.6 pct year-on-year last month to 34.79 billion U.S. dollars, accelerating from a 20.8 percent gain in June, according to the Ministry of Commerce.
Industrial product shipments soared 24.2 percent year-on-year, marking the 28th consecutive month of expansion, fueled by sales of video and audio equipment, as well as telephones, computers, and their related components.
Exports of agricultural goods increased for the first time in three months, rising 0.6 percent year-on-year in July, while agro-industrial products fell by 3.3 percent.
The July data also indicated that imports surged 36.7 percent from a year earlier to 38.40 billion dollars, resulting in a monthly trade deficit of 3.61 billion dollars.
For the first seven months of 2026, exports rose 18.2 percent to 231.53 billion dollars, while imports advanced 37.8 percent to 266.89 billion dollars, yielding a trade deficit of 35.35 billion dollars.
Looking ahead, Thai export growth is expected to remain robust in the remainder of 2026, supported by ongoing demand for artificial intelligence-related products, said Nantapong Chiralerspong, director-general of the ministry's trade policy and strategy office.
However, downward pressures from geopolitical tensions in the Middle East and uncertainties surrounding trade barriers remain risk factors that could hamper growth momentum, Nantapong told a news conference.
Last month, the ministry upwardly revised its export outlook to a rise between 5 percent and 11 percent this year, after a 13.1 percent expansion was recorded in 2025. ■

IN BRIEF: Kremlin briefing covers frozen assets, 'spooks' of Russia’s 'plans' against NATO
Unknown

MOSCOW, August 27. /TASS/. The protection of frozen Russian assets in the West, Europe’s aggressive policy toward Russia, and ongoing contacts over a Ukraine settlement were the main topics of Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov’s briefing.
TASS has compiled the key statements by the Kremlin spokesman.
On new rounds of Ukraine talks
Peskov said he had no information about the next round of talks between Russian and Ukrainian delegations: "I currently have no information on specific plans or dates for the next round of talks."
Russia continues contacts with the United States on Ukraine "at the working level."
Moscow remains open to further peace talks: "Of course, we remain open to pursuing peace talks."
Russia "would prefer to achieve its goals through peaceful means," but continues the special military operation because no such option exists to protect its interests in the Ukraine conflict.
On the West’s illegal use of frozen Russian assets
Moscow considers using its frozen assets to support Ukraine "blatantly illegal": "These actions would violate the law. They would carry legal consequences."
Russia will use all legal means to defend its interests if the EU moves to use frozen Russian assets to support Ukraine.
On the West’s aggressive policy
Moscow is facing an aggressive policy from European countries: "Russia faces a very aggressive policy from European countries. This aggression comes specifically from European countries."
Media reports alleging Russian aggression toward Western countries have nothing to do with reality: "Claims to the contrary distort reality and are nothing more than media rumors."

Trains operated by Ukrzaliznytsia (Ukrainian Railways), the state-run rail operator, are running with significant delays due to Russia's attacks on Ukraine. The worst-affected trains are those departing from frontline areas that have been subjected to Russian attacks for several consecutive days.
Source: information on delays on the Ukrainian Railways website

Background: Russian strikes have damaged 492 locomotives and 249 carriages belonging to Ukrainian Railways since the start of the full-scale invasion. A government action programme envisages repairing 70% of the damaged locomotives.

‘Strong signal’: South Korea raises rates again to fight inflation, rising home prices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
11:35:53 UTC
20:35:53 KST

‘Strong signal’: South Korea raises rates again to fight inflation, rising home prices
Bank of Korea Governor Shin Hyun-song says the pre-emptive moves aim to help ‘reduce the costs to the economy’
The Bank of Korea (BOK) lifted its benchmark rate by 0.25 percentage point to 3.0 per cent on Thursday, a month after an identical increase took it to 2.75 per cent in July.
The latest move brought the rate to its highest level since February 2025 and signalled a central bank willing to accept some damage to domestic demand to contain broader financial risks.
Households with housing-related loans, small businesses and other borrowers are expected to feel the pressure most acutely. But with semiconductor exports and investment driving stronger-than-expected growth, economists said the BOK had decided the greater danger lay in moving too slowly.
The Monetary Policy Board made that priority clear in its statement, saying: “It is important to prevent inflationary pressures from becoming widespread through pre-emptive action, and it is also necessary to continue paying attention to financial stability risks.
“The board will decide the timing and pace of further increases in the Base Rate while assessing trends in inflation and the domestic economy, as well as financial stability.”

Euribor nears 3%-mark as energy, inflation pressures persist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
11:35:00 UTC
20:35:00 KST

Euribor nears 3%-mark as energy, inflation pressures persist
Rises in the Euro Interbank Offered Rate (Euribor) are being driven by expectations of Increasing inflation due to higher energy prices, LHV economist Triinu Tapver told ERR.
The six‑month Euribor has risen to 2.765 percent over the past couple of weeks, compared with 2.637 percent just two weeks ago.
The 12‑month Euribor has hovered around the 3 percent-mark, at times rising above that level.
"For Europe – particularly large economies such as Italy and Germany – the price of natural gas, which has now risen to €69 per megawatt‑hour, is especially important. This means higher energy bills during the autumn‑winter heating season and, as a result, higher costs for production and other goods," Tapver, a macro analyst, said.
Rising inflation and energy prices have also made their effects known on European Central Bank (ECB) policy, Swedbank chief economist Tõnu Mertsina noted.
"While according to our forecast the ECB will raise its interest rate only in September and leave rates unchanged next year, markets see a greater likelihood of further monetary policy tightening. This has also influenced Euribor movements," Mertsina said.
Stronger economic activity, a tight labor market, higher defense and public spending, and green transition investments also point to rising inflation, he added.
Tapver, however, argued ECB decisions have less impact on Euribor than inflation forecasts. The 12‑month Euribor reflects the market's assessment of where interest rates could be a year from now.
"The 12‑month Euribor is generally more stable and always reacts more slowly to events. The current rise in the 12‑month Euribor could therefore be interpreted as a market expectation that interest rates will remain higher next year as well. The current situation in the Strait of Hormuz suggests that the six‑month Euribor will also continue rising toward the three‑percent level," Tapver said.
Mertsina took a different view. "It is quite a strong signal, but not a definite forecast. I would not draw a firm conclusion from the 12‑month Euribor that the six‑month Euribor will soon be above three percent. For that to happen, the market's expectation of further ECB tightening would first have to materialize. According to our forecast, the ECB's deposit facility rate will rise to 2.5 percent in September and remain at that level next year as well," Mertsina said.
The six‑month Euribor is currently 52 basis points above the central bank's rate, while over the past 10 years the average gap has been 15 basis points. Consequently, "soon above 3 percent" is not yet an inevitable outcome, he said.
Investors' expectation of a 0.25 percentage‑point ECB rate hike has largely been priced in. "If the central bank signals alongside the interest rate increase that there will be no further hikes, Euribor could even fall," Mertsina noted. However, if inflation remains a problem, the market will expect further hikes.
"That second risk is precisely what is present in the market right now," Mertsina said. "The rise in Euribor is not driven solely by today's central bank interest rate, but by the market reassessing how high the ECB will have to raise interest rates over the next six to 18 months in order to contain inflationary pressures stemming from energy prices and geopolitics."
Banks' loan portfolios are still growing, and there is no sign that customers are borrowing less. The economy's return to growth and continued income growth are enough to sustain borrowing.
"A six‑month Euribor at the 3‑percent level would probably not bring very significant changes to the ability of people and businesses to meet their payments, because the economy has started growing, including purchasing power and business volumes. The willingness to borrow would probably be affected, but not very broadly," Tapver noted.
High Euribor levels could affect new property developments, with buyers likely to focus on the secondary market, she added. Mertsina said a higher Euribor may not have a major impact on loan demand if the economy and incomes grow.
"If the economy and people's incomes grow, the labor market situation and confidence improve, and demand for new goods and services increases, borrowing can remain resilient. We see new customers coming in because their confidence regarding wages and the labor market has a positive outlook," he added.
The Euribor is the average interest rate that major European banks charge each other to borrow money. It affects ordinary people as many variable-rate home loans and car loans are tied to Euribor. When Euribor goes up, your monthly loan payments increase. When it goes down, your payments fall.
