The expansion of illegal Israeli settlements and outposts in the West Bank, alongside the ongoing horror of life in Gaza, makes the need for a two-state solution between Israel and Palestine more urgent and necessary than ever. International dithering and procrastination must stop to preserve any chance of sustainable peace.
This was our conclusion after visiting the West Bank as part of a wider Middle East trip that included meetings with Palestinian, Israeli, Lebanese, and Jordanian leaders.
It is clear to us that the Government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s policies threaten to make Palestine disappear politically, culturally, economically, and physically.
Traveling through the West Bank, we had a visceral sense of a land and people under deepening occupation. Everyday life is impeded at every turn. Settler violence is an integral part of this strategy, designed to intimidate and terrorize Palestinians off their land. Far from being the work of a small number of “juvenile delinquents” as he claims, it is a state-backed campaign undertaken with the active support of the Israel Defense Forces (IDF).
We saw at first-hand how state-backed settlement expansion operates. First, hillside outposts are established by a handful of settlers. Even though these are illegal under Israel’s own laws, we heard directly how they are systematically and swiftly protected by the IDF despite Israeli authorities from time to time condemning settler violence. Connections to water and electricity supplies typically follow, as do roads reserved for Israelis only.
The result is the physical and administrative carve-up of the West Bank. Palestinian communities are distanced from each other, their land, and the possibility of a future Palestinian state.
Among the blatant evidence of what is happening is the decades-old E1 settlement plan for Palestinian territory east of Jerusalem. On Aug. 18, the Israeli Housing Ministry issued a tender for over 1,200 units, setting off a process which, if completed, would sever East Jerusalem from the rest of the West Bank and thereby disrupt the territorial contiguity of a Palestinian state.
E1 has long been a red line even for Israel's staunchest allies. Previous Israeli governments, including those led by Prime Minister Netanyahu, have stopped short of actually proceeding, in part due to international pressure. Now that commercial tenders are being issued and construction contracts potentially signed, any companies and banks tempted to get involved would be breaching international law and have been warned to that effect by a number of Western countries and the European Commission.
Israel’s friends and allies must demand E1’s cancellation—not just postponement or freezing, but definitively ruling it out as a threat to the two-state solution which is necessary for both Israel and Palestine to have peace and security.
Many Israelis recognize this threat and oppose the growing extremism and intolerance in their politics and society at large. For instance, we met with President Isaac Herzog on our visit, who condemned settler violence. We also acknowledge the deep trauma Israel’s people suffered after the Hamas terror attacks of October 7, which included the detention of hostages contrary to all international law.
We take inspiration from the brave Israeli and Palestinian civil society activists we met. They remain determined to combat impunity for abuses and injustice, and to strive for a future for both peoples based on equality and respect for international law.
Yet this vision is far from the reality we saw on our visit. We saw how ongoing settlement of the West Bank and the sustained violence against and displacement of Palestinians threatens ethnic cleansing and annexation. Combined with the occupation of Gaza, including renewed calls by Israeli ministers for new settlements in the Strip, we are convinced that what is underway is the conquest and erasure of one state by another.
This is the logic of some of the bloodiest wars of previous centuries. It is what Russia is seeking to do in its illegal war of aggression against Ukraine. But it cannot be an acceptable way for a country which calls itself a democracy to behave in the 21st century.
Our visit ended in Brussels, where we met with representatives of the European Commission and EU member states. The EU was founded as a values-based organization to promote peaceful cooperation between nations. Given its significant trade relations with Israel, it could play a decisive role now in exerting pressure on Prime Minister Netanyahu and his government.
Yet what is lacking is the political will to take even basic steps. In line with international law, the EU considers Israeli settlements to be illegal, yet EU members continue to trade with Israel. Suspending preferential trade under the EU-Israel Association Agreement is another overdue step due to Israel’s failure to comply with human rights requirements, as already called for by the European Commission. Nor has the EU collectively sanctioned extremist ministers Smotrich and Ben Gvir.
There is still time to change course before it is too late, but only just.

Daily Update: Russia Loses 1,400 Troops, 4 Tanks, and 53 Artillery Systems in One Day
Russia lost an estimated 1,400 troops, 53 artillery systems and several armored vehicles over the past 24 hours, Ukraine’s General Staff reported on August 27.
According to the latest Ukrainian military figures, Russia’s total personnel losses since the start of its full-scale invasion on February 24, 2022, have reached approximately 1,482,150.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Russian forces also lost four tanks and seven armored combat vehicles over the past day, bringing their estimated cumulative losses to 12,304 tanks and 25,237 armored combat vehicles.
Total Russian artillery losses have reached 48,694 systems after another 53 were recorded over the latest reporting period. Ukraine also reported the destruction of three multiple-launch rocket systems and two air defense systems, bringing those totals to 2,065 and 1,590, respectively.
Russia’s estimated aviation losses remain at 440 aircraft and 354 helicopters.
The General Staff also reported that Russia lost 17 unmanned ground systems over the past day, raising the cumulative figure to 2,404. Another 1,762 operational-tactical UAVs were recorded as lost, bringing Russia’s total in that category to 483,367.
Russia’s other estimated losses stand at 5,052 cruise missiles, 35 ships and boats, two submarines, 140,248 vehicles and fuel tankers, and 4,602 pieces of special equipment.
Over the latest 24-hour period alone, Russian forces lost another 494 vehicles and fuel tankers and 10 pieces of special equipment, according to the General Staff.
Previously, reports emerged that several damaged vessels belonging to Russia’s Black Sea Fleet have been spotted sheltering in bays around temporarily occupied Sevastopol, including a damaged missile boat concealed beneath camouflage netting.

Estonia retail turnover up 4% in July, fuel sales lead
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
10:58:00 UTC
19:58:00 KST

Estonia retail turnover up 4% in July, fuel sales lead
The volume of retail trade turnover rose 4 percent on year to July and to a total of €982 million, Statistics Estonia reported.
Enterprises engaged in the retail sale of automotive fuel exerted the greatest impact on this increase, the agency said.
Commenting on the results, Johanna Linda Pihlak, leading analyst at Statistics Estonia, said the growth in the volume of retail trade turnover in July was also influenced by grocery stores and stores which sell manufactured goods. "However, the biggest boost to the volume of turnover in July was provided by enterprises engaged in the retail sale of automotive fuel, as their turnover volume grew by 7 percent year on year," Pihlak added.
The analyst noted that the turnover of enterprises engaged in the retail sale of automotive fuel covers not only the sale of motor fuels but reflects total sales, including income from food service, for example, and provision of other goods and services.
After two months of decline, turnover volume of stores selling manufactured goods rose 3 percent year‑on‑year in July, matching the 3 percent growth in grocery stores, which Pihlak attributed to slower food price rises. Monthly turnover rose 3 percent from June — 1 percent on a seasonally adjusted basis — while the first seven months of 2026 saw a 4 percent increase compared with the same period last year.
Statistics Estonia compiled the above report on behalf of the Ministry of Finance, using data from the Estonian Tax and Customs Board (MTA).
More detailed information is available from Statistics Estonia's website here, here and here.

World’s Largest Shipping Company Halts Bookings to Russia’s Black Sea Port of Novorossiysk After Drone Strike
MSC Mediterranean Shipping Co., the world’s largest container shipping company, has temporarily stopped accepting new bookings to and from Russia’s Black Sea port of Novorossiysk after one of its vessels was struck by a drone.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The suspension took effect immediately following an attack on the MSC ULSAN III as the vessel was sailing toward Novorossiysk, according to an MSC customer notice reviewed by Bloomberg on August 26. The company did not disclose when the strike occurred.
MSC said it was continuing to monitor security conditions in the area. In the meantime, customers have been advised to contact the company’s Russian agency to explore alternative arrangements for imports and exports until regular weekly services through Novorossiysk can resume.
According to Bloomberg, MSC significantly reduced its business in Russia following Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The international container traffic that has continued generally involves essential and civilian goods, including food, clothing, and medicines.
MSC has not halted operations at all Russian ports, however. The company continues to serve other locations, including St. Petersburg in northwestern Russia, the outlet reported.
The disruption in Novorossiysk comes amid a series of recent attacks on vessels operating near the key Russian Black Sea port.
On August 16, the Greek-operated Suezmax tanker Skiros was struck near Novorossiysk shortly after loading Russian-origin crude at the Caspian Pipeline Consortium terminal, Bloomberg reported. The vessel, which can carry approximately 1 million barrels of oil, was attacked soon after completing loading operations.
The incidents come amid a broader Ukrainian maritime campaign targeting Russian vessels and infrastructure in the Black Sea and Sea of Azov. Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces have reported striking a total of 218 Russian vessels during the month-long campaign.

Trial for 9/11 accused, including Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, set for June 2028
After two decades at Guantánamo Bay, trials for four alleged 9/11 conspirators have been set for 2028.
A US military judge has ordered Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the alleged mastermind of the September 11 attacks, and three co-defendants to stand trial, more than two decades after their arrest.
Air Force Lieutenant Colonel Michael Schrama issued the scheduling order on Wednesday, setting opening proceedings for June 5, 2028.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Guantanamo at 23: What’s next for the ‘lawless’ detention facility?
- list 2 of 3US charges woman for allegedly plotting attack on New York State Capitol
- list 3 of 3US court nixes guilty plea for alleged 9/11 attacks mastermind
The ruling comes after a US appeals court blocked plea deals that would have let Mohammed and two co-defendants avoid the death penalty.
The case has been stalled for years by disputes over evidence obtained while the men were held in CIA prisons and subjected to torture.
Schrama turned down a prosecution bid to open the trial in early 2027, arguing that timeline wouldn’t leave enough room to work through the disputes.
“A realistic trial date must account for the hearing and resolution of pretrial evidentiary and compliance motions,” he wrote.
Mohammed faces trial along with Walid bin Attash, Mustafa al-Hawsawi and Ali Abdul Aziz Ali.
Under the order, a jury of military service members will first be selected, with opening statements to follow 30 days later. The defence is due to begin presenting its case 60 days after prosecutors finish theirs and the trial will close with a sentencing phase.
Mohammed and two of his co-defendants struck a deal in 2024 that would have spared them the possibility of the death penalty in exchange for a guilty plea.
Then-Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin revoked that deal within days and an appeals court backed his move last month.
Mohammed was regarded as one of al-Qaeda chief Osama bin Laden’s key lieutenants until he was captured by US forces in Pakistan in March 2003. He spent three years in secret CIA prisons before arriving in Guantanamo in 2006.

Swiss army to create new drone centre
The Swiss army is turning to robotics and drones to ensure the country’s defence. To this end, the Federal Department of Defence (DDPS) is setting up a new drone battalion and recruit school.
Drones are becoming increasingly important and are being used more and more in hybrid conflicts. The number of drone flights over military and critical infrastructure in Switzerland is on the rise. The DDPS is therefore investing in this area.
Defence Minister Martin Pfister, Chief of the Armed Forces Benedikt Roos and the Director of armasuisse, Urs Loher, announced on Thursday at the Thun (BE) parade ground the creation of a new unmanned systems centre of excellence.
+ Several unidentified drones spotted over a Swiss military base
This centre will enable the development, testing and integration of these new technologies into the armed forces. The work is being carried out in collaboration with the scientific and business communities.
It is intended to bring together the needs of the troops, the technological expertise of armasuisse and the knowledge of universities and industry. The aim is to “develop new solutions together, test them and make them available to the army quickly”.
From 2028, the army will have a drone battalion for reconnaissance and defence. A specialised recruit school will be set up to train military personnel. The relevant regulations and legal framework will also be adapted.

U.S. Says Chinese Hackers Targeted Senate, NASA, Hospitals, and More
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
10:56:37 UTC
19:56:37 KST

Federal officials on Wednesday announced they had disrupted a yearslong Chinese hacking campaign that compromised or targeted several U.S. institutions, including NASA, the Federal Reserve, and even the Senate.
The Justice Department said in a statement it had seized internet domains used by two hacking platforms, called “QScan” and “QTRouter,” that were created and operated by a Chinese state-sponsored group. The platforms were used to target U.S. critical infrastructure and other sensitive networks. FBI Director Kash Patel said tools were used by Chinese government actors “to hide the origin of their attacks.”
An attached affidavit from an FBI agent accused the state-sponsored group, referred to as “QTFY,” of targeting the Department of Energy, Department of Justice, Department of Health and Human Services, and the National Institutes of Health. The group also allegedly targeted networks “operated by hospitals, telecommunications providers, power companies, financial institutions, and defense contractors.”
The DOJ’s announcement did not specify if anybody had been charged or apprehended in relation to the hacking, and the extent of what has been compromised remains unclear. TIME has reached out to the DOJ for comment.
The group’s hacking activity, which dates back to 2018 according to the FBI, adds to an ongoing record of U.S. allegations of Chinese state-backed cyberespionage operations.
A spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington, D.C. pushed back against the accusations in a statement to TIME, insisting that China is a “firm defender” of cybersecurity.
“China firmly opposes the U.S. overstretching the concept of national security and using it as a pretext to impose discriminatory restrictions on Chinese companies and will firmly safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese companies,” the spokesperson said, urging the U.S. to stop using such issues to “smear or discredit” the country.
A yearslong hacking campaign
QTFY members, according to the DOJ affidavit, include former members of the People’s Liberation Army—China’s military forces—who used their PLA relationships “to obtain contracts and subcontracts supporting offensive cyber operations.” The QTFY actors were allegedly employed by the Nanjing Xinjiuwei Network Technology Company, which “conducts malicious cyber activities” for the Chinese government, per the FBI.
The affidavit stated that not all of the attempted intrusions had been successful.
In August 2019, the group failed in attempting to break into NASA's server by exploiting a vulnerability in its virtual private network.
In September 2024, QTFY actors conducted computer intrusions at three unnamed laboratories of the Department of Energy, the NIH, an HHS agency, and another unnamed U.S. security device manufacturer.
Other efforts by the hacking group were detailed in a joint cybersecurity advisory authored by the FBI, the National Security Agency, and the U.S. Cyber Command's Cyber National Mission Force.
According to the advisory, the group conducted a vulnerability scan of the U.S. Senate and an American hospital system in March 2026, and of an unidentified U.S. election system in June 2026. Both attempts to gain access to these networks failed.
Speaking to Fox News, Attorney General Todd Blanche said Wednesday that the operation has been happening for many years and is a “major national security issue” for the U.S., adding that the authorities have not only stopped the operation, but have also shared the information with the private sector to stop further attempts.
Cybersecurity has been a source of tension between the U.S. and China—two geopolitical rivals.
The 2026 Annual Threat Assessment from the Office of the Director of National Intelligence says China “is the most active and persistent cyber threat to U.S. Government, private-sector, and critical infrastructure networks.”
In 2023, the U.S. identified and disrupted operations by Chinese state-sponsored group Volt Typhoon to intrude into U.S. energy, transportation and water networks, to potentially sabotage operations during geopolitical crises. The following year, Chinese government-linked hackers were said to have targeted the phone communications of President Donald Trump and Vice President J.D. Vance, who were then running for office, as part of a larger cyber-espionage campaign.
The Justice Department’s latest announcement comes a month before Trump’s counterpart Xi Jinping is expected to head to the U.S. amid continuing disputes in trade and technology.
As to whether Trump should bring up the alleged hacking from China when Xi visits, Blanche said he would not tell the President what to discuss.
“This is something that we have talked about with our counterparts in China for many, many years. And we know that it’s happening. And they know that we know that it’s happening. And it has to stop,” he added.

Chinese developer NetEase Games presented its largest-ever lineup to Gamescom. Among its five self-developed titles were ANANTA, an urban open-world role-playing game, and Sea of Remnants, an ocean fantasy role-playing game, both making their global debut at the event.
NetEase Games said it hopes to gather more direct feedback from overseas players, media and industry partners via Gamescom, which will help guide future development and content optimization.
"Internationalization is not a single distribution step after a product is finished, but should run throughout the entire process -- from R&D and product design to localization and long-term operations," said Riten Huang, general manager of marketing at NetEase Games.
During Gamescom Opening Night Live, HoYoverse unveiled Nodusfall, a cooperative action game set in a fantasy world inspired by mythologies from different cultures, including Chinese mythology documented in the ancient Classic of Mountains and Seas.
Game publisher 4Divinity showcased four games in the player zone, three of which were made by Chinese studios, including The Defiant, Showa American Story and Genigods: Nezha.
These games cover a wide range of genres, highlighting the diverse capabilities of Chinese game developers, said Tan Chor Yong, chief operating officer of 4Divinity.
"Players now realize that Chinese games can bring highly valuable experiences to global audiences, and the next wave is heading our way," Tan said, adding that this wave of new experiences is expected to grow stronger and arrive faster in the years ahead.
SHIFT TOWARD HOMEGROWN GLOBAL HITS
As Chinese-developed games gain wider attention from players worldwide, their distinctive Chinese cultural elements and perspectives are becoming key factors that set them apart from other games.
Igor Osadchev, a senior Unity developer at Volk Team, told Xinhua that Chinese culture is a major draw. "When I see a Chinese building or something like that, I am already interested in the game by default," he said.
Chris Hewish, president of Xsolla, a global video game commerce company, has also noticed a broader transformation in the industry. Chinese studios are increasingly creating standalone hits and original intellectual property (IP) for global audiences, he said.
Hewish added that many of the successful new games released over the past year have come from China rather than Western developers, marking a significant shift from the industry's historical pattern.
Wanzi, head of the Hypergryph global marketing center, told Xinhua that another significant shift is underway as the global market moves from simply "seeing" Chinese games to genuinely "understanding" them.
She said international audiences are increasingly looking beyond individual titles to their gameplay, storytelling, art design and technical performance, while also showing greater interest in the cultural influences and creative ideas behind them.
Steve Heng, a game industry professional, believes China's mythology and ancient stories offer rich material for games with international appeal. "If you have the courage to create cool games and tell cool stories, that will resonate internationally as well," he said.
More Chinese companies are transitioning from behind-the-scenes contributions to global game production to creating original IP and reaching global audiences directly, Tan said. "Further success along this path will only inspire more talent to follow suit, and this will indeed shape the global gaming market in the years to come."
DEEPER GLOBAL INTEGRATION
Chinese game companies are expanding their presence across the global gaming ecosystem. Beyond bringing more titles to international audiences, they are increasingly working with global teams and incorporating international perspectives into game development, technology and market operations.
Grace Pan, senior project manager at Cologne Exhibition Center, noted that Chinese game companies have accelerated their global expansion after several years of adapting to international markets.
She said Chinese game companies are increasingly involving international teams and incorporating perspectives at earlier stages of development, helping their games better connect with global players from the start and facilitating faster overseas expansion.
"The companies are not just making great games and bringing them to global markets, but they're starting to adopt a very global development approach," Hewish said.
Hewish pointed to Chinese companies setting up local offices in cities such as Toronto and Los Angeles, allowing them to stay closer to players in different markets.
Technology is becoming another area where Chinese developers are contributing to the wider gaming industry.
Hewish said Chinese studios have embraced artificial intelligence not only for game development but also for creating tools that can be shared across the sector. He cited Tencent's open-source AI development tools as an example.
Meanwhile, the boundaries between regional gaming markets are becoming increasingly blurred. Sebastian Szczepanski, a game industry professional, said the Chinese and Western markets, once relatively separate, are now moving closer together, with publishers increasingly operating across both.
Eric de Brocart, director and founder of GamerGen.com, said he hopes to establish direct ties with Chinese developers at Gamescom so that he can introduce more Chinese titles to French audiences through his website and videos.
For him, perceptions are already changing. Chinese games are no longer viewed as "obscure, complicated, or too Asian to be embraced." Instead, he sees a growing number of titles that remain relatively unknown overseas but deserve wider recognition.■

News Analysis: Europe's hydrogen push faces market test
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
18:55:31 CST
19:55:31 KST

WARSAW, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- Europe's hydrogen ambitions are entering a more demanding phase, as attention shifts from technological breakthroughs and policy targets to cost, market demand and supply-chain resilience.
Those issues dominated discussions at the 21st International Symposium on Hydrogen Power Theoretical and Engineering Solutions (HYPOTHESIS 2026), held in Warsaw from Aug. 23 to 27, pointing to a broader challenge: turning hydrogen from a promising decarbonization tool into a viable industry without creating new dependencies.
A COMPLEMENT, NOT A CURE-ALL
Europe sharply reshaped its energy supplies after the escalation of the Ukraine crisis, but its reliance on external sources has not disappeared.
Imported fossil fuels still account for 57 percent of energy consumed in the European Union and cost the bloc around 340 billion euros (about 394 billion U.S. dollars) in 2025, according to the European Commission. The Commission now describes faster clean-energy deployment as a socio-economic, competitiveness and security imperative.
Jakub Kupecki, chairman of HYPOTHESIS 2026 and director of Poland's National Centre for Nuclear Research, told Xinhua that the key to success and energy security lies in diversifying both supply sources and technologies which are used.
"Europe should avoid moving from one dependency into another imbalanced relationships," he said.
Hydrogen's role is also becoming more clearly defined as renewable power expands.
Jack Brouwer, director of the Clean Energy Institute, University of California, Irvine, said rising shares of wind and solar bring new challenges including curtailment, negative electricity prices and transmission constraints. Electrolysis offers a way to turn electricity into chemical energy and connect power systems with fuel and chemical markets, he said.
The case for hydrogen, in other words, is becoming less about using it everywhere and more about filling gaps where direct electrification is difficult, including manufacturing of steel, cement, chemicals.
THE COMMERCIAL GAP
Technical progress, however, has yet to create a mature low-carbon hydrogen market.
Global hydrogen demand surpassed 100 million tonnes in 2025, but low-emissions hydrogen production only reach almost 1 million tonnes, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA).
Investment data show a wide gap between announced ambitions and projects likely to materialize.
The IEA pointed out that investment momentum slowed in 2025. Committed projects and those with strong potential to be in operation by 2030 declined from 10 million tonnes to just above 6 million tonnes, due to delays in investment decisions, the IEA said in its 2026 Global Hydrogen Review.
Kupecki said taking a technology from the laboratory to the market requires "time, patience and funding."
The "hydrogen hype" of earlier years has cooled somewhat, which gives the industry time to re-examine technology pathways, assess costs under new economic realities, and re-define current priorities of companies and the national economies, he added.
RESILIENCE WITHOUT ISOLATION
Beyond cost, demand and investment, Europe faces another question: how to build hydrogen supply chains that are both resilient and competitive.
The EU's Net-Zero Industry Act has already brought supply-chain resilience into clean-technology procurement and renewable-energy auctions. Guidance issued by the European Commission in July said public spending should not reward price alone, but also take account of sustainability and resilience.
"Europe hopes to maintain a degree of technological independence, but this definitely does not mean not cooperating with other regions," Kupecki said, adding that market, value chains and competition are now global.
The issue is particularly relevant for electrolyzer, a core piece of equipment for producing renewable hydrogen.
IEA data show that China has emerged as the dominant market for new electrolyzer deployment. Global installed electrolysis capacity doubled in 2025 to exceed 4 GW, with China behind nearly three-quarters of new installations.
Kupecki noted that Polish and Chinese research institutions have already cooperated in areas such as materials and system designed, and as the technology matures, bilateral cooperation is expected to extend further into manufacturing, trade, and market applications.
"China can definitely be a wonderful off-taker of technologies," he said. ■

Lebanon accuses Israel of 'ecocide' in south

Breadcrumb
Lebanon accuses Israel of 'ecocide' as it systematically burns forest and farmland in south
Lebanese officials and residents report that the Israeli military is systematically sparking blazes that have burnt swathes of forest and farmland in the country's south as part of its policy of "ecocide".
In the village of Shaqra, Haidar Qoteish, 36, says he has watched fires devour fields and orchards in his hometown of Hula, just five kilometres (three miles) away but under Israeli military control.
"They've burnt everything. You can see the fields are all black," the father of four told AFP by telephone.
"Those whose land they didn't burn, they've bulldozed," he said. "It's a great loss, and there's nothing we can do."
Lebanon's governmental National Council for Scientific Research (CNRS) says Israeli military activity has caused 160 square kilometres of land, half of it agricultural, to go up in flames since hostilities between Israel and Hezbollah began in October 2023.
'Scorched earth' policy
Despite an alleged ceasfire since June, Israel continues to bomb the south and has been demolishing border villages.
Lebanon's Prime Minister Nawaf Salam said Israel is pursuing a "scorched-earth policy" in the south.
Hussein Fakih, the head of the civil defence agency for the Nabatieh region, said that since July his teams have observed fires both inside and adjacent to areas where Israeli troops are stationed.
He told AFP the blazes had been sparked by Israeli "bombs and drones" and sometimes incendiary phosphorous shells and cluster munitions.
In Kfarshuba, which abuts Israel's "security zone", mayor Qassem al-Qadri said an Israeli attack this month sparked a fire that spread across a broad area of "mostly forest".
He said residents desperately tried to fight the blaze themselves while waiting for the Israeli army to grant firefighters access to the area, in accordance with a ceasefire monitoring mechanism.
They only got the green light "the following day when the fire had burnt everything", said the civil defence's Fakih.
Kfarshuba residents with property close to Israeli positions are afraid to take fire prevention measures like clearing undergrowth, the mayor said.
"They talk about the 'security zone' but... we don't know where its (exact) boundaries are," Qadri added. "We feel like the whole area is under Israeli control."
'Ecocide'
Environment Minister Tamara Elzein has condemned what she called "ecocide" in the south, stressing Israel's army is "deliberately" burning swathes of Lebanese land.
CNRS director Chadi Abdallah told AFP "fires were limited to the border strip" during the 2023-2024 hostilities, but have broadened since the conflict reignited this year.
He said the Israeli army is "systematically burning land" and is "trying to create a buffer zone devoid of homes, people and the natural environment".
"During the previous war, around 8,500 hectares (85 square kilometres) of land was burnt," Abdallah said, while this year, "the Israelis have burnt around 7,500 hectares", including 350 hectares after the June deal.
CNRS satellite imagery showed formerly green areas that have now disappeared due to fires, as well as Israel's bulldozing and uprooting of vegetation.
Lebanon's state-run National News Agency this month said Israeli forces had uprooted 600 olive trees in one southern village alone.
Lebanese environmental group Green Southerners says it has recorded widespread damage to forest, woods and farmland since 2023.
This month, it warned that "major nature reserves in southern Lebanon have also been subjected to extensive and repeated destruction".
In Shaqra, Qoteish lamented the environmental losses.
"Demolished homes maybe can be rebuilt in a year, but trees don't grow back" so quickly, he said.

clarence perry’s ‘neighborhood unit’: the century-old idea behind today’s 15-minute city
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
10:50:51 UTC
19:50:51 KST

clarence perry and the evolution of the 15-minute city
Nearly a century before the 15-minute city became a shorthand for walkable urbanism, American sociologist and planner Clarence Perry was asking how close the things people need should be to where they live. Formalized in 1929 as The Neighborhood Unit: A Scheme of Arrangement for the Family-Life Community, part of the Regional Plan of New York and Its Environs, Perry’s model organized housing, schools, parks, civic facilities, and local services around a pedestrian catchment.
It was intended to protect residential life from the growing dangers of automobile traffic, creating a stronger sense of neighborhood community. Its legacy, however, is more complicated than the contemporary revival of proximity planning suggests. The same spatial boundaries designed to make neighborhoods safer and more coherent could also reinforce social and racial segregation.
Clarence Perry’s Neighborhood Unit, 1928 via Wikimedia Commons
walking distance turns into a planning formula
Perry developed his ideas against the upheavals of early twentieth-century American cities. Industrialization and rapid urban growth were transforming traditional street networks, while the growing presence of private automobiles made streets increasingly dangerous for pedestrians, particularly children. Perry imagined the neighborhood as a relatively self-contained social and spatial system within the larger metropolis. His thinking was influenced by his observations of Forest Hills Gardens in Queens, New York, a planned community designed by Frederick Law Olmsted Jr. and developed with support from the Russell Sage Foundation. There, Perry saw a model for organizing residential life around shared spaces and local institutions.
Perry proposed a population of approximately 5,000 to 6,000 residents, enough to support an elementary school serving around 1,000 to 1,200 pupils. The school would form the civic center of the neighborhood, surrounded by community facilities, recreational areas, and open space. The physical unit covered approximately 160 acres, or 65 hectares. This established a walking catchment of roughly a quarter to half a mile between the residential perimeter and the central civic facilities. Parks and playgrounds were intended to occupy approximately 10 percent of the unit.
Traffic was pushed toward the edges. Arterial roads would carry regional and commuter movement around the neighborhood, while internal streets were arranged to discourage through-traffic. Curving residential roads and cul-de-sacs were intended to create quieter environments for domestic life and children’s play. Commercial activity was similarly concentrated at the perimeter, where shops could serve local residents while remaining connected to larger traffic routes. Perry was attempting to make the physical city correspond to the everyday routines of family life, particularly the journey to school and the independent movement of children.
A diagram of Clarence Perry’s neighbourhood unit, illustrating the spatiality of the core principles of the concept, from the New York Regional Survey, Vol 7. 1929
From neighborhood unit to suburban superblock
Perry’s proposal belonged to a wider movement toward decentralized, human-scale planning. Ebenezer Howard’s Garden City model had already imagined smaller communities organized around shared infrastructure and green space, while Progressive Era planners were exploring the relationship between physical environments and social life.
In 1929, architects Clarence Stein and Henry Wright translated many of these principles into built form at Radburn, New Jersey. Its superblock arrangement separated pedestrian paths from automobile circulation and placed continuous interior parkland within the residential fabric.
Perry’s model subsequently became institutionalized through professional planning, housing policy, and municipal development. During the postwar suburban expansion, the neighborhood unit became a repeatable template for master-planned residential communities, helping establish the bounded neighborhood as one of the dominant forms of twentieth-century suburban development, but its success also exposed a fundamental problem: the assumption that physical design could produce particular forms of social behavior.
Greenway Terrace, Forest Hills Gardens. Queens, NY | image by Carol Betsch, 2001
The problem with designing community
The neighborhood unit was rooted in a form of physical determinism, the belief that spatial arrangement could help engineer social relationships and recreate the intimacy of smaller communities within the industrial metropolis, an assumption that became increasingly difficult to sustain as cities grew more mobile and socially complex. People’s work, education, friendships, cultural interests, and family relationships rarely remained within a single neighborhood. Metropolitan life depended on movement between multiple districts rather than on complete self-containment. More seriously, the neighborhood unit could provide a spatial framework for exclusion.
Reginald Isaacs’ 1948 critique pointed to a problem with the way the neighborhood unit divided the city. By setting clear boundaries around each neighborhood and placing an elementary school at its center, the model could make it easier to separate residents by race, culture, and income. Roads, green spaces, and school catchment areas were meant to protect the neighborhood, but they could also act as barriers between different communities. The problem, then, was not proximity itself. It was the way proximity was tied to fixed boundaries. Once schools, housing, and services were organized within these defined areas, those boundaries could also help produce more socially and economically uniform neighborhoods.
Jane Jacobs later challenged another central assumption of the model. In The Death and Life of Great American Cities, she argued that urban safety and vitality depended less on insulating residential areas from activity than on maintaining active streets, mixed uses, dense networks, and continuous pedestrian presence. For Jacobs, the city worked through permeability. Shops, homes, sidewalks, workplaces, and public spaces needed to overlap. Her concept of ‘eyes on the street’ offered an alternative to the neighborhood unit’s emphasis on protection through separation.
Airview. Radburn, New Jersey – safety film negatives, Library of Congress
The 15-minute city changes the metric from space to time
Carlos Moreno’s 15-minute city, introduced in 2016, returns to Perry’s basic proposition that essential activities should be close to where people live, but it changes the metric. Perry’s neighborhood unit is fundamentally spatial. Its boundaries are established through acreage, population, road hierarchy, and walking distance. Moreno’s chrono-urbanism instead treats time as a primary measure of urban accessibility.
The 15-minute city seeks to make six essential functions, that include living, working, supplying, caring, learning, and enjoying, accessible within roughly 15 minutes by walking or cycling, imagining a polycentric city in which multiple neighborhoods contain overlapping combinations of uses.
Where Perry concentrated commercial activity at neighborhood edges, contemporary proximity planning favors mixed-use streets and active ground floors. Where Perry’s model sought to protect an internal residential realm, the 15-minute city depends on permeable networks and multiple forms of mobility. The change is therefore not simply from a five- or 10-minute walk to a 15-minute one but a shift from designing a fixed physical container to reorganizing the temporal experience of urban life.
Perry’s neighborhood assigns relatively stable functions to specific spaces: the school is the school, the park is the park, and commerce belongs largely at the perimeter. Contemporary chrono-urbanism increasingly asks how the same infrastructure can support different activities at different times. Schoolyards can also become public recreational spaces outside school hours. Streets can shift between vehicular movement, pedestrian activity, dining, and public events. Civic buildings can accommodate cultural and community uses after their conventional working day. This temporal flexibility increases the effective capacity of existing urban infrastructure without necessarily requiring additional land and also responds to changes in how cities function. Remote work and digital connectivity have weakened the division between residential districts and centralized employment centers. The neighborhood can become a place not only to sleep, but also to work, socialize, learn, shop, and participate in civic life.
the Caoyang New Village in Shanghai is based on the neighborhood unit concept | Fayhoo, CC BY-SA 3.0 , via Wikimedia Commons
Proximity is only progressive if it is shared
The most important lesson from Perry’s model is that proximity alone does not guarantee a better city. A neighborhood can contain a school, park, grocery store, civic center, and local shops within walking distance while remaining socially exclusive. Housing costs, zoning, infrastructure, and uneven public investment determine who can access those amenities and who is pushed beyond them.
The 15-minute city inherits Perry’s belief that everyday life should not depend on long motorized journeys, but it has the opportunity to reject the cellular logic of the neighborhood unit. Its more ambitious goal is not to create perfectly self-contained communities, but to make essential resources broadly available while maintaining strong connections between neighborhoods.
Today, almost a century after Perry formalized the neighborhood unit, the central question is how a city can distribute services, public space, mobility, and time so that proximity becomes a shared urban condition. Perry imagined the metropolis as a collection of carefully bounded communities. The 15-minute city proposes a network of overlapping local worlds. The continuity between the two lies in the belief that urban quality begins close to home. The difference lies in what happens when the boundary disappears.
the superblocks model explained. Urban Mobility Plan of Barcelona 2013-2018

Is Iran war diplomacy ramping up, as Qatar, Oman, Pakistan officials visit?

Is Iran war diplomacy ramping up, as Qatar, Oman, Pakistan officials visit?
There are signs both sides could be ready to de-escalate, at least militarily, analysts say.
Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani is visiting Tehran on Thursday for talks about de-escalating tensions and reviving failed negotiations between Iran and the United States.
His visit comes amid a flurry of high-level delegations travelling to Tehran in recent days, with mediators rallying to persuade the warring sides back to the negotiating table despite continued hardline posturing on both sides.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Qatar’s prime minister to visit Tehran, seeking to revive US-Iran talks
- list 2 of 4Trump tells Al Jazeera ‘not in a hurry’ for Iran to return to talks
- list 3 of 4Iran, Oman agree on temporary Hormuz route: What we know
- list 4 of 4Iran emphasises self-sufficiency in battle against US economic war
Sheikh Mohammed, who is also Qatar’s foreign minister, will meet with “a number of Iranian officials” in Tehran to discuss ending hostilities and to “create the conditions conducive to dialogue”, a spokesperson said.
He will also address the issue of the critical Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf, and “the need for it to return to the status quo before February 28”. The narrow waterway has been mostly closed to shipping since early March, when Iran closed it, and shipping traffic, which carried more than one-fifth of global oil and gas supplies before the war, has collapsed, sending global energy markets into crisis.
Qatar is a key behind-the-scenes negotiator between Washington and Tehran and was pivotal in securing a memorandum of understanding (MoU) in June that briefly paused hostilities, but the deal has since expired.
Here’s what else we know about the renewed push for talks:
Who else is visiting Tehran?
On Monday, Pakistan’s army chief Asim Munir met with several high-ranking officials in Tehran, including Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran’s chief negotiator.
He also met with General Mohsen Rezaei, the recently appointed secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council.
On Tuesday, Oman’s Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi met his Iranian counterpart Abbas Araghchi in Tehran to discuss the Strait of Hormuz, which has become the biggest flashpoint in the conflict. The two countries have been negotiating how to jointly govern the shared passageway for weeks.
Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi on the same day announced the two sides had agreed to a new temporary shipping route in the strait that would see vessels enter through Iranian waters, and give Tehran partial control over exit routes. However, Iran emphasised that the strait will not reopen until the US lifts sanctions and unfreezes Iran’s assets.
What stage is the war at now?
Officially, the US and Iran are still at war and have each declared the other side as defeated, despite both suffering economically and politically from it.
Amid US news reports that the US may be running low on vital interceptor missiles and equipment in the Middle East, the Trump administration has shifted to a strategy of economic pressure on Iran, announcing new sanctions this week and threatening other countries which continue to do business with it with secondary sanctions.
A major obstacle is the closed Strait of Hormuz. Iran wants to continue controlling the waterway, which flows through the territorial waters of Iran and Oman, as it has done in the course of the conflict, but Washington opposes this stance and wants to return to the pre-war arrangement under which all shipping passed freely through the strait.
While Trump declared this week that all seamines had been removed from the strait, experts warn that some may have been missed, meaning this remains an additional risk to ships.
The US, meanwhile, is also continuing its naval blockade on Iranian ports in and around the strait, hampering Iranian oil exports.
Are there signs diplomacy is working?
Possibly. The breakthrough in talks between Iran and Oman over the Strait of Hormuz has been viewed by some experts as a sign that Tehran is open to negotiations.
The US will also begin returning diplomatic staff who were earlier evacuated from their Middle East stations as early as next week, according to the Reuters news agency on Thursday.
US staff and their family members were withdrawn after the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran in late February.
Staff were evacuated from Jordan, Bahrain, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Lebanon and Iraq, after the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran, and as Tehran retaliated on neighbouring countries.
US embassies in Saudi Arabia and Kuwait were temporarily shut down after coming under fire.
Now, posts in Jordan, Israel and Oman will be fully restored, US media reported.
In the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Lebanon, missions will be capped at 85 percent, while posts in Iraq, Kuwait and Bahrain will be limited to 75 percent.
It has not been confirmed whether the US decision to return embassy staff is connected with the ongoing diplomatic push. However, analysts say it demonstrates Washington’s confidence that the war will not escalate militarily, despite the breakdown of face-to-face talks.
What have the US and Iran said about peace talks?
Statements from both sides stand in stark contrast to the new push for peace, however.
US President Donald Trump told Al Jazeera on Wednesday he is in “no hurry” to resume talks with Iran and said he believes economic and military action against Tehran will both be effective.
Washington has notably shifted away from military operations to a strategy of increased economic pressure on Tehran, however. On Monday, a sweeping set of sanctions was unleashed on Iranian firms and Tehran’s trade partners.
More than 60 individuals and organisations were targeted across five sectors that Washington accuses of sustaining Iran’s economy: digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping. Oil and financial sectors have been under sanctions for some time.
The new sanctions affect entities in China, Hong Kong, the UK, Ukraine, Syria, France, Malaysia, Singapore and several other countries.
Iran, meanwhile, has rejected and condemned the new sanctions. In a letter to the United Nations on Wednesday, Iran’s Foreign Minister Araghchi described the US sanctions as an “act of state and economic terrorism”. He urged member states not to implement them.
High-ranking military officials recently appointed in a security cabinet shuffle have also continued to issue defiant statements. When Pakistan’s Munir visited, Supreme National Security Council secretary Rezaei reportedly told him that Iran “distrusts America”.
However, Iranian President Pezeshkian has sounded a slightly different tune.
Last week, he called for Iran to negotiate from a place of strength, not weakness, saying: “It is better that we bring the war to an end now as we are in a position of power and dignity.”
The Iranian president’s authority is, however, limited, as he is subordinate to Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei. Hardliners, especially in the military, have accused his government of conceding to the US by agreeing to the June MoU, although the president has pushed back against that criticism, saying the agreement did not represent capitulation.
What does the renewed diplomatic activity mean?
There’s no confirmation yet that the US is directly involved in the flurry of diplomatic activity seen this past week.
However, some analysts speculate that the US’s increased economic pressure on Iran could be a means to force Tehran to agree to negotiations.
Ali Vaez, of the International Crisis Group think tank, said Washington is looking to initiate a “financial apocalypse” in Iran by using the military blockade alongside sanctions on Iran’s already battered economy.
“The Islamic Republic has faced all of these before, though rarely in tandem and at a time when its challenges are already so acute,” Vaez said in a statement to journalists.
“The question is whether this new chapter in economic brinksmanship is intended to be a zero-sum campaign aimed at collapsing the regime, or leverage towards an agreement.”

Germany's 'extreme summer' sees record 15,800 heat-related deaths
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
10:41:00 UTC
19:41:00 KST

Germany has seen a record 15,800 heat-related deaths this summer as Europe endures a series of punishing heat waves, the country’s national public health institute said Thursday.
The worst affected group were people over 75, and around 9,600 deaths were recorded in one week in late June when Germany baked in temperatures over 40 degrees Celsius (104 degrees Fahrenheit), said the Robert Koch Institute (RKI).
Another 4,000 heat-related deaths were recorded between late July and mid-August, said the institute in its latest update.
Heat and drought have battered much of Europe this summer, fueling a spike in heat-related mortality, wildfires, devastating many crops and dropping water levels in major rivers. France, Britain and Spain have all reported thousands of excess summer deaths.
The institute said it has collected heat mortality data for the past decade and that the previous record was 8,900 deaths in 2018. A separate report by a medical publication had estimated 10,000 heat deaths in 1994.
Extreme heat can kill through heatstroke but mostly proves fatal when combined with existing conditions such as cardiovascular, lung or kidney diseases.
The RKI models heat-related mortality using statistical methods that compare deaths during summer weeks with and without heatwaves.
Climate change and heat adaptation were on the agenda of a two-day Cabinet retreat this week led by conservative Chancellor Friedrich Merz, but no new measures were announced.
Merz said Germany's 16 states are primarily responsible for heat protection and are already set to receive 100 billion euros ($116 billion) over the next 12 years from a special infrastructure and climate protection fund.
"There is no shortage of programs or of funds," Merz said Wednesday, adding that the government would examine potential aid for the agricultural and forestry sectors after drought and forest fires.
The parliamentary chief of Merz's CDU party, Thorsten Frei, meanwhile rejected a proposal by center-left SPD ministers to anchor climate protection in the German constitution as a joint task of national, state and local governments.
This model would carry the risk "that one level of government points the finger at another, and ultimately little gets done," he told Deutschlandfunk radio.
The group Environmental Action Germany charged the government was "irresponsible" because it had "failed to adopt a single effective measure for heat protection following an extreme summer that saw thousands of heat-related deaths."
It urged legal changes and funding to help municipalities and cities unseal paved surfaces that store heat and to plant vastly more trees.
"Future summers will be even hotter," said the group's director Barbara Metz. "Yet instead of finally ensuring our cities remain livable and people stay healthy, the government is merely tinkering with the symptoms."

Harald, who ascended the Norwegian throne in 1991, has had multiple health problems in recent years, forcing him to have a pacemaker fitted and to scale back his official schedule.
But he has always ruled out abdicating, arguing that he took a lifelong oath before the Norwegian parliament.

Six months of the Iran war – as told through Trump’s social media posts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
10:37:28 UTC
19:37:28 KST

Six months of the Iran war – as told through Trump’s social media posts
Visualising how a war was announced, prosecuted, declared won, negotiated and then reopened, all in the president’s own words.
This week marks six months since the United States and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran.
In that time, US President Donald Trump has published at least 319 posts mentioning Iran on Truth Social, his social media platform – roughly one every 14 hours.
Read in sequence, these posts, or “truths” as they are known on the platform, form a record of how a war was announced, prosecuted, declared won, negotiated and then reopened, all in the president’s own words.
Al Jazeera analysed these posts. Here is what we found.
Between February 28 and August 25, Trump posted at least 4,189 times on Truth Social, an average of 24 posts a day, or one every hour. One in every 13 mentioned Iran – 319 posts in total, or one every 14 hours.
While he posted at all hours, the most common time for his Iran posts was the morning in Washington, between 8 and 11am (13:00-16:00 GMT), corresponding to early evening in Tehran.
The word cloud below provides a snapshot of the most commonly used terms. “Iran” dominates at 510 mentions, more than three times the next word. But the two that follow are not Iran’s leaders or its nuclear programme: they are his own name and his own country.
Trump refers to himself as “President Donald J Trump” or “President DJT” 221 times, more often than he mentions the Strait of Hormuz, nuclear weapons and Israel combined.
His sign-off, “Thank you for your attention to this matter”, closes one in every four posts.
Before the war: ‘MAKE A DEAL!’
In the weeks leading up to February 28, Iran was an occasional subject, appearing in 17 posts between January 1 and February 27, roughly one every three days.
The messaging blended hardline threats with transactional diplomacy. Trump applauded Iranian leadership for cancelling more than 800 scheduled hangings and expressed support for anti-regime protesters. He also threatened 25 percent tariffs on nations doing business with Iran, and repeatedly urged Tehran to negotiate, declaring: “MAKE A DEAL!”
Then, on January 28, he announced that “a massive Armada is heading to Iran”.
Over the next month, the messaging escalated the threat of force with several mentions of “Operation Midnight Hammer”, the US military operation of June 2025 that targeted and severely damaged Iranian nuclear enrichment facilities towards the end of the 12-day war with Israel.
February 28: ‘Major combat operations’
On February 28 at 1:35am Eastern Time (06:35 GMT), US Central Command (CENTCOM) announced the commencement of Operation Epic Fury, at the direction of the president of the United States.
Fifty-five minutes later, at 07:30 GMT, US President Donald Trump posted an eight-minute video to Truth Social providing more details about the US’s “major combat operations” in Iran.
Later that evening, Trump posted: “Khamenei, one of the most evil people in History, is dead”, referring to Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who had led the country since 1989.
Over the next two weeks, Trump posted 40 more times, arguing he was right to launch the strikes and ruling out any settlement short of “UNCONDITIONAL SURRENDER!”
The Strait of Hormuz, which would come to dominate the next five months, went unmentioned until March 10.
On March 13, Trump announced that CENTCOM had “totally obliterated every MILITARY target in Iran’s crown jewel, Kharg Island,” adding that he had chosen not to destroy the island’s oil infrastructure “for reasons of decency”.
March 14: ‘We have already destroyed 100% of Iran’s Military capability.’
Two weeks into the war, on March 14, Trump posted: “We have already destroyed 100% of Iran’s Military capability.”
Trump spent much of the rest of March and April cataloguing destruction and issuing deadlines to Iran.
He announced strikes on Kharg island, bridges and power plants, set 48-hour and 10-day ultimatums over the Strait of Hormuz, and repeated that Iran’s navy, air force and leadership were “gone”.
Between the threats, he attacked NATO, France, the United Kingdom, the Democrats – which he repeatedly calls “Dumocrats” – and the “fake news” media.
April 7: ‘A whole civilization will die tonight’
On April 7, Trump warned that “a whole civilization will die tonight”, as he announced a “final” strike on Iran. It never came. Ten hours and 26 minutes later, he said Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Field Marshal Asim Munir had asked him to hold off, and that he had agreed to a two-week ceasefire on condition that Iran reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
April 12: ‘BLOCKADING any and all Ships’
On the morning of April 12, Trump posted an article floating a naval blockade as the “Trump card the president holds if Iran won’t bend”. Hours later he announced one, writing, “the United States Navy, the Finest in the World, will begin the process of BLOCKADING any and all Ships trying to enter, or leave, the Strait of Hormuz.”
The naval blockade, which he later nicknamed “A WALL OF STEEL”, became the one instrument he never traded away.
April 20: ‘Israel never talked me into the war with Iran’
On April 20, Trump posted that “Israel never talked me into the war with Iran”.
For a war the two countries launched together, however, Israel is almost absent from his account of it, appearing just 32 times, fewer than in one in 10 posts. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is named just twice.
The following day, Pakistan asked Trump to extend the ceasefire. He agreed, but kept the blockade. Iran, he repeated, was losing $500m a day as a result of his blockade.
The next three weeks are mostly attrition. At about 4am on April 29, Trump posted that “Iran has just informed us that they are in a ‘State of Collapse'” and wanted the strait to be opened before posting an AI-generated image of himself holding an assault-style rifle.
May 3: ‘Project Freedom will begin Monday morning’
On May 3, Trump announced Project Freedom, a US Navy operation to escort ships from uninvolved countries out of the strait, before pausing it three days later “Based on the request of Pakistan and other Countries”.
Between May and June, the war became a negotiation, conducted in public.
On May 18, Trump said he had cancelled a planned attack at the request of Gulf leaders. Five days later, he posted from the Oval Office after a call with the same leaders as well as officials from Pakistan, Turkiye, Egypt, Jordan and Bahrain, negotiating a Memorandum of Understanding on peace. Israel was not on the call. Trump said he had spoken to Netanyahu separately.
For the next four weeks, the war is fought through the blockade rather than by air, with Trump setting out his terms on May 29 and later going on to describe Iran as a “FAILED NATION” unable to pay its own military.
On June 11, Trump promised to hit Iran “VERY HARD TONIGHT”, then cancelled a few hours later.
June 14: ‘The Deal with the Islamic Republic of Iran is now complete’
On June 14, Trump declared the agreement complete and told the world’s ships to start their engines. The same day, he criticised an Israeli strike on Beirut, saying it “should not have happened”.
The deal started fraying immediately. On June 26, in between two posts about how good his approval ratings were, Trump said Iran had fired at least four drones at ships in the Strait, one striking the deck of a cargo carrier.
Two days after that, US aircraft hit Iranian missile stores and coastal radar “for violating the Cease Fire Agreement, AGAIN!”. Trump ended his post by stating: “There may come a point when we are no longer able to be reasonable, and will be forced to militarily complete the job that we very successfully started. If that happens, the Islamic Republic of Iran will no longer exist! President DJT”.
On July 8, Trump posted an image of a fire at Chabahar in southeastern Iran, reposted from a pro-Israel open-source intelligence account, saying it was “in retribution for yesterday’s bombing of ships by Iran”.
July 10: ‘The Cease Fire is OVER!’
On July 10, Trump wrote that the ceasefire was “OVER”. Three days later, the blockade returned – in his words, “we are reinstating the THE IRANIAN BLOCKADE”. On July 22, he set a rule: every time Iran shoots at a ship in the strait, the United States will destroy “ONE BRIDGE OR POWER PLANT”. On August 2, he cancelled another planned attack, this time at the request of Iran and unnamed regional countries.
August 10: ‘Donald Trump Won the Iran War’
On August 10, Trump posted a link to an article with the headline, “Donald Trump Won the Iran War”.
Through August, the war has become an economic one. The 60-day memorandum of understanding expired with nothing to replace it; Trump said he would declare the Strait a US “territory” and, on August 19, he announced the “MOST CRUSHING ECONOMIC OPERATION EVER TAKEN AGAINST ANY COUNTRY”, threatening any nation that offers Iran a financial lifeline.
All told, across 32,478 words, six months of war reached the public one post at a time, in the president’s own words.

New NASA photos reveal 16 galaxies from across the cosmos in dazzling detail
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
10:36:01 UTC
19:36:01 KST

NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory just dropped a new cache of photographs that capture the stunning beauty of different types of galaxies across the universe.
The 16 images include x-ray data that Chandra has collected over decades, combined with observations from other telescopes in space and across the world. These cosmic behemoths can tell us more about our own Milky Way galaxy’s history and the universe’s evolution over time.
NASA’s Chandra, launched in 1999, is the highest-resolution x-ray telescope in orbit and has captured everything from epic colliding galaxies to weird, dead stars.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Some of the images feature spiral galaxies, which have a concentration of stars in their center and “arms” that resemble a pinwheel—the Milky Way is a spiral galaxy.
The NGC 4631 galaxy, the spiral galaxy above, photographed from its side, has been nicknamed the “Whale Galaxy” because of its shape at this angle.
Other images reveal elliptical galaxies, which don’t have extending arms or much structure at all. These galaxies tend to include older stars and can grow larger than any other type of galaxy. The galaxy featured next, M104, is actually a mix of elliptical and spiral galaxies and is known as the “Sombrero Galaxy.”
The final group featured in the gallery are irregular galaxies, which, as the name suggests, can come in all shapes and sizes.
The images also provide clues into the transformations and collisions that shape galaxies, such as waves of stellar births and supermassive black holes. Both galaxy pairs featured above, Arp 143 and II Zw 096, highlight mergers and collisions between galaxies.

This file photo shows CIA Director Ratcliffe at a press conference.
The Kremlin Aug. 27 dismissed media speculation on the rare visit of the CIA director to Moscow earlier this week, after reports said U.S. intelligence chief John Ratcliffe warned Russia against attacking NATO.
“A lot of such scare stories are being published right now. Of course, they have nothing to do with reality,” said Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov, adding that Russia “is facing a very aggressive policy towards itself from European countries.”
Peskov’s remarks came after U.S. media reported on Aug. 26 that CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s visit was to warn Russia against any attack on NATO member states, after President Donald Trump sought to downplay the visit.
The Wall Street Journal and CBS News reported Ratcliffe aimed to dissuade Russia from attacking NATO members amid U.S. intelligence assessments that Moscow could seek to test the alliance.
The Journal specified that Putin could test NATO with a “limited assault” in the next few years.
Trump said Ratcliffe’s visit to Moscow on Aug. 25 was “semi-routine,” implying that the intelligence chief was in the Russian capital to discuss the Ukraine war.
“He’s there, very sort of semi-routine. I hate to disappoint people. We would like to see the war with Ukraine end,” Trump said in an interview with conservative radio host Glenn Beck.
Ratcliffe is one of the highest-ranking U.S. officials to visit Russia since its war with Ukraine started in 2022.
His visit came amid an escalation in Moscow’s offensive in Ukraine, with attacks this summer increasing the civilian death toll, while U.S.-brokered peace talks have stalled.
During his visit, Ratcliffe also discussed the war with Iran, warning of additional sanctions if the Strait of Hormuz doesn’t reopen to shipping traffic, CBS News reported, citing multiple people familiar with the matter.

Iran, Oman are back talking about Hormuz: Here's what we know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
10:33:39 UTC
19:33:39 KST

Breadcrumb
Iran, Oman are back talking about the Strait of Hormuz: Here's what we know
Speculation has returned over whether Iran and Oman may soon announce a temporary solution to the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz following a new round of negotiations in Muscat on Tuesday.
The two countries signed off the meeting with a statement that indicated progress but fell short of an agreement. Iranian officials have since painted a different picture, claiming that Oman has agreed to an arrangement that would give Tehran broad oversight of the strait.
Here's what we know about the talks.
What has been agreed?
That depends on who you ask.
Iran and Oman put out a joint statement following Tuesday's meeting that spoke of a "proposed framework" rather than a conclusive agreement.
On the table is a "joint temporary navigational corridor" and a "joint project to clear the strait of mines", the statement read.
But it stopped short of offering any details about the route, including its coordinates, when it would open, or how long it would remain active.
Efforts will continue to try and agree a permanent route and a way of administering traffic, it said.
But Iranian officials have subsequently claimed that a temporary corridor had been agreed.
In comments to state TV, Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said Oman had signed off on temporary entry and exit routes that would pass through Iran's territorial waters.
The Revolutionary Guards went further, claiming that Oman had agreed to Iran's controversial proposal to generate revenues from the strait.
"During negotiations with Oman, some agreements were made regarding each country's share of the waters of the Strait and Iran's and Oman's shares of its revenues," said IRGC spokesperson Hossein Mohebi.
Oman has not commented on Iran's claims.
Why are the revenues so controversial?
Iran's insistence on charging fees for using the strait is opposed by dozens of countries around the world.
That includes the US, which in July resumed its bombing campaign in a bid to force Iran to give up control of the waterway.
The subject is also highly sensitive among Gulf countries which remain heavily reliant on the strait to export oil, gas and other commodities. The UAE and Bahrain have been particularly vocal supporters of a maritime taskforce proposed by the UK and France that would keep the strait open after the war.
Oman has publicly opposed the introduction of fees and says it is committed to ensuring freedom of navigation.
What has Oman said?
Writing on X after Tuesday's talks, Oman's foreign minister Badr Albusaidi said he hoped that the two countries would soon announce the temporary route and "practical arrangements to restore safe navigation".
"Future management of the strait and a permanent solution will follow in due course," he added.
Will the strait be re-opened?
A temporary deal would be a big step towards resolving the strait's disputed status but would not immediately lead to its re-opening.
Iranian officials insist it will remain closed until the US meets its commitments under the June memorandum of understanding, including lifting its naval blockade and permanently ending the war.
"Before any action is taken to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, the United States must fully implement all the commitments it has breached," Gharibabadi said on Tuesday.
Are we any closer to a peace deal?
Although the 60-day memorandum officially expired earlier this month, regional mediators including Pakistan and Qatar are still trying to keep it alive. Both countries are pushing Iran and the US to return to the negotiating table and hammer out a peace deal to re-open the strait and end the war.
Pakistan sounded a note of optimism after its army chief Asim Munir held talks in Tehran earlier this week. Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman al-Thani will travel to Iran's capital on Thursday.
Publicly, neither country has expressed willingness to return to talks. Iran's hardline security and military chiefs have threatened to return to war in the coming weeks if the US does not meet its demands while Trump has doubled down on his "maximum pressure" strategy with a new round of sanctions aimed at strangling Iran's economy.
