Stop Touching Your Keyboard. Use This AI-Powered Microphone Instead
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

How much do you hate typing? The advent of large language models has rapidly advanced voice-to-text technology. Whether it's Wispr Flow joining your meetings to summarize discussions or Google debuting smarter on-device dictation in its latest Pixel smartphone, these tools do far more than transcribe: They intelligently strip filler words, clean up unscripted thoughts on the fly, and seamlessly mediate multilingual conversations.
Now, a new startup is entering the fray. Unlike its software-focused peers, Relay is building a dedicated, portable microphone for high-fidelity voice-to-text anywhere. Based in London, Relay was founded by two former Nothing employees: Cookie Xu, who was Nothing's head of AI and services, and Raymond Zhu, a hardware product manager. While the company is debuting its software today, the hardware—what it calls the Relay Q—won't be available until early 2027.
Zhu says when he and Xu worked at Nothing, they used Wispr Flow's transcription software to “type” most of their messages at work. He says it greatly helped with thinking out ideas, but they kept running into an issue: talking loudly in an office.
“In the office, we never really could get the right volume for input,” Zhu tells WIRED. “If I whisper too quietly, the Mac wouldn't be able to pick it up; too loud and my coworker next to me can hear. Sometimes I would actually pull out my earbud and go like this,” he says over a video call, holding an earbud in front of his mouth to demonstrate. “It calls for dedicated hardware.”
Relay is exclusive to macOS at launch, though the company has plans to bring it to Windows, iOS, and Android. It's starting with the desktop because Zhu believes conversations are most complex there. Chats with friends and family are simple on phones, but at work in front of a computer, you're sharing ideas, brainstorming, and using varied tone and formality.
Though the microphone is still months away from being ready, I've been using a beta version of Relay's macOS app, which works with or without the dedicated mic.
During setup, you'll need to choose a hotkey that will trigger Relay in any text field—the default is Fn. Press and hold the key while your cursor is in any text field, and Relay activates and handles the voice dictation. The voice-to-text engine is powered by Google's Gemini models.
It can also perform contextual actions—dubbed Skills—like asking it to message a colleague in Slack, which prompts Relay to launch the app, find the recipient, and draft the text. I had some trouble with this Slack skill, though it didn't have trouble crafting a calendar event in Google Calendar. Relay has some preset skills you can enable for popular apps like WhatsApp and Gmail, but you can make your own and connect other apps.
That automation requires sweeping system permissions. Relay needs access to your microphone, but you can grant it access to record a snapshot of your screen anytime it's activated, which is how it can execute those Skills. The company says it stores data locally on the user's device, where users can manually edit or delete it. When the data is sent for processing, it passes through Relay's servers in transit to Google's servers, but Relay does not retain the data. Still, granting AI models eyes on your operating system adds inherent privacy and security trade-offs, like with Microsoft's Recall.
Relay's transcription isn't nearly as impressive as what I've recently tried with Google's Rambler feature on its Pixel 11 series. It doesn't capture every word perfectly and can mess up punctuation sometimes. It can similarly understand when you misspeak and restate sentences, cutting the parts that don't matter. And yes, it can insert emoji for you, though it did this inconsistently in my tests. When I asked it to add a heart emoji, for example, it did it flawlessly. But when I tried to tack that on at the end of the sentence, it just wrote out “heart emoji.” How romantic.
It generally knows when you want it to perform an action that's separate from the message. For example, I sent a message via Relay to my wife saying I really want to eat at a particular restaurant, and in the same breath, I asked Relay to provide a Google Maps link to the spot—and it did. This can be a little hit or miss, though. I'll chalk it up to the beta.
I haven't used it long enough for the software to adapt to my way of speaking, but you can add notes in the Relay app to make it follow certain patterns. For example, I rarely end a sentence with a period in my Slack messages, so I told it to avoid adding periods, and it followed the rule. There's a good deal of customization for specific people that you regularly speak with, which it detects, so you can ensure your messages to your boss sound professional, while messages to your friends are casual. Or you can even set it so that messages to a coworker living in a different country are translated into their language.
I'm relying on a Mac Mini and the microphone in Apple's Studio Display monitor—some of these accuracy issues could be resolved once Relay's hardware arrives. For instance, right now there's a small delay when I press the function key on the keyboard and when Relay activates, but that delay would be far shorter with dedicated hardware.
Speaking of, the Relay Q is a cylindrical gizmo with a microphone at the end. You can hold down the top as you speak to trigger Relay on your computer or phone—exactly like the hot key—or take the button off the cylinder and clip it to a shirt if you don't want to hold it all the time. (Viewed from the top, the microphone looks like the letter Q, hence the name.) A double-tap can send the message. You can hold it up to your mouth and whisper as quietly as you'd like, and Zhu says it should be able to pick up what you say.
“One question was always in our mind when building this product,” Zhu says. “How long can you go with your workday without touching your keyboard?”
The idea of having a microphone—even a wearable one—for far more accurate voice-to-text isn't new. Last year, a startup called Sandbar unveiled the Stream Ring, and months later, Pebble showed off its own take, the Index 01. Both are rings designed for you to whisper your thoughts into them, and both are starting to ship right about now to initial buyers. Zhu says Relay considered a ring but ultimately decided against it, especially since so many smart rings are already on the market.
The Relay Q will come with a charging dock so you can neatly keep it on your desk when it's not in use. The company is also creating a separate MagSafe grip you can attach to the back of an iPhone or Qi2-enabled device where the Relay Q can attach, allowing you to press the button easily while using a phone to trigger Relay's voice-to-text on mobile, which it plans to launch alongside the Relay Q in the first quarter of 2027.
The Q will cost $150 and includes a year of the software, which will cost $15 per month afterward. (You don't need to buy the Relay Q to use the software.)

Teacher of Oscar-winning Russian filmmaker behind Mr Nobody Against Putin calls him a traitor
Aug 27 - Pavel Talankin, who filmed how one Russian school tried to justify the war in Ukraine to its students in a clandestine project for the Oscar-winning "Mr. Nobody Against Putin", was guilty of treachery, his former teacher told Russian state TV.
The documentary, by Talankin and David Borenstein, was based on two years of footage that Talankin recorded at a school where he was employed in the Chelyabinsk region, some 1,500 km (930 miles) southeast of Moscow.
Banned by the Russian authorities, the documentary shows how the school changed after Moscow sent its troops into Ukraine in 2022 and how some of the teachers — via history lessons and activities such as newly introduced patriotic hours — justified the war and sought to instil patriotism.
Talankin, who fled Russia in 2024, has said it was important to tell the world how Russian school children were being indoctrinated. He has defended the film as a record for posterity to show how "an entire generation became angry and aggressive".
But in an interview with TV programme Vesti, Nina Zabugornova, whom the broadcaster described as Talankin's first teacher in his hometown of Karabash, also in the Chelyabinsk region, said he was an ordinary boy not much different from others.
"I wanted to watch the documentary, to see what did Pashka film," said Zabugornova, standing in front of an Orthodox church in Karabash, where she is a bell-ringer.
"But it turned out that Pashka had decided to turn his back on his motherland. Isn't that a betrayal? Isn't that an evil?"
In March, Russia designated Talankin, who fled the country in 2024, as a foreign agent. Those given the label are subject to exacting bureaucratic requirements.
Zabugornova, who she said was a teacher for four decades, blamed herself that Talankin had committed "a betrayal".
"So I think that when he was little, when all these things were being formed in him, I must have overlooked something somewhere, didn't give him enough good lessons," she told Vesti. REUTERS

US and Canadian forces practise cruise missile defence
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
11:28:11 BST
19:28:11 KST

NORAD and US Northern Command are running Exercise Amalgam Dart across North America until 1 September, covering cruise missile defence scenarios and coordination with allied forces in the Arctic, the command stated.
The exercise began on 24 August and involves forces across the Alaskan, Canadian and Continental United States NORAD regions. According to the command, it is intended to sharpen the ability to detect, track, identify and respond to modern air domain threats.
American and Canadian personnel are integrating mixed fighter force operations, command and control organisations and air battle management, with aircraft flying as simulated adversaries. Training covers coordinated responses along both the eastern and western approaches to the continent, along with cruise missile defence scenarios using binational assets operating from 3 Wing Bagotville in Quebec.
The command describes the exercise as long-planned, routine and defensive.
That concept reflects a change in how the region is understood. NORAD was built around the shortest route between the Soviet Union and North America, which runs over the pole, and its warning and interception architecture faces north for that reason. The accession of Finland and Sweden to NATO has closed a gap on the European side of the same geography, and Russian long-range aviation operating from the Kola Peninsula presents a problem to both commands simultaneously rather than sequentially.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s economic outlook remained in the red in July, with the government’s monitoring indicator flashing a red light for the eighth consecutive month as strong AI demand continued to support growth.
The National Development Council said in a press release Thursday that the composite economic indicator scored 41 points in July, unchanged from June. The red light is one month short of the record nine consecutive red lights recorded in 2021.
Taiwan uses a five-color system to gauge the health of its economy, with colors ranging from blue to red. Blue signals contraction, yellow-blue indicates sluggish growth, green represents stable growth, yellow-red means the economy is warming up, and red indicates an overheated or booming economy.
The manufacturing business climate index rose from a green light to a yellow-red light, benefiting from continued strong AI demand. The M1B money supply indicator, which tracks cash and readily spendable bank deposits, saw its growth slow from a yellow-red to a green signal, partly due to foreign investors moving money out of Taiwan.
The council said leading and coincident indicators continued to rise, indicating that Taiwan’s economic growth momentum remains solid.
Looking ahead, the council said the deepening adoption of AI is expected to drive demand for computing power, while major global cloud service providers accelerate AI infrastructure investment. The stocking-up cycle for new consumer electronics products is also expected to support continued export growth.
Domestic semiconductor and AI supply chains are actively expanding capacity, while international companies are increasing investment and procurement in Taiwan. Government efforts to help small and medium-sized businesses and traditional industries upgrade and transform are also expected to boost private investment.
The council said strong profits among listed companies could encourage higher wages and dividend payments. In addition, the stable job market and the recovery in car sales are expected to boost consumption.
However, the council cautioned that international trade and economic conditions remain uncertain due to developments in the Middle East, changes in US tariff policies, shifts in monetary policy in major economies, and changes in fiscal policy. It said these factors will require close monitoring.

Iran war raises concerns over US weapons shortage for Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
10:27:28 UTC
19:27:28 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — US weapons shortages caused by the war with Iran are raising concerns among Taiwan and US allies in Asia about Washington’s ability to maintain its deterrence posture against China.
The massive expenditure of US munitions in the Middle East has depleted stockpiles and redirected military resources that could be critical in a potential war with China, per The Washington Post. The concerns come as Beijing continues to increase military pressure around Taiwan and Washington reduces some military activities in Asia.
On Aug. 16, President Donald Trump announced a reduction in joint military exercises with South Korea, citing costs, South Korea’s refusal to assist the US war effort against Iran, and his relationship with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, per Reuters. On Monday, the Pentagon canceled a joint amphibious landing exercise in South Korea scheduled for September, citing demands on US forces from the war in Iran, per The Hill.
South Korea, Japan, and Taiwan all rely heavily on Washington for major conventional weapons and face lengthy delivery backlogs. The Iran war has added pressure by consuming and reallocating resources needed for other contingencies, according to the Post.
Taiwan has nearly NT$965.5 billion (US$30 billion) in US weapons approved for sale but not yet delivered, including NT$28.4 billion in Patriot missiles, the Taiwan Security Monitor reported. The backlog includes other major systems such as HIMARS launchers and munitions.
Taiwanese defense officials told the Legislative Yuan in March that they still expected 102 Patriot missiles to be delivered this year. However, a Taiwanese official told the Post that deliveries of Patriot Advanced Capability-3 interceptors are expected to be significantly delayed because the Pentagon has depleted much of its interceptor stockpile in the Middle East.
Jennifer Kavanagh, director of military analysis at Washington-based Defense Priorities, told the Post that Taiwan is unlikely to receive the full order of about 100 missiles soon. She said Washington’s first priority would likely be replenishing its own stockpiles, followed by refilling supplies for Gulf Arab allies while the war with Iran continues.
Japan is facing similar concerns over US weapons deliveries. The Financial Times reported in May that deliveries of 400 Tomahawk cruise missiles to Japan could be delayed by as much as two years.
The diversion of US forces to the Middle East has also frustrated officials responsible for military operations in the Indo-Pacific, according to three sources. Mark Cancian, a retired Marine colonel and senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told the Post that CSIS war games conducted since 2023 found that defending Taiwan against an invasion would likely exceed current Pentagon supply plans, with many critical weapons exhausted within weeks.
Trump also described arms sales to Taiwan in May as a “good negotiating chip” with China, while a roughly NT$450.8 billion arms package for Taiwan was put on hold ahead of his summit with Xi in Beijing. The Post cited a Chinese official as warning that any signal from the White House approving new arms sales to Taiwan would seriously undermine prospects for further visits between the two leaders this year.
US intelligence officials say Xi has directed the Chinese military to be capable of invading Taiwan by 2027, although current assessments indicate that China’s leadership does not have imminent plans to launch an invasion. The 2027 deadline nonetheless highlights what analysts and officials describe as a vulnerability in US munitions stocks as Washington replenishes weapons consumed in the Middle East.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Residents and environmental groups opposed to a proposed incinerator in Nantou County’s Mingjian Township called Thursday for the project to be halted after infrared cameras reportedly recorded leopard cats near the site.
The Mingjian Anti-Incinerator Self-Help Association said cameras installed near the proposed 7.5-hectare site recorded leopard cats on July 29 and Aug. 19. The sightings suggest the area is an important habitat and movement corridor for the endangered species, per SETN.

The proposed site is on state-owned land designated as a special agricultural zone in Mingjian’s Xinmin Village. It is near about 2,250 hectares of tea plantations, rice-growing areas, and the Babao irrigation system.
At a news conference Thursday, residents and local farmers urged Nantou County Magistrate Hsu Shu-hua (許淑華) to reconsider the site. They said the project could affect agriculture, water resources, and local livelihoods.
Nantou County magistrate candidate Wen Shih-cheng (温世政) said more than 60% of Mingjian’s economy relies on the tea industry. While acknowledging that Nantou must address its waste-disposal problem, he said an incinerator in Mingjian should not be the only option.
Wen proposed combining waste reduction, improved sorting, food-waste recycling, and optimization of existing incineration facilities. The association called for an immediate halt to drilling and monitoring-well work, ecological surveys before further construction, and consideration of a leopard cat protection area along the Zhuoshui River.
The environmental bureau said that if official surveys confirm leopard cat activity, it would consider measures including avoidance, reducing the project’s scale, mitigation, and compensation.
Nantou has no municipal waste incinerator and relies on other cities and counties to process its waste. The county government’s proposed Nantou Waste Treatment and Renewable Energy Center completed its second-stage environmental impact assessment scope meeting in May.

A mysterious cosmic hum may come from 13-billion-year-old dark stars
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
10:26:04 UTC
19:26:04 KST

A mysterious cosmic hum may come from 13-billion-year-old dark stars
A mysterious gravitational-wave hum detected today may be an echo of the first giant black holes born more than 13 billion years ago.
- Date:
- August 27, 2026
- Source:
- Colgate University
- Summary:
- Today’s mysterious gravitational-wave background may preserve clues about how the Universe’s first supermassive black holes formed. Descendants of hypothetical Dark Stars could be responsible for a major portion of the signal, offering a surprising new way to investigate cosmic dawn and dark matter.
- Share:
A faint background of extremely low frequency gravitational waves detected through networks of pulsars could contain clues to events that unfolded more than 13 billion years ago, including the emergence of some of the Universe's earliest supermassive black holes.
In a study published as a Letter in Physical Review D, Colgate University researchers Sohan Ghodla and Cosmin Ilie examined whether supermassive black holes that originated in the early Universe could eventually produce a significant share of the gravitational wave background now being measured by Pulsar Timing Arrays, or PTAs.
The findings connect two areas of astronomy that may at first seem far apart. One involves observations of surprisingly massive black holes that already existed when the Universe was young. The other involves gravitational waves generated billions of years later by pairs of supermassive black holes spiraling toward one another.
The researchers found that one possible class of early black hole seeds, remnants left behind by supermassive Dark Stars, could potentially provide a dominant contribution to the PTA signal.
"Pulsar timing arrays are usually thought of as probes of supermassive black-hole binaries in the relatively recent Universe," said Ilie. "What our work shows is that the signal may also contain information about how the ancestors of those black holes formed at cosmic dawn. In that sense, gravitational waves observed today could provide a new window onto the birth of the first supermassive black holes."
Pulsars as Precise Cosmic Clocks
Pulsar Timing Arrays rely on rapidly spinning neutron stars known as pulsars, which act as extraordinarily precise clocks in space. When gravitational waves pass through the cosmos, they cause tiny changes in the timing of the radio pulses that eventually arrive at Earth. By tracking many pulsars over long periods, international research teams have found evidence for a stochastic gravitational wave background at nanohertz frequencies.
The most widely accepted astrophysical explanation for this background is a population of supermassive black hole binaries gradually spiraling inward. Systems whose black holes have a combined mass greater than roughly a billion Suns make especially important contributions at the frequencies detected by PTAs.
But explaining those enormous black holes raises a deeper question. Astronomers still want to know how their original seeds formed. Observatories including the James Webb Space Telescope and Chandra have discovered massive black holes at unexpectedly early stages of cosmic history, increasing interest in formation mechanisms capable of producing large black hole seeds very quickly.
Ghodla and Ilie investigated whether the descendants of such ancient seeds could persist through cosmic time, grow alongside their host galaxies, eventually pair up, and generate the gravitational wave background detected billions of years later.
Could Dark Stars Seed Giant Black Holes?
The researchers explored two possible routes for producing massive black hole seeds in the early Universe: direct collapse black holes and black holes formed through the collapse of supermassive Dark Stars.
Dark Stars are hypothetical primordial stars that would receive much of their energy from heating associated with dark matter instead of relying primarily on ordinary nuclear fusion. In the WIMP dark matter scenario considered in the study, these stars could remain relatively cool and extended while continuing to gather material. Under the right conditions, they might grow to a million times the mass of the Sun or more before collapsing into massive black holes.
Ghodla and Ilie modeled how black holes produced through these pathways would evolve over cosmic history. They followed the halos hosting the black holes, estimated how frequently the objects would merge, and calculated the gravitational wave background those mergers would produce.
Their results indicate that if remnants of supermassive Dark Stars existed at a number density of roughly 10-3 Mpc-3, their descendants could provide a large, and possibly dominant, share of the gravitational wave signal measured by PTAs.
The direct collapse black hole population considered in the study appears likely to have been much less common. With characteristic densities near 10-6 Mpc-3, those objects would contribute substantially less to the observed signal.
Using Gravitational Waves to Probe Cosmic Dawn
One of the study's key conclusions is that current PTA measurements can place limits on how common the earliest seeds of supermassive black holes could have been.
"Produce too many of these massive seeds and you end up over-producing the PTA-detected signal. Produce too few, and you need other sources to efficiently assemble these supermassive black holes later in the life of the universe to match PTA observations," said Ghodla.
Within the models examined by the researchers, seed densities around the 10-2 to 10-1 Mpc-3 range would begin generating more gravitational wave background than observations allow. The exact limit depends strongly on the masses of the dark matter halos where those seeds originally formed.
That gives PTA observations an unexpected ability to probe extremely ancient populations. They may be able to constrain objects that existed at redshifts greater than 10, even though the mergers of their descendants that create the gravitational waves happen much later in cosmic history.
The calculations also support an earlier finding that binaries with total black hole masses roughly above 109 solar masses dominate the predicted PTA signal. Binary systems containing less massive black holes contribute far less.
Connecting Dark Matter, Dark Stars, and Black Holes
The findings create a new observational link between several major questions in modern cosmology, including the nature of dark matter, the formation of the first luminous objects, the origins of supermassive black holes, and the gravitational waves that travel through the Universe.
"Dark Stars were originally proposed as objects that might be seen directly at cosmic dawn," Ilie said. "This work points to a completely different way of testing their possible role in cosmic history. Their descendants could leave a gravitational-wave imprint that persists all the way to the present-day Universe."
As Pulsar Timing Array measurements become more precise, and astronomers improve their understanding of distant black holes and the galaxies that hosted them, researchers may be able to distinguish more clearly among competing explanations for how the Universe's first supermassive black holes formed.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Colgate University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Sohan Ghodla, Cosmin Ilie. Reconstructing PTA measurements via early seeding of supermassive black holes. Physical Review D, 2026; 114 (4) DOI: 10.1103/hvfd-8fkr

Tate brothers to press for release from US jail during extradition fight

Andrew Tate's romantic partner testifies in his bid for release on bail
MIAMI, Aug 27 - A romantic partner of Andrew Tate testified on Thursday on behalf of the social media influencer as he and his brother Tristan Tate seek release on bail from a Miami jail as they contest extradition to Britain, where they are wanted on rape charges.
Natasha Sesay, who said she had been in a romantic relationship with Andrew Tate for 5-1/2 years, was questioned by defense lawyer Stephen Binhak as part of the Tate brothers' effort to persuade Miami-based U.S. Magistrate Judge Lauren Louis that they would not pose a danger to the community if released.
The former kickboxers have built a large online following promoting their views on masculinity and wealth. Andrew Tate has previously described himself as a misogynist.
Sesay, who said she shared an 8-month-old child with Andrew Tate and was expecting their second child next month, said his sometimes provocative comments online did not reflect who he truly was.
"It’s a very different character between the person that you see online and the person I know," Sesay said.
Andrew Tate, 39, and Tristan Tate, 38, looked back and forth between Binhak and Sesay during her testimony. They were seated at the defense table shackled at the feet, wearing beige prison garb and sporting beards to their hearing.
The Tate brothers were arrested in Miami on July 18 after Britain requested their extradition to face charges of rape, assault and facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation. The Tate brothers, who have dual U.S. and British citizenship, have denied any wrongdoing.
The arrests marked a new phase in their legal troubles. The Tates recruited dozens of women to work for a webcam pornography business starting in 2014, and later ran online courses called "Hustler's University," prosecutors with the Miami U.S. Attorney's office said in an August 10 court filing.
DEFENSE ARGUES AGAINST DETENTION
The prosecutors said in court filings there was a strong presumption in favor of detention in international extradition cases. They said the Tates could pose a danger to the community if released, citing British authorities' allegations that they strangled victims during forcible rapes, and that they could try to flee.
The prosecutors also pointed to allegations by authorities in Romania, where the brothers face human trafficking charges, that they sought to influence witnesses' statements while released on judicial supervision there. Romanian authorities say the Tates threatened to release private information about alleged victims and bribed an alleged victim, the U.S. prosecutors said.
Howard Srebnick, another lawyer for the Tates, said that they had regularly appeared in court in Romania, where they are on pretrial release, which he said was evidence they were not a flight risk.
"The brothers have been fully compliant with their conditions of release," Srebnick said.
Thomas Maniotis, defense lawyer, said the witnesses the Tates were alleged to have bribed were women who wanted to speak on their behalf, and said the Tates helped coordinate their travel to Bucharest and hired lawyers for them.
The defense lawyers proposed that Louis release them on the conditions they post bond, surrender their passports and submit to location monitoring.
BRITISH CHARGES SPAN SEVEN YEARS
The legal process for determining whether the Tate brothers may be extradited could take months. Britain has until September 16 to submit its full extradition request to the State Department, U.S. court records show.
The impetus for the brothers' arrests in Miami was new charges brought by Britain's Crown Prosecution Service relating to alleged offenses involving four alleged victims between July 2010 and August 2017.
They had previously faced rape and human trafficking charges in Britain related to three alleged victims, the CPS said. A British judge issued a warrant for their arrests in 2024. They have not appeared in British court to enter a plea to those charges.
Britain is seeking to extradite the brothers to face both sets of charges. REUTERS

Suspect arrested for allegedly killing influencer on livestream in Mexico
Mexico has arrested a man who allegedly shot and killed an influencer during a live broadcast, authorities said on Wednesday.
Cesar Gastelum was attacked on August 4 while livestreaming in Culiacan, the capital of Sinaloa state, which has been a battleground for warring drug factions.
Gastelum, who had more than 500,000 TikTok followers, was dressed as a food delivery worker and taking part in a social media challenge along with two friends when a motorcycle stopped next to him. In the recording of the livestream, seen by the Reuters news agency, the driver of the motorcycle appeared to fire a gun directly at Gastelum.
Security Minister Omar Garcia Harfuch said the alleged killer was located in the state of Puebla, in central Mexico.
During the arrest operation, police officers came under attack by three armed individuals and killed one of them, Harfuch wrote on X.
Authorities arrested the suspected killer of Gastelum and another person. Three firearms, ammunition and vehicles were seized at the scene, Harfuch said.
Preliminary investigation showed that the influencer's killing was related to his social media posts "alluding to a faction of a criminal group," Mexico's security secretariat said.
A sprawling war between the two main factions of the Sinaloa Cartel and associated armed groups has left thousands dead or missing in the northwestern state, even as President Claudia Sheinbaum seeks to contain criminal violence.
 The cartel was founded by Joaquin "El Chapo" Guzman, who is now imprisoned in the United States.
 
Influencers targeted in Mexico
Culiacan is ground zero for "narco-culture" celebrating the life of drug traffickers, and Mexican media report that social media influencers are often tied to disputing criminal gangs, leading to acts of intimidation or score-settling. Around a dozen influencers have been killed in recent years in Sinaloa, local media have reported.
Last year, Mexican social media influencer Valeria Marquez was shot dead at a beauty salon during a livestream on TikTok, where she had tens of thousands of followers. Prosecutors said she appeared to be murdered by a hit man and expressed fear before being killed.
In July, authorities announced the arrest in Jalisco of Ramon Angel Alvarez Ayala, whom officials linked to the killing of Marquez as well as the November 2025 murder of Uruapan Mayor Carlos Manzo, Reuters reported.
Marquez's murder shocked Mexico — where killings and kidnappings are a daily occurrence — and brought into sharp focus both its femicide epidemic and growing violence against influencers.
In January 2025, a small plane was reported to have dropped pamphlets in Culiacan threatening around 20 artists and YouTubers for alleged dealings with a warring faction of the Sinaloa drug cartel.
Influencers have been targeted in other parts of Latin America. Last year in Venezuela, police arrested an alleged accomplice in the murder of a TikTok influencer who was killed during a livestream after denouncing members of the Tren de Aragua criminal gang and allegedly corrupt police officers.

- Russia hit steel mills in the cities of Zaporozhye and Krivoy Rog, which supply goods for military production.
- A drone assembly workshop in the Kiev Region, producing the Hornet loitering munition, came under attack.
- Russian forces also carried out a massive strike on a transport and logistics center in Kiev (the San Park office and logistics complex), which is the largest storage and distribution center for strike FPV drones, as well as their ground control stations and components.
- The Russian army hit a transport and logistics center in Borispol (the Alexandrovsky office and logistics complex), which is the largest dual-use storage facility.
- Russia struck a workshop in the Odessa Region used for assembling drones and producing saltpeter for the Ukrainian army.
Situation in Ukraine
- Explosions were reported in Kiev during the night, with air raid alerts issued in most Ukrainian regions.
- Power outages have been recorded in five Ukrainian regions due to infrastructure damage, the Ukrenergo company reported on its Telegram channel.
- According to the company, some residents of the Dnepropetrovsk, Odessa, Poltava, Sumy, and Kharkov Regions are without power.
- The company urged Ukrainians to use high-power appliances only during daytime hours, when solar power plants operate most efficiently, in order to avoid overloading the grid.
- An enterprise and an energy infrastructure facility were damaged in the Poltava Region, head of the regional military administration Vitaly Dyakivnich said on Thursday morning.
- A major fire broke out on the premises of a warehouse in Borispol in the Kiev Region, the UNIAN news agency reported on its Telegram channel, which posted footage of the blaze and smoke.
- The Strana newspaper reported that in addition to the warehouse, a logistics facility of the Epizentr company also caught fire.

U.S.-based seaglider maker REGENT lands $240 million in new funding
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
10:20:43 UTC
19:20:43 KST

- REGENT Craft raised $240 million in Series B funding, bringing its total raised to date to $340 million across equity and debt.
- The company cited growing military interest, including an expanded $15 million U.S. Marine Corps contract for its Viceroy Seaglider platform.
REGENT Craft has raised $240 million in Series B funding, split evenly between equity and debt, the Rhode Island-based seaglider manufacturer announced Thursday.
The round was co-led by investment firms Mare Liberum and AE Ventures, with debt capital provided by Erebor Bank. The new funding brings REGENT’s total raised to date, across equity and debt, to $340 million.
REGENT builds Seaglider vessels, wing-in-ground effect craft that use hydrofoils to lift off the water and skim just above the surface within a wingspan’s height. The company describes the design as combining aircraft speed with the operational simplicity of a boat.
The company said the funding arrives ahead of several near-term milestones, including the first human flight of its Viceroy Seaglider prototype and the start of production at REGENT’s newly completed 255,000-square-foot (23,690 square meter) manufacturing facility in Rhode Island.
REGENT said it has seen growing military interest across its product line, which the company attributed to the Department of War’s focus on maritime operating areas. That interest includes an expanded U.S. Marine Corps contract, now valued at $15 million, for the Viceroy platform, along with rising interest in Squire, REGENT’s autonomous Seaglider drone.
Squire recently completed a demonstration at Silent Swarm, a military experimentation event sponsored by the Office of the Under Secretary of War for Research and Engineering, Quantum and Battlefield Information Dominance.
“This investment marks a critical inflection point for REGENT as we move from development into production,” said Billy Thalheimer, co-founder and CEO of REGENT. “We have built significant momentum across both our defense and commercial pipelines, and this funding enables us to scale manufacturing, execute key certification milestones, and deliver Seagliders to customers.”
“As maritime defense priorities evolve, operators need new capabilities that deliver greater speed, reach, and flexibility,” said Admiral Lorin Selby, General Partner at Mare Liberum. “REGENT is a leader in this emerging category with a strong track record of technical development and growing engagement with defense customers.”
Erebor Bank, which provided the round’s debt financing, was co-founded by Palmer Luckey, the entrepreneur who also founded military contractor Anduril.
“Rebuilding America’s industrial base means banking the companies actually willing to build things again,” said Owen Rapaport, co-founder and CEO of Erebor Bank. “REGENT is proof that American manufacturing can still move at startup speed.”
Other investors in the round include DCVC, along with returning backers Founders Fund, Caffeinated Capital, Lockheed Martin Ventures, Japan Airlines and Giant Step Capital.
REGENT said it has built a commercial order book spanning six continents, with multiple years of manufacturing capacity already booked. The company is also expanding internationally, continuing a partnership with the Abu Dhabi-based Strategic Development Fund on planned Seaglider operations and manufacturing in the United Arab Emirates. REGENT has separate partnerships with Balnord in Poland, focused on defense requirements in the Baltic Sea, and with iGrow in Greece for commercial operations across the Aegean Islands.
REGENT’s Squire autonomous seaglider drew attention earlier this year following a February defense briefing in Quonset, Rhode Island, attended by Secretary of War Pete Hegseth. In an interview with The Defence Blog at the time, Tom Huntley, General Manager of REGENT Defense, described Squire as designed to handle high-risk, repetitive logistics and ISR missions in contested littoral zones, freeing manned ships and aircraft for more complex combat roles. The Squire prototype has since been cleared for testing by the U.S. Coast Guard and remains in an ongoing envelope expansion campaign, according to Huntley.

New funding for long Covid research centre raised
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
10:18:53 UTC
19:18:53 KST

New funding for long Covid research centre raised
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The Long COVID Foundation (SLC) has launched a National Research & Innovation Center to investigate long covid in the Netherlands as government money has dried up.
With some €40 million the government provided for research having been spent and no new budget yet allocated, the foundation awarded €500,000 to seven researchers to keep their research going and to “translate scientific discoveries more quickly into diagnostics and targeted treatments for adults and children.”
“SLC wants to prevent years of investment, knowledge and research power from being lost.”
The money is being given to researchers from the hospitals Amsterdam UMC, the Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, UMC Utrecht and Erasmus MC. The foundation’s goal is that the centre, operating as an independent foundation and an open national research network, will be a central hub for stimulating and linking research under one national program.
Still no treatment
Calling long covid “one of the great unresolved medical challenges of our time”, the foundation estimates 400,000 people have been affected by it – 100,000 of them seriously. “Yet there are no proven healing treatment, effective diagnostics and targeted therapies yet.”
Long covid sufferers struggle with fatigue, brain fog, loss of concentration, and memory and immune system problems that have severely limited their ability to work and lead normal lives.
Targeted treatments
The foundation says it’s becoming increasingly clear that long covid suffers can be distinguished by groups. “An important task for the centre will be to better distinguish these groups and to investigate which treatments can work in which patients.”
The foundation is also looking into other the post-acute infection syndromes, such as ME/CFS, a chronic illness characterised by an inability to function.
In the future, says SLC, “long-term public and private financing is also needed”.
“The stronger and more structural the research is organized, the more likely it is that scientific discoveries will lead to the diagnostics and targeted treatments that patients have been waiting for so long.”

Syria's post-Assad prisons: Detainee death reignites fear
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
10:17:13 UTC
19:17:13 KST

Breadcrumb
Syrians fear the return of Assad's prisons as death of young detainee sparks anger
The mountain town of Al-Haffah in northwestern Syria's Lattakia governorate was engulfed in grief and anger last week amid the funeral of 29-year-old Mohammad Ghamira, a man who died in hospital after security officers allegedly beat him while in detention, an incident that has stirred traumatic memories of the former regime’s worst abuses.
Immediately upon his arrest over a financial dispute, Ghamira's family informed the police that he suffered from haemophilia, requiring special care and the strict avoidance of any physical trauma, as his blood lacked the ability to clot.
The family's warnings were ignored. After three days in detention, the young man's health deteriorated rapidly. Despite being rushed to hospital after his release, he died a week later.
As news of Ghamira's deteriorating condition spread, the Internal Security Command in Lattakia initiated an investigation.
Following the announcement of his death, authorities detained seven individuals who were present at the Al-Haffah police station holding cell during his detention.
On the evening of Sunday, August 16, the Minister of Interior issued an administrative order forming a committee to investigate the circumstances surrounding his death, mandating a report within 72 hours.
On Thursday, August 20, the committee announced its findings, confirming that an interrogator had slapped Ghamira on the neck.
Consequently, interrogator Ahmad Jawad was referred to the public prosecution in Lattakia, while the Ministry of Interior's disciplinary department was tasked with expanding its investigation into Captain Ahmad Shaker Al-Masri and interrogator Omar Youssef.
The incident has triggered widespread outrage among Syrians, many of whom see it as reminiscent of the Assad era, when police stations and detention centres were sites of unchecked violence and murder.
Bashar al-Assad was overthrown in December 2024, ending 54 years of the Assad family's rule that was marked by absolute control over politics and civic life and widespread human rights violations.
Questions remain over whether the new administration, led by former militant leader Ahmed al-Sharaa, will usher in genuine reform.
Syria's memories of torture
"For Syrians, prison is not merely a penal institution; it is tied to a deeply painful national memory of arbitrary detention, torture, forced disappearance, and death," said Almoutassim Al Kilani, a prominent Syrian human rights lawyer and legal expert specialising in international criminal law and transitional justice.
"Hearing news of a detainee being tortured or dying in a security facility after being released is not seen as an ordinary criminal incident, but as an alarm that touches the very meaning of liberation," Al Kilani added.
Ezzedine Ezzedine, a lawyer who has worked for years on detainee files documenting the abuses and crimes committed in Bashar al-Assad's prisons, called it "a massive shock" for him or any human rights lawyer who monitored the violations of the previous regime.
"We considered that the absolute minimum achievement of the regime's fall was the eradication of forced disappearance and torture," he said.
Ezzedine notes that his frustration, and that of other Syrians, stems from the persistence of violence in prisons and the fear that it could evolve from isolated incidents caused by inexperience into a general policy.
"We hope we are wrong," he adds. His fears are compounded by the lack of concrete legal measures to prevent such violations.
Forming investigative committees is insufficient, he said, because they lack judicial authority and are merely internal bodies formed by the Ministry of Interior.
"The idea of a committee is good, but the issue cannot be resolved by committees alone. Is it reasonable to form a committee every time a violation occurs? The solution lies in implementing radical procedures, applying the Code of Criminal Procedure, and empowering the law to take its true, independent role."
A legacy of fear
In the Syrian consciousness, prisons evoke deep fears and tragic stories. The mere thought of entering a police station is terrifying, let alone a political detention centre.
While mass detention and mistreatment in prison were not common during the period of national rule following the French mandate, from 1946 to 1963, torture emerged as a systemic tool of control when the Baath Party seized power.
The rise of Hafez al-Assad, who took over in 1970, marked a brutal turning point. In the 1980s, the regime filled prisons with thousands of political opponents, using torture as the primary means of subjugating detainees and quashing the opposition base.
From this point, and continuing under his son, Bashar al-Assad, Syria was ruled by an authoritarian security apparatus that infiltrated every aspect of the state and society.
It spread fear and silenced dissent, creating a profound lack of trust, where everyone felt monitored and suspected their neighbours might be informants, said civil and political activist Youssef Al-Banni.
"After the Syrian people suffered for 40 years under the father and 14 years under the son, sacrificing blood, enduring oppression and displacement, every Syrian has the right to react to any act of violence by security forces," said Al-Banni.
"This requires a courageous and clear stance on the necessity of investigation, follow-up, and holding those involved accountable, regardless of their rank or justification. Silence on such violations undermines the very goals for which the nation revolted."
Al Kilani agrees that the Assad legacy is heavy and changing it takes time. "Liberation does not mean violations will automatically disappear, because changing the authorities is much faster than changing institutional culture and power dynamics," he says.
"But the hallmark of the new phase must be how the state handles a violation. Under the previous regime, torture was part of a vast system that protected perpetrators and hid victims. After liberation, any assault must be treated as a criminal and exceptional act, to be exposed, investigated, and penalised."
Civil society is now stepping in to fulfil this monitoring role.
Following Ghamira's death, activists organised a protest in Aleppo, while another group planned a similar demonstration in Damascus, which was later postponed.
Journalist and activist Fadi Zeidan, one of the organisers of the postponed Damascus protest, explains that the organisers include independent activists and former detainees, collaborating with civil society and human rights representatives.
While the public was deeply shocked by the incident, Zeidan noted intense societal polarisation.
Some voices called for boycotting the protest, fearing it would be exploited by remnants of the former regime to attack the new government.
"Despite this, we are the children of the 2011 revolution, and we believe that safeguarding the path of freedom and dignity requires us not to remain silent about any violation, regardless of who committed it," Zeidan says.
The Damascus protest was postponed after political figures, parliamentarians, and Ministry of Information officials reached out to request time to address the protesters' demands.
The government was also concerned that the issue of deaths under torture could be exploited politically or internationally to undermine stability.
Accounts of abuse
But Ghamira's story is not an isolated incident.
In July of last year, a young man named Youssef Al-Labad was arrested after a verbal altercation with public security personnel at the Umayyad Mosque. He was transferred to the Hamidiyeh prison, run by Internal Security, where he died under mysterious circumstances.
His body was returned to his family bearing clear signs of torture.
Al-Labad had been a soldier in the Syrian regime's army before defecting at the start of the 2011 revolution to join the Free Syrian Army. He later sought asylum in Germany with his family, only to be killed two days after deciding to return to Syria.
Another case is that of activist Laith Al-Zoubi, who was arrested at his home on September 14, 2025, and released a week later. Now back in Syria, Al-Zoubi explains that while his initial arrest was non-violent, he was beaten and insulted upon arriving at the Sahnaya police station in rural Damascus after asking why he was detained. He was thrown into solitary confinement for seven days.
Despite informing them that he suffered from partial epilepsy and bipolar disorder and urgently needed his medication, he was denied medical care or visits from his family or lawyer. On the seventh day, he was forced to sign a document without reading it.
"I just wanted to get out and travel, and I will never return as long as this is how things are," he told The New Arab.
"It is not just my case. There are several people like me who were arbitrarily arrested and signed pledges, and I don't think I am the only one who was tortured. To this day, I do not know why I was arrested. They never informed me of the charges or interrogated me."
Calls for justice
Human rights organisations have documented arbitrary arrests, mistreatment, torture, and deaths in custody in post-Assad prisons.
Human Rights Watch's 2026 World Report cited accounts of such abuses in facilities run by transitional authorities, and the Syrian Network for Human Rights confirmed that these practices did not completely cease after the regime's fall.
Documented abuses like these, said Al Kilani, indicate that prisons remain in a dangerous transitional phase.
Legally, Syrian legislation contains provisions protecting detainees, but the problem often lies in enforcement and in the disregard for these provisions.
Ezzedine points out that the Anti-Torture Law No. 16 of 2022 explicitly penalises violence against detainees. Furthermore, the Code of Criminal Procedure guarantees a fair trial, bans violence against detainees, and upholds the presumption of innocence.
He notes that the Constitutional Declaration nullified all previous laws that granted immunity to security personnel and that violated international human rights treaties, which should serve as safeguards for detainees.
To ensure these laws are applied, Al Kilani stressed the need for a clear political and legal message that torture, beatings, insults, and the denial of medical treatment are crimes, not minor administrative errors.
He proposes closing all secret or unregistered detention centres, creating a unified national registry of detainees, and installing cameras in detention corridors.
Crucially, he suggests that medical services in prisons should fall under the technical and administrative jurisdiction of the Ministry of Health, rather than the Ministry of Interior, thereby allowing doctors to document injuries and order hospital transfers without pressure from security.
He also calls for permanent, qualified paramedics and binding protocols for critical conditions like haemophilia, diabetes, epilepsy, and heart disease.
These recommendations align with the demands of the postponed Damascus protest.
According to Zeidan, their sit-in was delayed in the hope that their demands would be met. These demands emphasise the strict criminalisation of torture, truth and accountability, the protection of detainees' rights, security sector reform, and human rights training for security personnel to ensure these practices do not return.
"For us in civil society, our role is to monitor the authorities' performance and not allow the legitimisation or justification of any violation under any pretext," said Zeidan.
"We will continue to apply pressure through all legislative and civil means, and we are currently preparing for field and legal mobilisation coinciding with the International Day of the Victims of Enforced Disappearances on August 30 to send a message that human dignity is a red line and the Syrian people will not be humiliated."
Mawada Bahah is an independent Syrian journalist with bylines in local, regional and international outlets

Five Kyiv Regional Council deputies were served with suspicion notices over a scheme involving budget funds, says the Prosecutor General
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
13:15:09 EEST
19:15:09 KST

Five Kyiv Regional Council deputies were served with suspicion notices over a scheme involving budget funds, says the Prosecutor General
Kyiv • UNN
Five deputies and four relatives are suspected of misappropriating funds from the “Care” program. Investigators allege the use of fictitious documents and personal expenditures.
Five deputies of the Kyiv Regional Council have been notified of suspicion of fraud involving budget funds through a scheme connected with the "Care" program, Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko said on Thursday on social media, UNN reports.
"Care" for their own: five deputies of the Kyiv Regional Council notified of suspicion of fraud involving budget funds
He noted that the "Care" program was created for people who genuinely need assistance: families of persons and children with disabilities, people facing difficult life circumstances and those affected by the war, veterans, military personnel, and families of fallen defenders. During 2021–2025, approximately UAH 384 million in budget funds was allocated for its implementation.
"I remember well how much effort it took to secure funding for this program when I headed the Kyiv Regional Military Administration. Every hryvnia had to work for those who truly needed support. And indeed, many deputies conscientiously performed their duties, communicated with people, determined their needs in difficult life circumstances, and genuinely helped," Kravchenko said.
"However, there were also those who, according to the investigation, turned the assistance mechanism into a scheme for personal enrichment. It was established that some of the budget funds under the "Care" program were received not by those for whom it had been created, but by relatives and close associates of certain deputies of the Kyiv Regional Council," the Prosecutor General noted.
According to him, "the scheme was simple." "Fictitious medical documents were prepared in the names of relatives. Based on them, the deputies applied for material assistance payments. At the same time, the recipients had no real need for treatment or social support. The money received from the budget was spent on aesthetic medicine services, the purchase of expensive cars, and other personal needs. In some cases, part of the assistance was returned to the deputies – tens of thousands of hryvnias were transferred directly to their personal bank cards," the Prosecutor General reported.
"Today, under the procedural guidance of the Prosecutor General's Office, five deputies of the Kyiv Regional Council and four of their relatives have been notified of suspicion," Kravchenko said. "Depending on their roles, their actions were qualified as organizing, carrying out, and aiding fraud committed on a large and especially large scale, including by an organized group – Parts 2, 3, and 5 of Article 27 and Parts 4 and 5 of Article 190 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine."
The investigation is ongoing. Other possible participants in the scheme are being identified, he added.
"Budget programs are created to help people, not to enrich those who have access to the distribution of funds. When money intended for people in difficult circumstances is directed to "their own," and part of it is subsequently returned to deputies, this is no longer "Care." It is fraud involving budget funds," the Prosecutor General emphasized.

Russia is preparing for the possible consequences of a new mobilization – the DIU and the FIS
Kyiv • UNN
Intelligence reports that the Russian Federation is preparing for a new mobilization and strengthening coercive measures. The decision may be made after the elections on September 18–20.
The Russian leadership is preparing measures in case of the social and economic consequences of tightening the martial regime. This information from the Main Intelligence Directorate and the Foreign Intelligence Service was published on the website of the Office of the President, reports UNN.
Details
The Russian leadership is preparing a set of forceful response measures to address the possible negative social and economic consequences of transferring cities and regions to a stricter martial regime. In internal Russian documents, the need for an additional wave of mobilization is justified by a significant increase in dissatisfaction with the war in the regions (dissatisfaction rates reach 69%) and, accordingly, a decrease in the number of people willing to voluntarily sign a contract
According to intelligence information, the greatest problems with recruiting contract soldiers are being recorded in the Oryol and Vladimir regions, as well as in Dagestan. In addition, a trend toward a further decline in the figures is being recorded in many other Russian regions.
Compared with 2025, in some regions the number of debtors, special contingents among convicts and criminal elements, migrants, and other categories that for a long time formed the main pool for contract recruitment to serve in the Russian army and participate in the war has decreased by 30–40%. The campaign to recruit students, in which the absolute majority of Russian higher education institutions was involved, has failed
The Russian leadership also plans to strengthen the personal responsibility of regional authorities and expand the powers of law enforcement agencies. Thus, a system for serving electronic mobilization orders is already in operation in the russian federation, and additional coercive measures are also being developed.
A ban on leaving russia, obtaining loans, buying / selling real estate, cancellation of a driver's license, blocking funds in bank accounts, and so on. At enterprises, the staffing of mobilization work and military registration departments is being expanded. As of the end of July 2026, more than 2.5 thousand new vacancies for staffing the aforementioned mobilization units at enterprises had already been posted on electronic employment platforms
According to the Main Intelligence Directorate of the Ministry of Defense and the Foreign Intelligence Service, the Russian leadership will most likely make a decision on a new mobilization after the "elections" to the State Duma of the russian federation, scheduled for September 18–20 this year.
To remind
Russian military personnel across the country are conducting exercises to test readiness for a possible new wave of mobilization, but the Kremlin has not yet made a corresponding decision.

Wrocław councillors approve resolution condemning attacks on Ukrainians
Wrocław city councillors have approved a resolution condemning ethnically motivated violence following a heated debate and remarks about "Ukrainians' ingratitude".
Source: Polish news portal Onet, as reported by European Pravda
Details: The draft resolution, submitted by councillors from the Left Forward (Lewicy Naprzód) group, condemned the recent wave of "aggression, hatred and ethnically motivated violence". It also stressed that the councillors oppose "any violence, regardless of the ethnicity of the perpetrator or victim".
"Everyone who has chosen Wrocław as their home and place to live is welcome here, regardless of ethnicity," the resolution states.
The resolution lists a number of incidents in Wrocław, including an attack by three men on a Ukrainian couple and a violent knife attack on a Polish woman by a Ukrainian man. During the debate, councillors also mentioned a recent bottle attack on a Belarusian taxi driver.
Councillors from the right-wing Law and Justice party attempted to add an amendment registering their protest against "generalised accusations of aggression, xenophobia or hatred on ethnic grounds against Poles, Polish women and the local Wrocław community". It also called on the government and Sejm to "immediately regulate the status of Ukrainian citizens of conscription age" who are in Poland without a valid permit, "so that they can return to their homeland and begin their service".
Law and Justice representative Sławomir Śmigielski, who presented the amendment, mentioned the enormous amount of aid Poland has provided to Ukraine. "And what did we get in return? Enormous ingratitude. President Zelenskyy has named a military unit after the heroes of the UPA. We believe this is a slap in the face for Poland and the Polish people," he said.
Robert Suligowski, a councillor from the Left Forward group, said Ukrainians living in Wrocław cannot be held responsible for the actions of the Ukrainian government. "These people expect our support; they should feel at home here. We should be greeting them with smiles and flowers, not knives and bottles," he said.
The debate was closed, although not all the councillors had an opportunity to speak. The council eventually adopted the resolution. Twenty-four councillors voted in favour, and Śmigielski of the Law and Justice party voted against. Six councillors abstained.

Nepalese rescue teams searched devastated areas Thursday for more than 1,300 people still missing a day after flash floods and landslides along the Nepal-Tibet border killed at least 353 and swept away entire villages.
Homes were engulfed and vehicles tossed around by the tsunami-like rumble of water and mud that struck villages and towns Wednesday morning on the path of two rivers, Bhote Koshi and Trishuli.
Many of the missing are foreign tourists, including scores of Hindu pilgrims to Tibet's sacred snow-capped Mount Kailash.
According to the U.S. Geological Survey, the disaster was caused by a glacial collapse that sent forth an overwhelming flow of icy debris.
Emergency teams were racing to evacuate survivors from affected zones, fearing new flash floods.
Nepali soldiers used sniffer dogs to search for bodies buried under thick grey sludge.
"Everything is finished," Omkar Joshi, 35, a Nepali customs agent rescued from a hilltop in the border town of Timure, told Agence France-Presse (AFP).
"It is a giant graveyard. All that is left are sand and pebbles, soaked red by human blood."
Nepali police said they had recovered 353 bodies.
Another 823 people, including 517 foreign tourists, were out of contact in the country. Beijing says 100 Chinese citizens are missing in Nepal.
In China, state media said the "mudslide disaster" at the Gyirong Port in Tibet killed three people, while 558 people, including 260 foreigners, are missing.
Chinese Premier Li Qiang visited the area Thursday, state media said, to oversee "emergency rescue and relief work, and to visit rescue workers and affected people."
In Nepal, rescuers waded through mud and sludge to look for survivors after floodwaters buried the lower floors of multi-story buildings.
Prime Minister Balendra Shah, who urged the Himalyan nation to "stand together" hours after the disaster, visited some of the hardest-hit areas Thursday.
Shah told local authorities to "provide immediate relief to displaced families" and to open blocked roads, his office said in a statement.
The foreigners out of contact were from 30 different countries, including Indians and others from Australia, Britain, Malaysia, the Netherlands, Portugal, South Africa, South Korea and the United States, Nepal's tourism board said.
The sudden rush of mud and debris was "like an inland tsunami," traveling nearly 170 kilometers (100 miles) south into Nepal, said environmental historian Ruth Gamble, of Australia's La Trobe University.
Rasuwa, in the north of Nepal, was the first district to be affected, but deaths have been reported as far south as Chitwan in the south, on the border with India.
Chinese government officials in Tibet mobilized nearly 800 emergency workers, as well as sniffer dogs and speed boats to help the rescue efforts, official news agency Xinhua said.
Promises of aid and assistance came in soon after reports of the scale of the disaster.
The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies said it was dispatching emergency supplies including blankets, first aid kits, stretchers and body bags.
The U.S. Geological Survey said the flood was sparked by a glacial collapse, that caused seismic activity and the "catastrophic" downstream impacts in Nepal and Tibet.
"This event was initially reported as a magnitude 4.4 earthquake," it said, but added that the seismic recordings were analyzed and found instead to be a "glacial collapse and debris flow."
Climate change is causing glaciers to melt worldwide, increasing the risks of glacial lake floods and glacial collapses.
Fears of potential further floods remain, with water trapped by the immense piles of debris blocking the valley.
"With a blockage still lodged upstream on the Nepal-China border river, authorities warn a second flood may occur," said Qianggong Zhang, head of climate and environmental risks at the Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development.
Li Qipu, a member of China's paramilitary People's Armed Police, cited "the instability of a reservoir lake upstream" and "the narrow mountain road" as elements complicating rescue efforts.
Scores of Hindu devotees from across the world are among the hundreds missing on the border, Indian spiritual leader Sadhguru said Thursday.
They had been returning from a holy pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, on the Chinese side of the frontier, when they were caught in the floods at an immigration post.
"The entire group was there in the building," Sadhguru said in a video message to his millions of followers, weeping as he spoke from Tibet, with the anguished wails of other pilgrims heard in the background.
"This is a terrible and extraordinary event."

"The tripods can be used on various types of surfaces, including soil, concrete pads, and prepared positions. Economic Watch: Dry ports deliver Chinese inland goods more efficiently to int'l market
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
18:08:58 CST
19:08:58 KST

CHANGSHA, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- Huaihua is a humble inland city that once saw its development hindered by geographical isolation. Despite breeding world-known hybrid rice, the city, located in deep mountains in central China's Hunan Province, long found it challenging to bring its high-quality agricultural products and manufactured goods to the global market.
However, its fortunes would take a positive turn in 2019, when the city was designated as an important node on the New International Land-Sea Trade Corridor -- a key international connectivity initiative now connecting more inland parts of China to the global market.
Local goods in Huaihua, now an international dry port, can undergo the custom clearance procedure just minutes after leaving the factory.
Then, the goods are loaded onto a freight train, sent to the coastal Qinzhou Port in Guangxi about 800 km away, and transferred to ships bound for customers overseas, said Tian Ping, a manager at Hunan Litong Hengyu Electrical Cables Tech Co., Ltd.
The company Tian worked for used to serve traditionally domestic power-grid customers. But now it is eyeing expansion into Southeast Asia, Central Asia, the Middle East and Africa.
"The dry port services and faster and cheaper transportation services are advantages of Huaihua that we value," Tian said.
Tian did the math. If companies shipped goods to Indonesia via Qingdao Port in east China, the logistics cost would be about 500 yuan (about 70 U.S. dollars) higher per tonne than using the rail-sea intermodal transport service available in Huaihua.
"In international competition, key advantages ultimately come down to production and logistics costs," said Tian.
Official figures show that the number of freight train services handled by Huaihua's dry port rose from 17 in 2021 to 1,220 in 2025. Its connectivity network now comprises seven major international logistics corridors and 200 domestic and international routes, reaching 216 ports and stations in 69 countries and regions.
More inland businesses are benefiting from such economically viable logistics option via dry port as China is encouraging inland regions to grow export-oriented economy and deeply integrate in Belt and Road cooperation.
In Ganzhou, east China's Jiangxi Province, its dry port is helping connect local furniture industry with suppliers and customers across Eurasia.
Six years ago, Jiangxi Sanyou Furniture Co., Ltd. could never have imagined making significant inroads into the European market. The furniture maker's opportunity for European expansion came when a staff member from the local dry port brought a Hungarian business delegation to visit.
One company from the Hungarian delegation placed an order worth 100,000 yuan, and Sanyou shipped the furniture by China-Europe freight train.
"It took only 20 days from loading the furniture to delivering it to Hungary, less than half the time required by sea," said Zhu Hao, Sanyou's marketing general manager. "The customer was satisfied with the furniture, and we saw the benefits."
The furniture company later established stable business relationships with customers in Hungary, Germany and Poland. Its European orders reached 7.36 million yuan in 2025.
By the end of 2025, Ganzhou International Land Port had handled more than 1,700 China-Europe freight trains. The trains have transported local products, ranging from porcelain tableware and toys to fresh farm produces and new-energy vehicles, to European customers. ■

Singapore launches liquid cooling standard for tropical data centers
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
18:08:30 CST
19:08:30 KST

SINGAPORE, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- Singapore has launched its standard for adopting liquid cooling technologies in tropical data centers, as the growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) drives demand for more energy-efficient digital infrastructure.
The new "Singapore Standard (SS) 726:2026 Liquid Cooling in Tropical Data Centres" is the world's first, according to a statement released Thursday.
"Tropical conditions such as high temperatures and humidity present additional challenges, including equipment corrosion, which can affect cooling efficiency and reliability," it said.
The standard equips data center operators with technical guidelines to design, deploy and operate various liquid cooling systems, manage potential risks, and integrate liquid cooling with existing air-cooled data centers.
It was jointly developed by the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) and Enterprise Singapore, through the Singapore Standards Council, in consultation with industry players.
"Liquid cooling is increasingly important to support the higher power densities required for AI and other advanced computing workloads, while improving cooling efficiency," said Aileen Chia, deputy chief executive at the IMDA.
As demand for digital infrastructure grows, Singapore will continue to develop industry-relevant standards that enable the safe, reliable and energy-efficient adoption of emerging technologies, said the statement. ■

Russian Oil Giant Lukoil Halts All Main Refineries After Ukrainian Drone Attacks
Russia’s oil giant Lukoil has emergency-halted crude processing and petroleum product manufacturing at its Nizhegorodnefteorgsintez (NORSI) refinery following a fire caused by a drone strike on August 26, three industry sources reported to Reuters.
With NORSI offline, all major Russian refineries belonging to Lukoil have ceased raw material processing, following earlier shutdowns at Permnefteorgsintez on August 21 and the Volgograd refinery on July 31.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The governor of the Nizhny Novgorod region, Gleb Nikitin, confirmed a drone attack on Wednesday that damaged an industrial facility in the area, though he did not name the specific company.
According to Reuters sources, the strike damaged individual processing units, inter-shop communications, and general plant utility systems. The sources were unable to provide a timeline for repairing the damage or resuming refining operations at NORSI.
NORSI ranks as Russia’s fourth-largest refinery by crude processing volume and second by gasoline production, with an annual capacity exceeding 15 million metric tons of crude oil.
The facility is capable of producing roughly 5 million metric tons of gasoline, over 5 million metric tons of diesel fuel, more than 2 million metric tons of fuel oil, and around 0.5 million metric tons of road bitumen per year.
The August 26 disruption follows multiple recent shutdowns at NORSI caused by drone strikes, with previous processing halts recorded on July 2, June 24, May 20, and April 5.
Following the production shutdown, Lukoil did not put up wholesale lots of motor gasoline, diesel fuel, or other petroleum products from the NORSI refinery for sale on the St. Petersburg International Mercantile Exchange on Wednesday.
According to satellite imagery analysis from the Dnipro Osint project on August 25, 2026, Russia’s LUKOIL-Permnefteorgsintez oil refinery lost approximately 86% of its primary crude-processing capacity—totaling roughly 11.3 million tons of crude oil per year—following Ukrainian drone strikes more than 1,500 kilometers from the border.
Several key atmospheric-vacuum distillation units sustained severe damage, including the AVT-5 unit with an annual capacity of 4.53 million tons, where distillation columns and crude oil dehydration systems were critically hit.
Additional repair work and crane activity were observed at the AVT-4 unit, which processes 4.94 million tons annually, while the AVT-1 unit, capable of handling 1.83 million tons per year, previously suffered a fire during the attack.

On July 29, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy offered to send specialists to help France battle massive wildfires that had burned across the country's southwestern regions for several days.
During a phone call with French President Emmanuel Macron, Zelenskyy noted that Ukraine was always ready to assist its allies, even while continuing to fight Russian aggression. The catastrophic blazes had already destroyed tens of thousands of hectares, forced widespread evacuations, and reportedly approached strategic industrial facilities producing rocket engines, missile components, and Rafale fighter jets.
Additionally, both leaders discussed diplomatic next steps following Zelenskyy's visit to Washington, as well as joint preparations for the upcoming winter, including air defense supplies and energy equipment.
