Malaria outbreak kills two workers at Germany’s busiest airport
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
10:06:47 UTC
19:06:47 KST

Malaria outbreak kills two workers at Germany’s busiest airport
Two employees at Germany’s Frankfurt Airport have died in a rare malaria outbreak caused by infected mosquitoes believed to have been accidentally brought in by plane from a malaria-endemic country.
The outbreak began in early July, according to the Frankfurt Public Health Department. The first worker died shortly afterward, with the malaria diagnosis confirmed posthumously. Authorities traced the outbreak to the airport, where operator Fraport set traps and captured several mosquitoes, sending them for genetic analysis to determine their origin. Staff were advised to seek medical attention if symptoms developed.
In mid-July, the Robert Koch Institute (RKI), Germany’s federal disease-control agency, confirmed four cases among airport employees.
“The affected individuals fell ill between July 4 and 6, 2026,” the RKI wrote in its Epidemiological Bulletin. “It is assumed that the infection was transmitted by an infected Anopheles mosquito imported by plane.”
Citing medical sources, local media later reported that a total of six male workers, largely in jobs handling luggage, had been infected.
On Wednesday, Frankfurt health authorities announced that a second infected worker had died. They insisted, however, that “for the population of Frankfurt, the risk is considered very, very low.”
“The disease is not transmissible from person to person but is always transmitted by mosquitoes,” the authorities said in a statement to German media. They did not confirm the total number of cases but said those affected were receiving treatment.
Frankfurt health chief Peter Tinnemann similarly sought to reassure residents, telling DPA news agency that “the risk to the Frankfurt population is insignificant.”
Malaria is a potentially fatal disease caused by Plasmodium parasites spread by infected female Anopheles mosquitoes. It typically causes fever, chills, headaches and fatigue, while severe cases can lead to organ failure, seizures and coma. The most dangerous form, malaria tropica, can become life-threatening within 24 hours if undetected, though malaria is generally considered preventable and curable with early treatment.
The disease is concentrated mainly in tropical regions, particularly sub-Saharan Africa. The latest WHO data shows an estimated 610,000 people died from malaria worldwide in 2024 out of roughly 282 million cases – around 9 million more infections than the previous year. More than half of the deaths occurred in Nigeria, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and Niger.
Malaria cases in Germany normally involve travelers who were infected in endemic countries. In rare cases, however, infected mosquitoes can be carried into the country aboard aircraft, including in luggage, and then bite people on the plane or at the airport – a phenomenon known as “airport malaria.” Europe’s last documented airport-acquired case also occurred at Frankfurt Airport in 2023, according to the RKI.

US Democrats increasingly oppose arming Israel: poll
Unknown

2026-08-27
10:05:05 UTC

Breadcrumb
US Democratic voters are rapidly shifting on Israel, favour presidential candidate opposing arms
There has been a significant shift within the US Democratic Party towards Israel, according to a recent poll that found an overwhelming majority of Democratic voters in the first six states to hold presidential primaries in 2028 would support electing a presidential candidate who pledges to halt military aid to Israel and impose an arms embargo on it.
The poll by the Policy Project at the Institute for Middle East Understanding with YouGov surveyed about 4,000 likely voters in the Democratic primaries in South Carolina, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Mexico, Michigan and Virginia, with a margin of error of plus or minus two percentage points.
The significance of the poll appears to lie in the fact that it extends to some states that do not have Arab and Muslim communities capable of influencing the course of elections, compared with the 2024 presidential election, in which Arab-American voters emerged as an influential bloc in states such as Michigan.
The results showed that most of Arab-Americans did not vote for presidential candidate Kamala Harris as punishment for her position on the genocide in Gaza. It also extends to states that predominantly vote Republican, such as South Carolina.
The shift in the general mood does not mean that this issue will determine the choice of the Democratic presidential candidate in 2028. But, it shows how Democratic voters view US military aid to Israel and the US position of providing it with unconditional support at the expense of Palestinian rights.
It should be noted that the party's presidential candidate is chosen through voters casting ballots for their preferred candidate in each state. Each candidate receives many delegates based on the proportion of votes they receive in each state, who pledge to support the candidate who selected them as delegates.
At the Democratic National Convention before the election, they vote to select the candidate. If no one secures a majority in the first round, senior delegates, including former presidents, state governors and members of Congress, vote in the second round. They account for about 15% of the delegates.
There are about 4,696 delegates to the party's national convention, including 3,949 pledged delegates and 747 known as senior delegates.
Some 75% of likely voters in New Hampshire, New Mexico and Michigan preferred a candidate who would prevent weapons from being sent to Israel, as did 74% in Nevada, 66% in Virginia and 65% in South Carolina.
Between 4% and 6% preferred a candidate who would send weapons to Israel.
Asked whether reducing US support for Israel would play a role in their vote, 65% of Michigan voters, 63% in New Hampshire, 61% in Nevada, 59% in New Mexico, 55% in Virginia and 46% in South Carolina answered "yes".
Some 70% in New Hampshire and New Mexico supported imposing US sanctions on Israel, compared with 68% in Nevada and Michigan, 61% in Virginia and 49% in South Carolina.
Meanwhile, 80% of likely voters in Michigan said they believed Israel was committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, compared with 78% in New Hampshire and Nevada, 76% in New Mexico, 72% in Virginia and 57% in South Carolina.
Reasons behind the shift
In this context, Dr Edmund Ghareeb, a professor of political science at American University in Washington, DC, listed the reasons for the shift in Democratic voters' mood, foremost among them Israel committing genocide in Gaza, which was broadcast publicly on social media; its attacks on Lebanon; and its crackdown on the student movement on university campuses over Gaza.
"There has been a major change in the position of Democratic voters, particularly in states with Democratic majorities," Dr Ghareeb told TNA.
He noted that most Americans sympathised with Israel following 7 October 2023, when the Hamas-led "Al-Aqsa Flood operation" took place, but Israeli policies, attacks on civilians, the commission of genocide, attacks on Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, the expulsion of residents and Christians from their homes, and the destruction in southern Lebanon all contributed to changing the positions of Democrats and independents, according to Ghareeb.
He said the US administration's handling of university student protests over Gaza, the dispersal of those protests, the arrests of students, and restrictions imposed on the right to protest and freedom of expression all significantly affected how American society viewed the issue, particularly students and young people under 35.
He pointed out that the decline in support for arming Israel had extended to a proportion of American Jews, who had begun adopting positions against arming Israel that did not align with Democratic political leaders.
He cited New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani receiving 33% of the vote among New York Jews, adding that rising food and petrol prices and their impact on the middle and ordinary classes because of the US-Israeli war on Iran had also had a significant effect on both Democrats and Republicans.
Ghareeb warned that this change in public opinion may not last long if there is no effective organisation to capitalise on this shift in voters' views and if new currents within the Democratic Party, such as progressives, fail to make significant use of the change.
He said the Gaza issue and its spread on social media, as well as Israeli policies, had pushed progressives to change their positions, reject the genocide and benefit from the movement on US streets.
"We see a split within both the Democratic and Republican parties, and even if President Donald Trump has control over the Republican Party, he is losing between 20% and 25% of his overall supporters, which represents a severe blow to him," he said.
He attributed this to the presence of Republican figures who oppose wars, such as Thomas Massie, Tucker Carlson and Marjorie Taylor Greene.

Bulgaria will get seven minehunter ships from Belgium and Netherlands to protect Black Sea
SOFIA, Aug 27 - Bulgaria has approved the purchase of seven minehunter ships from Belgium and the Netherlands, as the NATO alliance seeks to bolster its capabilities to clear naval mines and secure shipping routes in the Black Sea, local media reported on Thursday.
Along with Romania and Turkey, Bulgaria agreed at a NATO summit in July to expand a joint task force that clears mines floating in the Black Sea to include missions to protect critical infrastructure.
The three NATO states, which share the Black Sea with Georgia, Russia and Ukraine, formed the de-mining task force in 2024 to counter the threat of floating mines after Moscow's invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Under a sale agreement with the Netherlands approved by the Bulgarian parliament on Wednesday, Bulgaria will receive three ships equipped to seek and destroy mines and mine-like objects, while a separate transfer agreement between Belgium, the Netherlands and Bulgaria covers another four vessels.
The Netherlands has committed to restoring the technical capabilities and increasing the operational capacity of three ships before transferring ownership, with Bulgaria paying for repair and restoration work to bring all seven vessels to NATO operational readiness standards.
"These mine hunters are particularly necessary. We have three of the same type, and with these seven we will complement and further enhance our capabilities,” Defence Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said before lawmakers approved the deal.
“Bulgaria is part of the mine countermeasures group established together with our colleagues from Turkey and Romania, and it is working in excellent coordination to clear the maritime areas of the three countries.”
A memorandum of understanding covering the acquisition also includes crew training, spare parts and additional equipment. REUTERS

Famed U.S. drone maker accused of using Ukrainian drone footage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
10:03:13 UTC
19:03:13 KST

- A Ukrainian defense expert said AeroVironment's Switchblade 600 promotional video may show footage of a Ukrainian RAM-2X drone strike instead.
- He pointed to a targeting reticle repainted green and repositioned in the video as evidence, while also crediting Switchblade drones for a separate confirmed strike.
A Ukrainian defense expert has flagged an apparent discrepancy in a promotional video from American drone maker AeroVironment, saying footage the company presented as a successful Switchblade 600 strike actually shows the Ukrainian-made RAM-2X strike drone in action.
Bohdan Miroshnychenko, military analyst and editor-in-chief of the Ukrainian defense outlet Oboronka, raised the discrepancy in a post analyzing AeroVironment’s promotional video, which showcases the Switchblade 600 loitering munition’s use in Ukraine.
Miroshnychenko compared frames from the AeroVironment video against footage released separately by Ukrainian military personnel from a command post and a report from Ukraine’s Security Service, the SBU.
“It seems that the American manufacturer of the legendary Switchblade strike drones, in its promotional video, presented a strike by Ukrainian RAM-2X drones as the work of their own product,” Miroshnychenko wrote.
He pointed to a specific visual detail as evidence: the targeting reticle shown in the footage. A red reticle, which Miroshnychenko said is characteristic of the target-lock symbology used by the RAM-2X’s guidance system, appears repainted green in the AeroVironment video and shifted closer to the center of the vehicle shown on screen.
“The red targeting reticle, characteristic of target lock by the autonomous guidance system, was repainted the branded green and shifted closer to the center of the vehicle,” Miroshnychenko wrote.
Miroshnychenko framed the apparent mix-up as a sign that some Ukrainian-made weapons have reached a level of battlefield performance that allows them to be marketed internationally alongside established American systems.
“Another symptom that some Ukrainian weapons can already be brightly advertised with classic music under a beat and sold on the global market on par with American ‘hits,'” Miroshnychenko wrote. “Of course, as soon as we saturate our own Defense Forces with them and put things in order with the regulatory framework.”
Miroshnychenko also credited the Switchblade 600 for a separate, verified result in the same SBU operation he referenced. He said Switchblade drones were used effectively in that strike, which destroyed two Buk surface-to-air missile systems, two Tor-M2 systems, a Strela system and a Tunguska air defense system.
RAM-2X is a Ukrainian-developed strike drone. Switchblade 600 is a loitering munition built by AeroVironment that has been fielded by Ukrainian forces and, separately, by the U.S. Army, which has ordered additional units under an existing contract this year.

Nepal-Tibet floods: What is a glacial collapse, how common is it?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
10:01:48 UTC
19:01:48 KST

Nepal-Tibet floods: What is a glacial collapse, how common is it?
More than 165 people are killed, with thousands missing, in floods triggered by a huge glacial collapse near Nepal-China border.
More than 1,500 people are missing across Nepal and China’s Tibet, including more than 800 foreign tourists, after rare flash glacial-lake outburst floods submerged towns and communities under a sludge of mud and water.
More than 270 people have been killed, but officials say the toll is expected to rise as rescue teams attempt to reach farther areas that have been cut off by the floods, with several key bridges and highways also devastated.
With skies still clear above the Nepal-China border, and no rain pouring, officials earlier believed that a magnitude 4.4 earthquake could have triggered the downstream floods.
However, several experts and the United States Geological Survey have confirmed that “the seismic event” was a consequence of “a glacial collapse and debris flow that caused subsequent catastrophic impacts downstream” – rather than the other way around.
So, what is a glacial collapse, and is this a catastrophic outcome of worsening climate change?
What is glacial collapse?
In simple terms, a glacial collapse is the detachment of a large mass of glacier ice from its bed – sometimes involving millions of cubic metres of ice, rock, and water – that can transform into a highly mobile ice-rich avalanche or debris flow.
This collapse is not a formally defined scientific term in glaciology, but is widely used to describe the event.
Earth System Science Data, an international open-access scientific journal, describes this as gravity-driven failures of glacier ice on mountain slopes, including ice avalanches, glacier detachments, and rock-ice avalanches.
An initial study of Planet Labs satellite imagery showed a landslide of ice and rock unleashed a flood carrying debris in the Lhende River in Tibet, about 20km (12 miles) northeast of the Nepal-China border crossing in Rasuwagadhi, Nepal’s disaster management officials said on X.
Television images showed collapsed homes, floating cars and a metal bridge being washed away, while witnesses said the waters engulfed entire villages.
What happened in Nepal and Tibet?
The disaster struck the mountainous Nepal-Tibet border region, with some of the worst damage in Nepal’s Rasuwa district, immediately south of the Chinese border.
The initial surge entered the Lhende Khola, which feeds into the Bhote Koshi and then the Trishuli river, carrying floodwaters south through Nepal. Water levels in the Trishuli reportedly rose by as much as 9 metres (27ft) in just 30 minutes.
Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said the “glacier-inclusive flood” occurred in the Lhende River due to “an ice-rock avalanche on the Nepali side”, according to Prakash Pokharel, a geologist at the authority.
Vikram Gupta, who specialises in engineering geology and teaches at Sikkim University in India’s northeast state bordering Nepal, said it was “confirmed that a substantial portion of that glacier snout collapsed to initiate the event – probably including or entraining a fair amount of rock and sediment”.
Earth scientist Dan Shugar, an associate professor at the University of Calgary, said the imagery seemed to show that a large amount of snow had melted in the 24 hours before the disaster. “The lower part of a glacier broke off at about 5,200 metres and crashed onto the valley floor about 1,200 metres below,” Shugar said.
The disaster comes against a backdrop of rapid warming and glacial loss across the Himalayas.
Glaciers across the Hindu Kush Himalaya mountain range – which spans Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, China, India, Myanmar, Nepal and Pakistan – lost ice 65 percent faster between 2011 and 2020 than during the previous decade.
Nepal’s glaciers – sandwiched between two major carbon emitters, India and China – have lost close to one-third of their ice volume in roughly three decades due to global warming, the United Nations said in 2023.
“It was a huge gush of mud coming straight towards us,” said Keshav Prasad Baral, a 68-year-old survivor being treated in a Nepali hospital.
“As it got closer, it kept rising higher and higher. When I saw it enter our home, I tried to grab my wife’s hand and take her to the terrace. But she was swept away by the mud.”
A helicopter ferried him to safety four hours later. “My wife is still somewhere beneath the mud,” he added. “She’s gone.”
Did global warming cause it?
Experts note it is too soon to tell conclusively if global warming and worsening climate change were the cause behind the devastating floods.
The so-called glacial lake outburst floods (GLOF) – the sudden and catastrophic release of vast volumes of water from melting glacier-fed lakes – are among the dangers associated with such events in the region’s extreme topography.
Dorothy Heinrich, a researcher at the United Kingdom’s University of Reading, said GLOFs were among the hazards posed by a warming planet in the region.
“We do know what climate change trends look like in the Himalayas. There is high confidence of more heatwaves, glacial retreat, permafrost reduction, these sorts of things that can drive things like landslides and glacial outburst floods,” she said.
Hatim Sharif, a hydrologist at the University of Texas San Antonio, said the one thing that struck him was the lack of rainfall beforehand. “That defeats essentially every operational flood warning system in the world,” he said.
By the time you see the mud flow coming, it’s too late. “Running will not help,” nor will trying to flee by vehicle, Sharif said, because the mud and water moving at high speed form a lethal combination “like liquid concrete”.
Are glacial collapses common?
There have been a handful of instances of glacial collapse over the last decade, where scientists and geologists see them as highly unusual and rare.
Tibet has emerged as a hotspot for some of the world’s largest documented glacier collapses, although scientists say their causes are site-specific.
In July 2016, the lower part of a valley glacier in Tibet’s Aru Range – far western Tibet, near the Pangong Tso region – detached, sending about 68 million cubic metres of ice down the mountain and killing nine herders and hundreds of animals. Two months later, a nearby glacier collapsed, releasing about 83 million cubic metres of ice. NASA called it a rare occurrence.
Two years later, this time in Tibet’s Sedongpu Basin, two ice-rock avalanches occurred, spilling large quantities of glacier ice and debris into the Yarlung Tsangpo River, the upper Brahmaputra. Here, the debris blocked the river and created a dangerous temporary lake, showing how a glacier collapse can turn into a major downstream flood hazard.
In November 2022, about 40 million cubic metres of glacier ice detached from the Bukadaban Feng glacier in the Kunlun Mountains, and an ice avalanche crashed into a lake below, creating a 13-meter (42ft) high wave, according to analysis by the European Space Agency. It initially went completely unseen due to the site’s extremely remote location.
In India’s northern state of Uttarakhand in 2018, about 27 million cubic metres of rock and glacier ice collapsed from the steep north face of Ronti Peak, killing more than 200 people. But it was seen more as a rock avalanche, coupled with ice, rather than a straight-up glacier collapse.
In May last year, in Switzerland’s Blatten, a cascade of rock, soil, and ice roared down the mountainside in a vast cloud of dust, burying much of the village of Blatten. Experts have said the collapse was linked to climate change in the Alps.

Brazilian study provides objective data on breast proportion preferences
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
10:00:50 UTC
19:00:50 KST

A recent survey of medical students reveals a strong preference for symmetrical breast proportions and centrally located, smaller areolas. The findings aim to offer plastic surgeons objective data to guide patients seeking cosmetic breast procedures. The research was published in Revista Brasileira de Cirurgia Plástica.
Plastic surgeons regularly perform procedures to alter breast size and shape. However, surgical literature contains very few objective measurements regarding what constitutes an aesthetically pleasing breast. This lack of concrete data can make it difficult for doctors to advise patients and select the most appropriate surgical techniques.
Cosmetic surgery relies heavily on defined standards of beauty and proportion. For example, facial procedures often use precise geometric angles to plan a rhinoplasty. Gluteal surgeries follow established waist-to-hip ratios to produce consistent results. Historically, breast surgery has lacked similar standardized guidelines.
Researchers have long debated the ideal aesthetic parameters for breast reconstruction and augmentation. Earlier surgical pioneers proposed various proportional rules to help doctors achieve harmonious results. For instance, the renowned Brazilian surgeon Ivo Pitanguy helped establish early aesthetic principles for breast reconstruction, focusing heavily on proportional parameters.
Other specialists emphasized the geometry of the breast and the specific distances between the breast poles, which are the upper and lower halves of the breast mound. Previous studies have often suggested that a bottom-heavy breast is the most popular ideal. In these models, the lower pole carries slightly more volume than the upper pole.
To gather more contemporary and specific data, a team of researchers from the Universidade de Passo Fundo in Brazil initiated a new survey. Lead author Luís Gustavo Ramos Raupp Pereira and colleagues sought to evaluate visual preferences among medical students. They wanted to see if variables like gender influenced these aesthetic ideals. They aimed to provide updated information that could assist surgeons in preoperative planning.
The researchers conducted an observational, cross-sectional study. This type of research analyzes data from a specific population at a single point in time. They used an online questionnaire to gather responses.
The team sent the survey via institutional email to medical students at their university between May and September 2024. The questionnaire was based on parameters from previous international research on breast aesthetics. It asked participants to review a series of images and select their preferred breast shapes.
These visual aids displayed different volumetric ratios between the upper and lower poles of the breast. The options included a 40/60 ratio, a 50/50 ratio, and a 60/40 ratio. The images also showed variations in the position and size of the nipple and areola, known as the nipple-areola complex.
Alongside the visual choices, the researchers collected basic demographic information. They asked participants for their age and gender. They also inquired about education levels and physical exercise habits.
Participants were asked whether they had ever undergone breast surgery, such as augmentation or reduction. In total, 239 medical students completed the survey. The study group included 173 women and 66 men. The vast majority of respondents had no history of breast procedures, with only about eight percent reporting previous surgeries.
The group was also highly active. Nearly 90 percent reported participating in regular physical exercise. Almost half of the respondents stated they exercised up to five times a week.
The survey revealed a strong overall preference for symmetrical breast shapes. When asked to choose the most pleasing distribution of volume, 61.1 percent of participants selected a 50/50 ratio. This indicates they preferred an equal distribution of tissue between the upper and lower halves of the breast.
About 30 percent of the respondents preferred a 40/60 ratio. In this shape, the bottom half is slightly fuller than the top half. Less than 10 percent of the students preferred a 60/40 ratio, which features a fuller upper half.
Preferences regarding the placement of the nipple and areola were also consistent across the surveyed group. Nearly 60 percent of the students preferred a centrally located nipple-areola complex. About 26 percent chose a placement angled upward by 20 degrees.
Only 14 percent of the respondents favored a laterally positioned nipple. A lateral position means the nipple sits closer to the outside of the chest. When evaluating the size of the areola and nipple, the results leaned heavily toward smaller proportions.
Nearly 84 percent of all respondents selected the image depicting a smaller areola and nipple combination. Only 16 percent of the participants preferred the larger areola option presented in the survey. The researchers also compared the responses of male and female students to see if gender played a role in aesthetic preferences.
They found that the differences between men and women were not statistically significant. Both groups predominantly favored the 50/50 volume ratio, central nipple placement, and smaller areola size. Among women, roughly 63 percent preferred the symmetrical volume ratio. By comparison, 56 percent of men chose the exact same option.
Female respondents did show a slight preference for smaller areolas compared to men. About 85 percent of women chose the smaller size, versus 79 percent of men. However, the overall trends aligned closely between both sexes, showing a unified perspective on breast aesthetics.
The study authors noted a few limitations to their research. The sample size consisted entirely of medical students from a single university in southern Brazil. This specific population may possess a technical understanding of human anatomy.
This academic background could influence their visual preferences, potentially separating their views from standard cultural trends. Additionally, the participant group was unbalanced. The survey featured substantially more women than men.
This uneven distribution could affect how well the male preferences represent the broader population. A wider group of male respondents might have yielded slightly different percentages. The researchers suggest that future studies should include a broader variety of participants from different backgrounds and regions.
The study, “Breast Esthetic Preferences from the Perspective of Medical Students: A Cross-Sectional Study,” was authored by Luís Gustavo Ramos Raupp Pereira, Laura Librelotto Rubin Rodrigues, Maria Eduarda Caldato, Mateus Eduardo Giovelli, Karoline Scussel Ruhmke, Ana Luíza Fontana, and Eduardo Madalosso Zanin.

Why We Love Watching Robots Fail
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
10:00:03 UTC
19:00:03 KST

When Tiangong Ultra unofficially smashed Usain Bolt’s 100m world record in Beijing, China, unballetically flailing past the finish line in 8.86 seconds, he did not flash an Olympian grin down the camera lens. In fact, he has no face. He is a headless robot.
Ultra, the work of the Beijing Humanoid Robot Innovation Center, was competing in the penultimate day of the unapologetically dystopian World Humanoid Robot Games, which has been hosting 666 teams at China’s National Speed Skating Oval. At this event, more than 2,000 robots are put to the test in track and field events (like long jump and an obstacle course); sports (like table tennis and soccer); and “scenarios” (like bricklaying and firefighting).
The event produced several eye-catching moments, including when humanoids beat human records at the high jump and the 400m. Just a few days before Ultra’s race, Lightning, a robot developed by phone company Honor, ran the 100m in 9.39 seconds, again thundering home quicker than Bolt.
But these tumbling records will likely be, in the pop cultural consciousness, eclipsed by something far more entertaining: tumbling robots. Along with the epic wins, there have been some seriously old-school, epic fails. One humanoid at the weightlifting event lost its balance with a weedy 15kg barbell, started jerking and slammed into the judges’ table, its helpless arms aloft, as if to say, “Why me?” Most memorably, a robot ended his dash by careering into a safety mat, Tom and Jerry style, before cartoonishly arching backward and setting on fire. Each spark was like a beautiful firework.
These slapstick scenes are deliciously satisfying. It’s deeply reassuring to watch robots fizzle out into smithereens. I myself have fond memories of watching the fire-hazard creations on Robot Wars in the U.K. (the successor to BattleBots in the U.S.) get shredded into shrapnel. This time, it’s a reassuring reminder that we can beat robot replicants at our own games.
This robot schadenfreude is fuelled by a fear of the future. Pointing out their flaws makes humanity’s finish line feel further away, even if that’s a highly unintelligent thing to think.
In many ways, this feeling can be filed next to our twisted delight in belittling generative AI. ChatGPT’s past inability to spell “strawberry” has made it an object of ridicule online. Calling AI-generated content “slop” has become a knee-jerk reaction to artificial intelligence’s catastrophic metastasisation in the creative industries.
And our collective giddiness about technical mishaps is not reserved just for AI. For instance, we love to watch the armored glass windows of the Tesla Cybertruck break. One possible reason: it shatters the illusion that the future is here and already decided. Robots surely can’t replace us if we haven’t figured out car windows yet. This feeling is magnified when they are humanoids—ersatz versions of ourselves.
Seen through a sports lens, it mirrors how I felt with the Enhanced Games. The painfully brotastic event held in Las Vegas in May allowed athletes to take performance-enhancing drugs or wear banned gear. With social media instilling a chronic fatigue for actual human achievement, technophiles are moving the goalposts; if being pumped full of steroids or titanium plates makes you more likely to beat a world record, it’s worth it. Once again though, disappointment was on show. Just a single best-ever-time, in the men’s 50m freestyle, was (unofficially) recorded by Kristian Gkolovmeev; he wore an outlawed polyurethane skinsuit. Otherwise, the non-artificially-enhanced athletes dominated the competition.
My concern: when it comes to humanoids, at least, our schadenfreude is set to be a short-lived pastime. While advanced robots are still relatively primitive, their improvement is staggering. To put it into perspective, at last year’s World Humanoid Robot Games, Ultra won the 100 meters in 21.50 seconds, much closer to Bolt’s 200m record than his 100m time. They’re only getting stronger and faster. Dunking on “clankers,” a derogatory term for clumsy robots (like this one dancing to Billie Jean), may be the most classically human response: laughing off the impending doom.
Many futurists predict that in the near future, our factories and farms and battlefields and back gardens will be filled with humanoid helpers. In 2024, Elon Musk said that by 2040 there will probably be more humanoid robots than people. And according to research by Morgan Stanley over 1 billion humanoids may be in use by 2050 and the market could be worth $5 trillion.
Spectators from afar like me, viewing the drama on our phones, will continue to watch with a sort of futuristic gallows humour. Laughing at misfortune, however spiteful it may be, leads to social bonding—in this case, as an entire species, against robots—that humans desperately need right now.
Every time a clanker goes crash, bang, wallop, and kaput, it’s a visceral reminder that we still matter. And unlike them, when faced with their destruction, I’m able to smile.

Press review: SDF plans dissolution in Syria as Bangladesh invited to join Mecca pact
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

MOSCOW, August 27. /TASS/. Greece, Cyprus and Malta are prepared to challenge the EU’s decision to intercept Russian oil tankers, while the Kurdish-led SDF announces its dissolution. Meanwhile, the Saudis invite Bangladesh to join their defense alliance with Turkey and Pakistan. These stories topped Thursday's newspaper headlines across Russia.
Izvestia: Some in EU ready to contest bloc’s decision to intercept Russian tankers
The opposition in Greece will appeal to European courts and the EU Parliament regarding the detention of ships or tankers allegedly associated with Russia as part of the Irini mission, the leader of the Greek Solution right-wing party, Kyriakos Velopoulos, told Izvestia. According to him, the European Commission's plans may lead to a direct conflict between Europe and Russia as they also damage the economic interests of Athens. Cyprus and Malta, the two EU members that have also suffered from European restrictions on shipping, may join Greece. Experts argue that the chances of halting the Irini mission are low.
Any vessel that is not registered in an EU or G7 jurisdiction and is not insured in the West can be considered suspicious. The lack of legal clarity risks creating tensions not only with Russia, but also in relations with third countries, Luxembourgish MEP Fernand Kartheiser told Izvestia.
The Greek opposition can file a lawsuit with the EU court by initiating a complaint through the European Parliament on its own or jointly with shipowners whose interests may be affected. Or else legal action could be brought to a national authority, which will then refer the case to the European Court. Yegor Sergeyev, a senior researcher at the Institute of International Studies of the Moscow State Institute of International Relations (MGIMO), told Izvestia that the prospects for a lawsuit are still highly uncertain, given Athens' economic interest. Anti-Russian sentiments prevail among members of the European Parliament, so discussing the mission's mandate in this body is important more for attracting public attention than to make decisions.
Even as the Irini mission is allowed to inspect individual suspicious vessels, its ability to detain or seize them is extremely limited, Pavel Anisimov, deputy director of the International Relations and Political Science Institute at Russian State University for the Humanities, told Izvestia. The fact that the tanker is under EU sanctions does not give the mission a universal right to detain it on the high seas. Therefore, attempts to directly seize ships will be illegal in any case, he argued.
Media: Kurdish-led SDF in Syria announces plans to dissolve
On Tuesday evening, Mazloum Abdi, the leader of the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF), announced the Kurdish-led group’s dissolution and integration into the Syrian army, SANA news agency reported. The move may mark a milestone both in the final merger of Kurdish structures in northeastern Syria with the Syrian state and in efforts to resolve the long-standing Kurdish issue in the country.
A source familiar with the situation in Syria’s northeast confirmed the departure of SDF fighters and PKK commanders from the Kurds’ compact regions in the country to Vedomosti. He also said that the integration of local Kurdish armed formations into the new Syrian army has begun.
Nikolay Sukhov, a senior researcher at the Russian Academy of Sciences’ World Economy and International Relations Institute, told Vedomosti that the SDF agreed to dissolve after it suffered a military defeat at the hands of Damascus, the risk of a new Turkish military operation in the region emerged, and Washington supported the new Syrian government led by President Ahmed al-Sharaa. However, Kurdish leaders are not prepared to disarm every SDF fighter but instead plan to dissolve the SDF as a military and political force, Sukhov explained.
Ilya Shcherbakov, a political analyst specializing in Oriental studies, told Rossiyskaya Gazeta that the developments currently taking place in Syria indicate that Damascus is seeking to establish a unified power structure and restore the country’s territorial integrity. "Consistent steps on the international arena, including the removal of the country from the list of state sponsors of terrorism, as well as the dissolution of Kurdish-led armed formations demonstrate that the current administration is working to establish a permanent model of interaction with forces that previously remained in the ‘gray zone’ in relation to government-led structures," the expert maintained.
At the same time, the fact that Kurdish formations agreed to lay down arms does not mean that potential controversies will fade away, Shcherbakov warned. "Individual cells may remain, while an integrated force may try to influence Damascus’ policies through diplomatic means, especially in matters concerning the Kurds themselves. The Kurdish question has yet to be resolved," he emphasized.
Nezavisimaya Gazeta: Bangladesh invited to join Mecca pact
Saudi Arabia, the richest member of the Mecca pact, a military bloc with Turkey and Pakistan, invited the Republic of Bangladesh to join it, Bangladesh announced. The Mecca pact is an agreement between the three Sunni Muslim-majority countries, and 90% of the population in Bangladesh identifies with this faith.
Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan signed the mutual defense pact in Mecca on August 7. Their alliance was modeled on the NATO treaty, and Turkey being a NATO member with the bloc’s second-largest army was never an obstacle. Ankara confirmed that other countries may join the trilateral alliance.
Kollol Kibria, an expert in Dacca, said Bangladesh joining the pact may potentially complicate its relations not only with India but also with China, Japan, Iran, Oman, Kuwait, the UAE, Russia, and the United States. "Even as these ties will not be severed immediately, Dacca will have to make a choice," he warned, noting that Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan may have tensions with the aforementioned nations.
Kibria described the current relationship between Bangladesh and India as extremely challenging. Both nations are seeking to improve ties. India has invited the Bangladeshi head of state to visit New Delhi, but a visit would require favorable conditions, officials in Dacca say: Sheikh Hasina, the former prime minister of Bangladesh who resigned following a student-led mass uprising in 2024, fled to India, and a court in Dacca ordered the use of lethal force against her. Bangladesh has insisted on her extradition.
"The situation with Hasina, who can certainly expect a just and unbiased consideration of her case in a court in Bangladesh, will certainly have a major impact on the country’s relations with India. And joining the Mecca pact will further worsen them, for Pakistan alone will benefit from it. China will not be happy either. As a NATO member, Turkey is allied with America, China’s main geopolitical rival," Vinay Shukla, an Indian reporter, told Nezavisimaya Gazeta. He doubted that Moscow will benefit from Bangladesh’s departure from neutrality either, given Russia’s interests in the country where it is building a nuclear power plant.
Vedomosti: Natural gas output in Russia rises 3% in January-July
In January-July, natural gas production in Russia rose by 3% from the first seven months of last year to 397 billion cubic meters, data from Rosstat showed.
Last month, LNG production also continued its upward trend, showing a 14% increase from July 2025 to 2.3 million metric tons. In January-July, LNG output rose by 12% to 20.6 million metric tons.
The increase in natural gas output in January-July was due to weather conditions and a rise in both pipeline gas and LNG exports, analysts said.
The growth in gas exports comes amid supplies to European countries through the Turkish Stream pipeline and rising LNG supplies, Sergey Kaufman, an analyst at Finam, told Vedomosti. Russian gas exports to Central Asia have also been increasing, the expert added.
Russian LNG exports are growing primarily due to supplies from the Novatek-led Arctic LNG 2 project to China, Kaufman and Igor Yushkov, an expert at the Financial University under the Russian Government, explained. LNG exports have been increasing as well amid the military conflict in the Middle East, Kaufman noted. The global LNG deficit caused by the hostilities has enabled Russian LNG plants previously affected by sanctions to increase supplies, he said.
The growth in Russian LNG output will continue until the end of the year, although it may slow down, experts say. This will contribute to higher gas production in the country this year, Yushkov believes, mostly amid demand for Russian gas in China and Central Asia. Other experts also expect an increase in Russian gas output in 2026.
Nezavisimaya Gazeta: Siberia may play a role in Russia’s new digital economy
Data centers and artificial intelligence (AI) services are becoming a key element of the new digital economy worldwide, generating significant revenue and profit. According to some estimates, global investment in data centers could exceed $1 trillion this year. Against this backdrop, the Russian market looks modest but has substantial potential, particularly in Siberia, according to participants in a business breakfast hosted by the Stolypin Club.
Finding an "alternative oil" has been a popular trend in Russia over the past two decades, said Anton Sviridenko, executive director of the Stolypin Institute for the Economy of Growth. "We cannot abandon conventional oil for the time being. However, we cannot rely on traditional commodity-based revenues only in the longer term. Therefore, the search for new sources of growth must continue. An analysis of the global market shows that the distribution of revenues and profits will change dramatically, with new digital service industries, including data centers and artificial intelligence services, accounting for a major share of those," Nezavisimaya Gazeta quoted him as saying.
Russia has potential in this area, Sviridenko argued: "We have energy resources that are crucial for scaling AI systems, as well as a climate that can be beneficial for hosting and cooling data centers."
Anton Pyzhev, who heads the laboratory of the economy of climate change and environmentally-friendly development at Siberian Federal University, said while Russia has enormous potential for AI and industry infrastructure development, the country is still lagging behind in terms of the extent to which this technology is used. "And yet, compared to most countries, Russia remains a key player: many economies cannot afford to build a similar infrastructure on the required scale," Pyzhev argued.
Denis Khleborodov, CEO and founder of Cloud X, sees potential in Eastern Siberia as he points to a relatively cold climate and affordable energy as its advantages for efficient computing. And the region’s infrastructure can serve not only as a pillar for the Russian digital economy but also as a separate export industry, he emphasized.

'Too many cases': Mexico confronts U.S. over deaths of its citizens in ICE custody
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

‘Too many cases’: Mexico confronts U.S. over deaths of its citizens in ICE custody
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Mexico’s president is escalating pressure on U.S. authorities over 17 Mexican migrants who died in ICE custody or operations.
- Mexican diplomats have filed complaints with the Justice Department, eight attorneys general and 12 district attorneys.
- Prosecutors have announced no criminal cases, underscoring Mexico’s limited standing in U.S. courts.
MEXICO CITY — As increasing numbers of migrants perish during the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has vowed to ramp up pressure on U.S. authorities to investigate the deaths.
“There are too many cases,” Sheinbaum told reporters last week, referring to 17 Mexican citizens who have died while in U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody or during ICE operations. “Our obligation is to always defend Mexicans who are in the United States or whatever part of the world.”
The growing toll prompted Sheinbaum last month to direct Mexican diplomats to file complaints with state attorneys general and district attorneys across the United States, demanding that prosecutors investigate deaths that occurred in their jurisdictions.
“We cannot turn a blind eye to the Mexicans who have died,” Sheinbaum said following the most recent fatal incident — the ICE shooting in Houston last month of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, 52, a construction contractor from Mexico who had lived in the United States for three decades.
Mexico’s new strategy represents an escalation from the country’s traditional policy of filing protests through diplomatic channels while assisting families with legal advice, paperwork and shipping remains back to Mexico.
However, to date, Mexico’s stepped-up efforts have yielded few results.
There is no public confirmation of prosecutions in any of the 17 cases, despite the entreaties of the Mexican government to the U.S. Department of Justice, eight attorneys general and 12 district attorney’s offices.
“The Americans don’t seem to be paying much attention,” said Víctor Clark, a long-time human rights advocate in Tijuana. “What Mexico is doing is basically a bureaucratic step with no real response.”
From a legal standpoint, Mexico faces an uphill battle. Mexican authorities use the word denuncias (complaints) for their actions, but Mexico cannot directly file complaints in U.S. courts in these cases. U.S. prosecutors have no mandate to respond to Mexican inquiries.
“The reality of the matter is that the Mexican government has very little standing to file complaints in the United States,” said Aaron Reichlin-Melnick, a senior fellow at the American Immigration Council, a Washington-based research and advocacy group. “A request for investigation from the Mexican government probably has a little more of an impact than a request from a random private citizen.”
At least 52 migrants — including 14 Mexican citizens — have died while in ICE custody since the beginning of the second Trump administration, according to a report in June from Human Rights Watch and Physicians for Human Rights.
In addition, at least nine people have died during reported agency operations since 2025.
ICE says it thoroughly investigates all deaths of individuals in its custody or during agency actions. Critics charge that the Trump administration fails to pursue such cases adequately.
To date, Mexico has received partial or no responses to complaints sent to the eight states where the 17 deaths of Mexican citizens occurred, Roberto Velasco, Mexican’s foreign secretary, said last week.
Attorney generals in only four states — California, Texas, Florida and Illinois — even acknowledged receipt of Mexico’s demands, Velasco said.
The single definitive state reply came from Florida’s attorney general’s office, which concurred with ICE’s findings that the death of Royer Pérez Jiménez, 19, at the Glades County Detention Center was a “presumed suicide.”
According to Velasco, Ventura County was among only three of 12 local jurisdictions contacted — along with Cook County, Ill., and Harris Country, Texas — that said it was “evaluating” Mexico’s complaint.
But Joey Buttita, spokesperson for the Ventura County district attorney’s office, said the county had received no communication from Mexico.
Ventura was the site of one of ICE’s most sensational operations — the July 10, 2025, sweep at the Glass House Farms cannabis complex in Camarillo that resulted in hundreds of arrests as masked ICE agents descended on the facility.
One worker, Jaime Alanis García, 56, originally from Mexico’s Michoacán state, was fatally injured when he fell 30 feet from a greenhouse roof.
The farmworker who suffered fatal injuries while fleeing an immigration raid in Ventura County was buried in his Mexican hometown.
A flashpoint in the controversy is the private Adelanto ICE Processing Center in San Bernardino County, where some 1,500 detainees are held. At least four Mexican citizens have died at the Adelanto facility, which is operated by the Geo Group, a Florida-based company.
Representatives of detainees at Adelanto have filed a civil class-action lawsuit alleging widespread abuse — including systemic medical neglect, inadequate food and water and mold contamination.
In July, a federal judge ordered ICE to institute sweeping changes at the Adelanto center, mandating improvements in the provision of water, food, sanitation and medical care.
Both ICE and Geo Group have denied any abuse at the facility.
“For many illegal aliens this is the best healthcare they have received their entire lives,” according to a statement from Department of Homeland Security, ICE’s parent agency ,to The Times. “All detainees are provided with proper meals, water, medical treatment, and have opportunities to communicate with their family members and lawyers.”
In March, after the fourth death of a Mexican national at Adelanto , the Mexican government vowed that it would “exhaust every legal and diplomatic avenue to bring attention to conditions” at U.S. detention centers.
Mexican diplomats in Los Angeles presented relatives of José Guadalupe Ramos Solano, 52, who, according to an ICE statement, was found “unconscious and unresponsive” on March 25 at Adelanto. He had lived for 28 years in the United States and worked at an industrial laundromat, said his widow, Antonia Tovar.
“My husband was a good person, dedicated to his kids and to his wife,” Tovar said. “I just want justice and to fight for the people who are there. I want my husband’s case to be the last one.”
The San Bernardino County district attorney’s office has received three letters from the Mexican government about the deaths of at least two detainees at the Adelanto facility, said Jacquelyn Rodriguez, spokesperson for the district attorney’s office. But no criminal complaint has been filed.
Times staff writers McDonnell and Vives reported respectively from Mexico City and Los Angeles. Special correspondent Cecilia Sánchez Vidal in Mexico City contributed.

After six months, the Iran war has reached its endgame – a costly stalemate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
09:59:13 UTC
18:59:13 KST

News analysis
After six months, the Iran war has reached its endgame – a costly stalemate
- The US and Iran are in a costly stalemate, six months after American and Israeli forces rained missiles and bombs on the Islamic Republic.
- US sanctions aim to cut Iran’s financial lifelines, but Tehran relies on countries like China and India that are not aligned with American goals.
- Rising inflation and economic hardship risk sparking unrest in Iran, but the regime uses repression to maintain control.
AI generated
BEIRUT – The Iran war has reached its endgame: a costly stalemate.
Six months after US and Israeli forces attacked Iran, killing its supreme leader and maiming his son and successor, the Iranian government is under economic siege, but it still holds power and believes it has time on its side.
A threat by US President Donald Trump to impose crippling new sanctions on Iran faces a fundamental problem: Tehran is betting he will not take the final step to break the stalemate by aggressively enforcing secondary sanctions on the countries keeping its economy afloat, foremost among them China and India.
Washington’s latest measures, announced on Aug 24, mark a new phase in the conflict that began on Feb 28, shifting the battlefield from missiles and air strikes to Iran’s oil revenues, banks and trading partners.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has said the United States will cut off the financial lifelines sustaining Iran’s economy, while a US-led naval blockade restricts Tehran’s oil exports and access to hard currency.
“The (Trump) administration is groping in a sort of desperate fashion to try to find a pathway out of this,” said Aaron David Miller, a former US diplomat and senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment think-tank.
Bessent invoked the 1944 D-Day landings in France during World War II when he unveiled the sanctions, but Miller said: “To me, this isn’t D-Day. It’s Desperation Day. I don’t think the administration is any closer to finding a way out of this.”
Michael Knights, head of research at Horizon Engage, a New York-based strategic advisory, said the blockade may prove more consequential than the sanctions themselves because Iran’s immediate challenge is no longer how to survive economic pressure but how to break out of it.
Tehran has spent decades adapting to sanctions and endured previous “maximum pressure” campaigns without altering its behaviour, he said.
Mounting economic pressure, he said, may increase Iran’s incentive to raise the cost of the confrontation for its adversaries by pressuring Gulf states, particularly Saudi Arabia, to push Washington towards a diplomatic off-ramp.
Knights said Iran could increasingly adopt the model used by its Houthi allies in the Red Sea: periodic attacks, intermittent negotiations and a prolonged campaign of disruption short of all-out war, potentially targeting shipping, ports, energy infrastructure or other critical assets to make the conflict increasingly costly for Gulf states to tolerate.
Washington rejects that assessment and says the balance of power is in its favour.
“The Iranian economy is in free fall, and the regime’s military has been decimated,” US State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said in response to questions for this article. “President Trump holds all the cards, and we are cutting off every financial lifeline the regime has remaining.”
Replay of a tired playbook
Alan Eyre, a former US diplomat who worked on Iran, questioned whether Washington has the international support and bureaucratic machinery to make the sanctions stick.
He said that unlike the multilateral campaign preceding the 2015 nuclear deal between Tehran and major powers, which curbed Iran’s nuclear programme in exchange for lifting sanctions, the latest measures rely on public threats rather than sustained diplomacy with allies and trading partners.
Iranian officials dismiss the US strategy as a replay of a playbook that has already failed. One senior Iranian official told Reuters that countries such as China would not stop cooperating with Iran simply to serve US interests.
Some political analysts say the strategy faces a deeper flaw: From North Korea to Russia and Iran itself, sanctions have rarely forced governments to abandon goals they view as existential.
The senior Iranian official said Tehran believes Washington’s broader objective is to fuel domestic discontent in the hope that economic hardship could eventually translate into political unrest, but that the “maximum pressure” campaign failed during Trump’s first term and would fail again.
“If the pressure increases, Iran’s approach will change too,” he said, adding that Gulf Arab governments understood that squeezing Tehran further could put them at greater risk as well.
Threat is in popular unrest
For Iran’s rulers, the biggest threat may not be economic pain itself. It may be the risk that worsening hardship again spills into mass unrest, according to insiders and an Iranian official.
Annual inflation reached 66 per cent in July, while consumer prices were 87.9 per cent higher than a year earlier, according to Iran’s Statistical Centre. Food prices rose 128 per cent year on year.
President Masoud Pezeshkian acknowledged the severity of the squeeze last week, saying: “Our problems have multiplied several times over, while our income has also fallen.”
Economic grievances have repeatedly erupted into nationwide protests in recent years. In January, demonstrations over economic hardship were crushed by the Revolutionary Guards and the Basij militia, with thousands killed.
The appointment earlier in August of Hossein Taeb, a key architect of previous crackdowns, to lead the Basij was one of the clearest signs yet of official concern about renewed unrest, a former reformist official said.
The Basij, a paramilitary force affiliated with the Revolutionary Guards, has repeatedly been deployed by Iran’s clerical rulers to suppress protests.
That points to a paradox at the heart of Washington’s strategy: Sanctions may deepen Iran’s economic damage without forcing its rulers to change course. The leadership has historically answered domestic unrest with repression, and external pressure with threats of retaliation abroad.
‘Dangerous impasse’
For the Gulf states, the calculation is especially fraught.
They prefer economic and diplomatic pressure to another round of war, but fear an outcome that enables Iran to declare victory while retaining the ability to disrupt traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital global oil supply route that Tehran has effectively blocked, pushing up global oil prices.
Abdulaziz Sager, chairman of the Saudi-based Gulf Research Center, said Gulf governments are unconvinced that sanctions alone can rapidly alter Iran’s behaviour, given the leadership’s resilience and ability to maintain internal control.
Significant political change, or the collapse of Iran’s theocratic leadership, he said, is unlikely to come quickly.
The result is a dangerous impasse if mediated talks fail to produce a breakthrough: Washington wants Iran to abandon its leverage over Hormuz without conceding Tehran a role in managing the waterway, Iran wants the US naval blockade lifted without appearing to surrender, and Gulf states want the conflict contained without letting Iran emerge as the victor. Russia planning to mobilize 600,000 more troops this year and next, Ukrainian intel says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
09:59:00 UTC
18:59:00 KST

Russia planning to mobilize 600,000 more troops this year and next, Ukrainian intel says
According to Ukrinform, this was reported by the press service of the Office of the President, citing data from Ukrainian intelligence agencies.
“Ukraine has information that the Russian General Staff has already prepared a scenario for the additional mobilization of 600,000 people within the specified time frames this year and next. First and foremost, they plan to bring up to full strength the formations and military units fighting against Ukrainians, as well as units of the Russian armed forces that are currently being formed,” the statement said.
The report notes that Russia’s political leadership views another wave of mobilization as a response to the aggressor state’s loss of the initiative in the war, the continued rise in battlefield personnel losses and a significant slowdown in the recruitment of contract soldiers across the regions.
According to intelligence data, Russia’s personnel losses from January through July 2026 amounted to approximately 240,000, of whom at least 140,000 were irrecoverable losses. At the same time, fewer than that number – 232,000 people – were recruited under contract into the Russian occupation force during the same period.
As part of preparations for another mobilization wave and the recruitment of criminal elements under contract, Russia has begun amending relevant legislation and regulations. Military registration controls are being significantly tightened, mechanisms are being created to recruit people serving sentences in the Russian prison system, and additional coercive measures are being developed.
The categories of convicts eligible for military service in the occupation force have been expanded to include people with outstanding or unexpunged convictions under 11 articles of Russia’s Criminal Code. These include offenses involving the smuggling of toxic, radioactive and explosive substances, weapons and narcotics; banditry and organizing or participating in criminal gangs; organizing illegal migration; violating safety requirements at fuel and energy facilities; and the illegal handling, theft or extortion of nuclear or radioactive materials.
The Russian leadership has also approved extending mobilization or contract recruitment to certain significant categories of women serving sentences in prisons and penal colonies.
Preparations are also under way to establish quotas for law enforcement agencies – including the Ministry of Internal Affairs, the Federal Bailiffs Service, the Federal Penitentiary Service, the Investigative Committee – to send employees for military service under mobilization.
Depending on their level of training and the expected length of time they are likely to remain combat-effective, mobilized personnel may undergo between 15 to 60 days of training. Some of those mobilized could potentially be trained at military ranges in Belarus.
According to Ukrainian intelligence agencies, the Russian leadership is preparing a set of coercive measures to respond to possible negative social and economic consequences of placing cities and regions under a more restrictive wartime regime.
Internal Russian documents reportedly justify the need for another mobilization wave by citing a significant rise in regional dissatisfaction with the war. Dissatisfaction levels reportedly reach as high as 69%, accompanied by a decline in the number of people willing to voluntarily sign military contracts.
Problems with contract recruitment are most pronounced in the Oryol and Vladimir regions, as well as Dagestan. In the Kurgan region, monthly recruitment targets have been met at only 57–69% since the beginning of the year. In the Volgograd region, the number of potential contract recruits has fallen by 40% compared with 2025. A further decline is being recorded in many other Russian regions as well.
Compared with 2025, some regions have seen a 30–40% decline in the number of debtors, convicted prisoners and other criminal elements, migrants and other categories that had long served as the main pool for contract recruitment into the Russian army and participation in the war. A campaign to recruit students, involving the overwhelming majority of Russian universities, has also failed, according to the intelligence services.
In addition, the Russian leadership plans to increase the personal accountability of regional authorities and expand the powers of law enforcement agencies.
A system for issuing electronic mobilization orders has already been introduced, while expanded coercive measures are being developed, including bans on leaving Russia, obtaining loans, buying or selling real estate, revoking driver’s licenses and freezing funds in bank accounts. Enterprises are also expanding their mobilization and military-registration departments.
As of the end of July 2026, more than 2,500 new vacancies had already been posted on online employment platforms for staffing these mobilization units at enterprises.
The most likely scenario is that Russian leader Vladimir Putin will make a decision on mobilization after the “elections” to the Russian State Duma, scheduled for September 18–20 this year, the intelligence agencies concluded.
As reported by Ukrinform, President Volodymyr Zelensky previously said that Russia was preparing to launch a mobilization campaign after the so-called parliamentary elections in the fall.

EU States Push to Revive Russian-Asset ‘Reparations Loan’ for Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
09:56:32 UTC
18:56:32 KST

A group of EU countries is pushing Brussels to revive a stalled plan to use frozen Russian assets to finance Ukraine, as Kyiv faces a growing wartime budget shortfall.
Sweden, the Netherlands, Spain, and Poland are among the countries urging the European Commission to restart work on a proposed “reparations loan” and report on possible legal and technical ways to overcome Belgium’s opposition, the Financial Times (FT) reported on Thursday, citing four people familiar with the document.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The plan collapsed in December after Belgium objected. Almost all of the €210 billion ($244 billion) in Russian assets frozen in Europe are held at Euroclear, a Brussels-based securities depository.
Instead, the EU agreed to provide Ukraine with a €90 billion ($104 billion) loan backed by the bloc’s budget. EU governments also pledged to keep working on a separate reparations loan based on cash balances linked to the frozen Russian assets.
But little has changed since then, according to one FT source.
The renewed push comes as Ukraine faces mounting financial pressure after bringing forward spending to sustain its military campaign.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Monday that the defense ministry faces a €23.1 billion ($26.8 billion) funding gap that needs to be covered to keep the war effort going.
Ukraine shifted spending originally planned for the second half of the year into the first six months, helping fund a major campaign of medium- and long-range strikes against Russian military positions, logistics hubs and supply routes, including those serving occupied Crimea.
Ukrainian Drones Hit Ozon Logistics Hubs in Russia as Marketplace Warehouses Come Under Sustained Attack
The move has now left the defense ministry short of cash for military salaries, social support and weapons purchases. It also needs about €6 billion ($7 billion) in advance payments for weapons deliveries planned for early 2027.
Ukraine urgently needs additional funding as Russia continues its near-daily missile and drone attacks. Kyiv also needs to develop and produce interceptor missiles capable of defending against Russian ballistic missile strikes.
Swedish Foreign Minister Maria Malmer Stenergard said the time was right to reconsider how frozen Russian assets could be used.
“It is a fair and reasonable way to ensure that Ukraine can defend itself and all of Europe,” she said.
The EU has so far been unable to find a way around Belgium’s concerns over the legal and financial risks of using the frozen assets.
Zelensky has asked the EU to accelerate part of the €90 billion loan ($104 billion), with half scheduled for this year and the remainder next year. Brussels fears that changing the arrangement could undermine the fragile agreement on financing Ukraine and force the bloc to find additional money.
Still, an EU official familiar with the discussions told the FT that the bloc could revisit existing legal proposals if political conditions change.

"Ukrainian diplomats are in constant contact with competent authorities and services conducting search operations, relatives of the missing, as well as foreign diplomats in their countries of residence to coordinate international efforts to locate tour groups. Search teams and official authorities of the countries of residence have received full information from Ukrainian diplomatic missions regarding all Ukrainians with whom contact cannot be established. Searches continue," according to the commentary.
A group of employees from the Embassy of Ukraine in India has also traveled directly to the disaster zone. The Honorary Consul of Ukraine in Nepal is involved as well.
"The MFA, the Department of Consular Service, and the Embassies of Ukraine in India and China continue to monitor the situation and keep the case regarding the disappearance of 55 Ukrainian citizens under special control," the ministry emphasized.

Nine years on, a Rohingya survivor revisits the massacre that killed her family, and dreams of going home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
09:46:44 UTC
18:46:44 KST

Share & more
The rain on the plastic roof of the shelter in Bangladesh’s Kutupalong refugee camp takes Laila Begum back to the gloomy morning of 30 August 2017, the day her family went from nine to three people.
Then 18, Laila recounts what happened when the Myanmar military, accompanied by armed Rakhine villagers, surrounded her village of Tula Toli in northern Rakhine State and began shooting indiscriminately at Rohingya Muslims.
By the end of that morning, her parents and four of her six siblings were dead.
Now 27 and living with her husband and three children in the world’s largest refugee settlement in Cox’s Bazar, Laila says she wants to retell her story not only to highlight the Myanmar military’s continued impunity following its genocidal campaign – which killed thousands of Rohingya and drove more than 740,000 from their homes – but also to reaffirm her desire to return to her home country.
Over the last nine years, the harrowing experience of seeing her parents, siblings, and fellow Rohingya brutally killed has never left her.
She remembers the children burned alive.
She remembers how her people ran for their lives.
She remembers the plumes of smoke that rose from the burned-down homes.
She remembers people killed with gunfire and machetes.
She remembers her family.
Laila recalls the morning started with gunfire. Around 8am, the military shot dead a teenager in the street.
Many were gunned down while trying to escape; babies and children were thrown into fires and burned alive.
“I instantly fled towards a graveyard on the western edge of my village to hide,” she says. “Minutes later, a helicopter hovered overhead dropping ammunition and gasoline, and relentless gunshots across my village and the riverbank brought my heart to a standstill.”
From her hideout, she says she witnessed the military and armed Rakhine villagers slashing and shooting Rohingya they encountered: Many were gunned down while trying to escape; babies and children were thrown into fires and burned alive.
Laila says she saw one of her brothers shot and killed while he was trying to save his son, and as his pregnant wife was burned alive.
On the riverbank, women were separated from men.
“First, the men were separated and forced to drop to their knees, and then shot to death. Those who survived gunshots were later slashed with machetes,” she says. “The soldiers brought women into their homes in smaller groups; stayed for half an hour; the soldiers left; and then all that I saw was plumes of smoke rising from those houses.”
A well-documented massacre
The details in Laila’s account echo findings documented by Human Rights Watch, which interviewed Tula Toli survivors and found that soldiers and armed Rakhine villagers surrounded Rohingya gathered near the riverbank, separated men from women and children, and killed several hundred people that day. HRW also used satellite imagery to confirm that Tula Toli and the neighbouring Rohingya village of Dual Toli were extensively destroyed by arson.
“A night before the attack, the villagers had received warnings from a local Rakhine chairman,” Laila says. “He told us we would be safer if we gathered near the riverbank.”
Most of the villagers followed the advice.
“If the Rohingya weren’t advised to go to the riverbank, the military wouldn’t have been able to kill us at such a scale.”
Laila now believes that gathering helped the military to kill Rohingya en masse: “If the Rohingya weren’t advised to go to the riverbank, the military wouldn’t have been able to kill us at such a scale.”
After a couple of hours of killings, the soldiers, she says, piled up the dead bodies and set them on fire using gasoline.
“My only surviving brother from the gathering called on my husband’s phone, and told me that our father had been shot and mother had been burned alive. The call dropped.”
Later that day, Laila says she and her husband started walking through the forest towards Bangladesh.
The two-day journey on foot was gruelling. She felt she had lost everything and did not know whether her siblings were still alive.
Eventually, they reached the shore of the Naf River.
Laila had almost nothing left.
But she still had a gold nose pin. She used it to pay the boatman for passage across the river into Bangladesh.
On their third day, they reached Kutupalong.
She escaped the carnage, but she could not erase what she saw or what she lost.
Nine years have passed in the refugee camp, but the horrific scenes still reflect in her heart. She misses her parents and siblings. “I don’t have anyone to share with. I lost everything.”
For Laila, Tula Toli is more than a place of violence, it’s the place where she was born; it’s the place where she grew up with her family; it’s the place where she lost her parents and siblings.
She still wants to go back. “We just came to save our lives, not to stay,” she says. “I wish I had wings – I would fly back to Myanmar. Because that is our country.”
Laila says she wishes to see the soil where her family members were killed. “I couldn’t bury them, but I could at least see the soil where they were killed.”
Interviewed separately over the phone, her only surviving brother and sister echoed her feelings; they too want to go back to the place they still call home.
The slow-turning wheels of international justice
Laila's story is part of a much larger effort to establish accountability for the violence against the Rohingya.
The minority group has faced decades of discrimination and been treated as foreigners in their own country. The 1982 Citizenship Law rendered many Rohingya effectively stateless and entrenched their exclusion from full citizenship. During the 2017 genocidal campaign, then-government leader Aung San Suu Kyi, a Nobel Peace laureate, faced criticism for failing to condemn the military's actions and for downplaying allegations of atrocities. Two years later, she went further, defending Myanmar against genocide allegations at the International Court of Justice (ICJ), the UN’s top court.
Laila knows international justice cannot bring back what she has lost. But she wants it to create the conditions for her to return to her homeland with safety, dignity, and rights.
The Gambia brought Myanmar before the ICJ under the Genocide Convention, alleging that the state violated its obligations towards the Rohingya. In January 2020, the court ordered provisional measures requiring Myanmar to take steps to prevent genocidal acts against the Rohingya and preserve evidence related to the case. In 2022, it rejected Myanmar’s preliminary objections, finding that it had jurisdiction and that the case was admissible. The court heard arguments on the merits in January 2026 and is now deliberating.
Many Rohingya refugees want to return to Myanmar, and the military-backed government says it is prepared to receive verified returnees. But Rakhine remains embroiled in conflict between the Myanmar military and the Arakan Army – an ethnic Rakhine armed group that now controls much of the state – with both accused of abuses against Rohingya. UN agencies and rights groups say conditions are not yet safe for a voluntary, dignified, and sustainable return.
Laila knows international justice cannot bring back what she has lost. But she wants it to create the conditions for her to return to her homeland with safety, dignity, and rights.
Nine years away from home, she still wants to return because somewhere beneath the memories of that morning is another memory: of a place where her family once lived together.
It’s where her parents were killed.
It’s where she once called home.
Edited by Andrew Gully.
