How Shenzhen can win the ‘AI for science’ race
Rather than copy the research-focused models of Beijing and Shanghai, the tech hub must leverage its industrial depths to become a premier lab for experimentation and deployment
The opportunity is obvious: AI could become a new source of scientific productivity and industrial growth. The trap is copying what other cities are doing. Shenzhen should not try to become Beijing with more hardware, or Shanghai with a different set of industry labels; it should build around its own comparative advantage.
The first advantage is the structure of its innovation economy. Shenzhen invested 245.31 billion yuan in research and development in 2024, the highest R&D intensity among Chinese cities. Strikingly, companies accounted for over 93 per cent of that spending. Those figures describe a city where research, engineering and commercial deployment sit unusually close together. This matters in the AI-for-science drive because the hard part isn’t only inventing an algorithm, but turning it into a reliable scientific tool.

CDU's Volkmann: Ukraine aid is not charity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
08:30:00 UTC
17:30:00 KST

CDU's Volkmann: Ukraine aid is not charity
August 27, 2026
At 29, Johannes Volkmann is one of the youngest members of Germany's parliament — and one of the most dedicated supporters of Ukraine. When he was head of the council of the Lahn-Dill district in the state of Hessen, he launched a municipal partnership with the Ukrainian city of Brovary near the capital Kyiv to deliver supplies to those in need.
As a member of the Bundestag's Committee on Foreign Affairs and the United4Ukraine group, an international network of lawmakers, he continues to advocate for Ukraine. During his latest trip to the country, he spoke with DW about why he thinks aid to Ukraine is so important.
DW: Mr. Volkmann, you were last in Ukraine exactly a year ago. What has changed since then?
Johannes Volkmann: The number of airstrikes — and thus the threat to the civilian population — has increased significantly again. And at the same time, there is a sense that the Ukrainian people still want to stand their ground. I have utmost respect for that. Ukraine is demonstrating that freedom and democracy can defend themselves and fight back. That is a very important message of hope.
German support is particularly important for Ukraine's defense capabilities — Germany is the largest bilateral donor to Ukraine in Europe. At the same time, political forces in Germany oppose this support. The voters of these parties share this view and consider aid to Ukraine a waste of money. What would you say to them?
Everyone needs to understand that Ukraine today is not only defending itself, but also protecting Europe. Russian imperialism is not only a threat to Ukraine's borders, but also to those of our allies in the Baltic states and in Poland. That is why every euro we invest in Ukraine today is a good investment in our own security.
On top of that, Ukraine is able to help us more and more in Europe by sharing its experience on the battlefield with European armies — with regard to modern technologies, drones, the training of soldiers and modern tactics.
When it comes to experience, Ukraine has a tremendous lead in these areas. That is why Ukraine is now effectively a provider of security in Europe and no longer merely in need of security.
The Alternative for Germany (AfD), which currently leads the polls, has called for an end to German support for Ukraine. Many in Ukraine are wondering: What will happen if the AfD performs even better in the next German election and becomes part of the government?
I can understand this fear. The Bundestag was elected to serve until 2029. For me personally, as well as for my parliamentary group, the CDU/CSU, it is clear that Ukraine must be supported militarily because it is in our own interest in terms of security. For me, the AfD's position on Ukraine is an important reason why my party has ruled out any cooperation with them.
There is also a humanitarian responsibility: If millions of Ukrainians flee their homeland because Russia's war of aggression succeeds — and, of course, they won't want to live under Russian colonial rule — then that will destabilize our countries. That would place a much greater financial burden on us than supporting Ukrainians today in their defense of their homeland.
Do you view Russia as a military threat to Europe and Germany? Some are asking: If Russia has struggled so much in Ukraine militarily, what threat can it pose to NATO?
It is important to understand that Russia's hybrid attacks on Europe are not primarily aimed at military conquest but rather at achieving certain political objectives. These include the destruction of EU and NATO cohesion.
So, it is entirely possible that Russia, perhaps with threats involving nuclear weapons, could attempt to occupy specific areas in the Baltic region to test the significance of NATO's Article 5 — the solidarity clause. This is why it is all the more important that we remain vigilant about this issue and develop the capacity to defend ourselves in order to deter Russia from any such aggression. We can only protect peace through our own strength; weakness will be seen as an invitation to attack.
Germany was one of the countries particularly hesitant and cautious regarding Ukraine's possible accession to NATO. At the 2008 NATO summit in the Romanian capital Bucharest, it was against granting Ukraine a Membership Action Plan (MAP). Many in Ukraine believe that their country's rapid admission into NATO — or at least the granting of an MAP — could have prevented Russia's hybrid war in 2014 and the full-scale invasion in 2022. Was Germany's policy at the time a mistake?
It is clear that the hypothesis put forward by the German government at the time has turned out to have been wrong — the assumption that trade, for example in gas via the Nord Stream pipeline, would create mutual dependencies and thus prevent violence from occurring. The same applies to the assumption that neutrality would protect other countries.
It was a big mistake for Germany to not listen to the insights of our neighbors to the east, who, because of their own experiences with Moscow, historically have a much better understanding of what Russia actually wants.
Apart from accession to NATO, many Ukrainians view membership of the European Union as the best guarantee of security. But German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has ruled out Ukraine's accelerated admission to the bloc. Could Germany be making the same mistake again?
NATO membership and EU membership are two very different matters. The EU is a very comprehensive community based on the rule of law. There are 35 negotiating chapters necessary for accession. To rush through the process despite Ukraine not being ready in certain areas would do neither it nor the EU any favors.
At the same time — as the chancellor has also made clear — the idea is not to hold Ukraine back. It has to be clear that once certain milestones are met, the process of European integration will move forward.
Ukraine is fighting to be a European country. That is why I think it goes without saying that Ukraine, too, can be a full member of the European family with free self-determination. We should do everything in our power to support Ukraine on this path.
One issue many in Ukraine are concerned about is corruption and scandals — including those in President Zelenskyy's inner circle. How dangerous are such cases for the international support for Ukraine?
Personally, I am very worried about this. It would be even worse if corruption scandals were not exposed. It is good when corruption cases are thoroughly investigated and there are no false compromises when dealing with them. That is why we will be closely following the verdicts and consequences that result.
I can only encourage Ukrainian civil society, journalists, the public, members of parliament and the opposition to continue keeping a close eye on the situation and to ensure that Ukrainian and European funds are used properly.
Today, there aren't even any serious discussions about peace negotiations with Russia. The Kremlin insists on its maximum demands, which essentially amount to Ukraine's surrender. At the same time, there are forces in Germany, such as the AfD and the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), that have called for talks with Russia. Do you currently envisage any possibilities for diplomatic initiatives?
There have, of course, been numerous attempts by the Ukrainian president and Western states to start peace talks. At the same time, there are no serious signs that the Kremlin has any desire for peace. Such a desire for peace will only emerge when Putin recognizes the futility of his efforts for military conquest.
This requires an increase in military, financial and civil support for Ukraine. And above all, it requires a clear message that the Kremlin cannot hope that Europe will stop supporting Ukraine in 2027 or 2028. We stand with Ukraine — today and tomorrow.
This interview with Johannes Volkmann was conducted by Mykola Berdnyk.

55 Ukrainians missing in Nepal after floods - Foreign Ministry
Kyiv • UNN

In Nepal, 55 Ukrainians are considered missing due to the floods, according to information from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine updated as of 10:30 a.m. on August 27, UNN reports.

It is noted that search-and-rescue operations are ongoing. Access to many areas affected by the disaster is complicated by weather conditions. Local competent authorities are warning of the possibility of further floods and landslides.
The Embassies of Ukraine in India and the PRC, as noted, have posted safety recommendations on their official platforms. "Ukrainian diplomats are in constant contact with the competent authorities and services conducting search operations, relatives of those missing, as well as foreign diplomats in the countries of residence, in order to coordinate international efforts to locate the tourist groups," the statement said.
"Search teams and the official authorities of the countries concerned have received from Ukrainian diplomatic missions complete information about all Ukrainians with whom it has not been possible to establish contact. The search continues. A group of employees of the Embassy of Ukraine in India has also been dispatched directly to the disaster zone. The Honorary Consul of Ukraine in Nepal has been involved," the Ministry of Foreign Affairs noted.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Consular Service Department, and the Embassies of Ukraine in India and the PRC, as noted, continue to monitor the situation and are keeping the case concerning the disappearance of 55 Ukrainian citizens under special control.

Unknown

====================================================================================================

Fungal studies reveal new ways pathogens defeat human immunity
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
16:27:42 CST
17:27:42 KST

MELBOURNE, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- Scientists have discovered how the world's deadliest fungi explode immune cells and shape-shift to defeat the human immune system, providing new avenues for treatments and drug discovery.
Two studies focused on Candida auris and Candida albicans, microscopic fungi that cause life-threatening human infections, opening the door for treatments and antifungal drug discovery by identifying the nutrients the fungi and immune cells use to battle each other, according to a statement released Thursday by Australia's Monash University.
The study published in Nature Communications identified the naturally occurring amino acid alanine that reverses the process these fungi use to defeat the immune system.
When an immune cell swallows a fungal microbe to destroy it, the fungus can trigger a host protein called Ninjurin to form large pores, causing the immune cell to explode and release the fungal cells to spread the infection, researchers said, adding that higher doses of alanine blocked the protein and prevented the immune cells from bursting, thereby containing the fungal cells.
The second study, published in Nature Microbiology, discovered the shape-shifting ability of the mysterious Candida auris, which can adapt itself to stick to human tissue and remain invisible to human immune cells in different parts of the body.
Professor Ana Traven of the Monash Biomedicine Discovery Institute, senior author on both papers, said researchers were looking beyond ways to kill the fungus to explore how the patient's body could be nutritionally manipulated to give the immune system the energy and tools to fight back. ■

====================================================================================================

324-million-year-old insect fossil offers evolutionary link between water, land
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
16:27:40 CST
17:27:40 KST

NANJING, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- An international team led by Chinese researchers has uncovered an early insect species dating back roughly 324 million years that displays both aquatic and terrestrial features, providing direct evidence of how insects gradually made the transition from water to land.
The fossil specimen, named Chosha praecursor, was recovered from Carboniferous strata in the U.S. state of Texas. The work was carried out by scientists from the Nanjing Institute of Geology and Palaeontology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, in collaboration with colleagues from the United Kingdom, the United States, and Spain.
Although the insect already possessed the three pairs of walking legs typical of modern insects, its abdomen retained paddle-shaped lobes suited for swimming. The findings were published online Wednesday in the journal Nature.
Cai Chenyang, a researcher at the institute who led the study, said that abdominal appendages in extant insects are largely reduced, with only the three thoracic pairs remaining. Chosha praecursor, he noted, offers a snapshot of the transition: the ancestral aquatic appendages had not yet disappeared entirely but were being gradually modified and simplified as the insect adapted to life on land.
"This discovery serves as an evolutionary bridge between aquatic and terrestrial life forms," Cai said. "Around 320 million years ago, ancient insects at the water-land interface were progressively evolving new body structures suited to breathing and moving on land."
The fossil, identified as an adult female, measures about 3.2 cm in body length, extending to nearly 5 cm with its elongated tail structure, and has a fusiform shape.
Its thorax bore three pairs of walking legs, and its ovipositor and tail already showed typical insect features. However, segments one through nine of the abdomen still carried segmented appendages, with the rear pairs flattened into paddle-like forms.
Given that the fossil was found in nearshore, shallow-water deltaic deposits, the researchers conclude that Chosha praecursor inhabited humid transitional zones between land and water, retaining clear semi-aquatic characteristics. ■

Rescuers with rescue and relief supplies board a plane at the Chengdu Shuangliu International Airport in Chengdu, southwest China's Sichuan Province, Aug. 27, 2026. GYIRONG, Xizang, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- The first team of 141 rescuers has arrived at the mudslide-stricken border port of Gyirong in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region Thursday morning after the disaster caused significant casualties along the China-Nepal border, according to China's Ministry of Emergency Management.
A high-altitude helicopter has also arrived at the disaster-hit area, the ministry said.
The mudslide struck Gyirong Port in Gyirong County, Xizang, on Wednesday morning. As of 8 a.m. on Thursday, three people had been killed, 558 others remained missing, while two local villagers had been rescued, local authorities said.
Another batch of 111 rescuers from the China Search and Rescue team has arrived at Gyirong County as of 2:28 p.m. Thursday, and will head to Gyirong Port to carry out rescue operations.
An eight-member advance team from China Anneng, a state-owned engineering and rescue enterprise, arrived in Gyirong County early Thursday with communications and detection equipment to collect key data and support efforts to address an upstream blockage, which is a top priority.
Only after the risk posed by the blockage is addressed can the debris accumulated about 3 km upstream of the port be safely cleared, according to rescue personnel at the site.
Hundreds more rescuers, carrying equipment and supplies for detection, rescue, communications and logistical support, are rushing to the site. ■

Matildas follow Socceroo footsteps on path to World Cup

Unknown Publisher

17:21:10 KST

The Matildas will face South American giants Colombia in two matches ahead of next year's Women's World Cup, with young talent a focus.
Heather Garriock, Football Australia's executive director of football says coach Joe Montemurro will look to emulate Socceroos coach Tony Popovic who gave younger players an opportunity at the men's World Cup this year.
What's next?
The first game against Colombia will be in Canberra on November 28. The date and venue of the second match are yet to be revealed.
The Matildas are looking to follow the Socceroos' blueprint when they play in next year's FIFA Women's World Cup, and two friendlies against Colombia will be a key stepping stone.
On Thursday the Matildas announced they will play the first of two games against the South American giants on November 28 at Canberra Stadium.
The date and venue of the second clash are yet to be determined.
The matches will be an invaluable warm-up ahead of next year's World Cup, which kicks off in Brazil on June 24, with the final on July 25.
Loading Twitter content
And the Matildas, who finished fourth at the 2023 World Cup co-hosted by Australia and New Zealand, are keen to set up the team for long-term success.
With current players including Sam Kerr, Steph Catley, Emily van Egmond and Mackenzie Arnold entering the latter stages of their careers, there are concerns about the Matildas missing such a wealth of talent and experience once they retire.
Heather Garriock, Football Australia's executive director of football, said the friendlies against Colombia would make sure younger players are prioritised.
"We sat down with (coach) Joe (Montemurro) some 12 months ago when he started in the Matildas position, and we asked him what his ideal preparation was in the lead-up to the Women's World Cup," Garriock said on Thursday.
"It was very evident that different styles of play were important to him, but also trying to blood some of the next generation as well.
"We've seen that (younger players getting an opportunity) at the recent World Cup in the US with (Socceroos coach) Tony Popovic as well.
"Joe's style is very creative, very structured and process-driven."
The Socceroos' next generation shone at this year's World Cup in North America, with Nestory Irankunda, Alessandro Circati and Lucas Herrington subsequently earning contracts with major European teams.
The success of the Socceroos' young squad members came after Popovic integrated rising talent into the side in the lead-up to the tournament.
The Matildas are hoping to follow that blueprint, and 21-year-old goalkeeper Chloe Lincoln says getting game time in friendlies against top nations will help her confidence heading into Brazil.
"Playing them (Colombia) at the She Believes Cup, we got a sense of their style, and it's an amazing opportunity to (play) that opposition," Lincoln said.
"Now that the A-League is kicking off again, there's more opportunity for the local players and some of the younger girls playing in that competition to really put … their names forward.
"Especially in these friendly matches, every match really counts, building cohesiveness as a group and working on how we want to perform over in the World Cup."

mark francis turns sound and frequency into vibrating abstract paintings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
08:20:33 UTC
17:20:33 KST

With Chroma, Bernhard Knaus Fine Art presents a new body of work by Northern Irish painter Mark Francis, whose abstractions operate somewhere between what can be seen and what might almost be heard. On view from September 5 to November 21, 2026, the exhibition brings together paintings shaped by sound, frequency, and resonance, with vibrating fields of color, pulsating lines, and tightly structured rhythms turning the canvas into something closer to a visual soundscape.
For Francis, color behaves less like a static surface than an acoustic phenomenon. Lines appear to oscillate, overlap, and reverberate across the paintings, producing compositions that suggest echoes or layered frequencies without illustrating them literally. Titles including Sound Echo, Metronomic Sound, and Veil offer a few clues, but stop short of telling viewers exactly what they are looking at. Instead, the works occupy a deliberately unstable territory where seeing begins to borrow some of the language of listening.
Signals, 2026 | courtesy of Bernhard Knaus Fine Art, Frankfurt am Main
SCIENCE BECOMES A STARTING POINT, NOT AN ANSWER
The paintings often begin with structures recalling microscopic images, crystalline formations, networks, and cellular systems. Francis has long drawn from mathematical and biological models, particularly the hidden patterns revealed through scientific imaging. Rather than reproducing these systems faithfully, however, he removes them from their original context and treats their geometries as triggers for painting, allowing scientific order to gradually slip into something far less measurable.
As each composition develops, those initial structures begin to dissolve. Their origins remain only as traces: a grid that seems to fade, a line that vibrates without quite settling, or a pattern that feels familiar but refuses to become recognizable. This state between precision and ambiguity gives the paintings their tension. There is enough structure to suggest that something is happening beneath the surface, though thankfully no microscope is required to find out what.
Sonic Reflection, 2026 | courtesy of Bernhard Knaus Fine Art, Frankfurt am Main
CHROMA LETS CONTROL AND CHANCE SHARE THE CANVAS
That push and pull continues in Francis’ working process. His paintings are carefully conceived but often executed alla prima, allowing the image to develop directly on the canvas while paint, surface, gesture, and color respond to one another in real time. Planning provides the framework, while spontaneity introduces disruption, leaving control and chance to negotiate the final composition between themselves.
The resulting works function less as fixed images than as experiential fields of color, rhythm, and resonance. Chroma takes its title from the idea of a broad spectrum of sensory frequencies, proposing sound as something that shapes environments and perception even when it cannot be seen. Francis gives those invisible forces a painterly presence without attempting to pin them down. Alongside the Frankfurt exhibition, his work is also presented in Sea of Sound for the Republic of San Marino at the 2026 Venice Biennale, extending his investigation into that curious territory where the eye, apparently, develops an ear.
Audio Code, 2026 | courtesy of Bernhard Knaus Fine Art, Frankfurt am Main
Stalo, 2026 | courtesy of Bernhard Knaus Fine Art, Frankfurt am Main
Audio Division II, 2026 | courtesy of Bernhard Knaus Fine Art, Frankfurt am Main
Audio Division, 2026 | courtesy of Bernhard Knaus Fine Art, Frankfurt am Main
Plex, 2026 | courtesy of Bernhard Knaus Fine Art, Frankfurt am Main
Prismatic Zip, 2026 | courtesy of Bernhard Knaus Fine Art, Frankfurt am Main
Scaler, 2026 | courtesy of Bernhard Knaus Fine Art, Frankfurt am Main
project info:
name: Chroma artist: Mark Francis gallery: Bernhard Knaus Fine Art dates: September 5 – November 21, 2026
designboom has received this project from our DIY submissions feature, where we welcome our readers to submit their own work for publication. See more project submissions from our readers here.

====================================================================================================

EXPLAINER - What economic leverage does US still have over Iran?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
08:19:02 UTC
17:19:02 KST

After nearly six months of war without a lasting settlement, Washington is once again turning to economic pressure in its campaign against Iran, seeking to further squeeze Tehran's oil revenues, trade and access to the global financial system.
The latest push came this week with Operation Economic Outcast, a campaign aimed at further isolating Iran financially and expanding the reach of US secondary sanctions.
“Around the globe, our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in announcing the measures.
The campaign comes as Iran is already under intense economic pressure. Its Central Bank says oil exports have stopped, the rial has fallen to a record low and the International Monetary Fund expects the economy to contract 6.1% this year.
But Iran has endured decades of US sanctions and economic isolation without abandoning policies Washington has sought to change, raising a larger question: What economic cards does the US still have to play, and how much leverage can they give Washington over Tehran?
At the center of Washington's economic pressure is Iran's oil trade, one of Tehran's main sources of export revenue and foreign currency.
Central Bank Governor Abdolnaser Hemmati said last week that Iran's oil exports had fallen to zero amid the war and sanctions.
"There is no doubt that we face restrictions on oil exports," Hemmati said in a televised interview. "It is a reality that we are not exporting oil."
The US restored its naval blockade against vessels travelling to and from Iranian ports on July 14 after a temporary easing of restrictions.
According to commodities intelligence firm Kpler, Iranian crude loadings fell from an average of 893,000 barrels per day in July to just 156,000 through Aug. 17.
Hemmati's statement that exports have since fallen to zero suggests the pressure on Tehran's oil revenues has intensified further.
Max Gillman, Friedrich A. Hayek Professor of Economic History at the University of Missouri-St. Louis, said the blockade is likely to remain Washington's main instrument of economic pressure.
"I think the main enforcement measure will be the naval blockade on Iranian trade. I expect this to continue indefinitely," Gillman told Anadolu.
"The continued blockade serves to pressure the economic resources available to the ruling Iranian regime," he said.
Restricting Iran's ability to sell oil is only one side of Washington's strategy. The US can also make it more difficult for Tehran to access foreign currency it has already earned.
Hemmati said the Iranian government and Central Bank had prepared for the loss of revenue, but stressed that Iran faced an additional constraint because its foreign currency reserves remained blocked by Washington.
"The Americans have frozen our foreign currency reserves and do not allow us to withdraw them," he said.
He also said Iranian funds expected to be released under the Islamabad Memorandum, the framework agreement reached with Washington in June, had not yet been freed.
Access to those reserves has become increasingly important as pressure mounts on Iran's currency.
Iran has increasingly relied on alternative payment mechanisms, shadow banking networks, cryptocurrency and intermediaries in third countries to move export revenues and bypass sanctions.
US authorities have repeatedly targeted those channels, seeking to make it harder for Tehran to convert trade and energy earnings into usable foreign currency.
Washington can also target foreign companies, banks and individuals that do business with sanctioned Iranian entities, potentially threatening their access to the US financial system.
This week, the US Treasury announced new categories of Iranian economic activity that can expose foreign companies and individuals to sanctions, including digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping.
The Treasury also said it was developing sanctions against more than 60 entities, individuals and vessels around the world that it accused of helping Iran.
Teams from the Treasury and State departments and the US military are meeting foreign counterparts and setting deadlines for them to halt activities identified by Washington, he said.
"Every country has a defined timeline to shut down activities we have identified. If they do not take action, we will do so unilaterally through Treasury authorities," Bessent said.
He singled out Iran's Bank Melli, saying every branch must be shuttered, and issued a broader warning to institutions facilitating transactions Washington considers illicit.
"Any entity that facilitates money laundering on behalf of Iran will be removed from the US dollar system. The clock is ticking," he said.
Washington is tightening restrictions at a difficult moment for Iran's economy.
The IMF expects the economy to contract 6.1% in 2026, a downward revision of 7.2 percentage points from its January forecast, while average inflation is projected at 68.9%, up from 50.9% in 2025.
Labor-market conditions have also deteriorated. Iran's official unemployment rate rose to 9.1% in the spring, while the number of employed people fell by around 450,000 from a year earlier.
Meanwhile, the rial fell to a record low of about 2 million against the US dollar on the informal market Monday, while figures from the Statistical Center of Iran showed point-to-point consumer inflation reached 87.9% in July.
The weaker rial increases the local cost of imported goods, adding to pressure on households already confronting rapidly rising prices.
There are limits both to how far Washington can push its economic leverage and what that pressure can ultimately achieve.
Asked why the US was giving Iran's business partners an opportunity to halt targeted activities rather than immediately penalizing them, Bessent pointed to potential consequences for the wider financial system.
"We are giving everyone the opportunity to remedy bad behavior," he said. "Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?"
Restrictions on Iranian trade can also have consequences beyond Iran, particularly through their impact on energy markets.
Gillman said continued economic pressure could nevertheless prove less disruptive than renewed large-scale warfare, arguing that Washington appears to be seeking to pressure Tehran while avoiding sharper increases in oil prices.
Although the blockade itself puts upward pressure on oil prices, Gillman said keeping crude within the $70-$80 range would support wider economic stability and limit additional export revenues for Russia.
But the bigger question is whether even severe economic pressure can produce the political concessions Washington is seeking.
Iran has lived under varying degrees of US sanctions and economic isolation for decades, developing ways to circumvent restrictions while resisting pressure to abandon policies opposed by Washington.
The Trump administration argues that stronger enforcement can change Tehran's calculation.
Bessent also appealed directly to Iranian soldiers, pointing to the economic strain on the government.
"To the ordinary soldiers supporting this regime: As more and more of your paychecks stop or are supposedly 'just delayed,' ask whether your commanders are leading your country to triumph or to ruin," he said.
Yet despite the economic strain already facing Iran, nearly six months of war and pressure have so far failed to produce a lasting settlement.
The Islamic Republic's leadership has also long portrayed economic sacrifice and resistance to foreign pressure as part of defending the principles of the 1979 revolution.
Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, founder of the Islamic Republic, famously captured that thinking after the 1979 revolution: "We did not make the revolution for cheap melons, we made it for Islam."

Demolition of modernist arts complex in Tbilisi sparks outcry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
08:09:07 UTC
17:09:07 KST

Demolition of modernist arts complex in Tbilisi sparks outcry
TBILISI, Aug 27 - The demolition of a modernist arts complex in the Georgian capital Tbilisi has ignited outrage from some residents about the future of the city's skyline and from the Italian architects who designed it.
Known locally as the Rike Tubes, the Rike Park Music Theatre and Exhibition Hall was constructed between 2011 and 2012 under the previous government, led by pro-Western reformer Mikheil Saakashvili.
The governing Georgian Dream party came to power in 2012 and the complex was never fully completed and has gone largely unused.
Its tubular design has stood out in the old town skyline dominated by the conical roofs of Orthodox churches and 19th-century houses, making it a symbol of the pro-European approach of the previous government, while its disuse for some represented squandered opportunities.
"This ugliness does not befit our beautiful capital," Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze said in May this year.
MONTHS OF DEMOLITION WORK
In June, the Tbilisi City Hall's Architecture Service approved the demolition. The work began at the end of July and is scheduled to be completed by December 25, a city document shows.
Among local people who never liked the design, Elene Tsetskhladze nevertheless objected to its destruction.
"Personally, I don't like the way it looks visually, but I think that at this point, the state's priority should be construction, not destruction," she said. The money spent on demolition could be better used for free meals for schoolchildren and medicine for the poor, she added.
While they still can, tourists have flocked to snap photos of the 10,000-square-metre (12,000-square-yard) structure.
It was designed by the Italian architectural firm Fuksas Studio, led by husband and wife architects Massimiliano and Doriana Fuksas, who said they had received a deluge of support.
"We received thousands of emails. Every person said this was the most iconic building of Tbilisi," said Massimiliano.
The government had not told them the demolition was imminent and they are struggling to come to terms with it.
"You cannot cancel buildings, you cannot cancel memories," Massimiliano said. Doriana added: "You cannot cancel history."
Maqro Property, the parent company of Rike Dom, the company that owns the complex and requested its demolition, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. REUTERS

Search underway for 55 missing Ukrainians in Nepal and Tibet: further flooding possible
Fifty-five Ukrainians are considered missing following large-scale flooding in Nepal and Tibet. Local authorities are warning of the possibility of further flooding and landslides.
Source: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine in a comment to journalists
Details: Reports as of 10:30 Kyiv time indicate that more than 1,100 people in the region are considered missing, including more than 400 local residents and more than 700 tourists from nearly 30 countries. Among them are 55 Ukrainian citizens.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs said these are two tourist groups comprising 47 and 7 Ukrainians respectively, as well as one Ukrainian citizen who was part of a foreign tour group.
According to local authorities, at least 165 people have died in the disaster zone in total. As of now, there is no information indicating that Ukrainian citizens are among those killed or injured.
Search-and-rescue operations are ongoing. Access to many of the disaster-affected areas is difficult due to weather conditions. The ministry said the Nepalese authorities are warning of the possibility of further flooding and landslides.
Ukraine's embassies in India and China have posted safety advice on their official platforms. Ukrainian diplomats remain in constant contact with the local authorities and services in Nepal carrying out search operations, with relatives of those missing and with foreign diplomats in the countries concerned in order to coordinate international efforts to locate the tourist groups.
Search teams and official authorities in the host countries have received full information from Ukrainian diplomatic missions on all the Ukrainians with whom contact has not yet been established. Searches are continuing.
A group of staff from the Ukrainian embassy in India has also travelled directly to the disaster zone. Ukraine's honorary consul in Nepal has also been involved.
Quote: "The Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Consular Service Department and Ukraine's embassies in India and China continue to monitor the situation and are keeping the matter of the 55 missing Ukrainian citizens under special scrutiny."
Background:
- On the morning of 26 August, flooding hit the Rasuwa district, north of Nepal's capital, Kathmandu. Torrents of water and mud swept away houses, roads and bridges and damaged energy infrastructure.
- Early findings indicate that the disaster was caused by an avalanche of ice and rock from a glacier. The debris blocked the Lhende Khola River, sending a powerful surge of water, mud and debris downstream. Transport links have been disrupted in some areas, hampering search and rescue operations.
- On the evening of 26 August, Ukraine's Foreign Ministry reported that, according to Tourist Police Nepal, 53 Ukrainian citizens are considered missing following the severe flooding.

Move to slash amount of vitamin B6 considered safe by 72 per cent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
08:04:36 UTC
17:04:36 KST

Move to reduce amount of vitamin B6 considered safe by 72 per cent
In short:
The National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) has recommended reducing the upper limit of daily human consumption of vitamin B6 to 14 milligrams, down from the current 50mg.
Synthetic vitamin B6 is added to thousands of products sold in Australia, including supplements like multivitamins, protein powders and energy drinks,
What's next?
The Therapeutic Goods Administration says it is waiting for the NHMRC recommendation process to be completed before it commits to taking "further regulatory action" on products containing vitamin B6.
Months after taking vitamin supplements, Dominic Noonan-O'Keefe says he feared he was dying.
His body was overwhelmed by pain and numbness, his mind overcome with dread.
"Every millimetre of my body was exploding with misfiring, misdirected signals to my brain," he told 7.30.
"There were lightning bolts through my body 24 hours a day. It was the most awful thing I've ever lived through."
Today, more than two years after he stopped taking the supplements, he said the pain had "turned down", but he still lived with balance and vision problems, among a long list of symptoms he attributes to unknowingly consuming too much vitamin B6.
Amid a public health crackdown, Australia's peak health research body is moving to cut the amount of vitamin B6 considered safe to consume.
The medicines regulator has also confirmed it will act within weeks to bring in stronger warnings and labelling, as consumers are urged to check what is in their cabinets.
Proposed change to 'upper limit'
Vitamin B6 is an essential nutrient found naturally in foods like meat, fish and vegetables.
But the synthetic form, also known as pyridoxine, is added to thousands of products sold in Australia — from supplements like multivitamins, B-complex tablets, magnesium and zinc tablets, to fortified foods and drinks including protein powders, energy drinks and weight-loss shakes.
Since 2006, regulators, doctors and manufacturers have all worked from the same figure: the intake of up to 50 milligrams of vitamin B6 a day was safe.
That threshold is known as the "upper limit".
But after an extensive review of global evidence, Australia's peak health research body, the National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC), has now recommended reducing it by 72 per cent to 14mg.
"There's really no good reason to be taking 50mg of vitamin B6, unless of course you're suffering from severe malnutrition," said Tim Green, who co-chaired the working group behind the proposed change.
The amount of B6 people are advised to consume for good health — around 1.3mg a day — is not changing.
Professor Green said a deficiency would be rare.
"It wouldn't happen with a normal Australian diet," he said.
Matt Silsby, a neurologist and neurophysiologist, said B6 toxicity typically caused "primarily sensory symptoms, pins and needles or prickling or painful symptoms", and sometimes cramps or muscle twitches.
In more serious cases, he said it could "get quite severe and lead to nerve damage", and in a subset of those patients that damage can be permanent.
He was quick to stress that symptoms "could potentially have very many causes", and it's "not appropriate to just attribute everything to the vitamin B6 level".
Regulators, manufacturers face potential shake-up
The review followed years of mounting concern and, recently, a dramatic intervention by the medicines regulator.
In November last year the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) — which had conceded it had been too slow to act — moved to pull high-dose B6 products from general sale, while also asking the NHMRC to review the science behind the limit.
According to the recommendation, the new limit would apply to all adults, including during pregnancy and breastfeeding, with lower limits for children scaled down by body weight, to as little as 4mg a day for under-4s.
Alexandra Jones, a food policy expert at the George Institute for Global Health, told 7.30 the proposed reduction was "encouraging" and brought Australia "closer to the approach adopted by the European Food Safety Authority", which enforces some of the most conservative safety limits in the world.
The upper limit is also a key reference that medicine and food regulators draw on when deciding what can be sold, how it is labelled, and what sits behind the pharmacy counter.
"The outcomes of the NHMRC's work are not regulatory, but they do provide an important scientific foundation for updating guidance to consumers and potentially updating policy and regulation down the track," Dr Jones said.
The working group acknowledged the change could carry "cost implications for manufacturers", but said its decision was "made on the basis of population health".
"There's nobody who's going to be harmed by lowering it," Professor Green said, "but there will be people who may be harmed by keeping it at 50 milligrams."
'Hidden' in supplements and energy drinks
Just how many Australians have been affected is impossible to say.
Pathology clinics across the country sounded the alarm more than a year ago, noting a spike in concerning results.
But the TGA's surveillance of cases has been cumbersome.
The TGA publicly lists reports of potential issues related to medicines as "adverse events". As of August 13, the current number of potential peripheral neuropathy cases linked to pyridoxine (B6) since 2020 was 279.
But even by the TGA's own admissions, that number should not be considered an accurate reflection of prevalence in the community.
The Australian lobby group for complementary medicines, CMA, which represents major manufacturers, maintains that adverse events are "extremely rare".
A CMA spokesperson told 7.30 "high doses of vitamin B6 are often recommended by healthcare practitioners for specific therapeutic benefits or preventing deficiency".
Professor Green believes toxicity cases are under-reported and what has been recorded officially was "likely the tip of the iceberg", probably skewed towards the most "severely affected people".
Another issue in trying to understand prevalence is that toxicity symptoms exist on a spectrum and can often mimic other conditions.
Dr Silsby, who is researching the effect of B6 on nerves, said patients rarely realise how much they are taking and were often "absolutely shocked" when they figured out how many of their products contain B6.
"It can be hidden or unexpected in supplements … and we always ask them to go home and check through their cabinets and to stop anything that contains it,"
Professor Green himself admitted he unknowingly took B6 in a magnesium supplement for a while.
"If I can't figure it out, having been in this area for 20 years, how is the general public meant to?" he said.
For many people, though, the biggest source of hidden B6 is not vitamin supplements.
The NHMRC working group's analysis found that in 2023, nearly a third (32.9 per cent) of Australians' dietary vitamin B6 intake came from just three sources: electrolyte, energy and fortified drinks; cereal-based dishes like sandwiches and pasta; and poultry — but noted the latter two groups contain too little B6 to be a concern.
Dr Jones said the revised limit was "yet another good reason for energy drink consumers to rethink that habit".
While individual drinks are in the safe range of vitamin B6, problems could potentially arise if people consume multiple products containing synthetic B6.
"A single can of a popular energy drink can contain around 5 milligrams," she said, "so those drinking multiple cans, and particularly those combining energy drinks with supplements, need to take note."
But while the NHMRC offers advice, the rules governing what goes into foods and drinks are set separately by Food Standards Australia New Zealand (FSANZ).
Dr Jones told 7.30 the onus should not be on consumers "to maintain vigilance and read the fine print on everything," and said FSANZ should "consider updating guidance on an appropriate 'one day quantity' and potentially limiting the content of B6 permissible in energy drinks".
FSANZ said it would "carefully consider the final outcomes and any implications for food regulation", once a final recommendation was accepted.
The Australian Beverages Council, whose membership includes energy drink manufacturers, said it was consulting members over the proposal and would "comply with any relevant regulatory changes".
It noted the TGA's review had found supplements, not drinks, to be the largest source of dietary B6.
Complementary Medicines Australia — which represents about 80 per cent of the sector — played down the significance of the recommended change, noting the new figure is a dietary guideline, not a rule for medicines, and that supplements already carry warning labels and follow the regulations.
Previous safe limit set on 'biased' evidence
The NHMRC group behind the recommendation included toxicologists, pharmacologists, neurologists, a chemical pathologist, a GP, public health experts and a specialist in complementary medicines, as well as a member with lived experience of B6 toxicity.
An external review commissioned found the evidence behind the old 50mg figure was thin, resting largely on small, decades-old overseas studies that carried a "high risk of bias".
There had never been much solid data to work from, Professor Green said, because proper studies would mean deliberately harming people.
"People don't normally set out to poison people in studies," he told 7.30, adding that some of the earlier research would be considered "unethical" by modern standards.
What had changed, he said, was how much B6 people now consume, often without knowing, driven by the proliferation of supplements in recent years.
"The more people you start exposing to supplements, the more things that are going to come up that you didn't expect," he said, explaining that the committee primarily considered mounting adverse-event reports and recent international guidance, to "err on the side of caution."
The 'slow cogs' of progress
Mr Noonan-O'Keefe told 7.30 the NHMRC's recommendation was "fantastic" and "going in the right direction", and hoped the TGA was paying close attention.
"I hope they look at this latest body of evidence, which has existed for a long time, and recognise the level of action they've taken to date is insufficient," he said.
Under the TGA's current settings, products containing up to 50mg of vitamin B6 will remain on general sale until at least June 2027, more than three times the dose the new science says is safe.
In a statement to 7.30, the TGA said it had run a successful public safety campaign earlier this year and said "in the coming weeks" it intended to consult on further measures —including stricter labelling, as well as lowering the threshold at which products must carry a warning about nerve damage.
But the TGA spokesperson wouldn't commit to "further regulatory action", including considering scheduling changes, until the final NHMRC recommendations process was complete.
"A time frame for this work has not been decided," the spokesperson said.
That wait is hard to accept for people living with the consequences of toxicity.
"What are we waiting for?" Mr Noonan-O'Keefe said.
"A working group has established the issue, so the regulator knows and we expect them to be swift — not slow-turning cogs."
The NHMRC proposal is open for public submissions until September 30, with a final decision expected next year.
From there it would be up to the regulators to decide whether what's on the shelves should more closely match the recommendation.

Trial date set for alleged 9/11 mastermind
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Trial date set for alleged 9/11 mastermind
August 27, 2026
Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the alleged mastermind behind the terror attacks in the United States on September 11, 2001, has been given a trial date.
Mohammed was captured in 2003 and has spent nearly 20 years in detention at Guantanamo Bay prison in Cuba.
A US Air Force Judge late on Wednesday ordered that Mohammed and three co-defendants go before a military tribunal in June 2028.
The long-delayed procedure has been hampered by legal wrangling over confessions made after torture, finding a location where he could be tried, and intense emotions regarding the man widely regarded as the main planner of the 9/11 terror attacks .
An earlier plea deal in which Mohammed agreed to admit guilt in exchange for avoiding the death penalty was thrown out last year.
The new trial will see Mohammed, as well as Walid Muhammad Salih Mubarak bin 'Atash, Mustafa Ahmed Adam al Hawsawi, and Ali Abdul Aziz Ali stand trial in a US military court with service members acting as jury.
Who is Khalid Sheikh Mohammed?
Born in Kuwait in 1965, he is alleged to have been sympathetic to anti-Soviet Islamist causes before getting a degree in mechanical engineering from a US university in 1986.
He worked for a time as an engineer for the Qatari government. According to US intelligence agents, in the early 1990s he participated in a plot to bomb airliners traveling between the US and Asia that was never realized.
He is believed to have met al-Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden shortly after that. As the group's head of propaganda, he is accused of having helped plan the 1993 World Trade Center bombings, the 2002 Bali bombings in Indonesia, and the murder of US journalist Daniel Pearl as well as 9/11.
What is Mohammed charged with?
As the suspected mastermind of the September 11 attacks, he is charged with 2,977 counts of murder, terrorism, hijacking aircraft, and attacking civilians.
Because his charges are classified as war crimes, he will be tried by a military tribunal.
It is possible that he could be given the death penalty, but judges may seek to avoid that outcome because it can lead to a lengthy appeals process.

Patria drives armored vehicle in Finland from Tokyo desk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
08:01:11 UTC
17:01:11 KST

- Patria remotely operated an AMV armored vehicle in Finland from a control desk in Tokyo, a distance of more than 7,800 kilometers.
- The August 25-26 demonstration combined drive-by-wire technology, secure 5G connectivity and real-time situational awareness from multiple technology partners.
Finnish defense manufacturer Patria remotely operated an AMV armored vehicle located in Finland from a control desk in Tokyo, a distance of more than 7,800 kilometers (4,847 miles), the company said this week.
The demonstration took place August 25-26, hosted by the Embassy of Finland in Japan. The Patria AMV was positioned at the Parola military testing area in Finland while an operator in Tokyo controlled the vehicle in real time, using drive-by-wire vehicle technology connected over secure 5G networks.
“The demonstrations were a great success, drawing a large number of attendees from the Japan Ministry of Defence and defence-related companies,” said Janne Räkköläinen, Patria’s Vice President, Market Area World. “This event reflects the strong interest in Patria’s remote driving capabilities in Japan and internationally, as well as the confidence placed in our local partner, the Japan Steel Works.”
The demonstration relied on several outside technology partners. Patria’s own situational awareness system, Patria DOME, provided real-time monitoring of the vehicle and its surroundings, supplemented with satellite data from ICEYE. Nokia, SAVOX and Basemark contributed additional communications and visual awareness technology, while Telia provided the secure data connectivity linking Tokyo to Finland.
Patria has worked on remote and unmanned vehicle capabilities for the AMV platform for several years. The company demonstrated beyond-visual-line-of-sight remote control of an AMV 8×8 using commercial 5G and 4G networks in 2020, in a project conducted with the University of Tampere. In April 2025, Finnish telecom provider Telia separately demonstrated remote operation of a Patria AMV XP over a distance of nearly 100 kilometers (62 miles) during military exercises in Lapland, using a dedicated 5G network slice.
Patria has sold roughly 1,600 AMV vehicles to defense forces in multiple countries, including Finland, Poland, Sweden, Slovenia, Croatia, South Africa, the United Arab Emirates and Japan. Japan’s Ground Self-Defense Force received its first Patria AMV XP in September 2025 under the country’s Wheeled Armored Personnel Carrier program, with vehicles assembled locally at Japan Steel Works’ Muroran plant.
Patria said the same remote-operation concept demonstrated in Tokyo could support future applications including unmanned logistics, vehicle convoying and autonomous waypoint navigation.

A U.S. Army MH-60 Black Hawk helicopter crashed during a training flight.
Denver7 reported on this, citing a U.S. Army Special Operations Aviation Command spokesperson and the Gilpin County Sheriff’s Office.
The incident occurred on August 25 on the eastern slope of Thorodin Mountain in Colorado.
Four people were aboard the aircraft, and none were injured in the crash.
An investigation has been launched to determine the causes and circumstances of the accident.
The helicopter belonged to the U.S. Army’s 160th Special Operations Aviation Regiment, known as the Night Stalkers.
This elite unit specializes in nap-of-the-earth night flights and provides aviation support to special operations forces, including SEAL Team 6 and Delta Force.
To perform its missions, the regiment uses specially modified versions of helicopters, including the MH-60M Black Hawk.
These aircraft are equipped with more powerful engines, advanced aerial refueling systems, EW devices, and the latest electro-optical systems.
The MH-60 Black Hawk’s primary role in the unit is the covert insertion, deployment, and evacuation of assault groups in challenging terrain and weather conditions.
In July, an MH-60S Sea Hawk helicopter that was assigned to the aircraft carrier USS George H.W. Bush made an emergency water landing in the Arabian Sea.
Three out of the four helicopter’s crew members were found and evacuated from the water.

Afghan Relocations and Assistance Policy
Information and guidance on the Afghan Relocations and Assistance Policy.

Details
The Ministry of Defence, Defence Afghan Relocation and Resettlement and Home Office, UK Visas and Immigration Accountability Document was published under the 2022 to 2024 Sunak Conservative government.

USS George Washington marks 200,000th carrier landing
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
09:00:00 BST
17:00:00 KST

USS George Washington has completed its 200,000th fixed-wing aircraft recovery, with an F-35C Lightning II making the milestone landing while the carrier operated in the Indian Ocean.
The US Navy aircraft carrier USS George Washington has recorded its 200,000th fixed-wing aircraft recovery after 34 years of service, with the milestone achieved by an F-35C Lightning II operating in the Indian Ocean, the UK Defence Journal understands.
The landing took place on 18 August during routine operations in the US 7th Fleet area of responsibility. According to a US Navy news update, Lieutenant Steven Frazier of Strike Fighter Squadron 147 was flying the F-35C that completed the carrier’s 200,000th arrested landing.
Carrier landings, commonly known as “traps”, require a fixed-wing aircraft to catch one of the ship’s arresting wires with a tailhook as it touches down on the flight deck. The system rapidly brings the aircraft to a halt over a comparatively short distance, allowing sustained flight operations at sea without the runway length available at a conventional airfield.
Frazier said, as quoted in the news update: “For the George Washington, more than anything, it shows consistency over the last 34 years to be able to complete whatever mission the country calls upon it to do.”
He added: “For me personally, it shows that if this aircraft carrier launches me off of the ship, I’ll be able to come back and land on it.”
The Navy said George Washington can recover aircraft at a rate of around one per minute and typically handles approximately 70 recoveries across several flying periods during a day of sustained operations. Each recovery relies on coordination between pilots, landing signal officers, flight deck personnel, arresting gear crews working below deck and maintainers responsible for keeping the carrier’s aviation systems serviceable.
Rear Admiral Jeffrey L. Heames, commander of Carrier Strike Group 5, said: “Two hundred thousand traps is not just a number – it is a testament to the enduring strength of American naval aviation and the unmatching professionalism of the Sailors who make it possible.”
He added: “This milestone reminds the world that U.S. carriers remain ready to launch and recover aircraft anywhere, anytime, in defense of freedom and our allies.”
Over the course of its service, George Washington has recovered several generations of US naval aircraft. These have included F-14 Tomcats, F/A-18C/D Hornets and, more recently, F/A-18E/F Super Hornets, EA-18G Growlers, E-2 Hawkeyes and F-35C Lightning IIs. The 200,000th recovery therefore reflects aviation activity spanning the transition from Cold War-era carrier aircraft to the current generation of low-observable fighters and electronic warfare platforms.
Captain Nicholas DeLeo, commanding officer of USS George Washington, said the milestone represented the work of successive generations of sailors rather than a single flight crew. He said: “The 200,000th trap belongs to the arresting gear teams, the yellow shirts, the maintainers, and every watch-stander who ensures this afloat airfield stays full mission-capable.”
Carrier Air Wing Five commander Captain Brian Kesselring similarly described the achievement as the product of cooperation between the embarked air wing and the ship’s company. He said: “Every trap is a high-stakes ballet of skill, trust, and precision. Reaching 200,000 on George Washington is a shared achievement between the air wing and the ship’s company.”

Labor groups seek 15% employer pension contributions in Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
07:56:50 UTC
16:56:50 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Several labor groups on Thursday urged the government to raise employer pension contributions from 6% to 15%, increase wages, and give unions more say in migrant worker hiring, CNA reported.
Unite 4 Future Chair Ho Cheng-chia (何政家) said productivity has generally risen over the past two decades, while worker compensation has grown more slowly. He said the gap widened after 2019 and increased further after 2023 as Taiwan’s AI-related industries expanded.
Ho said workers are creating more economic value, but the gains are not fully reflected in their pay. Raising employer pension contributions would give workers a larger share of the value they create, he said.
Employers contributed an average of 6.04% of workers’ salaries to the pension system last year, according to labor insurance data cited in a government audit report. Ho said nearly 99% of employers contributed only about the legal minimum of 6%, per UDN.
Chunghwa Telecom Workers’ Union Chair Teng Ko-lien (鄧克廉) said higher pension contributions would work like a delayed pay raise. Workers would receive the money after retirement, giving them greater financial security later in life, per Economic Daily News.
Taoyuan Confederation of Trade Unions Chair Shih Shu-hua (施淑華) said some employers are unwilling to raise wages while continuing to recruit migrant workers. She said labor groups do not oppose migrant workers but oppose using lower-paid labor to hold down wages and working conditions.
Shih said employers should also be required to obtain union approval before hiring migrant workers. She added that unions in Taoyuan were seeking the right to strike and could strike over disputes involving wages and migrant worker hiring.
Under Taiwan’s labor pension system, employers must contribute at least 6% of a worker’s monthly salary to an individual pension account, while employees may make additional voluntary contributions. Raising the employer rate to 15% would increase companies’ labor costs but put substantially more money into workers’ retirement accounts without directly reducing their current wages.

Taiwan marks 100 years of Penglai rice with harvest in Yangmingshan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
07:56:49 UTC
16:56:49 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s Agriculture Ministry on Wednesday marked the centennial of Penglai rice by harvesting rice at the historic original seed field in Zhuzihu, Yangmingshan, where Japanese-type rice was successfully adapted to Taiwan a century ago, per CNA.
The ministry invited Japanese guests and agricultural experts to witness the harvest and taste rice varieties representing different stages of Taiwan’s rice-growing history.
Penglai rice was officially named in 1926 after years of efforts to adapt Japanese japonica rice to Taiwan’s climate. Japanese people living in Taiwan during the Japanese colonial period generally preferred the short-grain, sticky rice they were accustomed to eating in Japan over Taiwan’s native long-grain indica rice.
Japan began introducing Japanese rice varieties to Taiwan in the late 19th century, but the island’s warmer and more humid climate made cultivation difficult. Zhuzihu, a volcanic valley in Yangmingshan with a cooler microclimate, became an important experimental site.
The Nakamura strain was successfully cultivated at Zhuzihu in the 1920s, helping demonstrate that Japanese-type rice could be adapted to Taiwan. In 1926, the successfully improved Japanese-type rice was formally named “Penglai rice,” referring to the mythical Mount Penglai, associated in Chinese mythology with a legendary land of immortals.
Rice breeding and cultivation continued to improve after Penglai rice was introduced. Taichung 65, developed through breeding work led by Japanese agricultural experts, was officially named and promoted in 1936. It was high-yielding, adaptable, and suitable for cultivation in both rice-growing seasons, helping it become Taiwan’s leading rice variety before 1959.
Over the following decades, breeders continued developing varieties with greater yields, disease resistance, adaptability, and improved taste. Tainung 67 became a leading variety from 1979 to 1998, while Tainan 11 is currently Taiwan’s most widely cultivated variety, according to ministry officials, per CNA.
Agriculture Vice Minister Hu Jong-i (胡忠一) said the commemorative field was replanted with four classic varieties representing different periods: Nakamura, which was successfully cultivated experimentally in the 1920s; Taichung 65, the leading variety before 1959; Tainung 67, the leading variety from 1979 to 1998; and Tainan 11, currently the most widely cultivated.
“This year’s autumn harvest is not only a tribute to the land and history but also symbolizes Taiwan’s agricultural commitment to remembering its roots and continuing to thrive,” Hu said.
The event also featured a tasting of five rice varieties. A historical video chronicling the development of Penglai rice was shown, while Kaohsiung 147 was presented as an example of Taiwan’s modern rice breeding achievements. Kaohsiung 147 won gold awards at Japan’s International Contest on Rice Taste Evaluation in 2019 and 2024.
Hu said improvements to Penglai rice over generations, combined with growing recognition of the quality of Taiwanese rice in Japan, have helped expand the Japanese market. Japan imported about 12,500 tonnes of Taiwanese rice last year, he said.
Cho Akiro, chair of Sumitomo Corp. Taiwan, told Hu at the event that Taiwanese rice sold in Japan is considered by Japanese consumers to be comparable in quality and taste to Japanese rice and has received favorable reviews. The ministry said the development of Taiwan’s rice industry reflects a century of cross-border agricultural cooperation and technological exchange.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – Mandarin Airlines has received conditional approval from the Civil Aviation Administration to cut its weekly Hualien flights from Oct.1, reports said Thursday.
Mandarin and Uni Air applied to end all their Hualien flights because they were losing money. China Airlines subsidiary Mandarin operates seven flights a week between Kaohsiung and Hualien and three weekly flights between Taichung and Hualien, per Liberty Times.
The CAA has given its tentative approval for the airline to cut the number of flights between Kaohsiung and Hualien to five per week or three if the occupancy rate drops below 20%. Mandarin Airlines Chair Chen Ta-chun (陳大鈞) said the two flights lost NT$70 million (US$2.2 million) per year. One flight last year had only five passengers, he said, adding there were sufficient alternative modes of transportation, including trains and buses, to reach Hualien.
In June, EVA Air subsidiary Uni Air applied to end its four weekly flights between Taipei and Hualien. No decision has been made yet, the airline said.

The head of one of the district courts in Kyiv region and an intermediary have been notified of suspicion of creating a scheme intended to help a person liable for military service evade mobilization. The man handed the intermediary $2,500 for the judge. This was reported by the Office of the Prosecutor General, UNN reports.
Details
"Under the procedural guidance of the Office of the Prosecutor General, the head of one of the district courts in Kyiv region and an intermediary were notified of suspicion of obstructing the lawful activities of the Armed Forces of Ukraine during a special period (Part 1 of Article 114-1 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine). According to the investigation, the judge helped a person liable for military service evade conscription during mobilization," the post says.
According to the investigation, in March 2026, during a meeting arranged by the intermediary, the person liable for military service told the judge of his intention to evade mobilization. The judge advised him to arrange a housing rental and register as an internally displaced person so that the case could be heard precisely in the court he headed. Subsequently, the person liable for military service prepared an application to establish the fact that he was raising a child independently, along with the necessary documents.
"In May, the judge personally received these materials, and after the proceedings were opened, according to the investigation, he gave instructions regarding the further preparation of the documents and the position of the applicant's former wife. In July, he told the man that the case had been decided in his favor and named the time when a copy of the decision could be obtained. In August, the intermediary informed the person liable for military service that he needed to hand over $2,500 to the judge. Three days later, the man handed him the stated amount," the post says.
According to the investigation, this created grounds for evading conscription during mobilization, thereby obstructing the staffing of the Armed Forces of Ukraine and other military formations with personnel. The issue of selecting preventive measures for the suspects is currently being decided.
In addition, as stated, during the investigation, more than 100 other court decisions issued by the judge on similar matters will be examined.

Taiwan warns of surge in Chinese maritime gray zone tactics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
07:55:58 UTC
16:55:58 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Taiwan Coast Guard Administration (CGA) has warned of an intensifying situation as Beijing steps up maritime gray zone tactics around the country.
“When we say the situation is becoming increasingly severe, we mean that the number of their government vessels in the waters surrounding Taiwan has increased, and there was a marked increase in July,” a senior CGA official told Agence France-Presse (AFP). Chinese ships have been tracked 1,247 times around Taiwan since May, according to CGA figures.
The CGA detected Chinese government vessels around Taiwan’s main island a record 244 times in July, around eight per day, according to official data shared with AFP. Chinese ships were tracked 58 times last July.
Approximately 60% of the ships are coast guard cutters, while oceanographic research ships and other government ships make up the rest, according to AFP. This data excludes PLA vessels, which sail around Taiwan nearly every day.
The increasing number of ships has raised concerns that China could launch a maritime quarantine or full blockade by cutting off energy shipments and commercial shipping lanes, per AFP.
China has a fleet of more than 120 oceanographic research vessels, the CGA said, adding that it monitors 41 that operate near Taiwan, AFP reported. While civilian scientific organizations run these ships, the data they collect is shared with the Chinese military.
“That kind of data/knowledge is highly useful for Chinese naval forces, which will operate in these waters in the event of a conflict,” Ryan D. Martinson, a China maritime strategy specialist at the US Naval War College, told AFP. “It is especially important for anti-submarine warfare and submarine warfare.”
Martinson said he had noticed a recent rise in Chinese research vessels in waters east of Taiwan. “This is not a new ‘play’ in its ‘playbook.’ Rather, the novel aspect is that the scale of these operations around Taiwan is unprecedented,” he said.
The Chinese research vessel “Xiang Yang Hong 03” was recently observed operating over key undersea communication cables and deep-sea areas in Taiwan’s and Japan’s exclusive economic zones, according to Jason Wang, COO of geospatial firm ingeniSPACE. A Chinese coast guard cutter and a maritime militia fishing vessel accompanied the research vessel.
“This is the first time we have seen maritime militia escort a research vessel in Taiwan’s waters,” Wang said.
Wang explained that the ship aimed to collect “fresh hydrographic data of the Ryukyu Trench and East Taiwan Trench to conduct anti-submarine warfare” and “deny US and other allied vessels from doing the same.”
Martinson emphasized that these coordinated naval, militia, and scientific movements form a unified strategic campaign.
"All of these developments are connected, I believe," he said. "They represent a clear escalation in Beijing's efforts to exercise jurisdiction over the waters surrounding Taiwan, putting pressure on the country's leadership and undermining its sovereignty and sovereign rights."

What China can do to secure trade routes in its coming high-seas struggle with US

Unknown Publisher

What China can do to secure trade routes in its coming high-seas struggle with US
Di Dongsheng argues it could take three decades for China to dominate access to ports, straits, canals and shipping lanes around the world
China should forge a national consensus on “regaining mastery of the oceans” and direct overseas investment returns into defence spending to brace for sea-power competition with the US, according to a prominent Chinese academic.
Di Dongsheng, associate dean of Renmin University’s school of international studies in Beijing, warned on Tuesday that as economic ties between the United States, the dominant maritime power, and China, which relies heavily on sea-bound trade, shifted towards competition, the era of open oceans could be drawing to a close.
“We must prepare for struggle in a coming contest over sea power and the security of shipping routes,” Di wrote in a note on his social media channel.
He argued it could take about three decades for China to secure dominance over and access to ports, straits, canals and shipping lanes around the world in a step-by-step process.
“Before then, the possibility that a portion of [China’s] import and export trade relying on maritime transport would come under threats, or even partial shocks, still warrants close attention,” he said.
Di noted that Beijing had gained the “upper hand” in last year’s tariff and sanctions wars, forcing US President Donald Trump into a temporary compromise. However, his research indicated that the White House remained unconvinced and he said some viewed Washington as actively targeting China’s vulnerabilities and waiting for the right moment to act.
“One of China’s obvious soft spots is the maritime routes,” Di said.
He described geopolitical events since the second half of 2025 around the Panama Canal, Greenland and the Strait of Hormuz as “a series of warning signals that the openness of the seas is tending towards an end”.

U.S. Army awards $2.2 billion to build nuclear microreactors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
07:53:30 UTC
16:53:30 KST

- The U.S. Army selected five companies, including Westinghouse and Radiant, to build nuclear microreactors at five bases under its $2.2 billion Janus Program.
- Radiant's $750 million award, the largest of the five, covers 15 microreactors beginning with a three-unit installation at Fort Benning.
The U.S. Army has selected five companies to build and operate nuclear microreactors at military installations across the country, awarding up to $2.2 billion in combined funding under its Janus Program, the Army announced.
Westinghouse Government Services will supply its eVinci microreactor to Fort Drum, New York. Antares Nuclear will build at Fort Bragg, North Carolina. BWXT Advanced Technologies is set for Fort Campbell, Kentucky. General Atomics Electromagnetic Systems will deliver to Fort Hood, Texas. Radiant Industries will build at Fort Benning, Georgia.
The Janus Program is run in partnership with the Department of War Innovation Unit and is intended to move advanced microreactor technology beyond test programs and into sustained operation at defense installations, according to the Army.
“Reliable energy is fundamental to mission assurance, operational readiness and national security,” said Rich Rademacher, President of Westinghouse Government Services. “The selection of the eVinci microreactor for the Janus Project highlights the important role advanced nuclear technology can play in providing resilient, long-duration power to the warfighter.”
“The Janus Program is about transitioning from designs and experiments to reliable commercial hardware which secures our energy independence,” said Dr. Jeff Waksman, Principal Deputy Assistant Secretary of the Army for Installations, Energy and Environment. “The Janus Program vendors were selected through a deeply rigorous evaluation on technical, financial, and organizational capabilities conducted by an All-Star panel of dozens of experts from across the nation.”
The eVinci is a heat-pipe reactor Westinghouse says is designed to provide continuous electricity for eight years without refueling. The planned microreactors across the five installations will generate under 20 megawatts of electricity each and occupy less than five acres of land, according to the Army.
Radiant disclosed the largest agreement among the five vendors: up to $750 million to deploy 15 factory-built, 1-megawatt Kaleidos microreactors by 2030, beginning with a three-unit installation at Fort Benning. Radiant’s Kaleidos reactor is transportable by land, sea or air and is designed to be deployed directly at customer sites, according to the company.
“The Army’s $750 million award shows confidence in Radiant’s product and ability to manufacture, deploy and safely operate nuclear microreactors for the American military,” said Tori Shivanandan, president and chief operating officer of Radiant.
None of the planned reactors will use highly enriched, weapons-grade uranium, according to Waksman.
The Janus Program follows the Pentagon’s 2022 Project Pele initiative, which developed a portable 40-ton reactor capable of generating 1 to 5 megawatts of power. Army officials said the current program is funded for five years, with a target of having at least one microreactor producing usable electricity at an installation by September 30, 2028.
The five sites selected represent the first tranche of installations under Janus, with Army officials anticipating that additional private investment from the companies could bring the total number of microreactors across all installations to more than 20.
The push into military nuclear power comes as private companies increasingly move into a fuel-cycle sector long dominated by government programs. Christo Liebenberg, co-founder of uranium enrichment company LIS Technologies, told The Defence Blog in March that domestic enrichment capacity sits at the center of both civilian and defense nuclear infrastructure, and that private firms can move faster than institutional programs in developing fuel supply for smaller reactors built for remote or secure military installations.

Yayoi Kusama, Japan’s ‘queen of polka dots’, dies at 97
Unknown
