Push for import ban on 'pervert' smart glasses amid privacy concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
02:00:37 UTC
11:00:37 KST

Push for import ban on 'pervert' smart glasses amid privacy concerns
In short:
Smart glasses and other wearable recording devices would be subject to a 12-month import ban under a bill to be introduced to the Senate.
Experts warn Australian laws have not kept up with the privacy risks posed by the flood of cheap camera-enabled devices entering the country.
What's next?
The Greens intend to launch the bill when parliament resumes next month, with several independent crossbenchers also in support.
There is growing support for a ban on the import of so-called "smart glasses" amid an influx of low-cost devices that are being used to film people without their consent.
In recent weeks the devices, dubbed "pervert glasses" by some critics for their capacity to film in secret, have inspired two Australian petitions calling for restrictions on their sale and import which attracted tens of thousands of signatures.
Now the Greens, with support of independents, plan to launch a bill when parliament next sits to halt the import of such glasses as well as other wearable recording devices for at least 12 months, until tougher privacy protections are passed into law.
"If we end up having millions of these devices in the country, there'll be no place that's free for your privacy," Greens senator David Shoebridge said.
"And at the scale that you see these sorts of imports ramping up already, that is what we face".
While first generation smart glasses cost upwards of $500, newer entrants to the market are available for well under $100 from a number of online and shopfront retailers in Australia.
At both ends of the price range, they look like ordinary glasses and yet allow the wearer to record images, video and audio, mostly surreptitiously, with the press of a button.
It is not clear how many pairs of smart glasses are already in circulation domestically, but Senator Shoebridge warned the current crop was just the beginning for wearable cameras.
"Right now it's glasses, but in a month's time it's almost certainly going to be earbuds, maybe it'll be a lapel pin, maybe it'll just be your T-shirt, I don't know".
He said parliament had a narrow window of time to block their large scale importation before such devices "wash through society".
"Maybe we should think ahead for once," Senator Shoebridge said.
"The genie's not yet out of the bottle … let's put a little plug in it until we work out what we want it to do."
Alongside the proposed import ban, which would include carve-outs for legitimate uses, such as aiding people with a vision impairment, the Greens are pushing for new privacy protections.
The bill would amend the Privacy Act to prohibit filming, storing or sharing footage from a "wearable recording device" without a person's express consent.
The change would for the first time extend the Privacy Act from large organisations to individuals.
It also proposes extra powers and funding for the Privacy Commissioner, to enforce those rules.
Ban attracts crossbench support
Independents David Pocock and Kate Chaney are among the crossbenchers in favour of a temporary import ban.
"I do think it's sensible to be pausing the imports … while the parliament actually puts some laws in place," Senator Pocock said.
"I think it would reduce the number of these devices that are on the street."
Ms Chaney described the proposed import ban as an imperfect fix for a lag in Australia's privacy protections.
"An import pause is a temporary solution. We really need to make sure that we can regulate these devices in the long term," she said.
While bills from the crossbench such as this one have a low rate of success historically, the proposal reflects significant public and political pressure on the government to respond to the smart glasses' privacy risk.
Earlier this month Attorney-General Michelle Rowland aired her own concerns about the technology, asking the privacy commissioner to prioritise the issue.
When asked by the ABC, a spokesman for Ms Rowland did not say whether the government was considering an import ban of its own, but acknowledged that smart glasses do "raise privacy concerns".
"These concerns deserve to be met with balanced and holistic policies that protect Australians while preserving legitimate uses of technology," the spokesman said.
"The government is actively considering these issues as part of our second tranche of privacy reforms."
The government committed to a suite of changes to the Privacy Act in September of 2023 and passed an initial wave of amendments it called "tranche one" in December 2024, including anti-doxxing laws and Children's Online Privacy Code, but is yet to act on the majority of the recommendations it agreed to two years ago.
A spokesman for Shadow Attorney-General Michaelia Cash also declined to comment on the specific proposal for an import ban.
Australia already importing 'creepy' social media trends
In countries such as the US and the UK, where the technology is more widespread, it has facilitated doxxing, online shaming and harassment at gyms, beaches and a range of public and semi-public spaces.
One of the biggest concerns is that the incoming tide of cheaper alternatives will bring with it the social media trends which exploit tech like this.
One of the best known examples is "rizzing", where self-described pick-up artists and dating coaches hit on women in public, secretly film the encounter and post the footage online, without the subject's consent or knowledge.
That trend is still in its infancy in Australia, but the ABC was able to easily find local examples of the same practice.
Privacy advocates are worried about the trajectory, and say women and minorities tend to be more heavily targeted by surreptitious recording.
"We see women shamed for being dressed in a certain way, or maybe they're being drunk in public … [recordings are] very rarely used to shame men for the same sorts of behaviour," Tom Sulston from Digital Rights Watch said.
Initially sceptical about the prospect of an import ban, Mr Sulston was ultimately swayed by the growing expectation that Apple will release camera-enabled wireless headphones as soon as September.
"That would be a huge scale point for the amount of covert cameras being used in public in Australia,"
Electronic Frontiers Australia has been calling for a moratorium on the sale of the technology for several weeks, and said privacy violations were already appearing locally.
"I've seen a couple of real-life examples of devices being misused in a gym-type context and also on the beach," EFA chair John Pane said.
He said regardless of what laws were in place, the nature of this technology meant many victims would never find out they had been filmed, let alone have a chance to seek redress.
"It's all the more difficult with smart devices like these because you don't know when they're being used or not."
Mr Sulston said it was a moment for Australians and their government to decide how much surveillance they were willing to accept.
"That sense of being in the panopticon is really bad for us psychologically, and we cannot afford to end up there."

Chamber chairman Jacob Kam Chak-pui said Hong Kong performed well in research and innovation exchanges through its universities and scientific work, and in attracting leading global professionals through talent admission schemes.

Has Alien and Blade Runner filmmaker Ridley Scott lost the plot?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Aussie stars Jacob Elordi and Guy Pearce can't save this tepid dystopia
At several stages during Ridley Scott's latest movie about the downfall of humanity and the core of what keeps us strong, The Dog Stars, characters stare up at the night's glimmering star-scape.
Sadly, it only serves to remind us just how far he has fallen, as a filmmaker, since the heady heights of Alien (1979) and Blade Runner (1982).
Adapted from Peter Heller's 2012 novel of the same name by The Revenant writer Mark L Smith and Nixon scribe Christopher Wilkinson, you'd think they'd have a firm handle on survival in the wild and the political causes of our destruction, particularly with Scott's career-long interest in such things.
But what follows seems clinically uninterested in these thematic riches.
Fridging the plot
Frankenstein star Jacob Elordi is Hig, our main window into this fallen world that's been ravaged by a pandemic that should feel too close to the bone, coming so soon after our collective shave with mortality.
He was a mechanic, adoring of his pregnant wife, Melissa (Sai Bennett), with both her and their unborn child cruelly claimed by the rampaging disease.
But The Dog Stars isn't interested in Melissa.
She's just a convenient back story, a near-mute example of 'fridging', the heinous storytelling trope where a supporting character (usually a woman) is hurt or killed off simply to provide trauma-plot for the protagonist. (The term was coined by comic book writer Gail Simone after a particularly egregious example, with the brutal murder of Green Lantern's girlfriend, Alexandra DeWitt, whose dismembered body parts were stuffed in the superhero's refrigerator.)
Briefly glimpsed in flashbacks, Melissa's absence is simply fodder for Hig's woes, as he dreams of flying his Cessna into the side of a mountain. In fact, Hig's trusty pup, Jasper, gets more screen time, though this being a violent dystopian landscape, the risk of our four-legged friend also winding up in the metaphorical fridge is ever-present.
Despite being central to the narrative, Hig isn't granted a great deal of depth by Elordi, despite proving, in Justin Kurzel's The Narrow Road to the Deep North, that he's more than capable of inhabiting such a weary soul.
He shares this solitary life in an overgrown airport in Erie, Colorado, with Bangley (a charismatic, but unstretched Josh Brolin), a military-minded survivalist who has assembled something nearing The A-Team-style hilarious arsenal of murderous weapons.
Bangley's idea of keeping them safe involves shooting, without question, anyone who dares approach their ragged outpost. Which is maybe fair enough, given that, as is textbook in such fiction, for every reasonably sane person trying to maintain some small modicum of normality, post-apocalypse, there are ravaging hordes of those who choose violence, possibly because they are broken beyond repair.
They're dubbed Reapers (please find another term for such folks, dystopian writers). But much like Melissa, they're inconsequential; an indeterminate mass of tattooed maniacs. Without the sheer commitment to the absolute lunacy of the Mad Max franchise, you have to wonder why the Bad Guys™ appear to have a group chat to coordinate their fetish-forward look?
Whither do we wander?
While we're on the subject of unconvincing style, costume designer Janty Yates's only very artfully soiled and torn apocalypse styles mostly resemble a fashion shoot for a particular brand of 'hard-wearing' apparel that's apparently mandatory for a certain brand of straight man.
It's as unconvincing as Scott's thinly sketched world. The Dog Stars inexorably plods on, ticking off every dystopian trope dutifully — supply raids gone wrong, mysterious radio messages, the safe haven that isn't: check, check, check.
It ropes in another Aussie, Memento star Guy Pearce, as Pops, who is overbearingly protective of his plucky daughter, former med student Cima, played by The Substance star Margaret Qualley. In fairness, she has a fridged husband. Sadly, Qualley also has no discernible chemistry with Elordi. The film's not overly interested in their romantic potential anyway.
In an admittedly wild divergence from the book, Scott introduces Allison Janey as Darlene, a promisingly pantomime villain who's surreally decked in vintage flight attendant blue twin-suit and cap and terrifying drag queen makeup.
She holds court over a trippy cult that appears to be frozen in 60s glamour gone wrong. Guess what? Scott's not interested in them, either, with a far-too-fleeting sequence feeling as if the studio twisted editors Claire Simpson and Sam Restivo's arm. In the short-change stakes, Benedict Wong is even more hard done by, in a Mennonite subplot that's also surplus to Scott's requirements.
Drippy dystopia
Throw in a drippy acoustic guitar score from Harry Gregson-Williams, Scott's regular composer since Kingdom of Heaven, and a meandering pace, and even The Killer cinematographer Erik Messerschmidt's sweeping vistas can't save this insipid reading of Heller's already overly familiar novel.
There are copious finer examples out there, including Mary Shelley's The Last Man, published a few short years after Frankenstein, Cormac McCarthy's The Road, Stephen King's mythic The Stand, and Richard Matheson's 1954 novel I Am Legend, plus their many screen adaptations of admittedly varying quality.
Canadian author Emily St John Mandel's astonishing novel, Station 11, and Patrick Somerville's inspired miniseries adaptation, are the high bar, wrangling with what survival means in a near-dead world. They centre storytelling as the thread worth hanging on to.
Tragically, the latter-career Scott's grip on such stardust appears to have unravelled.
The Dog Stars is in Australian cinemas from August 27.

US allows imports of certain Russian diamond categories until September 1, 2027

10:58:40 KST

WASHINGTON, August 27. /TASS/. The United States has authorized transactions involving imports of certain categories of Russian diamonds into the country until September 1, 2027, according to a license published by the US Department of the Treasury.
According to the document, Russian-origin diamonds weighing 1 carat or more may be imported provided that they were located outside Russia and were not exported or reexported from Russia on or after March 1, 2024. In addition, the license permits imports of diamonds weighing 0.5 carats or more provided that they were located outside Russia and were not exported or reexported from Russia on or after September 1, 2024.
In December 2023, the Group of Seven countries announced restrictions on imports of diamonds mined or processed in Russia starting January 1, 2024. On March 1, the restrictions were extended to Russian diamonds processed in other countries.
In February 2024, US authorities announced that imports of unsorted diamonds and diamond jewelry from Russia would be banned starting March 1. They also prohibited imports into the United States of non-industrial diamonds from Russia weighing 1 carat or more starting March 1, 2024, and those weighing 0.5 carats or more starting September 1, 2024, regardless of whether they had been processed in third countries. In August of that year, US authorities authorized imports of certain categories of Russian diamonds until September 1, 2025. The license was later extended for another year.

America's visa squeeze: What’s at stake for asylum seekers, business travellers and tourists?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
01:56:41 UTC
10:56:41 KST

Washington, DC — Reports that the Trump administration is considering the revocation of up to 200,000 B1 and B2 visas tied to pending asylum claims have drawn attention well beyond the usual immigration policy circles.
The figure itself is significant, but so is the uncertainty surrounding it: which visa holders would be affected, under what criteria, and on what timeline are all questions the reports leave largely unanswered.
The implications, if the move proceeds, would extend past asylum seekers to encompass a broader population: tourists holding valid B2 visas and business travellers operating under B1 status, both groups now facing the possibility that a routine visa classification could carry unexpected consequences.
The B1 visa is generally issued to business travellers, while the B2 visa is given to tourists.
The administration's justification is that this is being used as a loophole to enter the country and put down roots while the asylum process takes its course, with Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau calling it "bogus asylum claims."
The administration didn't provide a specific number of visas that could be revoked, but the Associated Press cited State Department documents and US officials estimating the number at up to 200,000.
The move, if it happens, would mark the largest mass revocation in US history, and would likely be challenged.
What are the consequences?
It is worth noting that revoking a non-immigrant visa isn't the same as terminating an asylum case or claim. People who enter the country on a B1 or B2 visa and later apply for asylum generally derive their legal status from the pending asylum case, not from the original visa.
Based on this, the immediate impact on people with pending cases may be limited. However, the long-term consequences could be substantial.
"They would lose their status as temporary visitors, but they would not necessarily become immediately removable solely because their visa has been revoked. Their right to pursue an asylum application would generally remain intact until adjudication," Rut Bermejo Casado, Associate Professor at Rey Juan Carlos University and researcher in migration and asylum policies, tells TRT World.
With that being said, the move could have some consequences, including legal implications, as it could generate litigation over whether the administration is penalising individuals for exercising their right, which is protected under US asylum law.
As for the asylum seekers, many would depend entirely on their cases for legal status, and if those cases are dismissed, they would have no legal status in the country.
The measure could have symbolic significance, as it could signal a major shift toward treating post-entry asylum claims as evidence that temporary visas were used inconsistently with their intended purpose.
"In that sense, the policy may be more intended as a 'deterrent' and political statement than as a mechanism for immediate deportation," Bermejo Casado, who is also a non-resident senior fellow at the Elcano Royal Institute, says.
What do previous examples tell us?
In the United States, there were instances of mass visa revocations before.
In 1979, during the Iran hostage crisis, then-president Jimmy Carter issued an order — known as Executive Order 12172 — that gave the Secretary of State and the Attorney General power to limit or create exceptions for Iranian nationals holding non-immigrant visas.
The administration at the time ultimately invalidated visas and mandated that over 50,000 Iranian students report to immigration authorities in December of the same year to verify their status or face immediate deportation.
A federal appeals court reportedly backed the administration's right to single out Iranian students in this measure.
After the 9/11 attacks, the Department of Justice launched an initiative to locate, interview, and deport approximately 314,000 "absconders"— foreign nationals who stayed in the US despite final deportation orders.
But rather than pursuing that number equally, the George W. Bush administration prioritised people from the Middle East and South Asia.
However, these and other instances were primarily based on national security grounds, not on the claim that the holders later sought asylum.
"The closest comparisons are probably policies that seek to discourage asylum applications viewed by governments as abusive or opportunistic," Bermejo Casado says.
Over the past 20 years, Australia introduced a variety of measures aimed at deterring asylum claims after arrival. Similarly, a number of European governments introduced reforms intended to limit access to protection procedures.
"However, these measures have usually focused on procedural restrictions, offshore processing, or accelerated removal mechanisms rather than mass retroactive visa revocations," adds Bermejo Casado.
How could this be challenged?
Nearly every similar instance of this measure was legally challenged, though in most cases, courts upheld it.
In this case, if it comes to fruition, it is expected to face challenges, especially given that immigration and asylum rights are protected by US law and international obligations.
Although the Executive Branch has broad authority over the matter, courts may be asked to consider due process.
There could also be administrative hurdles, Bermejo Casado says, "as people fleeing serious insecurity or political persecution may continue to seek protection despite additional obstacles."
In short, the impact of this move would be limited, as it wouldn't prevent asylum seekers from pursuing their claims.
However, there could be long-term consequences given that it signals a tougher approach against irregular migration.

Airmen and Guardians Must Undergo Gas Mask Seal Tests as Part of Shaving Crackdown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
01:53:23 UTC
10:53:23 KST

The Department of the Air Force is giving Airman and Guardians until the end of the year to meet new requirements for ensuring they achieve a proper protective mask seal, part of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s crackdown on unauthorized facial hair.
The Department of the Air Force released instructions for Air Force and Space Force squadron-level unit commanders to appoint “mask fit validation monitors” that are trained to oversee protective mask seal testing, according to an Air Force tasking order posted Aug. 25 on the popular but unofficial Air Force amn/nco/snco Facebook page.
The service released guidance on the directive in a July 27 memo updating the Department of the Air Force Instruction on its Chemical, Biological, Radiological, Nuclear Defense Program, an Air Force official told Air & Space Forces Magazine Aug. 26.
“Every Airman and Guardian, including Air National Guard and Air Force Reserve members, must complete two new CBRN defense requirements … by Dec. 31, 2026,” the Air Force official said.
“The requirements are [to be] completed in order. First is the CBRN Defense Foundations Course, an annual web-based course taken through DAF e-Learning. Second is the mask validation, or negative pressure check, done in person with the unit mask fit validation monitor.”
The Air Force official added that the changes “align with the Secretary of War’s guidance titled ‘Grooming Standards for Facial Hair Implementation,’ and reinforce how these skills are critical not only for defense against CBRN threats, but also for other hazardous mission sets where respiratory protection may be required.”
Both requirements will then transition to annual requirements for Airmen and Guardians, according to the official.
Both the Navy and Marine Corps have also released similar guidance directing that all Sailors and Marines conduct annual protective mask seal testing, Task & Purpose reported.
The new guidance comes just short of a year after Hegseth told hundreds of U.S. military leaders he intended to impose stringent new grooming standards across the force aimed at beards, goatees, and other facial hair that could interfere with a proper seal on a chemical protective mask or firefighter respirator.
For service members with medical shaving profiles, Hegseth directed that all waivers be limited to 12 months and those with permanent conditions be evaluated for separation. Hegseth also directed that service members who wear beards under religious accommodations be reevaluated under the pre-2010 appearance standards that generally do not authorize facial hair waivers.
Hegseth’s memo also states that “noncompliant personnel—due to refusal, exemption denial, or failed tests—will be flagged as nondeployable in the appropriate Military Service personnel system. Repeated noncompliance may result in administrative separation.”
Airmen and Guardians can still wear mustaches and sideburns, but the services tightened regulations last fall to ensure they allow for a proper mask seal.
Airmen’s mustaches “must not go beyond the corners of the mouth or into a respirator seal zone,” according to an Oct. 29 memorandum updating portions of the Air Force regulations on dress and personal appearance.
The new guidance also takes a slightly stricter stance on sideburns. Airmen and Guardians had been authorized to wear sideburns that extended to the “bottom of the orifice of the ear opening,” according to a July 2025 policy update. The new policy dictates that sideburns “will be above the ear opening.”

10:43:33 KST

What we know about the environmental causes behind the Nepal landslide
Deadly floods along the Nepal-Tibet border on Wednesday highlighted the near-impossible task of predicting sudden landslides and mudflows in the Himalayas. Experts say the terrain can turn a blocked river into a devastating torrent within minutes, while climate change may be increasing the risks of such disasters.
Lethal surges of mud and water that hit "like liquid concrete" are nearly impossible to predict and cannot be outrun.
The cause of the deadly landslide and flood along the Nepal-Tibet border is not yet certain, but experts say the risk of such events is compounded by the extreme topography of the Himalayas.
At least 270 people were killed and nearly 1500 are missing in the wake of the disaster on Wednesday morning.
Video from the Chinese side shows a raging wall of mud and debris crashing over a building several storeys high, engulfing it and sweeping away buses and cars as if they were toys.
It is too soon to draw any firm links to climate change, but there are well-documented trends in the "Roof of the World" that have increased the likelihood of such hazards.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Landslide, then tremors, says USGS
Nepal's Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal said an earthquake likely triggered a landslide that in turn blocked a river, sending water gushing downstream after it eventually breached the obstruction.
But in a new note, the US Geological Survey said that while the event was initially reported as a magnitude 4.4 earthquake, "additional analysis of long period seismic waves indicate that the seismic energy was instead generated by a landslide".
A preliminary assessment by the Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) found "no anomalies" from the Chinese side of the border.
"We believe a rock-ice avalanche occurred in Nepal, blocking the Lhende river and causing the cascading flood event," Sarthak Shrestha, a remote sensing and geo-information analyst with the intergovernmental institute, told AFP.
Hatim Sharif, a hydrologist at the University of Texas San Antonio, told AFP one thing that struck him was the lack of rainfall beforehand.
"That defeats essentially every operational flood warning system in the world," he said.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Running won't help
By the time you see the mud flow coming, it is too late, said Sharif.
"Running will not help", nor will trying to flee by vehicle, Sharif added, because the mud and water moving at high speed form a lethal combination "like liquid concrete".
The only solution is to climb up a hill, at least 20 feet (six metres), he estimates.
One possible long-term remedy might be river-level gauges that relay changes to authorities in real time, giving residents 20-30 minutes of warning, he said.
Dorothy Heinrich, a researcher at the UK's University of Reading, told AFP: "In these mountain environments, the rivers can be quite narrow in areas."
Anything that blocks them, be it an avalanche or landslide, will lead to a "big accumulation of water, then it creates these incredibly fast floods".
Qianggong Zhang, head of climate and environmental risks at ICIMOD, warned of the potential for a second flood because of an ongoing blockage upstream.
Read moreDeadly flash floods near Nepal-Tibet border raze villages, leave hundreds missing
Climate change trends
Nepal is also prone to glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs) – the sudden and catastrophic release of vast volumes of water from melting glacier-fed lakes.
One such catastrophe in July 2025 originated in China's Gyirong County, then surged into Nepal's Rasuwa District, though authorities have not yet said a GLOF was responsible for the latest event.
In the coming days and weeks, scientists around the world will be investigating potential climate links through what are known as attribution studies, which analyse how likely an event was in the fossil-fuel-warmed climate of today, versus the pre-industrial era.
"We do know what climate change trends look like in the Himalayas. The high confidence of more heatwaves, glacial retreat, permafrost reduction, these sorts of things that can drive things like landslides and glacial outburst floods," said Heinrich.
She stressed, however, that a firm link could only be made through an event attribution study.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Humanitarian visas slashed: What we know so far about Labor's migration reforms

The Albanese government has denied plans to slash Australia’s humanitarian intake by a third, after reports the cut was being considered as part of a broader push to reduce net overseas migration.
On Thursday, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said in a statement the government's 20,000 humanitarian placements would "be continued in future years, consistent with Australia’s humanitarian commitments".
The statement followed reporting on Thursday morning by The Australian Financial Review newspaper that Labor appeared poised to reduce humanitarian placements from 20,000 to 13,750 at the start of the next financial year and that it had factored the decrease into migration forecasts.
A spokesman for Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke told SBS News earlier on Thursday that the final decision on next year's humanitarian intake had not yet been made and linked the process to next year's budget. At the time he did not rule out cuts.
But in his statement to SBS News, Albanese said the existing figure "remains government policy".

Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
In the wake of multiple international conflicts around the world, Labor has made a series of increases to the humanitarian intake, pushing it to its current high.
The confusion comes as the government is anticipated to announce an overhaul of its migration policy.
Labor had been expected to reveal details in a National Press Club address by Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke earlier this month, but the speech was cancelled after Burke failed to secure cabinet agreement on the best approach.
Since then, Albanese has refused to give further updates, telling ABC radio on Tuesday that there are a "series of plans in place" but there is still "more work to do" to finalise them. He declined to set a timeframe for immigration announcements, saying only that they would come at "appropriate times".
Migration targets have been the source of recent public debate, with One Nation pushing a tough anti-migration stance and gaining in the polls.
Both major parties have sought to restrict their own immigration policies while denying that this is in response to the minor party's growing popularity.
Opposition leader Angus Taylor has said the Coalition will cap net overseaos migration (NOM) at or below the number of homes built in Australia the previous year. Current building rates suggest their figure would be under 180,000; however, the Coalition is yet to announce where they would restrict immigration to reach that figure.
In 2024-2025, NOM was 306,000. Labor's budgetary forecasts suggest it will decline to 225,000 by 2027-2028, after the party has made concerted efforts to bring it down from a post-pandemic peak of 568,000.
One Nation has stated its preferred migration target is 130,000, although One Nation MP David Farley claimed the party would accept an additional 100,000 essential workers at the weekend. Party leader Pauline Hanson and MP Barnaby Joyce soon corrected him in a public fallout over targets.
What is Labor planning?
According to a report by The Australian newspaper on Wednesday, Labor is close to finalising its immigration crackdown, which will restrict international students and their families and limit visitor visas.
Burke is expected to reveal sweeping changes within weeks, with some measures thought to take effect in September.
The student visa changes could stop internationals from changing courses to extend their stay, reject onshore visa applications, limit the number of family members allowed on the visas, and halt the transfer of people from higher education into vocational or training programs.
Certain tourist visas are also expected to be cut from 12 months down to six.
The changes follow already substantial immigration reductions.
Australia's permanent migration program was brought down from a post-pandemic high of 195,000 to 185,000.
In July, the skilled visa program was overhauled, pushing overseas applicants to the back of the queue to slow the pace of new arrivals.
In addition, graduate visas have become more expensive, with lower age limits and stricter English-language requirements. Proof-of-funds requirements were also raised for international students to clamp down on illegal work.
While no government can dictate a net overseas migration (NOM) figure — a measurement of human movement, not a quota — it can adjust visas and entry requirements which impact NOM.
While Labor ministers are concerned that a more hardline approach to immigration will see them lose left-wing voter support, they are thought to be trying to ensure that the government can at least meet its own immigration forecasts.

USAF Gives Raytheon, Boeing $766M in Contracts for B-52 Radar Upgrades
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
01:39:06 UTC
10:39:06 KST

The Pentagon on Aug. 25 announced a pair of Air Force contracts to Raytheon and Boeing, totaling more than $766 million, for advance work on adding new radars to the B-52H Stratofortress.
The bigger of the two deals went to Raytheon Technologies as an indefinite-delivery, indefinite-quantity contract worth up to $603 million to equip B-52s with new AN/APQ-188 radars.
Boeing’s contract is for $163 million to build and deliver bomb rack modernization system kits to support the B-52’s Radar Modernization Program. That deal is a cost-plus-incentive fee, cost-plus-fixed fee cost-reimbursement, and firm-fixed-price delivery order, under the existing IDIQ contract for B-52 production and sustainment.
The Radar Modernization Program is meant to replace the legacy mechanical AN/APQ-166 radar with a modern active electronically scanned array radar and is a critical part of a large-scale upgrade of the Cold War-era B-52. That modernization, which is so extensive that B-52Hs who get it will be redesignated as B-52J models, will also include new engines, avionics, cockpit displays, weapons, communications, and other key systems.
Raytheon’s AN/APQ-188 is derived from the active electronically-scanned array radars now flown in the F-15 and F/A-18 fighters, and is intended to be able to better navigate and target in all weather conditions.
Raytheon’s work on the AN/APQ-188 radar will be performed in Forrest, Miss.; El Segundo, Calif.; McKinney, Texas; and Warner Robins, Ga., the contract announcement said, and is expected to be done by August 2031.
The Boeing work will be done in San Antonio, Texas, and should be finished by December 2028, the Pentagon said.
A B-52 outfitted with the APQ-188 flew from Boeing’s San Antonio, Texas, facility to Edwards Air Force Base, California, in December 2025, to carry out flight tests of the new radar. But tragedy struck in June, when that B-52 crashed at Edwards shortly after takeoff for a test sortie, killing all eight crew members aboard.
Air Force officials in July told reporters that a second B-52 was being modified with another APQ-188 to continue the radar’s testing, and that upgrade work was expected to be done by the end of the year. The June loss of the first test B-52 has put testing of the new radar on hold, likely for several months, while the newly upgraded bomber is still in the works. Officials at the Life Cycle Industry Days conference in Dayton, Ohio, said the Air Force’s B-52 modernization team may adjust its strategy and schedule as a result of the June crash.

In July, London Mayor Sadiq Khan criticised people online and abroad who “have been trying to talk London down”.
Louise Puddefoot, the Met’s deputy assistant commissioner for front-line policing, said discussion of crime in the capital was not something the force focused on.
She told Reuters: “I think my job is to show people that we’re tackling criminality, provide the data and the figures so they appreciate that we’re not the most dangerous capital city around, and provide that reassurance.

Stress gene more easily activated in brains of people with schizophrenia: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
09:31:49 CST
10:31:49 KST

SYDNEY, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- A gene involved in regulating the body's response to stress switches on more easily in the brains of people with schizophrenia, potentially opening the way for new psychiatric treatments, new research has found.
The study examined the FKBP5 gene and the corresponding FKBP51 protein, which help regulate the body's response to stress hormones such as cortisol, according to a statement released Wednesday by Australia's University of Sydney (USYD).
Using donated brain tissue, researchers found that in people with schizophrenia, chemical tags that normally keep the FKBP5 gene in check had been stripped away, leading to higher activity of the gene and opening up the possibility of developing new treatments targeting it.
"For people who have lost the chemical tags that keep their stress gene in check, it is like having the volume on their speaker stuck on high," said Natalie Matosin of the USYD School of Medical Sciences, senior author of the study published in the American Journal of Psychiatry.
The researchers from USYD and the Max Planck Institute of Psychiatry in Germany found that changes in the stress-response system become more pronounced with age, meaning the system may be switched on more easily and stay on for longer. These changes, in turn, increase vulnerability to psychiatric disorders such as schizophrenia later in life.
Matosin said the altered stress response was particularly concentrated in the brain's frontal cortex, an area of the brain that supports memory, decision-making and emotional control.
Having a persistently heightened stress response may mean that, as the brain ages, the circuits in the frontal cortex become more vulnerable to damage, increasing susceptibility to serious psychiatric illness, she added. ■

Feature: Modern Chinese tea culture takes root in Belgrade
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
09:31:19 CST
10:31:19 KST

by Xinhua writers Zhang Xuan, Nemanja Cabric
BELGRADE, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- "I have always loved Chinese tea culture and visited many places in China, but I never expected to enjoy authentic Hangzhou Longjing green tea right here in Serbia," said a Polish tourist identified as Emilia.
A self-professed tea enthusiast, Emilia was pleasantly surprised when she stumbled upon a "new Chinese-style" tea shop in Belgrade, the Serbian capital. "The tea leaves slowly unfurl and bloom like flowers in delicate cups. The whole process is incredibly elegant. I absolutely love the experience," she said.
Opened in 2024 near Knez Mihailova Street, a bustling pedestrian zone in central Belgrade, the shop, named "Tea Talk," has become a social media sensation. From shaved ice desserts served in traditionally patterned ceramic ware and paper cups adorned with ink-wash calligraphy to creative drinks featuring panda-shaped sweets alongside traditional ingredients such as red dates and goji berries, every detail reflects the charm of Chinese culture.
Shop owner Zhang Ruoqi, a graduate of China's Jingdezhen Ceramic University who previously taught ceramics in Singapore, sees her venture as more than just a beverage business.
Europeans are developing a deeper and evolving appreciation of Chinese tea culture, she said. By blending traditional tea, Chinese aesthetics, and ceramic art, Zhang aims to create youth-oriented and innovative drinks within an "experiential and accessible" cultural space.
"Serbia already has a long-standing coffee and afternoon tea culture," Zhang explained. "When we introduced Chinese tea, people started coming not just to drink tea, but also to talk about its aroma and flavor and admire the beauty of the teaware. These conversations naturally lead people to share life stories."
To deepen this engagement, the shop hosts a range of cultural events, including Hanfu (traditional Chinese attire) try-ons, tea ceremonies, and movie nights, helping local customers gain a better understanding of Chinese culture.
It was a movie night that first brought local resident Aleksic to the shop. As he put it, he "came for the movie, but stayed for the tea."
"After watching 'Farewell My Concubine,' I developed a strong interest in Peking Opera and hope to visit China one day," Aleksic said, adding that the shop's unique combination of visual, culinary, and cultural experiences sets it apart in Belgrade.
Meanwhile, another tea house in central Belgrade, "T-Element," is offering a different perspective on Chinese tea culture through the experience of a Russian expatriate.
Owner Leonid Nikitin speaks fluent Chinese and has been fascinated by Chinese tea since 2002. Since his first trip to China in 2006, he has visited the country at least twice a year, traveling to historic tea-producing provinces such as Yunnan, Fujian and Guangdong to study traditional tea-making techniques.
"Through communicating with Chinese tea sommeliers and studying traditional techniques in tea-producing regions, I came to understand the true essence of tea culture," Nikitin said. "Tea is not merely a ceremony or a social gathering; it is an integral part of everyday life."
His shop serves as an archive of his tea-centered journeys around the world. While it offers teas from Southeast Asia, Japan and Georgia, nearly half of its shelf space is devoted to Chinese varieties, including Pu'er, Anxi Tieguanyin and Fuding white tea, alongside porcelain, glass and Yixing clay teaware.
"Chinese tea culture spans thousands of years, but in Serbia, many people still mistakenly believe that tea is primarily medicinal," Nikitin said. "I want to introduce the rich flavors and cultural depth of Chinese tea and help more local people appreciate its unique charm."
As more Chinese tea houses open their doors, tea drinking is quietly emerging as a new lifestyle trend in Serbia.
"This subtle and gentle form of cultural exchange helps foster understanding, friendship, and mutual appreciation among people from different countries," said Tang Dasheng, cultural counselor at the Chinese Embassy in Serbia. He noted that the growing popularity of "new Chinese-style" tea in Europe demonstrates how cultural products can serve as a bridge for innovative cross-cultural communication. ■

SYDNEY, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- Qantas said on Thursday that its profit fell by almost 20 percent in the 2025-26 financial year amid a spike in fuel prices driven by the conflict in the Middle East.
The Qantas Group, which includes Qantas and budget carrier Jetstar, said in its full-year results that statutory profit after tax fell by 19.6 percent year on year to 1.29 billion Australian dollars (about 927 million U.S. dollars), while underlying profit before tax fell by 13.8 percent year on year to 2.06 billion Australian dollars.
Chief Executive Officer Vanessa Hudson said the group's fuel bill increased by 610 million Australian dollars because of the Middle East conflict, but fare and capacity adjustments and other mitigations limited the impact on earnings to 420 million Australian dollars.
"This year was defined by two very different operating environments, as a result of the conflict in the Middle East. In the first half, Qantas and Jetstar were both performing strongly, with demand growing across the domestic and international networks," Hudson said.
"The final four months of the year saw business and consumer confidence fall as the conflict and economic headwinds created uncertainty, and some large corporates and government responded by managing their costs more tightly, reducing demand for travel."
The Qantas Group said it took delivery of 17 new aircraft in 2025-26 and expects delivery of up to 31 aircraft in 2026-27, including the first of 12 Project Sunrise Airbus A350-1000ULR aircraft that will operate non-stop flights from eastern Australia to London and New York. ■

Wanted in Hong Kong: the theatrical equivalent of a hawker centre
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
01:30:13 UTC
10:30:13 KST

On a Saturday evening, Causeway Bay crackles with its famous retail energy, yet by 9 o’clock the streets begin their nightly death. There is nowhere magnetic to spill into – no late-night jazz den, immersive dinner theatre or playhouse humming with an experimental musical. Nearby, the 40,000-seat Hong Kong Stadium squats in silence while the catering rooms of the Happy Valley racecourse sit largely empty on non-race nights.
This dead zone between one of the world’s densest shopping districts and a historic sporting valley is a failure of urban imagination. The remedy is hiding in plain sight: demolish the obsolete stadium and replace it with a dense, dining-infused cluster of at least 20 small to medium-sized theatres, physically linked to both the racecourse and the 
Lee Garden retail corridor
.
International producers of 
first-run musicals
 routinely bypass our city. The hottest Broadway and West End transfers increasingly open in Shanghai or Shenzhen. The issue is simple: venue supply rather than audience taste or ticket pricing. Hong Kong’s cultural infrastructure remains trapped in a binary: a few cavernous halls or shoebox black boxes.
What every world city has – and what we lack – is the theatrical equivalent of a hawker centre: a dense, walkable precinct of contrasting performance spaces, each with integrated food and beverage options.
Happy Valley
’s stadium site is the only plausible venue. With the Rugby Sevens migrating to Kai Tak, the concrete bowl has lost its purpose. Raze it, and in its place build a theatre village of deliberately contrasting venues, clustered around a lantern-lit central piazza.
 Picture a doorway leading to a sumptuous 800-seat Cantonese opera house that evokes the lost glory of the 
original Lee Theatre
 – the fabled Percival Street venue that was the spiritual home of Cantonese theatrical tradition right in Causeway Bay’s heart. A new Lee Theatre within the cluster would reclaim that heritage.

Pro-Israel Democrats picked for top roles on key US House committee

Pro-Israel Democrats picked for top roles on key US House committee
The decision comes at a fractious time for the party amid a growing divide among its voters over US aid to Israel.
Three pro-Israel Democratic lawmakers have been selected for top roles on the Foreign Affairs Committee in the United States House of Representatives, also known as HFAC.
That comes despite shifting attitudes among Americans towards Israel, which is viewed in an increasingly negative light, particularly on the political left.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3US Arabs eye ‘historic’ Senate win for Abdul El-Sayed despite AIPAC attacks
- list 2 of 3Most US Democrats in early 2028 primary states oppose aid to Israel: Poll
- list 3 of 3California lawmaker overcomes pro-Israel spending to win special election
On Tuesday, Representative Jared Moskowitz of Florida was named as the top Democrat on the panel’s Middle East and North Africa Subcommittee (MENA), a position that will allow the outspoken supporter of Israel to help determine US policy in the region. Moskowitz will replace fellow Democratic Representative Brad Sherman of California.
Additionally, Representatives Debbie Wasserman Schultz of Florida and Wesley Bell of Missouri were appointed to seats on the subcommittees for oversight and intelligence and the Western Hemisphere, respectively.
All three politicians – Moskowitz, Wasserman Schultz and Bell – recently won their primaries against progressive Democratic challengers who targeted their pro-Israel positions.
One pro-Palestinian lawmaker, Representative Mark Pocan of Wisconsin, was named to the Africa Subcommittee.
The committee appointments spurred backlash from within the Democratic Party’s ranks, with some members denouncing the decisions as out of touch with voter sentiment.
Polls have consistently suggested a decline in support for Israel among voters in the US, particularly since the start of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023. In February, the US also partnered with Israel to attack Iran, launching an ongoing war.
A March poll from the Pew Research Center suggested that, overall, 60 percent of US adults had an unfavourable view of Israel, up from 42 percent in 2022.
More recently, a survey conducted last month by the news outlet CNN and the research firm SSRS showed an increase in the number of respondents who said they would support candidates who would cut aid to Israel.
Overall, 54 percent of respondents expressed openness to such a candidate. That number rose to 70 percent among Democratic-leaning voters.
Critics, including Congresswoman Rashida Tlaib of Michigan, have pointed to those numbers as evidence that the Foreign Affairs Committee appointments were misguided.
“A supermajority of Democratic voters have made it clear they want to end U.S. support for Israel’s genocide in Gaza and Trump’s assault on Iran,” Tlaib, the first Palestinian American elected to the US Congress, said in a statement to Al Jazeera.
She also pointed to statements from Moskowitz supporting Trump’s war effort against Iran.
“By elevating a genocide denier who has said he is ‘to the right’ of JD Vance on the war on Iran, Democratic leadership is once again ignoring the base of our party who want the funding of the genocide to end,” Tlaib said.
The decision to appoint three vocal supporters of Israel to key roles in the House comes at a fractious time for the party.
The US is in the midst of its midterm election season, and Democratic candidates are divided over what, if any, support the US should provide Israel after its controversial military campaigns in Gaza and Lebanon.
Several critics of Israel, including Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, have scored upsets this year in the Democratic Party primaries, beating pro-Israel rivals.
Ben Rhodes, who served as the deputy national security adviser to former President Barack Obama, was among those lambasting Tuesday’s selections, which he called a “giant f*** you from Democratic leadership to Democratic voters”.
“Dems are counting on people not noticing how they approach governing,” Rhodes wrote on social media. “Appointments on HFAC are a signal of what the party cares about and the disregard for war crimes and voter concerns could not be clearer.”
He predicted that the House leadership’s choices would leave voters feeling like their views were “completely ignored”.
The Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR), the largest Muslim advocacy group in the US, echoed the assessment, writing that it was “deeply concerned” by the appointments.
“Elevating these vocal supporters of funding the Israeli government’s ongoing crimes to the House Foreign Affairs Committee indicates that key House leaders intend to openly defy the will of the American people, including Democrats,” CAIR’s national deputy director, Edward Ahmed Mitchell, said in a statement.
But several top House Democrats doubled down on the choices, expressing optimism about the new party leadership on the Foreign Affairs Committee.
Representative Gregory Meeks of New York was among the Democrats who helped make the selections.
In a social media post, he indicated that he looked forward to “working closely” with the committee’s new members.
“Their experience, commitment, and expertise will strengthen our work and help guide the committee as it addresses urgent challenges in national security and diplomacy,” Meeks, a vocal supporter of Israel, added.
Meeks and Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic Party leader in the House, did not return Al Jazeera’s request for comment.
Currently, the House is narrowly controlled by the Republican Party. That allows it to name leaders to chair the chamber’s standing committees.
But the House majority could flip in the Democrats’ favour during November’s midterm races.
Mowkowitz, who has consistently opposed placing conditions or restrictions on US military aid to Israel, could become the chair of the MENA subcommittee if Democrats retake the House.
“I’ll work to strengthen America’s relationships with Israel and our Gulf allies, expand regional peace, advance American diplomacy, and ensure our foreign policy is grounded in strength, security, and reality,” Moskowitz wrote in a social media post on Tuesday.
“I’m ready to get to work.”

US-Canada trade war rolls into bathroom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
01:22:42 UTC
10:22:42 KST

US-Canada trade war rolls into bathroom
The US-Canada trade war is reaching the bathroom, with tariffs on paper products threatening to push up prices for toilet paper and other everyday essentials for Americans.
Trade talks between the two neighbors collapsed last Friday, with both sides accusing the other of making last-minute changes to a proposed comprehensive deal. US President Donald Trump immediately imposed 50% tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian imports, including wine, cement, plywood, and clothing. Not to be outdone, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney vowed to respond “dollar for dollar,” with Ottawa announcing duties of up to 50% on around 700 American products on Tuesday.
Paper products are among the hardest hit, with Canada targeting toilet paper and facial tissue with 25% duties, along with paper towels and napkins at 50%. Chemical wood pulp used to make such products also faces a 50% tariff.
Canada is the main source of US toilet paper imports, supplying $383.4 million worth in 2025 – about two-thirds of the imported total – according to US International Trade Commission data. Mexico was a distant second at $63 million. Canada is also the main foreign supplier of wood pulp to the US, including northern bleached softwood kraft pulp (NBSK), a key material in toilet paper and paper towels. Canadian pulp reportedly accounts for around 30% of US toilet paper and 50% of paper towel production.
If the tariffs take effect, US importers will bear the added cost of bringing Canadian products and pulp across the border, and given the reliance on Canadian supplies, at least some of that expense is likely to be passed on to consumers. This could prove particularly noticeable in a country that accounts for more than 20% of global tissue consumption, according to the 2019 report The Issue with Tissue by the Natural Resources Defense Council. Market research data shows the average American goes through around 141 rolls of toilet paper a year – roughly three a week – making the US the world’s top consumer, just ahead of Germany. At that rate, even a modest price hike could quickly add up.
Toilet paper is far from the only potential casualty of the trade war. Canada’s measures mirror many products targeted by Washington, with higher duties covering everything from fish, cheese, clothing, and cosmetics to steel and aluminum goods, motorcycles, smartphones, and exercise equipment. Canadian Industry Minister Melanie Joly said that the counter-tariffs were aimed primarily at protecting businesses while also applying political pressure ahead of the November 3 US midterm elections.
With Canada’s retaliatory tariffs not taking effect until September 8, however, some analysts hope that Washington and Ottawa still have time to strike a deal.
“That gives us this week. It gives us next week,” Christopher Sands, head of the Center for US-Canada Studies at Johns Hopkins University, told AP on Wednesday. “Time to take a breather and talk about how to avert an all-out trade war.”

Lawyer for Fed’s Lisa Cook, targeted by Trump, says there are no grounds for dismissal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
01:15:00 UTC
10:15:00 KST

Lawyer for Fed’s Lisa Cook, targeted by Trump, says there are no grounds for dismissal
- Lisa Cook’s lawyer denies mortgage fraud claims and says there is no legal reason for her removal from the Federal Reserve Board.
- Trump’s effort to fire Cook is unprecedented and seen as an attack on Fed independence, motivated by disagreements over monetary policy.
- The US Supreme Court blocked her removal but left open the question of cause; the White House recently challenged Cook again citing alleged false statements.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook’s lawyer on Aug 26 offered a detailed rebuttal to the accusations of mortgage fraud that US President Donald Trump asserts provide cause to fire her, saying they rely “on untried and unproven allegations of criminal wrongdoing.”
“Governor Cook has never committed mortgage fraud or any intentional wrongdoing, and there is no legally cognisable cause for removing her from the Federal Reserve Board,” Cook’s attorney Abbe David Lowell said in a letter to the White House.
Trump has been trying to sack Cook for more than a year in an unprecedented effort widely seen as part of a broader assault on the US central bank’s independence.
It’s the first time a US president has attempted to remove a central banker since the institution’s founding more than a century ago.
If he succeeded in removing Cook, Trump, who has long pushed for lower interest rates, would be able to install a replacement sympathetic to his view.
Mortgage fraud allegations against Cook, the first Black woman to serve as a Fed governor, were first levelled a year ago by Federal Housing Finance Agency director William Pulte.
The accusations were promptly amplified by Trump, who announced on social media that he was dismissing her over them.
Cook denied any wrongdoing, calling the allegations a pretext to remove her for monetary policy differences, and she sued to keep her job.
In June, the US Supreme Court refused to allow her removal in a 5-4 ruling that definitively protects Fed officials from being fired at will by a president. It has since returned the case to the lower court.
The decision left open the question of whether there was any wrongdoing that could serve as cause for termination, provided Cook was given the opportunity to defend herself.
Earlier in August, the White House took a fresh run at Trump’s firing effort, telling Cook in a letter dated Aug 5 that the president was “considering” removing her from her role “due to there being sufficient reason to believe that you made false statements on one or more mortgage agreements.”
The letter told Cook that “this is your chance to respond” and set a deadline of Aug 26.
“The Letter describes two acts by Governor Cook that, ‘taken together,’ supposedly constitute grounds for her removal,” Lowell’s response to the White House said.
“But neither of those acts shows intentional wrongdoing or amounts to a crime, and neither constitutes ‘cause’ under the Federal Reserve Act.”
Lowell said any mistakes on Cook’s mortgage applications indicating she was seeking a primary residence mortgage for a second home were inadvertent and were partly the result of errors on forms prepared by the lender.
“The pre-office conduct at issue, all of which took place in Governor Cook’s private capacity, was not fraudulent or criminal in any form, nor a basis for the President attempting to remove her,” Lowell said.
Lowell also surfaced news reports that Trump and other members of his administration had done essentially the same thing as Cook at various points in the past.
“Surely the President does not believe himself ‘unfit for office’ because he signed these contradictory ‘primary’ mortgage documents,” Lowell said, adding: “The conduct of others in this Administration further undercuts any notion that the allegations against Governor Cook are grounds for removal.”
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh has not addressed Cook’s case since taking the reins at the Fed in May.
But he has publicly echoed past Fed chiefs and the broader economic consensus that any loss of political independence for the central bank’s monetary policy decision-making would imperil its inflation-fighting credibility.
Trump repeatedly threatened to fire Warsh’s predecessor, Jerome Powell, for not lowering interest rates, and his Department of Justice pursued a criminal investigation of Powell over building renovations that a federal judge found to be a thinly disguised effort to pressure him into resigning.
Once Powell’s term as Fed chief ended and Warsh began his, the Republican president redirected his criticisms at other Fed board members, a majority of whom, including Cook, were appointed by Trump’s Democratic predecessor, Joe Biden.
In a criminal referral to the Justice Department a year ago, Pulte suggested Cook had committed bank fraud punishable by 30 years in prison because mortgage documents appeared to simultaneously claim more than one home as her primary residence.
The referral was one of several Pulte made containing similar allegations against other targets of Trump’s disfavour.
There has been no indication a criminal investigation into Cook is moving forward.
A Reuters report in 2025 showed Cook had indicated to a lender that one of the homes at issue was a vacation property.
Reuters also reported the local tax authority in Michigan said Cook had not broken rules for tax breaks on a home there that she declared as her primary residence.
The letter in August to Cook, signed by White House Deputy Chief of Staff Dan Scavino, said that even if there wasn’t fraud, Cook’s misstatements constitute negligence that calls into question her trustworthiness as a Fed governor. REUTERS

The trial of the alleged mastermind of the September 11 terrorist attacks has been scheduled for June 2028
Kyiv • UNN
A U.S. military court has scheduled the trial of Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and three co-defendants for June 2028. The case was delayed for years due to legal disputes.
A U.S. military court has scheduled the start of the trial of Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, who is accused of organizing the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, for June 2028. Three other defendants accused of conspiracy are also due to stand trial alongside him. NBC News reports, according to UNN.
Details
On Wednesday, U.S. Air Force Lieutenant Colonel Michael Shram, the military judge, rejected the date proposed by prosecutors for the start of the trial—January 2027. Instead, he scheduled the trial for approximately 18 months later—in June 2028.
Mohammed will stand trial alongside Walid bin Attash, Ali Abdul Aziz Ali, and Mustafa Ahmed al-Hawsawi. They are accused of conspiring to carry out the September 11 attacks, during which hijacked aircraft crashed into the World Trade Center in New York and the Pentagon. A fourth plane crashed in Pennsylvania.
Mohammed was detained in Pakistan in 2003 and transferred in 2006 to the U.S. military prison at Guantanamo Bay, Cuba. He was formally charged in 2008 with war crimes and murder in connection with the deaths of nearly 3,000 people in the attacks.
Years of delays and legal problems
The trial has been postponed for years because of legal disputes. In particular, last summer, a federal appeals court rejected a potential agreement that would have provided for Mohammed to plead guilty in exchange for a guarantee that he would not face the death penalty.
Defense attorneys also say that the delays are linked to the government's attempts to conceal information about torture that, they claim, the defendants endured in secret CIA prisons.
According to a 2014 U.S. Senate report, so-called "enhanced interrogation techniques" were used on Mohammed, including 183 instances of waterboarding.

China launches world’s first 100kW bamboo-built floating solar farm off Shandong coast

China launches world’s first 100kW bamboo-built floating solar farm off Shandong coast
The experimental platform is part of a broader push to replace steel and plastic components with more environmentally friendly materials
2-MIN READ2-MIN
2
 Listen
China has launched the world’s first 100-kilowatt (kW) floating solar farm built with bamboo frames, offering a more environmentally friendly approach to offshore energy.
The floating solar platform, named Jilin-2, is made of composite bamboo tubes and pipes. It has been deployed at a demonstration base off the coast of Yantai in the eastern province of Shandong.
It will supply power to an integrated hydrogen, ammonia and methanol production project, manufacturer Yantai CIMC Raffles Ocean Technology Group announced in late June.
“Compared to conventional steel or [high-density polythene] structures, the bamboo-based design significantly reduces marine environmental impact,” CIMC Raffles said.
The new platform builds upon an earlier 10kW prototype called Jilin-1 from 2023.
Jilin-2 was developed by the CIMC Offshore Engineering Research Institute, CIMC Raffles’ research arm, as well as China Forestry Group Corporation and Beijing Forestry University.

Asian shipper pays record US$5.3 million to cross Panama Canal
PANAMA CITY - A shipper needing to transit the Panama Canal bid a record US$5.3 million to secure its spot, according to people familiar with the matter.
South Korea-based SK Gas agreed to pay the sum to travel the canal on Sept 1, said the people, who could not be identified as the information was confidential.
The fee, determined through an auction run by the canal authority this week, breaks the previous high of US$4.6 million set earlier this month, also paid by a shipper controlling a South Korean vessel.
Demand to urgently pass through the waterway has soared after the Iran war upended global trade routes, particularly to Asia. 
Wait times at the canal have grown to as long as 17 days for vessels that arrive at the waterway without reservations, according to Argus Media.
The Panama Canal authority has also tightened restrictions on the number of slots starting in September, as well as on how much cargo ships can carry due to likely drought conditions in the region.
The winning auction bid allows the G. Spirit, a liquefied petroleum gas tanker, to travel north-bound through the canal. 
As of Aug 25, the ship was shown positioned on the Pacific side of the waterway, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.
SK Gas did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The Panama Canal Authority, through a spokeswoman, declined to provide comment on the record high auction price. 
The canal said in a statement that a majority of the vessels use a reservation booking system. 
Recent auction results have reflected “significantly stronger demand,” showing higher prices than the median auction price paid before February of around US$55,000.
The El Nino weather pattern brewing in the Pacific is another factor in shippers’ rising willingness to pay for reservations. That will likely bring severe drought to Panama, which would threaten the fresh water levels of the canal and shipping availability. BLOOMBERG

How to See the Partial Lunar Eclipse and Blood Moon on August 27
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
00:44:35 UTC
09:44:35 KST

If you missed the spectacular solar eclipse earlier this month, you have a chance to catch another stunning astronomical phenomenon: a partial lunar eclipse and “blood moon” that will occur on Thursday night into Friday early morning.
Earth’s shadow will cover nearly all of the bright lunar disk and will cast a reddish or orange hue on the moon’s surface.
The partial phase will last about three hours and 18 minutes. At its peak, it will have a threshold magnitude of 0.93, meaning that approximately 93 percent of the moon’s diameter will be within the darkest part of Earth’s shadow. Here’s what to expect and how to view it.
August Lunar Eclipse Timeline
While Europe was the prime viewing spot for the recent solar eclipse, the Americas will be the best location for viewing Thursday’s lunar event. The peak will occur at night across North and South America. Europe will also get a glimpse, but viewers there will have to wait until dawn. Even then, opportunities will be limited. In locations across Spain, for example, the breaking of day and the moon’s low altitude will make observation difficult. (Don’t feel too bad for folks there, though. They got a stunning view of the total solar eclipse a few weeks ago.)
Below is a list of the best times to observe the lunar eclipse in different cities, using local times for when the event will reach its peak. If you’re wanting to get the full experience, though, you can look toward the sky earlier and plan to stick around after.
- New York: 12:14 am
- Chicago: 11:14 pm
- Denver: 10:14 pm
- Los Angeles: 9:14 pm
- Mexico City: 10:14 pm
- Lima - 11:14 pm
- Buenos Aires: 1:14 am
- London: 5:12 am
What Causes a Blood Moon?
During a lunar eclipse, the moon usually takes on reddish tones. If the eclipse is total, it’s called a blood moon. The reason? Sunlight passes through Earth’s atmosphere before hitting the moon’s surface. During that passage, some of that light—specifically the blue wavelengths—is filtered out by the atmosphere leaving only the red end of the spectrum to reach the moon. The eclipse will be full enough that the effect will be pronounced.
“It’s as if all of the world’s sunrises and sunsets are projected onto the moon,” explains NASA.
How Can You Best View a Lunar Eclipse?
Unlike solar eclipses, you don’t need special eye protection to observe them. You can look directly at the moon during all phases of the event. However, there are a few tips that can significantly enhance your viewing experience.
The first is basic but very useful: Get away from areas with light pollution and try to find an unobstructed view of the sky. The roof or terrace of a house can be a good observation spot. Even if you can’t get out of the city, though, you’ll still be able to see the eclipse (weather permitting).
You can also pick out your spot to post up before the eclipse reaches it maximum extent. Observing earlier will allow you to appreciate how the Earth’s shadow gradually advances across the lunar surface.
If you have binoculars or a telescope, you should absolutely grab them or get set up beforehand. They’ll allow you to see more details of the moon and the advancing shadow across its surface. If you have a telescope, pay special attention to the boundary between the illuminated part of the moon and the area covered by Earth’s shadow. As the shadow advances, you’ll be able to see how it crosses craters, mountains, and other features.
No binoculars or telescope on hand, but still hoping to get a zoomed-in view? Check out your local science museum, observatory, or astronomy club to see if they’re having an eclipse party. And if it’s cloudy where you are, you can watch the eclipse unfold via a livestream. (Here’s where you’ll find Time and Date’s livestream, for example.)
Finally, don’t just look at the moon. As its brightness dims during the lunar eclipse, the stars surrounding it will become easier to make out. Near the peak of the eclipse, it’s worth putting down your binoculars or telescope for a few minutes to gaze at the entire sky.
This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

US military judge sets June 2028 trial date for alleged 9/11 mastermind
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
00:43:38 UTC
09:43:38 KST

A US military judge has ruled that the alleged mastermind of the September 11, 2001, attacks, Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, will stand trial starting in June 2028, multiple US media outlets reported.
Air Force Lt. Col. Michael Schrama, a military commissions judge, rejected a January 2027 start date proposed by prosecutors, scheduling proceedings for roughly 18 months later.
Mohammed will be prosecuted alongside three co-defendants suspected of conspiring in the attacks: Walid bin Attash, Ali Abdul Aziz Ali, and Mustafa Ahmed al-Hawsawi.
Mohammed is accused of orchestrating the plot to crash hijacked airliners into the World Trade Centre in New York and the Pentagon, alongside a third hijacked plane that crashed in a field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania.
Prolonged legal delays
Mohammed was considered one of Al Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden's top lieutenants before his capture in Pakistan in March 2003.
He was held in secret CIA facilities for three years before being transferred to the US naval base at Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, in 2006.
Mohammed was formally charged and arraigned in 2008 with war crimes and murder in connection with the nearly 3,000 people killed in the 9/11 attacks.
The legal process has faced repeated delays as the military commissions system encountered continuous procedural challenges.
Defence lawyers have argued that government efforts to suppress details of torture used at secret CIA black sites contributed significantly to the backlog.
A 2014 US Senate report revealed that the CIA subjected Mohammed to what it termed "enhanced interrogation techniques", including waterboarding him 183 times in what was described as "a series of near-drownings."
The scheduling ruling follows a federal appeals court decision last summer that threw out a proposed plea agreement that would have allowed Mohammed to plead guilty in exchange for taking the death penalty off the table.

CIA Director John Ratcliffe, during secretive trip, warned Russia not to attack NATO
CIA Director John Ratcliffe warned Russia not to attack NATO member states during his visit to Moscow this week, according to multiple people familiar with the matter, amid U.S. intelligence assessments that Russia could try to test NATO.
Ratcliffe also brought up Iran, warning of additional sanctions if the Strait of Hormuz does not reopen to shipping traffic, the people familiar with the matter told CBS News.
The secretive visit to the Russian capital came to light on Tuesday, after a U.S. Air Force jet was spotted flying into a Moscow airport and a diplomatic motorcade moved through the city. CBS News was first to report the trip, which is Ratcliffe's first known visit to Russia as CIA director. Ukraine was told that a U.S. delegation would travel to Moscow and was asked to hold off on strikes for the duration of the visit, according to a senior Ukrainian official.
The Wall Street Journal was first to report on Ratcliffe's warning not to attack NATO.
The CIA declined to comment on the reasons for Ratcliffe's trip.
President Trump confirmed the visit to Moscow in an interview with radio host Glenn Beck earlier Wednesday, but said it wasn't related to Iran or to Russian desires to test NATO, describing it as a "semi-routine" trip. Mr. Trump said "something may come out of" Ratcliffe's visit, pointing to his push to end Russia's war with Ukraine.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told reporters in Moscow that Ratcliffe spoke with Russian intelligence officials but didn't meet with President Vladimir Putin.
On Thursday, Peskov dismissed media reports about the purpose of Radcliffe's trip, French news agency AFP reports.
"A lot of such scare stories are being published right now. Of course, they have nothing to do with reality," Peskov said, adding that Russia "is facing a very aggressive policy towards itself from European countries."
Recent American intelligence assessments have indicated that Putin could be willing to authorize provocative actions on NATO territory, including cyberattacks, hybrid actions and other operations that fall short of conventional military action, CBS News reported earlier this month. The likely goal would not necessarily be to trigger a war, but instead to test NATO's unity and the Trump administration's willingness to defend NATO allies, according to U.S. officials.
A pattern of recent Russian actions has prompted concerns, the officials said, including drone incursions into Romania, a Russian missile that crossed into Poland last month and an uptick in alleged sabotage actions and cyberattacks in Europe.
Under Article 5 of the treaty that created NATO, members of the alliance are expected to come to each other's defense if attacked, a provision that the U.S. invoked after the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attacks. But Mr. Trump has long questioned NATO's reliability and criticized member states for — in his view — not contributing enough to their own defense.
Mr. Trump has also publicly pushed Russia and Ukraine to end their four-year-long war, though diplomatic efforts have appeared to stall.
Meanwhile, Russia has maintained its partnership with Iran during the U.S.'s war with the Middle Eastern state, providing intelligence to Iran on U.S. positions in the region, CBS News reported earlier this year. The two countries have also cooperated on drone manufacturing for years.

LOS ANGELES – A man arrested in August with a loaded gun near the Trump National Golf Club near Los Angeles must be evaluated by a mental health court before criminal proceedings can continue, a judge ruled on Aug 26.
The man, Jeanine John Taele of Downey, California, 38, was charged with weapons violations after authorities arrested him just days before President Donald Trump arrived to speak at a fundraiser.
On Aug 26, the judge, John J. Lonergan Jr of Los Angeles County Superior Court, ruled that Taele was unfit to face criminal proceedings. Lonergan denied bail to Taele, who appeared in court wearing a suicide prevention gown.
Anthony Bayne, a lawyer for Taele, said in court that his client was not able to understand or participate in his defence.
